### Text: `string` and `bytes`

Text is a `string`. Data that may not be text is `bytes`. They are two separate types, and you
convert between them with `as`.

A `string` is always valid text. Its length is the number of characters a person counts. An accented
letter, an emoji or a flag is one character, even when it needs several bytes. There is no
`$name[0]` syntax. `Core\Str::at` returns one character, and `Core\Str::slice` returns several.

`bytes` is for the content of a file, a reply from a network connection or a hash. Its length is the
number of bytes. `Core\Bytes::slice` takes a part of it by byte position.

**Good to know:** `$text as bytes` always works. `$data as string` checks the data first. If the
data is not valid text, it throws a `RuntimeError`.

**The examples below** show a name measured in characters and in bytes, the first character and a
short preview of a title, and uploads sorted into pictures and notes. The last one converts text to
bytes and back, and shows the error for data that is not text.

A `string` is always valid UTF-8. Its length counts graphemes (what a person counts as one
character). `"e\u{301}"` is an `e` with a combining accent: it has one grapheme and three bytes.

`$s[0]` does not compile for a `string` or for `bytes`: it is the error `E0482`. Use
`Core\Str::slice($s, $i, 1)` for a character, or `Core\Bytes::slice` for a byte position.

You cannot write a `bytes` value directly in the code. `"nvs" as bytes` gives the UTF-8 bytes of a
string. `Core\Encoding::fromHex` and `Core\Encoding::fromBase64` give any bytes you need.

`bytes` has no string form of its own. `echo $b` is the error `E0707`, so write `echo $b as string`.
If the bytes are not valid UTF-8, `$b as string` throws a `RuntimeError`. `$b as ?string` gives
`null` instead.

`==` tests whether two strings are equal. `"a" < "b"` is the error `E0715`, so use
`Core\Str::compare` to put strings in order. Text has no arithmetic: `"3" * 2` is the error
`E0716`. Join two strings with `.`, or convert a string to a number with `as int` or `as float`.

#### Example 01: check a name against two different limits

```nvs
<?nvs
// A display name is limited by what a reader sees; a database column is
// limited by what it stores. Those are two different numbers for the same
// name, so each one is measured with the type that owns it.

array<string> $names = ['Ann', 'Grüße', "Rene\u{301}e", 'Łukasz Szymański'];

foreach ($names as string $name) {
    uint $characters = Core\Str::length($name);
    uint $stored = Core\Bytes::length($name as bytes);
    echo $name, ': ', $characters, ' characters, ', $stored, " bytes\n";
}
```

```output
Ann: 3 characters, 3 bytes
Grüße: 5 characters, 7 bytes
Renée: 5 characters, 7 bytes
Łukasz Szymański: 16 characters, 18 bytes
```

#### Example 02: take the first character and a short preview

```nvs
<?nvs
// The syntax `$title[0]` does not exist, because the first character is not always the first byte.
// `Core\Str::at` returns one character, and `Core\Str::slice` returns several.
// Both return whole characters. A letter like `ö` is never cut in half.

array<string> $titles = ['Größenwahn', 'Ölzweig', 'Straße am Fluss'];

foreach ($titles as string $title) {
    string $initial = Core\Str::at($title, 0);
    string $preview = Core\Str::length($title) > 8
        ? Core\Str::slice($title, 0, 8) . '…'
        : $title;
    echo $initial, '  ', $preview, "\n";
}
```

```output
G  Größenwa…
Ö  Ölzweig
S  Straße a…
```

#### Example 03: sort uploads into pictures notes and neither

```nvs
<?nvs
// Files are often sent base64 encoded inside a JSON field.
// `Core\Encoding::fromBase64` returns `bytes`, because the data may not be text.
// The first bytes show if the file is a PNG picture.
// The data becomes a `string` only if it is valid text.

bytes $pngSignature = Core\Encoding::fromHex('89504e47');

array<string> $uploads = [
    'iVBORw0KGgo=', // the first bytes of a PNG
    'SGVsbG8sIHdvcmxkIQ==', // a short note
    'SGVsbG8s/w==', // a note with one byte that is not text
];

foreach ($uploads as string $encoded) {
    bytes $data = Core\Encoding::fromBase64($encoded);
    // `as ?string` converts the bytes to a string if they are valid text.
    // If they are not, the result is `null`.
    ?string $text = $data as ?string;
    if (Core\Bytes::startsWith($data, $pngSignature)) {
        echo 'picture, ', Core\Bytes::length($data), " bytes\n";
    } elseif ($text != null) {
        echo 'note: ', $text, "\n";
    } else {
        echo "neither a picture nor text\n";
    }
}
```

```output
picture, 8 bytes
note: Hello, world!
neither a picture nor text
```

#### Example 04: text to bytes and back

```nvs
<?nvs
// Converts text to bytes and back, and shows the error for bytes that are not text.

// `as bytes` gives the UTF-8 bytes of a string. This always works.
bytes $name = 'nvs' as bytes;
echo Core\Encoding::toHex($name), ' is ', $name as string, "\n";

// `fromHex` gives any bytes, here the two bytes `ff` and `00`.
bytes $raw = Core\Encoding::fromHex('ff00');
echo Core\Bytes::length($raw), " bytes\n";

// `ff` is not valid UTF-8, so `as string` throws a `RuntimeError`.
try {
    echo $raw as string, "\n";
} catch (RuntimeError $e) {
    echo $e->message, "\n";
}
```

```output
6e7673 is nvs
2 bytes
cannot convert `bytes` to `string`: not well-formed UTF-8 at byte 0
```

### `array<T>`

A list, or a lookup table, whose values all have the same type.

`var $ids = [1, 2];` creates an `array<int>`. The keys are not part of the type. Every value you add
later must have that type. Write the type yourself, as in `array<float> $weights = [2, 1];`, when the
array starts empty, when its values mix types, or when you will add values of a wider type later.

Keys are always strings: `$row[3]` and `$row["3"]` are the same entry. Entries keep the order you
added them in. An array of arrays is how you build a table or a grouped report.

An array is a value. When you pass it to a function, the function gets its own copy.

**Good to know:** reading a key that does not exist throws an error. Check first when a key may be
missing.

**The examples below** show a list made with `var` and one with a written type, then a lookup table,
then a grouped report that starts from an empty array. The last one shows how keys are numbered,
and that an assigned array is a copy.

An `array<T>` is an ordered table with `string` keys and values of the type `T`. Arrays can contain
arrays to any depth, such as `array<array<int>>`. `array<mixed>` can contain values of any type.

An `int` key is the same key as its digits written as a string, so `$a[1]` and `$a["1"]` read one
entry. The key variable of a `foreach` loop is always a `string`.

`$a[] = 60;` adds a value at the end. Its key is one more than the largest whole-number key, so after
`$a[5] = 50;` the next key is `6`.

Every value must have the type `T`. `array<int> $a = [1, "two"];` is the error `E0401`, and so is
`$a[] = "x";`. Reading a key that does not exist throws a `RuntimeError`: `undefined array key`.

Assigning an array to another variable copies it, the same as passing it to a function. A change through one variable is never seen
through the other.

An array has no string form: `echo $a` is the error `E0707`. `Core\Json::encode($a)` gives its text.
`$a + $b` with two arrays is the error `E0467`. `Core\Arr::underlay($a, $b)` combines them and keeps
the value of `$a` where both have a key.

#### Example 01: add up a list of prices

```nvs
<?nvs
// A basket of prices, shown one line at a time and then added up.

// Every value in this list is an `int`, so `var` gives `$prices` the type `array<int>`.
// Every value you add later must be an `int` too.
var $prices = [1299, 450];
$prices[] = 780;

var $total = 0;
foreach ($prices as var $price) {
    echo $price, "\n";
    $total = $total + $price;
}

echo 'total ', $total, ' over ', Core\Arr::count($prices), " items\n";

// A weight can have a fraction, so this list has the written type `array<float>`.
// With `var`, the list would be `array<int>`, and adding `0.5` would not compile.
array<float> $weights = [2, 1];
$weights[] = 0.5;

// This prints `weight 3.5 kg`.
echo 'weight ', Core\Arr::sum($weights), " kg\n";
```

```output
1299
450
780
total 2529 over 3 items
weight 3.5 kg
```

#### Example 02: look up a count by name

```nvs
<?nvs
// Stock counts kept under the name of the thing being counted.

// The keys are not part of the type. The values are all `int`,
// so `var` gives `$stock` the type `array<int>`.
var $stock = ['apples' => 3, 'pears' => 0];
$stock['figs'] = 7;

// `var $name` is a `string`, because every key is a string.
// `var $count` gets the type of the values, `int`.
foreach ($stock as var $name => var $count) {
    echo $name, ': ', $count, "\n";
}

// Reading a name that is not in the array throws an error.
// So check first with `Core\Arr::hasKey`. You can also write the types in a loop.
array<string> $asked = ['pears', 'plums'];
foreach ($asked as string $wanted) {
    echo $wanted, Core\Arr::hasKey($stock, $wanted) ? " is stocked\n" : " is not stocked\n";
}
```

```output
apples: 3
pears: 0
figs: 7
pears is stocked
plums is not stocked
```

#### Example 03: total a days orders per department

```nvs
<?nvs
// Totals a day's orders per department and prints the totals as JSON.
// `withServiceFee` gets a copy of `$totals` and changes only that copy.
// So the first line of output shows the original totals.

class Report
{
    public static function withServiceFee(array<int> $totals): array<int>
    {
        foreach ($totals as var $department => var $cents) {
            $totals[$department] = $cents + 250;
        }
        return $totals;
    }
}

// An array of arrays suits a grouped report.
// `var` gives `$lines` the type `array<array<int>>`.
var $lines = [
    'produce' => [1299, 450],
    'bakery' => [780],
];

// An empty array needs a written type. `var $totals = [];` does not compile,
// because the array has no value to take the type from.
array<int> $totals = [];
foreach ($lines as var $department => var $amounts) {
    $totals[$department] = Core\Arr::sum($amounts) as int;
}

var $billed = Report::withServiceFee($totals);

echo Core\Json::encode($totals), "\n";
echo Core\Json::encode($billed), "\n";
```

```output
{"produce":1749,"bakery":780}
{"produce":1999,"bakery":1030}
```

#### Example 04: keys and copies

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how keys are numbered, and that assigning an array copies it.

array<int> $a = [10, 20];
$a[5] = 50;

// `$a[]` adds a value with the next key after the largest one, here `6`.
$a[] = 60;

// `$a[1]` and `$a["1"]` read the same entry. This prints `2020`.
echo $a[1], $a['1'], "\n";

// `$copy` is a copy. The new key `x` is not added to `$a`, so this prints `4 5`.
array<int> $copy = $a;
$copy['x'] = 1;
echo Core\Arr::count($a), ' ', Core\Arr::count($copy), "\n";

echo Core\Json::encode($a), "\n";
```

```output
2020
4 5
{"0":10,"1":20,"5":50,"6":60}
```

### `callable`, classes, `object`, shapes

The types for things that are not plain values: a function you can pass around, a class, any
object, and an object described by the fields it has.

A `callable` is an anonymous function written with `fn`, or a method reference such as
`Core\Str::length`. A class, interface or enum name is a type, and `object` is the type every
instance fits. A shape describes an object by its fields. `as Point` checks that a value has those
fields and throws an error if not. `is Point` gives `true` or `false`.

To pick a class while the program runs, convert its name with `as class<T>`. A name from a setting
is checked when it runs, and `as ?class<T>` gives `null` for a wrong name.

**Good to know:** a call through a `callable` returns a `mixed` value, so convert the result where
you use it: `$f(4) as int`.

**The examples below** pass a pricing rule around, check a value against a shape, and pick a
report class from a name in quotes and from a setting. The last two get the class of an `object`
back, and show a shape without a name as a compile error.

A string is never a `callable`. `callable $f = "strlen";` is the error `E0418`. Write a method
reference such as `Core\Str::length` instead.

Any class instance can be assigned to an `object` variable. You can read a property through it by
name, and the result is `mixed`. A property the object does not have throws a `RuntimeError`.
`$o is Cell` tests the class, and `$o as Cell` converts to it. If the object is another class, `as`
throws a `RuntimeError`. `as ?Cell` is the error `E0473`, so use `is` to test first.

A `class<T>` variable contains a class, not an instance. `T` is a class or an interface, and every
class in the variable is `T` or extends or implements it. A `class<Dog>` can be assigned to a
`class<Animal>`. Two class references are equal when they are the same class.

`as class<T>` is the only way to get a class reference. A class name in quotes is checked when the
program compiles, and a name outside the hierarchy of `T` is the error `E0708`. A name in a variable
is checked when the program runs. A wrong name throws a `RuntimeError`, and `as ?class<T>` gives
`null` for it. `$cls as string` gives the class name.

Only three places take a class reference: `new $cls()`, `$cls::f()` and `$x is $cls`. A `string` in
any of the three is the error `E0496`. `Dog::class` is a `string`, the class name. Comparing a
`string` with a `class<T>` is the error `E0466`.

A shape cannot be written in front of a variable, because a `{` at the start of a statement opens a
block. `{ x: int } $p = …;` is the error `E0134`. Name the shape with `type` first.

A value assigned to a shape needs every field the shape names, with the type it gives. A missing
field or a field of another type is the error `E0401`. You can assign a new value to an existing
field of an anonymous object. Adding a field it does not have throws a `RuntimeError`.

`as Point` checks the type of each field too. `{ x: 5, y: "six" } as Point` throws a `RuntimeError`,
and `as ?Point` gives `null` for it.

#### Example 01: pass a pricing rule around

```nvs
<?nvs
// A discount rule written once and then handed around like any other value.
// A `callable` is an anonymous function or a method reference. A call through one
// returns `mixed`, so the code says the type of the result where it is used.

callable $tenPercentOff = fn(int $cents): int => $cents - Core\Math::intDiv($cents, 10);

class Till
{
    public static function apply(callable $rule, array<int> $prices): int
    {
        int $total = 0;
        foreach ($prices as int $price) {
            int $charged = $rule($price) as int;
            $total = $total + $charged;
        }
        return $total;
    }
}

array<int> $basket = [1000, 2500];
echo Till::apply($tenPercentOff, $basket), "\n";
echo $tenPercentOff(500) as int, "\n";
```

```output
3150
450
```

#### Example 02: describe a value by the fields it has

```nvs
<?nvs
// A point on a map, described by the fields it has and not by a class.
// A shape needs a name to be written in front of a variable, so it gets one with `type`.

type Point = { x: int, y: int };

class Grid
{
    public static function describe(Point $p): string
    {
        return '(' . ($p->x as string) . ', ' . ($p->y as string) . ')';
    }
}

// A value with more fields than the shape asks for still fits it.
Point $home = { x: 3, y: 4 };
var $pin = { x: 10, y: 20, label: 'office' };

echo Grid::describe($home), "\n";
echo Grid::describe($pin), ' ', $pin->label, "\n";

// A call through a `callable` returns a `mixed` value.
callable $findPlace = fn(string $name): mixed => $name == 'depot' ? { x: 7, y: 1 } : { city: $name };

// `as Point` checks that the value has an `int` field `x` and an `int` field `y`.
// If a field is missing, it throws an error. The second call shows this.
echo Grid::describe($findPlace('depot') as Point), "\n";

try {
    echo Grid::describe($findPlace('Vienna') as Point), "\n";
} catch (RuntimeError $e) {
    echo $e->message, "\n";
}

// `is Point` does the same check and gives `true` or `false`, so nothing is thrown.
mixed $place = $findPlace('Vienna');
echo $place is Point ? Grid::describe($place) : 'not on the grid', "\n";
```

```output
(3, 4)
(10, 20) office
(7, 1)
cannot convert a value of another type to `{ x: int, y: int }`
not on the grid
```

#### Example 03: pick the report format from a setting

```nvs
<?nvs
// Picks a report format from a setting. The setting is text, and the program needs a class.
// `as class<Renders>` converts a class name to a class reference.
// The program uses the reference to create the report and to call the static method `extension`.

interface Renders
{
    public function render(array<string> $rows): string;
    public static function extension(): string;
}

class CsvReport implements Renders
{
    public function render(array<string> $rows): string
    {
        return Core\Str::join($rows, ',');
    }

    public static function extension(): string
    {
        return 'csv';
    }
}

class LinesReport implements Renders
{
    public function render(array<string> $rows): string
    {
        return Core\Str::join($rows, "\n");
    }

    public static function extension(): string
    {
        return 'txt';
    }
}

array<string> $rows = ['north', 'south'];

// A class name written in quotes is checked when the program compiles.
// If `CsvReport` did not implement `Renders`, the program would not compile.
class<Renders> $default = 'CsvReport' as class<Renders>;

// A name from a setting is checked when the program runs. `as ?class<Renders>` gives `null`
// for a name that is not a `Renders` class. Then `??` uses the default format.
array<string> $settings = ['LinesReport', 'PdfReport'];

foreach ($settings as string $setting) {
    class<Renders> $format = ($setting as ?class<Renders>) ?? $default;
    Renders $report = new $format();

    echo $setting, ' writes a .', $format::extension(), " file:\n";
    echo $report->render($rows), "\n";
}
```

```output
LinesReport writes a .txt file:
north
south
PdfReport writes a .csv file:
north,south
```

#### Example 04: any object and its class

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows an `object` variable, and how `is` and `as` get its class back.

class Cell
{
    public int $n = 1;
}

class Row
{
    public int $n = 2;
}

// Any instance can be assigned to `object`. Reading `$o->n` gives a `mixed` value.
object $o = new Cell();
echo $o->n, "\n";

// `is Cell` tests the class. `as Cell` converts to it, so `->n` is an `int`. This prints `cell 1`.
echo ($o is Cell) ? 'cell' : 'other', ' ', ($o as Cell)->n, "\n";

// The object is not a `Row`, so `as Row` throws an error.
try {
    echo ($o as Row)->n, "\n";
} catch (RuntimeError $e) {
    echo $e->message, "\n";
}
```

```output
1
cell 1
cannot convert a value of another type to `Row`
```

#### Example 05: a shape needs a name

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that a shape needs a name before a variable can have it. A `{` at the start of
// a statement opens a block, so this program does not compile.
// proof: compile-error

{ x: int, y: int } $p = { x: 1, y: 2 };
```

```output
error[E0134]: a local declaration cannot be typed with a bare shape
  --> main.nvs:6:1
  |
6 | { x: int, y: int } $p = { x: 1, y: 2 };
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ `{` at the start of a statement already opens a block
  = help: give the shape a name first: `type Point = { x: int }; Point $point;`
```

### `mixed`

`mixed` is the one type Novis does not check. A `mixed` variable can contain a value of any type.

Input from outside the program has the type `mixed`: a query string, a form post, decoded JSON.
Convert each value to the type you need with `as`. If that is not possible, `as` throws an error.
`is` tests what the value is and does not convert it.

A `mixed` value is never converted to a narrower type for you. Passing one to a `string` parameter
does not compile until you write `as string`.

**Good to know:** an operation on a `mixed` value is slower than on a declared type. Convert the
value once, close to where it arrives.

**The examples below** read a page number from a query string, describe each field of a decoded
payload, and convert an order line. The last two use a `mixed` value directly and show the compile
error.

You can use a `mixed` value in arithmetic, as a condition, with `[]`, with `->`, with `.` and with
`is` or `as`. Each operation checks the value while the program runs. If the value has the wrong
type, it throws an error.

Arithmetic needs a number. `"abc" + 1` throws a `RuntimeError`, and so does `"5" + 1`. Convert text
first: `($m as int) + 1`. An `int` and a `float` add as they do without `mixed`: `5 + 1.5` is `6.5`.

`==` never converts a value. A `mixed` `"5"` is not equal to `5`.

`.` joins a number or a string. An array with `.` throws a `RuntimeError`. `[]` on a value that is
not an array throws a `RuntimeError`, and so does `->` for a field the object does not have.
Calling a method on a value that is not an object throws a `LogicError`.

A `mixed` value is never assigned to a narrower type without `as`. `int $i = $m;` is the error
`E0401`, and so is a `mixed` argument for a `string` parameter.

#### Example 01: read a page number out of a query string

```nvs
<?nvs
// Query parameters have the type `mixed`, because nothing has checked them yet.
// `as ?uint` converts a value to a whole number. If that is not possible,
// the result is `null`, and `??` gives the default value instead.

array<mixed> $query = ['page' => '3', 'size' => 'abc', 'sort' => 'name'];

uint $firstPage = 1;
uint $defaultSize = 20;

uint $page = ($query['page'] as ?uint) ?? $firstPage;
uint $size = ($query['size'] as ?uint) ?? $defaultSize;

echo 'page ', $page, ', ', $size, " per page\n";
```

```output
page 3, 20 per page
```

#### Example 02: say what each field of a decoded payload is

```nvs
<?nvs
// Describes each field of a decoded JSON document. Each field is a `mixed` value.
// `is` tests the type of a value and does not convert it.

array<mixed> $payload = ['id' => 4102, 'name' => 'Ada', 'paid' => true, 'note' => null];

foreach ($payload as tainted string $field => mixed $value) {
    if ($value is int) {
        echo $field, " is a whole number\n";
    } elseif ($value is string) {
        echo $field, " is text\n";
    } elseif ($value is bool) {
        echo $field, " is a yes or no\n";
    } else {
        echo $field, " was not sent\n";
    }
}
```

```output
id is a whole number
name is text
paid is a yes or no
note was not sent
```

#### Example 03: turn one untrusted order line into typed values

```nvs
<?nvs
// A handler converts each value once, at the start, and then works with typed values.
// If a value does not convert, `as` throws an error. The program reports the line and skips it.
// Only a line whose three values all converted is added to the total.

array<mixed> $lines = [
    ['sku' => 'A-1', 'quantity' => '2', 'price' => '9.95'],
    ['sku' => 'B-7', 'quantity' => 'many', 'price' => '4.00'],
    ['sku' => 'C-3', 'quantity' => 1, 'price' => '12.50'],
];

decimal $total = 0.00;
foreach ($lines as mixed $line) {
    try {
        tainted string $sku = $line['sku'] as string;
        uint $quantity = $line['quantity'] as uint;
        decimal $price = $line['price'] as decimal;
        $total = $total + $price * $quantity;
        echo $sku, ': ', $quantity, ' x ', $price, "\n";
    } catch (Throwable $e) {
        echo "skipped a line that did not convert\n";
    }
}
echo 'total ', $total, "\n";
```

```output
A-1: 2 x 9.95
skipped a line that did not convert
C-3: 1 x 12.50
total 32.40
```

#### Example 04: use a mixed value directly

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the operations you can use on a `mixed` value without converting it first.

mixed $m = 5;
mixed $row = ['k' => 'v'];
mixed $text = 'x';

// Each operation checks the value while the program runs. This prints `6 5 v xy X`.
echo $m + 1, ' ', $m as string, ' ', $row['k'], ' ', $text . 'y', ' ', Core\Str::upper($text as string), "\n";

// Arithmetic needs a number, so `"abc" + 1` throws an error.
mixed $bad = 'abc';
try {
    echo $bad + 1, "\n";
} catch (RuntimeError $e) {
    echo "no arithmetic on text\n";
}
```

```output
6 5 v xy X
no arithmetic on text
```

#### Example 05: convert before a typed parameter

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that a `mixed` value is not passed to a `string` parameter without `as string`.
// This program does not compile.
// proof: compile-error

mixed $text = 'x';
echo Core\Str::upper($text), "\n";
```

```output
error[E0401]: expected `string`, found `mixed`
  --> main.nvs:7:22
  |
7 | echo Core\Str::upper($text), "\n";
  |                      ^^^^^ this is `mixed`
```

### Nullable, union, single-value and enum-case types

A nullable type `?T` is the type `T` or `null`. A variable can be `null` only when its type allows
it. A union `A|B` is either of the two types. Test which one a value is with `is` before you use it
as one of them.

A single-value type is one value written as a type, such as `"asc"` or `3`. A union of them is a
list of allowed values. A setting that may only be one of three words has a type that names those
three words. Any other word is not accepted. An enum case is a type in the same way, so a function
can accept two cases of an enum and not the third.

**The examples below** show a setting that may be missing, a sort order limited to three words, and
a handler that converts an untrusted request into the values it accepts. The last three show each
kind of type at once, and two compile errors.

`null` is a type of its own, and `null $n = null;` compiles. `int $i = null;` is the error `E0401`.
A `?int` value is not used in arithmetic before it is tested. `$maybe + 1` is the error `E0716`.
Test it with `!= null` first, or give a default with `??`.

A union may mix any types, such as `object|int`. Inside `if ($id is int)`, `$id` is an `int`.

A value written in the code is checked against a single-value type when the program compiles.
`$mode = "delete";` for a `"read"|"write"` variable is the error `E0401`. A value converted with
`as` is checked when the program runs. If it is not in the list, `as` throws a `RuntimeError`.
A single-value type can be assigned to its wider type: a `1|2|3` value to an `int`.

An enum is a list of named whole numbers. `enum Mode { Read, Write }` numbers its cases from `0`.
`enum Mode: int { Read = 1 }` gives each case its number. `$m as int` gives the number of a case.
`1 as Mode` gives the case with that number. If no case has it, `as` throws a `RuntimeError`, and
`as ?Mode` gives `null`. `Mode::Read as string` is the error `E0708`.

`iterable` and an intersection `A&B` can be written for a parameter or a return type. No value can
be assigned to either of them. `iterable $i = $xs;` is the error `E0401`.

#### Example 01: a setting that may not be there

```nvs
<?nvs
// A setting may be missing. `?uint` is a whole number or `null`.
// `as ?uint` converts text to a whole number. If the text is not a number,
// the result is `null`, and `??` gives a default value.

array<string> $settings = ['page' => '3', 'limit' => 'many'];

?uint $page = $settings['page'] as ?uint;
?uint $limit = $settings['limit'] as ?uint;

echo 'page ', $page ?? 1, "\n";
echo 'limit ', $limit ?? 20, "\n";

// A variable can be `null` only when its type allows it, as `?string` does.
// So the reader can see on this line that `$note` may be empty.
?string $note = null;
echo 'note ', $note ?? '(none)', "\n";
```

```output
page 3
limit 20
note (none)
```

#### Example 02: a sort order that may only be one of three words

```nvs
<?nvs
// The type of `$order` is a set of three words. Only those words can be passed to `sortBy`,
// so `sortBy` does not need to check its argument. For any other word, `as` throws
// an error before the method is called.

class Report
{
    public static function sortBy("newest"|"oldest"|"name" $order): string
    {
        return 'sorting by ' . $order;
    }
}

array<string> $asked = ['newest', 'name', 'sideways'];
foreach ($asked as string $one) {
    try {
        echo Report::sortBy($one as "newest"|"oldest"|"name"), "\n";
    } catch (Throwable $e) {
        echo 'not a sort order: ', $one, "\n";
    }
}
```

```output
sorting by newest
sorting by name
not a sort order: sideways
```

#### Example 03: a handler that accepts only what it will act on

```nvs
<?nvs
// A handler converts each field of a request to the exact type it needs, once, at the top.
// The account is an `int` or a `string`, and the action is a case of the enum `Gate::Action`.
// `grant` accepts only the cases `Read` and `Write`. Converting `Delete`
// to that type throws an error, so `grant` is never called with it.

class Gate
{
    enum Action { Read, Write, Delete }

    public static function grant(Action::Read|Action::Write $action, int|string $account): string
    {
        array<string> $verbs = ['read', 'write', 'delete'];
        return 'account ' . ($account as string) . ' may ' . $verbs[$action as int];
    }
}

array<array<string>> $requests = [
    ['account' => '1042', 'action' => '0'],
    ['account' => 'ada', 'action' => '1'],
    ['account' => 'ada', 'action' => '2'],
];

foreach ($requests as array<string> $request) {
    try {
        string $raw = $request['account'];
        int|string $account = ($raw as ?int) ?? $raw;
        Gate::Action $asked = ($request['action'] as int) as Gate::Action;
        echo Gate::grant($asked as Gate::Action::Read|Gate::Action::Write, $account), "\n";
    } catch (Throwable $e) {
        echo "refused: this gate grants nothing else\n";
    }
}
```

```output
account 1042 may read
account ada may write
refused: this gate grants nothing else
```

#### Example 04: each kind of type

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a nullable type, a union, two single-value types and an enum case type.

enum Mode: int
{
    Read = 1,
    Write = 2,
}

?int $maybe = null;
int|string $id = 'abc';
"read"|"write" $mode = 'read';
1|2|3 $level = 2;
Mode::Read|Mode::Write $m = Mode::Write;

// `$m as int` gives the number of the case, here `2`. `1 as Mode` gives the case `Mode::Read`.
echo $maybe ?? -1, ' ', $id, ' ', $mode, $level, ' ', $m as int, ' ', (1 as Mode) == Mode::Read ? 'read' : 'other', "\n";

// No case has the number `9`, so `as Mode` throws an error.
try {
    Mode $none = 9 as Mode;
} catch (RuntimeError $e) {
    echo $e->message, "\n";
}

// `as ?Mode` gives `null` for the same number.
echo (9 as ?Mode) == null ? 'null' : 'case', "\n";
```

```output
-1 abc read2 2 read
`9` is not one of `Mode::Read`, `Mode::Write`
null
```

#### Example 05: a word outside the list

#### Example 06: nothing is an iterable

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that no value can be assigned to an `iterable` variable, not even an array.
// This program does not compile.
// proof: compile-error

array<int> $xs = [1, 2];
iterable $i = $xs;
```

```output
error[E0401]: expected `iterable`, found `array<int>`
  --> main.nvs:7:15
  |
7 | iterable $i = $xs;
  |               ^^^ this is `array<int>`

error: aborting due to 1 error
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```

### A member every class of a union declares

A variable of a union of classes, such as `Box|Circle`, is an object of one of those classes. You
can read a property or call a method of it when every class has that member with the same type. A
method needs the same parameters and return type. The member must also be visible where you use it.

Use `?->` on a union that may be `null`, such as `?Box|Circle`. A write compiles when no class makes
the property `readonly` and every class has the same `set` visibility. `isinit` does not compile on
a property of a union.

If one class does not have the member, the program does not compile. The same is true when the
types differ, or when the member is not visible in one class. The error is `E0881`, and its message
names the class. An interface is not allowed in such a union.

**The examples below** read a property of two shipping classes and call a method of two payment
classes. The last one is a compile error.

#### Example 01: a property both classes declare

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to read a property that every class of a union declares.

final class Courier
{
    public string $label = 'Courier, next day';
    public function constructor(public int $weight)
    { }
}

final class Pickup
{
    public string $label = 'Pickup at the shop';
    public function constructor(public int $weight)
    { }
}

final class Order
{
    // Small parcels go by courier. Heavy parcels are picked up at the shop.
    public static function shipping(int $weight): Courier|Pickup
    {
        if ($weight > 20) {
            return new Pickup($weight);
        }
        return new Courier($weight);
    }
}

// Both classes declare `string $label` and `int $weight`.
// So `$ship->label` compiles without a test of the class.
array<int> $weights = [3, 25];
foreach ($weights as int $weight) {
    Courier|Pickup $ship = Order::shipping($weight);
    echo $ship->weight, ' kg: ', $ship->label, "\n";
}

// `?->` reads a property of a union that may be `null`.
// Here the variable is `null`, so `??` prints `not chosen`.
?Courier|Pickup $later = null;
echo $later?->label ?? 'not chosen', "\n";

// A write works too, because `$label` has the same type in both classes.
Courier|Pickup $gift = new Courier(1);
$gift->label = 'Courier, gift wrapped';
echo $gift->label, "\n";
```

```output
3 kg: Courier, next day
25 kg: Pickup at the shop
not chosen
Courier, gift wrapped
```

#### Example 02: a method both classes declare

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to call a method that every class of a union declares.

final class Card
{
    public function constructor(public string $last4)
    { }

    public function fee(int $cents): int
    {
        return $cents >= 5000 ? 0 : 30;
    }

    public function describe(): string
    {
        return 'card ending ' . $this->last4;
    }
}

final class Transfer
{
    public function constructor(public string $bank)
    { }

    public function fee(int $cents): int
    {
        return $cents >= 100000 ? 0 : 50;
    }

    public function describe(): string
    {
        return 'transfer from ' . $this->bank;
    }
}

// Each call runs `fee` and `describe` of the class the value is.
// For 10000 cents, the card fee is `0` and the transfer fee is `50`.
array<Card|Transfer> $payments = [new Card('4242'), new Transfer('City Bank')];
foreach ($payments as Card|Transfer $payment) {
    echo $payment->describe(), ': fee ', $payment->fee(10000), " cents\n";
}
```

```output
card ending 4242: fee 0 cents
transfer from City Bank: fee 50 cents
```

#### Example 03: a member one class lacks

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that a property must exist in every class of the union.
// `Pickup` has no `$tracking`, so this program does not compile.
// proof: compile-error

final class Courier
{
    public string $tracking = 'TR-1001';
    public function constructor()
    { }
}

final class Pickup
{
    public string $shop = 'Main Street';
    public function constructor()
    { }
}

Courier|Pickup $ship = new Pickup();
echo $ship->tracking, "\n";
```

```output
error[E0881]: `Pickup` has no property `$tracking`
   --> main.nvs:21:6
   |
21 | echo $ship->tracking, "\n";
   |      ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ used through `Courier|Pickup` here
   = help: you can use a member through a union only when every class has it with the same type, and it is visible here. Otherwise, test the value with `is` first

error: aborting due to 1 error
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```

### `void`, `never`, `self`, `static`

Four return types say something an ordinary type cannot.

`void` means the method returns no value. You call it as a statement of its own. You cannot print
the result, store it in a variable or pass it to another method.

`never` means the method does not return to its caller. It always throws an error or ends the
program.

`self` and `static` both name a class. `self` is the class the method is written in. `static` is the
class the call names. So a method in a base class can return an instance of the child class it was
called on, and the caller gets that child class.

The examples show a method called only for what it does, a chain of calls on one object, and a base
class that creates an instance of whichever child class the call names. Example 04 shows that a
`void` result cannot be printed. Example 05 shows that a call to a `never` method ends the caller's
path.

`void` and `never` are allowed only as a return type. A parameter or a variable of type `void` or
`never` is the error `E0742`. `var $x = Helper::nothing();` is `E0742` too, because the
call returns `void`.

A `void` result is not a value. `echo Helper::nothing();` is the error `E0707`. Passing it to an
`int` parameter is `E0401`. A `void` method that returns a value is `E0403`.

A `never` method must not reach the end of its body. That is the error `E0739`. A `return;` in it is
`E0822`. Every path must throw, call `exit` or call another `never` method.

A call to a `never` method ends the caller's path. The caller needs no `return` after it. This is
true for a static method and for a method no child class overrides. A call to an overridden method
does not end the path, so the caller still needs a `return` there. Otherwise it is `E0739`.

`self` and `static` are only allowed inside a class. Outside one, `self` is `E0303`. `self` also
works as a parameter type and inside another type, such as `array<self>` or `?static`. `static` is
not allowed as a parameter type.

A method that returns `static` must return `$this` or `new static(...)`. `return new self();` is
`E0741`, because a child class may be the class the call names.

`self` and `static` are not values. `return self;` is the error `E0321`. To use a member of the
class, write `self::` and the member's name.

#### Example 01: a method called only for what it does

```nvs
<?nvs
// A method that returns no value has the return type `void`.
// Each call below is a statement of its own.

class Audit
{
    public static function note(string $what, uint $count): void
    {
        echo '[audit] ', $what, ' x', $count, "\n";
    }

    public static function line(string $text): void
    {
        echo $text, "\n";
    }
}

Audit::line('import starting');
Audit::note('rows read', 120);
Audit::note('rows skipped', 3);
Audit::line('import finished');
```

```output
import starting
[audit] rows read x120
[audit] rows skipped x3
import finished
```

#### Example 02: a chain of calls that each hand the object back

```nvs
<?nvs
// Each method returns `self`, the class it is written in, and returns `$this`.
// So you can call the next method on the result, all on one line.

final class Query
{
    public string $table = '';
    public array<string> $wheres = [];
    public uint $limit = 0;

    public function from(string $table): self
    {
        $this->table = $table;
        return $this;
    }

    public function where(string $clause): self
    {
        $this->wheres[] = $clause;
        return $this;
    }

    public function take(uint $rows): self
    {
        $this->limit = $rows;
        return $this;
    }

    public function text(): string
    {
        return 'select from '
            . $this->table
            . ' where '
            . Core\Str::join($this->wheres, ' and ')
            . ' limit '
            . $this->limit;
    }
}

Query $q = new Query();
echo $q->from('orders')->where('paid')->where('shipped')->take(25)->text(), "\n";
```

```output
select from orders where paid and shipped limit 25
```

#### Example 03: one base class that builds whichever kind was asked for

```nvs
<?nvs
// The base class `Record` has one `load` method for every subclass.
// `load` returns `static`, the class named in the call. So `Invoice::load` returns an `Invoice`.
// `refuse` returns `never`, because it always throws an error.

class Record
{
    public function constructor(public uint $id)
    {}

    public static function load(uint $id): static
    {
        if ($id == 0) {
            Record::refuse('a record id is never zero');
        }
        return new static($id);
    }

    public static function refuse(string $why): never
    {
        throw new RuntimeError($why);
    }

    public function label(): string
    {
        return 'record #' . $this->id;
    }
}

final class Invoice extends Record
{
    public function label(): string
    {
        return 'invoice #' . $this->id;
    }
}

final class Customer extends Record
{
    public function label(): string
    {
        return 'customer #' . $this->id;
    }
}

Invoice $invoice = Invoice::load(1042);
Customer $customer = Customer::load(7);
echo $invoice->label(), "\n";
echo $customer->label(), "\n";

try {
    Invoice::load(0);
} catch (Throwable $e) {
    echo "refused an impossible id\n";
}
```

```output
invoice #1042
customer #7
refused an impossible id
```

#### Example 04: a void result cannot be printed

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that the result of a `void` method cannot be printed.
// This program does not compile.
// proof: compile-error

class Helper
{
    public static function nothing(): void
    {}
}

echo Helper::nothing();
```

```output
error[E0707]: `void` has no string form
   --> main.nvs:12:6
   |
12 | echo Helper::nothing();
   |      ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ converted to `string` here
   = help: a call that returns `void` has no value at all, so there is nothing here to print

error: aborting due to 1 error
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```

#### Example 05: a never call ends the path

```nvs
<?nvs
// `first` needs no `return` after `Report::fail`, because `fail` returns `never`.

class Report
{
    public static function fail(string $why): never
    {
        throw new RuntimeError($why);
    }

    public static function first(array<int> $rows): int
    {
        if (Core\Arr::count($rows) > 0) {
            return $rows[0];
        }
        Report::fail('no rows');
    }
}

echo Report::first([3, 4]), "\n";

try {
    Report::first([]);
} catch (RuntimeError $e) {
    echo 'error: ', $e->message, "\n";
}
```

```output
3
error: no rows
```

### `type` aliases

A `type` alias gives a type a short name. After `type UserId = uint;`, `UserId` and `uint` are the
same type. A value of one is a value of the other, so you never convert between them.

You write an alias at the top level of a file, or inside a class, interface or enum. An alias
inside a class belongs to that class. Outside the class, you write the class name first:
`Basket::Lines`.

An alias cannot be a second name for one class, because a class already has a name. Use an alias
for a type that is long to write: a union, a nested array, or the fields of an object a method
returns.

An alias exists only while the program compiles. It has no cost while the program runs.

Example 04 names a nullable class and a union. Example 05 shows that an alias of one class does not
compile.

An alias name is written in PascalCase. `type user_id = uint;` is the error `E0110`.

An alias at the top level of a file can be used anywhere in that file, also above its declaration.
An alias inside a method body or a block, such as an `if`, is the error `E0233`.

An alias inside a class, interface or enum has no visibility. `public type Lines = …;` is the error
`E0133`. Inside its class you write the short name. Everywhere else you write `Owner::Name`.

A child class does not inherit an alias. `Lines` in a child class of `Basket` is the error `E0303`.
Write `Basket::Lines` there.

An alias of a single class, interface or enum is the error `E0307`. `?Foo`, a union, an object
shape and `array<Foo>` are allowed.

An alias may use another alias, such as `type Ids = array<Id>;`. An alias that contains itself is
the error `E0310`, such as `type Tree = array<Tree>;`. Use a class for a type that contains itself.

Two declarations with the same name are the error `E0304`. This is also true for an alias and a
class with the same name.

#### Example 01: a short name for a long type

```nvs
<?nvs
// Three aliases at the top of the file give three types a short name.
// An alias and its type are the same type, so a value moves between them without `as`.

type UserId = uint;
type Answer = int|string;
type Grid = array<array<float>>;

class Report
{
    public static function line(UserId $id, Answer $answer): string
    {
        return 'user ' . ($id as string) . ' answered ' . ($answer as string);
    }
}

UserId $id = 1042;
uint $plain = $id; // the alias and `uint` are one type, in both directions

echo Report::line($id, 7), "\n";
echo Report::line($plain, 'maybe'), "\n";

Grid $grid = [[1.5, 2.0], [0.5]];
echo $grid[0][1], ' ', $grid[1][0], "\n";
```

```output
user 1042 answered 7
user 1042 answered maybe
2 0.5
```

#### Example 02: a name that belongs to a class

```nvs
<?nvs
// You can declare a type alias inside a class. Inside that class, you write
// the short name `Lines`. Outside it, you write `Basket::Lines`.
// A subclass does not inherit the alias.

final class Basket
{
    type Lines = array<string>;

    public function constructor(public Lines $lines)
    {}

    public function add(string $line): Lines
    {
        $this->lines[] = $line;
        return $this->lines; // inside the class: the short name
    }
}

class Printer
{
    public static function show(Basket::Lines $lines): void
    { // outside the class: the class name first
        foreach ($lines as string $line) {
            echo '- ', $line, "\n";
        }
    }
}

Basket $basket = new Basket(['two coffees']);
Printer::show($basket->add('one tea'));
```

```output
- two coffees
- one tea
```

#### Example 03: the shape a method hands back

```nvs
<?nvs
// `type Invoice` gives a name to the fields that these methods return.
// Each method uses the name `Invoice`, so the fields are written only once.
// To add a field, you change only this one line.

type Invoice = { number: string, total: decimal, paid: bool };

class Billing
{
    public static function build(string $number, decimal $total): Invoice
    {
        return { number: $number, total: $total, paid: false };
    }

    public static function settle(Invoice $invoice): Invoice
    {
        return { number: $invoice->number, total: $invoice->total, paid: true };
    }

    public static function line(Invoice $invoice): string
    {
        return $invoice->number
            . ' '
            . ($invoice->total as string)
            . ($invoice->paid ? ' (paid)' : ' (open)');
    }
}

Invoice $draft = Billing::build('INV-1042', 19.99 as decimal);
echo Billing::line($draft), "\n";
echo Billing::line(Billing::settle($draft)), "\n";
```

```output
INV-1042 19.99 (open)
INV-1042 19.99 (paid)
```

#### Example 04: a nullable class and a union

```nvs
<?nvs
// `MaybeUser` is a `User` or `null`. `Id` is an `int` or a `string`.

class User
{
    public int $n = 7;
}

type Id = int|string;
type MaybeUser = ?User;

Id $a = 1;
Id $b = 'x';
MaybeUser $u = new User();
echo $a, $b, ' ', $u?->n, "\n";
```

```output
1x 7
```

#### Example 05: an alias of one class

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that an alias cannot name one class on its own. `Foo` already has a name.
// This program does not compile.
// proof: compile-error

class Foo
{
    public int $n = 1;
}

type Bar = Foo;
```

```output

   --> main.nvs:11:12
   |
11 | type Bar = Foo;
   |            ^^^ aliases exactly one class-shaped atom
   = help: a class already has its own name, so write the class name. An alias can name a union, an intersection or an `array<...>`

error: aborting due to 1 error
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```

### Values written in the code

You can write a value directly in your program: a number, a string, `true`, `false` or `null`.

A number can have underscores between its digits, and it can be written in base 16, base 2 or
base 8. A leading zero has no special meaning, so `017` is seventeen. A number followed by a unit,
such as `30s` or `1h30m`, is a duration (a length of time).

A string in single quotes keeps every character as you typed it. A string in double quotes inserts
the values of your variables and reads escapes such as `\n`. A heredoc is a string that covers
several lines.

An html template, written ``html`...` ``, is a piece of a web page. Its type is `Core\Html\Markup`.
Every value you insert into it is escaped, so a value cannot add a tag.

**The examples below** show the ways to write a number, the two kinds of quotes, a message built
from a template, a page fragment with inserted values, the escapes of a double-quoted string,
durations, and a program that joins markup with `.` and does not compile.

A float can also be written `1E-2` or `1_000.5`. The keywords `true`, `false` and `null` are values
too.

A single-quoted string has two escapes: `\\` is one backslash and `\'` is a quote. Every other
backslash is printed as it is, so `'a\nb'` prints `a\nb`.

A double-quoted string has the escapes `\\`, `\"`, `\$`, `\n`, `\t`, `\r`, `\v` and `\f`. It also
has an octal escape from `\0` to `\777`, `\xHH` and `\u{HHHH}`. An octal or `\x` escape writes one
byte. The bytes of the string must form valid UTF-8, so `"\xff"` is the error `E0431`. An escape the
language does not know keeps its backslash, so `"\q"` prints `\q`.

A string cannot contain the `ESC` character. This is the error `E0011`. It is the same for the raw
byte and for `\e`, `\x1b`, `\033` and `\u{1b}`. To style text in a terminal, use `Core\Cli\Text`.

In a double-quoted string, `$name[key]` and `$name[0]` read one array element. A second `[...]`
after it is text, so `"$s[0][1]"` prints the element and then `[1]`. For more, use braces. The
expression in braces must start with a variable, and then it can be any expression, such as
`{$a + $b}`. A `{` with no `$` after it is text. `"${name}"` prints `${name}`.

A value in a string is converted the way `echo` converts it. A number, a `bool`, a `string` and
`null` work. `bytes`, an array and an enum case are the error `E0707`. An object of a class that
does not implement `Stringable` is the error `E0412`.

In a heredoc, every line must start with the same spaces as the closing marker. Those spaces are
removed. A line with less indentation is the error `E0433`.

A duration has the units `ns`, `us`, `ms`, `s`, `m`, `h`, `d` and `w`. A duration is an object, so
`==` checks whether two variables are the same object. `1h == 1h` is `false`. To compare two
durations, use `compareTo`, which returns `0` when they are equal.

An anonymous object at the start of a statement must be in parentheses: `({ x: 1 });`. Without them
it is the error `E0117`. The same is true for the body of an arrow function.

An html template keeps every byte between the backticks, also the spaces and line breaks. Write a
backtick in it as `` \` ``. Write `\{` for a `{` that opens no hole. A variable after it is still
filled in, so `\{$n}` prints `{`, the value and `}`.

A brace that is not followed by `$` is text. `{Page::TITLE}` prints as it is written, and the
compiler gives the warning `W1012`. Write `<?= Page::TITLE ?>` for a constant or a method call.

`<?= ... ?>` in an html template takes any expression. Spaces around it are allowed. A `}` inside it
is an ordinary brace. The first `?>` that is not inside a string or a template closes it. A `<?nvs`
block inside a template is the error `E0010`. A template is one expression. To repeat markup in a
loop, build the fragments in code and join them.

A `string` in a hole is escaped, also when it is tainted. A `Core\Html\Markup` in a hole is written
as it is. A secret value in a hole is the error `E0790`. A value with no string form is the error
`E0707`.

`+` joins two `Core\Html\Markup` values. `Core\Html::join($parts, $separator)` joins a list of
them. `.` with a `Core\Html\Markup` is the error `E0710`. The text it would make is escaped a second
time when it is printed.

`html"..."` with double quotes does not compile. The error `E0319` says to write it with backticks.

`"<p>x</p>" as Core\Html\Markup` converts a string that is written directly in the code. Any other
string is the error `E0417`. To turn a computed string into markup, use `Core\Html::escape` or
`Core\Html::sanitize`.

#### Example 01: the ways to write a number

```nvs
<?nvs
// A number can be written in more than one way. Underscores between digits make
// a long number easier to read, and the value stays the same. You can also write
// a number in base sixteen (`0x`), base two (`0b`) or base eight (`0o`).

int $seats = 1_000_000;
int $mask = 0xFF;
int $flags = 0b1011;
int $mode = 0o644;

echo $seats, ' ', $mask, ' ', $flags, ' ', $mode, "\n";

// A zero at the front is only a zero, so `017` is seventeen.
// PHP and C read `017` as base eight, which is fifteen.
int $seventeen = 017;

echo $seventeen, "\n";

// A number with a dot or an exponent in it is a float. The digits before the
// dot or after it may be left out.
float $half = .5;
float $five = 5.;
float $thousand = 1e3;

echo $half, ' ', $five, ' ', $thousand, "\n";
```

```output
1000000 255 11 420
17
0.5 5 1000
```

#### Example 02: the two kinds of quote

```nvs
<?nvs
// Single quotes keep the text exactly as you typed it. Double quotes fill in
// the values of your variables and turn an escape such as `\n` into the
// character it stands for.

class Guest
{
    public string $name = 'Ada';

    public function shouting(): string
    {
        return Core\Str::upper($this->name);
    }
}

string $who = 'Ada';

echo 'Dear $who,', "\n";
echo "Dear $who,", "\n";

// Braces let you put a whole expression in the text. Anything that starts
// with a variable works: a key of an array, a property, or a method call.
array<string> $city = ['home' => 'Vienna'];
Guest $guest = new Guest();

echo "You are in $city[home] today.\n";
echo "Room for {$guest->name}, who signs as {$guest->shouting()}.\n";

// A brace with no variable after it is just a brace, and a backslash the
// language does not know keeps its backslash.
echo "{plain} and \q\n";
```

```output
Dear $who,
Dear Ada,
You are in Vienna today.
Room for Ada, who signs as ADA.
{plain} and \q
```

#### Example 03: a message to a customer

```nvs
<?nvs
// A confirmation message, written as one block with a heredoc. The text sits
// in the program the way it will look to the customer, and the values are
// filled in where they appear. The closing marker sets the indentation, so
// the lines can stay lined up with the code.

string $who = 'Ada';
int $order = 1042;
decimal $total = 24.90;
Core\Time\Duration $window = 2w;

echo <<<TEXT
    Hi $who,

    Order #$order is on its way. The total was $total euro.
    You can send it back within $window.

    Thank you!
    TEXT;
echo "\n";

// The second kind of heredoc quotes the marker, and then nothing is filled
// in. It is what you want for a template you hand to something else.
echo <<<'TEXT'
    Hi $who, your order #$order is on its way.
    TEXT;
echo "\n";
```

```output
Hi Ada,

Order #1042 is on its way. The total was 24.90 euro.
You can send it back within 2w.

Thank you!
Hi $who, your order #$order is on its way.
```

#### Example 04: an html template with a hole for any expression

```nvs
<?nvs
// A piece of a web page, written as an html template. The text between the
// backticks is written to the page as it is. Every hole is escaped, so a
// value cannot add a tag of its own.

class Shop
{
    public const string NAME = 'Kettle & Co';

    public static function price(int $cents): string
    {
        return Core\Str::format('%d.%02d €', $cents / 100, $cents % 100);
    }

    public static function badge(): Core\Html\Markup
    {
        return html`<span class="badge">new</span>`;
    }
}

// `{$name}` is a hole for a variable. It prints `&lt;b&gt;Ann&lt;/b&gt;`,
// so the `<b>` stays text on the page.
tainted string $name = '<b>Ann</b>';
echo html`<p>Welcome, {$name}</p>`, "\n";

// `<?= ... ?>` is a hole for any expression: a constant, a method call, a
// calculation. A `string` result is escaped, so the `&` prints as `&amp;`.
echo html`<h1><?= Shop::NAME ?></h1><p class="price"><?= Shop::price(5990) ?></p>`, "\n";

// A result of type `Core\Html\Markup` is written as it is, tags included.
bool $isNew = true;
echo html`<h2>Teapot <?= $isNew ? Shop::badge() : html`` ?></h2>`, "\n";

// Two fragments are joined with `+`. The result is one `Core\Html\Markup`.
Core\Html\Markup $page = html`<header><?= Shop::NAME ?></header>` + html`<main>{$name}</main>`;
echo $page, "\n";
```

```output
<p>Welcome, &lt;b&gt;Ann&lt;/b&gt;</p>
<h1>Kettle &amp; Co</h1><p class="price">59.90 €</p>
<h2>Teapot <span class="badge">new</span></h2>
<header>Kettle &amp; Co</header><main>&lt;b&gt;Ann&lt;/b&gt;</main>
```

#### Example 05: escapes in a double quoted string

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the escapes of a double-quoted string, and what is printed for each one.

// `\t` is a tab, `\"` is a quote, `\$` is a dollar sign and `\\` is one backslash.
string $who = 'Ada';
echo "tab[\t] quote[\"] dollar[\$who] backslash[\\]\n";

// `\101` (octal), `\x41` (hex) and `\u{41}` (a code point) all print `A`.
echo "oct[\101] hex[\x41] code point[\u{41}]\n";

// An escape the language does not know keeps its backslash, so this prints `\q`.
echo "unknown[\q]\n";

// In braces, any expression that starts with a variable is filled in. This prints `30`.
array<int> $n = [10, 20];
echo "sum {$n[0] + $n[1]}\n";
```

```output
tab[	] quote["] dollar[$who] backslash[\]
oct[A] hex[A] code point[A]
unknown[\q]
sum 30
```

#### Example 06: durations

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to write a length of time. A number followed by a unit is a `Core\Time\Duration`.

// Units can follow each other. `1h30m` is one hour and thirty minutes.
Core\Time\Duration $wait = 1h30m;
echo $wait, ' is ', $wait->toSeconds(), " seconds\n";

// The other units are `ns`, `us`, `ms`, `s`, `d` and `w`.
echo 250us->toNanoseconds(), ' ', 1d->toSeconds(), "\n";

// `compareTo` returns `0` when two durations are equal. `==` only checks for the same object.
echo $wait->compareTo(90m), "\n";
```

```output
1h30m is 5400 seconds
250000 86400
0
```

#### Example 07: markup joined with a dot

```nvs error
// This program does not compile.

```

```output
  --> main.nvs:7:13
  |

  = help: escaping is not idempotent, so text made out of a `Markup` is escaped a second time at the sink — write the markup to the sink directly, compose it with `+`, or say `Core\Html::toSource($markup, "why")` if the bytes really are what you want
```

### Widening without `as`

Some values are converted to a wider type without `as`. This happens when you assign a value, pass
an argument, return a value or put an element in an array.

An `int` or a `uint` is converted to a `float`. A value is converted to a nullable type, to a union
that contains its type, and to `mixed`. An object is converted to a parent class, to an interface its
class implements, and to `object`. A single-value type such as `"read"` is converted to `string`.

Only the conversion to `float` changes the value. It is checked while the program runs. A number
above 2^53 cannot be stored exactly in a `float`, so the program throws an `ArithmeticError`.

No other conversion happens without `as`. A `string` to a number, a number to a `string`, and an
`int` to a `uint` each need `as`.

**The examples below** show a whole number used as a `float`, the wider types, a price list with
both kinds of number, an anonymous object at a shape, and a program that assigns an `int` to a `uint`
and does not compile.

A number written in the code without a type takes the type of the place it goes to. It can be an
`int`, a `uint`, a `float` or a `decimal`. `decimal $d = 3;` and `array<float> $xs = [1, 2];` both
compile.

An `int` or a `uint` above 9007199254740992 (2^53) throws an `ArithmeticError` when it is converted
to a `float`. This is also true for a number that a `float` could store exactly, such as
9007199254740994.

A single-value type is converted to its base type. A `"read"|"write"` value is converted to `string`,
and a `true` value to `bool`.

These assignments each need `as` or a test that narrows the type. Without it, each is the error
`E0401`:

- an `int` to a `uint`, and a `uint` to an `int`
- a number to a `string`, and a `string` to a number
- a `float` to an `int`
- a `mixed` value to any other type
- a `?int` to an `int`. The help suggests `$value ?? 0`.

An anonymous object written at a shape type has its fields converted too. `{ x: 2 }` at `{ x: float }`
stores `2.0`. A shape value that already exists is not converted. A `{ x: int }` value at
`{ x: float }` is the error `E0401`. Build a new value instead: `{ x: $old->x }`.

#### Example 01: a whole number where a fraction is wanted

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows an `int` used where a `float` is needed, with no `as`. This works in an
// assignment, an argument, a return value and a calculation.

class Cart
{
    public static function withTax(float $amount): float
    {
        return $amount * 1.2;
    }

    public static function base(int $units): float
    {
        return $units;
    }
}

int $units = 3;

float $stored = $units;
echo $stored, "\n";

echo Cart::withTax($units), "\n";
echo Cart::base($units), "\n";

float $rate = 1.5;
echo $rate + $units, "\n";
```

```output
3
3.6
3
4.5
```

#### Example 02: into a place that holds more

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a value assigned to a wider type with no `as`: a nullable type, a union
// and `mixed`.

interface Sends
{
    public function send(): string;
}

class Email implements Sends
{
    public function send(): string
    {
        return 'sent by e-mail';
    }
}

class Invoice extends Email
{}

int $count = 3;

?int $optional = $count;
int|string $either = $count;
mixed $anything = $count;

echo $optional ?? 0, ' ', $either as string, ' ', $anything as string, "\n";

// An object is assigned to its parent class, to an interface its class
// implements, and to `object`.
Email $parent = new Invoice();
Sends $contract = new Invoice();
object $plain = new Invoice();

echo $parent->send(), "\n";
echo $contract->send(), "\n";
echo $plain is Email, "\n";
```

```output
3 3 3
sent by e-mail
sent by e-mail
1
```

#### Example 03: a price list that mixes both

```nvs
<?nvs
// A price list for a small shop. Some prices are whole numbers and some are not.
// A list with the type `array<float>` accepts both, and you do not write `as`.

// `var $prices = [4, 2.5, 3];` does not compile, because the values are `int` and `float`.
// So the type is written here.
array<float> $prices = [4, 2.5, 3];
var $total = 0.0;

foreach ($prices as var $price) {
    echo $price, "\n";
    $total = $total + $price;
}

echo 'total ', $total, "\n";
```

```output
4
2.5
3
total 9.5
```

#### Example 04: an anonymous object at a shape

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows that the fields of an anonymous object are converted to the types of the shape.

type Point = { x: float, y: float };

// `x` and `y` are written as whole numbers. They are stored as `float` values.
Point $p = { x: 2, y: 3 };
echo $p->x / 4, ' ', $p->y / 4, "\n";

// A function that returns the shape converts its fields the same way.
class Origin
{
    public static function point(): Point
    {
        return { x: 0, y: 1 };
    }
}

echo Origin::point()->y / 4, "\n";
```

```output
0.5 0.75
0.25
```

```nvs error

// This program does not compile.
// proof: compile-error

int $i = 3;
uint $u = $i;
```

```output

  --> main.nvs:7:11
  |
```

### The conversion operator `as`

Changing a value into another type is written one way in Novis: `as`, followed by the type you want.

A conversion gives a value of that type, or it throws an error. It never rounds, never drops a
fraction, and never uses a zero or an empty string instead. With `as ?int`, the result is `null` where the plain form would throw. Add `??` to
use a default value instead.

`as` also checks an object against a shape, such as `as Point`, and turns a class name into a class
reference with `as class<T>`.

**Good to know:** `as` converts only the value directly before it, so `$a + $b as float` converts
`$b` alone.

**The examples below** read numbers out of text from outside the program, add up an order total, and
skip a row that throws an error. Then they show which error each conversion throws and choose a class
by its name. The last two do not compile.

`as` can be written more than once: `$m as int as string` converts to `int` and then to `string`.

A conversion that fails while the program runs throws one of two errors. A number that does not fit
throws an `ArithmeticError`. These conversions throw it:

- a `float` or a `decimal` with a fraction to `int`
- a negative number to `uint`
- an `int` above 2^53 to `float`

Every other failure throws a `RuntimeError`.

Text converts to a number only when the whole text is one number. `" 42"`, `"42 "`, `""`, `"0x1A"`,
`"1_000"` and `"12.0"` all throw when converted to `int`. `"+5" as int` is `5`. `"1e3" as float` is
`1000`, and `".5"` and `"5."` are also valid `float` values. `"inf"` and `"NAN"` throw.

A `float` converts to `decimal` at the value it prints as. `0.1 as decimal` is `0.1`, not a long
binary fraction. A string converts to `decimal` the same way: `"1e3" as decimal` is `1000`.

`true as string` is `"1"`. `false as string` and `null as string` are `""`. A `bool` does not convert
to a number. `$b as int` is the error `E0708`, so write `$b ? 1 : 0`. Any value converts to `bool`
by the truthiness table: `"0"`, `""`, `0.0` and `null` are `false`.

`string as bytes` always works. `bytes as string` throws a `RuntimeError` when the bytes are not
valid UTF-8.

An enum case converts to `int` or `uint` and gives its number. `5 as Rank` throws a `RuntimeError`
when no case of `Rank` has the number `5`. An enum case does not convert to `string`.

A conversion between two types that has no rule is the error `E0708`, and the message names both
types. An `array`, `bytes` and an enum case to `string` are three of them.

A `mixed` value converts by the type of the value it contains. Text from a `mixed` value is
tainted: `$value as string` gives a `tainted string`.

`array<T> as array<U>` checks each element. An element must already be a `U`, or be a number that
widens to one, such as an `int` in an `array<float>`. The elements are not converted from text:
`["1", "2"] as array<int>` throws a `RuntimeError`.

`?int as int` throws a `RuntimeError` when the value is `null`. `$object as Foo` throws a
`RuntimeError` when the object is not a `Foo`.

A value converts to a set of allowed values, such as `"read"|"write"`, only when it equals one of
them. Otherwise it throws a `RuntimeError` that lists the allowed values.

`as ?T` is not allowed where `as T` cannot fail. `$i as ?int` on an `int` is the error `E0709`. A
class is not allowed either: `$o as ?Foo` is the error `E0473`, so use `$o is Foo`.

`as class<T>` checks a class name written in the code while the program compiles. That is
`Foo::class` or a string literal such as `'Shop\Dog'`. A name that is not a class is the error
`E0303`, and a class that is not a `T` is `E0708`. This is the same with `as ?class<T>`. Every
other string, including a class constant, is checked while the program runs. `as class<T>` then
throws a `RuntimeError`, and `as ?class<T>` gives `null`.

A class name in a string is always the full name with its namespace. No `namespace` and no `use`
applies to it. Inside `namespace Shop`, `"Dog" as ?class<Animal>` is `null`, and
`"Shop\Dog"` finds the class.

A `class<Dog>` converts to `class<Animal>` without a check when `Dog` extends `Animal`. Back from
`class<Animal>` to `class<Dog>`, the class it contains is checked, and the conversion throws a
`RuntimeError` when that class is not a `Dog`.

#### Example 01: numbers out of text that came from outside

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how `as` converts text from a file, a form or a command line to a number.
// The whole text must be a number.

array<string> $fields = ['12', '-4', '2.5', '19.90'];

int $units = $fields[0] as int;
int $adjustment = $fields[1] as int;
float $weight = $fields[2] as float;
decimal $price = $fields[3] as decimal;

echo $units + $adjustment, "\n";
echo $weight * 2, "\n";

// `as string` converts a number to text. A `decimal` keeps its two decimal places,
// so this prints `19.90`.
echo $price as string, "\n";
echo ($units as string) . ' units', "\n";
```

```output
8
5
19.90
12 units
```

#### Example 02: when the text might not be a number

```nvs
<?nvs
// Input from users is often not a valid number. `as ?int` converts text to a whole number.
// If that is not possible, the result is `null` and the program continues.
// Only "30" converts here. The other three give `null`.

array<string> $answers = ['30', 'thirty', '30.5', ''];

// `??` replaces `null` with a default value. Here the default is 14 days.
foreach ($answers as string $answer) {
    int $days = ($answer as ?int) ?? 14;
    echo 'a trial of ', $days, " days\n";
}

// To tell the user which answers were wrong, compare the result with `null` yourself.
foreach ($answers as string $answer) {
    if (($answer as ?int) == null) {
        echo "not a whole number: \"", $answer, "\"\n";
    }
}
```

```output
a trial of 30 days
a trial of 14 days
a trial of 14 days
a trial of 14 days
not a whole number: "thirty"
not a whole number: "30.5"
not a whole number: ""
```

#### Example 03: an order total read from a form

```nvs
<?nvs
// An order is sent as rows of text: a quantity and a price.
// `as uint` converts the quantity to a whole number that is not negative.
// `as decimal` converts the price to an exact amount of money.
// If a conversion fails, it throws an error. The program prints the row and skips it.

class Order
{
    public static function lineTotal(array<string> $row): decimal
    {
        uint $quantity = $row[0] as uint;
        decimal $price = $row[1] as decimal;

        // `as decimal` converts only `$quantity`, the value directly before it.
        // The result is then multiplied by `$price`.
        return $quantity as decimal * $price;
    }
}

array<array<string>> $rows = [
    ['3', '19.90'],
    ['1', '4.05'],
    ['two', '9.99'],
];

decimal $total = 0.00;

foreach ($rows as array<string> $row) {
    try {
        $total = $total + Order::lineTotal($row);
    } catch (RuntimeError $e) {
        echo 'left out a row whose quantity is not a number: ', $row[0], "\n";
    }
}

echo 'total ', $total as string, "\n";
```

```output
left out a row whose quantity is not a number: two
total 63.75
```

#### Example 04: which error a conversion throws

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the order in which `as` runs, and which error a failed conversion throws.

// `as` converts only the value directly before it. `7 / 2 as int` is `7 / (2 as int)`.
echo 7 / 2 as int, ' ', (7 / 2) as string, ' ', 1 + 2 as float, "\n";

string $digits = '42';
int $n = $digits as int;
echo $n + 1, ' ', '1e3' as float, ' ', 3.0 as int, "\n";

// `true` converts to "1". `false` and `null` convert to an empty string.
echo true as string, '|', false as string, '|', null as string, "|\n";

float $f = 3.9;
string $word = 'abc';
int $neg = -1;

// A number that does not fit throws an `ArithmeticError`.
try {
    echo $f as int, "\n";
} catch (ArithmeticError $e) {
    echo $e->message, "\n";
}
try {
    echo $neg as uint, "\n";
} catch (ArithmeticError $under) {
    echo $under->message, "\n";
}

// Text that is not a number throws a `RuntimeError`.
try {
    echo $word as int, "\n";
} catch (RuntimeError $text) {
    echo $text->message, "\n";
}

// `as ?int` gives `null` for each value that `as int` cannot convert.
echo ($word as ?int) ?? -1, ' ', ($f as ?int) ?? -1, ' ', ($digits as ?int) ?? -1, "\n";
```

```output
3.5 3.5 3
43 1000 3
1|||
cannot convert `float` 3.9 to `int`
cannot convert `int` -1 to `uint`
cannot convert string "abc" to `int`
-1 -1 42
```

#### Example 05: a class name read while the program runs

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how `as class<T>` turns a class name into a class reference.

class Animal
{
    public function speak(): string
    {
        return '...';
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal
{
    public function speak(): string
    {
        return 'woof';
    }
}

// `Dog::class` is checked while the program compiles.
class<Animal> $folded = Dog::class as class<Animal>;

// A name in a variable is checked while the program runs.
string $name = 'Dog';
class<Animal> $picked = $name as class<Animal>;
Animal $pet = new $picked();
echo $pet->speak(), ' ', ($pet is $folded) ? 'a Dog' : 'not', "\n";

// No class `Cat` exists, so the conversion throws a `RuntimeError`.
string $missing = 'Cat';
try {
    class<Animal> $bad = $missing as class<Animal>;
    echo (new $bad())->speak(), "\n";
} catch (RuntimeError $e) {
    echo $e->message, "\n";
}
```

```output
woof a Dog
cannot convert `Cat` to `class<Animal>`: it does not name a class that is a `Animal`
```

#### Example 06: a configured class with a default

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a class chosen by a setting, with a default class when the setting names no class.

interface Renders
{
    public static function extension(): string;
}

class CsvReport implements Renders
{
    public static function extension(): string
    {
        return 'csv';
    }
}

// The default is checked while the program compiles.
class<Renders> $fallback = 'CsvReport' as class<Renders>;

// No class `PdfReport` exists, so `as ?class<Renders>` gives `null`, and `??` uses the default.
string $setting = 'PdfReport';
class<Renders> $format = ($setting as ?class<Renders>) ?? $fallback;
echo $format::extension(), "\n";
```

```output
csv
```

#### Example 08: a conversion that cannot fail

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that `as ?int` is not allowed on a value that is already an `int`.
```
