### Calls

A call runs a method and returns the method's result.

You write the class or the object, the name of the method, and the arguments in brackets. You can
call a method on the result of a call directly. Arguments go in the order of the parameters. You can
also write them by name, in any order. A name also lets you leave out a parameter in the middle that
has a default. A variadic parameter, written `...$rest`, takes any number of arguments. `...$list`
at the call passes each value of an array as an argument. An `inout` parameter writes its new value
back to the variable you passed. You write `inout` at the call as well.

**Good to know:** you call a `callable` through the variable, the array element or the property
that contains it. Its arguments are checked when the program runs.

**The examples below** take these in turn: calling and chaining, naming the arguments you pass, and
pricing an order with the handler the customer chose. The last one shows each way to write a call in
one program.

The arguments run in the order they are written, also when they are named. In
`A::f(b: A::v(2), a: A::v(5))`, `A::v(2)` runs first.

A static method may also be called on an object: `$p->s()` calls the static method `s`. An
instance method called on the class, such as `P::i()`, is the error `E0778`. A method the class does
not have is the error `E0405`. On a nullable object, such as a `?P`, `$p->hi()` is the error `E0459`.
Use `$p?->hi()`, which gives `null` when `$p` is `null`.

`...$list` only fills a variadic parameter. Before a method with only fixed parameters, it is the
error `E0489`. Arguments may come before it, and several `...` arguments may follow each other:
`A::f(3, ...$xs)` and `A::f(...$xs, ...$xs)` both work. The type of the array must match the
variadic parameter, so an `array<string>` for `int ...$a` is the error `E0401`. The keys of the
array are kept: `["x" => 1, "y" => 2]` arrives with the keys `"x"` and `"y"`.

A call through a `callable` gives `mixed`. `int $r = $f(1)` is the error `E0401`, so write
`$f(1) as int`. The arguments are checked when the call runs. An argument of the wrong type throws a
`LogicError`: ``argument 1 to a `callable` must be of type int, string given``. Too few arguments
throw a `LogicError` too, and extra arguments are ignored.

A `callable` in a property needs brackets around it: `($this->cb)(1)`. Without them,
`$this->cb(1)` calls a method named `cb`, and is the error `E0405` when the class has none.

A call that returns `void` has no value. At an `int` variable it is the error `E0401`, and after
`echo` it is the error `E0707`.

#### Example 01: calling a method and chaining the result

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how a call is written and how calls chain. A static method is called
// on the class and an instance method on an object. You can call a method on
// the object that a call returns directly.

class Greeting
{
    public function constructor(private string $word)
    {}

    // Builds a greeting so the caller does not have to know the word for each
    // language.
    public static function in(string $language): Greeting
    {
        return new Greeting(match ($language) {
            'de' => 'Hallo',
            'fr' => 'Bonjour',
            default => 'Hello',
        });
    }

    public function to(string $name): string
    {
        return $this->word . ', ' . $name . '!';
    }
}

// The static call returns an object, and `->to` is called on it.
// This prints: Bonjour, Ada!
echo Greeting::in('fr')->to('Ada'), "\n";

// `new` chains in the same place, with no brackets around it.
// This prints: Hello, Bob!
echo new Greeting('Hello')->to('Bob'), "\n";

// When you need the object more than once, store it in a variable first.
// This prints: Hallo, Cem! Hallo, Dara!
Greeting $german = Greeting::in('de');
echo $german->to('Cem'), ' ', $german->to('Dara'), "\n";
```

```output
Bonjour, Ada!
Hello, Bob!
Hallo, Cem! Hallo, Dara!
```

#### Example 02: naming the arguments you pass

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the ways to write the arguments of a call: by position, by name in
// any order, and as an array passed to a method that takes any number of
// arguments.

class Ticket
{
    // The last two parameters have a default, so a caller may write one
    // argument or all three.
    public static function price(int $seats, int $each = 20, int $booking = 3): int
    {
        return $seats * $each + $booking;
    }

    // `...$prices` collects everything left over into one array.
    public static function cheapest(int ...$prices): int
    {
        int $best = 0;

        foreach ($prices as int $price) {
            if ($best == 0 || $price < $best) {
                $best = $price;
            }
        }

        return $best;
    }
}

// By position: the first argument is for the first parameter, and so on.
// This prints 43.
echo Ticket::price(2, 20, 3), "\n";

// By name, in any order. The parameter `each` in the middle is left out, so
// it has its default of 20. This prints 26.
echo Ticket::price(booking: 6, seats: 1), "\n";

// Any number of arguments. This prints 26.
echo Ticket::cheapest(43, 26, 33), "\n";

// `...` passes each value of an array as one argument. This prints 26.
array<int> $offers = [43, 26, 33];
echo Ticket::cheapest(...$offers), "\n";
```

```output
43
26
26
26
```

#### Example 03: pricing an order at checkout

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows calls doing the work of a checkout. The basket totals itself, and the
// shipping charge comes from the handler the customer chose. The running total
// is added up through a parameter that is written back. All amounts are in
// cents.

class Basket
{
    public function constructor(private array<int> $lines)
    {}

    public function goods(): int
    {
        int $total = 0;

        foreach ($this->lines as int $line) {
            $total = $total + $line;
        }

        return $total;
    }
}

class Checkout
{
    // `inout` writes the new value back into the caller's own variable, so
    // every step adds to the same total without assigning the result.
    public static function add(inout int $total, int $amount): void
    {
        $total = $total + $amount;
    }

    // Most callers take the standard rate, so it has a default and is named
    // at the call that needs a different one.
    public static function tax(int $amount, int $rate = 20): int
    {
        return Core\Math::intDiv($amount * $rate, 100);
    }
}

// One handler per shipping method, chosen by the name that arrives with the
// order. Each one is given the value of the goods and returns the charge.
array<callable> $shipping = [
    'standard' => fn(int $goods): int => $goods >= 5000 ? 0 : 495,
    'express' => fn(int $goods): int => 1295,
    'collect' => fn(int $goods): int => 0,
];

Basket $basket = new Basket([1299, 450, 2600]);
string $method = 'standard';

int $total = 0;
Checkout::add(inout $total, $basket->goods());
Checkout::add(inout $total, $shipping[$method]($basket->goods()) as int);
Checkout::add(inout $total, Checkout::tax($basket->goods()));

// This prints: goods 4349 shipping standard total 5713
echo 'goods ', $basket->goods(), ' shipping ', $method, ' total ', $total, "\n";

// The argument `rate: 5` sets a reduced tax rate. This prints: reduced total 5061
int $reduced = 0;
Checkout::add(inout $reduced, $basket->goods());
Checkout::add(inout $reduced, $shipping[$method]($basket->goods()) as int);
Checkout::add(inout $reduced, Checkout::tax($basket->goods(), rate: 5));
echo 'reduced total ', $reduced, "\n";
```

```output
goods 4349 shipping standard total 5713
reduced total 5061
```

#### Example 04: every way to write a call

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows each way to write a call: chained, named, variadic, `inout` and through a `callable`.

class Greeter
{
    public function constructor(private string $greeting)
    {}

    public function greet(string $name, string $mark = '!'): string
    {
        return $this->greeting . ', ' . $name . $mark;
    }

    public static function make(): Greeter
    {
        return new Greeter('Hi');
    }

    public static function sum(int ...$xs): int
    {
        int $t = 0;
        foreach ($xs as int $x) {
            $t += $x;
        }
        return $t;
    }

    public static function twice(inout int $n): void
    {
        $n = $n * 2;
    }
}

// A chained call, and named arguments in any order. This prints: Hi, Ada! Yo, Bob?
echo Greeter::make()->greet('Ada'), ' ', new Greeter('Yo')->greet(mark: '?', name: 'Bob'), "\n";

// `sum` takes any number of arguments, also none. `twice` changes `$n` to 8.
// This prints: 6 9 0 8
array<int> $xs = [4, 5];
int $n = 4;
Greeter::twice(inout $n);
echo Greeter::sum(1, 2, 3), ' ', Greeter::sum(...$xs), ' ', Greeter::sum(), ' ', $n, "\n";

// A `callable` in a variable, in an array element, and an anonymous function called directly.
// The extra argument `99` is ignored. This prints: 2 2 8 40
callable $f = fn(int $x): int => $x + 1;
array<callable> $ops = ['dbl' => fn(int $x): int => $x * 2];
echo $f(1), ' ', $f(1, 99), ' ', $ops['dbl'](4), ' ', (fn(int $x): int => $x * 10)(4), "\n";
```

```output
Hi, Ada! Yo, Bob?
6 9 0 8
2 2 8 40
```

### The pipeline operator

Passes a value through several steps, written from left to right in the order they run.

You write the value, then `|>`, then the step. Inside the step, `$_` is the place where the
value goes. Each step takes the result of the step before it. To trim a string and then convert it
to lower case, you write two steps.

Without `|>` you write one call inside another, and you read the steps from the inside to the
outside. Both forms do the same work, and `|>` adds no cost when the program runs.

**Good to know:** each step needs exactly one `$_`. A step with none, or with two, does not
compile. The right side of `|>` is the call itself, with `$_` in it.

**The examples below** clean up a form field in two steps, build a URL slug in five steps and
tidy a list of tags. Example 04 uses `|>` with other operators. Examples 05 and 06 do not compile.

The compiler replaces `$_` with the value on the left. So a pipeline has the same type, the same
errors and the same result as the nested calls it replaces. A `tainted string` stays tainted, and a
`?string` value on the left is the error `E0401` at a step that needs a `string`. The value on the
left runs once.

A step is a call, an array index, a property, a method call or an expression in brackets.
`$xs |> $_[1]`, `$p |> $_->name`, `4 |> $p->add($_)`, `2 |> self::f($_)` and `3 |> new Point($_)`
all work. For any other expression, write brackets around it: `$n |> ($_ * 2)`.

The step ends where the call, index or brackets end. In `$n |> $_ * 2`, the step is only `$_`, and
then the result is multiplied by 2. The result is the same here, but `$n |> 10 - $_` does not
compile: the step is `10`, which has no `$_`.

`$_` may be deep inside the step. `$s |> Core\Str::lower(Core\Str::trim($_))` works. So does a
second pipeline in an argument, or an anonymous function in an argument that uses `$_`.

These are the three errors:

- A step without `$_` is the error `E0129`. A method reference such as `Core\Str::upper` and an
  anonymous function are steps without `$_` too.
- A step with `$_` twice is the error `E0130`. Store the value in a variable first.
- `$_` anywhere else is the error `E0131`. This includes `$_` as a parameter name, and the second
  `$_` in `$n |> $_ * $_`.

`|>` runs after a prefix `-` and before every operator with two sides. `"a" . "b" |> Core\Str::upper($_)`
prints `aB`, and `$s ?? "d" |> Core\Str::upper($_)` is `$s ?? Core\Str::upper("d")`. `!` runs after
`|>`, so `!$a |> f($_)` is `!f($a)`.

#### Example 01: clean up a form field

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to clean up an email address from a signup form in two steps.
// `|>` gives the value on its left to the step on its right. `$_` is the place
// where the value goes. The steps run from left to right.
// The first address prints as ada@example.com.

array<string> $submitted = ['  Ada@Example.COM ', 'BOB@example.com', ' carol@Example.Com  '];

foreach ($submitted as string $raw) {
    string $email = $raw |> Core\Str::trim($_) |> Core\Str::lower($_);
    echo $email, "\n";
}
```

```output
ada@example.com
bob@example.com
carol@example.com
```

#### Example 02: make a url slug

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to make the slug for a URL from the title of an article, in five steps.
// Each step is on a line of its own, and the steps run from the top to the bottom.
// The first title prints as hello-world.

array<string> $titles = ['Hello World', '  Novis Ships 1.0  ', 'Web  Servers, Fast'];

foreach ($titles as string $title) {
    string $slug = $title
        |> Core\Str::trim($_)
        |> Core\Str::lower($_)
        |> Core\Str::replace($_, ',', '')
        |> Core\Str::replace($_, '  ', ' ')
        |> Core\Str::replace($_, ' ', '-');
    echo $slug, "\n";
}
```

```output
hello-world
novis-ships-1.0
web-servers-fast
```

#### Example 03: tidy a tag field

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to tidy the tags that a person typed into one form field, separated by commas.
// The steps split the text, trim each tag, delete the duplicates and sort the tags.

string $field = 'web, cli , web,  jit ,security';

array<string> $tags = $field
    |> Core\Str::split($_, ',')
    |> Core\Arr::map($_, fn(string $t): string => Core\Str::trim($t))
    |> Core\Arr::unique($_)
    |> Core\Arr::sort($_);

// `$tags` is a normal variable, so a new pipeline can start from it.
// This prints cli,jit,security,web and then 4 tags.
echo $tags |> Core\Str::join($_, ','), "\n";
echo $tags |> Core\Arr::count($_), " tags\n";
```

```output
cli,jit,security,web
4 tags
```

#### Example 04: pipelines beside other operators

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how `|>` works together with the operators around it.

string $s = '  Novis  ';
echo $s |> Core\Str::trim($_) |> Core\Str::lower($_), "\n";

// A prefix `-` runs first, so `Core\Math::abs` gets 7. `|>` runs before `>`,
// so the second value compares the length with 5. This prints 7 1.
int $n = -7;
echo -$n |> Core\Math::abs($_), ' ', $s |> Core\Str::length($_) > 5, "\n";

// The right side may be any expression in brackets. This prints a-b-c 10.
array<string> $xs = ['c', 'a', 'b'];
echo $xs |> Core\Arr::sort($_) |> Core\Str::join($_, '-'), ' ', 5 |> ($_ * 2), "\n";
```

```output
novis
7 1
a-b-c 10
```

### Anonymous functions

An anonymous function is a small function you write where you need it. You can keep it in a
variable, pass it to another call or store it in a list.

`fn` is the only way to write one. After the arrow comes one expression, whose value the function
returns, or a block in braces. Every parameter has a type. A block declares its return type.
The function copies each outside variable it uses when the function is written.

`$fn->bindTo($obj)` and `$fn->bind($obj)` return a copy that uses `$obj` as `$this`.
`$fn->call($obj, ...)` makes that copy and calls it. The object must be of the class the function
was written in, or a subclass. Any other object, or `null`, throws a `LogicError`.

**Good to know:** there is no `use (...)` list. A call through a `callable` returns `mixed`.

**The examples below** write functions, show captures and check a form.
Example 04 reads `$this`, 05 calls itself, and 06 does not compile.

These forms do not compile:

- `function (int $x) { … }` is the error `E0222`.
- `fn(int $x) use ($k) => …` is the error `E0223`.
- `static fn(…) => …` is the error `E0210`.
- An `inout` parameter is the error `E0493`, and `int &$x` is the error `E0237`.
- A parameter without a type is the error `E0808`.
- A block body without a return type is the error `E0450`.

With an expression body, the return type may be left out. The function then returns the type of the
expression. A value of the wrong type is the error `E0401` in an expression body, and the error
`E0403` after `return` in a block.

A captured variable is a copy. The function may change its copy, and the outside variable keeps its
value. Each call starts again from the value that was captured: a function that adds 1 to its copy
of `$k = 1` returns `2` on every call. An object is not copied. A function that captured `$b` reads
a property of `$b` that changed after the function was written.

A function cannot use the variable it is stored in. In `callable $f = fn(…) => … $f(…) …`, the inner
`$f` is the error `E0301`, because `$f` has no value yet. Give the function a name instead:
`fn fact(int $n): int => …` can call `fact(…)`. The call is checked against the function's
parameters and return type. Outside the function, `fact` is the error `E0320`.

`$this` outside a method, or inside a `static` method, is the error `E0779`.

A method reference names a method without calling it. `Core\Str::length`, `self::f` and
`static::f` each give a callable. On an object, write `(...)` in place of the arguments:
`$p->add(...)`. A method that does not exist is the error `E0405`.

`bindTo`, `bind` and `call` can throw a `LogicError` for the wrong object. Its message starts
``this callable uses `$this`, so it can only be bound to an object of class `A` ``. A function that does not use `$this` is returned unchanged, so any object works. A second
argument is the error `E0402`.

An anonymous function can be called where it is written: `(fn(int $x): int => $x * 10)(4)` gives
`40`.

#### Example 01: writing a small function where you need it

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the two ways to write an anonymous function. After the arrow comes
// either one expression, whose value the function returns, or a block in braces
// that runs several lines and returns.

// One expression. The result is the value of `$x + 1`.
callable $next = fn(int $x): int => $x + 1;

// A block, for work that takes more than one line. A block says what it
// returns; only the one-expression form may leave the type out.
callable $total = fn(array<int> $amounts): int => {
    int $sum = 0;

    foreach ($amounts as int $amount) {
        $sum = $sum + $amount;
    }

    return $sum;
};

// An anonymous function is called through its variable. The call returns `mixed`,
// so write `as` to say which type you are reading. This prints 8 12.
array<int> $prices = [3, 4, 5];
echo $next(7) as int, ' ', $total($prices) as int, "\n";

// An anonymous function is a value, so you can pass it directly to a call.
// This prints: BAG,BOX
array<string> $names = ['bag', 'box'];
array<mixed> $shouted = Core\Arr::map($names, fn(string $name) => Core\Str::upper($name));
echo Core\Str::join($shouted as array<string>, ','), "\n";
```

```output
8 12
BAG,BOX
```

#### Example 02: what an anonymous function captures

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows what an anonymous function captures. It copies every outside variable it
// uses when the function is written. Changing that variable afterwards does not
// change what the function reads.

string $greeting = 'Hello';
callable $greet = fn(string $name): string => $greeting . ', ' . $name;

// The variable changes. The copy inside the function stays the same.
// This prints: Hello, Ada
$greeting = 'Goodbye';
echo $greet('Ada') as string, "\n";

// One anonymous function per round, each with that round's number. This prints 0,1,2
array<callable> $labels = [];
int $round = 0;

while ($round < 3) {
    $labels = Core\Arr::append($labels, fn(): string => $round as string);
    $round = $round + 1;
}

// `$label()` returns `mixed`, and `as string` converts it to a `tainted string`.
// So the array has the type `array<tainted string>`.
array<tainted string> $printed = [];

foreach ($labels as callable $label) {
    $printed = Core\Arr::append($printed, $label() as string);
}

echo Core\Str::join($printed, ','), "\n";

class Discount
{
    public function constructor(private int $percent)
    {}

    // Inside a method the object is captured too, so the function reads the
    // property through it. This returns a callable the caller can keep.
    public function rule(): callable
    {
        return fn(int $price): int => $price - Core\Math::intDiv($price * $this->percent, 100);
    }
}

// The callable still has the discount, wherever it is used.
// This prints 900 450
Discount $tenth = new Discount(10);
callable $apply = $tenth->rule();
echo $apply(1000) as int, ' ', $apply(500) as int, "\n";
```

```output
Hello, Ada
0,1,2
900 450
```

#### Example 03: checking a form with one rule per field

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a common use of anonymous functions. One rule per field is kept in an
// array. Each rule is an anonymous function that returns the message for a bad
// value. The same loop then checks any form, so adding a field is adding a line.

class Form
{
    // Each rule gets the value of its field. It returns an empty string when
    // the value is fine.
    public static function check(array<string> $values, array<callable> $rules): array<tainted string>
    {
        array<tainted string> $problems = [];

        foreach ($rules as string $field => callable $rule) {
            tainted string $message = $rule($values[$field] ?? '') as string;

            if ($message != '') {
                $problems = Core\Arr::append($problems, $field . ': ' . $message);
            }
        }

        return $problems;
    }
}

// The shortest length is written once and carried into the rule that uses it.
int $shortest = 8;

array<callable> $rules = [
    'name' => fn(string $value): string => $value == '' ? 'please give a name' : '',
    'email' => fn(string $value): string => Core\Str::contains($value, '@') ? '' : 'needs an @',
    'password' => fn(string $value): string =>
        Core\Str::length($value) < $shortest ? 'needs ' . $shortest . ' characters' : '',
];

array<string> $filled = [
    'name' => 'Ada',
    'email' => 'ada@example.com',
    'password' => 'correct horse',
];

// Nothing is wrong with this one, so the list of problems is empty.
// This prints: filled in: 0 problem(s)
echo 'filled in: ', Core\Arr::count(Form::check($filled, $rules)), " problem(s)\n";

array<string> $empty = [
    'name' => '',
    'email' => 'ada.example.com',
    'password' => 'short',
];

// This prints one line per field that failed its rule.
foreach (Form::check($empty, $rules) as tainted string $problem) {
    echo $problem, "\n";
}
```

```output
filled in: 0 problem(s)
name: please give a name
email: needs an @
password: needs 8 characters
```

#### Example 04: a function that reads this

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows an anonymous function that reads `$this`, one that captures a variable,
// and one with a block body.

class Counter
{
    public int $base = 10;

    // Inside a method, the function can read `$this`.
    public function adder(): callable
    {
        return fn(int $x): int => $this->base + $x;
    }
}

// The function copies `$prefix` when it is written, so it still uses "one".
string $prefix = 'one';
callable $tag = fn(string $s): string => $prefix . ':' . $s;
$prefix = 'two';

callable $sum = fn(array<int> $xs): int => {
    int $t = 0;
    foreach ($xs as int $x) {
        $t += $x;
    }
    return $t;
};

// This prints one:x 6 15.
array<int> $ns = [1, 2, 3];
Counter $c = new Counter();
echo $tag('x'), ' ', $sum($ns), ' ', $c->adder()(5), "\n";
```

```output
one:x 6 15
```

#### Example 05: a function that calls itself

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows an anonymous function that calls itself. Its name comes after `fn`,
// and the name works only inside the function.

callable $factorial = fn fact(int $n): int => $n <= 1 ? 1 : $n * fact($n - 1);

// The name also works with a block body.
callable $fib = fn fib(int $n): int => {
    if ($n <= 1) {
        return $n;
    }
    return fib($n - 1) + fib($n - 2);
};

// This prints 120 55.
echo $factorial(5), ' ', $fib(10), "\n";
```

```output
120 55
```

#### Example 06: the function keyword

```nvs error

// Shows that `function` does not make an anonymous function. Write `fn` instead.
// proof: compile-error

callable $f = function (int $x): int { return $x + 1; };
```

### Arrays in expressions

An array is a list of values, or a table where every value has a name.

You write an array as `[10, 20]` or `["city" => "Graz"]`. `var $prices = [10, 20]` takes the type
from the values, so `$prices` is an `array<int>`. An empty array, or one whose values have different
types, needs the type written: `array<int> $prices = []`. `$prices[] = 30` adds a value at the end.
Every key is text, so `$prices[8]` and `$prices["8"]` are one entry. Reading a key that is not there
throws a `RuntimeError`. Write `$prices["milk"] ?? 0` where a missing key is normal.

**Good to know:** an array is a value. Assigning, passing or returning it gives a copy, so a change
on one side is never seen on the other.

**The examples below** build a list and a price table, read missing keys and group rows.
Example 04 shows keys, spread and nested arrays, 05 destructuring, and 06 does
not compile.

`var $a = [];` is the error `E0414`, because an empty array has no values to take a type from.
`var $a = [1, "x"];` is `E0414` too. Its help names the type to write: `array<int|string>`.

A key is an `int`, a `uint` or a `string`. A `float`, `bool` or `null` key is the error `E0434`.
`"08"` and `"8"` are two different keys.

`$a[] = 1` uses the largest whole-number key plus one, and a negative key counts too. In an empty
array, after `$a[-5] = 1;` the next key is `-4`. `unset` does not number the keys again, so after
`[10, 20, 30]` loses key `1`, the next `$a[]` gets key `3`. `$a[]` can only be written to. Reading
it is the error `E0481`.

`[...$a, 30]` copies the entries of `$a` into the new array. A whole-number key, such as `"5"` or
`"-3"`, gets the next number of the new array. Every other key is kept. When two entries have the same key, the later
one wins: `["k" => 5, ...$a, "k" => 7]` has one `k`, and it is `7`. The values of `$a` must fit the
new array's type. An `array<int>` spread into an `array<string>` is the error `E0401`.

A write into a key that is not there creates every inner array on the way:
`$g["a"]["b"]["c"] = 1;` works on an empty `$g`. A read does not. `$g["a"]["b"]` throws a
`RuntimeError` for the first key that is missing: `undefined array key `a``. `??` and `isset` test
every level, so `isset($g["a"]["b"])` is `false`. `isset` is also `false` for a key whose value is
`null`.

`unset($a["k"])` does nothing when the key is not there. It also works on an inner array:
`unset($g["r"]["0"])`.

A function result is not stored anywhere, so `A::f()["k"] = 1;` is the error `E0700`. Assign the
result to a variable first.

Destructuring reads by key, not by order. `[int $a] = $p;` reads key `"0"`, wherever it is in `$p`.
Entries that no variable names are skipped, and a missing key throws `undefined array key`. A
positional variable and a `"key" =>` variable can be mixed, and a key can be a variable:
`[$k => int $v] = $row;`.

Each variable in a destructuring needs its type. `[$a, $b] = $p;` is the error `E0101`, and
`[var $a] = $p;` is the error `E0102`. Each type must match the array's value type, or it is the
error `E0401`. The right side must be an `array<T>`. A `mixed` or a `?array<int>` value is the error
`E0482`. A `foreach` variable cannot be a destructuring pattern, which is the error `E0101`.
`list($a, $b) = $p;` is the error `E0230`.

#### Example 01: a shopping list and a price table

```nvs
<?nvs
// Builds a shopping list and a table of prices, then reads both back.

// `var` takes the type from the values. Every value is a string, so
// `$basket` is an `array<string>`.
var $basket = ['bread', 'milk'];
// `$basket[] = ...` adds a value at the end. Its key is the next number.
$basket[] = 'coffee';

foreach ($basket as string $position => string $item) {
    echo $position, ': ', $item, "\n";
}

// You can also write the type yourself. `[...$basket]` copies every value
// of the list into the new list.
array<string> $withGift = [...$basket, 'flowers'];
echo Core\Arr::count($withGift), " items\n";

// A table gives every value a name you choose. Every value is an `int`, so
// `$prices` is an `array<int>`.
var $prices = ['bread' => 250, 'milk' => 120];
$prices['coffee'] = 890;
echo 'milk costs ', $prices['milk'], " cents\n";

// An empty array has no values to take a type from, so its type is written.
array<int> $discounts = [];
$discounts['milk'] = 20;
echo 'milk costs ', $prices['milk'] - $discounts['milk'], " cents on sale\n";

// Every key is text. `$shelf[8]` and `$shelf["8"]` are the same entry, so a
// number used as a key always finds the value you stored under it.
var $shelf = [8 => 'tea'];
echo $shelf['8'], "\n";
```

```output
0: bread
1: milk
2: coffee
4 items
milk costs 120 cents
milk costs 100 cents on sale
tea
```

#### Example 02: keys that may be missing

```nvs
<?nvs
// Reads settings where a key may be missing. Reading a key that is not
// there throws an error, so this shows the two safe ways to ask for one.

var $settings = ['theme' => 'dark', 'language' => 'de'];

// `??` gives the value on the right when the key is missing.
echo $settings['theme'] ?? 'light', "\n";
echo $settings['timezone'] ?? 'UTC', "\n";

// `isset` tells you whether a key is there.
if (isset($settings['timezone'])) {
    echo "a timezone is set\n";
} else {
    echo "no timezone is set\n";
}

// `unset` removes one entry. Every other entry keeps its key.
unset($settings['language']);
echo Core\Arr::count($settings), " setting left\n";

// Without a guard the missing key throws a `RuntimeError`, which you can catch.
try {
    echo $settings['language'], "\n";
} catch (RuntimeError $e) {
    echo $e->message, "\n";
}
```

```output
dark
UTC
no timezone is set
1 setting left
undefined array key `language`
```

#### Example 03: grouping orders for a report

```nvs
<?nvs
// Groups orders by country and adds up what each country spent, the way a
// small report does. Writing into a key that is not there yet creates the
// inner array for you.

// Every order is an `array<string>`, so `var` makes `$orders` an
// `array<array<string>>`.
var $orders = [
    ['country' => 'AT', 'total' => '42'],
    ['country' => 'DE', 'total' => '17'],
    ['country' => 'AT', 'total' => '8'],
];

// The report starts empty, so its type is written out.
array<array<string>> $byCountry = [];

foreach ($orders as string $position => array<string> $order) {
    // Destructuring reads two keys of one order into two variables.
    ['country' => string $country, 'total' => string $total] = $order;

    // The first order of a country creates the list under its name.
    $byCountry[$country][] = $total;
}

foreach ($byCountry as string $country => array<string> $totals) {
    uint $sum = 0;
    foreach ($totals as string $index => string $amount) {
        $sum = $sum + ($amount as uint);
    }
    echo $country, ': orders ', Core\Arr::count($totals), ', total ', $sum, "\n";
}
```

```output
AT: orders 2, total 50
DE: orders 1, total 17
```

#### Example 04: keys spread and nested arrays

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how keys are numbered, how a spread copies entries, and how a write
// creates an inner array.

array<int> $a = [10, 20];
$a[] = 30;
$a['k'] = 40;
$a[-5] = 50;

// The largest whole-number key is `2`, so this value gets key `3`.
$a[] = 60;
foreach ($a as string $k => int $v) {
    echo $k, ':', $v, ' ';
}
echo "\n";

// The spread numbers `-5` again, and keeps `k`. This prints `7 40`.
array<int> $b = [...$a, 'j' => 70];
echo Core\Arr::count($b), ' ', $b['k'], "\n";

// `unset` removes one entry. `$a[0]` and `$a["1"]` still work, so this
// prints `5 30`.
unset($a['k']);
echo Core\Arr::count($a), ' ', $a[0] + $a['1'], "\n";

// This write creates the inner array under `r`.
array<array<int>> $g = [];
$g['r']['c'] = 1;
$g['r'][] = 2;
echo Core\Json::encode($g), "\n";

// `??` covers both keys, so this prints `9`.
echo $g['x']['y'] ?? 9, "\n";
```

```output
0:10 1:20 2:30 k:40 -5:50 3:60
7 40
5 30
{"r":{"c":1,"0":2}}
9
```

#### Example 05: destructuring a pair a row and points

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows destructuring: reading the entries of an array into variables.

array<int> $pair = [1, 2];
[int $a, int $b] = $pair;

// An empty place skips an entry. `$second` is `2`.
[, int $second] = $pair;
echo $a, ' ', $b, ' ', $second, "\n";

// A key on the left reads that key, in any order.
array<string> $row = ['id' => '7', 'name' => 'ada'];
['name' => string $name, 'id' => string $id] = $row;
echo $id, ' ', $name, "\n";

// A pattern inside a pattern reads an inner array.
array<array<int>> $points = [[1, 2], [3, 4]];
[[int $x1, int $y1], [int $x2, int $y2]] = $points;
echo $x1, $y1, $x2, $y2, "\n";

// A missing key throws a `RuntimeError`.
try {
    [int $one, int $two, int $three] = $pair;
    echo $three, "\n";
} catch (RuntimeError $e) {
    echo $e->message, "\n";
}
```

```output
1 2 2
7 ada
1234
undefined array key `2`
```

#### Example 06: list does not exist

```nvs error

// Write `[int $a, int $b] = $pair;` instead.
// proof: compile-error

list(int $a, int $b) = $pair;
```

```output
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ use `[...]` instead — it is the only destructuring spelling Novis keeps
  = help: the elements are written the same way inside `[...]`
```

### Anonymous objects

An anonymous object is an object with exactly the fields you write. You do not declare a class for
it.

You write it as `{ x: 1, y: 2 }` and read or change a field with `$point->x`. Its type is the shape
`{ x: int, y: int }`, and a `type` alias gives that shape a short name. Any object with at least those
fields fits where the shape is needed. So two parts of a program work together when they name the
same fields.
A field that may be missing is written `label?: string`, and `??` gives a value for the times it is
not there.

**Good to know:** an object is a handle and not a value. Two variables can name one object, and `==`
checks whether they do. It does not compare the fields, so two anonymous objects with equal values are
never equal.

**The examples below** build a point and change it, then pass shapes into a method and back out,
then return the result of a check as an object. Example 04 returns an object from an anonymous
function, and example 05 does not compile.

A field name is a plain name with no quotes. `{"x": 1}` is the error `E0101`, and so is
`{...$p, y: 2}`, because there is no spread for an object. A comma after the last field is allowed,
and `{}` is an object with no fields. A field name written twice is the error `E0494`.

At the start of a statement and directly after the `=>` of an anonymous function, `{` starts a
block. An anonymous object there is the error `E0117`. Write it in parentheses: `({ x: 1 });` and
`fn(int $x): Point => ({ x: $x, y: 0 })`.

The type of a field does not change. `$p->x = "a";` on `{ x: 1 }` is the error `E0401`. A
field with another anonymous object in it, or a function, is allowed. Call that function as
`($p->f)(1)`. `$p->f(1)` is the error `E0477`, because an anonymous object has no methods.

Reading a field the object does not have compiles, and throws a `RuntimeError` when it runs:
`` `$shape{x}` has no field `y` ``. A field written `b?: int` is optional. Reading it when it is not
there throws the same error, so read it with `$r->b ?? 0`. `isset($r->b)` is `false` when it is not
there.

An object of a class fits a shape when it has public properties with those names and types.
`$v is Point` checks every field and its type when the program runs.
`$v as Point` runs the same check. If the check fails, it throws a `RuntimeError`.

`clone $p` gives a new object with the same fields, so `$p == clone $p` is `false`.
`Core\Json::encode($p)` writes the fields sorted by name. `echo $p` compiles, and throws a
`RuntimeError` when it runs, because an anonymous object has no string form.

#### Example 01: a point and what holds it

```nvs
<?nvs
// Builds a small object with the fields you name, then reads and changes
// them.

type Point = { x: int, y: int };

Point $start = { x: 1, y: 2 };
// A field is read and written with `->`.
echo $start->x, ',', $start->y, "\n";
$start->x = 10;
echo $start->x, "\n";

// `var` works out the type of an anonymous object for you, and a field can
// contain another anonymous object.
var $marker = { label: 'home', at: { x: 3, y: 4 } };
echo $marker->label, ' at ', $marker->at->x, ',', $marker->at->y, "\n";

// An object is a handle. Both variables name the same object here, so the
// change is visible through both of them.
Point $alias = $start;
$alias->y = 99;
echo $start->y, "\n";

// `==` checks whether two variables name one object. It does not compare the
// fields, so these two are different even with equal values.
Point $twin = { x: 10, y: 99 };
if ($start == $twin) {
    echo "one object\n";
} else {
    echo "two objects\n";
}
```

```output
1,2
10
home at 3,4
99
two objects
```

#### Example 02: a shape as an input and a result

```nvs
<?nvs
// Uses a named shape as the type of what a method takes and of what it
// returns. Any object with at least those fields fits.

type Money = { amount: int, currency: string };

class Prices
{
    // The parameter takes any object that has these two fields.
    public static function format(Money $price): string
    {
        return ($price->amount as string) . ' ' . $price->currency;
    }

    // A shape is also a return type, and the anonymous object is the result.
    public static function double(Money $price): Money
    {
        return { amount: $price->amount * 2, currency: $price->currency };
    }
}

Money $coffee = { amount: 350, currency: 'EUR' };
echo Prices::format($coffee), "\n";
echo Prices::format(Prices::double($coffee)), "\n";

// This object has a third field. It still fits, because it has the two
// fields the shape needs.
var $line = { amount: 120, currency: 'EUR', note: 'milk' };
echo Prices::format($line), "\n";
```

```output
350 EUR
700 EUR
120 EUR
```

#### Example 03: the result of a check

```nvs
<?nvs
// Returns the result of a check as an object and turns it into JSON, the
// way a small web handler does.

type Result = { ok: bool, message: string, code?: int };

class Signup
{
    public static function check(string $email): Result
    {
        if (Core\Str::contains($email, '@')) {
            return { ok: true, message: 'welcome' };
        }

        return { ok: false, message: 'that is not an email address', code: 422 };
    }
}

array<string> $tried = ['ada@example.com', 'ada'];

foreach ($tried as string $position => string $email) {
    Result $result = Signup::check($email);

    // `code` is written `code?: int`, so it may be missing. `??` gives a
    // value for the times it is not there.
    echo $result->message, ' (', $result->code ?? 200, ")\n";
    echo Core\Json::encode($result), "\n";
}
```

```output
welcome (200)
{"message":"welcome","ok":true}
that is not an email address (422)
{"code":422,"message":"that is not an email address","ok":false}
```

#### Example 04: an object from an anonymous function

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows an anonymous function that returns an anonymous object.

type Point = { x: int, y: int };

// After `=>`, a `{` starts a block. The parentheses make it an object.
var $onXAxis = fn(int $x): Point => ({ x: $x, y: 0 });

Point $p = $onXAxis(5);
$p->y = 7;
echo $p->x + $p->y, "\n";

// Each call creates a new object, so `==` gives `false` here.
Point $q = $onXAxis(5);
echo ($p == $p) ? 'same' : 'different', ' ', ($p == $q) ? 'same' : 'different', "\n";
```

```output
12
same different
```

#### Example 05: an object at the start of a statement

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that a `{` at the start of a statement starts a block, so this
// program does not compile. Write `({ x: 1 });` instead.
// proof: compile-error

{ x: 1 };
```

```output
error[E0117]: an anonymous object here is ambiguous with a block
  --> main.nvs:6:1
  |
6 | { x: 1 };
  | ^^^^^^^^ `{` already means a block in this position
  = help: wrap it in parentheses: `({...})`

error: aborting due to 1 error
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```

### Refused in expression position

Some ways of writing code that PHP allows do not exist in Novis. Writing one is a compile error.

The list is `eval`, `extract`, `settype`, `compact` and the other free functions, variable variables
such as `$$name` and `${$expr}`, `list(...)`, casts such as `(int)$x`, the `@` sign, `=&`,
backticks, `die`, `include` and `require_once`, `yield` used as a value, and `self`, `static` or
`parent` written outside a class. Each error but the backtick's names what to write instead: a
method under `Core` for a free function, `as` for a conversion, `[...]` for taking a list apart,
`require` for reading another file, and `exit` for ending a program.

**Good to know:** you meet all of these when you compile, never while the program is running.

**The examples below** show the three replacements you need most often: a `Core` method in place of
a free function, `as` in place of a cast, and `[...]` in place of `list(...)`. The last example shows
the error for a variable variable.

Each form below is a compile error with its own code. The help line of the error names what to
write instead.

- `eval(…)` is `E0201`. Put the code in a file and `require` it, or run it with `spawn script`.
- `extract($a)` is `E0205`. Use destructuring, or read each key.
- `settype($x, "int")` is `E0208`. Convert into a new variable with `as`.
- `compact(…)`, `strlen(…)` and every other free function is `E0320`. Use a `Core` method such as
  `Core\Str::length($s)`.
- `$$name` and `${$expr}` are `E0202`. Use an `array<T>` with a key for each name.
- `list($a, $b) = $p;` is `E0230`. Write `[int $a, int $b] = $p;`.
- `(int)$x` and the other casts are `E0225`. Write `$x as int`.
- `@$a["k"]` is `E0236`. Catch the error with `try` and `catch`.
- `$b =& $a;` is `E0701`. Write `$b = $a;`, which copies the value.
- `die` is `E0228`. Write `exit`.
- `include` and `require_once` are `E0221`. Write `require`.
- In a generator, a `yield` whose value is used, such as `mixed $x = yield 1;`, is `E0448`. Write `yield 1;` as a
  statement of its own.
- `self`, `static` and `parent` outside a class are `E0303`. This is the same for `self::X`,
  `static::$x`, `parent::f()` and `new self()`. Write the class name.

A backtick is the one form with no replacement. `` echo `ls`; `` is the error `E0001`, an unexpected
character, and its message names nothing else. To run another program, use `Core\Process::run` with
the path and an array of arguments.

#### Example 01: a core method in place of a php function

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the `Core` methods that replace PHP's free functions. In Novis
// every built-in is a method on a class, so `strtoupper($s)` is written
// `Core\Str::upper($s)`.

use Core\Str;

array<string> $names = ['ada lovelace', 'grace hopper'];

foreach ($names as string $name) {
    // `Str::upper` returns the text in capitals, and `Str::length` returns the
    // number of characters. The first line prints `ADA LOVELACE (12)`.
    echo Str::upper($name), ' (', Str::length($name), ")\n";
}

// `Str::replace` puts one text in place of another. This prints
// `grace-hopper`.
echo Str::replace('grace hopper', ' ', '-'), "\n";
```

```output
ADA LOVELACE (12)
GRACE HOPPER (12)
grace-hopper
```

#### Example 02: as in place of a cast

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `as`, the one way to convert a value in Novis. PHP writes `(int)$x`
// or `settype($x, "int")`; neither exists here, and both are replaced by this
// one syntax.

string $typed = '42';

// `as int` converts the text to a whole number, and the result goes into a new
// variable. This prints `44`.
int $age = $typed as int;
echo $age + 2, "\n";

// A conversion that cannot work throws an error. `as ?int` returns `null`
// instead, so you can test the result. This prints `not a number`.
?int $maybe = "twelve o'clock" as ?int;
echo $maybe ?? 'not a number', "\n";

// `as` never changes the variable it reads. `$typed` is still the text it was
// given, so this prints `42`.
echo $typed, "\n";
```

```output
44
not a number
42
```

#### Example 03: reading a row into variables

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to read the parts of a row into variables, the way a program does
// when it imports a file. PHP offers `list(...)`, `extract` and `$$name` for
// this; Novis has `[...]` for a list and an array you index by name.

array<string> $line = ['2026-09-19', 'ada@example.com', '19.99'];

// `[...]` on the left takes the elements in order, one variable each. This
// prints the three values on one line.
[string $date, string $email, string $amount] = $line;
echo $date, ' ', $email, ' ', $amount, "\n";

array<string> $form = ['email' => 'grace@example.com', 'country' => 'US'];

// A row whose parts have names is an array with string keys. You read the key
// you want, and `??` gives a value for a key that is not there.
echo $form['email'], "\n";
echo $form['phone'] ?? 'no phone given', "\n";

// The key can come from a variable. This replaces a variable variable such as
// `$$name`, and the result still has a type: here it is a `string`.
string $wanted = 'country';
echo $form[$wanted], "\n";
```

```output
2026-09-19 ada@example.com 19.99
grace@example.com
no phone given
US
```

#### Example 04: a variable variable

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that a variable variable such as `$$name` does not exist, so this
// program does not compile. Use an array with a key for each name instead.
// proof: compile-error

string $name = "value";
string $value = "x";
echo $$name;
```

```output
error[E0202]: variable variables (`$$name` / `${expr}`) are not supported
  --> main.nvs:8:6
  |
8 | echo $$name;
  |      ^^^^^^ defeats name resolution and type inference
  = help: use an explicit `array<T>` instead — its keys are `string`, so one entry per name

error: aborting due to 1 error
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```

<a id="lang-statements"></a>
## A.4 Statements and control flow

Keywords: statement, block, scope, definite assignment, if, elseif, else if, else, endif, alternative syntax, while, endwhile, do while, for, foreach, endforeach, as, key, value, inout, by reference, Iterator, Iterable, switch, case, default, fallthrough, break, continue, break 2, continue 2, levels, return, catch, echo, print, unset, exit, yield, goto, label, declare, global, static variable

### Expression statements, blocks and declarations

A statement is one step of a program. Most statements are an expression followed by `;`: a call, an
assignment, an `echo`. The value is thrown away, and the work still happens. A `;` on its own is an
empty statement.

A declaration is a statement too. Write the type, or write `var` and the type comes from the value.
A variable belongs to the whole function, so each name is declared once.

Braces `{ … }` group statements into a block. A block does not open a new scope. You may read a
variable only where every path has given it a value. A variable assigned in one branch of an `if`
is readable after the `if` when every branch assigns it.

**The examples below** show the statements, a variable declared before its value is
known, and a program that prices an order. The last one reads a variable that only one branch
declares, and does not compile.

A variable is declared once in a function. A second declaration of the same name does not compile: it
is the error `E0406`. This is also true inside a block, and for the variable of a second `for` loop.

A declaration inside a loop body is one statement. It runs on every round of the loop, and it gives the
variable its first value again each time.

A variable declared inside one branch of an `if` has no value on the other paths. Reading it after the
`if` does not compile: it is the error `E0301`.

#### Example 01: the statements a program is made of

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the kinds of statement a program is made of: a declaration, an
// assignment, a call written for what it does, and an empty statement.

class Report
{
    // Prints one line and returns how many characters it printed.
    public static function line(string $text): uint
    {
        echo $text, "\n";
        return Core\Str::length($text);
    }
}

// A declaration is a statement. It gives `$total` a type and a first value.
int $total = 0;

// An assignment followed by `;` is a statement.
$total = $total + 7;

// This call is a statement. The program runs it for what it prints, and the
// number it returns is thrown away.
Report::line('counted');

// A `;` on its own is an empty statement. It does nothing.
;

// This prints 7.
echo $total, "\n";
```

```output
counted
7
```

#### Example 02: declaring a variable before its value is known

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the two ways to declare a variable, and how to declare one before you
// know its value.

// A declaration names the type. `$attempts` is a whole number from here on.
int $attempts = 3;

// `var` takes the type from the value on the right, so `$service` is a string.
var $service = 'payments';

// You can declare a variable without a value. You may read it only after every
// path has given it one, so both branches below assign it.
string $plan;
if ($attempts > 1) {
    $plan = 'retry';
} else {
    $plan = 'give up';
}

// Braces group statements into a block. A block does not open a new scope, so
// `$wait` is still there after the closing brace.
{
    int $wait = $attempts * 2;
}

// This prints: payments: retry after 6 seconds
echo $service, ': ', $plan, ' after ', $wait, " seconds\n";
```

```output
payments: retry after 6 seconds
```

#### Example 03: pricing an order step by step

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows these statements in a program that prices an order: a variable
// declared before its price is known, a call written for what it records, and
// a block that groups one step.

class Audit
{
    // Writes one line about a decision and returns whether it was written.
    public static function note(string $text): bool
    {
        echo 'audit: ', $text, "\n";
        return true;
    }
}

array<int> $order = ['items' => 4, 'weight' => 1200];

// The shipping price is not known yet. Every branch below gives it a value, so
// it can be read after the `if`.
int $shipping;
if ($order['weight'] > 1000) {
    $shipping = 900;
    // The result of this call is thrown away. The line is still written.
    Audit::note('heavy parcel');
} elseif ($order['items'] > 3) {
    $shipping = 400;
    Audit::note('more than three items');
} else {
    $shipping = 250;
}

// The block groups the discount step. `$discount` can be read after it,
// because a block does not open a new scope.
{
    int $discount = 0;
    if ($shipping > 500) {
        $discount = 100;
    }
}

// This prints 800.
echo $shipping - $discount, "\n";
```

```output
audit: heavy parcel
800
```

#### Example 04: a variable declared in one branch cannot be read after it

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that a variable declared in one branch of an `if` cannot be read after
// the `if`. When `$flag` is false, `$x` has no value, so this program does not
// compile.
// proof: compile-error

bool $flag = true;
if ($flag) {
    int $x = 1;
}
echo $x;
```

```output
error[E0301]: `$x` is read before any assignment reaches it
   --> main.nvs:11:6
   |
11 | echo $x;
   |      ^^ not definitely assigned here

error: aborting due to 1 error
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```

### `if`, `elseif`, `else`

`if` runs a block of code when its condition is true. `else` gives the block that runs when it is
not. `elseif` adds a further condition to test in between. You may write `else if` instead, and the
two are the same.

The arms are tested from top to bottom, and only the first one whose condition is true runs. `else`
comes last and takes everything the arms above it did not.

The condition is any expression, and it does not have to be a `bool`. The value is read as a
condition: `0`, `0.0`, `""`, `"0"`, `[]`, `null` and `false` count as false, and every other value
counts as true.

A body of one statement needs no braces. `if ($n > 1) echo "big\n";` is allowed. Braces around every
body are still the safer habit.

**The examples below** show a chain that picks one arm, then conditions that are not `bool` values,
then a shipping price worked out from several rules in order.

#### Example 01: picking one arm of a chain

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows an `if`/`elseif`/`else` chain. The arms are tested from top to bottom,
// and only the first one whose condition is true runs.

class Band
{
    public static function of(int $score): string
    {
        if ($score >= 90) {
            return 'excellent';
        } elseif ($score >= 75) {
            return 'good';
        } elseif ($score >= 50) {
            return 'pass';
        } else {
            return 'fail';
        }
    }
}

array<int> $scores = [95, 80, 60, 20];

foreach ($scores as int $score) {
    // This prints one line per score: 95 excellent, 80 good, 60 pass, 20 fail.
    echo $score, ' ', Band::of($score), "\n";
}
```

```output
95 excellent
80 good
60 pass
20 fail
```

#### Example 02: a condition that is not a bool

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows conditions that are not `bool` values. The value is read as a
// condition, so an empty array, an empty string and the number 0 are false.

array<string> $names = [];
if ($names) {
    echo "there are names\n";
} else {
    // This line runs. An empty array counts as false.
    echo "no names yet\n";
}

int $unread = 0;
if ($unread) {
    echo "you have unread messages\n";
} else {
    // This line runs. The number 0 counts as false.
    echo "your inbox is empty\n";
}

// The text "0" counts as false as well. Test the length when you mean
// "this text is not empty".
string $answer = '0';
if ($answer) {
    echo "the answer counts as true\n";
} elseif (Core\Str::length($answer) > 0) {
    // This line runs.
    echo "the answer is not empty, and it still counts as false\n";
}
```

```output
no names yet
your inbox is empty
the answer is not empty, and it still counts as false
```

#### Example 03: working out a shipping price

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows several rules tested in order, the way a program works out a price.
// The first rule that fits decides, so the order of the arms is part of the
// rules. Prices here are in cents.

class Shipping
{
    public static function priceFor(string $country, int $grams, bool $isMember): int
    {
        if ($isMember && $grams <= 2000) {
            return 0;
        } elseif ($country != 'DE') {
            return 1490;
        } elseif ($grams > 10000) {
            return 990;
        } elseif ($grams > 2000) {
            return 590;
        }
        return 390;
    }
}

// This prints 0. The member rule is first, so it wins over every rule below it.
echo Shipping::priceFor('DE', 800, true), "\n";
// This prints 1490. A parcel outside Germany takes the same price at any weight.
echo Shipping::priceFor('FR', 800, false), "\n";
// This prints 990.
echo Shipping::priceFor('DE', 12000, false), "\n";
// This prints 390. No arm matched, so the line after the chain decides.
echo Shipping::priceFor('DE', 800, false), "\n";
```

```output
0
1490
990
390
```

### `while` and `do … while`

`while (condition) { … }` runs its body again and again for as long as the condition is true. The
condition is tested first, so a condition that is false at the start means the body never runs.

`do { … } while (condition);` runs the body first and tests the condition afterwards. The body
therefore always runs at least once. Note the semicolon after the closing bracket.

`break` leaves the loop. `continue` skips the rest of the body and goes to the next test. In a
`do … while` loop, `continue` goes to the test at the bottom, and does not restart the body.

The condition is read the same way an `if` condition is. It does not have to be a `bool`.

Use `while` when you do not know how many rounds you need, such as reading until nothing is left.
Use a `for` or a `foreach` loop when you are counting or walking a collection.

**The examples below** show a `while` loop that drains a queue of work, then a `do … while` loop
that always runs once, then a retry that stops on success or after a limit.

#### Example 01: working through a list until it is empty

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a `while` loop. The condition is tested before every round, including
// the first one, so a list that is already empty means no round at all.

class Queue
{
    public static function drain(array<string> $jobs): int
    {
        int $done = 0;
        int $at = 0;
        while ($at < Core\Arr::count($jobs)) {
            echo 'running ', $jobs[$at as string], "\n";
            $done = $done + 1;
            $at = $at + 1;
        }
        return $done;
    }
}

array<string> $jobs = ['backup', 'send mail', 'clean up'];
// This prints one line per job, then 3.
echo Queue::drain($jobs), "\n";

array<string> $none = [];
// This prints 0. The condition was false at the start, so the body never ran.
echo Queue::drain($none), "\n";
```

```output
running backup
running send mail
running clean up
3
0
```

#### Example 02: asking once before testing anything

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `do … while`. The body runs before the condition is tested, so it
// always runs at least once. Note the semicolon after the closing bracket.

// A page of results is fetched, and another page only while a full one came
// back. The first page is always fetched.
class Pages
{
    public static function sizeOf(int $page): int
    {
        if ($page < 3) {
            return 100;
        }
        return 12;
    }
}

int $page = 1;
int $rows = 0;
int $size = 0;
do {
    $size = Pages::sizeOf($page);
    $rows = $rows + $size;
    echo 'page ', $page, ' gave ', $size, " rows\n";
    $page = $page + 1;
} while ($size == 100);

// This prints 212.
echo $rows, "\n";

// The same loop written with `while` would fetch nothing here, because the
// condition is false from the start.
int $count = 0;
do {
    $count = $count + 1;
} while (false);
// This prints 1.
echo $count, "\n";
```

```output
page 1 gave 100 rows
page 2 gave 100 rows
page 3 gave 12 rows
212
1
```

#### Example 03: trying again until it works or the limit is reached

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a `while` loop with two ways to end: the work succeeded, or the limit
// was reached. A program does this around a call that sometimes fails.

class Upload
{
    // Fails on the first two attempts and succeeds on the third.
    public static function send(int $attempt): bool
    {
        return $attempt >= 3;
    }
}

int $attempt = 0;
bool $sent = false;

while ($sent == false && $attempt < 5) {
    $attempt = $attempt + 1;
    $sent = Upload::send($attempt);
    if ($sent) {
        echo 'sent on attempt ', $attempt, "\n";
    } else {
        echo 'attempt ', $attempt, " failed\n";
    }
}

if ($sent == false) {
    echo 'gave up after ', $attempt, " attempts\n";
}

// This prints 3.
echo $attempt, "\n";
```

```output
attempt 1 failed
attempt 2 failed
sent on attempt 3
3
```

### `for`

A `for` loop counts. Its header has three parts, separated by semicolons: where the counter starts,
how long the loop runs, and how the counter changes after every round. `for (var $i = 0; $i < 10;
$i++)` runs the body while `$i` is below 10.

The first part is either one new variable, or assignments to variables declared above the loop. The
second and third parts may each be a list separated by commas. Any part may be empty, and `for (;;)`
runs until a `break`.

The counter belongs to the function, not to the loop. After the loop, it has the value that ended
it. A second loop in the same function needs a different name. `continue` runs the third part before
the next test.

**The examples below** show a `var` counter, two counters that meet in the middle, `uint` counters,
a `for (;;)` loop, and a header that does not compile.

The first part of the header declares one variable at most. `for (int $a = 0, int $b = 0; …)` is
the error `E0125`. Declare the second variable above the loop.

The first part is either one declaration or a list of expressions. It cannot have both. `for (var $i
= 0, $j = 1; …)` is the error `E0124`.

The second part can be a list separated by commas. Before each test, the loop runs every expression
in the list. The last expression decides if the loop runs again. The expressions before it also run
on the test that ends the loop.

Two loops in one function cannot declare the same counter. The second declaration is the error
`E0406`.

#### Example 01: numbering every line of a list

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the three parts of a `for` header: where the counter starts, how long
// the loop runs, and how the counter changes after every round.

var $steps = ['unpack the archive', 'check the files', 'install'];

// `var $i = 0` declares the counter. It is an `int`, the type of `0`.
for (var $i = 0; $i < Core\Arr::count($steps); $i++) {
    // The counter is also the position in the array.
    echo $i + 1, '. ', $steps[$i], "\n";
}

// You can read the counter after the loop. It holds the value that ended the
// loop, so this prints 3.
echo $i, "\n";
```

```output
1. unpack the archive
2. check the files
3. install
3
```

#### Example 02: walking a list from both ends

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a loop with two counters. The first and the third part of the header
// are lists separated by commas, so both counters start and move together.

array<string> $names = ['Ada', 'Grace', 'Alan', 'Edsger'];

uint $front = 0;
uint $back = 0;

for ($front = 0, $back = Core\Arr::count($names) - 1; $front < $back; $front++, $back--) {
    string $keep = $names[$front];
    $names[$front] = $names[$back];
    $names[$back] = $keep;
}

// The counters meet in the middle, and every pair has changed places. This
// prints ["Edsger","Alan","Grace","Ada"].
echo Core\Json::encode($names), "\n";
```

```output
["Edsger","Alan","Grace","Ada"]
```

#### Example 03: sending rows in batches

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a counter that moves by more than one. A program does this to send a
// long list in batches, because one request per row would be too many requests.

class Store
{
    // Writes one batch and returns how many rows it held.
    public static function write(array<int> $rows): uint
    {
        echo 'writing ', Core\Json::encode($rows), "\n";
        return Core\Arr::count($rows);
    }
}

array<int> $ids = [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17];
uint $total = Core\Arr::count($ids);
uint $written = 0;

// The counters write their type, `uint`, in place of `var`. A `uint` is never
// negative, and neither is a position in a list.
for (uint $start = 0; $start < $total; $start = $start + 3) {
    array<int> $batch = [];
    // The inner loop stops at the end of the batch or at the end of the list,
    // whichever comes first.
    for (uint $at = $start; $at < $start + 3 && $at < $total; $at++) {
        $batch[] = $ids[$at];
    }
    $written = $written + Store::write($batch);
}

// Seven rows do not divide into batches of three, so the last batch is
// shorter. This prints 7.
echo $written, "\n";
```

```output
writing [11,12,13]
writing [14,15,16]
writing [17]
7
```

#### Example 04: a loop that ends with break

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a `for` loop with an empty header. `for (;;)` has no test, so only
// `break` ends it.

int $tries = 0;

for (;;) {
    $tries++;
    echo 'try ', $tries, "\n";
    if ($tries == 3) {
        break;
    }
}

// The loop ran three times. This prints 3.
echo $tries, "\n";
```

```output
try 1
try 2
try 3
3
```

#### Example 05: the header declares one variable

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that the first part of a `for` header declares one variable at most.
// This header declares two, so this program does not compile.
// proof: compile-error

for (int $row = 0, int $column = 0; $row < 3; $row++) {
    echo $row, "\n";
}
```

```output
error[E0125]: a `for` init clause declares at most one binding
  --> main.nvs:6:20
  |
6 | for (int $row = 0, int $column = 0; $row < 3; $row++) {
  |                    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ this is the second declaration
  = help: declare the second variable above the loop. The variable can be used in the whole function either way

error: aborting due to 1 error
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```

### `foreach`

`foreach` visits every element of an array, a generator or any object you can iterate. Write
`foreach ($subject as var $value)`, and the body runs once for each element.

`var` gives the variable the type of the subject's values. Over an array you may get the key too,
with `var $key => var $value`. The key is always a `string`. You can write the type in place of
`var`, as in `string $key => int $value`, and the compiler checks it. A variable with neither does
not compile.

The value variable is a copy. With `inout`, as in `foreach ($rows as inout var $row)`, each element
goes back into the array when the body ends. The syntax `&$value` does not compile. A plain
loop walks a copy of the array, so adding or removing elements in the body does not change what
it visits.

**The examples below** show values, then keys with values, then `inout`, each with `var` first and
a written type after. Then come a loop over what a function returns, a generator, a wider type, and
two loops that do not compile.

One header can use `var` for one variable and a written type for the other. A variable without
either is the error `E0101`.

`var` on the value keeps every qualifier of the element type. Over an `array<tainted string>`, the
value variable is a `tainted string`.

A written type can be wider than the element type. Write `int|float $v` over an `array<int>` if the
body stores a `float` in `$v`. The compiler checks that each element fits the written type.

A generator, an `Iterator<T>` and an `Iterable<T>` give values of type `T` and have no key. A key
variable over one of them is the error `E0444`.

The word `as` in the header belongs to `foreach`. To convert the subject, put the conversion in
parentheses: `foreach (($m as array<int>) as var $v)`. A `mixed` subject without a conversion is the
error `E0443`.

An array literal can be the subject when the value variable uses `var`. All its elements need the
same type. Elements of different types are the error `E0414`, and so is an empty array `[]`. With a
written type, an array literal does not compile. Put it in a typed variable first.

An `inout` loop walks the array itself. An element that the body adds at the end is visited too.

A later `foreach` in the same function can declare the same variable again with the same type. With
another type, the second declaration is the error `E0406`.

#### Example 01: adding up the values of an array

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the simplest `foreach`. The body runs once for each element of the array.

var $lineTotals = ['shirt' => 1990, 'socks' => 450, 'belt' => 2500];
var $sum = 0;

// `var $cents` gets the type of the array's values, so `$cents` is an `int`.
foreach ($lineTotals as var $cents) {
    $sum = $sum + $cents;
}

// This prints 4940. Prices here are in cents.
echo $sum, "\n";

// The array can also be written in the loop header. All its values are strings,
// so `$tag` is a `string`.
foreach (['new', 'sale', 'last one'] as var $tag) {
    echo '[', $tag, '] ';
}
echo "\n";

// You can write the type in place of `var`. The compiler checks that the array
// contains that type, and the reader sees the type in the loop header.
int $largest = 0;
foreach ($lineTotals as int $cents) {
    if ($cents > $largest) {
        $largest = $cents;
    }
}

// This prints 2500.
echo $largest, "\n";
```

```output
4940
[new] [sale] [last one]
2500
```

#### Example 02: reading the key with the value

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the key form of `foreach`. Write `$key => $value` to get both. With `var`,
// the key is a `string` and the value has the type of the array's values.

var $stock = ['shirt' => 4, 'socks' => 0, 'belt' => 12];

foreach ($stock as var $item => var $left) {
    if ($left == 0) {
        echo $item, ": out of stock\n";
    } else {
        echo $item, ': ', $left, " left\n";
    }
}

// You can write both types instead. An array key is always a `string`, even when
// it looks like a number.
array<string> $byId = ['1' => 'Ada', '2' => 'Grace'];
foreach ($byId as string $id => string $name) {
    // This prints: id 1 is Ada, then id 2 is Grace.
    echo 'id ', $id, ' is ', $name, "\n";
}
```

```output
shirt: 4 left
socks: out of stock
belt: 12 left
id 1 is Ada
id 2 is Grace
```

#### Example 03: correcting every row in place

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `inout`, which writes the value back into the array. A program does
// this to clean up a table of input before it stores or sends the table.

var $form = [
    'name' => '  Ada Lovelace ',
    'city' => 'London  ',
    'note' => '',
];

// `inout var $field` is a `string`, because every value in `$form` is a string.
foreach ($form as inout var $field) {
    $field = Core\Str::trim($field);
}

// This prints: {"name":"Ada Lovelace","city":"London","note":""}
echo Core\Json::encode($form), "\n";

// This loop writes the type `int` in place of `var`. Without `inout`, the
// variable is a copy, and the array keeps its values.
array<int> $counts = ['a' => 1, 'b' => 2];
foreach ($counts as int $copy) {
    $copy = $copy * 100;
}
// This prints: {"a":1,"b":2}
echo Core\Json::encode($counts), "\n";
```

```output
{"name":"Ada Lovelace","city":"London","note":""}
{"a":1,"b":2}
```

#### Example 04: walking what a function returns

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `var` over the result of a function call. The loop variable gets its type
// from the function, so the type is not written anywhere in this file.

var $order = "2 x coffee\n1 x filter\n\n3 x mug\n";
var $count = 0;

// `Core\Str::lines` returns an array of strings, so `$line` is a `string`.
foreach (Core\Str::lines($order) as var $line) {
    if (Core\Str::isEmpty($line)) {
        continue;
    }
    $count++;
    echo $count, '. ', $line, "\n";
}

// The empty line is skipped, so this prints 3.
echo $count, "\n";
```

```output
1. 2 x coffee
2. 1 x filter
3. 3 x mug
3
```

#### Example 05: walking a generator

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `foreach` over a generator. The function returns an `Iterator<int>`,
// so `$page` is an `int`. A generator has no keys.

class Pages
{
    // Gives the numbers from 1 to `$last`, one at a time.
    public static function upTo(int $last): Iterator<int>
    {
        int $page = 1;
        while ($page <= $last) {
            yield $page;
            $page++;
        }
    }
}

foreach (Pages::upTo(3) as int $page) {
    echo 'page ', $page, "\n";
}
```

```output
page 1
page 2
page 3
```

#### Example 06: a wider type and a converted subject

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a loop variable with a wider type than the array, and a subject that
// is converted in the header.

var $prices = ['apple' => 3, 'pear' => 8];

// The values are `int`, but the body stores a `float` in `$amount`.
// So the variable needs the type `int|float`.
foreach ($prices as string $name => int|float $amount) {
    if ($amount > 6) {
        $amount = $amount * 0.25;
    }
    // This prints apple=3, then pear=2.
    echo $name, '=', $amount, "\n";
}

// `$data` is `mixed`, so the loop converts it first. The conversion needs
// parentheses, because `as` also separates the subject from the variable.
mixed $data = [7, 8];
foreach (($data as array<int>) as var $n) {
    echo $n, "\n";
}
```

```output
apple=3
pear=2
7
8
```

#### Example 07: the variable needs a type

