### `switch`

`switch (value) { … }` compares one value with a list of labels and runs the body of the first label
that is equal to it. Each label is written as `case something:`, and `default:` is what runs when no
label matched. Nothing happens when no label matched and there is no `default`.

A body runs on into the next body until a `break` stops it. That is called falling through, and it
lets several labels share one body: write them one under the other, with nothing in between. A body
that ends with `return` also leaves the `switch`.

The labels are tried in the order you wrote them, and `default` is tried last wherever you put it.
`switch (true)` compares against `true`, so every label is a condition, and the first condition that
is true is the one that runs.

**The examples below** show a choice between three answers, then labels that share a body, then
`switch (true)` sorting a number into bands, then a `default` between two labels.

`switch` compares the value with each label using `==`. A label whose type can never be equal to the
value is the error `E0466`. An `int` value with the label `"5"` is one such case.

A body falls through into the body written after it, even when that is `default`. `default` is
still tried last, after every `case`. When it matches, the bodies after it run too, until a
`break`.

#### Example 01: choosing one answer out of several

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a `switch` that picks one answer out of several. The subject is
// compared with each `case` in order, and `default` runs when none matched.

array<string> $statuses = ['new', 'sent', 'lost'];

foreach ($statuses as string $status) {
    string $text = '';
    switch ($status) {
        case 'new':
            $text = 'waiting to be packed';
            break;
        case 'sent':
            $text = 'on its way';
            break;
        default:
            $text = 'we do not know';
    }
    echo $status, ': ', $text, "\n";
}
```

```output
new: waiting to be packed
sent: on its way
lost: we do not know
```

#### Example 02: two labels that share one body

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows labels that share a body, and a body without `break`. A body without
// `break` runs on into the next body, which is called falling through.

array<string> $keys = ['a', 's', 'q'];

foreach ($keys as string $key) {
    echo $key, ': ';
    switch ($key) {
        case 'a':
        case 's':
            echo 'saving';
            break;
        case 'q':
            echo 'saving, ';
        // There is no `break` here, so the next body runs as well.
        default:
            echo 'leaving';
    }
    echo "\n";
}
```

```output
a: saving
s: saving
q: saving, leaving
```

#### Example 03: sorting a number into bands

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `switch (true)`, which tests one condition after another and runs the
// first one that is true. A program does this to sort a number into bands.

class Shipping
{
    public static function band(uint $grams): string
    {
        switch (true) {
            case $grams <= 500:
                return 'letter';
            case $grams <= 2000:
                return 'small parcel';
            case $grams <= 20000:
                return 'parcel';
            default:
                return 'freight';
        }
    }
}

array<uint> $weights = [120, 1500, 9000, 45000];

foreach ($weights as uint $grams) {
    // This prints letter, small parcel, parcel and freight, one per line.
    echo $grams, 'g: ', Shipping::band($grams), "\n";
}
```

```output
120g: letter
1500g: small parcel
9000g: parcel
45000g: freight
```

#### Example 04: a default in the middle

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a `default` written between two labels. It is still tried last, and
// it falls through into the body after it.

array<int> $codes = [1, 2, 9];

foreach ($codes as int $code) {
    echo $code, ': ';
    switch ($code) {
        case 1:
            echo 'one, ';
        default:
            echo 'other, ';
        case 2:
            echo 'two';
    }
    echo "\n";
}

// This prints "1: one, other, two", then "2: two", then "9: other, two".
```

```output
1: one, other, two
2: two
9: other, two
```

### `break` and `continue`

`break` stops a loop immediately. `continue` skips the rest of the current iteration and starts the
next one.

Both act on the loop closest to them. Inside a `switch`, `break` leaves the `switch`, and a plain
`continue` starts the next iteration of the loop around it, because a `switch` has no iterations of
its own.

Write a number after either word to leave more than one level at once. `break 2` leaves the loop
around the loop you are in. Levels count from 1 at the closest statement, and every loop and every
`switch` is one level. The number has to be written directly in the code, so a variable is not
allowed there.

**Good to know:** a level with no matching loop or `switch` does not compile. A wrong number is an
error you see before the program runs.

**The examples below** take these in turn: a search that stops at the first match, a loop that skips
the rows it does not want, and an order check that leaves two loops at once. The last two show a
`switch` inside a loop, and a `continue` that does not compile.

Inside a `switch` that is inside a loop, `continue`, `continue 1` and `continue 2` do the same thing.
Each one starts the next iteration of the loop.

`break 1` is the same as `break`, and `continue 1` is the same as `continue`. The smallest level is 1,
so `break 0` does not compile.

These programs do not compile, because no statement matches the level:

- `break` or `continue` outside any loop or `switch`.
- `continue` inside a `switch` with no loop around it.
- `break 3` inside only one loop.

#### Example 01: stopping a search at the first match

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how `break` stops a loop as soon as the work is done. This loop looks
// for the first reading above 100 and stops there.

array<int> $readings = [12, 40, 96, 140, 3, 220];

int $found = 0;
foreach ($readings as int $reading) {
    if ($reading > 100) {
        $found = $reading;
        break;
    }
    echo 'checked ', $reading, "\n";
}

// The loop stopped at 140 and never read the two values after it.
// This prints 140.
echo 'first above 100: ', $found, "\n";
```

```output
checked 12
checked 40
checked 96
first above 100: 140
```

#### Example 02: skipping the rows you do not want

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how `continue` skips the rest of one iteration and starts the next
// one. This loop greets every name in the list and skips the empty entries.

array<string> $names = ['Ada', '', 'Grace', '   ', 'Alan'];

int $greeted = 0;
foreach ($names as string $name) {
    // `Core\Str::trim` removes the spaces at both ends of the text.
    string $clean = Core\Str::trim($name);
    if ($clean == '') {
        continue;
    }
    $greeted = $greeted + 1;
    echo 'hello ', $clean, "\n";
}

// Two of the five entries were skipped, so this prints 3.
echo $greeted, " greeted\n";
```

```output
hello Ada
hello Grace
hello Alan
3 greeted
```

#### Example 03: leaving two loops at once in an order check

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `continue 2` and `break 2`, which act on the second level out. Level 1
// is the inner loop and level 2 is the outer one. A shop checks its orders for
// one product, and an order holding a `pen` is not shipped at all.

class Order
{
    public function constructor(public string $id, public array<string> $items)
    {}
}

array<Order> $orders = [
    new Order('A-1', ['book', 'pen', 'lamp']),
    new Order('A-2', ['cup', 'mug']),
    new Order('A-3', ['ring', 'box']),
];

string $wanted = 'ring';
string $foundIn = '';

foreach ($orders as Order $order) {
    echo 'order ', $order->id, "\n";
    foreach ($order->items as string $item) {
        if ($item == 'pen') {
            // `continue 2` starts the outer loop's next iteration, so the rest
            // of this order and the line after the inner loop are both skipped.
            echo "  holds a pen, skipping this order\n";
            continue 2;
        }
        if ($item == $wanted) {
            $foundIn = $order->id;
            // `break 2` leaves both loops, so the `box` after it is never read.
            break 2;
        }
        echo '  ', $item, "\n";
    }
    echo "  order checked\n";
}

// This prints A-3.
echo 'found in ', $foundIn, "\n";
```

```output
order A-1
  book
  holds a pen, skipping this order
order A-2
  cup
  mug
  order checked
order A-3
found in A-3
```

#### Example 04: a switch inside a loop

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `break` and `continue` inside a `switch` that is inside a loop.
// This log printer skips debug lines and marks errors.

array<string> $levels = ['info', 'debug', 'error', 'info'];
array<string> $messages = ['started', 'cache is warm', 'disk is full', 'stopped'];

for (int $i = 0; $i < 4; $i++) {
    switch ($levels[$i]) {
        case 'debug':
            // `continue` starts the next line, so the `echo` below does not run.
            continue;
        case 'error':
            echo '!! ';
            // `break` leaves only the `switch`. The message below is still printed.
            break;
        default:
            echo '   ';
    }
    echo $messages[$i], "\n";
}
```

```output
   started
!! disk is full
   stopped
```

#### Example 05: continue needs a loop

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that `continue` needs a loop around it. A `switch` alone is not
// enough, so this program does not compile.
// proof: compile-error

string $command = 'skip';

switch ($command) {
    case 'skip':
        continue;
}
```

```output
error[E0475]: `continue` is not inside a loop
   --> main.nvs:10:9
   |
10 |         continue;
   |         ^^^^^^^^^ no enclosing loop to leave

error: aborting due to 1 error
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```

### `return`

`return $value;` leaves the method it is in and gives the value to whoever called the method. The
lines after it do not run, and neither does the rest of any loop it is inside. A method may have as
many `return` statements as you need, and the first one that runs ends the method.

The value has to fit the return type the method declares. A method declared `void` gives nothing
back, so its `return` carries no value and is written `return;` alone. Writing a value there does
not compile.

`return` also works outside any method, at the top level of a file. There it ends the file. In the
file you started, that ends the program.

**The examples below** show a method that returns as soon as it has found what it was looking for,
then a `void` method that ends early, then a program that stops because it has nothing to do. The
last one shows a `void` method with a value in its `return`, which does not compile.

A method with a return type other than `void` needs a value in every `return`. In such a method,
`return;` alone does not compile.

Every way through such a method has to end with a `return` or a `throw`. If one way reaches the end of
the method body, the program does not compile.

A file that another file loads with `require` can end with `return $value;` at its top level. The
`require` expression then gives that value.

#### Example 01: giving a value back to the caller

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `return`, which leaves a method and gives a value back to the caller.
// The first `return` that runs ends the method, so the loop stops there.

class Basket
{
    // Gives the first price over the limit, or 0 when there is none.
    public static function firstOver(array<int> $prices, int $limit): int
    {
        foreach ($prices as int $price) {
            if ($price > $limit) {
                return $price;
            }
        }
        return 0;
    }
}

array<int> $prices = [300, 1200, 4500];

// This prints 1200. The method ends at the first price over 1000, so 4500 is
// never looked at.
echo Basket::firstOver($prices, 1000), "\n";

// This prints 0. No price is over 9000, so the last line of the method runs.
echo Basket::firstOver($prices, 9000), "\n";
```

```output
1200
0
```

#### Example 02: leaving a method that has no value

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `return;` with no value. A `void` method gives nothing back, so its
// `return` carries no value, and it is how such a method ends early.

class Mailer
{
    public static function send(string $address, string $text): void
    {
        if ($address == '') {
            echo "no address, nothing sent\n";
            return;
        }

        echo 'sent to ', $address, ': ', $text, "\n";
    }
}

// The first call ends at the `return`, so it prints one line about the missing
// address. The second call prints the message it sent.
Mailer::send('', 'your order is on its way');
Mailer::send('ada@example.com', 'your order is on its way');
```

```output
no address, nothing sent
sent to ada@example.com: your order is on its way
```

#### Example 03: ending a program that has nothing to do

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `return` outside any method, which ends the file. In the file you
// started, that ends the program. A script does this when it has no work.

array<string> $jobs = [];

if (Core\Arr::count($jobs) == 0) {
    echo "nothing to do\n";
    return;
}

// This line never runs, because the `return` above ended the program.
echo 'running ', Core\Arr::count($jobs), " jobs\n";
```

```output
nothing to do
```

#### Example 04: a void method cannot return a value

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that a `void` method cannot return a value. This `return` has a
// value, so this program does not compile.
// proof: compile-error

class Counter
{
    public static function reset(): void
    {
        return 0;
    }
}

Counter::reset();
```

```output
error[E0403]: this method declares `void` but returns `int`
   --> main.nvs:10:16
   |
10 |         return 0;
   |                ^ this is `int`

error: aborting due to 1 error
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```

### `catch` as an expression

`catch` written after an expression gives that expression a value to fall back on when it throws an
error. It saves writing a whole `try` block for one value.

Write the expression, then `catch (SomeError $e) => fallback`. If the expression runs normally, its
own value is the result. If it throws an error the arm matches, the arm's value is the result. You
may write several arms after one expression; they are tried in order, and the first class that
matches wins. An error no arm matches keeps travelling, as it would without the `catch`. An arm
holds an expression, so `throw` is allowed there and `return` is not.

**Good to know:** `catch (Throwable) => value` with no variable and no `throw` gives a warning. It
hides every error, including the ones you never thought about.

**The examples below** show a fallback for a row that is missing, then several arms tried in order,
then a report line whose division is guarded and a low-level error replaced by a clear one. The last
two show the type of the result, and a `return` in an arm that does not compile.

Every arm checks the error that the expression on the left threw. In `f() catch (LogicError $a) => x
catch (IOError $b) => y`, the `IOError` arm does not check `x`.

An arm for a parent class that is written before an arm for its subclass matches first. The later
arm never runs. This compiles without a warning.

`catch` covers everything to its left up to an assignment. In `$x = $a / $b catch (ArithmeticError
$e) => 0`, it covers the whole division. It also covers a whole `?:` and a whole `??` chain.

The variable is optional: `catch (IOError) => 0` is allowed. An arm names one class.
`catch (IOError | LogicError $e)` does not compile: it is the error `E0245`.

An arm's variable can only be used inside that arm. After the arm, you may declare the same name
again. The name must not already be a variable of the function when the arm starts: that is the
error `E0406`.

The type of the result includes the type of the expression and the type of every arm. If `get`
returns `int` and an arm gives `null`, the result is `?int`. Writing that result into an `int`
variable does not compile: it is the error `E0401`. An arm that throws adds nothing to the type.

`return`, `break` and `continue` in an arm do not compile: that is the error `E0126`.

This form has no `finally`. When the error leaves the expression, the `finally` block of the `try`
around it runs as usual.

The warning for `catch (Throwable) => value` is `W1006`. An arm with a variable does not get it.

#### Example 01: a fallback when a row is missing

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how a `catch` arm after an expression supplies a fallback value.
// `Repo::price` throws when it has no row for a product.

class Repo
{
    public static function price(string $sku): int
    {
        if ($sku == 'lamp') {
            return 1200;
        }
        throw new IOError('no row for ' . $sku);
    }
}

// The lookup worked, so the result is the call's own value. This prints 1200.
echo Repo::price('lamp') catch (IOError $missing) => 0, "\n";

// The lookup threw, so the result is the arm's value. This prints 0.
echo Repo::price('ring') catch (IOError $missing) => 0, "\n";

// The arm can read the error it caught. This prints `no row for ring`.
echo Repo::price('ring') catch (IOError $e) => $e->message, "\n";
```

```output
1200
0
no row for ring
```

#### Example 02: several arms tried in order

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows several arms written after one expression. They are tried in order and
// the first class that matches wins. The arms belong to the expression on the
// left, not to each other.

class Field
{
    public static function toAmount(string $text): int
    {
        if ($text == '') {
            throw new LogicError('the field is empty');
        }
        if ($text == '?') {
            throw new IOError('the field is unreadable');
        }
        return 42;
    }
}

// Nothing threw, so the result is the call's own value. This prints 42.
echo Field::toAmount('42') catch (LogicError $l) => -1 catch (IOError $io) => -2, "\n";

// The first arm matches. This prints -1.
echo Field::toAmount('') catch (LogicError $l) => -1 catch (IOError $io) => -2, "\n";

// The second arm matches. This prints -2.
echo Field::toAmount('?') catch (LogicError $l) => -1 catch (IOError $io) => -2, "\n";

// An error no arm matches keeps travelling, so the `try` around it catches it.
try {
    echo Field::toAmount('') catch (IOError $io) => -2, "\n";
} catch (LogicError $left) {
    echo 'left the expression: ', $left->message, "\n";
}
```

```output
42
-1
-2
left the expression: the field is empty
```

#### Example 03: a report line that survives an empty row

```nvs
<?nvs
// A report page shows an average for every row, and a price list turns a
// missing rate into a clear error. `catch` binds looser than the arithmetic,
// so the guard covers the whole division.

class Report
{
    public static function line(string $label, int $total, int $count): string
    {
        // A row with no entries would stop the page with an error. The arm
        // supplies 0 instead.
        var $average = $total / $count catch (ArithmeticError $zero) => 0;
        return $label . ': ' . $average as string;
    }
}

class Rates
{
    public static function read(string $code): int
    {
        throw new IOError('no rate for ' . $code);
    }

    // An arm may throw instead of giving a value. The caller then sees an error
    // that says what went wrong at this level.
    public static function forCode(string $code): int
    {
        return Rates::read($code)
            catch (IOError $e) => throw new RuntimeError('price list is incomplete: ' . $e->message);
    }
}

// This prints `north: 300`, then `south: 0`, then `east: 0`.
echo Report::line('north', 900, 3), "\n";
echo Report::line('south', 120, 0), "\n";
echo Report::line('east', 0, 7), "\n";

try {
    echo Rates::forCode('EUR'), "\n";
} catch (RuntimeError $stopped) {
    echo $stopped->message, "\n";
}
```

```output
north: 300
south: 0
east: 0
price list is incomplete: no rate for EUR
```

#### Example 04: the result type includes every arm

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows that the type of the result includes the type of every arm.

class Repo
{
    public static function get(int $id): int
    {
        if ($id < 0) {
            throw new IOError('no such row');
        }
        return $id * 2;
    }
}

// `get` returns `int` and the arm gives `null`, so the result is `?int`.
?int $found = Repo::get(-1) catch (IOError) => null;
// This prints `none`.
echo $found ?? 'none', "\n";

// One arm gives a string and the other gives an int, so the variable is `mixed`.
// The second arm matches. This prints -1.
mixed $either = Repo::get(-1) catch (LogicError $logic) => 'logic' catch (IOError $io) => -1;
echo $either, "\n";
```

```output
none
-1
```

#### Example 05: an arm cannot return

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that an arm is an expression, so `return` is not allowed there.
// Write a `try` block when you need a statement. This program does not compile.
// proof: compile-error

class Repo {
    public static function get(int $id): int {
        return $id;
    }
}

int $n = Repo::get(1) catch (IOError $e) => return 0;
echo $n, "\n";
```

```output
error[E0126]: a `catch` arm is an expression, and `return` is a statement
   --> main.nvs:12:45
   |
12 | int $n = Repo::get(1) catch (IOError $e) => return 0;
   |                                             ^^^^^^ `return` cannot appear here
   = help: `throw` is an expression, so `catch (E $e) => throw new …` is allowed here; for an early return write the block form, `try { … } catch (E $e) { return …; }`

error: aborting due to 1 error
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```

### `echo`, `print`, `unset`, `exit`, `yield`

`echo`, `print`, `unset`, `exit` and `yield` are five short statements: they write output, remove an
array entry, end the program, and produce values one at a time.

`echo a, b, c;` writes several values in order with nothing between them. `print $value;` writes one
value, and its result is `1`. Both turn a value into text the same way `.` does: `true` writes `1`,
and `false` and `null` write nothing.

`unset($a["k"]);` removes that entry from the array `$a`, and nothing else. Every variable and every
property in Novis always has a value, so `unset($x)` and `unset($o->p)` do not compile. Assign `null`
instead, where the type allows it.

`exit;` ends the program with status 0. `exit(3);` ends it with status 3, and `exit("bye")` writes the
text and then ends with status 0.

`yield $value;` goes inside a method that returns `Iterator<T>`. It sends one value to the loop that
reads it. A `yield` is a statement, so `$x = yield 1;` does not compile.

**The examples below** show `echo` and `print`, then `unset` on array entries, then a check that
reads rows with `yield` and stops with `exit`. The last one is an `unset` that does not compile.

One `unset` can remove several entries: `unset($a["k"], $a["j"]);`. Removing a key that is not in
the array does nothing. The entries after a removed one keep their keys.

`unset($x)` on a variable does not compile: it is the error `E0234`. `unset($o->p)` on a property
does not compile either: that is the error `E0413`.

`exit("bye")` writes the text to standard output. `exit` is also an expression, so
`int $n = $value ?? exit(4);` ends the program with status 4 when `$value` is `null`.

`yield` outside a generator does not compile: it is the error `E0445`. A method that contains `yield`
must return `Iterator<T>`, or it is the error `E0446`.

`yield from` does not exist: it is the error `E0448`. Write a `foreach` loop that yields each value
instead.

#### Example 01: writing values with echo and print

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how `echo` and `print` write values. `echo` takes several values at
// once and writes them in order with nothing between them.

string $name = 'Ada';
int $orders = 3;

// This prints: Ada has 3 orders
echo $name, ' has ', $orders, ' orders', "\n";

// `print` writes one value.
print "report finished\n";

// A value becomes text the same way `.` does. `true` writes `1`, and `false`
// and `null` write nothing, so this line prints 1|||
echo true, '|', false, '|', null, '|', "\n";
```

```output
Ada has 3 orders
report finished
1|||
```

#### Example 02: removing the entries you are done with

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how `unset` removes entries from an array. Only an array entry can be
// removed. A variable always has a value in Novis, so `unset($x)` does not
// compile.

array<int> $stock = ['apple' => 4, 'pear' => 0, 'plum' => 7, 'fig' => 0];

// One call removes several entries. This prints {"apple":4,"plum":7}
unset($stock['pear'], $stock['fig']);
echo Core\Json::encode($stock), "\n";

array<int> $counts = [10, 20, 30];

// Removing an entry in the middle leaves a gap. The entries after it keep the
// keys they had, so this prints {"0":10,"2":30}
unset($counts[1]);
echo Core\Json::encode($counts), "\n";

// Removing a key that is not in the array does nothing, and is not an error.
// There are still 2 entries.
unset($counts[99]);
echo Core\Arr::count($counts), "\n";
```

```output
{"apple":4,"plum":7}
{"0":10,"2":30}
2
```

#### Example 03: ending a check at the first bad row

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a small check program. It reads rows one at a time with `yield`,
// writes a line for each good row, and ends with `exit` at the first bad one.

class Rows
{
    // Each `yield` sends one row to the loop below.
    public static function all(): Iterator<string>
    {
        yield 'ada,42';
        yield 'grace,17';
        yield 'broken row';
        yield 'alan,9';
    }
}

foreach (Rows::all() as string $row) {
    if (Core\Str::contains($row, ',') == false) {
        // `exit` with a text writes it and ends the program with status 0.
        // The rows after this one are never read.
        exit('stopped at a bad row: ' . $row . "\n");
    }
    echo 'ok: ', $row, "\n";
}

echo "every row is good\n";
```

```output
ok: ada,42
ok: grace,17
stopped at a bad row: broken row
```

#### Example 04: unset needs an array entry

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that `unset` only removes array entries. A variable always has a
// value, so `unset($x)` does not compile.
// proof: compile-error

int $x = 1;
unset($x);
```

```output
error[E0234]: `unset()` takes an array element of a named holder
  --> main.nvs:7:7
  |
7 | unset($x);
  |       ^^ this is not an array element
  = help: `unset()` removes an array element and nothing else. A variable always has a value. If its type is nullable, assign `null` to it

error: aborting due to 1 error
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```

### Statement forms that do not parse

Novis reads PHP syntax, but not all of it. A few PHP statement forms do not parse. For most of them, the
compiler error names what to write instead.

`goto` and its labels are gone: use a loop, an early `return`, or a flag. `declare(strict_types=1)`
is not needed, because every Novis file is strict already. The alternative syntax `if (…): … endif;`
is not accepted: write braces. Instead of `global $x;`, pass the value as a parameter, or keep it in
a `private static` property. That property is also what replaces a `static` variable inside a
function. Write `[int $a, int $b] = …` instead of `list($a, $b) = …`, and `require` instead of `include` or
`require_once`. A `class`, `interface`, `enum`, `type`, `namespace`, `use` or `autoload` statement
goes at the top of a file, never inside a body.

**The examples below** show what to write instead of `goto`, instead of `global` and a `static`
variable, and instead of `list()` and the alternative syntax. The last two are a `goto` and an
`if (…): … endif;` that do not compile.

Each form has its own error code:

- `goto` is the error `E0203`.
- `global $x;` is the error `E0204`.
- `static $n = 0;` inside a method is the error `E0209`.
- `list($a, $b) = …` is the error `E0230`.
- `include` and `require_once` are the error `E0221`.
- A `class`, `interface`, `enum`, `type`, `namespace` or `use` statement inside a body is the error
  `E0233`.

A label, `declare(…)` and the alternative syntax give a general syntax error. That error does not
name what to write instead. The alternative syntax is the colon form of `if`, `while`, `for`,
`foreach` and `switch`, with `endif`, `endwhile`, `endfor`, `endforeach` and `endswitch`.

In `[int $a, int $b] = …`, each variable needs its type. `[$a, $b] = …` does not compile, even when
`$a` and `$b` are already declared.

#### Example 01: what to write instead of goto

```nvs
<?nvs
// `goto` and its labels do not parse. Shows the three ways to leave a piece of
// work early instead: an early `return`, a `break`, and a flag.

class Orders
{
    // Returns the first total above the limit, or 0 when there is none.
    public static function firstOver(array<int> $totals, int $limit): int
    {
        foreach ($totals as int $total) {
            // An early `return` leaves the method at once.
            if ($total > $limit) {
                return $total;
            }
        }
        return 0;
    }
}

array<int> $totals = [400, 1200, 250, 3000];

// This prints 1200.
echo Orders::firstOver($totals, 1000), "\n";

// `break` leaves a loop. This one stops at the first total below 300.
int $small = 0;
foreach ($totals as int $total) {
    if ($total < 300) {
        $small = $total;
        break;
    }
}

// This prints 250.
echo $small, "\n";

// A flag carries the decision to the statements after the loop.
bool $found = $small > 0;
if ($found) {
    echo "one small order\n";
}
```

```output
1200
250
one small order
```

#### Example 02: what to write instead of global and a static variable

```nvs
<?nvs
// `global $x;` and a `static` variable inside a function do not parse. Shows
// what to write instead: a parameter, and a `private static` property.

class Retry
{
    // The count belongs to the class, so it is still there on the next call.
    private static int $attempts = 0;

    // The limit arrives as a parameter. Nothing is read from outside.
    public static function attempt(int $limit): bool
    {
        self::$attempts = self::$attempts + 1;
        return self::$attempts <= $limit;
    }

    public static function attempts(): int
    {
        return self::$attempts;
    }
}

int $round = 0;
while ($round < 3) {
    // The first two calls are allowed, the third is not.
    if (Retry::attempt(2)) {
        echo 'attempt ', Retry::attempts(), ": allowed\n";
    } else {
        echo 'attempt ', Retry::attempts(), ": too many\n";
    }
    $round = $round + 1;
}
```

```output
attempt 1: allowed
attempt 2: allowed
attempt 3: too many
```

#### Example 03: what to write instead of list and the alternative syntax

```nvs
<?nvs
// `list($a, $b) = …` and the alternative syntax `if (…): … endif;` do not
// parse. Shows the two replacements in a program that reads contact lines.

array<string> $lines = ['Ada Lovelace|ada@example.com', 'Grace Hopper|'];

foreach ($lines as string $line) {
    // Brackets replace `list()`. Each name is written with its type, as
    // everywhere else.
    [string $name, string $mail] = Core\Str::split($line, '|');

    // Braces replace `if (…): … endif;`.
    if ($mail == '') {
        echo $name, " has no address\n";
    } else {
        echo $name, ' <', $mail, ">\n";
    }
}
```

```output
Ada Lovelace <ada@example.com>
Grace Hopper has no address
```

#### Example 04: goto does not compile

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that `goto` is not allowed. The compiler error names the three ways
// to write it instead. This program does not compile.
// proof: compile-error

int $n = 0;
while ($n < 3) {
    $n++;
    if ($n == 2) {
        goto done;
    }
}
```

```output
   --> main.nvs:10:9
   |
10 |         goto done;
   |         ^^^^^^^^^^ makes the control-flow graph unstructured
   = help: restructure with a loop, an early `return`, or a boolean flag

error: aborting due to 1 error
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```

#### Example 05: the alternative syntax does not compile

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that the alternative syntax `if (…): … endif;` is not allowed. Write
// braces instead. This program does not compile.
// proof: compile-error

int $n = 2;
if ($n == 2):
    echo "two";
endif;
```

```output

  --> main.nvs:7:13
  |

  |             ^ not found here

  --> main.nvs:7:13
  |
7 | if ($n == 2):
  |             ^ not found here

  --> main.nvs:9:1

  = help: every constant belongs to a class, so write `Class::NAME`. A built-in constant is on its `Core` class, such as `Core\Math::PI`
```

<a id="lang-classes"></a>
## A.5 Classes, interfaces and objects

Keywords: class, constructor, __construct, new, public, protected, private, static, self, parent, $this, abstract, final, extends, implements, interface, trait, delegation, by, readonly, lateinit, isinit, LateInit, initProperty, property hooks, get, set, PropertyGuard, beforePropertySet, beforePropertyUnset, PropertyObserver, Stringable, __toString, Comparable, compareTo, clone, __clone, is, object, ?->, nullsafe, __get, __set, __call, __callStatic, __invoke, __destruct, anonymous class, const, ::class, class<T>, class reference, new $cls, late static binding

### Declaring a class

A class is a type you write yourself. It holds some data and the functions that work on that data. You
create one with `new`.

Every member of a class writes `public`, `protected` or `private`. A `public` member is reachable from
anywhere. A `protected` member is reachable from the class and from the classes that extend it. A
`private` member is reachable only from the class that declares it. There is no default, so a member
written without one of those three words does not compile.

The constructor is a method named `constructor`. It runs once, when `new` creates the object. It must
give a value to every property that has no default. A class where every property already has a default
needs no constructor.

**Good to know:** a visibility keyword in front of a constructor parameter declares a property of that
name and fills it with the argument.

**The examples below** show a class with data and methods, a constructor that declares its
properties, and a class that keeps its data private. The last two show a property with no visibility,
which does not compile, and a class with no constructor.

A property, a method or a constant written without `public`, `protected` or `private` does not
compile (`E0122`). A method named `__construct` does not compile either (`E0114`). The error tells you
to name it `constructor`. A class name is PascalCase, so `class point` is the error `E0110`.

Reading a property or calling a method where its visibility does not allow it is the error `E0471`.
That includes a `private` property read in a class that extends the declaring class. A `private`
constructor works the same way. `new A()` outside `A` is `E0471`, and a `static` method of `A` may
still call `new A()`.

A class is declared at the top level of a file. A class or an interface inside a class body is the
error `E0233`. Only an `enum` or a `type` alias may be declared there. A class inside a method or an
`if` block is `E0233` too.

A wrong number of arguments is the error `E0402`. An unknown method or property is `E0405`, for a
read and for a write. A class with no `constructor` takes no arguments, so `new Counter(1)` is
`E0402`. A class that extends another and declares no constructor uses its parent's: with
`class B extends A {}`, `new B(4)` calls `A`'s constructor.

A visibility keyword is allowed only on a parameter of `constructor`. On any other method it is the
error `E0722`. A promoted parameter may also be `readonly`: `public readonly int $x`.

`new A` without parentheses is the same as `new A()`. A constructor may declare the return type
`void`, and it may have no return type at all.

#### Example 01: a class with data and methods

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to declare a class, create an object with `new`, and use it.
// Every member writes `public`, `protected` or `private`.

class User
{
    public string $name;
    public string $email;
    private string $role = 'member';

    public function constructor(string $name, string $email)
    {
        $this->name = $name;
        $this->email = $email;
    }

    public function label(): string
    {
        return $this->name . ' <' . $this->email . '>';
    }

    public function roleName(): string
    {
        return $this->role;
    }
}

var $user = new User('Ada Lovelace', 'ada@example.com');

// A `public` property is read and written from anywhere with `->`.
$user->email = 'ada@example.org';

// This prints `Ada Lovelace <ada@example.org>`.
echo $user->label(), "\n";

// `$role` is `private`. Only `User`'s own methods read it, so this class gives
// you a method for it. This prints `member`.
echo $user->roleName(), "\n";
```

```output
Ada Lovelace <ada@example.org>
member
```

#### Example 02: a constructor that declares the properties

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows constructor promotion. A visibility keyword on a constructor parameter
// declares a property of that name and type, and assigns the argument to it.

class Product
{
    // These three lines declare three properties and fill them. There is no
    // second place where `$name`, `$priceCents` and `$currency` are written.
    public function constructor(
        public string $name,
        public int $priceCents,
        private string $currency = 'EUR',
    )
    {}

    public function price(): string
    {
        return $this->priceCents . ' ' . $this->currency;
    }
}

var $book = new Product('The Art of Computer Programming', 8990);

// A default on the parameter is a default for the argument. `$currency` is
// `EUR` here, because the third argument was left out.
var $mug = new Product('Coffee mug', 1250, 'CHF');

// This prints `The Art of Computer Programming: 8990 EUR`.
echo $book->name, ': ', $book->price(), "\n";

// This prints `Coffee mug: 1250 CHF`.
echo $mug->name, ': ', $mug->price(), "\n";
```

```output
The Art of Computer Programming: 8990 EUR
Coffee mug: 1250 CHF
```

#### Example 03: a class that collects and sums its own data

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the shape most classes in a program have: private data, and public
// methods that are the only way to reach it.

class Cart
{
    private array<int> $prices = [];

    public function constructor(private string $currency)
    {}

    public function add(int $priceCents): void
    {
        $this->prices[] = $priceCents;
    }

    public function total(): int
    {
        int $sum = 0;
        foreach ($this->prices as int $price) {
            $sum = $sum + $price;
        }
        return $sum;
    }

    public function summary(): string
    {
        return Core\Arr::count($this->prices) . ' items, ' . $this->total() . ' ' . $this->currency;
    }
}

var $cart = new Cart('EUR');
$cart->add(1250);
$cart->add(399);
$cart->add(8000);

// Nothing outside `Cart` can change the prices, so `total` is always the sum of
// what `add` was given. This prints `3 items, 9649 EUR`.
echo $cart->summary(), "\n";
```

```output
3 items, 9649 EUR
```

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that every property needs `public`, `protected` or `private`.
// `$balance` has none, so this program does not compile.
// proof: compile-error

class Account
{
    int $balance = 0;
}
```

```output
  --> main.nvs:8:9
  |
8 |     int $balance = 0;
  |         ^^^^^^^^ no visibility written here

error: aborting due to 1 error
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```

#### Example 05: a class with no constructor

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a class with no constructor. Every property has a default, so `new`
// takes no arguments.

class Counter
{
    public int $n = 0;
}

var $c = new Counter();
$c->n = $c->n + 1;

// This prints `1`.
echo $c->n, "\n";
```

```output

```

### Properties

A property is a named value that each object of a class has.

Every property declares its type and its visibility. A property without a default value must be
assigned in the constructor, on every path out of it. A default value must
be a constant: a number, a string, a `bool`, an enum case, a class constant, `[]` or `null`.

Three keywords change when a property gets its value. `readonly` means the constructor sets it once
and no later code can change it. `lateinit` means another part of the program sets it after `new`
returns. Reading it before that first write throws an error. `static` means there is one value for
the whole class, and it starts every request at the value you declared.

**The examples below** show defaults, a constructor, `readonly`, `static` and `lateinit`. Others
show a constructor that does not compile, a `lateinit` read that throws, `isinit`, a `readonly`
write and `static::` on a property.

Only a plain `=` assigns a property in the constructor. `$this->n += 1;` reads the property first, so
a constructor with only that line is the error `E0409`. A `?T` property with no default and no
assignment starts as `null`.

A `return` in a constructor has no value. `return 1;` is the error `E0248`. A bare `return;` leaves
the constructor early, and every property must already have its value on that path. If one does
not, it is `E0409`.

A `lateinit` property may have any type, and a default too. If a method reads it before any write on
the same path, the read does not compile (`E0428`). Any other read with no value first throws a
`LogicError` when it runs. Example 06 prints its message. `isinit` works only on a `lateinit` property. On any other property it is the error
`E0853`. A property cannot be both `lateinit` and `readonly` (`E0427`).

A `readonly` property has no default, and that includes a `static readonly` one (`E0249`). Every
write after the constructor is the error `E0782`: `=`, a compound operator such as `+=`, and an
append with `[]`. A write in another method of the class is `E0782` too, and so is a write in a
subclass constructor after `parent::constructor()`. A second write on the same path through the
constructor is `E0782` as well. `unset($a->v)` is the error `E0413` for every declared property.

A `static` property with no default and a type that is not nullable is the error `E0409`. A
subclass shares the same value with its parent: `B::$n = 5;` also changes `A::$n`. `static::$n`
is the error `E0499`. Write `self::$n` or the class name. `++`, `--` and every compound operator
work on a `static` property. An unknown one is the error `E0309`, and a `private` one read outside
its class is `E0471`.

#### Example 01: defaults and a constructor

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the two ways a property gets its first value: a default written in the
// class, or an assignment in the constructor.

class Invoice
{
    // These three have a default, so the constructor does not touch them.
    public string $currency = 'EUR';
    public int $total = 0;
    public array<string> $lines = [];

    // This one has no default. The constructor must give it a value.
    public string $customer;

    public function constructor(string $customer)
    {
        $this->customer = $customer;
    }

    public function add(string $line, int $amount): void
    {
        $this->lines[] = $line;
        $this->total = $this->total + $amount;
    }
}

var $invoice = new Invoice('Ada Lovelace');
$invoice->add('Keyboard', 4900);
$invoice->add('Cable', 900);

// This prints: Ada Lovelace owes 5800 EUR for 2 lines.
echo $invoice->customer, ' owes ', $invoice->total, ' ', $invoice->currency;
echo ' for ', Core\Arr::count($invoice->lines), " lines.\n";
```

```output
Ada Lovelace owes 5800 EUR for 2 lines.
```

#### Example 02: readonly values that never change

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `readonly`. The constructor gives each property its value, and no other
// code can change it.

final class Money
{
    public function constructor(public readonly int $cents, public readonly string $currency)
    {}

    // The two amounts cannot change, so adding them returns a third object.
    public function plus(Money $other): Money
    {
        return new Money($this->cents + $other->cents, $this->currency);
    }
}

var $coffee = new Money(350, 'EUR');
var $cake = new Money(425, 'EUR');
var $order = $coffee->plus($cake);

// This prints 350 + 425 = 775 EUR. The first two objects still have their own
// values.
echo $coffee->cents, ' + ', $cake->cents, ' = ', $order->cents, ' ', $order->currency, "\n";
```

```output
350 + 425 = 775 EUR
```

#### Example 03: a shared counter and a logger attached later

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a `static` property, which belongs to the class itself, and a `lateinit`
// property, which is written after the object is created.

class Printer
{
    public function write(int $number, string $subject): void
    {
        echo '#', $number, ' ', $subject, "\n";
    }
}

class Ticket
{
    // One value for the whole class. Every request starts it again at 0.
    public static int $issued = 0;

    // The printer is chosen elsewhere, so it arrives after `new` returns.
    public lateinit Printer $printer;

    public readonly int $number;

    public function constructor(public string $subject)
    {
        self::$issued = self::$issued + 1;
        $this->number = self::$issued;
    }

    // A class may read its own `lateinit` property once a write came first on
    // the same path. This method does both.
    public function printWith(Printer $printer): void
    {
        $this->printer = $printer;
        $this->printer->write($this->number, $this->subject);
    }
}

var $printer = new Printer();

var $first = new Ticket('The printer is out of paper');
$first->printWith($printer);

var $second = new Ticket('A new keyboard');
$second->printWith($printer);

// This prints 2. The counter belongs to the class, so both tickets added to it.
echo 'tickets so far: ', Ticket::$issued, "\n";
```

```output
#1 The printer is out of paper
#2 A new keyboard
tickets so far: 2
```

#### Example 06: reading lateinit too early

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows what happens when code reads a `lateinit` property before it has a
// value. The read throws a `LogicError`.

class Logger
{
    public function name(): string
    {
        return 'log';
    }
}

class Widget
{
    public lateinit Logger $logger;

    public function attach(Logger $l): void
    {
        $this->logger = $l;
    }
}

var $w = new Widget();

// Nothing has set `$logger` yet, so this prints the error message.
try {
    echo $w->logger->name(), "\n";
} catch (Throwable $e) {
    echo 'threw: ', $e->message, "\n";
}

// After `attach`, the read works. This prints `log`.
$w->attach(new Logger());
echo $w->logger->name(), "\n";
```

```output
threw: `Widget`'s property `$logger` is read before it is initialized
log
```

#### Example 07: isinit checks for a value

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `isinit`. It returns `true` when a `lateinit` property has a value.
// It does not read the property, so it never throws.

class Post
{
    public lateinit ?string $note;
}

var $p = new Post();

// This prints `no`.
echo isinit($p->note) ? 'yes' : 'no', "\n";

// `null` is a value too. This prints `yes`.
$p->note = null;
echo isinit($p->note) ? 'yes' : 'no', "\n";
```

```output
no
yes
```

### Methods, `self`, `static` and `parent`

A method is a function that belongs to a class.

An instance method runs on one object, and `$this` is that object. A `static` method belongs to the
class itself. It has no `$this`, and you call it as `Class::method()`.

Three keywords call a method without writing the class name. `self` is the
class the code is written in. `static` is the class the call was made on, which may be a subclass.
`parent` is the class this one extends, so `parent::format()` calls the parent's version.

**Good to know:** a method that says it returns `static` must return the object it was called on, or
a new object of the same class.

**The examples below** show the two kinds of method, `self` beside `static` in a subclass, and a
subclass that calls its parent's version. The last two show a chain of calls with an anonymous
function that keeps `$this`, and a return type `static` that does not compile.

An anonymous function written inside a method keeps that method's `$this`. It may read the class's
`private` properties and call its `private` methods.

A `static` method may also be called on an object: `$a->s()` calls `A::s()`. `$a::s()` is the error
`E0496`, because the left side of `::` must be a class name. An instance method called through the
class, such as `A::i()`, is the error `E0778`. `$this` inside a `static` method is the error `E0779`.

`self`, `static` and `parent` work only inside a class. Outside one, `self::class` and
`static::class` are the error `E0702`. `parent::` in a class that extends no class is the error
`E0303`. When the parent declares a constructor, the child's constructor must call
`parent::constructor(...)` on every path. A path without the call is the error `E0410`.

A method that returns `self` returns the class the method is written in. On a subclass object, the
result has the parent's type, so a method only the subclass has is the error `E0405`. Declare the
return type `static` to keep the subclass. `self` also works as a parameter type.

A method that returns `static` may return `$this`, `new static(...)` or the result of a `static::`
call. `new self()` or `new A()` there is the error `E0741`. `new self()` in a `static` method
always creates the class the code is written in, even when the call was made on a subclass.
`static::method()` reaches an `abstract static` method that a subclass writes.

`static::` inside an anonymous function is the error `E0834`. `self::m()` and `parent::m()` inside
one call the class the function is written in.

#### Example 01: an instance method and a static method

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the two kinds of method. An instance method works on one object through
// `$this`. A static method belongs to the class and needs no object.

class Temperature
{
    public function constructor(public readonly int $celsius)
    {}

    // An instance method. `$this` is the object the method was called on.
    public function isFreezing(): bool
    {
        return $this->celsius <= 0;
    }

    // A static method. It has no `$this`, so everything it needs is a parameter.
    public static function warmer(Temperature $a, Temperature $b): Temperature
    {
        if ($a->celsius > $b->celsius) {
            return $a;
        }
        return $b;
    }
}

var $morning = new Temperature(-4);
var $noon = new Temperature(11);

// Only the first of these two prints a line.
if ($morning->isFreezing()) {
    echo "the morning is freezing\n";
}
if ($noon->isFreezing()) {
    echo "the noon is freezing\n";
}

// This prints 11, which is the warmer of the two.
echo 'warmer: ', Temperature::warmer($morning, $noon)->celsius, "\n";
```

```output
the morning is freezing
warmer: 11
```

#### Example 02: self is where the code is static is who called it

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the difference between `self` and `static`. `self` is the class the code
// is written in. `static` is the class the call was made on.

class Document
{
    public static function kind(): string
    {
        return 'document';
    }

    // `new static()` creates an object of the class that was called, so a
    // subclass gets one of its own kind.
    public static function create(): static
    {
        return new static();
    }

    public function describe(): string
    {
        return static::kind() . ' (this code is written in ' . self::kind() . ')';
    }
}

class Invoice extends Document
{
    public static function kind(): string
    {
        return 'invoice';
    }
}

echo Document::create()->describe(), "\n";
echo Invoice::create()->describe(), "\n";
```

```output
document (this code is written in document)
invoice (this code is written in document)
```

#### Example 03: a subclass calls the version its parent wrote

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `parent`. A subclass runs the constructor and the methods of the class
// it extends, and adds its own work around them.

class Notification
{
    public function constructor(public string $subject)
    {}

    public function format(): string
    {
        return '[note] ' . $this->subject;
    }
}

class UrgentNotification extends Notification
{
    public function constructor(string $subject, public string $team)
    {
        // The parent's constructor assigns the properties the parent declares.
        parent::constructor($subject);
    }

    public function format(): string
    {
        // `parent::format()` is the version above this one, not this one, so
        // this method does not call itself.
        return parent::format() . ' for ' . $this->team;
    }
}

var $normal = new Notification('Backup finished');
var $urgent = new UrgentNotification('Disk is full', 'operations');

echo $normal->format(), "\n";
echo $urgent->format(), "\n";
```

```output
[note] Backup finished
[note] Disk is full for operations
```

#### Example 04: chaining and a function that keeps this

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a method that returns `$this`, so calls can be chained. It also shows
// an anonymous function that keeps the object it was made on.

class Acc
{
    private int $n = 0;

    public function bump(): self
    {
        $this->n = $this->n + 1;
        return $this;
    }

    // The function reads `$this->n` when it is called, not when it is made.
    public function adder(): callable
    {
        return fn(int $k): int => $this->n + $k;
    }
}

var $a = new Acc();
var $f = $a->adder();
$a->bump()->bump();

// `$n` is 2 now, so this prints `5`.
echo $f(3) as int, "\n";
```

```output
5
```

```nvs error
// A call on a subclass would get the wrong class, so this does not compile.
// proof: compile-error

class Builder
{
    public function copy(): static
    {
        return new self();
    }
}
```

```output
   |                ^^^^^^^^^^ not the called class
```

### Constants and `::class`

A class can hold named values that never change, and every class knows its own name.

A constant is written `public const int MAX = 3;`, with its type. Code inside the
class reads it as `self::MAX`, and code anywhere else as `Limits::MAX`. The value must be written
directly in the code, as one value or a list.

A subclass can give a constant a new value. In a method, `static::MAX` reads the value of the class
the call was made on. `self::MAX` reads the value of the class the code is written in. `static::`
works only for a single value, not inside an anonymous function.

`Limits::class` gives the name of a class as a string. `$order::class` gives the class a value
really is.

A constant list gives you a new list on every read.

**The examples below** show `self::` and `static::`, class names as text, a constant list, and
`static::` with a list, which does not compile.

A constant name is SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE, so `const int max` is the error `E0113`. `static` on a
constant is the error `E0106`. An unknown constant is `E0309`. A constant cannot be assigned:
`A::N = 2;` is the error `E0105`, and `A::L[] = 2;` is `E0700`. A constant is read through the class
name, so `$a::N` is the error `E0496` and `$a->N` is `E0405`.

A subclass that declares the same constant again keeps its type, or a narrower one. An `int|string`
constant may become `int`. A `string` in place of an `int` is the error `E0833`. An interface may
declare a constant, and a class that implements it may declare it again. In a default method,
`static::NAME` reads the value of the class, or the interface's value when the class has none.

`static::NAME` works for `string`, `int`, `uint`, `bool` and `float` constants. For an `array` or a
`?int` constant it is the error `E0832`. A parameter default cannot use `static::` (`E0831`), and
`self::NAME` works there.

`Class::class`, `self::class` and `parent::class` are fixed when the program compiles.
`static::class` and `$obj::class` are read when the program runs. The result is a `string`, so
`int $n = A::class;` is the error `E0401`. `$v::class` on a `mixed`, a `?A` or an anonymous object is
the error `E0702`. Check the value with `is` first. On a `class<A>` value it is `E0702` too. Write
`$c as string` to get the name.

`foreach` works on an array constant like on any other array.

#### Example 01: values that never change

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a class holding values that never change. Every constant writes its
// type, and code inside the class reads it with `self::` or `static::`.

class Upload
{
    public const uint MAX_BYTES = 1048576;
    public const string FOLDER = 'uploads';
    // The element type is `float`, so this constant holds 1.0 and 2.5.
    public const array<float> STEP_SECONDS = [1, 2.5];

    // Returns true when a file of this size may be stored. `static::MAX_BYTES`
    // reads the constant of the class the call was made on.
    public static function fits(uint $bytes): bool
    {
        return $bytes <= static::MAX_BYTES;
    }

    // `self::MAX_BYTES` always reads the value written in this class.
    public static function describe(): string
    {
        return static::MAX_BYTES as string . ' of ' . self::MAX_BYTES as string . ' bytes';
    }
}

// A subclass gives the constant a smaller value.
class AvatarUpload extends Upload
{
    public const uint MAX_BYTES = 65536;
}

// From outside the class, the name of the class comes first. This prints
// 1048576 and then uploads.
echo Upload::MAX_BYTES, "\n";
echo Upload::FOLDER, "\n";

// `fits` uses `static::`, so each class checks against its own limit.
if (Upload::fits(500000)) {
    echo "500000 bytes fit an upload\n";
}
if (!AvatarUpload::fits(500000)) {
    echo "500000 bytes do not fit an avatar\n";
}

// This prints `65536 of 1048576 bytes`. The first number comes from
// `static::`, the second from `self::`.
echo AvatarUpload::describe(), "\n";

// The first value is written as a whole number. The declared type makes it a
// float, so this division prints 0.5.
echo Upload::STEP_SECONDS[0] / 2, "\n";
```

```output
1048576
uploads
500000 bytes fit an upload
500000 bytes do not fit an avatar
65536 of 1048576 bytes
0.5
```

#### Example 02: the name of a class as text

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to get the name of a class as a string. On a value, `::class`
// gives the class that value really is.

class Notification
{
    public static function label(): string
    {
        // `static::class` is the class the call was made on. It is not always
        // the class this method is written in.
        return static::class;
    }
}

class EmailNotification extends Notification
{}

class SmsNotification extends Notification
{}

// `Class::class` is the name of that class, written as text. This prints
// Notification.
echo Notification::class, "\n";

// The call decides what `static::class` gives. This prints EmailNotification
// and then SmsNotification.
echo EmailNotification::label(), "\n";
echo SmsNotification::label(), "\n";

// A variable declared as the parent class can hold a subclass. `::class` gives
// the class the value was created from, so this prints SmsNotification.
Notification $sent = new SmsNotification();
echo $sent::class, "\n";
```

```output
Notification
EmailNotification
SmsNotification
SmsNotification
```

#### Example 03: a constant list as an allow list

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a constant list checked on the way in, which is what a service does
// with a small fixed table of allowed values.

class Images
{
    public const array<string> TYPES = ['image/png', 'image/jpeg', 'image/webp'];

    // Returns true when this service stores files of that type.
    public static function allowed(string $type): bool
    {
        return Core\Arr::contains(self::TYPES, $type);
    }
}

array<string> $uploads = ['image/png', 'application/pdf', 'image/webp'];
foreach ($uploads as string $type) {
    if (Images::allowed($type)) {
        echo $type, " is stored\n";
    } else {
        echo $type, " is rejected\n";
    }
}

// Every read of the constant gives a new list. This one adds a type to the
// list it got, and the constant still holds three types, so this prints 4 3.
array<string> $mine = Images::TYPES;
$mine[] = 'image/gif';
echo Core\Arr::count($mine), ' ', Core\Arr::count(Images::TYPES), "\n";
```

```output
image/png is stored
application/pdf is rejected
image/webp is stored
4 3
```

```output
   |                                ^^^^^^^^^^^^^ read through `static::`
   = help: a `static::` constant is read when the program runs, and only a `string`, `int`, `uint`, `bool` or `float` constant can be read that way. Write `self::` or the class name, or make the constant one of those types
```

### Inheritance

A class can build on another class. `extends` names the parent, and the new class starts with
everything the parent has.

The subclass keeps every property and method of the parent, and may write its own version of a
method. `parent::` reaches the version the parent wrote. When the parent has a constructor, the
subclass constructor must call `parent::constructor(...)`.

An `abstract` class is not finished. You cannot create an object of it, and a subclass must write
each method it declares without a body. A `final` class cannot be extended, and a `final` method
cannot be replaced. `$x is T` tests whether an object is a `T`.

**Good to know:** a class extends one parent only. To share behaviour between classes that are not
related, use an interface.

**The examples below** show a subclass that adds to its parent, then an abstract class every
subclass fills in, then a class the program picks while it runs. Examples 06, 09 and 10 show an
`abstract static` method, `is` and a static call through a class value. The others show what does
not compile.

`extends` names one class. `extends A, B` is a syntax error. A class that is not declared is the
error `E0303`, and so is an interface after `extends`. A class that extends itself, directly or
through another class, is the error `E0305`.

When the parent has a constructor, every path through the subclass constructor must call
`parent::constructor(...)`. A call inside one `if` branch only is the error `E0410`. Code may run
before the call, and a second call runs the parent's constructor again. When the parent has no
constructor, the subclass does not call one, and `parent::constructor()` is the error `E0309`. A
subclass with no constructor uses the parent's constructor.

A subclass reaches the parent's `public` and `protected` members. A `private` member is the error
`E0471` in the subclass. `parent::` in a class with no parent is `E0303`. `parent::f()` runs the
nearest version above the class, so it reaches a grandparent when the parent does not declare `f`.
A default parameter value comes from the declared type of the variable. Say `A::f(int $x = 1)` is
replaced by `B::f(int $x = 2)`. A call on an `A` variable uses `1`, even when it contains a `B`.

A class that does not write every `abstract` method of its parent is the error `E0449`. An
`abstract` class that extends another one does not need to write them. `new` on an `abstract` class
or on an interface is the error `E0785`. `new static()` inside an `abstract` class compiles, because
it makes an object of the subclass the call was made on. A method without a body in a class that is
not `abstract` is the error `E0786`, and so is an `abstract` method there. A method cannot be both
`abstract` and `final`: that is the error `E0106`.

An `abstract static` method has no body, so a call to it must reach a subclass. `self::title()` and
`static::title()` in a static method call the class the method was called on. `Page::title()` on the
`abstract` class is the error `E0835`. `self::title()` inside an anonymous function is `E0835` too,
because it calls the class the function is written in.

A class that extends a `final` class is the error `E0783`. A method that replaces a `final` method
is the error `E0784`, also in a grandchild class. Other methods of the same class can be replaced as
usual.

`$x is T` is true for the object's own class, every parent class, and every interface they
implement. It is false for any other class, and false when `$x` is `null`. Inside the `if`, the
variable has the type `T`. The right side of `is` is a class name or a `class<T>` value. A `string`
there is the error `E0496`.

A `class<T>` value works in three places: `new $cls(...)`, `$cls::f(...)` and `$x is $cls`. A
`string` in any of them is the error `E0496`. `$obj->$name` with a string is the error `E0235`. A
static call through a `class<T>` value runs the subclass's method, and `static::` in it is that
subclass. `new $cls(...)` checks the arguments against the constructor of `T`. When a subclass of `T`
has a constructor that cannot take those arguments, the `new` is the error `E0794`. Convert to the
subclass, as in `as class<Strict>`, or give the subclass a constructor that fits. A class name
written in the code that is not a subclass of `T` is the error `E0708` at `as class<T>`.

#### Example 01: a subclass adds to what its parent does

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `extends`. A subclass starts with everything its parent has, and
// `parent::` runs the version the parent wrote.

class Invoice
{
    public function constructor(public string $customer, public int $cents)
    {}

    public function line(): string
    {
        return $this->customer . ': ' . $this->cents . ' cents';
    }
}

class OverdueInvoice extends Invoice
{
    public function constructor(string $customer, int $cents, public int $days)
    {
        // The parent's constructor assigns the properties the parent declares.
        parent::constructor($customer, $cents);
    }

    public function line(): string
    {
        // `parent::line()` is the version above this one, so this method adds
        // to that text instead of writing it again.
        return parent::line() . ', ' . $this->days . ' days late';
    }
}

// A subclass fits everywhere its parent fits, so both objects go in the
// same array.
array<Invoice> $book = [
    new Invoice('Ada', 1200),
    new OverdueInvoice('Bo', 3400, 12),
];

// Each object runs its own version of `line`.
foreach ($book as Invoice $invoice) {
    echo $invoice->line(), "\n";
}
```

```output
Ada: 1200 cents
Bo: 3400 cents, 12 days late
```

#### Example 02: an abstract class every subclass fills in

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `abstract` and `final`. An abstract class says which methods a
// subclass has to write, and writes the work that is the same for all of them.

abstract class Exporter
{
    public function constructor(public string $title)
    {}

    // This method has no body. Every subclass writes it.
    abstract public function row(string $value): string;

    // This one has a body, and it calls the method that does not.
    public function render(array<string> $values): string
    {
        string $out = $this->title . "\n";
        foreach ($values as string $value) {
            $out = $out . $this->row($value) . "\n";
        }
        return $out;
    }
}

// `final` says no class extends this one.
final class CsvExporter extends Exporter
{
    public function row(string $value): string
    {
        return "\"" . $value . "\"";
    }
}

final class ListExporter extends Exporter
{
    public function row(string $value): string
    {
        return '- ' . $value;
    }
}

array<string> $names = ['Ada', 'Bo'];

// There is no object of `Exporter` itself. `array<Exporter>` still holds both
// subclasses, because both are exporters.
array<Exporter> $exporters = [new CsvExporter('names.csv'), new ListExporter('Names')];
foreach ($exporters as Exporter $exporter) {
    echo $exporter->render($names);
}
```

```output
names.csv
"Ada"
"Bo"
Names
- Ada
- Bo
```

#### Example 03: a class the program picks while it runs

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `class<T>` and `is`. A job runner reads the name of a class from its
// queue, makes an object of that class, and runs it.

class Task
{
    public function constructor(public string $subject)
    {}

    public function run(): string
    {
        return 'nothing to do for ' . $this->subject;
    }
}

class EmailTask extends Task
{
    public function run(): string
    {
        return 'email sent to ' . $this->subject;
    }
}

class ReportTask extends Task
{
    public function run(): string
    {
        return 'report written for ' . $this->subject;
    }
}

// In a real program these names come from a queue or a configuration file, so
// they are text.
array<string> $queue = ['EmailTask', 'ReportTask'];

foreach ($queue as string $name) {
    // `as class<Task>` converts the text to a class. It throws an error when
    // the text is not the name of a class that extends `Task`.
    class<Task> $cls = $name as class<Task>;

    // `new $cls(...)` makes an object of that class.
    Task $task = new $cls('Ada');
    echo $task->run(), "\n";
}

// `is` tests what an object really is. `$first` is declared `Task`, and the
// object in it is an `EmailTask`, so this prints the line below.
Task $first = new EmailTask('Bo');
if ($first is EmailTask) {
    echo "the first task is an email task\n";
}
```

```output
email sent to Ada
report written for Ada
the first task is an email task
```

#### Example 06: an abstract static method

```nvs

{
```

#### Example 09: is checks the class its parents and its interfaces

```nvs

// and every interface they implement.

{
    public function mark(): string;
}

{
    public function mark(): string
    {
        return 'base';
    }

{}

{}
```

### `covariant`

`covariant` lets a subclass give a method parameter or a property a narrower type than its parent
gives it. The parent takes any `Animal`, and the subclass takes only a `Dog`.

You write `covariant` before the type: `public function feed(covariant Dog $a)` for a parameter, and
`public covariant Dog $pet;` for a property. Code that uses the parent's type can still pass any
`Animal`. So Novis checks each value when it enters. A parameter is checked before the method body
runs. A property is checked each time it is written. A value of the wrong type throws a
`LogicError` that names both types.

**Good to know:** a narrower type without `covariant` does not compile. The error message tells you
to add it.

**The examples below** show a narrower parameter, the error a wrong value throws, a narrower
property and `compareTo` in a subclass. The last one does not compile.

`covariant` is allowed on a parameter of a method that replaces a parent's method or implements an
interface's method. Static methods and `compareTo` are included. It is also allowed on an instance
property that the parent class already declares. Anywhere else it is the error `E0882`. That
includes a method that replaces nothing and a constructor parameter that is not promoted. It also
includes an anonymous function, a static property, a constant and a `readonly` property.

The type must be one that `is` can test quickly: a class, an interface, an enum, a scalar, or a
nullable type or union of those. An array, a shape, a callable, a `class<T>` and a `property<T>` are
the error `E0883`. For those, take the wider type and test the value inside the method.

The new type must be narrower than the type in the first class that declares the parameter or the
property. The same type or a wider type with `covariant` is `E0882`, because the check would test
nothing. A grandchild class that repeats its parent's narrower type writes `covariant` too. A
`tainted` or `secret` type keeps that word. If the first class gives the parameter a default value,
the narrower type must accept that value, or the method is the error `E0884`.

An `inout` parameter is checked when the method is entered. A variadic parameter checks each value,
and the error names the first one that fails. A property is checked on every write. That includes a
write through `object` or `mixed`, a `property<T>` key, `Core\Reflect` and the parent's
constructor. A property with a `set` hook is checked before the hook runs. Reading a value is never
checked.

#### Example 01: a method that takes a narrower type

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a subclass method that takes a narrower parameter type with `covariant`.

class Animal
{
    public function constructor(public string $name)
    {}
}

class Dog extends Animal
{
    public function bark(): string
    {
        return $this->name . ' barks';
    }
}

class Shelter
{
    public function admit(Animal $a): string
    {
        return $a->name . ' is admitted';
    }
}

class DogShelter extends Shelter
{
    // `covariant Dog` means this method takes only a `Dog`.
    // Inside the body, `$a` is a `Dog`, so `bark` can be called.
    public function admit(covariant Dog $a): string
    {
        return $a->bark() . ' and is admitted';
    }
}

// The variable has the parent type, and the object is a `DogShelter`.
Shelter $shelter = new DogShelter();

// A `Dog` passes the check, so this prints "Rex barks and is admitted".
echo $shelter->admit(new Dog('Rex')), "\n";
```

```output
Rex barks and is admitted
```

#### Example 02: a wrong value throws a logic error

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the `LogicError` a `covariant` parameter throws when the value has the wrong type.

class Animal
{}
class Dog extends Animal
{}
class Cat extends Animal
{}

class Shelter
{
    public function admit(Animal $a): string
    {
        return 'admitted';
    }
}

class DogShelter extends Shelter
{
    public function admit(covariant Dog $a): string
    {
        return 'a dog is admitted';
    }
}

Shelter $shelter = new DogShelter();

// The parent type takes any `Animal`, so this call compiles.
// `DogShelter::admit` takes only a `Dog`, so the call throws before the body runs.
try {
    echo $shelter->admit(new Cat()), "\n";
} catch (LogicError $e) {
    echo $e->message, "\n";
}
```

```output
The parameter `$a` of `DogShelter::admit` has the type `Dog`. The argument is an object of class `Cat`.
```

#### Example 03: a property with a narrower type

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a subclass property with a narrower type, and the check on each write.

class Animal
{}
class Dog extends Animal
{}
class Cat extends Animal
{}

class Owner
{
    public function constructor(public Animal $pet)
    {}
}

class DogOwner extends Owner
{
    // This property has the type `Dog` in a `DogOwner`.
    public covariant Dog $pet;

    public function constructor(Dog $pet)
    {
        parent::constructor($pet);
    }
}

Owner $owner = new DogOwner(new Dog());

// A `Dog` passes the check.
$owner->pet = new Dog();
echo 'the new pet is a ', $owner->pet::class, "\n";

// The parent type allows a `Cat`, so this write compiles.
// The object is a `DogOwner`, so the write throws and the property keeps its `Dog`.
try {
    $owner->pet = new Cat();
} catch (LogicError $e) {
    echo $e->message, "\n";
}
echo 'the pet is still a ', $owner->pet::class, "\n";
```

```output
the new pet is a Dog
The property `$pet` of `DogOwner` has the type `Dog`. The value is an object of class `Cat`.
the pet is still a Dog
```

#### Example 04: compare to in a subclass

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `compareTo(covariant Price $other)` in a subclass of a `Comparable` class.

class Amount implements Comparable
{
    public function constructor(public int $cents)
    {}

    public function compareTo(self $other): int
    {
        return $this->cents <=> $other->cents;
    }
}

class Price extends Amount
{
    public function constructor(int $cents, public string $currency)
    {
        parent::constructor($cents);
    }

    // A `Price` compares only with another `Price`, so it can read `currency`.
    public function compareTo(covariant Price $other): int
    {
        if ($this->currency != $other->currency) {
            throw new LogicError('The two prices have different currencies.');
        }
        return $this->cents <=> $other->cents;
    }
}

Price $tea = new Price(250, 'EUR');
Price $cake = new Price(400, 'EUR');

// `<` calls `compareTo` on two `Price` objects. This prints `true`.
echo $tea < $cake ? 'true' : 'false', "\n";

// A call through the type `Amount` can pass a plain `Amount`.
// `Price::compareTo` takes only a `Price`, so the call throws.
Amount $amount = $tea;
try {
    echo $amount->compareTo(new Amount(100)), "\n";
} catch (LogicError $e) {
    echo $e->message, "\n";
}
```

```output
true
The parameter `$other` of `Price::compareTo` has the type `Price`. The argument is an object of class `Amount`.
```

#### Example 05: a narrower type needs covariant

```nvs error
<?nvs

// proof: compile-error

{}

    public function admit(Animal $a): void
```

```output
   --> main.nvs:18:21
   |
18 |     public function admit(Dog $a): void
   |                     ^^^^^ `$a` is `Dog`, and a call to `Shelter::admit` passes `Animal`
   = help: a call through `Shelter` passes what `Shelter::admit` takes and reads what it returns. Keep its parameters, its `static` and its visibility. Each parameter may accept a wider type, and the return type may be narrower. To take a narrower type, write `covariant` before it. Each value is then tested when the method is called

error: aborting due to 1 error
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```
