<a id="lang-iteration"></a>
## A.7 Iteration and generators

Keywords: foreach, Iterable, Iterator, iterate, advance, current, yield, generator, Generator, yield from, Core\Arr::from, lazy, finally, ObjectMap, ObjectSet, Heap, Channel

### What `foreach` walks

`foreach` is the loop that walks a collection of values and gives you one value at a time.

It accepts three kinds of subject: an array, an object whose class implements `Iterable`, and an
object whose class implements `Iterator`. A method that contains `yield` returns an `Iterator`, so it
is a subject too. Write `var` for the loop variable, and it gets the type of the subject's values. Or
write the type, and the compiler checks it. Over an array the loop may get the key as well as the
value. The other two subjects have no keys, so a loop over one gets the value alone.

**Good to know:** a method that takes `Iterable<T>` as a parameter type works with every class that
can be walked. One function can then read a list, a cart or a database result the same way.

**The examples below** show an array with and without its keys, then an object and a generator, then
a checkout that adds up a shopping cart. Each one uses `var` first and a written type after it.
Example 04 shows a second loop over the same iterator.

The key of an array is always a `string`, also when the array was written as a list. `var $k` is a
`string`, and `int $k` is the error `E0723`. Convert the key in the loop body if you need a number.

A written value type is checked against the element type. `string $v` over an `array<int>` is the
error `E0401`. This is the same over an `Iterable<int>` and an `Iterator<int>`.

Any other subject is the error `E0443`. That covers an object whose class implements neither
interface, an `int`, a `string` and a `?array<int>`. Check a nullable array for `null` before the
loop.

A loop over an `Iterator` walks the iterator itself. A second loop over the same iterator starts
where the first one stopped. After a complete loop, the second loop gets no values. After a
`break`, the second loop gets the values that are left.

#### Example 01: walking an array with and without its keys

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the two ways a `foreach` loop walks an array: the values alone, and the keys
// together with the values.

var $scores = ['ada' => 31, 'bob' => 27, 'cleo' => 44];

// The loop gives one value per step. `var $score` gets the type of the values, `int`.
var $total = 0;
foreach ($scores as var $score) {
    $total = $total + $score;
}
// This prints 102.
echo $total, "\n";

// An array also has keys. `string $name => int $score` gets both, and writes their types.
foreach ($scores as string $name => int $score) {
    echo $name, ' scored ', $score, "\n";
}
```

```output
102
ada scored 31
bob scored 27
cleo scored 44
```

#### Example 02: walking an object and an iterator

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the other two subjects a `foreach` loop accepts: an object whose class
// implements `Iterable`, and an `Iterator` returned by a method that contains `yield`.

class Weekdays implements Iterable<string>
{
    // `foreach` calls `iterate()` once and walks the iterator it returns.
    public function iterate(): Iterator<string>
    {
        yield 'Monday';
        yield 'Tuesday';
        yield 'Wednesday';
    }
}

class Steps
{
    // A method with `yield` returns an `Iterator`, which `foreach` walks directly.
    public static function upTo(int $last): Iterator<int>
    {
        int $i = 1;
        while ($i <= $last) {
            yield $i;
            $i = $i + 1;
        }
    }
}

// The subject is an object. `Weekdays` is an `Iterable<string>`, so `$day` is a
// `string`. This prints the three names.
foreach (new Weekdays() as var $day) {
    echo $day, "\n";
}

// The subject is an iterator. This loop writes the type `int` in place of `var`.
// This prints 1, 2 and 3.
foreach (Steps::upTo(3) as int $n) {
    echo $n, "\n";
}
```

```output
Monday
Tuesday
Wednesday
1
2
3
```

#### Example 03: adding up a shopping cart

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows one method that adds up a shopping cart. Its parameter type is `Iterable<Item>`,
// so it walks any class that can be walked and never needs to know how the cart stores
// its items.

class Item
{
    public function constructor(
        public string $name,
        public int $cents,
        public int $quantity,
    )
    {}
}

class Cart implements Iterable<Item>
{
    private array<Item> $items = [];

    public function add(Item $item): void
    {
        $this->items[] = $item;
    }

    public function iterate(): Iterator<Item>
    {
        // `var $item` is an `Item`, because `$this->items` is an `array<Item>`.
        foreach ($this->items as var $item) {
            yield $item;
        }
    }
}

class Checkout
{
    public static function total(Iterable<Item> $items): int
    {
        int $cents = 0;
        foreach ($items as Item $item) {
            $cents = $cents + $item->cents * $item->quantity;
        }
        return $cents;
    }
}

var $cart = new Cart();
$cart->add(new Item('Coffee', 749, 2));
$cart->add(new Item('Filter', 399, 1));

// This prints 1897, the price of the whole cart in cents.
echo Checkout::total($cart), "\n";
```

```output
1897
```

#### Example 04: an iterator continues where it stopped

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows that a second loop over the same `Iterator` starts where the first
// loop stopped. A loop over an `Iterable` starts again from the first value.

class Queue implements Iterable<string>
{
    public function iterate(): Iterator<string>
    {
        yield 'first';
        yield 'second';
        yield 'third';
    }
}

Queue $queue = new Queue();
Iterator<string> $jobs = $queue->iterate();

// The first loop stops after one value. This prints `first`.
foreach ($jobs as string $job) {
    echo $job, "\n";
    break;
}

// The same iterator gives the values that are left. This prints `second` and `third`.
foreach ($jobs as string $job) {
    echo $job, "\n";
}

// The object calls `iterate()` again for a new loop. This prints `first`.
foreach ($queue as string $job) {
    echo $job, "\n";
    break;
}
```

```output
first
second
third
first
```

### The two interfaces

Two interfaces make a class walkable by a `foreach` loop: `Iterator<T>` and `Iterable<T>`. There are
no others.

`Iterator<T>` is the cursor. `advance()` moves it to the next element and returns `false` once there
are none left. `current()` returns the element the last `advance()` moved to. `Iterable<T>` has one
method, `iterate()`, which returns a fresh `Iterator<T>`. A class declares one of the two at a
concrete type, such as `Iterator<int>`. Both names also work as a parameter type or a variable type.

**Good to know:** `foreach` calls `iterate()` once per loop, so one `Iterable<T>` object can be
walked twice, or nested inside a loop over itself. A cursor has no keys, so a loop over one cannot
bind a key.

**The examples below** show a cursor written by hand, then a class that gives out a fresh cursor per
loop, then a search result read page by page. Example 04 shows that a loop over a cursor cannot get
a key.

`implements Iterator` with no type argument is the error `E0442`. Write the element type, such as
`Iterator<int>`. A class of your own cannot declare a type argument. `class Box<T>` and
`interface Pair<T>` do not compile.

A class that implements `Iterator<T>` without `advance()` or `current()` is the error `E0449`. The
same is true for `Iterable<T>` without `iterate()`.

A class may implement both interfaces. `iterate()` may then return `$this`.

The three types are separate. An `array<int>` and an `Iterator<int>` are not an `Iterable<int>`, and
an `Iterable<int>` object is not an `Iterator<int>`. Passing one where another is needed is the error
`E0401`. The element type must match too: an `Iterable<int>` object is not an
`Iterable<int|string>`.

`current()` called before the first `advance()`, or after `advance()` returned `false`, throws a
`LogicError`. The message is `current() outside the iteration protocol: it answers only after
advance() returned true`.

#### Example 01: a cursor written by hand

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the `Iterator<T>` interface. A class that has `advance()` and `current()` can be
// walked by a `foreach` loop, and by a `while` loop that calls the two methods itself.

class Letters implements Iterator<string>
{
    // The cursor starts before the first element, so the first `advance()` reaches it.
    private int $at = -1;

    public function constructor(private array<string> $items)
    {}

    // Moves to the next element. The result is `false` once there are none left.
    public function advance(): bool
    {
        $this->at = $this->at + 1;
        return $this->at < (Core\Arr::count($this->items) as int);
    }

    // Returns the element the last `advance()` moved to.
    public function current(): string
    {
        return $this->items[$this->at];
    }
}

array<string> $abc = ['a', 'b', 'c'];

// The two methods are the whole protocol, so this loop does what a `foreach` does.
var $byHand = new Letters($abc);
while ($byHand->advance()) {
    echo $byHand->current();
}
echo "\n";

// The same three letters, with the loop calling the two methods for you.
foreach (new Letters($abc) as string $letter) {
    echo $letter;
}
echo "\n";
```

```output
abc
abc
```

#### Example 02: a fresh cursor for every loop

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the `Iterable<T>` interface. Its one method `iterate()` returns a cursor, and
// `foreach` calls it once per loop. Every loop therefore starts at the beginning.

class Countdown implements Iterable<int>
{
    public function constructor(private int $from)
    {}

    // A method with `yield` returns an `Iterator<int>`, which is what this must give.
    public function iterate(): Iterator<int>
    {
        int $i = $this->from;
        while ($i > 0) {
            yield $i;
            $i = $i - 1;
        }
    }
}

var $three = new Countdown(3);

// The same object is walked twice, and the second loop starts at 3 again.
foreach ($three as int $n) {
    echo $n;
}
echo "\n";
foreach ($three as int $n) {
    echo $n;
}
echo "\n";

// One loop inside another over the same object. Each loop has its own cursor, so this
// prints all nine pairs.
foreach ($three as int $outer) {
    foreach ($three as int $inner) {
        echo $outer, $inner, ' ';
    }
}
echo "\n";
```

```output
321
321
33 32 31 23 22 21 13 12 11
```

#### Example 03: reading a search result page by page

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a real use: a search result stored in pages. The class implements `Iterable<string>`,
// so the program reading the names never handles a page itself. A page the loop does not
// reach is never read.

class Results implements Iterable<string>
{
    public function constructor(private array<array<string>> $pages)
    {}

    public function iterate(): Iterator<string>
    {
        foreach ($this->pages as array<string> $page) {
            echo "(reading a page)\n";
            foreach ($page as string $name) {
                yield $name;
            }
        }
    }
}

var $results = new Results([
    ['Ada Lovelace', 'Alan Turing'],
    ['Grace Hopper', 'Edsger Dijkstra'],
    ['Barbara Liskov'],
]);

// The loop stops after three names, so the third page is never read.
int $shown = 0;
foreach ($results as string $name) {
    echo $name, "\n";
    $shown = $shown + 1;
    if ($shown == 3) {
        break;
    }
}
```

```output
(reading a page)
Ada Lovelace
Alan Turing
(reading a page)
Grace Hopper
```

#### Example 04: an iterator has no key

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that a loop over an `Iterator` cannot get a key. This loop does not
// compile. Write `as int $v` alone, or count the steps in your own variable.
// proof: compile-error

class Steps
{
    public static function upTo(int $n): Iterator<int>
    {
        int $i = 0;
        while ($i < $n) {
            yield $i;
            $i = $i + 1;
        }
    }
}

foreach (Steps::upTo(3) as string $k => int $v) {
    echo $k, '=', $v, "\n";
}
```

```output
error[E0444]: an `Iterable`/`Iterator` subject has no key to bind
   --> main.nvs:18:28
   |
18 | foreach (Steps::upTo(3) as string $k => int $v) {
   |                            ^^^^^^^^^ no key exists here
   = help: an iterator has values but no keys. Remove the `$k =>`, or loop over an `array<T>`

error: aborting due to 1 error
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```

### Generators

A generator is a method that gives out its values one at a time, as a loop asks for them.

Write `yield` in the body and declare `Iterator<T>` as the return type. Calling the method runs none
of the body. It returns a cursor, and each step of a `foreach` loop runs the body as far as the next
`yield`. When the loop ends, the body stops where it is. This makes a generator cheap. It has one
value at a time, and it can give a sequence that goes on forever.

**Good to know:** a generator is walked once. A second `foreach` over the same cursor sees nothing,
and calling the method again gives you a new cursor that starts at the beginning.

You cannot `clone` a generator. `clone Gen::count(3)` does not compile. If the generator is in a
`mixed` or `Iterator<T>` variable, `clone` throws a `LogicError`. To start again, call the method
again.

**The examples below** show a small generator first, then a sequence with no end, then two
generators reading one report together. Then they show separate cursors and `return;`, a `finally`
block, an error thrown in a generator, and two code examples that do not compile.

A method with `yield` in its body must return `Iterator<T>`. Any other return type is the error
`E0446`. This is true for `Iterable<T>`, `array<T>` and `void`. `Generator` is not declared, so it is
the error `E0303`. A method that returns `Iterator<T>` but has no `yield` is an ordinary method. It
must return a value, or it is the error `E0739`.

`yield` works only in the body of the generator itself. A `yield` at the top level of a file, or in
an anonymous function, is the error `E0445`. This is also true for an anonymous function inside a
generator.

A static method, an instance method and `iterate()` may each be a generator. An `iterate()` that
yields gives a new generator for each loop, so the object can be walked many times.

`yield` is a statement and has no value. These forms are the error `E0448`:

- `int $x = yield 2;`, since nothing is sent back into a generator.
- `yield "a" => 1;`, since an `Iterator<T>` has no keys.
- `yield;` with no value.
- `yield from G::inner();`. Write `foreach (G::inner() as int $v) { yield $v; }` instead.

The value of a `yield` must have the type `T`. `yield "a";` in an `Iterator<int>` is the error
`E0401`.

`return;` ends the sequence early. `return 5;` is the error `E0447`, because a generator has no
return value.

A generator cannot take an `inout` parameter. That is the error `E0492`. The arguments are copied
when the method is called. A change to the caller's array after the call is not seen by the
generator.

`current()` called before the first `advance()`, or after `advance()` returned `false`, throws a
`LogicError`. Once the sequence has ended, every later `advance()` returns `false`.

A loop over a generator cannot have a key. `foreach (G::g() as string $k => int $v)` is the error
`E0444`.

`clone G::g()` is the error `E0858`. `clone` of a generator in a variable throws a `LogicError` with
the message `clone(): a generator is a suspended frame, so it has no meaning on the other side of a
copy boundary`.

A `finally` block around a `yield` runs when the body reaches its end. It also runs when the loop
stops early with `break`, before the code after the loop. A generator that was advanced and then
freed runs its `finally` too. This happens when its last variable gets a new value. A generator that
was never advanced runs nothing.

A `throw` in the body reaches the `foreach` loop or the `advance()` call that resumed the generator.
The values yielded before it have already been given to the loop. A `try` and `catch` inside the body
can catch the error, and the body can then go on yielding.

A generator can read another generator with `foreach`, and a generator can call itself in the same
way. A generator stored in a `mixed` variable is an `Iterator<T>` for `is`. A `foreach` over the
`mixed` variable is the error `E0443`.

#### Example 01: a method that yields its values

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to write a generator: a method whose body contains `yield`. It gives
// out one value at a time, and the body runs only as far as the loop asks.

class Countdown
{
    // A generator declares `Iterator<T>` as its return type. Each `yield` gives one `T`.
    public static function from(int $start): Iterator<int>
    {
        echo "the body starts\n";
        int $n = $start;
        while ($n > 0) {
            yield $n;
            $n = $n - 1;
        }
        echo "the body ends\n";
    }
}

// Calling the method runs none of the body. It returns a cursor, and prints nothing.
Iterator<int> $numbers = Countdown::from(3);
echo "the cursor exists\n";

// The loop is what runs the body. This prints 3, 2 and 1.
foreach ($numbers as int $n) {
    echo $n, "\n";
}
```

```output
the cursor exists
the body starts
3
2
1
the body ends
```

#### Example 02: a sequence with no end

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a generator whose loop has no end. The body runs one step per value, so a
// sequence without an end is safe to write and safe to walk.

class Backoff
{
    // Every wait is twice the one before it: 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on.
    public static function delays(int $first): Iterator<int>
    {
        int $wait = $first;
        while (true) {
            yield $wait;
            $wait = $wait * 2;
        }
    }
}

int $attempt = 0;
foreach (Backoff::delays(1) as int $seconds) {
    $attempt = $attempt + 1;
    echo "attempt {$attempt} waits {$seconds}s\n";
    // `break` leaves the generator where it stopped. The body runs no further,
    // so the loop above ends after four values.
    if ($attempt == 4) {
        break;
    }
}
```

```output
attempt 1 waits 1s
attempt 2 waits 2s
attempt 3 waits 4s
attempt 4 waits 8s
```

#### Example 03: scanning a report line by line

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows two generators working together: one reads the lines of a report, the other
// keeps the lines that matter. A program uses this shape to scan a long report while
// holding one line at a time.

class Report
{
    // Gives out the lines of the text, one per `yield`.
    public static function lines(string $text): Iterator<string>
    {
        foreach (Core\Str::lines($text) as string $line) {
            yield $line;
        }
    }

    // Reads the generator above and keeps only the failures. A `foreach` with a
    // `yield` inside it is how one generator reads another.
    public static function failures(Iterator<string> $lines): Iterator<string>
    {
        foreach ($lines as string $line) {
            if (Core\Str::startsWith($line, 'ERROR')) {
                yield $line;
            }
        }
    }
}

string $log = "INFO started\nERROR disk full\nINFO retry\nERROR timeout\nINFO done\n";

// This prints the two `ERROR` lines. The report is walked once, and neither
// generator builds a list of its own.
foreach (Report::failures(Report::lines($log)) as string $failure) {
    echo $failure, "\n";
}
```

```output
ERROR disk full
ERROR timeout
```

#### Example 04: each call gives its own cursor

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows that each call gives a new cursor, that `return;` ends the values early,
// and that a cursor is walked once.

class Numbers
{
    public static function count(int $n): Iterator<int>
    {
        int $i = 0;
        while ($i < $n) {
            yield $i;
            $i = $i + 1;
        }
    }

    public static function early(bool $stop): Iterator<int>
    {
        yield 1;
        if ($stop) {
            return;
        }
        yield 2;
    }
}

// Two calls give two cursors. Each one keeps its own place, so this prints 10.
Iterator<int> $a = Numbers::count(3);
Iterator<int> $b = Numbers::count(3);
$a->advance();
$a->advance();
$b->advance();
echo $a->current(), $b->current(), "\n";

// `return;` stops the values. This prints 1, then 12.
foreach (Numbers::early(true) as int $v) {
    echo $v;
}
echo "\n";
foreach (Numbers::early(false) as int $v) {
    echo $v;
}
echo "\n";

// The second loop over the same cursor gets no values. This prints 01 once.
Iterator<int> $once = Numbers::count(2);
foreach ($once as int $v) {
    echo $v;
}
foreach ($once as int $v) {
    echo $v;
}
echo "\n";
```

```output
10
1
12
01
```

#### Example 05: finally runs when the loop stops

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows that a `finally` block in a generator runs when the body ends, and also
// when the loop stops early with `break`.

class Rows
{
    public static function read(int $n): Iterator<int>
    {
        try {
            int $i = 0;
            while ($i < $n) {
                yield $i;
                $i = $i + 1;
            }
        } finally {
            echo '[closed]';
        }
    }
}

// The body reaches its end, so this prints 012[closed].
foreach (Rows::read(3) as int $v) {
    echo $v;
}
echo "\n";

// `break` stops the loop after 1. The `finally` block still runs, so this prints 01[closed].
foreach (Rows::read(5) as int $v) {
    echo $v;
    if ($v == 1) {
        break;
    }
}
echo "\n";
```

```output
012[closed]
01[closed]
```

#### Example 06: an error thrown by a generator

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows that an error thrown in a generator reaches the loop that reads it.

class Feed
{
    public static function upTo(int $n): Iterator<int>
    {
        int $i = 0;
        while ($i < $n) {
            if ($i == 2) {
                throw new RuntimeError('bad element 2');
            }
            yield $i;
            $i = $i + 1;
        }
    }
}

// The loop gets 0 and 1 first. Then the error reaches the `catch` block,
// so this prints 0;1;caught: bad element 2.
try {
    foreach (Feed::upTo(5) as int $v) {
        echo $v, ';';
    }
} catch (RuntimeError $e) {
    echo 'caught: ', $e->message, "\n";
}
```

```output
0;1;caught: bad element 2
```

#### Example 07: yield from does not exist

```nvs error
    }

    public static function all(): Iterator<int>

}
```

### `Core` collections are `Iterable`

A `foreach` loop walks a `Core` collection the same way it walks an array.

Four classes work this way. `Core\ObjectSet` gives you its members and `Core\ObjectMap` gives you its
keys, both in the order you added them. `Core\Heap` gives you its elements smallest first, and leaves
the heap full. `Core\Task\Channel` gives you each value another task sent, and the loop ends when that
task calls `close`.

A set, a map and a heap take a copy of their contents when the loop starts. The loop walks that copy,
so your code may add or remove inside the loop body. The loop still visits what was there at the
start, and your changes are in the collection when it ends.

**The examples below** show a set and a map first, then a heap, then a channel between two tasks.

`Core\ObjectSet<T>`, `Core\Heap<T>` and `Core\Task\Channel<T>` are each an `Iterable<T>`.
`Core\ObjectMap<K, V>` is an `Iterable<K>`. You can pass each one to a parameter of that type.

A loop over a map gives the keys, never the values. `int $v` over an `ObjectMap<string, int>` is the
error `E0401`. A key variable is not allowed: `foreach ($map as string $k => int $v)` is the error
`E0444`. The written type of the loop variable must be the element type, or the error is `E0401`.
`var $v` takes the element type.

A heap made with a compare function gives its elements in the order that function sets. A heap of
`Comparable` objects gives them in the order of `compareTo`.

A set, a map and a heap can be walked many times, and each loop gives every element again.

A loop over a channel takes each value out of it. A second loop over the same closed channel gets no
values. Values sent before `close` are still given to the loop.

#### Example 01: walking a set and a map

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to walk a `Core\ObjectSet` and a `Core\ObjectMap` with `foreach`.

var $tags = new Core\ObjectSet<string>();
$tags->add('blue');
$tags->add('green');
$tags->add('blue');

// A set holds each value once, so "blue" is in it once. The loop gives you the
// members in the order you added them. This prints blue and then green.
foreach ($tags as string $tag) {
    echo $tag, "\n";
}

var $stock = new Core\ObjectMap<string, int>();
$stock->set('apples', 12);
$stock->set('pears', 4);

// A loop over a map gives you the keys. Use `get` to read the value for a key.
foreach ($stock as string $name) {
    echo $name, ' ', $stock->get($name), "\n";
}
```

```output
blue
green
apples 12
pears 4
```

#### Example 02: reading a heap without emptying it

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to read every element of a `Core\Heap` in priority order.

var $costs = new Core\Heap<int>();
$costs->push(30);
$costs->push(5);
$costs->push(17);

// The loop gives you the elements smallest first. This prints 5, 17 and 30.
foreach ($costs as int $cost) {
    echo $cost, "\n";
}

// The loop takes nothing out of the heap. All three elements are still there,
// so this prints 3.
echo $costs->count(), "\n";

// `pop` is what removes one. This prints 5, the same element the loop saw first.
echo $costs->pop(), "\n";
```

```output
5
17
30
3
5
```

#### Example 03: a worker task reading its jobs

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a worker task taking its jobs from a `Core\Task\Channel` with `foreach`.

class Report
{
    public static string $done = '';
}

// The channel holds 2 jobs at a time. A sender waits while it is full, so a fast
// sender cannot fill up the memory of a slow worker.
var $jobs = new Core\Task\Channel<string>(2);

Core\Task::all({
    fill: fn(): int => {
        array<string> $queue = ['resize-logo', 'resize-banner', 'resize-icon'];
        foreach ($queue as string $job) {
            $jobs->send($job);
        }
        // `close` ends the loop in the other task. Without it, that loop waits forever.
        $jobs->close();
        return 0;
    },
    work: fn(): int => {
        // The loop gives you each job that was sent, in the order it was sent.
        foreach ($jobs as string $job) {
            Report::$done = Report::$done . $job . ' ';
        }
        return 0;
    },
});

// Both tasks have finished here, so this prints all three job names.
echo Report::$done, "\n";
```

```output
resize-logo resize-banner resize-icon
```

### Materialising a sequence: `Core\Arr::from`

`Core\Arr::from` turns a sequence into a plain array.

It takes whatever a `foreach` loop takes: an array, a generator, an object you can walk, or a `Core`
collection. The result is an `array<T>` numbered from `0`, holding the values in the order the
sequence gave them. Use it when you need the whole sequence at once, to count it, to sort it, or to
read it more than once. A generator is walked once and is then spent, so keep the array you get
back.

**Good to know:** the `limit` option stops the walk after the number of values you name. A sequence
with no end needs it, or the call never returns.

**The examples below** show a generator collected into an array, then `limit` on a sequence with no
end, then a `Core` collection sorted.

The element type of the result is the element type of the sequence. A generator of `int` gives an
`array<int>`, and a `Core\ObjectMap<string, int>` gives an `array<string>`. Assigning the result to
another array type is the error `E0401`.

An array literal written in the call gives an `array<mixed>`. `array<int> $b =
Core\Arr::from([1, 2, 3]);` is the error `E0401`. Put the array in a typed variable first.

The keys of an array are not kept. An array with the keys `"x"` and `"y"` gives an array with the
keys `0` and `1`.

The argument must be an array, an `Iterable<T>`, an `Iterator<T>` or a `Core` collection. Any other
type is the error `E0401`, and this is true for `mixed` too.

`limit` is a `uint`. A negative number or a string is the error `E0401`. `limit: 0` gives an empty
array, and the body of a generator does not run. A limit larger than the sequence gives the whole
sequence. Any other option name is the error `E0454`.

With `limit`, a generator stops where the limit is reached. A later loop or a later
`Core\Arr::from` over the same generator continues with the next value.

A heap is not emptied. `Core\Arr::from` gives its elements in priority order, and the heap still has
them all.

An error thrown by a generator reaches the code that called `Core\Arr::from`.

#### Example 01: a generator as an array

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to collect the values of a generator into a plain array.

class Fibonacci
{
    public static function first(int $many): Iterator<int>
    {
        int $a = 1;
        int $b = 1;
        int $n = 0;
        while ($n < $many) {
            yield $a;
            int $next = $a + $b;
            $a = $b;
            $b = $next;
            $n = $n + 1;
        }
    }
}

// `Core\Arr::from` walks the generator to its end and keeps every value.
array<int> $numbers = Core\Arr::from(Fibonacci::first(7));

// The keys start at 0. This prints 7, then 13.
echo Core\Arr::count($numbers), "\n";
echo $numbers[6], "\n";

// The values are in an array now, so you can read them as often as you like.
// This prints 33.
echo Core\Arr::sum($numbers), "\n";
```

```output
7
13
33
```

#### Example 02: taking the first few values

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the `limit` option, which stops the walk after the number of values you name.

class Ids
{
    // This generator has no end.
    public static function forever(string $prefix): Iterator<string>
    {
        int $n = 1;
        while (true) {
            yield "{$prefix}-{$n}";
            $n = $n + 1;
        }
    }
}

// `limit` is what makes this call return. It stops the walk after three values.
array<string> $batch = Core\Arr::from(Ids::forever('order'), { limit: 3 });

// This prints order-1, order-2 and order-3.
foreach ($batch as string $id) {
    echo $id, "\n";
}
```

```output
order-1
order-2
order-3
```

#### Example 03: sorting what a collection holds

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to take a `Core` collection into an array and sort it. A program does this
// when it gathers values while it works and puts them in order at the end.

var $seen = new Core\ObjectSet<string>();
$seen->add('marta');
$seen->add('ada');
$seen->add('kofi');
$seen->add('ada');

// A set gives its members in the order you added them, and keeps each one once.
// This prints 3.
array<string> $names = Core\Arr::from($seen);
echo Core\Arr::count($names), "\n";

// `Core\Arr::sort` needs every value at once, which is why the array above is made
// first. This prints ada, kofi and marta.
foreach (Core\Arr::sort($names) as string $name) {
    echo $name, "\n";
}
```

```output
3
ada
kofi
marta
```

### What does not exist

PHP's iteration helpers do not exist in Novis. Naming one is a compile error.

There is no `ArrayAccess`, `Countable`, `IteratorAggregate`, `Traversable` or `Generator`, and no
`iterator_to_array`, `count`, `current`, `next` or `reset`. Each one has a replacement. A class
becomes walkable by implementing `Iterable<T>` or `Iterator<T>`. A generator returns an
`Iterator<T>`, so it needs no class of its own. `Core\Arr` holds what the free functions did:
`Core\Arr::count` counts, and `Core\Arr::from` reads a sequence into an array. Reading an element of
an object, `$basket[0]`, has no interface behind it. Give the class a method and name it yourself.

**Good to know:** you meet all of these when you compile, never while the program is running.

**The examples below** show the three replacements: `Iterable<T>` for `IteratorAggregate`, `Core\Arr`
for the free functions, and methods of your own for `ArrayAccess` and `Countable`. The last two
examples show `Countable` and `iterator_to_array` as compile errors.

`Countable`, `ArrayAccess`, `IteratorAggregate`, `Traversable` and `Generator` are not declared. A
class that implements one, or a parameter of one of these types, is the error `E0303`. The message
names no replacement.

`iterator_to_array`, `iterator_count`, `count`, `current`, `next`, `reset` and `array_walk` are not
functions. A call to one is the error `E0320`.

`$obj[0]` on an object is the error `E0482`, for a read and for a write. Only an array can be read
with `[ ]`.

A `foreach` loop over an object that implements neither `Iterable<T>` nor `Iterator<T>` is the error
`E0443`. A method named `getIterator` does not change this. A loop never reads an object's
properties.

#### Example 01: iterable in place of iteratoraggregate

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the replacement for PHP's `IteratorAggregate` and `Traversable`. A class becomes
// walkable by implementing `Iterable<T>` and writing one method, `iterate()`.

class Playlist implements Iterable<string>
{
    private array<string> $tracks = [];

    public function add(string $title): void
    {
        $this->tracks[] = $title;
    }

    // This replaces `getIterator()`. The return type names what the loop reads.
    public function iterate(): Iterator<string>
    {
        foreach ($this->tracks as string $title) {
            yield $title;
        }
    }
}

var $playlist = new Playlist();
$playlist->add('Blue in Green');
$playlist->add('So What');

// The object is now a subject a `foreach` loop accepts.
foreach ($playlist as string $title) {
    echo $title, "\n";
}
```

```output
Blue in Green
So What
```

#### Example 02: core arr in place of the free functions

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the replacements for PHP's `iterator_to_array` and `count`. Both live on `Core\Arr`,
// so there is no free function to call.

class Series
{
    public static function squares(int $upTo): Iterator<int>
    {
        int $i = 1;
        while ($i <= $upTo) {
            yield $i * $i;
            $i = $i + 1;
        }
    }
}

// `Core\Arr::from` reads a sequence into an array. This replaces `iterator_to_array`.
array<int> $squares = Core\Arr::from(Series::squares(5));
echo $squares[0], ',', $squares[4], "\n";

// `Core\Arr::count` returns the number of elements. This replaces `count`.
echo Core\Arr::count($squares), "\n";
```

```output
1,25
5
```

#### Example 03: methods of your own in place of arrayaccess

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a real use: a basket that PHP would give `ArrayAccess` and `Countable`. Novis has
// neither interface, so the class names its own methods. A reader of this code sees what
// each one does without looking the interface up.

class Line
{
    public function constructor(public string $sku, public int $quantity)
    {}
}

class Basket implements Iterable<Line>
{
    private array<Line> $lines = [];

    public function put(string $sku, int $quantity): void
    {
        $this->lines[] = new Line($sku, $quantity);
    }

    // This replaces `offsetGet`, and the name says which line it returns.
    public function lineAt(int $position): Line
    {
        return $this->lines[$position];
    }

    // This replaces `count`, and it returns the number of lines.
    public function size(): int
    {
        return Core\Arr::count($this->lines) as int;
    }

    public function iterate(): Iterator<Line>
    {
        foreach ($this->lines as Line $line) {
            yield $line;
        }
    }
}

var $basket = new Basket();
$basket->put('COFFEE-1KG', 2);
$basket->put('FILTER-100', 1);

// This prints 2 lines, then COFFEE-1KG.
echo $basket->size(), " lines\n";
echo $basket->lineAt(0)->sku, "\n";

foreach ($basket as Line $line) {
    echo $line->sku, ' x', $line->quantity, "\n";
}
```

```output
2 lines
COFFEE-1KG
COFFEE-1KG x2
FILTER-100 x1
```

```nvs error
// Shows that `iterator_to_array` is not a function, so this call does not compile.

// proof: compile-error
```

```output
   = help: every function is a method of a class. The built-in functions are in the `Core` namespace. Write `Core\Str::length($s)`, or write `use Core\Str;` and then `Str::length($s)`
```

<a id="lang-errors"></a>
## A.8 Errors, exceptions and limits

Keywords: Throwable, Exception, Error, LogicError, RuntimeError, IOError, ParseError, TimeoutError, RecursionError, ArithmeticError, throw, try, catch, finally, multi-catch, rethrow, previous, backtrace, location, message, getMessage, getPrevious, getTrace, getCode, uncaught exception, error handler, fatal, FATAL, memory limit, onLimit, capability, fs.read, script.spawn, Core\Fatal, Core\Debug, dump a value, assertion, Core\Test\Failure

### The throwable tree

Every error in Novis is an object of a class under `Throwable`, and the whole tree is short. There
is no `Exception` and no `Error`.

`LogicError` means a bug in your own program, such as a `match` with no arm for the value it was
given. `RuntimeError` means the world said no: a missing array key, a value that cannot be
converted, a file you are not allowed to read. `IOError`, `ParseError`, `TimeoutError` and
`RecursionError` are kinds of `RuntimeError`. `ArithmeticError` is its own branch, for division by
zero and for a number that does not fit.

A `catch` arm also catches every class under the one it names, so `catch (Throwable $e)` catches
everything.

**The examples below** show which class each common failure throws, how one arm takes a whole
branch, and a job that treats a bug and a bad input differently. The last one shows the error for
`Exception`.

`Exception` and `Error` are not declared. `class ConfigError extends Exception`, `catch (Error $e)` and
`new Exception("…")` are each the error `E0303`. Write `Throwable`, `LogicError` or `RuntimeError`.

`Throwable` is a class. You can create one with `new Throwable("…")`, and you can extend it directly.

`ArithmeticError` extends `Throwable`, not `RuntimeError`. A `catch (RuntimeError $e)` clause does not
catch it. These are the messages it has:

- Division by zero gives `Division by zero`.
- `%` by zero gives `Modulo by zero`.
- An `int` addition past the largest `int` gives `Integer addition overflowed`.
- `2.5 as int` gives ``cannot convert `float` 2.5 to `int` ``. A `float` with a fraction does not
  convert to `int`.

Your own class can extend any class in the tree, `ArithmeticError` and `ParseError` too. A class that
extends `ParseError` has `issues`, and the list is empty. A class in the tree may be `final` or
`abstract`.

`Core\Test\Failure` is the class of a failed assertion. It extends `Throwable` directly, and your own
class cannot extend it: that is the error `E0303`.

`Core\Script::finish()` ends the program, and no `catch` catches it. A `finally` block still runs.

#### Example 01: which class a failure throws

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows which class each common failure throws. The class tells you what kind
// of problem it is, so you can catch only the kind you can handle.

int $zero = 0;
array<int> $stock = ['mugs' => 4];
mixed $text = 'abc';

// Division by zero is an `ArithmeticError`.
try {
    echo 1 / $zero, "\n";
} catch (ArithmeticError $divided) {
    echo $divided->message, "\n";
}

// A key that is not in the array is a `RuntimeError`.
try {
    echo $stock['plates'], "\n";
} catch (RuntimeError $missing) {
    echo $missing->message, "\n";
}

// A value that cannot be converted is a `RuntimeError` as well.
try {
    echo $text as int, "\n";
} catch (RuntimeError $bad) {
    echo $bad->message, "\n";
}

// A `match` with no arm for the value is a bug in the program, so it is a
// `LogicError`.
try {
    echo match ($zero) { 1 => 'one' }, "\n";
} catch (LogicError $noArm) {
    echo $noArm->message, "\n";
}
```

```output
Division by zero
undefined array key `plates`
cannot convert this value to `int`
no `match` arm matched the subject
```

#### Example 02: one arm takes a whole branch

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows that a `catch` arm also catches every class under the one it names.
// `IOError`, `ParseError` and `TimeoutError` are kinds of `RuntimeError`.

final class Feed
{
    public static function fetch(string $source): tainted string
    {
        if ($source == 'slow') {
            throw new TimeoutError('the feed did not answer in time');
        }
        if ($source == 'gone') {
            throw new IOError('the feed file is missing');
        }
        return Core\Json::encode(Core\Json::decode($source));
    }
}

array<string> $sources = ["{\"ok\": true}", 'slow', 'gone', "{\"ok\": }"];
foreach ($sources as string $source) {
    try {
        echo Feed::fetch($source), "\n";
    } catch (ParseError $bad) {
        // The narrow arm goes first. It takes the parse errors and nothing else.
        echo 'bad input: ', $bad->message, "\n";
    } catch (RuntimeError $other) {
        // The wide arm takes the rest of the branch, here a timeout and a
        // missing file.
        echo 'the feed said no: ', $other->message, "\n";
    }
}
```

```output
{"ok":true}
the feed said no: the feed did not answer in time
the feed said no: the feed file is missing
bad input: Core\Json::decode(): expected value at line 1 column 8
```

#### Example 03: a bug and a bad input

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a job that treats the two halves of the tree differently. A
// `RuntimeError` is bad input, so the job reports the line and carries on. A
// `LogicError` is a bug in the program, so the job stops.

final class Cart
{
    public static function total(array<int> $line): int
    {
        // A field that is not there throws a `RuntimeError`.
        int $price = $line['price'];
        int $count = $line['count'];
        if ($count < 0) {
            // A count below zero can only come from our own code.
            throw new LogicError('a line with a count below zero');
        }
        return $price * $count;
    }
}

array<array<int>> $lines = [
    ['price' => 250, 'count' => 2],
    ['price' => 400],
    ['price' => 100, 'count' => 0 - 1],
];

int $sum = 0;
foreach ($lines as array<int> $line) {
    try {
        $sum = $sum + Cart::total($line);
    } catch (RuntimeError $input) {
        echo 'skipped a line: ', $input->message, "\n";
    } catch (LogicError $bug) {
        echo 'stopping, this is a bug: ', $bug->message, "\n";
        break;
    }
}
echo 'total ', $sum, "\n";
```

```output
skipped a line: undefined array key `count`
stopping, this is a bug: a line with a count below zero
total 500
```

#### Example 04: exception is not a class

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that `Exception` does not exist. Extend `RuntimeError` or
// `LogicError` instead.
// proof: compile-error

class ConfigError extends Exception
{
}
```

```output
error[E0303]: `Exception` is not declared
  --> main.nvs:6:27
  |
6 | class ConfigError extends Exception
  |                           ^^^^^^^^^ no matching declaration

error: aborting due to 1 error
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```

| Class | Extends | Own properties |
|---|---|---|
| `Throwable` | — (the root) | `$message`, `$previous`, `$backtrace`, `$location` |
| `LogicError` | `Throwable` | — |
| `RuntimeError` | `Throwable` | — |
| `IOError` | `RuntimeError` | — |
| `ParseError` | `RuntimeError` | `$issues` |
| `TimeoutError` | `RuntimeError` | — |
| `RecursionError` | `RuntimeError` | — |
| `ExtensionError` | `RuntimeError` | — |
| `ArithmeticError` | `Throwable` | — |
| `Core\Test\Failure` | `Throwable` | — |
| `Core\Cli\NotInteractive` | `RuntimeError` | — |
| `Core\Db\DbError` | `RuntimeError` | `$kind`, `$sqlState`, `$driverCode`, `$constraint`, `$sql` |
| `Core\Db\RolledBack` | `RuntimeError` | `$reason` |
| `Core\Ldap\LdapError` | `RuntimeError` | `$kind`, `$code` |
| `Core\DeprecatedError` | `LogicError` | — |
| `Core\Script\Finished` | — (the root) | — |

### Properties, not accessors

You read a caught error through its properties. There are no accessor methods.

`getMessage()`, `getPrevious()`, `getTrace()`, `getFile()`, `getLine()` and `getCode()` do not
exist. Write `$e->message` instead.

Every error has the same four properties. `message` is the text it was created with. `previous` is
the error that caused it, or `null`. `backtrace` is one line per function the throw came out of,
innermost first. `location` is the file and the line of the `throw`. A `ParseError` adds `issues`,
one entry per problem the parser found, each with a `path` and a `message`.

**Good to know:** there is no error code anywhere. The class of the error is what says what kind of
problem it is.

**The examples below** show where a throw came from, the list of problems in a parse error, and one
log line built out of a caught error. The last one shows the error for `getMessage()`.

`getMessage()`, `getPrevious()`, `getTrace()`, `getTraceAsString()`, `getFile()`, `getLine()` and
`getCode()` are each the error `E0405`. The help names the property to read instead. For `getCode()` it
lists the four properties, because there is no error code. `$e->code` is the error `E0405` too.

All four properties are `readonly`. `$e->message = "…"` is the error `E0782`.

`location` is the empty string until the object is thrown. When the same object is thrown a second
time, `location` changes to the line of the second `throw`.

`backtrace` has one line for each method the throw left. A throw in the top-level code of a file has
one line, `<script>() at main.nvs:2`. An object that was never thrown has an empty `backtrace`.

`previous` is a `?Throwable`. `$e->previous->message` is the error `E0459`, because `previous` may be
`null`. Write `$e->previous?->message`.

`issues` exists on `ParseError` and its subclasses. On any other class, `$e->issues` is the error
`E0405`. A `ParseError` that your own code creates has an empty `issues` list.

`Core\Debug::dump($e)` prints the four properties. `echo $e` is the error `E0412`, and
`Core\Json::encode($e)` throws a `RuntimeError`. Build the text from `$e->message` and the other
properties.

#### Example 01: where a throw came from

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the two properties that say where an error came from. `location` is the
// file and the line of the `throw`. `backtrace` has one line per function the
// throw came out of, the innermost one first.

final class Prices
{
    public static function of(string $item): int
    {
        throw new RuntimeError('no price for ' . $item);
    }

    public static function totalOf(string $item): int
    {
        return Prices::of($item) * 2;
    }
}

try {
    echo Prices::totalOf('blue mug'), "\n";
} catch (RuntimeError $failed) {
    echo $failed->message, "\n";
    echo 'thrown at ', $failed->location, "\n";
    foreach ($failed->backtrace as string $frame) {
        echo '  ', $frame, "\n";
    }
}
```

```output
no price for blue mug
thrown at main.nvs:10
  Prices::of() at main.nvs:10
  Prices::totalOf() at main.nvs:15
```

#### Example 02: every problem in one list

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the extra property of a `ParseError`. `issues` has one entry per
// problem the parser found. This form has two bad fields, and both of them are
// in the list.

array<string> $form = ['name' => 'Ada', 'age' => 'not a number', 'active' => 'yes'];

try {
    Core\Arr::shapeAs<{ name: string, age: int, active: bool }>($form);
    echo "the form is good\n";
} catch (ParseError $bad) {
    echo $bad->message, "\n";
    foreach ($bad->issues as ({ path: string, message: string }) $issue) {
        // `path` names the field, and `message` says what is wrong with it.
        echo '  ', $issue->path, ': ', $issue->message, "\n";
    }
}
```

```output
Core\Arr::shapeAs(): 2 value(s) of `$shape{active,age,name}` did not match
  active: expected bool, found a string
  age: expected int, found a string
```

#### Example 03: one log line for a failure

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows one log line built out of a caught error. It says what went wrong,
// where it was thrown, and which error caused it. The chain is followed to the
// first cause.

class CheckoutFailed extends RuntimeError
{
    public function constructor(string $message, ?Throwable $cause)
    {
        parent::constructor($message, { previous: $cause });
    }
}

final class Checkout
{
    public static function pay(string $order): string
    {
        try {
            throw new TimeoutError('the payment service did not answer');
        } catch (TimeoutError $slow) {
            throw new CheckoutFailed('order ' . $order . ' was not paid', $slow);
        }
    }
}

try {
    echo Checkout::pay('4021'), "\n";
} catch (Throwable $failed) {
    string $line = $failed->message . ' at ' . $failed->location;
    var $cause = $failed->previous;
    bool $more = true;
    while ($more) {
        // `previous` is `null` at the end of the chain. So the code copies it
        // into a variable and checks it before it reads `message`.
        var $here = $cause;
        if ($here == null) {
            $more = false;
        } else {
            $line = $line . ', caused by: ' . $here->message;
            $cause = $here->previous;
        }
    }
    echo $line, "\n";
    echo 'frames: ', Core\Arr::count($failed->backtrace), "\n";
}
```

```output
order 4021 was not paid at main.nvs:21, caused by: the payment service did not answer
frames: 1
```

#### Example 04: getmessage does not exist

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that `getMessage()` does not exist. The error tells you to read the
// `message` property instead.
// proof: compile-error

try {
    throw new LogicError('boom');
} catch (Throwable $e) {
    echo $e->getMessage();
}
```

```output
error[E0405]: `Throwable` has no method named `getMessage`
  --> main.nvs:9:10
  |
9 |     echo $e->getMessage();
  |          ^^ referenced here
  = help: an exception has properties and no accessor methods. Write `->message`. The properties are `message`, `previous`, `backtrace`, `location`

error: aborting due to 1 error
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```

### Constructing and subclassing

Every error is built the same way: `new` with a message, and an optional second argument naming the
error that caused this one.

You can write an error class of your own. It extends `Throwable` or any class under it. A class that
writes no constructor uses the one it inherits, so `new OutOfStock("no mugs left")` works with
nothing else to write. A class that wants more can write its own constructor, add properties, and
pass the message on with `parent::constructor($message)`.

A message is always required. `new RuntimeError()` does not compile.

**Good to know:** both arguments have names, so you can write
`new RuntimeError(message: "the server said no")` and read the call without counting positions.

**The examples below** show an error class of your own, one that adds properties in its own
constructor, and a loader that keeps the error it caught as the cause of the error it throws.

The message must be a `string`. `new RuntimeError(5)` is the error `E0401`. A `tainted string` is the
error `E0401` too, so check text from outside the program before you put it in a message.

`previous` takes a `Throwable` or `null`. Another type is the error `E0401`. Any other option, such as
`{ cause: $e }`, is the error `E0454`, and its help lists `previous`.

With names, the arguments may come in any order:
`new RuntimeError(options: { previous: $e }, message: "…")`. A subclass that writes no constructor
accepts the names too.

A subclass with its own constructor must call `parent::constructor(...)` on every path. A path without
the call is the error `E0410`. `parent::constructor()` with no message is the error `E0402`.

A subclass may add properties with a default value, such as `public int $status = 500;`, without a
constructor of its own.

#### Example 01: your own error class

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to write an error class of your own. The class extends `Throwable`
// and writes no constructor, so it uses the one it inherits. You pass a message
// to `new` and nothing else.

class OutOfStock extends Throwable
{
}

final class Warehouse
{
    public static function pack(string $item, int $inStock): string
    {
        if ($inStock == 0) {
            throw new OutOfStock('no ' . $item . ' left');
        }
        return 'packed one ' . $item;
    }
}

try {
    // This prints `packed one blue mug`.
    echo Warehouse::pack('blue mug', 4), "\n";
    echo Warehouse::pack('red mug', 0), "\n";
} catch (OutOfStock $empty) {
    // `message` is the text you passed to `new`. This prints `no red mug left`.
    echo $empty->message, "\n";
}

// The message may also be passed by name.
try {
    throw new OutOfStock(message: 'the shelf is empty');
} catch (OutOfStock $shelf) {
    echo $shelf->message, "\n";
}
```

```output
packed one blue mug
no red mug left
the shelf is empty
```

#### Example 02: a constructor of its own

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows an error class that writes its own constructor. It adds two properties
// and passes the message to the class it extends.

class HttpError extends RuntimeError
{
    // `public int $status` and `public string $url` declare the properties and
    // fill them from the arguments in one step.
    public function constructor(string $message, public int $status, public string $url)
    {
        parent::constructor($message);
    }
}

final class Api
{
    public static function get(string $url, int $status): string
    {
        if ($status >= 400) {
            throw new HttpError('the server said no', $status, $url);
        }
        return 'body of ' . $url;
    }
}

try {
    echo Api::get('/health', 200), "\n";
    echo Api::get('/orders/91', 404), "\n";
} catch (HttpError $failed) {
    // This prints `404 /orders/91: the server said no`.
    echo $failed->status, ' ', $failed->url, ': ', $failed->message, "\n";
}

// `HttpError` extends `RuntimeError`, so a `RuntimeError` arm catches it too.
try {
    echo Api::get('/orders/92', 503), "\n";
} catch (RuntimeError $any) {
    echo 'as a runtime error: ', $any->message, "\n";
}
```

```output
body of /health
404 /orders/91: the server said no
as a runtime error: the server said no
```

#### Example 03: say which error caused it

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how one error names the error that caused it. A settings loader catches
// the error from the JSON reader and throws its own, with the first one kept as
// the cause. The person reading the log then sees both.

class ConfigError extends RuntimeError
{
    public function constructor(string $message, public string $file, ?Throwable $cause)
    {
        // `{ previous: $cause }` is the options bag of the inherited constructor.
        parent::constructor($message, { previous: $cause });
    }
}

final class Settings
{
    public static function read(string $file, string $text): mixed
    {
        try {
            return Core\Json::decode($text);
        } catch (ParseError $bad) {
            throw new ConfigError('cannot start without ' . $file, $file, $bad);
        }
    }
}

try {
    echo Core\Json::encode(Settings::read('app.json', "{\"port\": 8080}")), "\n";
    echo Core\Json::encode(Settings::read('cache.json', "{\"port\": }")), "\n";
} catch (ConfigError $stop) {
    echo $stop->message, "\n";
    echo 'the file is ', $stop->file, "\n";
    // `previous` is the error that was caught inside `read`.
    echo 'caused by: ', $stop->previous?->message ?? 'nothing', "\n";
}
```

```output
{"port":8080}
cannot start without cache.json
the file is cache.json
caused by: Core\Json::decode(): expected value at line 1 column 10
```

### `throw`

`throw` reports an error and stops the work in progress. It takes an object of a class under
`Throwable`, such as `LogicError`, `IOError`, or a class you wrote yourself. The nearest `catch`
clause whose class matches takes over, and the lines after the `throw` never run.

`throw new RuntimeError("the reason");` is the usual form. The message is the first argument, and a
class may add more. If no `catch` matches, the program ends with status 1.

`throw` is a statement, and it is also an expression. You can write it where a value is expected:
after `??` when a value may be missing, in the `default` arm of a `match`, and in a ternary
arm. In each of those places the program either has a value or throws, so
every line after it can use the value.

**The examples below** show `throw` after `??` for a missing field, in the `default` arm of a
`match` over order statuses, and in the checks a program runs before it ships an order. The last
one shows a method that throws for a value it cannot use, and a `catch` around the call.

`throw "x"`, `throw 5` and `throw new Foo()` for a class not under `Throwable` are each the error
`E0780`. A variable whose type is an interface is `E0780` too, even when the object in it extends
`RuntimeError`.

A `?LogicError` variable may be thrown. When it is `null`, the `throw` throws a `LogicError` with the
message `Can only throw objects`. A `mixed` variable may be thrown as well. When its value is not a
`Throwable`, the result is the same `LogicError`.

`throw` as a value can stand after `??` and `?:`, in a `match` arm, in either arm of a ternary, after
`||`, and after `echo`. Its type is `never`. At a typed
variable or a method argument, `int $x = throw …;` is the error `E0401`. In arithmetic such as
`1 + throw …`, the result is `mixed`.

A method whose return type is `int` may end with a `throw` and no `return`. A method may also have the
return type `never` and always throw.

`throw LogicError("x")` without `new` is the error `E0320`.

#### Example 01: a value that may be missing

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `throw` written after `??`. The value on the left is used when it is
// there. When it is missing, the `throw` on the right stops the method with an
// error.

final class Rows
{
    public static function email(array<string> $row): string
    {
        // `??` gives the value stored under `"email"`. If the row has no such
        // key, `throw` raises a `LogicError` and the method returns nothing.
        return $row['email'] ?? throw new LogicError('the row has no email');
    }
}

array<string> $complete = ['id' => '7', 'email' => 'ada@example.com'];
array<string> $partial = ['id' => '8'];

// This prints ada@example.com.
echo Rows::email($complete), "\n";

try {
    echo Rows::email($partial), "\n";
} catch (LogicError $missing) {
    // This prints "the row has no email".
    echo $missing->message, "\n";
}
```

```output
ada@example.com
the row has no email
```

#### Example 02: a status the program does not know

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `throw` in a `match` arm. Every status the program knows has an arm of
// its own. An unknown status reaches the `default` arm, and that arm throws.

final class Orders
{
    public static function nextStep(string $status): string
    {
        return match ($status) {
            'paid' => 'pack the order',
            'packed' => 'print the label',
            'shipped' => 'nothing left to do',
            // A `match` arm may be a `throw`. The method then returns nothing
            // for this subject, and the caller gets the error.
            default => throw new LogicError('unknown order status: ' . $status),
        };
    }
}

array<string> $statuses = ['paid', 'packed', 'returned'];

// The first two lines print a step. The third prints the error message,
// because "returned" has no arm.
foreach ($statuses as string $status) {
    try {
        string $step = Orders::nextStep($status);
        echo $status, ': ', $step, "\n";
    } catch (LogicError $unknown) {
        echo $status, ': ', $unknown->message, "\n";
    }
}
```

```output
paid: pack the order
packed: print the label
returned: unknown order status: returned
```

#### Example 03: checking an order before it ships

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the checks a program runs before it ships an order. Each check either
// gives a value or throws, so the last line can use both values.

final class Shipment
{
    public static function forOrder(int $quantity, ?string $address): string
    {
        // The ternary gives `$quantity` when it is positive. For 0 it throws.
        int $items = $quantity > 0
            ? $quantity
            : throw new LogicError('an order needs at least one item');
        // `??` covers the second case: an address nobody filled in.
        string $to = $address ?? throw new LogicError('an order needs an address');
        return 'ship ' . $items . ' item(s) to ' . $to;
    }
}

// This prints: ship 3 item(s) to 12 Baker Street
echo Shipment::forOrder(3, '12 Baker Street'), "\n";

try {
    echo Shipment::forOrder(0, '12 Baker Street'), "\n";
} catch (LogicError $empty) {
    echo $empty->message, "\n";
}

try {
    echo Shipment::forOrder(2, null), "\n";
} catch (LogicError $nowhere) {
    echo $nowhere->message, "\n";
}
```

```output
ship 3 item(s) to 12 Baker Street
an order needs at least one item
an order needs an address
```

#### Example 04: reporting a value the method cannot use

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how `throw` reports a value a method cannot work with. The method
// stops at the `throw`, and the `catch` around the call runs instead.

class Age
{
    public static function of(int $birthYear, int $thisYear): int
    {
        if ($birthYear > $thisYear) {
            throw new RuntimeError('a birth year in the future: ' . $birthYear);
        }
        return $thisYear - $birthYear;
    }
}

// This prints 41
echo Age::of(1985, 2026), "\n";

try {
    echo Age::of(2040, 2026), "\n";
    echo "this line is never reached\n";
} catch (RuntimeError $e) {
    // This prints: cannot use that row: a birth year in the future: 2040
    echo 'cannot use that row: ', $e->message, "\n";
}
```

```output
41
cannot use that row: a birth year in the future: 2040
```

### `try`, `catch`, `finally`

`try` guards a block of code that can throw. Write `try { … }`, then `catch` clauses, a `finally`
block, or both. Each `catch` clause names one class from the throwable tree.

A clause matches its own class and every class under it, so `catch (RuntimeError $e)` also takes an
`IOError`. The clauses are tried from top to bottom, so the narrow classes go first. You may leave
the variable out when you do not need the error itself.

`finally` runs on every way out of the block: after the body, after a `catch`, and on `return`,
`break`, `continue` or an error that nothing caught.

**The examples below** show two clauses picked by class, a `catch` that throws a new error with a
cause, and the clean-up around a job that reads rows. Then they show a loop that carries on after a
row that fails, two clauses with one variable name, which does not compile, and a `finally` that
runs on `continue`.

A `try` needs at least one `catch` clause or a `finally` block. A `try` with neither does not compile:
it is the error `E0242`.

A `catch` clause may name an interface. It then matches every class that implements that interface.

A clause for a parent class that is written before a clause for its subclass catches that error
first. The later clause never runs. This compiles without a warning.

`catch (LogicError | IOError $e)` does not compile: it is the error `E0245`. Write two clauses.

The variable of a `catch` clause is a variable of the whole function. Two clauses in one function may
use the same name when they catch the same type. When the types are different, the second clause does
not compile: that is the error `E0406`.

A `catch` clause may throw as well. The other clauses of the same `try` do not catch the new error.
The `finally` block of that `try` runs first, and then the next `try` outside handles the error. This
is how one layer reports an error of its own and keeps the caught one as its `previous`.

When one `try` is inside another, the inner `finally` block runs before the outer one.

A `return` inside a `finally` block does not compile: it is the error `E0250`. Change the result in
the `try` or in a `catch`, or after the whole block.

A `break` or `continue` that would leave a `finally` block does not compile: it is the error `E0251`.
This is also true for `break 2` from a loop inside the `finally`. A loop that is written completely
inside the `finally` block may use `break` and `continue`.

A `yield` inside a `finally` block does not compile: it is the error `E0255`. A generator cannot
pause there. Write the `yield` in the `try` block or after the whole block.

A `finally` block may contain its own `try` and `catch`. An error caught there does not leave the
block.

When the `try` returns a value, the value is computed first. The `finally` block runs after that, so
a change it makes does not change the value that the function returns.

When no `catch` handles an error, the `finally` blocks still run. Then the error leaves the function,
or ends the program at the top level.

A `finally` block can throw while an error is leaving the block. The handler outside then gets the
new error, and its `previous` is the first error. A method called in the `finally` that throws does
the same. If the new error already has a `previous`, it keeps that `previous`, and the first error is
lost.

#### Example 01: two clauses picked by class

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows two `catch` clauses in the order they are tried. `TimeoutError` is a
// kind of `RuntimeError`, so the narrow clause is written first. A
// `RuntimeError` clause written first would take both errors.

final class Feed
{
    public static function read(string $name): string
    {
        if ($name == 'slow') {
            throw new TimeoutError('the feed did not answer');
        }
        if ($name == 'gone') {
            throw new RuntimeError('the feed is not there');
        }
        return '3 rows';
    }
}

array<string> $names = ['daily', 'slow', 'gone'];

foreach ($names as string $name) {
    try {
        string $rows = Feed::read($name);
        echo $name, ': ', $rows, "\n";
    } catch (TimeoutError $slow) {
        echo $name, ': timed out, ', $slow->message, "\n";
    } catch (RuntimeError $other) {
        echo $name, ': failed, ', $other->message, "\n";
    }
}
```

```output
daily: 3 rows
slow: timed out, the feed did not answer
gone: failed, the feed is not there
```

#### Example 02: a catch that reports its own error

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a `catch` that cannot handle what it caught. It throws an error of its
// own and gives the caught one as the cause. That new error leaves the `try` it
// was thrown in, and the caller handles it.

final class Settings
{
    public static function port(array<string> $raw): int
    {
        try {
            return $raw['port'] as int;
        } catch (RuntimeError $unusable) {
            throw new LogicError('the port setting is unusable', { previous: $unusable });
        }
    }
}

array<string> $withoutPort = ['host' => 'localhost'];
array<string> $withText = ['port' => 'eight'];

try {
    echo Settings::port($withoutPort), "\n";
} catch (LogicError $first) {
    echo $first->message, "\n";
    // The cause says what the inner error was.
    echo 'caused by: ', $first->previous?->message ?? 'nothing', "\n";
}

try {
    echo Settings::port($withText), "\n";
} catch (LogicError $second) {
    echo $second->message, "\n";
    echo 'caused by: ', $second->previous?->message ?? 'nothing', "\n";
}
```

```output
the port setting is unusable
caused by: undefined array key `port`
the port setting is unusable
caused by: cannot convert string "eight" to `int`
```

#### Example 03: cleaning up around every row

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the clean-up a program runs around a job that reads rows. Every row has
// a `finally` of its own, and the whole job has one around it. The inner block
// runs first.

final class Import
{
    public static int $rowsClosed = 0;
    public static int $jobsClosed = 0;

    public static function rows(array<string> $lines): int
    {
        try {
            int $total = 0;
            foreach ($lines as string $line) {
                try {
                    if ($line == '') {
                        throw new RuntimeError('an empty row stopped the job');
                    }
                    $total = $total + 1;
                } finally {
                    Import::$rowsClosed = Import::$rowsClosed + 1;
                }
            }
            return $total;
        } finally {
            Import::$jobsClosed = Import::$jobsClosed + 1;
        }
    }
}

array<string> $complete = ['a', 'b', 'c'];
array<string> $withHole = ['a', '', 'c'];

// This prints 3.
echo Import::rows($complete), "\n";

try {
    echo Import::rows($withHole), "\n";
} catch (RuntimeError $stopped) {
    echo $stopped->message, "\n";
}

// The failed job closed its row and then itself, so both counts went up.
echo 'rows closed: ', Import::$rowsClosed, "\n";
echo 'jobs closed: ', Import::$jobsClosed, "\n";
```

```output
3
an empty row stopped the job
rows closed: 5
jobs closed: 2
```

#### Example 04: finally runs before the caller gets the value

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows when `finally` runs for a function that returns. It runs before the
// caller gets the value, so "checked" prints first.

final class Loader
{
    public static int $reads = 0;

    public static function load(string $key): string
    {
        try {
            if ($key == 'bad') {
                throw new IOError('cannot read ' . $key);
            }
            return 'value-of-' . $key;
        } finally {
            Loader::$reads = Loader::$reads + 1;
            echo 'checked ', $key, "\n";
        }
    }
}

echo Loader::load('host'), "\n";

// The `IOError` passes the `LogicError` clause. The second clause catches it.
try {
    echo Loader::load('bad'), "\n";
} catch (LogicError $wrongClause) {
    echo "not this one\n";
} catch (IOError $io) {
    echo 'io: ', $io->message, "\n";
}

// The `finally` block ran for both calls, so this prints 2.
echo 'reads: ', Loader::$reads, "\n";
```

```output
checked host
value-of-host
checked bad
io: cannot read bad
reads: 2
```

#### Example 05: a return in finally does not compile

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows a `return` inside `finally`. It does not compile, because it would
// replace the value of the `try` and any error that is leaving the block.
// proof: compile-error

final class Counter {
    public static function next(int $n): int {
        try {
            return $n + 1;
        } finally {
            return 0;
        }
    }
}

echo Counter::next(1), "\n";
```

```output
error[E0250]: a `return` never leaves a `finally` block
   --> main.nvs:11:13
   |
11 |             return 0;
   |             ^^^^^^^^^ this discards what the region was leaving with
   = help: return from the `try` or a `catch` to change the result, or write it after the whole region

error: aborting due to 1 error
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```

#### Example 06: carrying on after a row that fails

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the block form of `try`. The `catch` clause runs when the code inside
// the `try` block throws an error, and the program carries on after the block.

class Amount
{
    public static function of(string $text): int
    {
        ?int $value = $text as ?int;
        if ($value == null) {
            throw new RuntimeError('not a whole number: ' . $text);
        }
        return $value;
    }
}

array<string> $rows = ['12', 'seven', '30'];
int $total = 0;

foreach ($rows as string $row) {
    try {
        $total = $total + Amount::of($row);
    } catch (RuntimeError $e) {
        // This prints: skipped: not a whole number: seven
        echo 'skipped: ', $e->message, "\n";
    }
}

// This prints 42. The row that failed added nothing.
echo $total, "\n";
```

```output
skipped: not a whole number: seven
42
```

#### Example 07: two clauses need two names

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that two `catch` clauses for different types need two variable names.
// Both clauses below use `$e`, so this program does not compile.
// proof: compile-error

class Twice
{
    public static function run(): string
    {
        try {
            throw new LogicError('x');
        } catch (LogicError $e) {
            return 'a';
        } catch (Throwable $e) {
            return 'b';
        }
    }
}

echo Twice::run(), "\n";
```

```output
error[E0406]: `$e` is already declared
   --> main.nvs:12:29
   |
12 |         } catch (LogicError $e) {
   |                             -- first declared here
...
14 |         } catch (Throwable $e) {
   |                            ^^ second declaration

error: aborting due to 1 error
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```

#### Example 08: finally runs on continue

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows that `finally` also runs when `continue` leaves the `try` block.

int $i = 0;

while ($i < 3) {
    $i++;
    try {
        if ($i == 2) {
            // The rest of the block is skipped, but `finally` still runs.
            continue;
        }
        echo 'body', $i, ' ';
    } finally {
        echo 'fin', $i, ' ';
    }
}

// The loop above prints: body1 fin1 fin2 body3 fin3
// The second pass prints only fin2.
echo "\n";
```

```output
body1 fin1 fin2 body3 fin3
```

### Rethrowing

`throw $e;` inside a `catch` sends the same error on to the next handler.

The object does not change. Its `message`, its `previous` and its class stay as they were. Only
`location` moves to the line of the rethrow, so a log line written later says where the error was
sent on. Rethrow when the code you are in has something to do first, such as closing a file or
counting a failure, and cannot handle the error itself.

**Good to know:** to add information of your own, do not rethrow. Throw a new error and give it the
caught one as its cause, with `{ previous: $e }`. A handler further out then has both messages.

**The examples below** show a plain rethrow, a rethrow after a log line, and a retry that gives up
and sends the last error on.

`throw $e;` may also throw an error that was caught earlier and saved in a variable or a property.
Each throw moves `location` to the line of that `throw`. The object stays the same, so `==` with the
saved variable is `true`.

A clause that catches a wide class, such as `catch (Throwable $e)`, does not change the class of the
error. After `throw $e;`, a `catch (TimeoutError $t)` further out still catches a `TimeoutError`.

After a rethrow, `backtrace` still starts at the function that threw first. For the function that
rethrew, the line in `backtrace` is the line of `throw $e;`.

The `finally` block of the `try` that rethrows runs before the error leaves that `try`.

When nothing catches the rethrown error, it ends the program like any uncaught throw. The report on
the error output names the function that threw first.

#### Example 01: send the same error on

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a plain rethrow. `throw $io;` inside the `catch` sends the same object
// on, so the handler further out reads the same message and the same class.

final class Relay
{
    public static function go(): void
    {
        try {
            throw new IOError('the socket closed');
        } catch (IOError $io) {
            echo "the relay saw it\n";
            throw $io;
        }
    }
}

try {
    Relay::go();
} catch (Throwable $sent) {
    echo $sent->message, "\n";
    // `location` is the line of the rethrow, which is line 13 here.
    echo 'sent on at ', $sent->location, "\n";
}
```

```output
the relay saw it
the socket closed
sent on at main.nvs:13
```

#### Example 02: do something first

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the common reason to rethrow. This code counts the failure and writes a
// line about it. It cannot decide what to do next, so it sends the error on.

final class Uploads
{
    public static int $failures = 0;

    public static function send(string $name): string
    {
        try {
            if ($name == 'photo.raw') {
                throw new IOError('the upload was cut off');
            }
            return 'sent ' . $name;
        } catch (IOError $cut) {
            Uploads::$failures = Uploads::$failures + 1;
            echo 'upload ', $name, " failed\n";
            throw $cut;
        }
    }
}

echo Uploads::send('notes.txt'), "\n";

try {
    echo Uploads::send('photo.raw'), "\n";
} catch (IOError $failed) {
    echo 'giving up: ', $failed->message, "\n";
}

echo 'failures so far: ', Uploads::$failures, "\n";
```

```output
sent notes.txt
upload photo.raw failed
giving up: the upload was cut off
failures so far: 1
```

#### Example 03: a retry that gives up

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a retry. The call is tried three times. The first two errors are caught
// and the loop tries again. The third one is sent on, because there is nothing
// left to try.

final class Payments
{
    public static int $calls = 0;

    public static function charge(int $order): string
    {
        Payments::$calls = Payments::$calls + 1;
        throw new TimeoutError('the payment service did not answer');
    }

    public static function chargeWithRetries(int $order, int $tries): string
    {
        int $attempt = 1;
        while ($attempt <= $tries) {
            try {
                return Payments::charge($order);
            } catch (TimeoutError $slow) {
                echo 'attempt ', $attempt, " timed out\n";
                if ($attempt == $tries) {
                    // The last attempt sends the error on unchanged.
                    throw $slow;
                }
            }
            $attempt = $attempt + 1;
        }
        return 'not reached';
    }
}

try {
    echo Payments::chargeWithRetries(4021, 3), "\n";
} catch (TimeoutError $gaveUp) {
    echo 'gave up after ', Payments::$calls, ' calls: ', $gaveUp->message, "\n";
}
```

```output
attempt 1 timed out
attempt 2 timed out
attempt 3 timed out
gave up after 3 calls: the payment service did not answer
```

### An uncaught throw

A throw that no `catch` handles ends your program.

The program stops at the line that threw. Everything it printed before that line is still printed.
The exit status is 1. The error output gets a report with the error class, the message, and one line
for each function the throw passed through, innermost first.

There is no global handler that catches everything for you and lets the program carry on. Catch the
error where you can do something about it, or let it end the program.

Two methods let you watch this ending without changing it. `Core\Fatal::onUncaughtThrow` gives you
the error itself. `Core\Script::onExit` runs at every ending, normal or not. Both run before the
program exits, and the exit status is still 1.

**The examples below** show the plain ending first, then each of these two methods.

The report goes to the error output, and the normal output does not get it. By default the report is
one line of JSON. `msg` is the message, `fields.class` is the error class, and `nodes` has one entry
for each function with `function`, `file` and `line`. The last entry is `<script>`, the top level of
the file.

With `format = "text"` in the `[log]` table of `nvs.toml`, the report is text. The first line is
`[error]` and the message. The next line is the class. Then each function gets one line, such as
`#0 Repo::get() at main.nvs:4`.

The report has the class of your own error, such as `BadInput`, when you throw one.

The report does not have the error in `previous`. To see the cause, catch the error and print
`$e->previous?->message` yourself.

Before the program ends, every `finally` block that the error leaves still runs. What it prints
stays in the normal output.

The exit status is 1 for every uncaught throw.

#### Example 01: the program stops here

```nvs exit=1
<?nvs
// Shows what happens when no `catch` handles a throw. The program ends at
// the line that threw, with exit status 1.
// proof: exit 1

class Repo
{
    public static function get(int $id): string
    {
```
