```nvs exit=1
        throw new RuntimeError('no row ' . $id);
    }
}

// This prints. Everything printed before the throw stays printed.
echo "loading order 7\n";

// Nothing catches this error, so the program ends here. The error output gets
// the class `RuntimeError`, the message, and one line for each function.
echo Repo::get(7), "\n";

// This line never runs.
echo "done\n";
```

```output
loading order 7
```

#### Example 02: print your own message

```nvs exit=1
<?nvs
// Shows how to print your own message when an error ends the program.
// proof: exit 1

// This anonymous function runs when a throw reaches the top of the program and nothing
// caught it. The program still ends, and the exit status is still 1.
Core\Fatal::onUncaughtThrow(fn(Throwable $e): void => {
    echo 'import stopped: ', $e->message, "\n";
    echo "check your file, then run the import again\n";
});

class Import
{
    public static function row(string $line): string
    {
        if (Core\Str::length($line) == 0) {
            throw new RuntimeError('an empty line is not a row');
        }
        return $line;
    }
}

echo Import::row('ada,lovelace'), "\n";

// The second row is empty, so this throw ends the program. The anonymous function above
// runs first and prints the two lines you wrote for your user.
echo Import::row(''), "\n";
```

```output
ada,lovelace
import stopped: an empty line is not a row
check your file, then run the import again
```

#### Example 03: write a summary at every ending

```nvs exit=1
<?nvs
// Shows how to write a summary line even when an error ends the program.
// proof: exit 1

final class Counter
{
    public static int $written = 0;
}

// This anonymous function runs at every ending: a normal one, an `exit`, and an error
// that nothing caught. `status()` is 1 for an ending an error caused.
Core\Script::onExit(fn(Core\Script\ExitReport $report): void => {
    echo '--- rows written: ', Counter::$written, "\n";
    echo '--- exit status: ', $report->status(), "\n";
    echo '--- error: ', $report->error()?->message ?? 'none', "\n";
});

class Rows
{
    public static function write(string $row): void
    {
        if (Core\Str::length($row) == 0) {
            throw new RuntimeError('row ' . Counter::$written . ' is empty');
        }
        Counter::$written = Counter::$written + 1;
        echo 'wrote ', $row, "\n";
    }
}

Rows::write('ada,lovelace');
Rows::write('grace,hopper');

// This row is empty, so the program ends here. The summary above is still
// printed, and it reports the two rows that did get written.
Rows::write('');
```

```output
wrote ada,lovelace
wrote grace,hopper
--- rows written: 2
--- exit status: 1
--- error: row 2 is empty
```

#### Example 04: finally runs before the end

```nvs exit=1
<?nvs
// Shows that `finally` still runs when nothing catches the error. The clean-up
// prints, and then the program ends with exit status 1.
// proof: exit 1

echo "start\n";

try {
    throw new RuntimeError('the job failed');
} finally {
    // This line runs before the program ends.
    echo "clean-up done\n";
}

// This line never runs.
echo "after\n";
```

```output
start
clean-up done
```

### Recursion depth

A function that calls itself without ever returning is stopped. When the call stack grows past the
depth Novis allows, the innermost call throws a `RecursionError`. The limit is on the size of the
stack rather than on a number of calls, so how deep you can go depends on what each call holds. A
small function reaches a few thousand calls.

A `RecursionError` is a kind of `RuntimeError`, so `catch (RecursionError $e)` and
`catch (RuntimeError $e)` both handle it, and the program carries on. The frames are already gone
when the handler runs, so the handler has the whole stack available again and may keep working.
Uncaught, a `RecursionError` ends the program like any other error.

This is what makes a recursive walk over data you did not write safe. Input nested far deeper than
you expected, or a cycle in a table you follow, gives you an error you can report instead of a
crash.

**The examples below** show a runaway recursion caught, a walk a thousand calls deep that finishes,
and a redirect chain that loops back on itself.

The message of the error is `the call stack is too deep`. `$e is RuntimeError` is `true`.

A function with a few parameters and locals reaches fewer calls than a function with one. The exact
number can change between versions of Novis, so do not write code that needs it.

A `catch` in any of the calls handles the error. The calls inside it are gone, and the calls outside
it go on as usual. The program may call the deep function again after a `catch`, and it throws a
`RecursionError` again.

`finally` blocks in each call run while the error leaves the calls.

`backtrace` has one entry for each call, so a `RecursionError` has a few thousand entries. An
uncaught one prints all of them in the report.

You may throw a `RecursionError` yourself with `new RecursionError("…")`.

#### Example 01: catching a runaway recursion

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a function that calls itself with no way out. The runtime stops it at
// the depth limit with a `RecursionError`, the `catch` handles it, and the
// program carries on.

final class Down
{
    public static function forever(int $n): int
    {
        return Down::forever($n + 1) + 1;
    }
}

try {
    echo Down::forever(0), "\n";
} catch (RecursionError $tooDeep) {
    // This prints "stopped: the call stack is too deep".
    echo 'stopped: ', $tooDeep->message, "\n";
}

echo "the program carries on\n";
```

```output
stopped: the call stack is too deep
the program carries on
```

#### Example 02: a deep walk that finishes

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how much room recursion has. This function calls itself a thousand
// times before it returns, which stays inside the limit, so it finishes and
// prints its result.

final class Sum
{
    public static function upTo(int $n): int
    {
        if ($n == 0) {
            return 0;
        }
        return $n + Sum::upTo($n - 1);
    }
}

// This prints 500500.
echo Sum::upTo(1000), "\n";
```

```output
500500
```

#### Example 03: a redirect chain that loops

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a recursive walk over a table somebody else filled in. Two entries that
// point at each other make the walk endless, and the depth limit turns that
// into an error you can report.

final class Links
{
    public static function follow(array<string> $targets, string $from): string
    {
        string $next = $targets[$from] ?? '';
        if ($next == '') {
            return $from;
        }
        return Links::follow($targets, $next);
    }
}

array<string> $plain = ['/old' => '/new', '/new' => '/home'];
array<string> $loop = ['/a' => '/b', '/b' => '/a'];

// This prints /home.
echo Links::follow($plain, '/old'), "\n";

try {
    echo Links::follow($loop, '/a'), "\n";
} catch (RecursionError $endless) {
    echo "the redirect chain does not end\n";
}
```

```output
/home
the redirect chain does not end
```

#### Example 04: a catch in the middle of the calls

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a `catch` in one of the calls of a deep recursion. The calls inside it
// are gone. The calls outside it go on and return a value.

final class Down
{
    public static int $caughtAt = -1;

    public static function count(int $depth): int
    {
        int $next = $depth + 1;
        if ($depth == 100) {
            try {
                return Down::count($next);
            } catch (RecursionError $tooDeep) {
                Down::$caughtAt = $depth;
                return 0;
            }
        }
        return Down::count($next) + 1;
    }
}

// The call at depth 100 returns 0, and each of the 100 calls outside it adds 1.
// This prints "100 calls returned, caught at depth 100".
echo Down::count(0), ' calls returned, caught at depth ', Down::$caughtAt, "\n";
```

```output
100 calls returned, caught at depth 100
```

### Fatal errors: limits no `catch` sees

A resource limit stops your program at once, and no `catch` sees it.

`nvs.toml` sets four limits for a program: `memory`, `cpu_time`, `wall_time` and `max_output`. A
program that goes past one of them is stopped where it stands. This is a `FATAL`. It is not a
`Throwable`, so no `catch` clause matches it and no `finally` runs. The program writes a line starting
with `FATAL:` to standard error and ends with status 1.

One hook runs before that end. `Core\Fatal::onLimit` registers a function that runs once when a limit
stops the program, and it is told which limit fired. Use it to write a last note about what the
program was doing. Registering a second function replaces the first. The program still ends after the
handler.

**The examples below** show a limit that no `catch` and no `finally` sees, and a handler that names
the limit that fired. The third is a job that records the order it stopped on.

The `FATAL:` line on standard error names the limit and the numbers. For `memory` it gives the bytes
the program held, the limit, and the part of the limit kept for the handler. With `memory = "16M"`,
1 megabyte is kept for the handler, so the program itself can use 15 megabytes. When `nvs.toml` sets
no `memory` limit, the limit is `128M`.

The handler receives an array with one key, `limit`. Its value is the name of the limit as
`nvs.toml` writes it: `memory`, `cpu_time`, `wall_time` or `max_output`. The handler may also declare
no parameter. A handler with a parameter of another type, such as `fn (int $x): void`, is the error
`E0401`.

`Core\Fatal::onLimit` keeps one handler. A second call replaces the first, so only the last handler
runs.

The handler runs once. If it throws an error, the error is not shown, and the program still writes
the `FATAL:` line and ends with status 1. After the `max_output` limit, what the handler prints with
`echo` still reaches standard output.

Two more errors end the program in the same way: `send` on a closed `Core\Task\Channel`, and
`new Core\Task\Channel<int>(0)`. Each writes a `FATAL:` line that names the method, and the program
ends with status 1. No `catch` and no `finally` runs. The `onLimit` handler does not run either,
because no limit fired.

#### Example 01: no catch sees a limit

```toml file=nvs.toml
### Each example in this folder may use at most 16 megabytes of memory.
[limits]
memory = "16M"
```

```nvs exit=1
<?nvs
// Shows what a memory limit does to a program. `nvs.toml` gives this program
// 16 megabytes. Holding more than that stops it where it stands. No `catch`
// and no `finally` runs, and the program ends with status 1.
// proof: exit 1

echo "before the limit\n";

try {
    array<string> $ballast = [];
    int $slab = 0;
    while ($slab < 4) {
        $ballast[] = Core\Str::repeat('x', 8388608);
        $slab = $slab + 1;
    }
    echo "not reached\n";
} catch (Throwable $never) {
    // A limit is not a throw, so no class matches it. `Throwable` is the widest
    // clause there is, and it does not run either.
    echo "not reached: the catch ran\n";
} finally {
    echo "not reached: the finally ran\n";
}

echo "not reached: the program went on\n";
```

```output
before the limit
```

#### Example 02: a handler for the last moment

```toml file=nvs.toml
### Each example in this folder may use at most 16 megabytes of memory.
[limits]
memory = "16M"
```

```nvs exit=1
<?nvs
// Shows the one hook a limit runs. `Core\Fatal::onLimit` registers a function
// that runs when a limit stops the program. The function receives the name of
// the limit that fired. The program still ends after it.
// proof: exit 1

Core\Fatal::onLimit(fn(array<string> $report): void => {
    echo 'stopped by the ', $report['limit'], " limit\n";
});

echo "working\n";

array<string> $ballast = [];
int $slab = 0;
while ($slab < 4) {
    $ballast[] = Core\Str::repeat('x', 8388608);
    $slab = $slab + 1;
}

echo "not reached\n";
```

```output
working
stopped by the memory limit
```

#### Example 03: a job that says where it stopped

```toml file=nvs.toml
### Each example in this folder may use at most 16 megabytes of memory.
[limits]
memory = "16M"
```

```nvs exit=1
<?nvs
// Shows how to leave a note when a limit stops a job. The handler prints the
// order the job was on, so the person reading the log can start again from
// there.
// proof: exit 1

final class Job
{
    // The handler reads this. An anonymous function copies the variables it
    // captures when it is written, so a variable would still have its first value here.
    public static string $current = 'none';
}

Core\Fatal::onLimit(fn(array<string> $report): void => {
    echo 'stopped on order ', Job::$current, ', limit: ', $report['limit'], "\n";
});

array<string> $orders = ['A-1001', 'A-1002', 'A-1003', 'A-1004'];
array<string> $labels = [];

foreach ($orders as string $order) {
    Job::$current = $order;
    echo 'packing ', $order, "\n";
    $labels[] = Core\Str::repeat('x', 8388608);
}

echo "not reached\n";
```

```output
packing A-1001
packing A-1002
stopped on order A-1002, limit: memory
```

### Capability denials are catchable

A call your program is not allowed to make throws a `RuntimeError`.

Reading a file, writing a file and starting another script each need a capability. A capability is
permission to do one kind of thing. The person who runs the server grants it in `nvs.toml`. A
program you start from the command line may read and write any file. A server program may read its
application folder and write only its own temporary folders.

A call without the grant throws before it does any work. The message names the method, the capability
it needed and the path it was given. A `help:` line under it says where to write the grant. This is an
ordinary throw, so `catch (RuntimeError $denied)` takes it and the program keeps running.

Your program can use that. Try the call, catch the error, and do the work another way if it is not
allowed.

**The examples below** show a call nobody allowed, and a grant that lets one call through while a
second call is still denied. The third is a program that finishes its work without the capability.

The message has two lines. The first is ``Core\IO::read needs the capability `fs.read` for <path>,
which is not granted``, with the full path of the file. The second is the line to add to `nvs.toml`:
``help: add `read = ["<folder>"]` under `[capabilities.fs]` in nvs.toml``. `<folder>` is the
full path of the folder that contains the file.

`fs.read` covers every call that looks at a file, such as `Core\IO::exists`, and not only
`Core\IO::read`. `fs.write` is a separate capability. A grant of `read` for a folder does not let your
program write there.

A grant lists folders. Novis resolves each path to its real full path before it checks it. A `..` that
leads out of a granted folder is denied, and so is a symbolic link that points out of one. A path
with `..` that ends inside a granted folder is allowed.

A file that does not exist inside a granted folder is not a denial. The call throws `IOError`, a
subclass of `RuntimeError`, with the operating system's message. A path that does not exist outside
every granted folder is denied like any other path.

`spawn script "job.nvs"` needs `script.spawn`. Its message starts with ``spawn script` needs the
capability `script.spawn` ``, and the `help:` line names `[capabilities.script]`.

#### Example 01: a call nobody allowed

```toml file=nvs.toml
### Example 01 may not read any file.
[[app]]
entry = "main.nvs"

[app.capabilities.fs]
read = []
```

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows what a program sees when it reads a file and `nvs.toml` does not allow
// it. The call throws a `RuntimeError`. The `catch` takes it, and the program
// keeps running.

try {
    echo Core\IO::read('orders.csv');
} catch (RuntimeError $denied) {
    // The message names the method, the capability and the full path of the file.
    // This prints the part before the path.
    echo Core\Str::before($denied->message, ' for '), "\n";
    // The second line of the message is the line to add to `nvs.toml`.
    // It also contains the full path of the folder. This prints `...` in its place.
    string $help = Core\Str::after($denied->message, "\n") ?? '';
    echo Core\Str::before($help, "\""), '...]', Core\Str::after($help, "\"]"), "\n";
}

echo "still running\n";
```

```output
Core\IO::read needs the capability `fs.read`
help: add `read = [...]` under `[capabilities.fs]` in nvs.toml
still running
```

#### Example 02: a grant in nvs toml

```text file=data/notice.txt
The shop closes at 18:00.
```

```toml file=nvs.toml
### Example 02 may read the files in the `data` folder. It may not write any file.
[[app]]
entry = "main.nvs"

[app.capabilities.fs]
read = ["data"]
write = []
```

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a program with one capability and not the other. `nvs.toml` grants
// `fs.read` for one directory, so reading a file there works. Writing a file
// needs `fs.write`, and this program does not have it.

echo Core\Str::trim(Core\IO::read('data/notice.txt')), "\n";

try {
    Core\IO::write('data/notice.txt', 'The shop is open all night.');
} catch (RuntimeError $denied) {
    // The message names the full path of the file. This prints the part before it.
    echo Core\Str::before($denied->message, ' for '), "\n";
}
```

```output
The shop closes at 18:00.
Core\IO::write needs the capability `fs.write`
```

#### Example 03: a report when the disk is closed

```toml file=nvs.toml
### Example 03 may not write any file.
[[app]]
entry = "main.nvs"

[app.capabilities.fs]
write = []
```

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a program that does its work without a capability. It saves a report
// to a file. Writing is not allowed here, so it prints the report instead.

string $report = 'orders: 3, total: 41.50';

try {
    Core\IO::write('report.txt', $report);
    echo "the report is in report.txt\n";
} catch (RuntimeError $denied) {
    echo "report.txt cannot be written, so here is the report\n";
    echo $report, "\n";
}
```

```output
report.txt cannot be written, so here is the report
orders: 3, total: 41.50
```

### Assertion failures

An assertion that fails throws `Core\Test\Failure`.

Every `Core\Test::assert…` method either returns and lets your code carry on, or throws. The message
names the method that failed and the values it compared, so you can read what went wrong without
opening the file again. The `message` option puts your own sentence in front of that text.

`Core\Test\Failure` is not a `RuntimeError`. It sits directly under `Throwable`, so a `catch
(RuntimeError $e)` in the code you are testing never catches it by accident. A `catch (Throwable $e)`
does catch it.

Inside a `#[Test]` method the test runner catches the failure and reports that test as failed.
Outside one it is an ordinary throw: catch it, or it ends your program.

**The examples below** show the message, the `catch` arm that takes it, and a check outside a test.

`$failure is RuntimeError` and `$failure is LogicError` are both `false`. Only a `catch` for
`Core\Test\Failure` or for `Throwable` takes a failed assertion.

An assertion that passes returns nothing and prints nothing.

You can create a failure yourself with `new Core\Test\Failure("…")`. Your own class cannot extend it.

A failure that nothing catches ends the program with status 1, like any uncaught error. The report on
standard error has the class `Core\Test\Failure` and the message.

#### Example 01: what a failure says

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows what a failed assertion throws, and what its message says.

// Every `Core\Test::assert...` method throws `Core\Test\Failure` when it fails.
try {
    Core\Test::assertEquals(41, 42);
} catch (Core\Test\Failure $failure) {
    // The message names the method and both values it compared.
    echo $failure->message, "\n";
}

// The `message` option puts your own sentence in front of that text.
try {
    Core\Test::assertTrue(false, { message: 'the flag should be set' });
} catch (Core\Test\Failure $failure) {
    echo $failure->message, "\n";
}

// `location` is the file and the line of the assertion that failed.
try {
    Core\Test::assertCount(['order', 'customer'], 3);
} catch (Core\Test\Failure $failure) {
    echo $failure->message, "\n";
    echo 'raised at ', $failure->location, "\n";
}
```

```output
Core\Test::assertEquals failed: `$actual` is 41, `$expected` is 42
the flag should be set: Core\Test::assertTrue failed: `$actual` is false
Core\Test::assertCount failed: `$actual` holds 2 entries, `$expected` is 3
raised at main.nvs:21
```

#### Example 02: only a throwable arm catches it

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows which `catch` arm takes a failed assertion. `Core\Test\Failure` is not
// a `RuntimeError`.

class Cart
{
    public static function total(array<int> $prices): int
    {
        int $sum = 0;
        foreach ($prices as int $price) {
            $sum = $sum + $price;
        }
        return $sum;
    }
}

// The `RuntimeError` arm does not match a failure. The `Throwable` arm is the
// one that runs.
try {
    Core\Test::assertEquals(Cart::total([100, 250]), 999);
} catch (RuntimeError $error) {
    echo "the RuntimeError arm caught it\n";
} catch (Throwable $failure) {
    echo "the Throwable arm caught it\n";
    echo $failure->message, "\n";
}
```

```output
the Throwable arm caught it
Core\Test::assertEquals failed: `$actual` is 350, `$expected` is 999
```

#### Example 03: a check that ends the script

```nvs exit=1
<?nvs
// Shows a check outside a test. Nothing catches the failure, so the program
// ends with exit status 1.
// proof: exit 1

array<string> $config = ['host' => 'localhost', 'port' => '5432'];

echo "checking the configuration\n";

// This assertion passes, so the program carries on.
Core\Test::assertCount($config, 2);

// This one fails. Outside a `#[Test]` method a failure is an ordinary throw,
// so it ends the program here and the error output gets the message.
Core\Test::assertTrue(
    Core\Arr::hasKey($config, 'password'),
    { message: 'the password is missing' },
);

echo "this line never runs\n";
```

```output
checking the configuration
```

### Inspecting a value

Two members show you what a value really is while you are working on a program. `Core\Debug::dump`
writes one rendering per argument to standard error. `Core\Debug::render` builds the same rendering
and returns it as a `Core\Cli\Text` value. You can print it or put it in a log line.

A rendering names the type of every value, the length of every string and the class of every object.
Control bytes such as a tab are made visible, a structure that is very deep or very long is cut
short, a value that points back at itself is marked, and a property declared `secret` is shown as
`[redacted]`.

`dump` never writes to standard output, and a captured buffer never swallows it. What your program
prints stays exactly what it printed, so a `dump` you forget to remove cannot change a response.

**The examples below** show a rendering printed, a `dump` beside a program's own output, and a
password that stays hidden.

`Core\Debug::render` returns a `Core\Cli\Text`, not a `string`. `echo` prints it. Call `->text()` to
get the `string`, for example to compare it: `Core\Debug::render(1)->text() == "int(1)"` is `true`.
Two `Core\Cli\Text` values are objects, so `==` on them compares the objects, not the text.

Each value shows its type. `null` is `null`, and a number is `int(1)`, `uint(3)`, `float(1.5)` or
`decimal(2.50)`. An enum case shows its number, such as `int(1)`. A function shows the number of its
parameters, such as `callable(1 parameter)`. A string shows its length in bytes, so `"café"` is
`string(5)`.

A newline is shown as `\n` and a tab as `\t`. Other control bytes and the characters that change the
direction of text are shown as visible symbols.

An array shows its first 100 entries, then `[elided: 200 of 300 entries]` for the rest. A string over
1024 bytes shows its first 1024 bytes, as `string(1024+) "…" [elided: 3976 bytes]`. A structure shows
eight levels, and a deeper value is `[elided: below the depth cap]`. An object that was already shown
higher up is `[cycle -> #1]`, with the number of that object.

`Core\Debug::dump()` with no value writes nothing. Output from `dump` inside `Core\Out::capture` is
not captured. It still goes to standard error.

A `secret` property is shown as `[redacted]`. A `secret` variable cannot be passed to `dump` or
`render` at all: that is the error `E0724`.

Inside a web request, `dump` writes a log record at the `Debug` level. In production, that record is
kept only when `[log] level` is `"Debug"`.

#### Example 01: seeing what a value is

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `Core\Debug::render`. It returns the rendering of a value as text, so
// this program prints it. Every value says what type it is, and a string says
// how many bytes it has.

final class Order
{
    public function constructor(public int $id, public string $customer)
    {
    }
}

echo Core\Debug::render(new Order(1042, 'Ada')), "\n";

// A tab inside a string is shown as `\t`, so you can see it.
echo Core\Debug::render(['paid' => true, 'note' => "two\tcolumns"]), "\n";
```

```output
Order#1 (2) {
  $id => int(1042)
  $customer => string(3) "Ada"
}
array(2) [
  "paid" => bool(true)
  "note" => string(11) "two\tcolumns"
]
```

#### Example 02: a dump beside your own output

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `Core\Debug::dump`. It writes to standard error, so it appears in your
// terminal while the program's own output stays unchanged. The lines below are
// the output; the two renderings arrive on standard error.

final class Basket
{
    public function constructor(public int $items, public int $cents)
    {
    }
}

var $basket = new Basket(3, 4599);

Core\Debug::dump($basket);

// One call takes several values and renders each of them.
Core\Debug::dump($basket->items, $basket->cents, 'still here');

echo 'total: ', $basket->cents, " cents\n";
echo 'items: ', $basket->items, "\n";
```

```output
total: 4599 cents
items: 3
```

#### Example 03: a password that stays hidden

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows what happens to a password in a rendering. A property declared `secret`
// is printed as `[redacted]`. You can inspect a configuration object without
// putting its password in your terminal or your log file.

final class DbConfig
{
    public function constructor(
        public string $host,
        public string $user,
        public secret string $password,
    )
    {
    }
}

var $config = new DbConfig('db.internal', 'orders', 'hunter2');

// The host and the user are shown. The password is not.
echo Core\Debug::render($config), "\n";
```

```output
DbConfig#1 (3) {
  $host => string(11) "db.internal"
  $user => string(6) "orders"
  $password => [redacted]
}
```

<a id="lang-concurrency"></a>
## A.9 Tasks, channels and isolates

Keywords: Core\Task, all, map, limit, deadline, TimeoutError, sleep, Core\Task\Channel, send, close, spawn script, await, Core\Script\Handle, isolate, ScriptResult, script.spawn, args, output, capture, inherit, async, await, fibers, fork, parallel, concurrent requests, threads, workers, shared state

### No colouring: I/O just waits

Novis has no `async`, no `await` on a promise, no `Fiber` and no callback style. A function that
waits is an ordinary function. When it reads a file, sleeps or takes a value from a channel, it
stops the task that called it and returns when the answer is there. The result is the value itself,
with nothing to unwrap, and the lines around the call run in their own order.

The same function works when you call it on its own line and when you call it inside a group of
tasks.

You get concurrency by running several tasks, not by marking functions. While one task waits,
another runs. A task belongs to the call that started it, and that call does not return while any
of its tasks is still running.

**The examples below** show an ordinary function that waits, two tasks taking turns, and a page
that asks for two slow answers at once.

`async`, `await` and `Fiber` are not keywords or classes. `async function` and `await $x` do not
compile, and `new Fiber(…)` is `E0303`.

A task runs until it waits. Two tasks that never wait run one after the other, each from its first
line to its last.

A task may start its own group of tasks. The inner `Core\Task::all` or `Core\Task::map` returns
before the outer task goes on.

What a task prints with `echo` is kept until the group is done. Then each task's output is printed
in the order the tasks were written, not in the order they finished. For `Core\Task::map`, that is
the order of the array. The output of a task that was stopped or that threw is printed too.

A static property has one value, and every task of the program reads and writes that same value.

#### Example 01: a function that waits is an ordinary function

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows that waiting needs no special syntax. `Core\Time::sleep` stops this task
// until the time has passed. The lines around it run one after another, in order.

class Report
{
    public static function rows(): array<string>
    {
        // A real program reads a file or asks a database here. Both of those wait.
        Core\Time::sleep(10ms);
        return ['north', 'south'];
    }
}

echo "asking for the rows\n";

// The result is the array itself. There is nothing to unwrap.
array<string> $rows = Report::rows();

echo 'got ', Core\Arr::count($rows), " rows\n";

foreach ($rows as string $row) {
    echo $row, "\n";
}
```

```output
asking for the rows
got 2 rows
north
south
```

#### Example 02: while one task waits another runs

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows what a wait does inside a group of tasks. `slow` waits 40 milliseconds and
// `quick` waits 5. While `slow` waits, `quick` runs and finishes first. The steps are
// kept in a variable, because a task collects what it prints until the group is done.

class Trace
{
    public static string $steps = '';

    public static function note(string $what): void
    {
        Trace::$steps = Trace::$steps . $what . "\n";
    }
}

Core\Task::all({
    slow: fn(): void => {
        Trace::note('slow starts');
        Core\Time::sleep(40ms);
        Trace::note('slow is done');
    },
    quick: fn(): void => {
        Trace::note('quick starts');
        Core\Time::sleep(5ms);
        Trace::note('quick is done');
    },
});

// Both tasks start, and `quick` is done long before `slow`.
echo Trace::$steps;
```

```output
quick starts
slow starts
quick is done
slow is done
```

#### Example 03: a page asks for two slow answers at once

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a real use: a page needs a customer and their orders, and both answers come
// from somewhere slow. These are ordinary functions, so the page can ask for them at
// the same time or one at a time. The functions are written the same way either way.

class Store
{
    public static function customer(): string
    {
        Core\Time::sleep(5ms);
        return 'Ada Lovelace';
    }

    public static function orders(): array<string>
    {
        Core\Time::sleep(5ms);
        return ['A-1001', 'A-1002'];
    }

    public static function banner(): string
    {
        Core\Time::sleep(5ms);
        return 'Free delivery this week';
    }
}

// Neither answer needs the other, so both are asked for at the same time.
var $page = Core\Task::all({
    customer: Store::customer,
    orders: Store::orders,
});

echo $page->customer, "\n";

foreach ($page->orders as string $order) {
    echo 'order ', $order, "\n";
}

// The same kind of function, called on its own line.
string $banner = Store::banner();
echo $banner, "\n";
```

```output
Ada Lovelace
order A-1001
order A-1002
Free delivery this week
```

### `Core\Task::all`: a fixed set of tasks

`Core\Task::all` runs a fixed set of jobs at the same time and gives you all their results together.

You give it a shape: a value with named fields, written `{ rows: …, label: … }`. Each field holds a
function that takes no arguments. `Core\Task::all` returns a shape with the same field names, and
each field has the type that job's function returns. You read `$page->rows` straight away, with no
conversion. A variable of type `callable`, with no signature, gives you `mixed` for that field alone.

`Core\Task::all` returns only when every job has finished, so nothing from the group is still
running afterwards. The subject has to be a shape of functions. An array of functions does not
compile.

**The examples below** show three jobs read by name, the three ways to write a job, a product
page that loads its parts at the same time, and an array of functions that does not compile.

The type of a field in the result is the return type of its function. For `fn(): int => …` it is
`int`. A `fn` with an expression body and no return type gives the type of that expression. A
variable of type `callable`, with no signature, gives `mixed`. A variable of type `callable(): int`
gives `int`.

A field of type `mixed` converted with `as string` is a `tainted string`.

A function that returns `void` gives a `void` field. `echo $r->a` on it is `E0707`.

Reading a field that the shape does not have compiles and throws `RuntimeError` when it runs.

`Core\Task::all({})` has no tasks and returns at once.

Each field must be a function. A field with another value, such as `{ a: 1 }`, is `E0401`. An array
of functions is `E0401` too.

#### Example 01: three jobs read by name

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to run three jobs at the same time. `Core\Task::all` takes one field per
// job and returns one field per result, under the same names.

var $page = Core\Task::all({
    rows: fn(): array<int> => [10, 20, 30],
    label: fn(): string => 'orders',
    total: fn(): int => 60,
});

// Each field already has the type its own function returns, so nothing needs converting.
// This prints orders: 3 rows, 60 in total.
echo $page->label, ': ', Core\Arr::count($page->rows), ' rows, ', $page->total, " in total\n";
```

```output
orders: 3 rows, 60 in total
```

#### Example 02: the three ways to write a job

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows that where a job is written does not matter. A field can hold a function
// written in place, a method named with `(...)`, or a function kept in a variable.

class Stock
{
    public static function onHand(): int
    {
        return 42;
    }
}

var $kept = fn(): string => 'from a variable';

var $group = Core\Task::all({
    here: fn(): string => 'written in place',
    method: Stock::onHand,
    kept: $kept,
});

// This prints written in place, then 42, then from a variable.
echo $group->here, "\n";
echo $group->method, "\n";
echo $group->kept, "\n";
```

```output
written in place
42
from a variable
```

#### Example 03: a product page loads its parts at once

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a real use: a product page needs three things before it can be drawn, and
// none of them needs the others. Running them together takes as long as the slowest
// one, instead of as long as all three added up.

class Catalog
{
    public static function product(): string
    {
        return 'Espresso machine';
    }

    public static function stock(): int
    {
        return 12;
    }

    public static function reviews(): array<string>
    {
        return ['fast', 'quiet'];
    }
}

var $page = Core\Task::all({
    product: Catalog::product,
    stock: Catalog::stock,
    reviews: Catalog::reviews,
});

echo $page->product, "\n";
echo 'in stock: ', $page->stock, "\n";

foreach ($page->reviews as string $review) {
    echo '- ', $review, "\n";
}
```

```output
Espresso machine
in stock: 12
- fast
- quiet
```

#### Example 04: an array of functions does not compile

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that `Core\Task::all` needs named fields. An array of functions has no
// names, so this program does not compile.
// proof: compile-error

var $results = Core\Task::all([fn(): int => 1, fn(): int => 2]);
```

```output
error[E0401]: expected `{ name: callable(): T, ... }`, found `array<mixed>`
  --> main.nvs:6:31
  |
6 | var $results = Core\Task::all([fn(): int => 1, fn(): int => 2]);
  |                               ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ this is `array<mixed>`

error: aborting due to 1 error
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```

### `Core\Task::map`: one task per element

`Core\Task::map` calls one function once per element of an array, each call at the same time as the
others, and gives you the results as an array.

The results come back under the input's own keys and in the input's own order. The order the jobs
finished in does not change anything you see. The function receives the value and the key, in that
order, and you may write only the value if the key is not needed. The result is an array of the
type the function returns.

`Core\Task::map` returns only when every element has been handled, so nothing from the group is
still running afterwards. If one job throws, the rest are stopped and the error reaches you at the
call.

**The examples below** show one job per element, a function that reads the key as well, and an
import that checks every row of a file at the same time.

The function may take no parameters, the value, or the value and the key. A third parameter is
`E0401`. The key is always a `string`, so `fn(int $v, int $k)` is `E0401`. The value parameter
must have the type of the array's elements.

The result is an array of the function's return type. `Core\Task::map([1, 2], fn(int $v): int => …)`
returns an `array<int>`.

The function can be written in place, or be a method reference such as `Prices::of`. A
variable of type `callable(int): int` works too. A variable of type `callable`, with no signature,
is `E0401`.

The first argument must be an array. An `Iterator` or a `mixed` value is `E0401`.

An empty array starts no tasks, and the result is an empty array.

#### Example 01: one job for every element

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to run one job for every element of an array. `Core\Task::map` calls the
// function once per element, all at the same time, and returns the results as an array.

array<int> $prices = ['apple' => 3, 'pear' => 4, 'plum' => 5];

var $cents = Core\Task::map($prices, fn(int $euros): int => $euros * 100);

// The results keep the input's keys and the input's order.
// This prints apple=300, then pear=400, then plum=500.
foreach ($cents as string $fruit => int $amount) {
    echo $fruit, '=', $amount, "\n";
}
```

```output
apple=300
pear=400
plum=500
```

#### Example 02: the function can read the key too

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the two parameters the function may take. The first is the element's value.
// The second is its key. You write the second one only when you need it.

array<int> $stock = ['Hamburg' => 12, 'Munchen' => 0, 'Koln' => 7];

// Only the value. This prints 24, 0 and 14.
var $doubled = Core\Task::map($stock, fn(int $count): int => $count * 2);
foreach ($doubled as int $count) {
    echo $count, "\n";
}

// The value and the key. This prints Hamburg has 12, and so on for the other two.
var $lines = Core\Task::map($stock, fn(int $count, string $city): string => $city . ' has ' . $count);
foreach ($lines as string $line) {
    echo $line, "\n";
}
```

```output
24
0
14
Hamburg has 12
Munchen has 0
Koln has 7
```

#### Example 03: an import checks every row at once

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a real use: an uploaded file has one order per row, and every row has to be
// checked before any of them is saved. No row needs another row, so all of them are
// checked at the same time. The answers come back in the file's own order.

class Row
{
    public static function check(string $line): string
    {
        array<string> $parts = Core\Str::split($line, ',');
        if (Core\Arr::count($parts) != 2) {
            return 'needs two columns';
        }

        if (Core\Str::length($parts[1]) == 0) {
            return 'the amount is empty';
        }

        return 'ok';
    }
}

array<string> $upload = [
    'COFFEE-1KG,2',
    'FILTER-100',
    'MUG-BLUE,',
    'CUP-RED,4',
];

var $verdicts = Core\Task::map($upload, fn(string $line): string => Row::check($line));

// An array's key is always a `string`, so the row number is converted before it is used.
foreach ($verdicts as string $key => string $verdict) {
    echo 'row ', ($key as int) + 1, ': ', $verdict, "\n";
}
```

```output
row 1: ok
row 2: needs two columns
row 3: the amount is empty
row 4: ok
```

### `limit` and `deadline`

`Core\Task::all` and `Core\Task::map` both take a second argument with two fields, `limit` and
`deadline`. Both fields are optional, and they are the only two bounds a group of tasks has.

`limit` says how many tasks may run at the same time. The others wait for a free place, and none of
them is refused. Without a `limit`, every task starts at once. A `limit` of `0` throws `LogicError`.

`deadline` is a time limit for the whole call, not for each task. When it passes, every task still
running is stopped. The call waits for those tasks to stop, and then throws `TimeoutError`. A
stopped task runs no more of its own code: not its `catch`, and not the line after the one it was
waiting on.

**The examples below** show a deadline for a whole call, two tasks running at a time, and a price
list that is polite to a slow service.

The options must be written at the call as `{…}`. Options kept in a variable are `E0453`. A field
that is not `limit` or `deadline` is `E0454`, and its help lists the two.

`limit` is a `uint`. `limit: -1` and an `int` variable are `E0401`. A `limit` larger than the
number of tasks is allowed. The waiting tasks start in the order they were written.

`deadline` is a `Core\Time\Duration`, such as `20ms`. A number such as `20` is `E0401`.

The `TimeoutError` message is `Core\Task::map: the deadline expired before every child returned`,
with `Core\Task::all` for that call. `TimeoutError` is a `RuntimeError`. The `LogicError` message
for `limit: 0` starts with `Core\Task::map:` or `Core\Task::all:` too.

`deadline: 0ms` throws `TimeoutError`, even when no task waits.

A stopped task does not run its `finally` blocks either.

A task can start its own group with a shorter deadline, and catch that group's `TimeoutError`. The
outer group then goes on. When the outer deadline passes first, it stops the inner groups too, and
the outer call throws its own `TimeoutError`.

#### Example 01: a deadline for the whole call

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to give a group of tasks a time limit. The deadline covers the whole
// call. When it passes, every task still running is stopped and the call throws
// `TimeoutError`.

try {
    Core\Task::all({
        quick: fn(): int => 1,
        slow: fn(): int => {
            Core\Time::sleep(500ms);
            return 2;
        },
    }, { deadline: 20ms });
    echo "both tasks finished\n";
} catch (TimeoutError $late) {
    // This is the line that prints. `slow` needs half a second, and the group has
    // 20 milliseconds.
    echo "the group ran out of time\n";
}
```

```output
the group ran out of time
```

#### Example 02: no more than two tasks at a time

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to say how many tasks may run at the same time. There are six tasks
// here, and `limit` lets two of them run at once. The other four wait for a free
// place. None of them is refused.

class Gauge
{
    public static int $running = 0;
    public static int $most = 0;
}

var $results = Core\Task::map(Core\Arr::range(1, 6), fn(int $n): int => {
    Gauge::$running += 1;
    if (Gauge::$running > Gauge::$most) {
        Gauge::$most = Gauge::$running;
    }
    Core\Time::sleep(5ms);
    Gauge::$running -= 1;
    return $n * 10;
}, { limit: 2 });

// This prints 2. Two tasks ran at the same time, and never three.
echo 'most at once: ', Gauge::$most, "\n";
// All six tasks ran, so the last result is 60.
echo 'last result: ', $results[5], "\n";
```

```output
most at once: 2
last result: 60
```

#### Example 03: a price list that is polite and gives up

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a real use: a report needs the price of six products from a slow service.
// `limit` asks for no more than two prices at a time, so the service is not flooded.
// `deadline` stops the whole report after one second.

class Prices
{
    public static function of(string $sku): int
    {
        // A real program asks another server here.
        Core\Time::sleep(5ms);
        return Core\Str::length($sku) as int * 100;
    }
}

array<string> $skus = ['cup', 'mug', 'kettle', 'spoon', 'pot', 'tray'];

try {
    var $prices = Core\Task::map(
        $skus,
        fn(string $sku): int => Prices::of($sku),
        { limit: 2, deadline: 1s },
    );
    foreach ($prices as int $price) {
        echo $price, "\n";
    }
} catch (TimeoutError $late) {
    // The report prints this when the service does not answer in time.
    echo "the price service was too slow\n";
}
```

```output
300
300
600
500
300
400
```

### A child's throw

`Core\Task::all` and `Core\Task::map` run several tasks at the same time. When one task throws an
error, the whole group stops.

The first error wins. The other tasks are cancelled, and none of them is still running when your
`catch` runs. The error you catch is the one the task threw. It has the same class, the same message,
and your own properties if you wrote your own error class. Nothing wraps it.

A cancelled task runs nothing more. Its own `catch` does not run, and neither do the lines after it.

**The examples below** show a group where one task fails, an error class of your own crossing out of a
task, a page that loads three things and reports the one that was missing, and two tasks that throw
before they wait.

A task runs until it waits, for example in `Core\Time::sleep` or a `send` on a full channel. The other
tasks are stopped at the place where they wait. A task that throws before it waits for anything is
not stopped in time. When two tasks throw that way, your `catch` gets the first error. The second
error is printed on standard error as `uncaught in a cancelled sibling: second`, and the program goes
on. With `Core\Task::map`, the first error is the one of the first element.

A stopped task runs none of its own `catch` and `finally` blocks. What it printed before it stopped is
still printed.

The error you catch is the same object the task threw. `==` with a copy the task saved is `true`. A
`catch (Throwable $e)` gets it too, and `$e is LogicError` is still `true` for a `LogicError`.

The `backtrace` of the error has one entry: the task's function, at the line of the `throw`.

A task can start its own group. An error in the inner group passes through the outer group to your
`catch`, and the other tasks of the outer group are stopped too.

When nothing catches the error, the program ends with exit status 1 and the usual error report.

When a `deadline` passes before any task throws, the call throws `TimeoutError`, and the later error
is not thrown.

#### Example 01: one task fails and the group stops

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows what happens when one task in a group throws an error. The group stops
// and your `catch` gets the error that task threw.

class Trace
{
    public static int $finished = 0;
}

try {
    Core\Task::all({
        // This task waits, so the other one throws first.
        slow: fn(): int => {
            Core\Time::sleep(2s);
            Trace::$finished = Trace::$finished + 1;
            return 1;
        },
        quick: fn(): int => {
            throw new RuntimeError('the price list is empty');
        },
    });
    echo "the group finished\n";
} catch (RuntimeError $e) {
    echo 'caught: ', $e->message, "\n";
}

// The slow task was cancelled, so it never reached its last line.
echo Trace::$finished, " tasks finished\n";
```

```output
caught: the price list is empty
0 tasks finished
```

#### Example 02: an error class of your own

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows an error class of your own crossing out of a task. The class and the
// properties you gave it are still there in the `catch`.

class ImportFailed extends RuntimeError
{
    public int $row;

    public function constructor(string $message, int $row)
    {
        $this->row = $row;
        parent::constructor($message);
    }
}

try {
    // One task for each file. The second file has a row this program cannot read.
    Core\Task::map([1, 2, 3], fn(int $file): int => {
        if ($file == 2) {
            throw new ImportFailed('this row has no price', 31);
        }
        return $file;
    });
    echo "all three files were imported\n";
} catch (ImportFailed $e) {
    echo $e->message, "\n";
    echo 'row ', $e->row, "\n";
}
```

```output
this row has no price
row 31
```

#### Example 03: a page that loads three things

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a page that loads three things at the same time. One of them is not
// there, so the page says so instead of showing half of itself.

class Store
{
    public static function user(): string
    {
        return 'Ada';
    }

    public static function orders(): int
    {
        return 3;
    }

    public static function recommendations(): int
    {
        throw new RuntimeError('the recommendation service is down');
    }
}

try {
    var $page = Core\Task::all({
        user: fn(): string => {
            return Store::user();
        },
        orders: fn(): int => {
            return Store::orders();
        },
        recommendations: fn(): int => {
            return Store::recommendations();
        },
    });
    echo $page->user, ' has ', $page->orders, " orders\n";
} catch (RuntimeError $e) {
    echo 'this page cannot be built: ', $e->message, "\n";
}
```

```output
this page cannot be built: the recommendation service is down
```

#### Example 04: two tasks throw before they wait

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows two tasks that both throw before they wait for anything. Your `catch` gets
// the first error.

try {
    Core\Task::all({
        first: fn(): int => {
            throw new RuntimeError('the first file is missing');
        },
        // This task runs before the group can stop it. Its error is printed on
        // standard error, and your program goes on.
        second: fn(): int => {
            echo "the second task started\n";
            throw new RuntimeError('the second file is missing');
        },
    });
} catch (RuntimeError $e) {
    echo 'caught: ', $e->message, "\n";
}
echo "the program goes on\n";
```

```output
the second task started
caught: the first file is missing
the program goes on
```

### `Core\Task\Channel<T>`: a bounded queue between tasks

A `Core\Task\Channel<T>` is a queue that one task fills and another empties. You give it a capacity
when you make it, and it holds that many values. `send` puts one value in. If the channel is full,
`send` waits until there is room, so the queue never grows.

You read a channel with a `foreach` loop. It takes the values out one at a time, in the order they
were sent. The loop waits while the channel is empty, and ends once it is empty and closed.

`close` says that no more values are coming. Values already in the queue are still delivered, and
closing twice does nothing. A task that never closes leaves the reading task waiting forever.
Sending into a closed channel stops the program with an error, and so does a capacity of `0`.

**The examples below** show two tasks passing values, what the capacity does, and orders billed
while they are still being read.

The capacity is a `uint`. `-1` and an `int` variable are `E0401`. A capacity of `0` stops the program
with `FATAL: Core\Task\Channel's constructor expected a capacity of at least 1, got 0` and exit
status 1.

You must write the value type. `new Core\Task\Channel(1)` is `E0442`. A `send` of another type is
`E0401`, and so is a `foreach` variable of another type. `foreach ($chan as var $v)` gives `$v` the
channel's value type. A key, as in `foreach ($chan as $k => int $v)`, is `E0444`.

A channel has the methods `send` and `close`. There is no `receive` method (`E0405`). A `foreach` loop
is the way to take values out.

A `send` on a closed channel stops the program with `FATAL: Core\Task\Channel::send was called on a
closed channel` and exit status 1. No `catch` block and no `finally` block runs.

Nothing checks that another task will read or send. A `send` on a full channel with no reader waits
forever. So does a `foreach` on an empty channel that nobody closes. This is true inside a task group
and outside one. A `deadline` on the group stops that wait.

A second `foreach` over a channel that is closed and empty runs nothing.

An object you send is the same object in the reading task. A change the reader makes to it is seen by
the sender.

You can pass a channel to a method. The parameter type is `Core\Task\Channel<int>`, with the value
type.

#### Example 01: two tasks pass values through a queue

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how one task sends values to another through a channel. `close` tells the
// reading task that no more values are coming.

var $lines = new Core\Task\Channel<string>(4);

Core\Task::all({
    write: fn(): void => {
        $lines->send('first');
        $lines->send('second');
        $lines->send('third');
        // Close the channel when you are done sending. Without this the reading
        // task waits forever.
        $lines->close();
    },
    read: fn(): void => {
        // The loop takes one value at a time. It ends when the channel is empty
        // and closed.
        foreach ($lines as string $line) {
            echo $line, "\n";
        }
        echo "no more lines\n";
    },
});
```

```output
first
second
third
no more lines
```

#### Example 02: the queue holds a fixed number of values

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows what the capacity of a channel does. This one holds 2 values. `send` waits
// while the channel is full, so the queue never holds more than 2 values. The memory
// it uses is the same for 8 values and for 8 million.

var $jobs = new Core\Task\Channel<int>(2);

var $done = Core\Task::all({
    fill: fn(): int => {
        foreach (Core\Arr::range(1, 8) as int $n) {
            $jobs->send($n);
        }
        $jobs->close();
        return 8;
    },
    work: fn(): int => {
        int $sum = 0;
        foreach ($jobs as int $n) {
            echo 'handled job ', $n, "\n";
            $sum = $sum + $n;
        }
        return $sum;
    },
});

// This prints 8 and 36.
echo $done->fill, ' jobs, total ', $done->work, "\n";
```

```output
handled job 1
handled job 2
handled job 3
handled job 4
handled job 5
handled job 6
handled job 7
handled job 8
8 jobs, total 36
```

#### Example 03: orders are billed while they are still being read

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a real use: one task reads orders and another writes a receipt for each one.
// The channel holds 2 orders, so the reading task waits for the writer. A list of a
// million orders uses the same memory as a list of three.

class Order
{
    public function constructor(public string $id, public int $cents)
    {}
}

class Shop
{
    public static function orders(): array<Order>
    {
        return [
            new Order('A-1001', 1250),
            new Order('A-1002', 900),
            new Order('A-1003', 4300),
        ];
    }
}

var $queue = new Core\Task\Channel<Order>(2);

var $till = Core\Task::all({
    read: fn(): int => {
        int $count = 0;
        foreach (Shop::orders() as Order $order) {
            $queue->send($order);
            $count = $count + 1;
        }
        $queue->close();
        return $count;
    },
    bill: fn(): int => {
        int $cents = 0;
        foreach ($queue as Order $order) {
            echo 'receipt ', $order->id, ': ', $order->cents, " cents\n";
            $cents = $cents + $order->cents;
        }
        return $cents;
    },
});

// This prints 3 and 6450.
echo $till->read, ' orders, ', $till->bill, " cents in total\n";
```

```output
receipt A-1001: 1250 cents
receipt A-1002: 900 cents
receipt A-1003: 4300 cents
3 orders, 6450 cents in total
```

### Isolates: `spawn script` and `await`

`spawn script "file.nvs"` runs another file while your program keeps going. It gives you a handle.
`await $handle` waits for that file and returns its result.

The result has four fields. `ok` is true when the file finished without an error. `value` is what the
file returned, and you convert it with `as`. `output` is what the file printed, when you wrote
`output: "capture"`. `error` has the class name and the message when the file stopped with an error.

A path in quotes starts at the folder of the file that contains it. A path you build at run time
must be a full path, or `spawn script` throws `RuntimeError`. Build one with `Core\Path::join`. You
can also start a static method, written `Class::method`.

A static method and a file inside your application folder need no capability. A file outside that
folder needs the `script.spawn` capability. You can await one handle once. A second `await` of the
same handle throws `LogicError`.

`spawn script` gives a `Core\Script\Handle`. The handle has no properties, so `$h->ok` is `E0405`.
`await` needs a handle. `await $n` on an `int` is `E0401`.

The entry is a path or a static method. An anonymous function is `E0802`.

`with(…)` takes the options `args`, `limits`, `grants`, `output` and `on`. Another name is `E0101`, and
its help lists the five.

`on:` must be the word `"worker"` or `"here"`, written at the spawn. Another word is `E0818`, and so is
a variable. To choose the core while the program runs, write two spawns in an `if`.

`output:` may be a variable. A value that is not `"capture"` or `"inherit"` throws `LogicError` with
the message ``` `spawn script`'s `output:` is `'capture'` or `'inherit'`, got `'keep'` ```.

The type of `output` in the result is `Core\Html\Markup|Core\Cli\Text`, not `string`. So `string $s =
$r->output;` is `E0401`. `echo $r->output` works, and `$r->output as string` gives the text.

With `output: "inherit"`, the child's output is printed when you `await` its handle. It comes after
everything the parent printed before that `await`. The `output` field is then empty.

A handle that is never awaited prints nothing. The program ends when the parent ends, even while the
child still runs.

`value` is `mixed`, so `int $v = $r->value;` is `E0401`. `$r->value as string` gives a `tainted
string`. A child with no `return` gives `null`. A child that calls `exit` also gives `null`, and `ok`
is `true`.

A child cannot return an object. When it does, `ok` is `false`, and the class in `error` is `Error`.
This is true for an anonymous object too, and for a class the parent also declares.

`args:` copies its value at the spawn. A change the parent makes later is not seen by the child.
Without `args:`, `Core\Script::args()` returns `null`. A file cannot receive an object in `args:`. The
spawn then throws `LogicError` in the parent.

A static method gets each entry of `args:` as the argument with the same name. Write `args:` as an
array with string keys, such as `["n" => 5]`. Here an object can be passed. A method with parameters
and no `args:` is `E0402`, and a key that names no parameter is `E0486`. When an entry is missing
while the program runs, the spawn throws `LogicError`. When an entry has the wrong type, the child
fails with a `LogicError`, and `ok` is `false`.

A path built while the program runs must be absolute. For a relative one, the message is ``
`spawn script` needs an absolute path, and `child.nvs` is relative ``. A second line names
`Core\Path::join` and `Core\Path::fromCwd`.

`limits: { memory: "1M" }` gives the child a memory limit. A child that goes over it ends with `ok`
`false` and a `RuntimeError`. `grants: []` gives the child no capabilities, so a `spawn script` inside
it throws `RuntimeError`.

A child can start its own child. A task in `Core\Task::all` can start a child and `await` it.

#### Example 01: run another file and wait for it

```nvs file=jobs/add-up.nvs
<?nvs
// This file reads the value the parent gave in `args:`.
array<int> $numbers = Core\Script::args() as array<int>;
int $total = 0;
foreach ($numbers as int $n) {
    $total += $n;
}
return $total;
```

```nvs file=jobs/build-report.nvs
<?nvs
// The examples in the folder above start this script. It adds up last month's
// sales and returns one line of text about them.

int $total = 0;
foreach (Core\Arr::range(1, 30) as int $day) {
    $total += $day * 100;
}

return 'Sales last month: ' . $total;
```

```nvs file=jobs/count-rows.nvs
<?nvs
// The examples in the folder above start this script. It reads an order file
// and returns the number of rows it read.

echo "read the order file\n";
return 1200;
```

```nvs file=jobs/fetch-prices.nvs
<?nvs
// The examples in the folder above start this script. It collects prices and
// returns how many it found.

echo "prices are ready\n";
return 3;
```

```nvs file=jobs/fetch-stock.nvs
<?nvs
// The examples in the folder above start this script. It counts the items in
// stock and returns that number.

echo "stock is ready\n";
return 5;
```

```nvs file=jobs/say-hello.nvs
<?nvs
echo "the child says hello\n";
```

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to run another file and collect its result. `spawn script` starts
// the file. `await` waits for it to finish and gives you a result to read.

// The path starts at the folder of this file.
var $handle = spawn script 'jobs/count-rows.nvs' with(output: 'capture');

// The file is running now. Your program can do other work on this line.
echo "the file was started\n";

var $result = await $handle;

// `ok` is true when the file finished without an error.
echo 'ok: ', $result->ok ? 'true' : 'false', "\n";

// `value` is what the file returned. Convert it with `as`.
int $rows = $result->value as int;
echo 'rows: ', $rows, "\n";

// `output` is everything the file printed, because this spawn asked to keep it.
echo 'it printed: ', $result->output;
```

```output
the file was started
ok: true
rows: 1200
it printed: read the order file
```

#### Example 04: print the child s output and await once

```nvs file=jobs/add-up.nvs
<?nvs
// This file reads the value the parent gave in `args:`.

foreach ($numbers as int $n) {
    $total += $n;
}
return $total;
```

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `output: "inherit"`. The child's output is printed when you `await` it.
// A second `await` of the same handle throws `LogicError`.

var $hello = spawn script 'jobs/say-hello.nvs' with(output: 'inherit');
echo "the parent prints first\n";

// The child's line is printed here, at the `await`.
var $done = await $hello;
echo 'ok: ', $done->ok ? 'true' : 'false', "\n";

try {
    var $again = await $hello;
} catch (LogicError $e) {
    echo $e->message, "\n";
}
```


### A child shares nothing

A script you start with `spawn script` runs on its own. It shares nothing with the program that started
it.

Every class static in the started script begins at its declared value, whatever your program wrote in its
own copy. A write inside the script stays there. Your own values are the same after the script has
finished as they were before it began. Two scripts started one after another share nothing either.

Printing works the same way. With `output: "capture"` the text the script prints comes back to you in the
`output` field of the result, and nothing reaches the screen. With `output: "inherit"` the script prints
to your screen, and `output` is then empty.

**The examples below** show a script that cannot change your numbers, the two ways to handle what a
script prints, and a health check made of three scripts that cannot disturb each other.

A static property with an array value starts at its declared value in the child too. An entry the
parent added is not there, and an entry the child adds does not reach the parent.

A child started with `on: "here"` runs on the same core as the parent. It shares nothing with the
parent either.

A task in `Core\Task::all` can start a child. All tasks of the program share one value of each static
property, but the child still gets its own copy.

The child is a separate program. It does not need the classes the parent declares, and it cannot read
the parent's variables. A child that uses `$x` without declaring it does not compile. The error is
`E0301`, and `spawn script` throws `RuntimeError` in the parent.

#### Example 01: the script cannot change your data

```nvs file=scripts/count-orders.nvs
<?nvs
// The examples in the folder above start this script. It prints the number it
// reads, then writes a new number in its place.

final class Orders
{
    public static int $counted = 0;
}

echo 'the script read ', Orders::$counted, "\n";
Orders::$counted = 42;
echo 'the script wrote ', Orders::$counted, "\n";
```

```nvs file=scripts/say-what-it-did.nvs
<?nvs
// The examples in the folder above start this script. It prints one line and
// returns the number of files it removed.

echo "removed 3 old files\n";
return 3;
```

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows that a script you start with `spawn script` cannot change your data.
// It gets its own copy of every class static, and your own copy stays as it is.

final class Orders
{
    public static int $counted = 0;
}

Orders::$counted = 7;
echo 'before: ', Orders::$counted, "\n";

// The path starts at the folder of this file.
var $handle = spawn script 'scripts/count-orders.nvs' with(output: 'capture');
var $result = await $handle;

// The script printed two lines while it ran. With `capture` they come back as
// text. It read 0, because its own copy of `Orders::$counted` starts at 0.
echo $result->output;

// The script set `Orders::$counted` to 42. This still prints 7.
echo 'after: ', Orders::$counted, "\n";
```

```output
before: 7
the script read 0
the script wrote 42
after: 7
```

#### Example 02: keep what the script prints or show it

```nvs file=scripts/count-orders.nvs
<?nvs
// The examples in the folder above start this script. It prints the number it
// reads, then writes a new number in its place.

final class Orders
{
    public static int $counted = 0;
}

echo 'the script read ', Orders::$counted, "\n";
Orders::$counted = 42;
echo 'the script wrote ', Orders::$counted, "\n";
```

```nvs file=scripts/say-what-it-did.nvs
<?nvs
// The examples in the folder above start this script. It prints one line and
// returns the number of files it removed.

echo "removed 3 old files\n";
return 3;
```

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the two ways to handle what a started script prints. A script has its
// own place to print to. You decide where that text goes.

// `output: "capture"` keeps the text for you. Nothing reaches the screen while
// the script runs. The path starts at the folder of this file.
var $first = spawn script 'scripts/say-what-it-did.nvs' with(output: 'capture');
var $kept = await $first;
echo 'the script said: ', $kept->output;

// `value` is what the script returned. Convert it with `as`.
int $files = $kept->value as int;
echo 'it removed ', $files, " files\n";

// `output: "inherit"` sends the text to your own screen instead. All of it is
// there once `await` has returned.
var $second = spawn script 'scripts/say-what-it-did.nvs' with(output: 'inherit');
var $shown = await $second;

// `output` is empty this time, because the text went to the screen.
// `as string` converts it to a `string`, so `Core\Str::length` can count it.
echo 'kept text: ', Core\Str::length($shown->output as string), " characters\n";
```

```output
the script said: removed 3 old files
it removed 3 files
removed 3 old files
kept text: 0 characters
```

#### Example 03: a health check of three scripts

```nvs file=checks/disk-space.nvs
<?nvs
// One health check. The example in the folder above starts it. It counts the
// problems it found in its own `Report::$problems`, and returns that number.

final class Report
{
    public static int $problems = 0;
}

echo "two disks are above 90 percent\n";
Report::$problems = Report::$problems + 2;
return Report::$problems;
```

```nvs file=checks/mail-queue.nvs
<?nvs
// One health check. The example in the folder above starts it. Its own
// `Report::$problems` starts at 0, whatever the other checks wrote in theirs.

final class Report
{
    public static int $problems = 0;
}

echo "the mail queue is empty\n";
return Report::$problems;
```

```nvs file=checks/old-sessions.nvs
<?nvs
// One health check. The example in the folder above starts it. It removes old
// sessions and counts the ones it could not remove.

final class Report
{
    public static int $problems = 0;
}

echo "one session is older than a year\n";
Report::$problems = Report::$problems + 1;
return Report::$problems;
```

```nvs file=scripts/count-orders.nvs
<?nvs
// The examples in the folder above start this script. It prints the number it
// reads, then writes a new number in its place.

final class Orders
{
    public static int $counted = 0;
}

echo 'the script read ', Orders::$counted, "\n";
Orders::$counted = 42;
echo 'the script wrote ', Orders::$counted, "\n";
```

```nvs file=scripts/say-what-it-did.nvs
<?nvs
// The examples in the folder above start this script. It prints one line and
// returns the number of files it removed.

echo "removed 3 old files\n";
return 3;
```

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a health check made of three scripts. Each script has its own data. One
// check cannot change what another check counted. This program adds the three
// numbers up itself.

final class Report
{
    public static int $problems = 0;
}

// `#[Core\Path]` says that a parameter is a file path. A relative path in
// quotes passed to it starts at the folder of this file.
class Here
{
    public static function path(#[Core\Path] string $path): string
    {
        return $path;
    }
}

// `$dir` is a full path, so a path built from it works from any folder.
string $dir = Here::path('checks');
array<string> $checks = ['disk-space', 'mail-queue', 'old-sessions'];

foreach ($checks as string $name) {
    string $path = Core\Path::join($dir, $name . '.nvs');
    var $handle = spawn script $path with(output: 'capture');
    var $result = await $handle;

    // All three scripts declare `Report::$problems` and start it at 0. The
    // number each one returns is its own count.
    int $problems = $result->value as int;
    Report::$problems = Report::$problems + $problems;

    echo $name, ': ', $problems, " problem(s)\n";
    echo '  ', $result->output;
}

// This program added the three numbers up itself. The scripts could not.
echo 'total: ', Report::$problems, " problem(s)\n";
```

```output
disk-space: 2 problem(s)
  two disks are above 90 percent
mail-queue: 0 problem(s)
  the mail queue is empty
old-sessions: 1 problem(s)
  one session is older than a year
total: 3 problem(s)
```

### A child's failure is a value

A script you start with `spawn script` runs on its own. When it fails, the failure comes back to you as
a value.

`await` returns a result. `ok` is false when the script ended with an error it did not catch. `error` has
the class name and the message of that error. `output` still has everything the script printed before it
failed. Your program keeps running.

A mistake in your own program is different. A file name that points to nothing throws an error in your
program. So does a file that does not compile, or a misspelled `output:` setting. Those errors happen at
the line that starts the script, and you catch them with `try`.

**The examples below** show a failed script read as a result, your own mistake told apart from the
script's failure, and a group of jobs where one fails and the other two still finish. The last one
shows the error when your program may not start scripts.

The type of `error` is `null|{ class: string, message: string }`. It is `null` when `ok` is `true`. So
`$r->error->message` is `E0459`. Read it with `?->`, or test `$r->error != null` first.

`error` has two fields, `class` and `message`. It has no `backtrace` and no `line`. `$r->error?->line`
compiles, and throws a `RuntimeError` when it runs: `` `$shape{class,message}` has no field `line` ``.

`class` is the name of the class the child threw. For a class the child declares itself, such as
`ImportFailed`, the result has that name. A `RecursionError` in the child gives the class
`RecursionError` and the message `the call stack is too deep`. A division by zero gives
`ArithmeticError`.

A failure in the child never throws in the parent. A `try` around `await` catches nothing, and `ok`
is `false`. With `output: "inherit"`, what the child printed is printed at `await`, and then `ok` is
`false` too.

A child that calls `exit(3)` gives `ok` `true` and `error` `null`. The result has no status number.

A missing file and a file that does not compile give the same message in the parent:
`` `spawn script '<path>'`: `<path>` could not be compiled; see the errors above ``. The compiler's
errors are printed to standard error. For a missing file, that is a `could not read` line with the
message of the operating system.

Without the grant, the message is `` `spawn script` needs the capability `script.spawn` for <path>,
which is not granted ``. A second line starts with `help:` and names `[capabilities.script]` in
`nvs.toml`.

#### Example 01: a job that fails

```nvs file=jobs/build-invoices.nvs
<?nvs
// The examples in the folder above start this script. It writes one invoice
// for each order it was given.

echo "wrote 2 invoices\n";
```

```nvs file=jobs/import-orders.nvs
<?nvs
// The examples in the folder above start this script. It reads orders and
// stops at the first row it cannot read.

echo "read 2 orders\n";
throw new RuntimeError('row 3 has no price');
```

```nvs file=jobs/send-receipts.nvs
<?nvs
// The examples in the folder above start this script. It sends one receipt
// for each invoice it was given.

echo "sent 2 receipts\n";
```

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows what you get when a script you started fails. `await` returns a result
// with `ok` set to false, and `error` has the class name and the message.

// The path starts at the folder of this file.
var $handle = spawn script 'jobs/import-orders.nvs' with(output: 'capture');
var $result = await $handle;

echo 'ok: ', $result->ok ? 'true' : 'false', "\n";
// `error` is empty when the script worked, so read it with `?->`.
echo 'error: ', $result->error?->class, ': ', $result->error?->message, "\n";
// The script printed this line before it failed. The failure did not lose it.
echo 'output: ', $result->output;
echo "this program is still running\n";
```

```output
ok: false
error: RuntimeError: row 3 has no price
output: read 2 orders
this program is still running
```

#### Example 02: my mistake or the scripts

```nvs file=jobs/build-invoices.nvs
<?nvs
// The examples in the folder above start this script. It writes one invoice
// for each order it was given.

echo "wrote 2 invoices\n";
```

```nvs file=jobs/import-orders.nvs
<?nvs
// The examples in the folder above start this script. It reads orders and
// stops at the first row it cannot read.

echo "read 2 orders\n";
throw new RuntimeError('row 3 has no price');
```

```nvs file=jobs/send-receipts.nvs
<?nvs
// The examples in the folder above start this script. It sends one receipt
// for each invoice it was given.

echo "sent 2 receipts\n";
```

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the two ways starting a script can go wrong. A mistake in this program
// throws here. A failure inside the script comes back as a result.

// This file name points to nothing, so `spawn script` throws in this program.
// Each path starts at the folder of this file.
try {
    spawn script 'jobs/no-such-job.nvs';
} catch (RuntimeError $mine) {
    echo "my mistake: there is no script at that path\n";
}

// `output:` takes "capture" or "inherit". Any other word is a `LogicError`.
try {
    spawn script 'jobs/import-orders.nvs' with(output: 'capturr');
} catch (LogicError $typo) {
    echo 'my mistake: ', $typo->message, "\n";
}

// This script starts, runs and then fails. That is a result, not a throw.
var $handle = spawn script 'jobs/import-orders.nvs' with(output: 'capture');
var $result = await $handle;
echo 'the script failed: ', $result->error?->message, "\n";
```

```output
my mistake: there is no script at that path
my mistake: `spawn script`'s `output:` is `'capture'` or `'inherit'`, got `'capturr'`
the script failed: row 3 has no price
```

#### Example 03: a nightly run of three jobs

```nvs file=jobs/build-invoices.nvs
<?nvs
// The examples in the folder above start this script. It writes one invoice
// for each order it was given.

echo "wrote 2 invoices\n";
```

```nvs file=jobs/import-orders.nvs
<?nvs
// The examples in the folder above start this script. It reads orders and
// stops at the first row it cannot read.

echo "read 2 orders\n";
throw new RuntimeError('row 3 has no price');
```

```nvs file=jobs/send-receipts.nvs
<?nvs
// The examples in the folder above start this script. It sends one receipt
// for each invoice it was given.

echo "sent 2 receipts\n";
```

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a program that runs three jobs and reports each one. The first job
// fails, and the other two still run. This is what a nightly job runner does.

// `#[Core\Path]` says that a parameter is a file path. A relative path in
// quotes passed to it starts at the folder of this file.
class Here
{
    public static function path(#[Core\Path] string $path): string
    {
        return $path;
    }
}

// `$jobs` is a full path, so a path built from it works from any folder.
string $jobs = Here::path('jobs');
array<string> $names = ['import-orders', 'build-invoices', 'send-receipts'];

int $failed = 0;
foreach ($names as string $name) {
    string $path = Core\Path::join($jobs, $name . '.nvs');
    var $handle = spawn script $path with(output: 'capture');
    var $result = await $handle;
    // A failed job is a result you can read, so the loop goes on to the next.
    if ($result->ok) {
        echo $name, ": done\n";
    } else {
        echo $name, ': failed, ', $result->error?->message, "\n";
        $failed = $failed + 1;
    }
}

echo $failed, " of 3 jobs failed\n";
```

```output
import-orders: failed, row 3 has no price
build-invoices: done
send-receipts: done
1 of 3 jobs failed
```



```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows what happens when this program may not start scripts. Its `nvs.toml`
// sets `spawn = false`, so `spawn script` throws a `RuntimeError`.

// The path starts at the folder of this file. The script never runs.
try {
    var $handle = spawn script 'jobs/send-receipts.nvs';
    var $result = await $handle;
} catch (RuntimeError $denied) {
    // The message goes on with the full path of the script.
    // `Core\Str::before` keeps only the text before it.

echo "this program is still running\n";
```

```output
this program is still running
```
