### `Core\Program::implementing<I>()`: every class that is an `I`

`Core\Program::implementing<I>()` gives you one object for every class in your program that
implements the interface `I`. Novis works that list out while it compiles your program, so nothing is
registered while it runs and no list of classes is written anywhere. A class joins the list by
implementing the interface.

The array is sorted by the full class name. The order is the same on every machine and never depends
on the file system. An `abstract` class is not in the list, because `new` cannot create one. Every
class in the list needs a constructor that takes no arguments, and what a class needs arrives through
the interface's own methods instead. An interface that no class implements gives an empty array.

The objects are created where the call is, each time it runs, like any other `new`. Two calls give
you two separate sets of objects.

The examples show a list of checks, which classes end up in the list, and one table written in every
format a program knows. The last example is a class whose constructor needs an argument, which does
not compile.

`I` can also be a class. Then the list has every class that extends it, and `I` itself when it is
not `abstract`. An `abstract` base class is a good `I` when the classes share code. A class that
implements an interface which extends `I` is in the list too. The test for each class is the same
as `$object is I`.

`I` must be an interface or a class that your program declares. An enum, a shape, a scalar,
`mixed` and `object` are `E0743`. A built-in interface or class, such as `Stringable` or
`RuntimeError`, is `E0743` as well. A name that nothing declares is `E0303`.

The call takes exactly one type argument, so `implementing()` and `implementing<I, J>()` are
`E0442`. It takes no value argument, so `implementing<I>(1)` is `E0402`.

A class whose constructor has a parameter without a default is `E0744`, and the message names the
class. A constructor whose parameters all have defaults is allowed, and each parameter gets its
default. To pass arguments to the constructors, use `Core\Program::constructors` instead.

The result is an `array<I>`. Storing it in an `array<J>` of another type is `E0401`, and `var`
gives the variable the type `array<I>`.

Each call runs every constructor again. Two calls return two different objects for each class, so
`==` between them is `false`.

The full class name includes the namespace, so `Alpha\Zebra` comes before `Middle`, and `Middle`
before `Zed\Apple`. The list has the classes of every file in the program. It also has the classes
under each `autoload` folder, even when no code names those classes or their files.

#### Example 01: every class that implements an interface

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to reach every class that implements an interface.
// `Core\Program::implementing` gives you one new object per class. Novis finds
// the classes while it compiles your program, so a new class joins the list by
// existing.

interface Check
{
    public function describe(): string;
}

class DiskSpace implements Check
{
    public function describe(): string
    {
        return 'disk space is fine';
    }
}

class Certificates implements Check
{
    public function describe(): string
    {
        return 'certificates are valid';
    }
}

class Backups implements Check
{
    public function describe(): string
    {
        return 'backups ran last night';
    }
}

// The list is sorted by class name, so `Backups` comes first. The order never
// depends on the order the classes are written in.
foreach (Core\Program::implementing<Check>() as Check $check) {
    echo $check->describe(), "\n";
}
```

```output
backups ran last night
certificates are valid
disk space is fine
```

#### Example 02: which classes the list contains

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows which classes end up in the list. A class is in it when it implements
// the interface and `new` needs no arguments for it. An interface no class
// implements gives you an empty array.

interface Check
{
    public function name(): string;
}

// An `abstract` class cannot be created with `new`, so it is not in the list.
abstract class BaseCheck implements Check
{
    public function name(): string
    {
        return 'base';
    }
}

// This one extends the abstract class, so it implements `Check` as well.
class DiskCheck extends BaseCheck
{
    public function name(): string
    {
        return 'disk';
    }
}

class MailCheck implements Check
{
    public function name(): string
    {
        return 'mail';
    }
}

// This class has the same method and implements nothing, so it stays out.
class Report
{
    public function name(): string
    {
        return 'report';
    }
}

interface Rule
{
    public function apply(): string;
}

// This prints `disk` and then `mail`.
foreach (Core\Program::implementing<Check>() as Check $check) {
    echo $check->name(), "\n";
}

// No class implements `Rule`, so this prints 0.
echo Core\Arr::count(Core\Program::implementing<Rule>()), "\n";
```

```output
disk
mail
0
```

#### Example 03: one table in every format

```nvs
<?nvs
// Writing one table in every format a program knows. Adding a format means
// adding a class. There is no list of formats to keep up to date, and nothing
// has to be registered.

interface Exporter
{
    public function format(): string;
    public function render(array<string> $rows): string;
}

class CsvExporter implements Exporter
{
    public function format(): string
    {
        return 'csv';
    }

    public function render(array<string> $rows): string
    {
        string $out = '';
        foreach ($rows as string $row) {
            $out = $out == '' ? $row : $out . ',' . $row;
        }
        return $out;
    }
}

class JsonExporter implements Exporter
{
    public function format(): string
    {
        return 'json';
    }

    public function render(array<string> $rows): string
    {
        return Core\Json::encode($rows);
    }
}

class TextExporter implements Exporter
{
    public function format(): string
    {
        return 'text';
    }

    public function render(array<string> $rows): string
    {
        string $out = '';
        foreach ($rows as string $row) {
            $out = $out . '- ' . $row . ' ';
        }
        return Core\Str::trim($out);
    }
}

array<string> $rows = ['cup', 'plate', 'bowl'];

// One line per format, in alphabetical order by class name.
foreach (Core\Program::implementing<Exporter>() as Exporter $exporter) {
    echo $exporter->format(), ': ', $exporter->render($rows), "\n";
}
```

```output
csv: cup,plate,bowl
json: ["cup","plate","bowl"]
text: - cup - plate - bowl
```

```nvs error
class SmtpSender implements Sender

    public function send(string $text): string
    {
        return 'sent to ' . $this->host . ': ' . $text;

}

foreach (Core\Program::implementing<Sender>() as Sender $sender) {
    echo $sender->send('hello'), "\n";
}
```

```output
   --> main.nvs:30:10

   |          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ this enumeration would write `new SmtpSender()`
   = help: every class in the result is created with no arguments. Give `SmtpSender` a `constructor` with no required parameters. Or use `Core\Program::constructors<Sender, callable(...): Sender>()`, which passes the arguments you give it
```

### `Core\Program::implementingWith<I, T>($member)`: every implementor with one attribute

`Core\Program::implementingWith<I, T>($member)` gives you one row for every class in your program
that implements the interface `I`, with one of that class's attributes beside it.

Each row has two fields. `instance` is the object, and `attribute` is the one attribute on that
class's `$member` whose fields match the shape `T`. Without such an attribute, it is `null`. `$member` is the name of a method or a property, or an empty string for the attributes written
on the class itself. Rows are sorted by full class name.

Novis finds the classes and their attributes while it compiles your program. A framework uses this
to read the settings of the classes it found.

**Good to know:** two attributes on one class that both match `T` are an error. Use a narrower
shape, or read that class with `Core\Attributes::all<T>`.

The examples show a report label, class attributes, an admin menu, each page's route path, and a
missing member, which does not compile.

`I` follows the same rules as for `Core\Program::implementing`. The list has the same classes in
the same order, and `E0743`, `E0744` and `E0442` are given for the same mistakes. The call takes two
type arguments.

`$member` is a `string`, and an `int` is `E0401`. Without an argument, `$member` is the empty
string, so the rows have the attributes on each class itself. A second argument is `E0402`.

Write `$member` as a string in quotes. Novis reads it while it compiles. A variable, a class
constant or a joined string such as `"m" . "m"` also compiles, but every row's `attribute` is
then `null`.

A method name finds the method in each class, also a `static` or a `private` one. `"constructor"`
finds the attributes on the constructor. A property is written without the `$`, as `"total"`. In
double quotes, `"$total"` is a variable in the string, so it is `E0301` when no such variable
exists. A promoted constructor parameter is a property, and its name gives the attributes written
on that parameter. A constructor parameter that is not promoted is not found. To read its
attributes, use `Core\Attributes::get` with `Report::constructor` and the parameter's name.

A name that one of the classes does not have is `E0798`, and the message names that class. A
method that a class inherits counts as one it has. Its attributes are not read, so that row's
`attribute` is `null`. A class that overrides a method has only the attributes on its own version.
An attribute on the interface's method is not read either.

The attribute matches `T` when it has every field of `T` with the right type. It may have more
fields. Two attributes that both match on one class are `E0728`, and the message names the class and
the member. A shape with a field that only one of them has picks that one. A `T` that is not a shape,
such as `int` or a class, is `E0729`.

Each row has the type `{ instance: I, attribute: ?T }`. Storing the result in an
`array<{ instance: I, attribute: T }>` is `E0401`, because `attribute` may be `null`.

The attributes Novis reads itself can be read this way too. `{ path: string }` reads the path of each
class's `#[Core\Route]`.

When no class implements `I`, the result is `[]`, whatever `$member` is.

#### Example 01: every class with the attribute it declares

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to read one attribute from every class that implements an
// interface. Each row holds the object and the attribute found on it.

type Label = { text: string };

interface Report
{
    public function rows(): int;
}

class SalesReport implements Report
{
    #[Label(text: 'Sales')]
    public function rows(): int
    {
        return 12;
    }
}

class StockReport implements Report
{
    #[Label(text: 'Stock')]
    public function rows(): int
    {
        return 7;
    }
}

// The rows are sorted by class name, so `SalesReport` comes first.
// This prints `Sales: 12` and then `Stock: 7`.
foreach (Core\Program::implementingWith<Report, Label>('rows') as { instance: Report, attribute: ?Label } $row) {
    echo $row->attribute?->text ?? '(none)', ': ', $row->instance->rows(), "\n";
}
```

```output
Sales: 12
Stock: 7
```

#### Example 02: a class that carries no attribute

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the two things that are not a method attribute: an empty member name,
// which reads the attributes on the class itself, and a class carrying none.

type Owner = { team: string };

interface Job
{
    public function run(): string;
}

#[Owner(team: 'billing')]
class Invoices implements Job
{
    public function run(): string
    {
        return 'invoices';
    }
}

class Cleanup implements Job
{
    public function run(): string
    {
        return 'cleanup';
    }
}

// `Cleanup` has no `#[Owner]`, so its attribute is `null` and `??` supplies
// the text instead. This prints `cleanup: nobody` and then `invoices: billing`.
foreach (Core\Program::implementingWith<Job, Owner>('') as { instance: Job, attribute: ?Owner } $row) {
    echo $row->instance->run(), ': ', $row->attribute?->team ?? 'nobody', "\n";
}
```

```output
cleanup: nobody
invoices: billing
```

#### Example 03: build an admin menu from the pages

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows what a framework does with this: every page in the program, beside the
// menu entry that page declares for itself.

type Menu = { title: string, order: int };

interface AdminPage
{
    public function path(): string;
}

class Dashboard implements AdminPage
{
    #[Menu(title: 'Dashboard', order: 1)]
    public function path(): string
    {
        return '/admin';
    }
}

class Users implements AdminPage
{
    #[Menu(title: 'Users', order: 2)]
    public function path(): string
    {
        return '/admin/users';
    }
}

class Health implements AdminPage
{
    // This page is reachable and stays out of the menu, because it declares
    // no `#[Menu]`.
    public function path(): string
    {
        return '/admin/health';
    }
}

// Adding a page to the menu is adding the attribute to the page, and no list
// of pages can go out of date. This prints `1. Dashboard -> /admin` first.
foreach (Core\Program::implementingWith<AdminPage, Menu>('path') as { instance: AdminPage, attribute: ?Menu } $row) {
    ?Menu $entry = $row->attribute;
    if ($entry != null) {
        echo $entry->order, '. ', $entry->title, ' -> ', $row->instance->path(), "\n";
    }
}
```

```output
1. Dashboard -> /admin
2. Users -> /admin/users
```

#### Example 05: each page beside its route

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to read the path of each page's `#[Core\Route]`, so each path is
// written only once.

interface Page
{
    public function render(): string;
}

class Index implements Page
{
    #[Core\Route(path: '/', method: Core\Http\Method::Get)]
    #[Core\Access(allow: Core\Audience::Public)]
    public function render(): string
    {
        return 'home';
    }
}

class Contact implements Page
{
    #[Core\Route(path: '/contact', method: Core\Http\Method::Get)]
    #[Core\Access(allow: Core\Audience::Public)]
    public function render(): string
    {
        return 'contact us';
    }
}

class Draft implements Page
{
    public function render(): string
    {
        return 'not routed';
    }
}

// `Draft` has no route, so its `attribute` is `null`.
// This prints `/contact -> contact us` first, because `Contact` comes first.
foreach (Core\Program::implementingWith<Page, { path: string }>('render') as { instance: Page, attribute: ?{ path: string } } $row) {
    echo $row->attribute?->path ?? '(no route)', ' -> ', $row->instance->render(), "\n";
}
```

```output
/contact -> contact us
(no route) -> not routed
/ -> home
```

<a id="lang-testing"></a>
## A.11 Testing

Keywords: test, #[Test], nvs test, test directory, test suite, bootstrap, assertEquals, assertSame, assertTrue, assertNull, assertCount, assertThrows, expected exception, data rows, TestWith, Fixture, property, Property, property-based testing, generated inputs, random inputs, shrink, counterexample, setup, skip, retries, flaky, Core\Test, Core\Test\Failure, --format json, junit, fixed clock, seed, .nvst, how to test, unit test, which test, expected output, benchmark, Bench, #[Bench], nvs test --bench, count, allocations

### A test is a method marked `#[Test]`

A test is a method with `#[Test]` written above it.

Any class in your program may have tests. There is no base class to extend, and no name a test
class or a test method has to have. You write `use Core\Test;` once, put `#[Test]` above a method,
and run `nvs test yourfile.nvs`. The compiler collects every `#[Test]` method while it checks your
program.

A test method is `public`, is not `static`, and returns `void`. A method that breaks one of those
three rules does not compile. A test that checks nothing fails, so every test calls at least one
assertion.

**Good to know:** `nvs run` on the same file runs your program and runs no test.

`#[Test]` and `#[Core\Test]` are the same attribute. `use Core\Test;` makes the short name work for the
attribute and for the assertions, such as `Test::assertSame`.

A `#[Test]` method that is `static`, `private` or `protected`, or that returns a value, is `E0733`.
The message names the rule the method breaks.

A test method may declare parameters. A fixture or a data row fills each one. A parameter that
nothing fills is `E0736`.

The report lists the classes in name order. Inside a class, the tests run in the order they are
written. Each test line starts with a mark: `✓` passed, `✗` failed, `-` skipped and `!` flaky.

A test that calls no assertion fails with the message `it asserted nothing`. To test that a call
finishes without an error, write `Core\Test::assertDoesNotThrow`.

A test that throws an error fails, and the error's message is printed under the test.

What a test prints with `echo` is not shown when the test passes. When the test fails, its output
is printed under the failure, after `output:`. `nvs test --show-output` prints the output of every
test.

A `#[Test]` method in an `abstract` class runs only in each class that extends it. A `#[Test]` on a
method of an interface does nothing.

A file with no `#[Test]` method runs no test. The summary is `0 failed, 0 passed, 0 skipped, 0
flaky`, and the exit status is `0`.

`nvs run` on a file with tests runs the statements outside the classes and runs no test.

#### Example 01: a test beside the code it checks

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to write a test. `#[Test]` above a method makes that method a
// test. `nvs test` on this file runs every `#[Test]` method it finds.

use Core\Test;

class Slug
{
    public static function of(string $title): string
    {
        return Core\Str::replace(Core\Str::lower($title), ' ', '-');
    }
}

class SlugTest
{
    #[Test]
    public function spacesBecomeDashes(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Slug::of('Hello World'), 'hello-world');
    }

    #[Test]
    public function capitalsBecomeSmallLetters(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Slug::of('ORDER Form'), 'order-form');
    }
}

// `nvs run` runs the program and leaves the tests alone.
// This prints `hello-world`.
echo Slug::of('Hello World'), "\n";
```

```output
hello-world
```

#### Example 02: a class that holds its own tests

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows that any class may have tests. There is no base class to extend and no
// name a test class must have, so a small class can keep its tests inside it.

use Core\Test;

class Basket
{
    public static function shippingCents(int $totalCents): int
    {
        if ($totalCents >= 5000) {
            return 0;
        }
        return 499;
    }

    #[Test]
    public function aSmallBasketPaysForShipping(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Basket::shippingCents(1200), 499);
    }

    #[Test]
    public function theLimitItselfShipsFree(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Basket::shippingCents(5000), 0);
    }
}

// This prints 499 and then 0.
echo Basket::shippingCents(1200), "\n";
echo Basket::shippingCents(9900), "\n";
```

```output
499
0
```

#### Example 03: one marked method for each rule

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a test class written the way you would write one at work. Every rule
// gets its own `#[Test]` method, and the name of the method says what the rule
// is. A method without `#[Test]` is an ordinary method.

use Core\Test;

class PasswordPolicy
{
    public static function problem(string $password): string
    {
        if (Core\Str::length($password) < 12) {
            return 'too short';
        }
        if (Core\Str::lower($password) == $password) {
            return 'needs a capital letter';
        }
        return 'none';
    }
}

class PasswordPolicyTest
{
    #[Test]
    public function aShortPasswordIsRefused(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame($this->problemFor('Short1'), 'too short');
    }

    #[Test]
    public function aPasswordWithoutCapitalsIsRefused(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame($this->problemFor('correcthorsebattery'), 'needs a capital letter');
    }

    #[Test]
    public function aLongPasswordWithACapitalLetterPasses(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame($this->problemFor('CorrectHorseBattery'), 'none');
    }

    // This method has no `#[Test]`, so `nvs test` does not run it. The tests
    // above call it like any other method.
    private function problemFor(string $password): string
    {
        return PasswordPolicy::problem($password);
    }
}

// This prints `too short` and then `none`.
echo PasswordPolicy::problem('Short1'), "\n";
echo PasswordPolicy::problem('CorrectHorseBattery'), "\n";
```

```output
too short
none
```

#### Example 04: the report of a run

```nvs test exit=1
<?nvs
// Shows the report `nvs test` prints for a test that passes, one that is
// skipped and one that fails.
// proof: test
// proof: exit 1

use Core\Test;

final class ArithmeticTest
{
    // The report shows `✓` for this test.
    #[Test]
    public function additionCommutes(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(2 + 3, 3 + 2);
    }

    // The report shows `-` for this test, and prints the reason.
    #[Test(skip: 'division is not written yet')]
    public function divisionRounds(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(7 / 2, 4.0);
    }

    // The report shows `✗` for this test, and prints both values.
    #[Test]
    public function thisOneFails(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(2 + 2, 5);
    }
}

// `nvs test` does not run this line.
echo 'this line runs only under nvs run', "\n";
```

```output
  ArithmeticTest
    ✓ additionCommutes
    - divisionRounds
      skipped: division is not written yet
    ✗ thisOneFails
      Core\Test::assertSame failed: `$actual` is 4, `$expected` is 5

  1 failed, 1 passed, 1 skipped, 0 flaky
```

#### Example 05: a static test does not compile

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that a test method cannot be `static`. The runner calls each test on a
// new object of its class.
// proof: compile-error

use Core\Test;

final class ShapeTest
{
    #[Test]
    public static function aTestIsNotStatic(): void
    {
        Test::assertTrue(true);
    }
}
```

```output
error[E0733]: the `#[Test]` method `aTestIsNotStatic` is `static`
   --> main.nvs:11:28
   |
11 |     public static function aTestIsNotStatic(): void
   |                            ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ is `static`
   = help: a test is run against a fresh instance, so drop the `static`

error: aborting due to 1 error
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```

### Every test is its own isolate, and the constructor is `setUp`

Every test runs on its own, and shares no stored value with any other test.

A `static` value that one test writes is back at its declared starting value in the next test. The
test class is built again for every test, so a property one test changes starts fresh in the next
one. The constructor of a test class is where you prepare what a test needs. It runs once before
every test body.

A test class constructor takes no parameters. One that takes a parameter is reported as that test
failing. Values that a test method itself needs come from a fixture or from a data row.

**The examples below** show a `static` that starts fresh in each test, a constructor that prepares
the same starting point for every test, and two tests that register the same address.

Each row of a `#[TestWith]` test runs on its own too. A `static` value one row writes is back at
its declared value in the next row.

The attempts of one test share their `static` values. With `retries:`, a counter that the first
attempt raised still has that value in the second attempt.

A constructor that throws an error makes the test fail, with the error's message.

A fixture is built outside the tests. A `static` value that a fixture method writes is back at its
declared value in every test.

A test that starts a script with `spawn script` and does not `await` it fails. The message says the
test left a task still running. `Core\Task::all` and `Core\Task::map` wait for every task they start,
so a test that uses them does not fail this way.

#### Example 01: a static starts fresh in each test

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows that one test cannot change what another test sees. A `static` value
// written by one test is back at its declared value in the next test.

use Core\Test;

class Counter
{
    public static int $hits = 0;
}

class CounterTest
{
    #[Test]
    public function theFirstTestWrites(): void
    {
        Counter::$hits = Counter::$hits + 1;
        Test::assertSame(Counter::$hits, 1);
    }

    #[Test]
    public function theSecondTestStartsFresh(): void
    {
        // The test above added one. This test reads `0` again.
        Test::assertSame(Counter::$hits, 0);
    }
}

// Outside a test there is one counter for the whole program, so it keeps both
// of these. This prints `2`.
Counter::$hits = Counter::$hits + 1;
Counter::$hits = Counter::$hits + 1;
echo Counter::$hits, "\n";
```

```output
2
```

#### Example 02: the constructor prepares each test

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the constructor of a test class. It runs once before every test, so
// every test starts from the same prepared state.

use Core\Test;

class Basket
{
    public array<string> $items;

    public function constructor()
    {
        $this->items = [];
    }

    public function add(string $item): void
    {
        $this->items[] = $item;
    }
}

class BasketTest
{
    private Basket $basket;

    // This runs again before each test below, so each test gets a new basket.
    public function constructor()
    {
        $this->basket = new Basket();
        $this->basket->add('bread');
    }

    #[Test]
    public function itStartsWithThePreparedItem(): void
    {
        Test::assertCount($this->basket->items, 1);
    }

    #[Test]
    public function itAddsToThePreparedItem(): void
    {
        // The item this test adds is gone before the next test starts.
        $this->basket->add('milk');
        Test::assertCount($this->basket->items, 2);
    }
}

// This prints `2`.
var $basket = new Basket();
$basket->add('bread');
$basket->add('milk');
echo Core\Arr::count($basket->items), "\n";
```

```output
2
```

#### Example 03: two tests that register the same address

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows why this matters at work. Two tests register the same address, and
// both expect one account, because neither test sees the other's account.

use Core\Test;

class Registry
{
    public static array<string> $accounts = [];

    public static function register(string $email): void
    {
        Registry::$accounts[] = $email;
    }

    public static function count(): uint
    {
        return Core\Arr::count(Registry::$accounts);
    }
}

class RegistryTest
{
    #[Test]
    public function itRegistersAnAddress(): void
    {
        Registry::register('ada@example.com');
        Test::assertSame(Registry::count(), 1);
    }

    // The same address again. This test starts with an empty registry, so it
    // needs no code to remove what the test above registered.
    #[Test]
    public function itRegistersTheSameAddressAgain(): void
    {
        Registry::register('ada@example.com');
        Test::assertSame(Registry::count(), 1);
    }
}

// Outside a test the registry keeps both addresses. This prints `2`.
Registry::register('ada@example.com');
Registry::register('grace@example.com');
echo Registry::count(), "\n";
```

```output
2
```

### `#[Test(...)]` options

`#[Test(...)]` takes options that change how one test runs. Every option is optional, and a test that
needs none is written as plain `#[Test]`.

`skip:` states a reason, and the test is reported as skipped without being run. `at:` fixes the clock
at one instant, so a test of dates and times reads the same time on every run. `Core\Test::advance`
moves that fixed clock forward. `seed:` fixes the numbers `Core\Random` draws, so the test draws the
same sequence on every run. `retries:` allows more attempts after a failure, and needs `because:`
beside it to state why. A test that fails and then passes is reported as flaky, never as passed.
`timeout:` gives one test its own time limit. `tags:` labels a test, and `nvs test --tag` runs only the
tests with that label.

**Good to know:** an option with a wrong name does not compile, so a typo is found before the tests
run.

**The examples below** show a skipped test, a fixed clock, a test class that uses several options
together, a time limit, and tags.

The options are `skip: string`, `at: string`, `seed: int`, `retries: int`, `because: string`,
`db: string`, `server: bool`, `timeout: string` and `tags: array<string>`. An option with another name is `E0454`, and its help lists them. A
value of the wrong type is `E0401`, so `skip: true` does not compile. An option given twice is
`E0304`.

A skipped test is not built, so its constructor does not run. The fixtures only it needs are not
built either. The report prints the reason after `skipped:`.

`at:` takes a time in the RFC 3339 format, such as `"2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"`. `Core\Time::now()`
returns that time in the test. A text in another format compiles, and the test fails with a message
that shows the format.

`Core\Test::advance` moves the fixed clock forward by a duration, such as `90m`. In a test without
`at:`, it throws a `LogicError`. It throws the same error under `nvs run`. The clock of the computer
never moves.

With `seed:`, `Core\Random` and `Core\Uuid::v7` give the same values on every run. Two tests with the
same seed get the same values. A test without `seed:` gets different values on every run.

`retries:` without `because:` is `E0734`. `because:` alone compiles and changes nothing.

A test that fails and then passes is reported as flaky. The mark is `!`, and the report prints the
message of the failed attempt. A test that fails every attempt is reported as failed, with the
message of the last attempt.

`db: "main"` opens a transaction on the database connection `[db.main]` before the test, and
rolls it back after the test. The test sees the database as it was, and leaves no change in it. If no
`[db.main]` block is configured, the test fails with a message that says so.

`server: true` starts a real HTTP server for the test, on a free port of the local computer.
`Core\Test::serverUrl()` returns its address. In a test without `server: true`, it returns `null`.

#### Example 01: skip a test and say why

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to skip a test and say why. `skip:` needs a reason. The runner
// reports the test as skipped and does not run its body.

use Core\Test;

class Coupon
{
    public static function percentFor(string $code): uint
    {
        if ($code == 'SPRING24') {
            return 15;
        }
        return 0;
    }
}

class CouponTest
{
    #[Test]
    public function itGivesFifteenPercentForTheSpringCode(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Coupon::percentFor('SPRING24'), 15);
    }

    // The reason is part of the report, so anybody reading a run sees why
    // this test did not run.
    #[Test(skip: 'the refund table is not written yet')]
    public function itGivesNothingOnARefundedOrder(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Coupon::percentFor('SPRING24'), 0);
    }
}

// This prints `15 0`.
echo Coupon::percentFor('SPRING24'), ' ', Coupon::percentFor('AUTUMN24'), "\n";
```

```output
15 0
```

#### Example 02: a fixed clock for one test

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to fix the time a test reads. `at:` sets the clock at one instant
// for that test. `Core\Test::advance` then moves the clock forward.

use Core\Test;
use Core\Time;

class Receipt
{
    public static function stampedAt(string $iso): string
    {
        return 'receipt at ' . $iso;
    }
}

class ReceiptTest
{
    // The clock stands still at this instant, for this test only.
    #[Test(at: '2026-01-01T00:00:00Z')]
    public function itStampsTheTimeTheClockShows(): void
    {
        string $first = Receipt::stampedAt(Time::now()->toIso());
        Test::assertSame($first, 'receipt at 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z');

        // This moves the fixed clock forward by 90 minutes.
        Test::advance(90m);

        string $later = Receipt::stampedAt(Time::now()->toIso());
        Test::assertSame($later, 'receipt at 2026-01-01T01:30:00Z');
    }
}

// This prints `receipt at 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z`, the text the test checks first.
echo Receipt::stampedAt('2026-01-01T00:00:00Z'), "\n";
```

```output
receipt at 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z
```

#### Example 03: options in a real test class

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the options a real test class uses: a fixed clock, a fixed seed, an
// allowance of extra attempts with the reason for it, and a skip.

use Core\Random;
use Core\Test;
use Core\Time;

class Invite
{
    public static function code(string $draw): string
    {
        return 'INV-' . $draw;
    }

    public static function isWellFormed(string $code): bool
    {
        return Core\Str::length($code) == 8;
    }
}

class InviteTest
{
    // With `at:` this test reads the same time on every run.
    #[Test(at: '2026-03-01T09:00:00Z')]
    public function itReadsOneFixedTime(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Time::now()->toIso(), '2026-03-01T09:00:00Z');
    }

    // With `seed:` `Core\Random` draws the same numbers on every run.
    #[Test(seed: 42)]
    public function itBuildsACodeFromADrawnNumber(): void
    {
        int $draw = Random::int(1000, 9999);
        Test::assertTrue(Invite::isWellFormed(Invite::code($draw as string)));
    }

    // The payment sandbox fails now and then, so this test gets two more
    // attempts. `because:` is what a reader of the report has instead of the run.
    #[Test(retries: 2, because: 'the payment sandbox is slow to start')]
    public function itAcceptsACodeTheSandboxReturns(): void
    {
        Test::assertTrue(Invite::isWellFormed('INV-1234'));
    }

    // This test waits for work that is not done. It is reported as skipped.
    #[Test(skip: 'the refund endpoint is not built yet')]
    public function itRefundsAnInvite(): void
    {
        Test::assertTrue(Invite::isWellFormed('INV-0000'));
    }
}

// This prints `INV-1234`.
echo Invite::code('1234'), "\n";
```

```output
INV-1234
```

#### Example 04: a test reported as flaky

```nvs test
<?nvs
// Shows a fixed clock, a fixed seed, and a test that passes on its second
// attempt. The report shows `!` for that test, because it is flaky.
// proof: test

use Core\Random;
use Core\Test;
use Core\Time;

final class DeterminismTest
{
    // `Core\Test::advance` moves the fixed clock forward by 90 minutes.
    #[Test(at: '2026-01-01T00:00:00Z')]
    public function theClockIsFixedAndMovable(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Time::now()->toIso(), '2026-01-01T00:00:00Z');
        Test::advance(90m);
        Test::assertSame(Time::now()->toIso(), '2026-01-01T01:30:00Z');
    }

    // With the same seed, `Random::int` returns the same number on every run.
    #[Test(seed: 42)]
    public function aSeedIsRepeatable(): void
    {
        int $first = Random::int(0, 999);
        Test::assertTrue($first >= 0);
    }

    // The attempts of one test share their `static` values. The first
    // attempt fails, and the second one passes.
    #[Test(retries: 2, because: 'a counter replaces a slow network')]
    public function itPassesOnTheSecondAttempt(): void
    {
        Attempts::$n = Attempts::$n + 1;
        Test::assertSame(Attempts::$n, 2);
    }
}

final class Attempts
{
    public static int $n = 0;
}
```

```output
  DeterminismTest
    ✓ theClockIsFixedAndMovable
    ✓ aSeedIsRepeatable
    ! itPassesOnTheSecondAttempt
      flaky: it passed on attempt 2, having failed with:
      Core\Test::assertSame failed: `$actual` is 1, `$expected` is 2

  0 failed, 2 passed, 0 skipped, 1 flaky
```

#### Example 05: retries need a reason

```nvs error
<?nvs
// Shows that `retries:` needs `because:` beside it. Without a reason, the test
// does not compile.
// proof: compile-error

use Core\Test;

final class NetworkTest
{
    #[Test(retries: 2)]
    public function itReachesTheServer(): void
    {
        Test::assertTrue(true);
    }
}
```

```output
error[E0734]: `retries` is given with no `because`
   --> main.nvs:10:12
   |
10 |     #[Test(retries: 2)]
   |            ^^^^^^^^^^ retried for no stated reason
   = help: a test that passes only after a retry is reported as flaky. Write the reason for the retries: `#[Test(retries: 2, because: "real DNS")]`

error: aborting due to 1 error
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```

#### Example 06: a time limit for one test

```nvs test exit=1
<?nvs
// Shows how to give one test a time limit. `timeout:` sets the limit for that
// test. A test that runs past it is stopped, and the report shows it as failed.
// proof: test
// proof: exit 1

use Core\Test;

class Basket
{
    public static function total(array<int> $prices): int
    {
        int $sum = 0;
        foreach ($prices as int $price) {
            $sum = $sum + $price;
        }
        return $sum;
    }
}

class BasketTest
{
    // This test finishes long before its limit of 2 seconds.
    #[Test(timeout: '2s')]
    public function itAddsThePrices(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Basket::total([4, 8, 15]), 27);
    }

    // This loop never ends. The test is stopped after 50 milliseconds.
    #[Test(timeout: '50ms')]
    public function itStopsALoopThatNeverEnds(): void
    {
        int $count = 0;
        while (true) {
            $count = $count + 1;
        }
    }
}
```

```output
  BasketTest
    ✓ itAddsThePrices
    ✗ itStopsALoopThatNeverEnds
      the test ran past its wall-time limit of 50ms, set by `#[Test(timeout: "50ms")]`

  1 failed, 1 passed, 0 skipped, 0 flaky
```

#### Example 07: tags select which tests run

```nvs test
<?nvs
// Shows how to label tests with `tags:`. `nvs test --tag db` runs only the tests
// labelled `db`, and `nvs test --skip-tag slow` runs every test except the slow ones.
// proof: test

use Core\Test;

class Order
{
    public static function withShipping(int $cents): int
    {
        return $cents + 500;
    }
}

class OrderTest
{
    // A test without `tags:` runs when no `--tag` is given.
    #[Test]
    public function itAddsTheShippingCost(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Order::withShipping(1000), 1500);
    }

    // A test may have several tags. `--tag db` and `--tag slow` both select it.
    #[Test(tags: ['db', 'slow'])]
    public function itAddsShippingToEveryStoredOrder(): void
    {
        array<int> $stored = [500, 1000, 2500];
        int $total = 0;
        foreach ($stored as int $cents) {
            $total = $total + Order::withShipping($cents);
        }
        Test::assertSame($total, 5500);
    }

    // `--skip-tag slow` leaves out this test.
    #[Test(tags: ['slow'])]
    public function itAddsShippingToAMillionOrders(): void
    {
        int $total = 0;
        for (int $i = 0; $i < 1000000; $i++) {
            $total = $total + Order::withShipping(100);
        }
        Test::assertSame($total, 600000000);
    }
}
```

```output
  OrderTest
    ✓ itAddsTheShippingCost
    ✓ itAddsShippingToEveryStoredOrder
    ✓ itAddsShippingToAMillionOrders

  0 failed, 3 passed, 0 skipped, 0 flaky
```

### `#[Core\Test\Fixture]`: built once, injected by type

A fixture is a value your tests share. It is built once, and every test that needs it is called with
it.

You write a `public static` method and put `#[Fixture]` above it. The type that method returns is
what the fixture supplies. Every test in the same class that declares a parameter of that type is
called with the value. The name of the parameter does not matter, only its type. A fixture may
declare a parameter as well, so one fixture can be built from another.

The method runs once for the whole class, before the tests. Each test then works on its own copy, so
a change one test makes is not visible to another. Setup that costs time, such as reading a file or
building a large object, happens one time. Each test runs on its own, so without a fixture this setup
runs once for every test.

**Good to know:** a fixture belongs to its own class, and a test cannot use another class's fixture.
A parameter that no fixture supplies does not compile.

A fixture method that is not `static` or not `public`, or that returns `void`, is `E0735`. A
`#[Fixture]` with a field, such as `#[Fixture(name: "x")]`, is `E0454`.

Two fixtures of one class that return the same type are `E0304`. Fixtures that need each other, such
as `s` needing `r` and `r` needing `s`, are `E0737`, and the message shows the cycle.

The type must be the same. A fixture that returns a subclass `S2` does not fill a parameter of type
`S`, and that parameter is `E0736`. A fixture may return any type, such as `int`, `?int` or
`array<int>`.

A fixture is built only when a test that runs needs it. A fixture that only skipped tests need is
not built.

A fixture that throws an error makes each test that needs it fail, with the error's message. The
other tests of the class still run.

A variadic or `inout` parameter on a test method is `E0733`.

A fixture method is test code, like a test method. Only a test, a fixture or a class hook may call
it. A call from other code is the compile error `E0889`. `nvs run` and `nvs build` do not compile it.

#### Example 01: one value for every test

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how every test gets one value. `#[Fixture]` goes above a `public static`
// method, and the type that method returns is what it supplies.

use Core\Test;
use Core\Test\Fixture;

class ShippingRates
{
    public function constructor(public int $baseCents, public int $perItemCents)
    {}

    public function totalCents(int $items): int
    {
        return $this->baseCents + $this->perItemCents * $items;
    }
}

class ShippingRatesTest
{
    // This method runs once for the whole class. Every test below that declares
    // a `ShippingRates` parameter is called with what it returns.
    #[Fixture]
    public static function rates(): ShippingRates
    {
        return new ShippingRates(499, 120);
    }

    #[Test]
    public function threeItemsPayTheBaseAndThreeItems(ShippingRates $rates): void
    {
        Test::assertSame($rates->totalCents(3), 859);
    }

    // The type of the parameter says which fixture fills it. The name is yours
    // to choose.
    #[Test]
    public function anEmptyOrderPaysTheBase(ShippingRates $anyNameYouLike): void
    {
        Test::assertSame($anyNameYouLike->totalCents(0), 499);
    }
}

// This prints 859.
ShippingRates $rates = new ShippingRates(499, 120);
echo $rates->totalCents(3), "\n";
```

```output
859
```

#### Example 02: a fixture built from another fixture

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows a fixture built from another fixture. A `#[Fixture]` method may declare
// a parameter too, and it is filled the same way a test's parameter is.

use Core\Test;
use Core\Test\Fixture;

class Settings
{
    public function constructor(public string $host)
    {}
}

class Mailer
{
    public function constructor(public Settings $settings)
    {}

    public function route(string $address): string
    {
        return $address . ' via ' . $this->settings->host;
    }
}

class MailerTest
{
    #[Fixture]
    public static function settings(): Settings
    {
        return new Settings('smtp.example.com');
    }

    // This fixture needs a `Settings`, so it is built after the one above. The
    // order you write the two methods in does not matter.
    #[Fixture]
    public static function mailer(Settings $settings): Mailer
    {
        return new Mailer($settings);
    }

    #[Test]
    public function itRoutesThroughTheConfiguredHost(Mailer $mailer): void
    {
        Test::assertSame($mailer->route('ana@example.com'), 'ana@example.com via smtp.example.com');
    }

    // A test may declare both. Each parameter is filled from its own type.
    #[Test]
    public function bothFixturesReachOneTest(Mailer $mailer, Settings $settings): void
    {
        Test::assertSame($mailer->settings->host, $settings->host);
    }
}

// This prints `ana@example.com via smtp.example.com`.
Mailer $mailer = new Mailer(new Settings('smtp.example.com'));
echo $mailer->route('ana@example.com'), "\n";
```

```output
ana@example.com via smtp.example.com
```

#### Example 03: setup that happens once

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the use a fixture is really for. Setup that costs time happens one time
// for the whole class, and each test works with the result.

use Core\Test;
use Core\Test\Fixture;

// A user as a login form checks it: a name and a stored password hash.
class Account
{
    public function constructor(public string $name, public string $hash)
    {}

    public function logIn(secret string $typed): bool
    {
        return Core\Password::verify($typed, $this->hash);
    }
}

class AccountTest
{
    // `Core\Password::hash` takes a long time, so guessing a password is slow.
    // This fixture runs it once. Without the fixture, every test runs it.
    #[Fixture]
    public static function account(): Account
    {
        return new Account('ada', Core\Password::hash('correct horse'));
    }

    #[Test]
    public function theRightPasswordLogsIn(Account $account): void
    {
        Test::assertTrue($account->logIn('correct horse'));
    }

    #[Test]
    public function aWrongPasswordDoesNotLogIn(Account $account): void
    {
        Test::assertSame($account->logIn('wrong horse'), false);
    }

    #[Test]
    public function anEmptyPasswordDoesNotLogIn(Account $account): void
    {
        Test::assertSame($account->logIn(''), false);
    }
}

// This prints `true`.
Account $account = new Account('ada', Core\Password::hash('correct horse'));
echo $account->logIn('correct horse') ? 'true' : 'false', "\n";
```

```output
true
```

### `#[Core\Test\TestWith]`: data rows

A data row gives one test a set of values. You write one row for each set, and each row is reported
as its own case.

`#[TestWith(name: value, …)]` goes above a `#[Test]` method. Each field of the row names one
parameter of that method, and the value is a constant. Repeat `#[TestWith]` for every set of values
you want. The runner calls the method once per row, in the order you wrote the rows, and reports
them as `method#0`, `method#1` and so on. A row that fails is reported on its own, and the rows
after it still run.

Rows and fixtures work together in one test. A parameter that a row names is filled by the row. A
parameter that no row names is filled by the fixture of that type.

**Good to know:** every row of a method fills the same parameters, and a field that names no
parameter does not compile.

A row value is a literal of the parameter's type: an `int`, `uint`, `float`, `bool` or `string`
written in the code. An `int` literal also fills a `float` parameter. A class constant, an enum case,
an array and a negative number for a `uint` are `E0738`.

A field that names no parameter is `E0738`, and so is a value of the wrong type. A field given twice
in one row is `E0304`. A row that leaves out a parameter that another row fills is `E0738`.

`#[TestWith]` on a method without `#[Test]` is `E0738`. A parameter with no row and no fixture is
`E0736`.

When a row and a fixture can both fill a parameter, the row is used.

`skip:` on a test with rows skips every row, and each row is reported as skipped. With `retries:`,
each row gets its own attempts.

`--filter` selects a single row by its name, such as `--filter SlugTest::itSlugs#1`.

#### Example 01: one row for each case

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to give one test several sets of values. Each `#[TestWith]` row is
// its own case, so a row that fails does not stop the rows after it.

use Core\Test;
use Core\Test\TestWith;

class Band
{
    public static function of(uint $orders): string
    {
        if ($orders >= 100) {
            return 'gold';
        }
        if ($orders >= 10) {
            return 'silver';
        }
        return 'bronze';
    }
}

class BandTest
{
    // Each field of a row names one parameter below. The values are constants.
    #[TestWith(orders: 0, want: 'bronze')]
    #[TestWith(orders: 10, want: 'silver')]
    #[TestWith(orders: 100, want: 'gold')]
    #[Test]
    public function itNamesTheBandOfAnOrderCount(uint $orders, string $want): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Band::of($orders), $want);
    }
}

// This prints `bronze silver gold`.
echo Band::of(0), ' ', Band::of(10), ' ', Band::of(100), "\n";
```

```output
bronze silver gold
```

#### Example 02: rows and a fixture in one test

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows rows and a fixture in one test. A parameter a row names is filled by the
// row. A parameter no row names is filled by the fixture of that type.

use Core\Test;
use Core\Test\Fixture;
use Core\Test\TestWith;

class Vat
{
    public function constructor(public int $percent)
    {}

    // The tax on an amount in cents. 19 percent of 1000 cents is 190 cents.
    public function on(int $cents): int
    {
        return Core\Math::intDiv($cents * $this->percent, 100);
    }
}

class VatTest
{
    // The same rate for every row, built once for the whole class.
    #[Fixture]
    public static function vat(): Vat
    {
        return new Vat(19);
    }

    // `$cents` and `$want` come from the row. `$vat` comes from the fixture.
    #[TestWith(cents: 100, want: 19)]
    #[TestWith(cents: 1000, want: 190)]
    #[TestWith(cents: 0, want: 0)]
    #[Test]
    public function itTaxesAnAmountInCents(int $cents, int $want, Vat $vat): void
    {
        Test::assertSame($vat->on($cents), $want);
    }
}

// This prints 190.
Vat $vat = new Vat(19);
echo $vat->on(1000), "\n";
```

```output
190
```

#### Example 03: a table of permissions

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the rows for a check that returns `true` or `false`. There is one row
// for each combination of the inputs, and each row gives the expected result.

use Core\Test;
use Core\Test\TestWith;

class Access
{
    // An editor may change any article. Anybody else may change only their own.
    public static function canEdit(string $role, bool $isAuthor): bool
    {
        if ($role == 'editor') {
            return true;
        }
        return $isAuthor;
    }
}

class AccessTest
{
    // Four rows for the four combinations, so no case is left untested.
    #[TestWith(role: 'editor', isAuthor: true, want: true)]
    #[TestWith(role: 'editor', isAuthor: false, want: true)]
    #[TestWith(role: 'writer', isAuthor: true, want: true)]
    #[TestWith(role: 'writer', isAuthor: false, want: false)]
    #[Test]
    public function itAnswersEveryCombination(string $role, bool $isAuthor, bool $want): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Access::canEdit($role, $isAuthor), $want);
    }
}

// This prints `true` and then `false`.
echo Access::canEdit('editor', false) ? 'true' : 'false', "\n";
echo Access::canEdit('writer', false) ? 'true' : 'false', "\n";
```

```output
true
false
```

### `#[Core\Test\Property]`: generated inputs

A property is a test that runs many times, with new inputs on every call. You say what must be
true for every input, and the runner looks for an input where it is false.

`#[Property]` goes on a method with the same shape as a `#[Test]` method. Each parameter gets a
generated value of its declared type. The runner calls the method 100 times, and `runs:` changes
that number. `gen: { level: "0..1000" }` gives `$level` a whole number from 0 to 1000.

When a call fails, the runner tries smaller inputs that still fail. The report shows the smallest
input it found, the input that failed first, and the seed. Write that seed as
`#[Property(seed: n)]`, and the test runs with the same inputs again.

**Good to know:** a generated string can have any character, including emoji and accents. A
property that only holds for English letters fails.

A parameter can have any of these types: a number, `bool`, `decimal`, `string`, `bytes`, an enum, `mixed`,
`?T`, `array<T>`, a shape, a union, and a class of your program with a `public` constructor. A class
is built with `new`, so its constructor runs. A function, an interface, an abstract class, a `Core`
class and a `secret` value are `E0890`.

`gen:` takes a range for a parameter, written as `"low..high"`. Both ends are included. On a
number, the range is the value. On a `string`, `bytes` or `array<T>`, the range is the length, up
to 10000. A string's length counts characters as a person reads them. On `?T`, the range is for
`T`. A range that names no parameter, or that does not fit the type, is `E0890`.

The options are those of `#[Test]`, without `retries:` and `because:`. `runs:` is from 1 to 100000.
A property never uses a `#[TestWith]` row or a fixture.

The seed also sets the test's own random numbers. Without `seed:`, every run has a new seed.

The runner tries at most 1000 smaller inputs. It also stops at the test's time limit. One call's
inputs have at most 1048576 elements, bytes and characters together. A property that needs more
fails before its first call.

In the JSON report, a failed property has a `counterexample` field. A subclass runs every property
it inherits, the same way it runs an inherited `#[Test]`.

#### Example 01: a property holds for every input

```nvs test
<?nvs
// Shows a property: a test that runs many times, with new inputs on every call.
// proof: test

use Core\Test;
use Core\Test\Property;

final class Money
{
    public static function add(int $a, int $b): int
    {
        return $a + $b;
    }
}

final class MoneyTest
{
    // `$a` and `$b` are whole numbers from -1000 to 1000. The test runs 100 times.
    #[Property(gen: { a: '-1000..1000', b: '-1000..1000' })]
    public function itAddsInEitherOrder(int $a, int $b): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Money::add($a, $b), Money::add($b, $a));
    }
}
```

```output
  MoneyTest
    ✓ itAddsInEitherOrder

  0 failed, 1 passed, 0 skipped, 0 flaky
```

#### Example 02: a failure shrinks

```nvs test exit=1

use Core\Test;

final class Volume
```
