### Hooks: `#[BeforeClass]`, `#[AfterClass]` and `#[AfterEachTest]`

A hook is a method that the test runner calls around your tests. You use one to clean up something a
test leaves outside itself, such as a file or a database table.

- `#[BeforeClass]` runs once, before the tests of the class. It is a `public static` method.
- `#[AfterClass]` runs once, after the last test. It is a `public static` method. It can take a
  `Core\Test\Summary`, which has the counts of passed and failed tests.
- `#[AfterEachTest]` runs after each test, on the same object as the test. It can take a
  `Core\Test\Outcome`, which has the name of the test and whether it passed.

The after hooks also run when a test fails. `#[AfterClass]` also runs when `#[BeforeClass]` throws
an error.

To prepare each test, use the constructor. To share a value with the tests, use a fixture.

**Good to know:** a class has at most one hook of each kind. A subclass inherits the hooks of its
parent class.

`#[BeforeClass]` takes no parameters. `#[AfterClass]` may take one `Core\Test\Summary`, and
`#[AfterEachTest]` one `Core\Test\Outcome`. A hook with another parameter is `E0862`. So is a hook
that returns a value or is not `public`. A class hook must be `static`, and `#[AfterEachTest]` must
not be. Each of those is `E0862` too.

A second hook of one kind in a class is `E0304`.

`#[BeforeClass]` and `#[AfterClass]` may not write a `static` property. That is `E0863`. Each test
reads the declared value, so a fixture is the way to give the tests a value. `#[AfterEachTest]`
runs with the test, and it may write one.

The class hooks run in this order: `#[BeforeClass]`, then the fixtures, then the tests, then
`#[AfterClass]`. They run when every test of the class is skipped. They do not run for a class with
no test, or for a class that `--filter` leaves out.

What a class hook prints with `echo` is part of the report, under the class name. What
`#[AfterEachTest]` prints belongs to the test, so it is shown only when the test fails.

`#[AfterEachTest]` runs after every attempt. It sees the properties the test set on the object.

`Core\Test\Outcome` has `class()`, `name()`, `attempt()`, `passed()` and `failures()`, the messages
of the failed assertions. `Core\Test\Summary` has `class()`, `passed()`, `failed()`, `skipped()`,
`flaky()` and `failedTests()`, the names of the failed tests.

When `#[BeforeClass]` throws an error, each test fails. The message names the hook and gives the
error's message. `#[AfterClass]` still runs.

When `#[AfterClass]` throws an error, the report has a line marked `✗` with the hook's name, and
the exit status is `1`. When `#[AfterEachTest]` throws an error, that attempt fails.

A subclass runs the tests, the fixtures and the hooks of its parent under its own name. The parent
also runs them under its name, unless it is `abstract`. A method that overrides a hook or a test
without its attribute is `E0862` or `E0733`.

There is no `#[BeforeEachTest]`. The constructor of the test class runs before each test.

#### Example 01: remove the file a test wrote

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `#[AfterEachTest]` removing the file a test wrote, so the next run starts
// without it.

use Core\IO;
use Core\Path;
use Core\Test;
use Core\Test\AfterEachTest;

class ShoppingList
{
    public static function text(array<string> $items): string
    {
        string $text = '';
        foreach ($items as string $item) {
            $text = $text . '- ' . $item . "\n";
        }
        return $text;
    }
}

class ShoppingListTest
{
    public string $file;

    public function constructor()
    {
        $this->file = Path::fromCwd('shopping-list-test.txt');
    }

    #[Test]
    public function itWritesOneLinePerItem(): void
    {
        IO::write($this->file, ShoppingList::text(['bread', 'milk']));
        Test::assertSame(IO::readText($this->file), "- bread\n- milk\n");
    }

    // This runs after the test, also when the test fails.
    #[AfterEachTest]
    public function removeTheFile(): void
    {
        IO::remove($this->file);
    }
}

// This prints `- bread`, then `- milk`.
echo ShoppingList::text(['bread', 'milk']);
```

```output
- bread
- milk
```

#### Example 02: create a table once for the class

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows `#[BeforeClass]` creating a database table once for the class, and
// `#[AfterClass]` deleting it after the last test.

use Core\Db;
use Core\Test;
use Core\Test\AfterClass;
use Core\Test\BeforeClass;

class Seed
{
    // This builds one `insert` statement for many products.
    public static function insertProducts(array<string> $names): string
    {
        string $values = '';
        foreach ($names as string $name) {
            if ($values != '') {
                $values = $values . ', ';
            }
            $values = $values . "('" . $name . "')";
        }
        return 'insert into products (name) values ' . $values;
    }
}

class ProductTest
{
    // The table is outside every test, so a hook creates it one time.
    #[BeforeClass]
    public static function createTable(): void
    {
        var $db = Db::connect('test');
        $db->execute('create table products (name text)', []);
        $db->execute(Seed::insertProducts(['tea', 'cake']), []);
    }

    // `db: "test"` undoes what the test writes, so every test sees two rows.
    #[Test(db: 'test')]
    public function itFindsTheSeededProducts(): void
    {
        var $rows = Db::connect('test')->query('select name from products', []);
        Test::assertCount($rows->all(), 2);
    }

    // This runs after the last test, also when a test failed.
    #[AfterClass]
    public static function dropTable(): void
    {
        Db::connect('test')->execute('drop table products', []);
    }
}

// This prints the statement `createTable` runs.
echo Seed::insertProducts(['tea', 'cake']), "\n";
```

```output
insert into products (name) values ('tea'), ('cake')
```

#### Example 03: keep the log of a failed test

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows hooks that keep the log of a failed test and delete the log of a passed
// one. A build server can then show the logs of the failed tests.

use Core\IO;
use Core\Path;
use Core\Test;
use Core\Test\AfterClass;
use Core\Test\AfterEachTest;
use Core\Test\Outcome;
use Core\Test\Summary;

class Evidence
{
    // A retry is a new attempt, so the attempt number is part of the name.
    public static function fileName(string $class, string $test, int $attempt): string
    {
        return $class . '-' . $test . '-' . $attempt . '.log';
    }
}

class CheckoutTest
{
    public string $log;

    public function constructor()
    {
        $this->log = Path::fromCwd('checkout-test.log');
    }

    #[Test]
    public function itAddsTheShippingCost(): void
    {
        // The prices are in cents.
        IO::write($this->log, "total 1250, shipping 490\n");
        Test::assertSame(1250 + 490, 1740);
    }

    // `Outcome` says which test ran and whether it passed.
    #[AfterEachTest]
    public function keepTheLogIfItFailed(Outcome $outcome): void
    {
        if ($outcome->passed()) {
            IO::remove($this->log);
        } else {
            string $name = Evidence::fileName($outcome->class(), $outcome->name(), $outcome->attempt());
            IO::move($this->log, Path::fromCwd($name));
        }
    }

    // `Summary` has the counts for the whole class.
    #[AfterClass]
    public static function report(Summary $summary): void
    {
        echo $summary->failed(), " failed, their logs are kept\n";
    }
}

// This prints `CheckoutTest-itAddsTheShippingCost-2.log`.
echo Evidence::fileName('CheckoutTest', 'itAddsTheShippingCost', 2), "\n";
```

```output
CheckoutTest-itAddsTheShippingCost-2.log
```

#### Example 04: the order the hooks run in

```nvs test
<?nvs
// Shows the order the hooks run in. `#[BeforeClass]` runs before the tests,
// and `#[AfterClass]` runs after them with the counts.
// proof: test

use Core\Test;
use Core\Test\AfterClass;
use Core\Test\AfterEachTest;
use Core\Test\BeforeClass;
use Core\Test\Outcome;
use Core\Test\Summary;

final class HookTest
{
    #[BeforeClass]
    public static function createTable(): void
    {
        echo "create the table\n";
    }

    #[AfterClass]
    public static function dropTable(Summary $summary): void
    {
        echo 'drop the table, ', $summary->passed(), " passed\n";
    }

    // This hook runs after each test. Its output is shown only when the
    // test fails, so this run does not print it.
    #[AfterEachTest]
    public function removeFiles(Outcome $outcome): void
    {
        echo 'remove the files of ', $outcome->name(), "\n";
    }

    #[Test]
    public function first(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(1 + 1, 2);
    }

    #[Test]
    public function second(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(2 + 2, 4);
    }
}
```

```output
  HookTest
create the table
    ✓ first
    ✓ second
drop the table, 2 passed

  0 failed, 2 passed, 0 skipped, 0 flaky
```

### Assertions

An assertion checks one thing about a value. When the check is false, the test fails.

Every assertion is a static method of `Core\Test`. You write the value your code produced first,
and the value you expect second. An assertion that passes returns and does nothing. One that fails
records the failure and throws `Core\Test\Failure`, and the error message names both values. You
may add `{ message: "..." }` at the end of any assertion to put your own sentence in front of that
message.

Catching a `Core\Test\Failure` does not make a test pass. The runner keeps a record of every failed
assertion, so a test that caught its own failure still fails. The report lists every failed
assertion of a test.

**Good to know:** both sides of an assertion have the same type, so `assertSame(1, "1")` does not
compile.

`Core\Test::assertSame` compares numbers, strings and arrays by value. Two objects pass only when
they are the same object, so `assertSame(new P(1), new P(1))` fails.

`assertEquals` is the same as `assertSame`, but it compares two objects with their `compareTo`
method. It passes when `compareTo` returns `0`. For a class without `compareTo`, it throws a
`RuntimeError`, and the test fails.

`assertEqualsDeep` compares arrays entry by entry and objects property by property. The message
names the first place where the two differ, such as `$actual->rows["1"]->name`. A `secret`
property is compared, and the message shows `«redacted»` in place of its value.

Both sides of `assertSame`, `assertEquals` and `assertEqualsDeep` have one type. `assertSame(1, "1")`
and `assertSame(1, 1.0)` are `E0401`. `assertTrue` takes a `bool`, so `assertTrue(1)` is `E0401`.

`assertCount` counts every entry, with any keys.

`assertThrows` passes when the function throws the class you name or a subclass of it. Its message
names the class that was thrown instead, or says that the function returned. `assertDoesNotThrow`
fails with the message of the error the function threw.

An assertion that fails inside the function you give `assertThrows` still makes the test fail. To
test that an assertion fails, use `Core\Test::expectFailure`. It passes when an assertion inside the
function failed, and that failure does not count against the test. It fails when no assertion
inside the function failed.

A failing assertion throws, so the lines after it in the test do not run. A test that catches each
`Core\Test\Failure` goes on, and the report lists every failed assertion.

`Core\Test\Failure` is a `Throwable`. It is not a `RuntimeError` and not a `LogicError`.

Under `nvs run`, an assertion that fails throws the same `Core\Test\Failure`. If nothing catches it,
the program ends with exit status `1`.

`Core\Test::advance` is not an assertion. It moves the clock that `#[Test(at:)]` fixed.

#### Example 01: the assertions you reach for first

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the four assertions most tests use. Each one takes the value your code
// produced, and then the value you expect. `nvs test` on this file runs the
// `#[Test]` methods.

use Core\Test;

class Order
{
    public array<string> $lines = [];
    public ?string $couponCode = null;

    public function add(string $line): void
    {
        $this->lines[] = $line;
    }

    public function isEmpty(): bool
    {
        return Core\Arr::count($this->lines) == 0;
    }
}

class OrderTest
{
    #[Test]
    public function aNewOrderIsEmpty(): void
    {
        var $order = new Order();
        Test::assertTrue($order->isEmpty());
        Test::assertCount($order->lines, 0);
        Test::assertNull($order->couponCode);
    }

    #[Test]
    public function addingALineKeepsItsText(): void
    {
        var $order = new Order();
        $order->add('2 x Coffee');
        Test::assertCount($order->lines, 1);
        Test::assertSame($order->lines[0], '2 x Coffee');
    }
}

var $order = new Order();
$order->add('2 x Coffee');

// This prints `2 x Coffee`.
echo $order->lines[0], "\n";
```

```output
2 x Coffee
```

#### Example 02: what a failing assertion tells you

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows what a failing assertion tells you. It throws `Core\Test\Failure`, and
// the message names both sides. This program catches the error and prints that
// message, so you can see each one.

use Core\Test;

try {
    Test::assertSame(2 + 2, 5);
} catch (Core\Test\Failure $f) {
    echo $f->message, "\n";
}

// A trailing `{ message: "..." }` puts your own sentence in front of the report.
try {
    Test::assertSame(0, 1, { message: 'a fresh counter is one' });
} catch (Core\Test\Failure $f) {
    echo $f->message, "\n";
}

// `assertEqualsDeep` compares two arrays entry by entry. The message names the
// first place where they differ.
array<string> $sent = ['Berlin', '10115'];
array<string> $stored = ['Berlin', '10117'];
try {
    Test::assertEqualsDeep($sent, $stored);
} catch (Core\Test\Failure $f) {
    echo $f->message, "\n";
}
```

```output
Core\Test::assertSame failed: `$actual` is 4, `$expected` is 5
a fresh counter is one: Core\Test::assertSame failed: `$actual` is 0, `$expected` is 1
Core\Test::assertEqualsDeep failed: the two differ at `$actual["1"]`: `$actual` is "10115", `$expected` is "10117"
```

#### Example 03: checking that a call throws

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to check that a call throws. `assertThrows` runs the function you
// give it, and passes when that function throws the class you name.
// `assertDoesNotThrow` passes when the function returns.

use Core\Test;

class Age
{
    public static function fromText(string $text): int
    {
        ?int $value = $text as ?int;
        if ($value == null) {
            throw new ParseError('`' . $text . '` is not a number');
        }
        return $value;
    }
}

// The call throws `ParseError`, so this assertion passes and prints nothing.
Test::assertThrows(fn(): void => { Age::fromText('tomorrow'); }, ParseError::class);
echo 'bad input throws', "\n";

// The call returns a number, so this assertion passes too.
Test::assertDoesNotThrow(fn(): void => { Age::fromText('41'); });
echo 'good input does not throw', "\n";
```

```output
bad input throws
good input does not throw
```

#### Example 04: an assertion of your own

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows an assertion of your own. `Core\Test\Failure` is an ordinary error, so
// a method can catch one and throw a new one with a better message.

use Core\Test;

final class Checks
{
    public static function assertEven(int $n): void
    {
        try {
            Test::assertSame($n % 2, 0);
        } catch (Core\Test\Failure $inner) {
            throw new Core\Test\Failure($n . ' is odd: ' . $inner->message);
        }
    }
}

// 4 is even, so this assertion passes and returns.
Checks::assertEven(4);
echo '4 passed', "\n";

// 3 is odd. The message starts with your own text.
try {
    Checks::assertEven(3);
} catch (Core\Test\Failure $f) {
    echo $f->message, "\n";
}

// `{ message: … }` puts your own sentence in front of the report.
try {
    Test::assertEquals(1, 2, { message: 'a new counter is one' });
} catch (Core\Test\Failure $f) {
    echo $f->message, "\n";
}

// A `ParseError` is a `RuntimeError`, so this assertion passes.
Test::assertThrows(fn(): void => { throw new ParseError('bad input'); }, RuntimeError::class);
echo 'a ParseError is a RuntimeError', "\n";
```

```output
4 passed
3 is odd: Core\Test::assertSame failed: `$actual` is 1, `$expected` is 0
a new counter is one: Core\Test::assertEquals failed: `$actual` is 1, `$expected` is 2
a ParseError is a RuntimeError
```

### Running tests: `nvs test`

`nvs test main.nvs` compiles a program and runs every method that has the `#[Test]` attribute. It
prints one line for each test and a count at the end.

Tests can be in the same file as the code, or in a class of their own. The statements outside a
class do not run under `nvs test`.

`nvs test .` runs every `.nvs` file in a folder and its subfolders as one program. Run it in your
project folder, so every test can use the classes your `autoload` line loads. A `tests` folder
needs one file that requires your entry file.

`--filter <text>` runs only the tests whose name, `Class::method`, contains that text.
`--list` prints each test and its file, and runs none. `--format json` and `--format junit` print a
report for a build server. The exit status is `1` when a test failed, and `0` otherwise.

The examples show two tests, two test classes with a filter, and a report for a build server.

`nvs test main.nvs` runs the tests in `main.nvs` and in the files it loads. `autoload` loads only the
classes the program uses. A test class that the program never names does not run. `nvs test .`
runs it.

`nvs test tests/` runs every `.nvs` file in `tests/` and its subfolders as one program. One file
there requires the entry file of your application, and its name can be anything. The statements
outside the classes do not run, in any of the files.

A `.nvst` file, or a folder of `.nvst` files, is a different kind of test. Each file has a
`--TEST--` title, a program under `--FILE--` and its expected output under `--EXPECT--`. The report
is one line, such as `1 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped`.

A folder with both `.nvs` and `.nvst` files is an error. `nvs test` takes one program at a time, so
a `.nvs` path and a `.nvst` path in one call are an error too. `--format`, `--list` and `--update`
do not work with `.nvst` files.

`--format json` prints one JSON document at the end. It has `schemaVersion` `2`, a `summary` with
`total`, `passed`, `failed`, `skipped`, `flaky` and `durationMs`, and a `tests` list. Each test has
`class`, `method`, `file`, `line`, `column`, `verdict` and `durationMs`. `line` and `column` are
where the method's name is written, counted from `1`. A skipped test also has `reason`. A failed or
flaky test has `failures`, and a flaky test has `attempts`.

`--coverage-lcov`, `--coverage-clover` and `--coverage-cobertura` write which lines the tests ran.
With one of them, the JSON document has `schemaVersion` `3`, and each test has `coverage`. It maps
each file name to the lines that test ran.

`--format junit` prints JUnit XML, with one `<testsuite>` for each class and one `<testcase>` for
each test. A test has `<skipped>`, `<failure>` or `<flakyFailure>` inside it. The `message` of a
failure is its first message, and the text inside is every message.

With `--format json` or `--format junit`, standard output has only the document. The output of a
test that fails goes to standard error.

`--list` prints each test and where it is written, such as `T::a  main.nvs:6`, and runs nothing. A
test with data rows has one line for each row. With `--format json`, it prints a document with
`schemaVersion` `2` and a `listed` list of `class`, `method`, `file`, `line` and `column`.

`--filter` is case-sensitive, so `--filter t::` does not select the class `T`. A data row
is `Class::method#0`, `Class::method#1` and so on. A class with no selected test is not printed, and
its fixtures are not built.

The exit status is `1` when a test failed, and `0` otherwise. It is the same in every format.

#### Example 01: run the tests of a program

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the program you give to `nvs test`. `nvs test 01-run-the-tests-of-a-program.nvs`
// compiles it, runs both tests below, and prints a line for each one.

use Core\Test;

class Greeting
{
    public static function forName(string $name): string
    {
        if ($name == '') {
            return 'Hello!';
        }
        return 'Hello, ' . $name . '!';
    }
}

class GreetingTest
{
    #[Test]
    public function itGreetsSomebodyByName(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Greeting::forName('Ada'), 'Hello, Ada!');
    }

    #[Test]
    public function itGreetsSomebodyWithNoName(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Greeting::forName(''), 'Hello!');
    }
}

// The lines outside a class do not run under `nvs test`. Under `nvs run` they
// do, and this prints `Hello, Ada! Hello!`.
echo Greeting::forName('Ada'), ' ', Greeting::forName(''), "\n";
```

```output
Hello, Ada! Hello!
```

#### Example 02: run only some of the tests

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows how to run part of a test suite. A test's name is `Class::method`, so
// `nvs test --filter CartTest::` runs the three tests of `CartTest` and none
// of `ShippingTest`.

use Core\Test;

class Cart
{
    public static function total(array<uint> $prices): uint
    {
        uint $sum = 0;
        foreach ($prices as uint $price) {
            $sum = $sum + $price;
        }
        return $sum;
    }
}

class Shipping
{
    public static function costFor(uint $total): uint
    {
        if ($total >= 5000) {
            return 0;
        }
        return 499;
    }
}

class CartTest
{
    #[Test]
    public function itAddsNothingForAnEmptyCart(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Cart::total([]), 0);
    }

    #[Test]
    public function itAddsOnePrice(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Cart::total([1250]), 1250);
    }

    #[Test]
    public function itAddsSeveralPrices(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Cart::total([1250, 750, 3000]), 5000);
    }
}

class ShippingTest
{
    // `--filter CartTest::` does not run this test, and its class is not
    // printed at all.
    #[Test]
    public function itShipsALargeOrderForFree(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Shipping::costFor(5000), 0);
    }
}

// This prints `5000 0`.
echo Cart::total([1250, 750, 3000]), ' ', Shipping::costFor(5000), "\n";
```

```output
5000 0
```

#### Example 03: the report a build server reads

```nvs
<?nvs
// Shows the program a build server runs. `nvs test --format json` prints one
// JSON document holding every test and its result. The exit status is `1`
// when a test failed, which is what stops the build.

use Core\Test;

class Password
{
    public static function isStrongEnough(string $text): bool
    {
        return Core\Str::length($text) >= 12;
    }
}

class PasswordTest
{
    #[Test]
    public function itAcceptsALongPassword(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Password::isStrongEnough('correct horse battery'), true);
    }

    #[Test]
    public function itRejectsAShortPassword(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Password::isStrongEnough('horse'), false);
    }

    // `--list` prints this test and where it is written, without running it.
    #[Test]
    public function itRejectsAnEmptyPassword(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Password::isStrongEnough(''), false);
    }
}

// This prints `strong weak weak`.
echo (Password::isStrongEnough('correct horse battery') ? 'strong' : 'weak'), ' ',
     (Password::isStrongEnough('horse') ? 'strong' : 'weak'), ' ',
     (Password::isStrongEnough('') ? 'strong' : 'weak'), "\n";
```

```output
strong weak weak
```

### `#[Bench]` and `nvs test --bench`

`#[Bench]` marks a method as a bench. A bench measures how much work a piece of code does.
`nvs test --bench main.nvs` runs every bench in the program, one at a time. It runs no test, and a
plain `nvs test` runs no bench.

A bench method has the same shape as a `#[Test]` method. Write `use Core\Test\Bench;` at the top of
the file, and `#[Bench]` above the method.

The report prints a `count:` line under each bench. It counts statements, calls, allocations,
allocated bytes and runs of the garbage collector. These counts are the same on every run and on
every computer. The line also prints the time the bench took, marked `(advisory)`, because that
time changes on every run.

A bench passes without an assertion. With `--format json`, a build server can compare the counts
with the last run.

**Good to know:** a new version of Novis can give the same program different counts.

The examples show a bench beside a test, two ways to write the same work, and benches that a build
server checks.

A bench method is `public`, it is not `static`, and it returns `void`. If an assertion inside a
bench fails, the bench fails. `#[Bench(skip: "reason")]` skips a bench and prints the reason.

The counts tell you if your code does more work. They do not tell you if Novis got faster.

Each bench runs once. Its counts are the same on every run, so a second run gives no new
information.

Each bench runs on its own, the same way each test does. A value that one bench puts in a `static`
property is not there when the next bench runs. So the counts of a bench do not depend on the
benches that ran before it.

A bench can have a `#[Fixture]` parameter. The fixture is built before the counting starts, so its
work is not part of the counts.

A bench cannot fix the clock or the random numbers. A bench that reads `Core\Time::now()` or calls
`Core\Random` can do different work on each run, and then its counts change too.

`#[Bench]` has two options, `skip:` and `because:`. Both are strings. Every other option of
`#[Test]`, such as `retries:`, `seed:` or `at:`, does not compile on a bench. A `#[TestWith]` row on
a bench does not compile either. A method that has `#[Bench]` and also `#[Test]` or `#[Fixture]`
does not compile.

`--filter` works with `--bench` and selects benches by `Class::method`. `--bench` does not work with
`--jobs` or `--mutate`, and it does not work with a `.nvst` file.

In the JSON report, a bench that ran has `counts` with `statements`, `calls`, `allocations`,
`bytes` and `gc`. It also has `advisoryWallMs`, the time it took in milliseconds. A skipped bench
has `reason` and no `counts`.

The exit status is `1` when a bench failed, and `0` otherwise.

#### Example 01: a bench beside a test

```nvs test
<?nvs
// Shows a bench beside a test. `nvs test --bench` runs the bench and not the test.
// proof: test --bench

use Core\Test;
use Core\Test\Bench;

final class Slug
{
    public static function of(string $title): string
    {
        return Core\Str::replace(Core\Str::lower(Core\Str::trim($title)), ' ', '-');
    }
}

final class SlugTest
{
    // `nvs test` runs this test. `nvs test --bench` does not.
    #[Test]
    public function itJoinsTheWordsWithDashes(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Slug::of(' Hello World '), 'hello-world');
    }

    // A bench needs no assertion. The report prints a `count:` line under it.
    // `statements` is how many statements ran, and `calls` is how many calls were made.
    #[Bench]
    public function slugsOfOneHundredTitles(): void
    {
        for (int $i = 0; $i < 100; $i++) {
            Slug::of('Release Notes ' . $i);
        }
    }
}
```

```output
  SlugTest
    ✓ slugsOfOneHundredTitles
      count: statements=302 calls=400 allocations=505 bytes=26674 gc=0

  0 failed, 1 passed, 0 skipped, 0 flaky
```

#### Example 02: two ways to build one line

```nvs test
<?nvs
// Shows two benches that compare two ways to build one line of a CSV file.
// proof: test --bench

use Core\Test\Bench;

final class CsvLine
{
    // This method adds one cell at a time, in a loop.
    public static function byLoop(array<string> $cells): string
    {
        string $line = '';
        foreach ($cells as string $cell) {
            if ($line != '') {
                $line = $line . ',';
            }
            $line = $line . $cell;
        }
        return $line;
    }

    // This method makes one call to `Core\Str::join`.
    public static function byJoin(array<string> $cells): string
    {
        return Core\Str::join($cells, ',');
    }
}

final class CsvLineBench
{
    // Both benches build the same 200 cells first.
    // So the difference in their counts is the work of building the line.
    private static function cells(): array<string>
    {
        array<string> $cells = [];
        for (int $i = 0; $i < 200; $i++) {
            $cells[] = 'cell' . $i;
        }
        return $cells;
    }

    #[Bench]
    public function byLoop(): void
    {
        CsvLine::byLoop(CsvLineBench::cells());
    }

    // This bench runs 1000 fewer statements than the bench above.
    #[Bench]
    public function byJoin(): void
    {
        CsvLine::byJoin(CsvLineBench::cells());
    }
}
```

```output
  CsvLineBench
    ✓ byLoop
      count: statements=1406 calls=2 allocations=423 bytes=32373 gc=0
    ✓ byJoin
      count: statements=406 calls=3 allocations=418 bytes=30336 gc=0

  0 failed, 2 passed, 0 skipped, 0 flaky
```

#### Example 03: benches a build server checks

```nvs test
<?nvs
// Shows benches that a build server checks on every change to the program.
// proof: test --bench

use Core\Test\Bench;
use Core\Test\Fixture;

final class Catalog
{
    public function constructor(public array<int> $prices)
    {}

    public function priceOf(string $sku): ?int
    {
        if (!Core\Arr::hasKey($this->prices, $sku)) {
            return null;
        }
        return $this->prices[$sku];
    }
}

final class CatalogBench
{
    // A fixture is built before the counting starts.
    // So the 500 prices it adds are not part of the counts below.
    #[Fixture]
    public static function catalog(): Catalog
    {
        array<int> $prices = [];
        for (int $i = 0; $i < 500; $i++) {
            $prices['sku-' . $i] = 100 + $i;
        }
        return new Catalog($prices);
    }

    // `nvs test --bench --format json` prints a `counts` object for this bench.
    // The counts are the same on every machine. A build server can compare them with the last run.
    #[Bench]
    public function oneHundredLookups(Catalog $catalog): void
    {
        for (int $i = 0; $i < 100; $i++) {
            $catalog->priceOf('sku-' . $i);
        }
    }

    // `skip:` stops a bench from running, and the report prints the reason.
    #[Bench(skip: 'the import file is not in this repository')]
    public function importTheWholeCatalog(): void
    {}
}
```

```output
  CatalogBench
    ✓ oneHundredLookups
      count: statements=402 calls=200 allocations=205 bytes=8902 gc=0
    - importTheWholeCatalog
      skipped: the import file is not in this repository

  0 failed, 1 passed, 1 skipped, 0 flaky
```

# Part B — The `Core` library

Every function and constant in Novis is a member of a class under the reserved `Core` namespace; there are no free functions. The sections below are in the registry's own order. A class with type parameters (`Core\ObjectMap<K, V>`) is written with them at `new`.

<a id="core-core-str"></a>
### `Core\Str`

Keywords: string, text, grapheme, unicode, length, substring, slice, search, index of, contains, starts with, ends with, count occurrences, compare, natural order, case-insensitive, split, join, replace, trim, pad, repeat, reverse, word wrap, lowercase, uppercase, capitalize, case conversion, normalize, character code, printf-style formatting, length, at, isEmpty, contains, startsWith, endsWith, slice, indexOf, lastIndexOf, countOf, compare, before, after, join, split, parts, chunk, lines, graphemes, codePoints, replace, replaceAll, replaceRange, padStart, padEnd, trim, trimStart, trimEnd, repeat, reverse, wrap, lower, upper, upperFirst, lowerFirst, fold, normalize, fromCodePoint, fromCodePoints, format

Every member of `Core\Str` is a static function over a `string` that answers a new value; none
changes its argument. Every position, length and count is in **graphemes** — user-perceived
characters — so `length("👍🏽")` is `1`, no `slice` or `chunk` ever splits a character, and a byte
count is `Core\Bytes::length`. A string has no `$s[0]` and no `<`/`>`: `Core\Str::at`,
`Core\Str::slice` and `Core\Str::compare` are those spellings. A position or a cut that does not
exist is `null` — `indexOf`, `lastIndexOf`, `before`, `after` — never `false`.

```nvs
<?nvs
string $s = Core\Str::trim('  Grüße aus Köln  ');
echo Core\Str::length($s), ' ', Core\Str::upper($s), "\n";
echo Core\Str::slice($s, 0, 5), '|', Core\Str::at($s, 2), '|', Core\Str::reverse('café'), "\n";
echo Core\Str::indexOf($s, 'aus') ?? 'none', ' ', Core\Str::indexOf($s, 'Bonn') ?? 'none', "\n";
echo Core\Str::contains($s, 'Köln') ? 'yes' : 'no', ' ', Core\Str::countOf($s, 'ü'), "\n";
array<string> $words = Core\Str::split($s, ' ');
echo Core\Arr::count($words), ' ', Core\Str::join(Core\Arr::reverse($words), '-'), "\n";
echo Core\Str::replace($s, 'Köln', 'Bonn'), '|', Core\Str::before($s, ' ') ?? 'none', "\n";
echo Core\Str::padStart('7', 3, '0'), ' ', Core\Str::repeat('ab', 3), ' ', Core\Str::upperFirst('ßig'), "\n";
echo Core\Str::format('%-6s|%05.1f|%x', 'id', 3.14159, 255), "\n";
echo Core\Str::compare('img10', 'img9'), ' ', Core\Str::compare('img10', 'img9', { natural: true }), "\n";
```
```output
14 GRÜSSE AUS KÖLN
Grüße|ü|éfac
6 none
yes 1
3 Köln-aus-Grüße
Grüße aus Bonn|Grüße
007 ababab SSig
id    |003.1|ff
-1 1
```

<a id="core-core-str-length"></a>
#### `Core\Str::length`

```nvs skip
Core\Str::length(string $s): uint
```

Counts the graphemes in `$s`. A grapheme is what a person counts as one character, so a letter with a combining accent counts once. Every `Core\Str` function counts in graphemes. The result is never a byte count.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$s` | `string` (neutral) | The string to measure. |

**Returns** `uint` — The number of graphemes. The empty string gives `0`.

<a id="core-core-str-at"></a>
#### `Core\Str::at`

```nvs skip
Core\Str::at(string $s, int $index): string
```

Returns the one character at position `$index` of `$s`. A character is what a person sees as one letter, so `"é"` is one character.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$s` | `string` | The string to read from. |
| `$index` | `int` | The position of the character. The first character is at `0`. A negative position counts from the end, so `-1` is the last character. |

**Returns** `string` — A string with exactly one character in it.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — There is no character at `$index`. The position is at or past the length of `$s`, counting from either end.

<a id="core-core-str-isempty"></a>
#### `Core\Str::isEmpty`

```nvs skip
Core\Str::isEmpty(string $s): bool
```

Checks whether `$s` is the empty string `""`. A string of spaces is not empty, and neither is `"0"`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$s` | `string` (neutral) | The string to check. |

**Returns** `bool` — `true` when `$s` has no characters, otherwise `false`.

<a id="core-core-str-contains"></a>
#### `Core\Str::contains`

```nvs skip
Core\Str::contains(string $haystack, string $needle): bool
```

Checks whether `$needle` appears anywhere in `$haystack`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$haystack` | `string` (neutral) | The string to search in. |
| `$needle` | `string` (neutral) | The text to search for. The search is case-sensitive. |

**Returns** `bool` — `true` when `$needle` is in `$haystack`, otherwise `false`. An empty `$needle` is in every string, so the result is `true`.

<a id="core-core-str-startswith"></a>
#### `Core\Str::startsWith`

```nvs skip
Core\Str::startsWith(string $s, string $prefix): bool
```

Checks whether `$s` starts with `$prefix`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$s` | `string` (neutral) | The string to check. |
| `$prefix` | `string` (neutral) | The text `$s` must start with. The check is case-sensitive. |

**Returns** `bool` — `true` when `$s` starts with `$prefix`, otherwise `false`. An empty `$prefix` is at the start of every string, so the result is `true`.

Checks whether `$s` ends with `$suffix`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|

| `$suffix` | `string` (neutral) | The text `$s` must end with. The check is case-sensitive. |

**Returns** `bool` — `true` when `$s` ends with `$suffix`, otherwise `false`. An empty `$suffix` is at the end of every string, so the result is `true`.

<a id="core-core-str-slice"></a>
#### `Core\Str::slice`

```nvs skip
Core\Str::slice(string $s, int $offset, ?int $length = null): string
```

Returns the part of `$s` that starts at `$offset` and has `$length` characters. Positions count characters as a person sees them, so "é" is one character.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$s` | `string` | The string to take the part from. |
| `$offset` | `int` | Where the part starts. The first character is at `0`. A negative offset counts from the end. |
| `$length` | `?int` (default `null`) | How many characters to take. A negative length stops that many characters before the end. `null` takes everything to the end. |

**Returns** `string` — The part as a new string. It is `""` when the part is empty or the offset is past the end. `$s` does not change.

<a id="core-core-str-indexof"></a>
#### `Core\Str::indexOf`

```nvs skip
Core\Str::indexOf(string $haystack, string $needle, { from?: int, caseInsensitive?: bool }): ?uint
```

Finds the first place where `$needle` appears in `$haystack` and returns its position. The first character is position `0`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$haystack` | `string` (neutral) | The string to search in. |
| `$needle` | `string` (neutral) | The string to search for. An empty needle matches where the search starts. |
| `{ from: … }` | `int` (default `0`) | The position where the search starts. A negative value counts from the end. The default is `0`. |
| `{ caseInsensitive: … }` | `bool` (default `false`) | When `true`, upper-case and lower-case letters match each other. Each character is compared by its lower-case form, so `ß` does not match `SS`. The default is `false`. |

**Returns** `?uint` — The position of the first match at or after `from`, counted in characters as `Core\Str::length` counts them. You can pass it to `Core\Str::slice`. The result is `null` when there is no match.

<a id="core-core-str-lastindexof"></a>
#### `Core\Str::lastIndexOf`

```nvs skip
Core\Str::lastIndexOf(string $haystack, string $needle, { before?: int, caseInsensitive?: bool }): ?uint
```

Finds the last place where `$needle` appears in `$haystack` and returns its position. The first character is position `0`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$haystack` | `string` (neutral) | The string to search in. |
| `$needle` | `string` (neutral) | The string to search for. |
| `{ before: … }` | `int` (default `9223372036854775807`) | Searches only the characters in front of this position, so a match must end here or earlier. A negative position counts back from the end. The default is the whole string. |
| `{ caseInsensitive: … }` | `bool` (default `false`) | When `true`, upper-case and lower-case letters count as the same. The default is `false`. |

**Returns** `?uint` — The position of the last match, or `null` when there is none. Matches may overlap, so `lastIndexOf("aaa", "aa")` returns `1`.

<a id="core-core-str-countof"></a>
#### `Core\Str::countOf`

```nvs skip
Core\Str::countOf(string $haystack, string $needle): uint
```

Counts how many times `$needle` appears in `$haystack`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$haystack` | `string` (neutral) | The string to search in. |
| `$needle` | `string` (neutral) | The text to count. The search is case-sensitive. It must not be empty. |

**Returns** `uint` — The number of times `$needle` appears, or `0` when it does not appear. Matches do not overlap, so `countOf("aaa", "aa")` is `1`.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `$needle` is empty.

<a id="core-core-str-compare"></a>
#### `Core\Str::compare`

```nvs skip

```

Compares two strings to sort them.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$a` | `string` (neutral) | The first string. |
| `$b` | `string` (neutral) | The second string. |

<a id="core-core-str-split"></a>
#### `Core\Str::split`

```nvs skip
Core\Str::split(string $s, string $separator, { limit?: int }): array<string>
```

Splits `$s` into parts at every place where `$separator` is found.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$s` | `string` | The string to split. |
| `$separator` | `string` | The text to split at. Upper and lower case are different. It must not be empty. |
| `{ limit: … }` | `int` (default `9223372036854775807`) | A positive limit gives at most that many parts. The last part contains the rest of the string. A negative limit deletes that many parts from the end. `0` gives the whole string as one part. The default is no limit. |

**Returns** `array<string>` — The parts in order, without the separator. The empty string gives `[""]`. A negative limit that deletes every part gives `[]`.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `$separator` is empty.

<a id="core-core-str-parts"></a>
#### `Core\Str::parts`

```nvs skip
Core\Str::parts(string<K> $text): array<string|K>
```

Splits a string with holes into its text and its holes.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$text` | `string<K>` | A string with holes, such as `string<propertyPath<Order>>`. Each `{name}` in it is a hole. |

**Returns** `array<string|K>` — The text and the holes in order. The array starts and ends with text, and text and holes take turns. So an even index is text and an odd index is a hole. Text can be the empty string. In text, `{{` is already `{` and `}}` is already `}`. If `$text` is `tainted`, the text is `tainted` too. The holes are not.

<a id="core-core-str-chunk"></a>
#### `Core\Str::chunk`


Divides `$s` into pieces of `$size` characters each. A piece never cuts a character in half.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |

**Returns** `array<string>` — The pieces in order. Only the last piece can be shorter than `$size`. The result is `[]` for the empty string.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `$size` is `0`.

<a id="core-core-str-lines"></a>
#### `Core\Str::lines`

```nvs skip
Core\Str::lines(string $s): array<string>
```

Splits `$s` into its lines. A line ends at `\n`, at `\r\n` or at `\r`, on every system.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$s` | `string` | The text to split. |

**Returns** `array<string>` — One string for each line, without its line break. A line break at the very end does not add an empty line. An empty line in the middle is kept as `""`. An empty string gives `[]`.

<a id="core-core-str-graphemes"></a>
#### `Core\Str::graphemes`

```nvs skip
Core\Str::graphemes(string $s): array<string>
```

Divides `$s` into its characters, the way a person counts them. An accented letter, a flag or an emoji with a skin tone is one character, even when it is several code points. These are the characters `Core\Str::length` counts.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$s` | `string` | The string to divide. |

**Returns** `array<string>` — One string for each character, in order. An empty string gives `[]`.

<a id="core-core-str-codepoints"></a>
#### `Core\Str::codePoints`

```nvs skip
Core\Str::codePoints(string $s): array<uint>
```

Lists the code points of `$s`. A code point is the number Unicode gives to one symbol. One character a person sees can be several code points.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$s` | `string` (neutral) | The string to read. |

**Returns** `array<uint>` — One `uint` for each code point, in order. Each number is between `0` and `0x10FFFF` and is never a surrogate. The result is `[]` for the empty string.

<a id="core-core-str-replace"></a>
#### `Core\Str::replace`

```nvs skip
Core\Str::replace(string $s, string $search, string $replacement, { caseInsensitive?: bool, limit?: uint }): string
```

Replaces every occurrence of `$search` in `$s` with `$replacement`. Matches are found from left to right and do not overlap. The new text is not searched again.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$s` | `string` | The string to change. |
| `$search` | `string` | The text to find. An empty `$search` matches nothing. |
| `$replacement` | `string` | The text that replaces each match. |
| `{ caseInsensitive: … }` | `bool` (default `false`) | If `true`, upper-case and lower-case letters match each other, so `"A"` finds `"a"`. The default is `false`. |
| `{ limit: … }` | `uint` (default `18446744073709551615`) | The most matches to replace, counted from the left. `0` replaces nothing. The default is every match. |

**Returns** `string` — The changed string. If nothing matched, the result is `$s` unchanged.

<a id="core-core-str-replaceall"></a>
#### `Core\Str::replaceAll`

```nvs skip
Core\Str::replaceAll(string $s, array<string> $pairs, { caseInsensitive?: bool }): string
```

Replaces several texts in `$s` in one call. Each key of `$pairs` is a text to find, and its value is the text that replaces it. The string is read once, from left to right. Where several keys match at the same place, the longest one is used. The new text is not searched again.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$s` | `string` | The string to change. |
| `$pairs` | `array<string>` | The replacements. Each key is the text to find, and its value is the text that replaces it. An empty key is ignored. |
| `{ caseInsensitive: … }` | `bool` (default `false`) | If `true`, upper-case and lower-case letters match each other. If two keys then match the same text, the key written first is used. The default is `false`. |

**Returns** `string` — The changed string. If `$pairs` is empty or nothing matched, the result is `$s` unchanged.

<a id="core-core-str-replacerange"></a>
#### `Core\Str::replaceRange`

```nvs skip
Core\Str::replaceRange(string $s, int $offset, ?int $length, string $replacement): string
```

Replaces a part of `$s` with `$replacement`. The part is the text `Core\Str::slice` returns for the same `$offset` and `$length`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$s` | `string` | The string to change. |
| `$offset` | `int` | The character where the part starts. `0` is the first character. A negative offset counts from the end. |
| `$length` | `?int` | How many characters the part has. A negative length stops that many characters before the end. `null` means the part runs to the end. |
| `$replacement` | `string` | The text that replaces the part. `""` deletes the part. |

**Returns** `string` — The changed string. If the part is empty, for example with a `$length` of `0`, `$replacement` is inserted at `$offset`.

<a id="core-core-str-wrap"></a>
#### `Core\Str::wrap`

```nvs skip
Core\Str::wrap(string $s, uint $width, { breakWith?: string, cutLongWords?: bool }): string
```

Splits `$s` into lines of at most `$width` characters. It breaks a line at a space and writes `breakWith` in place of that space. A character is what a person sees as one character, so `"é"` counts as one.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$s` | `string` | The text to wrap. |
| `$width` | `uint` | The longest line, in characters. With `0`, every space is a line break. |

| `{ cutLongWords: … }` | `bool` (default `false`) | With `true`, a word longer than `$width` is cut into pieces of `$width` characters. With `false`, the default, a long word stays whole on a line of its own. |

**Returns** `string` — The wrapped text. A text of at most `$width` characters is returned unchanged. A result over the memory limit stops the request.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `breakWith` is `""`, or `$width` is `0` and `cutLongWords` is `true`.

<a id="core-core-str-fold"></a>
#### `Core\Str::fold`

```nvs skip
Core\Str::fold(string $s): string
```

Case-folds `$s`: every letter changes to one fixed form, so text that differs only in upper and lower case gives the same result.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$s` | `string` | The string to fold. |

**Returns** `string` — The folded string. It is a key for comparing, not text to show: `ß` becomes `ss` and `ﬁ` becomes `fi`. `fold("STRASSE") == fold("straße")` is `true`.

<a id="core-core-str-normalize"></a>
#### `Core\Str::normalize`

```nvs skip
Core\Str::normalize(string $s, Core\Str::NormalForm $form): string
```

Changes `$s` into one of the four Unicode normal forms. Two ways to write the same text then give the same string.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$s` | `string` | The string to normalize. |
| `$form` | `Core\Str::NormalForm` | Which form to use. `Nfc` and `Nfd` keep every character's meaning. `Nfkc` and `Nfkd` also replace look-alike characters: `ﬁ` becomes `fi`. |

**Returns** `string` — The normalized string. `Nfc` is the form to store and compare text in. A string of ASCII characters is returned unchanged.

<a id="core-core-str-fromcodepoint"></a>
#### `Core\Str::fromCodePoint`

```nvs skip
Core\Str::fromCodePoint(uint $codePoint): string
```

Builds a string of one code point. A code point is the number Unicode gives to one symbol. To build one byte, use `Core\Bytes`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$codePoint` | `uint` | The number of the symbol. It is at most `0x10FFFF` and is not in the surrogate range `0xD800` to `0xDFFF`. |

**Returns** `string` — A string that contains that one code point. `0x20AC` gives `"€"`.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `$codePoint` is above `0x10FFFF`, or it is in the surrogate range `0xD800` to `0xDFFF`. Unicode gives no symbol to these numbers.

<a id="core-core-str-fromcodepoints"></a>
#### `Core\Str::fromCodePoints`

```nvs skip
Core\Str::fromCodePoints(array<uint> $codePoints): string
```

Builds a string from a list of code points, in order. It does the opposite of `Core\Str::codePoints`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$codePoints` | `array<uint>` | The numbers of the symbols, in order. Each one is at most `0x10FFFF` and is not in the surrogate range `0xD800` to `0xDFFF`. |

**Returns** `string` — The string. An empty array gives `""`.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — An element is above `0x10FFFF`, or it is in the surrogate range `0xD800` to `0xDFFF`. No part of the string is returned.

<a id="core-core-str-format"></a>
#### `Core\Str::format`

```nvs skip
Core\Str::format(string $template, mixed ...$arguments): string
```

Fills the placeholders in `$template` with `$arguments` and returns the text. The placeholders are `%s %d %u %f %e %g %x %X %o %b %%`, with flags, a width, a precision and positions such as `%1$s`. The result never depends on the locale.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$template` | `string` (sink) | The template. It must be trusted text, so a tainted string is not allowed. When the template is written directly in the code, its placeholders are checked when the program compiles. |
| `...$arguments` | `mixed` | The values for the placeholders, in order, or by position with `%1$s`. Every value must be used by at least one placeholder. |

**Returns** `string` — The filled-in text. A width or a precision counts characters, as `Core\Str::length` does. `%f` always writes `.` before the decimals.

**Throws** `LogicError` — A placeholder is not valid, the template uses more arguments than were passed, an argument is not used, or a value does not fit its placeholder. For example, `%d` does not accept an array.; `RuntimeError` — A width or a precision is larger than any string this process can hold. A smaller one that is over the memory limit stops the request.

<a id="core-core-arr"></a>
### `Core\Arr`

Keywords: array, list, dictionary, count, filter, map, reduce, keys, values, first, last, search, slice, chunk, push, pop, append, prepend, pad, reverse, flip, fill, range, combine, column, merge, overlay, underlay, diff, intersect, unique, sum, product, average, min, max, sort, natural sort, stable sort, isset, array + array, group by, copy-on-write, immutable, count, filter, map, mapKeys, groupBy, reduce, find, findKey, any, all, isEmpty, hasKey, contains, keyOf, isList, keys, values, first, last, firstKey, lastKey, slice, replaceRange, chunk, append, prepend, withoutFirst, withoutLast, withoutNull, padStart, padEnd, reverse, flip, flatten, flattenDeep, column, sort, sortByKey, fill, fillKeys, range, fromKeysAndValues, from, overlay, overlayDeep, underlay, appendAll, diff, intersect, countBy, unique, min, max, sum, product, average, shapeAs

`Core\Arr` has the array functions as static methods. Each one returns a **new** array and never
changes its argument. `Core\Arr::sort` returns the sorted array, and `append` returns the longer one.
Keys are always `string`: `$a[0]` and `$a["0"]` are the same entry, `keys` returns `array<string>`,
and a callback's key parameter is `string`. A callback receives `($value, $key)` and may declare
fewer parameters. `reduce` passes the carry first. A missing value is `null`: `first`, `last`,
`find`, `keyOf` and `min` return `null` for an empty array. `count` returns a `uint`. `$a + $b` does
not compile. `overlay` and `underlay` combine maps, and `appendAll` joins lists.

`shapeAs<T>` is the one member that answers something other than an array. It reads its subject as the
type written at the call site — an inline shape, `{ name: string, score: int }`, or a class carrying
`#[Core\Json\Derive]` — converting every named field with `as` and leaving every key the type does not
name behind, so a form carrying a CSRF token does not break a handler reading two fields out of it.
That is the whole story for loose input: an `array<T>` is homogeneous and there is no per-key-typed
one, so a form, a query string or a decoded document is converted **once, at the boundary**, where a
failure is still a `400` — and nothing downstream is left holding a `mixed` to check. A field that is
absent, or that holds a value `as` refuses for its declared type, throws `ParseError` carrying every
field that failed at its own dotted path, rather than the first of them. `{ name?: T }` marks a key that
may be absent, and `??` and `isset` read one without throwing. `Core\Request::queryAs` and `postAs`
are this member over what a request carried. Text that came from outside the program, such as a form
or an `array<mixed>`, is `tainted`. A text field it fills must then be declared `tainted` too.

```nvs
<?nvs
array<int> $scores = ['ada' => 92, 'bo' => 67, 'cy' => 85, 'di' => 74];
var $passed = Core\Arr::filter($scores, fn(int $n): bool => $n >= 70);
echo Core\Json::encode($passed), "\n";
var $ranked = Core\Arr::sort($passed, { order: Core\Arr::Order::Desc, preserveKeys: true });
echo Core\Json::encode(Core\Arr::keys($ranked)), "\n";
echo Core\Arr::first($ranked) ?? 0, ' ', Core\Arr::firstKey($ranked) ?? '-', "\n";
var $labels = Core\Arr::map($scores, fn(int $n, string $k): string => $k . ':' . ($n as string));
echo Core\Str::join(Core\Arr::values($labels), ' '), "\n";
echo Core\Arr::sum($scores), ' ', Core\Arr::count($scores), ' ', Core\Arr::average($scores) ?? 0, "\n";
int $total = Core\Arr::reduce($scores, fn(int $carry, int $n): int => $carry + $n, 0);
echo $total, ' ', Core\Arr::max($scores) ?? 0, "\n";
array<int> $evens = Core\Arr::filter(Core\Arr::range(1, 10), fn(int $n): bool => $n % 2 == 0);
echo Core\Json::encode(Core\Arr::values($evens)), ' ', Core\Arr::contains($evens, 4) ? 'yes' : 'no', "\n";
var $byLength = Core\Arr::groupBy(['fig', 'pear', 'kiwi', 'plum'], fn(string $w): int => Core\Str::length($w) as int);
echo Core\Json::encode($byLength), "\n";
echo Core\Json::encode($scores), "\n";
var $entry = Core\Arr::shapeAs<{ name: string, score: int, note?: string }>(['name' => 'ada', 'score' => '92', 'csrf' => 't0ken']);
echo $entry->name, ' ', $entry->score as string, ' ', $entry->note ?? 'no note', "\n";
```
```output
{"ada":92,"cy":85,"di":74}
["ada","cy","di"]
92 ada
ada:92 bo:67 cy:85 di:74
318 4 79.5
318 92
[2,4,6,8,10] yes
{"3":["fig"],"4":{"1":"pear","2":"kiwi","3":"plum"}}
{"ada":92,"bo":67,"cy":85,"di":74}
ada 92 no note
```

#### `Core\Arr::count`

```nvs skip
Core\Arr::count(array<T> $a): uint
```

Returns the number of entries in `$a`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$a` | `array<T>` | The array to count. |

**Returns** `uint` — The number of entries; `0` for the empty array.

<a id="core-core-arr-filter"></a>
#### `Core\Arr::filter`

```nvs skip
Core\Arr::filter(array<T> $a, callable(T, string): bool $predicate): array<T>
```

Returns the entries for which `$predicate` returns a truthy value. The callback receives `($value, $key)` and may declare fewer parameters.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$a` | `array<T>` | The array to filter. |
| `$predicate` | `callable(T, string): bool` | Called as `($value, $key)` per entry. A truthy result keeps the entry. Truthy means the same here as in an `if` test. |

**Returns** `array<T>` — The kept entries under their own keys, never renumbered; an empty array when nothing passes.

<a id="core-core-arr-map"></a>
#### `Core\Arr::map`

```nvs skip
Core\Arr::map(array<T> $a, callable(T, string): U $fn): array<U>
```

Replaces every value with the result of `$fn` for it. The keys stay the same.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$a` | `array<T>` | The array to map. |
| `$fn` | `callable(T, string): U` | Called as `($value, $key)` per entry, and may declare fewer parameters; its return type is the result's `U`. |

**Returns** `array<U>` — One entry per entry of `$a`, under the same key. Its value is the callback's result.

<a id="core-core-arr-mapkeys"></a>
#### `Core\Arr::mapKeys`

```nvs skip
Core\Arr::mapKeys(array<T> $a, callable(T, string): int|string $fn): array<T>
```

Stores every value under the key that `$fn` returns for it.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$a` | `array<T>` | The array to re-key. |
| `$fn` | `callable(T, string): int\|string` | Called as `($value, $key)` per entry, and may declare fewer parameters. It returns the entry's new key, an `int` or a `string`. |

**Returns** `array<T>` — The values under their new keys, in first-occurrence order. When two entries get the same key, the last one is kept. `1` and `"1"` are the same key.

<a id="core-core-arr-groupby"></a>
#### `Core\Arr::groupBy`

```nvs skip
Core\Arr::groupBy(array<T> $a, callable(T, string): int|string $key): array<array<T>>
```

Puts the entries into groups. `$key` is called for each entry, and its result is the name of the group the entry goes into.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$a` | `array<T>` | The array to partition. |
| `$key` | `callable(T, string): int\|string` | Called as `($value, $key)` per entry, and may declare fewer parameters. It returns the group's name, an `int` or a `string`. |

**Returns** `array<array<T>>` — One inner array per distinct result, in first-occurrence order. Each inner array keeps its entries under their own keys. `1` and `"1"` name the same group.

<a id="core-core-arr-reduce"></a>
#### `Core\Arr::reduce`

```nvs skip
Core\Arr::reduce(array<T> $a, callable(U, T, string): U $fn, U $initial): U
```

Combines the entries into one value, starting from `$initial`. The callback receives `($carry, $value, $key)` and may declare fewer parameters.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$a` | `array<T>` | The array to reduce. |
| `$fn` | `callable(U, T, string): U` | Called as `($carry, $value, $key)` per entry. It returns the next carry. |
| `$initial` | `U` | The starting value. Its type is `U`, which is also the type of the result. |

**Returns** `U` — The last carry; `$initial` itself over an empty array, with no call made.

<a id="core-core-arr-slice"></a>
#### `Core\Arr::slice`

```nvs skip
Core\Arr::slice(array<T> $a, int $offset, ?int $length = null, { preserveKeys?: bool }): array<T>
```

Returns the entries in one range of positions. A position counts entries from the start, whatever the keys are.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$a` | `array<T>` | The array to take from. |
| `$offset` | `int` | The position where the range starts. A negative offset counts back from the last entry. An offset before the first entry starts at the first entry. |
| `$length` | `?int` (default `null`) | How many entries the range has. A negative length stops that many entries before the end, and `null` takes every entry to the end. |
| `{ preserveKeys: … }` | `bool` (default `false`) | Keeps every entry's own key. By default every key is discarded, string keys included, and the result is renumbered from `"0"`. |

**Returns** `array<T>` — The entries in the range; the empty array when the range ends before it starts.

<a id="core-core-arr-replacerange"></a>
#### `Core\Arr::replaceRange`

```nvs skip
Core\Arr::replaceRange(array<T> $a, int $offset, ?int $length, array<T> $replacement = []): array<T>
```

Returns a copy of the array with one range of positions replaced by the values of `$replacement`. The original array does not change.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$a` | `array<T>` | The array to edit. |
| `$offset` | `int` | The position where the range starts. A negative offset works as in `slice`. An offset at the end appends. |
| `$length` | `?int` | How many entries the range has. A negative length works as in `slice`. `0` inserts at the position, and `null` reaches the end. |
| `$replacement` | `array<T>` (default `[]`) | The values to put in place of the range. Without it, the range is removed. |

**Returns** `array<T>` — A list renumbered from `"0"`, kept entries and replacement alike.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `$size` is `0`.

Returns the array with every given value added after its last entry. It works like `$a[] = $v`, written as an expression.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|

| `...$values` | `T` | The values to add, in written order. |

**Returns** `array<T>` — The entries of `$a` under their own keys, then each value under the next free integer key. That key is one past the largest key present. With no values, the result is `$a` itself.

<a id="core-core-arr-flip"></a>


Makes every value a key, and every key its value.

<a id="core-core-arr-column"></a>
#### `Core\Arr::column`

```nvs skip
Core\Arr::column(array<array<T>> $a, int|string $column, { indexBy?: int|string }): array<T>
```

Takes the cell with one key out of every row.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$a` | `array<array<T>>` | The rows, each an array. |
| `$column` | `int\|string` | The key of the cell to take; `0` and `"0"` name one cell, as `$row[0]` and `$row["0"]` do. |
| `{ indexBy: … }` | `int\|string` (default `null`) | The key of the cell to use as the result's key. By default the result gets new integer keys. |

**Returns** `array<T>` — The cells in row order. A row without the column is skipped. A row without the `indexBy` cell goes under the next free integer key. When two rows have the same `indexBy` value, the last one is kept.

<a id="core-core-arr-sort"></a>
#### `Core\Arr::sort`

```nvs skip
Core\Arr::sort(array<T> $a, { by?: callable, order?: Core\Arr::Order, comparator?: callable, preserveKeys?: bool }): array<T>
```

Returns the entries in order. The sort is stable, so equal entries keep their order. Four options choose the sort value, the direction, the comparison and the keys.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$a` | `array<T>` | The array to sort. |
| `{ by: … }` | `callable` (default `null`) | Called once per entry as `($value, $key)`, and may declare fewer parameters. Its result is compared instead of the entry. |
| `{ order: … }` | `Core\Arr::Order` (default `Core\Arr::Order::Asc`) | `Core\Arr::Order::Asc` (the default) or `Core\Arr::Order::Desc`. `Desc` reverses the comparison, so equal entries keep their relative order. |
| `{ comparator: … }` | `callable` (default `null`) | Called as `($a, $b)` on two values, or on two results of `by`. It returns a negative number, zero or a positive number. It replaces the natural order. |
| `{ preserveKeys: … }` | `bool` (default `false`) | Keeps the key of each entry. By default, the result has new keys from `"0"`. |

**Returns** `array<T>` — The sorted entries. A natural order exists only between two numbers, two strings (compared byte by byte), two bools or two nulls. `"10"` sorts before `"9"`.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — Two entries have no natural order and no `comparator` was given. An `int` and a `string` have no natural order, and neither does any object. The error is also thrown when the comparator returns `NaN`.

<a id="core-core-arr-sortbykey"></a>
#### `Core\Arr::sortByKey`

```nvs skip
Core\Arr::sortByKey(array<T> $a, { order?: Core\Arr::Order, comparator?: callable, keys?: array<int|string> }): array<T>
```

Returns the entries in key order. The sort is stable, and every key is kept.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$a` | `array<T>` | The array to sort. |
| `{ order: … }` | `Core\Arr::Order` (default `Core\Arr::Order::Asc`) | `Core\Arr::Order::Asc` (the default) or `Core\Arr::Order::Desc`. `Desc` reverses the comparison, so equal keys keep their insertion order. |
| `{ comparator: … }` | `callable` (default `null`) | Called as `($a, $b)` on two keys, both `string`s. It returns a negative number, zero or a positive number. It replaces the natural order. |
| `{ keys: … }` | `array<int\|string>` (default `null`) | The keys to put first, in this order. The other keys follow in their current order. A listed key that `$a` does not have is skipped. With `Desc`, the other keys come first, then the listed keys from last to first. |

**Returns** `array<T>` — The same entries under the same keys, ordered by key; the natural order is bytewise, so `"10"` precedes `"9"`.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The comparator returned `NaN`.; `LogicError` — The call gives both `keys` and `comparator`.

<a id="core-core-arr-fill"></a>


Returns `$count` copies of `$value` under the keys `"0", "1", …`. There is no start index. Use `fillKeys` to choose the keys.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$count` | `uint` | How many entries; `0` yields the empty array. |
| `$value` | `T` | The value of every entry. |

**Returns** `array<T>` — A list of `$count` entries.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The result for `$count` is larger than the largest array this process can store.

<a id="core-core-arr-fillkeys"></a>
#### `Core\Arr::fillKeys`

```nvs skip

```

Stores `$value` under every key in `$keys`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$keys` | `array<int\|string>` | The keys to store under, given as the array's *values*. Each is an `int` or a `string`. The array's own keys are ignored. |
| `$value` | `T` | The value of every entry. |

**Returns** `array<T>` — One entry per distinct key, in first-occurrence order; `1` and `"1"` are one key.

<a id="core-core-arr-range"></a>
#### `Core\Arr::range`

```nvs skip
Core\Arr::range(int $start, int $end, { step?: int }): array<int>
```

Returns the integers from `$start` to `$end`, both included. When `$start` is greater than `$end`, it counts down.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$start` | `int` | The first value. |
| `$end` | `int` | The last value that may appear. When a step goes past it, the list stops at the last value inside the range. |
| `{ step: … }` | `int` (default `1`) | The distance between two neighbouring values, `1` by default. It is always positive, because `$start` and `$end` set the direction. |

**Returns** `array<int>` — A list from `$start` towards `$end`; one entry when the two are equal.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `step` is `0` or negative.

<a id="core-core-arr-fromkeysandvalues"></a>

```nvs skip

```

Pairs the entries of `$keys` and `$values` in order. Each value is stored under its key.

|---|---|---|

| `$values` | `array<T>` | The values, in the same order. The array's own keys are ignored. |

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The two arrays have different numbers of entries.

<a id="core-core-arr-from"></a>
#### `Core\Arr::from`

```nvs skip
Core\Arr::from(array<T>|Iterable<T>|Iterator<T> $items, { limit?: uint }): array<T>
```

Reads a sequence into an array. The sequence can be an `Iterable<T>`, an `Iterator<T>` or an array: anything `foreach` accepts.

<a id="core-core-arr-overlay"></a>
#### `Core\Arr::overlay`

```nvs skip
Core\Arr::overlay(array<T> $base, array<U> ...$layers): array<T|U>
```

Writes the entries of every layer over `$base`. Where two have the same key, the value from the later array is kept. Integer keys and string keys work the same way.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$base` | `array<T>` | The array underneath. |
| `...$layers` | `array<U>` | The arrays to write over it, in order. A later layer replaces the values of an earlier one. |

**Returns** `array<T|U>` — Every key of every argument. An existing key keeps its position and takes the last value written under it. A new key is appended.

<a id="core-core-arr-overlaydeep"></a>

```nvs skip
Core\Arr::overlayDeep(array<T> $base, array<U> ...$layers): array<T|U>
```

Works like `overlay`. Where both sides of a key are arrays and neither is a list, it combines them the same way. A list is replaced as a whole.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$base` | `array<T>` | The array underneath. |
| `...$layers` | `array<U>` | The arrays to write over it, in order. A later layer replaces the values of an earlier one. |

**Returns** `array<T|U>` — Every key of every argument, as `overlay` returns them. When both values under one key are maps, they are combined the same way, and the later map does not replace the earlier one.

<a id="core-core-arr-diff"></a>
#### `Core\Arr::diff`

```nvs skip
Core\Arr::diff(array<T> $a, array<T> $b, { on?: Core\Arr::SetOn, by?: callable, comparator?: callable }): array<T>
```

Returns the entries of `$a` that `$b` does not have. Entries are compared by strict identity. The options choose what is compared, and how.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$a` | `array<T>` | The array whose entries are kept. |
| `$b` | `array<T>` | The entries of `$a` that are also in this array are removed. |
| `{ on: … }` | `Core\Arr::SetOn` (default `Core\Arr::SetOn::Values`) | Which part of an entry is compared: `Core\Arr::SetOn::Values` (the default), `Core\Arr::SetOn::Keys` or `Core\Arr::SetOn::Both`. |
| `{ by: … }` | `callable` (default `null`) | Called once per entry as `($value, $key)`, and may declare fewer parameters. Its result replaces the part `on` selected. Under `Core\Arr::SetOn::Keys`, that part is the key. |
| `{ comparator: … }` | `callable` (default `null`) | Called as `($a, $b)` on two selected parts. It returns a negative number, zero or a positive number. It replaces identity, and every entry of `$a` is then compared with every entry of `$b`. |

**Returns** `array<T>` — The kept entries of `$a` under their own keys, in `$a`'s order.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The comparator returned `NaN`.

<a id="core-core-arr-intersect"></a>

| `{ by: … }` | `callable` (default `null`) | Called once per entry as `($value, $key)`, and may declare fewer parameters. Its result replaces the part `on` selected. Under `Core\Arr::SetOn::Keys`, that part is the key. |
| `{ comparator: … }` | `callable` (default `null`) | Called as `($a, $b)` on two selected parts. It returns a negative number, zero or a positive number. It replaces identity, and every entry of `$a` is then compared with every entry of `$b`. |

**Returns** `array<T>` — The kept entries of `$a` under their own keys, in `$a`'s order.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The comparator returned `NaN`.

<a id="core-core-arr-countby"></a>
#### `Core\Arr::countBy`

```nvs skip
Core\Arr::countBy(array<T> $a, { by?: callable }): array<uint>
```

Counts how many entries have each distinct value. With `by`, it counts how many entries give each result of `by`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$a` | `array<T>` | The array to count over. |
| `{ by: … }` | `callable` (default `null`) | Called once per entry as `($value, $key)`, and may declare fewer parameters. It returns the group's name, an `int` or a `string`. Without it, the value itself is the group. |

**Returns** `array<uint>` — One `uint` per distinct group, keyed by the group in first-occurrence order. `1` and `"1"` are the same group.

<a id="core-core-arr-unique"></a>
#### `Core\Arr::unique`

```nvs skip
Core\Arr::unique(array<T> $a, { by?: callable }): array<T>
```

Returns the entries whose value has not appeared before. Values are compared by strict identity, so `1` and `"1"` are two different values.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$a` | `array<T>` | The array to deduplicate. |
| `{ by: … }` | `callable` (default `null`) | Called once per entry as `($value, $key)`, and may declare fewer parameters. Its result is compared by identity, but the entry itself is what is kept. |

**Returns** `array<T>` — The first occurrence of each value, under its own key and in its own position.

<a id="core-core-arr-min"></a>
#### `Core\Arr::min`

```nvs skip
Core\Arr::min(array<T> $a): ?T
```

Returns the smallest entry. Entries are compared in the order `sort` uses without a comparator.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$a` | `array<T>` | The array to search. |

**Returns** `?T` — The smallest value, the first of equals; `null` for the empty array. Two strings compare bytewise, so `min(["1e2", "50"])` is `"1e2"`.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — Two entries have no natural order, such as an `int` and a `string`, or any object.
