<a id="core-core-bytes-pack"></a>
#### `Core\Bytes::pack`

```nvs skip
Core\Bytes::pack(string $format, mixed ...$values): bytes
```

Writes `$values` as bytes, in the layout `$format` describes. The format uses a fixed set of codes. `a`, `A` and `Z` write a buffer padded with NUL bytes, padded with spaces, or padded with NUL bytes and ended with a NUL. `c` and `C` write one byte. `n`/`v`, `N`/`V` and `J`/`P` write 16, 32 and 64 bits, with the most or the least significant byte first. `G`/`g` write a binary32 float and `E`/`e` a binary64 float, in the same two byte orders. `x` writes one NUL byte. A code without a count takes the whole argument, not one byte. An integer field accepts any value that fits its width as signed or unsigned, in two's complement.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$format` | `string` (sink) | The format string. It must be written directly in the code. A code may be followed by a count or `*`. For a number code, the count is how many values it takes. For a buffer code, it is the width in bytes. |
| `...$values` | `mixed` | The values to write: one per number field, and one buffer per buffer field. An integer field takes an `int` or a `uint`. A float field takes a `float`. No value is converted. |

**Returns** `bytes` — The packed buffer.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `$format` has a code that is not in the table, has `x*`, or has a count larger than the biggest buffer. The codes `s`, `S`, `i`, `I`, `l`, `L`, `q`, `Q`, `f`, `d`, `h`, `H`, `X` and `@` are not allowed. The error names what to use instead. A value is missing, has the wrong type, or does not fit the width of its field. A `float` is outside the binary32 range, or a buffer is wider than its field. Or the format uses fewer values than the call passes.

<a id="core-core-bytes-unpack"></a>
#### `Core\Bytes::unpack`

```nvs skip
Core\Bytes::unpack(bytes $b, string $format): array<mixed>
```

Reads `$b` back with `$format`, using the codes of `pack` in reverse. So `unpack(pack($f, ...$v), $f)` gives `$v` again, field for field. Bytes that the format does not describe throw an error.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$b` | `bytes` | The buffer to read. |
| `$format` | `string` (sink) | The same format string that `pack` takes. It must be written directly in the code. Fields have no names, so the result is a list. |

**Returns** `array<mixed>` — The fields as a list, in order. A `c` field gives an `int`, and every other integer code gives a `uint`. `G`, `g`, `E` and `e` give a `float`. A buffer code gives `bytes`, with the padding of `A` and `Z` removed.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `$format` has a code that is not in the table, or a count larger than the biggest buffer. Or a field reads past the end of `$b`, or bytes are left after the last field.

<a id="core-core-path"></a>
### `Core\Path`

Keywords: path, file name, file extension, directory name, parent directory, join paths, path separator, absolute path, relative path, normalize, .., basename, dirname, extension, withExtension, join, split, normalize, isAbsolute, relativeTo, fromCwd, thisFile, thisDir

`Core\Path` is string algebra over path text: no member reads the disk, so nothing here needs a
capability, follows a symlink or checks that a file exists — that is `Core\IO`. Both `/` and `\`
are accepted on every platform, and a member that answers a path renders it with
`Core\Path::SEPARATOR` — `\` on Windows, `/` elsewhere. `join` only appends: a segment's own leading
separator or drive is dropped rather than allowed to replace the base. `normalize` resolves `.` and
`..` lexically; neither member makes an untrusted path safe, which is `Core\IO::within`. Absence
is `null`: `extension` on a name without one, `relativeTo` where no relative path exists.

```nvs
<?nvs
class Show
{
    // A rendered path carries the platform's separator; print it as `/` either way.
    public static function slash(string $p): string
    {
        return Core\Str::replace($p, Core\Path::SEPARATOR, '/');
    }
}
string $p = '/var/www/html/index.php';
echo Core\Path::basename($p), ' ', Core\Path::basename($p, { withoutExtension: true }), ' ', Core\Path::extension($p) ?? 'none', "\n";
echo Show::slash(Core\Path::dirname($p)), ' ', Show::slash(Core\Path::dirname($p, { levels: 2 })), "\n";
echo Show::slash(Core\Path::withExtension($p, 'html')), "\n";
echo Show::slash(Core\Path::join('/var/www', 'html', '/index.php')), "\n";
echo Show::slash(Core\Path::normalize('/var/www/../log/./app.log')), "\n";
echo Show::slash(Core\Path::relativeTo('/var/log/app.log', '/var/www') ?? 'none'), "\n";
echo Core\Str::join(Core\Path::split('etc//hosts/'), ','), ' ', Core\Path::isAbsolute('C:/tmp') ? 'abs' : 'rel', ' ', Core\Path::isAbsolute('tmp') ? 'abs' : 'rel', "\n";
echo Core\Path::extension('Makefile') ?? 'none', "\n";
```
```output
index.php index php
/var/www/html /var/www
/var/www/html/index.html
/var/www/html/index.php
/var/log/app.log
../log/app.log
etc,hosts abs rel
none
```

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Path::basename`](#core-core-path-basename) | `basename(string $path, { withoutExtension?: bool }): string` |
| [`Core\Path::dirname`](#core-core-path-dirname) | `dirname(string $path, { levels?: uint }): string` |
| [`Core\Path::extension`](#core-core-path-extension) | `extension(string $path): ?string` |
| [`Core\Path::withExtension`](#core-core-path-withextension) | `withExtension(string $path, ?string $extension): string` |
| [`Core\Path::join`](#core-core-path-join) | `join(string $base, string ...$segments): string` |
| [`Core\Path::split`](#core-core-path-split) | `split(string $path): array<string>` |
| [`Core\Path::normalize`](#core-core-path-normalize) | `normalize(string $path): string` |
| [`Core\Path::isAbsolute`](#core-core-path-isabsolute) | `isAbsolute(string $path): bool` |
| [`Core\Path::relativeTo`](#core-core-path-relativeto) | `relativeTo(string $path, string $base): ?string` |
| [`Core\Path::fromCwd`](#core-core-path-fromcwd) | `fromCwd(string $path): string` |
| [`Core\Path::thisFile`](#core-core-path-thisfile) | `thisFile(): string` |
| [`Core\Path::thisDir`](#core-core-path-thisdir) | `thisDir(?string $join = null): string` |
| `Core\Path::SEPARATOR` | `string` = `"/" ("\" on Windows)` — The path separator of this platform. It is `\` on Windows and `/` on every other platform. Every method writes it, and every method accepts both `/` and `\`. |

<a id="core-core-path-basename"></a>
#### `Core\Path::basename`

```nvs skip
Core\Path::basename(string $path, { withoutExtension?: bool }): string
```

Returns the last part of `$path`: the file name, or the name of the last folder. A separator at the end is ignored, so `/srv/shop/` gives `shop`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` | The path. `/` and `\` are both separators on every platform. |
| `{ withoutExtension: … }` | `bool` (default `false`) | When `true`, the extension is removed, so `report.pdf` gives `report`. The default is `false`. |

**Returns** `string` — The name. For a path that is only a root, such as `/` or `C:\`, the result is the empty string.

<a id="core-core-path-dirname"></a>
#### `Core\Path::dirname`

```nvs skip
Core\Path::dirname(string $path, { levels?: uint }): string
```

Returns the folder that contains `$path`. The option `levels` goes up more than one folder.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` | The path. `/` and `\` are both separators on every platform. |
| `{ levels: … }` | `uint` (default `1`) | How many parts to remove from the end. The default is `1`. With `0`, the result is the path with its separators cleaned up. A number larger than the path stops at the root. |

**Returns** `string` — The folder, written with `Path::SEPARATOR`. When nothing is left, the result is the root for an absolute path and `.` for a relative one. `dirname('')` is `.`.

<a id="core-core-path-extension"></a>
#### `Core\Path::extension`

```nvs skip
Core\Path::extension(string $path): ?string
```

Returns the extension of the last part of `$path`: the text after the last `.`, without the dot.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` | The path. `/` and `\` are both separators on every platform. |

**Returns** `?string` — The extension, or `null` when there is none. A name that starts with a dot, such as `.gitignore`, has none. A name that ends with a dot, such as `report.`, has none too.

<a id="core-core-path-withextension"></a>
#### `Core\Path::withExtension`

```nvs skip
Core\Path::withExtension(string $path, ?string $extension): string
```

Returns `$path` with the extension of its last part changed to `$extension`. When `$extension` is `null`, the extension is removed.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` | The path. `/` and `\` are both separators on every platform. |
| `$extension` | `?string` | The new extension, without its dot, the same way `Core\Path::extension` returns it. It may have a dot inside, such as `tar.gz`. `null` removes the extension. |

**Returns** `string` — The new path, written with `Core\Path::SEPARATOR`.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `$extension` is empty, starts with a `.`, or contains `/` or `\`. Or `$path` has no file name, such as `/` or `''`.

<a id="core-core-path-join"></a>
#### `Core\Path::join`

```nvs skip
Core\Path::join(string $base, string ...$segments): string
```

Adds each of `$segments` to the end of `$base`, with one separator between each part. The result always starts where `$base` starts. A segment that starts with `/` or a drive is added after `$base` and does not replace it.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$base` | `string` | The first path. The result starts where this path starts. |
| `...$segments` | `string` | Any number of paths to add, in order. A leading `/`, `\` or drive in one of them is removed. |

**Returns** `string` — The joined path, written with `Core\Path::SEPARATOR`. With no segments, the result is `$base` with its extra separators removed. A `..` segment stays in the result and still means the parent folder.

<a id="core-core-path-split"></a>
#### `Core\Path::split`

```nvs skip
Core\Path::split(string $path): array<string>
```

Splits `$path` into its parts: the folders and the file name, in order. `Core\Path::join` puts the parts back together into the same path.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` | The path. `/` and `\` are both separators on every platform. |

**Returns** `array<string>` — The parts in order. When the path starts at a root, the root is the first part: `/`, a drive such as `C:\`, or a share such as `\\server\share\`. The root is written with `Core\Path::SEPARATOR`. No part is empty, because a repeated separator or one at the end adds nothing. The empty path gives an empty array.

<a id="core-core-path-normalize"></a>
#### `Core\Path::normalize`

```nvs skip
Core\Path::normalize(string $path): string
```

Removes the `.` and `..` parts from `$path` and writes it with `Core\Path::SEPARATOR`. The method works on the text only and never looks at the disk. The result can still point outside a folder, so it does not make a path safe. `Core\IO::within` checks that.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` | The path. `/` and `\` are both separators on every platform. |

**Returns** `string` — The same path without `.` parts, and with each `..` removing the folder before it. A `..` at the start of a relative path stays. A `..` that would go above a root is removed, because a root has no parent. A repeated separator or one at the end is removed. The empty path gives `.`.

<a id="core-core-path-isabsolute"></a>
#### `Core\Path::isAbsolute`

```nvs skip
Core\Path::isAbsolute(string $path): bool
```

Checks whether `$path` starts at a root. A root is a separator, a drive followed by a separator, or a network share. The check is the same on every platform.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (neutral) | The path. `/` and `\` are both separators on every platform. |

**Returns** `bool` — `true` for `/tmp`, `\tmp`, `C:/log` and `\\server\share`. `false` for a relative path such as `logs/app.log`, for `C:log`, and for the empty string.

<a id="core-core-path-relativeto"></a>
#### `Core\Path::relativeTo`

```nvs skip
Core\Path::relativeTo(string $path, string $base): ?string
```

Returns the path that leads from the folder `$base` to `$path`. The `.` and `..` parts of both paths are removed first, as `Core\Path::normalize` does.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` | The place the result leads to. |
| `$base` | `string` | The folder the result starts from. The result has one `..` for each folder of `$base` that `$path` does not share. |

**Returns** `?string` — A relative path, written with `Core\Path::SEPARATOR`. It is `.` when both paths name the same place. It is `null` when no relative path exists: one path is absolute and the other is not, the paths start at different roots, or `$base` starts with more `..` parts than `$path` does. Folder names are compared byte for byte. A drive letter and a server name ignore upper and lower case.

<a id="core-core-path-fromcwd"></a>
#### `Core\Path::fromCwd`

```nvs skip
Core\Path::fromCwd(string $path): string
```

Joins `$path` to the folder the program was started from, and returns the full path. Use it for a path that a user typed on the command line.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (launder) | The path. A relative path is joined to the working folder. A full path is returned as it is, with its `.` and `..` parts removed. |

**Returns** `string` — A full path, written with `Core\Path::SEPARATOR`, with its `.` and `..` parts removed. The method does not check that the file exists. The result is not `tainted`, so you can pass a path from `Core\Cli::arguments` to `Core\IO::read`.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The program is handling a web request. A server has no working folder that belongs to the app.

<a id="core-core-path-thisfile"></a>
#### `Core\Path::thisFile`

```nvs skip
Core\Path::thisFile(): string
```

Returns the full path of the source file that contains this call. The compiler writes the path in place of the call, so the call costs nothing when the program runs.

**Returns** `string` — The full path of the file, written with `Core\Path::SEPARATOR`. In a bundled program, the folder is the one beside the executable.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The source was given to the compiler as text, so there is no file to name.

<a id="core-core-path-thisdir"></a>
#### `Core\Path::thisDir`

```nvs skip
Core\Path::thisDir(?string $join = null): string
```

Returns the full path of the folder that contains this source file. The compiler writes the path in place of the call, so the call costs nothing when the program runs.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$join` | `?string` (default `null`, neutral) | A relative path, written directly in the code as a string such as `'data'`. It is added to the folder. A variable or a full path does not compile. Use `Core\Path::join(Core\Path::thisDir(), $part)` for a part the program builds. |

**Returns** `string` — The full path of the folder, with `$join` added when you give one, and with its `.` and `..` parts removed.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The source was given to the compiler as text, so there is no folder to name.

<a id="core-core-io"></a>
### `Core\IO`

Keywords: file, read a file, write a file, file system, fs.read, fs.write, capability, permission, nvs.toml, path, read, write, append, writeStream, exists, isFile, isDir, isReadable, isWritable, size, modifiedAt, stat, copy, move, remove, makeDir, removeDir, list, walk, temporaryDir, canonicalize, within, readText, lines, open, stdin

`Core\IO` reads or replaces a whole file as text. Every call is a capability check first: the path
must fall under a root that `nvs.toml` grants as `fs.read` or `fs.write`, and a read grant is not a
write grant. A path the configuration does not grant throws a `RuntimeError` naming the capability,
and the program may catch it and carry on; a path the configuration allows but the operating system
refuses — no such file, a directory — throws an `IOError`. The check resolves the path through its
deepest existing directory, so a file that does not exist yet is spelled from one — `./out.txt`, not
`out.txt` — or the check refuses it as not granted. Without an `nvs.toml`, every call is refused.

```toml file=nvs.toml
[capabilities.fs]
read = ["."]
write = ["."]
```
```txt file=data.txt
alpha
beta
```
```nvs
<?nvs
string $text = Core\IO::read('data.txt');
echo Core\Str::length($text), " bytes\n";

Core\IO::write('./copy.txt', $text . "gamma\n");
echo Core\Str::trim(Core\IO::read('./copy.txt')), "\n";

try {
    Core\IO::read('./missing.txt');
} catch (IOError $io) {
    echo "missing: no such file\n";
}
try {
    Core\IO::read('../outside.txt');
} catch (RuntimeError $denied) {
    echo "outside: refused\n";
}
```
```output
11 bytes
alpha
beta
gamma
missing: no such file
outside: refused
```

|---|---|

| [`Core\IO::isDir`](#core-core-io-isdir) | `isDir(string $path): bool` |
| [`Core\IO::isReadable`](#core-core-io-isreadable) | `isReadable(string $path): bool` |

| [`Core\IO::stdin`](#core-core-io-stdin) | `stdin(): tainted string` |

<a id="core-core-io-read"></a>
#### `Core\IO::read`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::read(string $path): string
```

Returns the whole content of a file as text. It needs the `fs.read` capability for the path. The check uses the resolved path, so a symlink or a `..` that leaves the allowed folders throws an error.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (sink) | The file to read. A relative path must be a string written directly in the code. It is joined to the folder of the file that contains it. |

**Returns** `string` — The file's content as a `string`, with nothing stripped. The content must be UTF-8 text; `readText` reads a file written in another charset.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant `fs.read` for this path. The message names the capability the way `nvs.toml` writes it. Or the file is larger than `[limits] max_output`, the limit for a single read in a request. The same setting limits the captured output of a child process. Or the file is not valid UTF-8, and the message names the byte where the text stops.; `IOError` — The capability allowed the call, but the operating system did not. The file does not exist, is a directory, or could not be read.

<a id="core-core-io-write"></a>
#### `Core\IO::write`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::write(string $path, string $content): void
```

Replaces a file's whole content. It creates the file if it does not exist. It needs the `fs.write` capability for the path. Permission to read a folder does not give permission to write in it.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (sink) | The file to write. A relative path must be a string written directly in the code. It is joined to the folder of the file that contains it. |
| `$content` | `string` (neutral) | The bytes to write. They become the file's entire content. `append` is the method that adds to what is already there. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. A failure throws an error. It never returns `false`, so a caller that ignores the result does not miss a failure.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant `fs.write` for this path. This is checked before anything is created, so the failed write leaves no file behind.; `IOError` — The capability allowed the call, but the operating system did not. A directory is missing, the filesystem is read-only, or the process does not have permission.

<a id="core-core-io-append"></a>
#### `Core\IO::append`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::append(string $path, string $content): void
```

Adds content to the end of a file. It creates the file if it does not exist. It needs the `fs.write` capability for the path.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (sink) | The file to add to. A relative path must be a string written directly in the code. It is joined to the folder of the file that contains it. |
| `$content` | `string` (neutral) | The bytes to add. The file's current content is kept, and these bytes come after it. The operating system finds the end of the file when it writes. The file is not read first. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. A failure throws an error. It never returns `false`, so a caller that ignores the result does not miss a failure.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant `fs.write` for this path. This is checked before anything is created, so the failed append leaves no file behind.; `IOError` — The capability allowed the call, but the operating system did not. A directory is missing, the filesystem is read-only, or the path is a directory.

<a id="core-core-io-writestream"></a>
#### `Core\IO::writeStream`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::writeStream(string $path, array<bytes>|Iterable<bytes>|Iterator<bytes> $src, { max?: uint, overwrite?: bool }): void
```

Writes a sequence of `bytes` chunks to `$path` as they arrive. Only one chunk is in memory at a time. Examples are an upload part, a response body or a decompressed archive. It needs the `fs.write` capability for the path.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (sink) | The file to write. It must not already exist unless `overwrite` says otherwise. |
| `$src` | `array<bytes>\|Iterable<bytes>\|Iterator<bytes>` | The chunks, in order: an `array<bytes>`, an `Iterable<bytes>` or an `Iterator<bytes>`. Each chunk is written and then freed, so memory use does not grow with the length of the source. |
| `{ max: … }` | `uint` (default `18446744073709551615`) | The most bytes to accept across the whole stream. When it is not given, there is no limit. Nothing else limits the size of a file on disk, so this is the only limit. |
| `{ overwrite: … }` | `bool` (default `false`) | Whether an existing file may be replaced. It is `false` by default, because the file name usually comes from a client. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. If a write fails part-way through, the partial file is removed before the error is thrown. A later reader never finds a cut-off file that the program thinks is complete.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant `fs.write` for this path, or the stream ran past `max` bytes.; `IOError` — Something is already at the path and `overwrite` is `false`. Or the operating system did not allow the file to be created or written.

<a id="core-core-io-exists"></a>
#### `Core\IO::exists`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::exists(string $path): bool
```

Checks whether anything is at `$path`. The result is `true` for a directory as well as a file. It needs the `fs.read` capability. The capability is checked before the path is used, so a path outside it throws an error.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (sink) | The name to look for. A relative path must be a string written directly in the code. It is joined to the folder of the file that contains it. |

**Returns** `bool` — `true` if something is at the path, `false` if nothing is there. A missing path is a normal result here and not an error. `size` throws an error for it.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant `fs.read` for this path. This error is different from `false`. A program without access to a folder cannot use this method to learn what is in it.; `IOError` — The operating system could not say whether the path exists. For example, the process may not open a parent directory. That is not the same as a missing path.

<a id="core-core-io-isfile"></a>
#### `Core\IO::isFile`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::isFile(string $path): bool
```

Checks whether `$path` is a regular file. Symbolic links are followed, so a link to a file gives `true`. It needs the `fs.read` capability, which is checked before the path is used.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (sink) | The path to check. A relative path must be a string written directly in the code. It is joined to the folder of the file that contains it. |

**Returns** `bool` — `true` for a regular file. `false` for a directory, for any other kind of entry, and for a path where nothing exists. A missing path gives `false` and does not throw an error.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant `fs.read` for this path. This error is different from `false`, as it is for `exists`.; `IOError` — The operating system could not say whether the path is a file. For example, the process may not open a parent directory. That is not the same as a missing file.

<a id="core-core-io-isdir"></a>
#### `Core\IO::isDir`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::isDir(string $path): bool
```

Checks whether `$path` is a directory. Symbolic links are followed, so a link to a directory gives `true`. It needs the `fs.read` capability.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (sink) | The path to check. A relative path must be a string written directly in the code. It is joined to the folder of the file that contains it. |

**Returns** `bool` — `true` for a directory. `false` for a file, for any other kind of entry, and for a path where nothing exists. A path can exist and still give `false` for both `isFile` and `isDir`.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant `fs.read` for this path.; `IOError` — The operating system could not say whether the path is a directory. For example, the process may not open a parent directory.

<a id="core-core-io-isreadable"></a>
#### `Core\IO::isReadable`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::isReadable(string $path): bool
```

Checks whether this process can read what is at `$path` right now. It needs the `fs.read` capability, which is checked first. A path outside that capability throws an error.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (sink) | The file or directory to check. A relative path must be a string written directly in the code. It is joined to the folder of the file that contains it. |

**Returns** `bool` — `true` if the operating system would allow a read, `false` if it would not. A path where nothing exists gives `false`. The result is only true at the moment of the call, so a read after it can still fail.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant `fs.read` for this path.

<a id="core-core-io-iswritable"></a>
#### `Core\IO::isWritable`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::isWritable(string $path): bool
```

Checks whether this process can write to what is at `$path` right now. It needs the `fs.write` capability. A program that may only read cannot check where it could write.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (sink) | The file or directory to check. A relative path must be a string written directly in the code. It is joined to the folder of the file that contains it. |

**Returns** `bool` — `true` if the operating system would allow a write, `false` if it would not. A path where nothing exists gives `false`. As with `isReadable`, the result is only true at the moment of the call.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant `fs.write` for this path.

<a id="core-core-io-size"></a>
#### `Core\IO::size`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::size(string $path): uint
```

Returns the size of the file at `$path` in bytes, as the operating system reports it. It needs the `fs.read` capability.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (sink) | The file to measure. A relative path must be a string written directly in the code. It is joined to the folder of the file that contains it. |

**Returns** `uint` — The byte count as a `uint`. For a text file this counts bytes, not characters. `Core\Str::length` gives the length of a `string` in graphemes (what a person counts as one character).

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant `fs.read` for this path.; `IOError` — The capability allowed the call, but the operating system did not. Nothing is at the path, or its metadata could not be read. A missing file has no size, so this method throws an error. `exists` returns `false` for it.

<a id="core-core-io-modifiedat"></a>
#### `Core\IO::modifiedAt`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::modifiedAt(string $path): Core\Time\Instant
```

Returns the time the file at `$path` was last written, as a `Core\Time\Instant`. It needs the `fs.read` capability.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (sink) | The file or directory to check. A relative path must be a string written directly in the code. It is joined to the folder of the file that contains it. |

**Returns** `Core\Time\Instant` — The modification time as an exact point in time, with no time zone. Call `->in($zone)` to get a calendar date and time.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant `fs.read` for this path.; `IOError` — Nothing is at the path, or its metadata could not be read. Or the platform does not record a modification time, or the recorded time is outside the range of a `Core\Time\Instant`.

<a id="core-core-io-stat"></a>
#### `Core\IO::stat`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::stat(string $path): Core\IO\Metadata
```

Returns what the operating system reports about `$path`, as a `Core\IO\Metadata`. A program that needs several facts about a file makes only one system call. It needs the `fs.read` capability.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (sink) | The file or directory to measure. A relative path must be a string written directly in the code. It is joined to the folder of the file that contains it. |

**Returns** `Core\IO\Metadata` — A `Core\IO\Metadata`. Its values are from the moment of the call. They do not change when the file changes later.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant `fs.read` for this path.; `IOError` — Nothing is at the path, or its metadata could not be read. A missing file has no metadata, so this method throws an error. `exists` returns `false` for it.

<a id="core-core-io-copy"></a>
#### `Core\IO::copy`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::copy(string $from, string $to): void
```

Copies a file. It needs `fs.read` for the source and `fs.write` for the destination. Permission to read a folder never gives permission to write in it.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$from` | `string` (sink) | The file to read. It is left exactly as it was. |
| `$to` | `string` (sink) | The file to create. Anything already at this path is replaced, as `write` replaces it. The program names this path itself, together with the source. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. A failure throws an error. It never returns `false`, so a caller that ignores the result does not miss a failure.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant `fs.read` for the source or `fs.write` for the destination. Both are checked before either is used, so a failed check copies nothing.; `IOError` — The capability allowed the call, but the operating system did not. Nothing is at the source, the destination directory does not exist, or the process does not have permission. A destination that is the source file itself, however the path is written, also throws an error. The file stays as it was. The message names both paths.

<a id="core-core-io-move"></a>
#### `Core\IO::move`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::move(string $from, string $to): void
```

Moves a file by renaming it. It needs `fs.write` for **both** paths. The source needs `fs.write` too, because a move removes the source file.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$from` | `string` (sink) | The path that stops existing. |
| `$to` | `string` (sink) | The new path of the file. Anything already there is replaced. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. The operating system does the rename, so it is atomic. The destination always has either the whole new file or the file it had before. A move between filesystems fails. It is not done as a copy and a delete, because that is not atomic and needs different capabilities. To do that, call `copy` and then `remove`.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant `fs.write` for one of the two paths. Both are checked before either is used.; `IOError` — The capability allowed the call, but the operating system did not. Nothing is at the source, the destination directory does not exist, or the two paths are on different filesystems. The message names both paths.

<a id="core-core-io-remove"></a>
#### `Core\IO::remove`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::remove(string $path): void
```

Deletes the file at `$path`. It needs the `fs.write` capability, because deleting a file is a write.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (sink) | The file to delete. To delete a directory, use `removeDir`. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. Removing a path where nothing exists throws an error. A program that deleted nothing is never told that it succeeded.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant `fs.write` for this path. Permission to read a folder does not give permission to delete from it.; `IOError` — The capability allowed the call, but the operating system did not. Nothing is at the path, it is a directory, or the process may not delete it.

<a id="core-core-io-makedir"></a>
#### `Core\IO::makeDir`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::makeDir(string $path): void
```

Makes sure a directory exists at `$path`. It also creates every missing parent directory. It needs the `fs.write` capability.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (sink) | The directory that must exist. Every missing directory above it is created too. All of them are inside the path the capability is checked for. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. A directory that already exists is a success, not an error. The method only promises that the directory exists afterwards, so a caller needs no `exists` check first. `removeDir` works differently. It does not delete directories recursively.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant `fs.write` for this path. This is checked before anything is created, so the failed call leaves no directory behind.; `IOError` — The capability allowed the call, but the operating system did not. The path is empty, a part of the path exists and is a file, or the process may not create a directory there.

<a id="core-core-io-removedir"></a>
#### `Core\IO::removeDir`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::removeDir(string $path): void
```

Deletes the **empty** directory at `$path`. It needs the `fs.write` capability. There is no recursive form, so one wrong argument cannot delete a whole tree. To empty a directory, a program walks it and removes each entry.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (sink) | The directory to delete. It must be empty. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. A failure throws an error. It never returns `false`.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant `fs.write` for this path.; `IOError` — The capability allowed the call, but the operating system did not. Nothing is at the path, it is not a directory, or it still has entries in it.

<a id="core-core-io-list"></a>
#### `Core\IO::list`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::list(string $path): array<string>
```

Returns the names of the entries in the directory at `$path`, as an `array<string>`. The list never contains `.` and `..`. It needs the `fs.read` capability. The order is the operating system's own, and the list is not sorted. `Core\Arr::sort` sorts it.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (sink) | The directory to read. A file throws an error. |

**Returns** `array<string>` — One `string` per entry. Each one is a name, not a path. The caller joins it to `$path`. Use `within` to make that join safe when the name came from outside the program. The whole list is in memory at once, so use this method for a directory that fits in memory. `walk` reads the whole tree under a directory.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant `fs.read` for this path.; `IOError` — The capability allowed the call, but the operating system did not. Nothing is at the path, it is not a directory, or an entry could not be read partway through the listing.

<a id="core-core-io-walk"></a>
#### `Core\IO::walk`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::walk(string $path): Core\IO\Walk
```

Returns every entry in the tree under `$path`, as an `Iterable<string>` of paths relative to `$path`. `list` reads one directory, and this method reads the whole tree. It needs the `fs.read` capability for **every** directory it enters, including the first one. A symbolic link is returned as an entry and is never followed, so the walk always ends.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (sink) | The directory the walk starts at. A file throws an error, as it does for `list`. |

**Returns** `Core\IO\Walk` — One `string` per entry anywhere under `$path`. Each one is a path *relative to* `$path`, written with `Core\Path::SEPARATOR`. The caller joins it to `$path`, and `within` makes that join safe. All entries of a directory come before any entry inside them. Within one directory, the order is the operating system's own.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant `fs.read` for a directory the walk tried to read. The message names the directory where the walk stopped. That is the start directory, unless the capability covers only part of the tree.; `IOError` — The capability allowed the call, but the operating system did not. Nothing is at the path, it is not a directory, or a directory inside the walk could not be read to the end.

<a id="core-core-io-temporarydir"></a>
#### `Core\IO::temporaryDir`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::temporaryDir(): string
```

Creates a new, empty, private directory and returns its path. The directory is under `[io] temp_root`, or under the `tmp` folder in the data folder. It is created at once, so no other program can take its name first. It needs the `fs.write` capability **for the path it creates**. A configuration that allows only the working directory does not cover the temporary folder.

**Returns** `string` — The absolute path of a directory that exists, is empty, and belongs to this script. Novis deletes it and everything in it when the script ends. This happens after the last line of your code runs, however the script ends. A program never has to delete it, and it is never left behind. You may remove it earlier, and that is not an error. A file that must stay after the script ends does not belong in a temporary directory.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant `fs.write` for the temporary folder. The message names the path that the capability must cover.; `IOError` — The capability allowed the call, but no directory could be created. The temporary folder is full, read-only or missing. Or there is no temporary folder, because `[io] temp_root` is not set and the data folder cannot be used.

<a id="core-core-io-canonicalize"></a>
#### `Core\IO::canonicalize`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::canonicalize(string $path): string
```

Returns the absolute path that `$path` resolves to. The operating system follows every `.`, `..` and symbolic link. It needs the `fs.read` capability, because resolving a name reads the directories on the way. **This is not a path traversal check.** Use `within` for a path from outside: it resolves the path and checks that it stays inside a folder.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (sink) | The path to resolve. A relative path must be a string written directly in the code. It is joined to the folder of the file that contains it. Every part of the path must exist, including the last one. |

**Returns** `string` — The resolved absolute path. Resolving the result again gives the same path, so you can compare two results for equality. `Core\Path::normalize` cannot do this. Two different ways to write the path of one file normalize to different strings. They canonicalize to the same string.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant `fs.read` for this path.; `IOError` — The capability allowed the call, but the operating system did not. A part of the path does not exist or is not a directory, or a symbolic link loops. A missing path cannot be resolved, so this method throws an error. `exists` returns `false` for it.

<a id="core-core-io-within"></a>
#### `Core\IO::within`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::within(string $base, string $path): string
```

Resolves `$path` against `$base` and then **checks** that the result is still inside `$base`. This is the path traversal check, so its result is accepted where a `tainted` string is not. `Core\Path::normalize` cannot make this check. It removes `..` from the text, but a symbolic link in the path can still lead somewhere else. It needs the `fs.read` capability for both paths, because resolving a path reads the directories above it.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$base` | `string` (sink) | The directory the result must stay inside. It must exist, because the check uses its canonical path. |
| `$path` | `string` (launder) | The path to resolve against `$base`. This is the untrusted part, and the reason to use this method. A relative `$path` is joined to `$base`, also when it is written directly in the code. It is not joined to the folder of the file that calls `within`. An absolute path is resolved too, and then the same check makes it fail. |

**Returns** `string` — The resolved absolute path, as a plain `string`. It has no `..`, no symbolic links and no repeated separators. It is the path the operating system itself uses for the file.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The resolved path is not inside `$base`. The message names the base and the argument, but never the place the argument led to. So the error shows nothing about the target of a symbolic link. If the configuration does not grant `fs.read` for either path, the same error class is thrown earlier.; `IOError` — The capability allowed the call, but nothing could be resolved. `$base` does not exist or is not a directory, or no parent directory of the joined path exists.

<a id="core-core-io-readtext"></a>
#### `Core\IO::readText`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::readText(string $path, { charset?: Core\Charset }): string
```

Returns the whole content of a file, converted from the charset it is written in. If a byte cannot be converted exactly, it throws an error. It needs the `fs.read` capability for the path, as `read` does.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (sink) | The file to read. A relative path must be a string written directly in the code. It is joined to the folder of the file that contains it. |
| `{ charset: … }` | `Core\Charset` (default `Core\Charset::Utf8`) | The encoding of the file's bytes. It is `Core\Charset::Utf8` when it is not given. Novis strings are UTF-8, so UTF-8 text is read unchanged. |

**Returns** `string` — The file's content as a `string`, converted from `$charset`. It never contains a replacement character, because a conversion that cannot be exact throws an error.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant `fs.read` for this path. Or the file's bytes are not valid `$charset`. In that case the message names the offset of the first invalid sequence.; `IOError` — The capability allowed the call, but the operating system did not. The file does not exist, is a directory, or could not be read.

<a id="core-core-io-lines"></a>
#### `Core\IO::lines`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::lines(string $path): Core\IO\Lines
```

Returns every line of a file, without its line ending. The file is split into lines the same way `Core\Str::lines` splits a string. It needs the `fs.read` capability for the path, as `read` does.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (sink) | The file to read. A relative path must be a string written directly in the code. It is joined to the folder of the file that contains it. |

**Returns** `Core\IO\Lines` — An `Iterable<string>`. A `foreach` loop gives the lines in file order, and you can loop over it again as often as you like. `\n`, `\r\n` and a single `\r` each end a line. A line ending at the end of the file does not add an empty last line. An empty file has no lines.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant `fs.read` for this path.; `IOError` — The capability allowed the call, but the operating system did not. The file does not exist, is a directory, or could not be read.

<a id="core-core-io-open"></a>
#### `Core\IO::open`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::open(string $path, Core\IO::FileMode $mode): Core\IO\File
```

Opens a file and returns a handle to read and write it. The mode is an enum value. It needs `fs.read` for `Read`, `fs.write` for `Write` and `Append`, and both for `ReadWrite`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (sink) | The file to open. A relative path must be a string written directly in the code. It is joined to the folder of the file that contains it. |
| `$mode` | `Core\IO::FileMode` | What the handle may do, as a `Core\IO::FileMode` case. |

**Returns** `Core\IO\File` — An open `Core\IO\File`. It is closed by `close`, and by the end of the request if the program never calls it.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant a capability this mode needs for this path.; `IOError` — The capability allowed the call, but the operating system did not. The mode is `Read` and nothing is at the path, the path is a directory, or this process may not open it.

<a id="core-core-io-stdin"></a>
#### `Core\IO::stdin`

```nvs skip
Core\IO::stdin(): tainted string
```

Reads everything from the program's standard input in one call. The result is `tainted`, because the bytes come from whoever started the program. It needs no capability, because the program starts with its standard input already open.

**Returns** `tainted string` — Every byte until the end of input, as one `tainted string`. It is the empty string when the input is already closed. A program started with no input gets that. Input ends when the writer closes it, so at a terminal this call waits for the user. To ask the user a question, use the prompts in `Core\Cli`, which have a time limit.

**Throws** `IOError` — The read failed in the operating system. The process writing to the pipe stopped, or standard input was not open for reading.; `RuntimeError` — The input is not valid UTF-8. The message gives the position of the first byte that is not text.

<a id="core-core-io-file-read"></a>
#### `Core\IO\File->read`

```nvs skip
$file->read(uint $max): string
```

Reads up to `$max` bytes from the handle's position and moves the position past them. It needs no capability of its own, because `open` already checked it.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$max` | `uint` | The most bytes to read. Fewer are returned when the file ends first. |

**Returns** `string` — The bytes read, as a `string`. The text always ends with a whole character. When `$max` ends inside a character, that character stays in the file for the next read. An empty string means the end of the file.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The handle has already been closed.; `RuntimeError` — The bytes are not valid UTF-8, or the next character is longer than `$max`. The handle does not move, so the next read starts at the same byte.; `IOError` — The read itself failed, or the handle was not opened for reading.

<a id="core-core-io-file-readline"></a>
#### `Core\IO\File->readLine`

```nvs skip
$file->readLine(): ?string
```

Reads the next line and moves the handle past it. The line ending is read but not returned. `\n`, `\r\n` and `\r` all end a line, as they do for `Core\Str::lines` and `Core\IO::lines`.

**Returns** `?string` — The line without its line ending, or `null` at the end of the file. Because of the `null`, there is no separate `eof` method. A last line with no line ending is still a line.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The handle has already been closed.; `RuntimeError` — The line is not valid UTF-8. The handle does not move, so the next call reads the same line.; `IOError` — The read itself failed, or the handle was not opened for reading.

<a id="core-core-io-file-write"></a>
#### `Core\IO\File->write`

```nvs skip
$file->write(string|bytes $data): uint
```

Writes `$data` at the handle's position and moves the position past it. It needs no capability of its own, because `open` already checked it.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$data` | `string\|bytes` (neutral) | The data to write, as a `string` or as `bytes`. It is written exactly as it is. |

**Returns** `uint` — How many bytes were written. This is always every byte of `$data`. A partial write is retried until it is complete, so a caller never needs a loop.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The handle has already been closed.; `IOError` — The write itself failed, or the handle was not opened for writing.

<a id="core-core-io-file-seek"></a>
#### `Core\IO\File->seek`

```nvs skip
$file->seek(uint $offset): void
```

Moves the handle to `$offset` bytes from the start of the file. You can move past the end of the file. If you then write, the gap is filled with zeroes.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$offset` | `uint` | How many bytes from the start of the file the next read or write happens at. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. Use `tell` to get the position.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The handle has already been closed.; `IOError` — The seek itself failed. For example, the handle is a pipe or a terminal, which has no position.

<a id="core-core-io-file-tell"></a>
#### `Core\IO\File->tell`

```nvs skip
$file->tell(): uint
```

Returns the handle's position, in bytes from the start of the file. The next `read` or `write` happens at this position. Every method of this class leaves the position just after the bytes it used.

**Returns** `uint` — The position, as a `uint`. Zero on a handle nothing has read or written yet, unless `FileMode::Append` put it at the end.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The handle has already been closed.; `IOError` — Getting the position failed. For example, the handle is a pipe or a terminal, which has no position.

<a id="core-core-io-file-truncate"></a>
#### `Core\IO\File->truncate`

```nvs skip
$file->truncate(uint $size): void
```

Sets the file's length to `$size` bytes. A smaller size deletes everything after it. A larger size fills the new part with zeroes.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$size` | `uint` | How long the file is to be afterwards, in bytes from its start. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. The handle's position does not move. After a file is shortened, the position can be past its new end. `tell` still returns the old position. A write there leaves a gap filled with zeroes before the written bytes.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The handle has already been closed.; `IOError` — The resize itself failed. The most common cause is a handle opened with `FileMode::Read`, which the operating system does not resize.

<a id="core-core-io-file-flush"></a>
#### `Core\IO\File->flush`

```nvs skip
$file->flush(): void
```

Sends everything written on this handle to the operating system. Novis writes directly to the operating system, so there is never data waiting in the handle.

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. This method does not wait until the data is on the disk.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The handle has already been closed.; `IOError` — The flush itself failed in the operating system. No method of this class causes this error now, but the operating system may still report one.

<a id="core-core-io-file-lock"></a>
#### `Core\IO\File->lock`

```nvs skip
$file->lock(): void
```

Takes an exclusive lock on the file. The lock lasts until the handle closes. It never waits: if another handle has the lock, it throws an error at once.

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. There is no `unlock`. The lock lasts as long as the handle, so `close` releases it, and so does the end of the request.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The handle has already been closed.; `IOError` — Another handle already has the lock, or the operating system did not allow it. Whether the lock stops reads and writes by handles that do *not* have the lock depends on the platform.

<a id="core-core-io-file-close"></a>
#### `Core\IO\File->close`

```nvs skip
$file->close(): void
```

Closes the handle and frees the file descriptor. Calling it is optional, because every open handle is closed when the request ends.

**Returns** `void` — Nothing.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The handle has already been closed. Closing twice is a bug in the program, so it throws an error and is not ignored.

<a id="core-core-io-metadata"></a>
### `Core\IO\Metadata`

Keywords: size, modifiedAt, isFile, isDir

| Member | Signature |

| [`Core\IO\Metadata->isFile`](#core-core-io-metadata-isfile) | `isFile(): bool` |
| [`Core\IO\Metadata->isDir`](#core-core-io-metadata-isdir) | `isDir(): bool` |

<a id="core-core-io-metadata-size"></a>
#### `Core\IO\Metadata->size`

```nvs skip
$metadata->size(): uint
```

The file's size in bytes at the moment `stat` was called. It needs no capability, because `stat` already checked the path.

**Returns** `uint` — The byte count as a `uint`. For a directory, the number depends on the platform and has no portable meaning.

<a id="core-core-io-metadata-modifiedat"></a>
#### `Core\IO\Metadata->modifiedAt`

```nvs skip
$metadata->modifiedAt(): Core\Time\Instant
```

When the file was last written, as a `Core\Time\Instant`. It is the same value that `Core\IO::modifiedAt` returns, taken from this `stat` result.

**Returns** `Core\Time\Instant` — The modification time as an exact point in time, with no time zone.

<a id="core-core-io-metadata-isfile"></a>
#### `Core\IO\Metadata->isFile`

```nvs skip
$metadata->isFile(): bool
```

Whether the path was a regular file. Most paths are either a file or a directory, but not all. A socket, a device node and a named pipe give `false` for both `isFile` and `isDir`.

**Returns** `bool` — `true` for a regular file, `false` for anything else that was there.

<a id="core-core-io-metadata-isdir"></a>
#### `Core\IO\Metadata->isDir`

```nvs skip
$metadata->isDir(): bool
```

Whether the path was a directory. As with `isFile`, some paths are neither a file nor a directory.

**Returns** `bool` — `true` for a directory, `false` for anything else that was there.

<a id="core-core-process"></a>
### `Core\Process`

Keywords: run, spawn

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Process::run`](#core-core-process-run) | `run(string $path, array<string> $argv, { cwd?: string, env?: array<string>, timeout?: Core\Time\Duration }): Core\Process\Result` |
| [`Core\Process::spawn`](#core-core-process-spawn) | `spawn(string $path, array<string> $argv, { cwd?: string, env?: array<string>, timeout?: Core\Time\Duration }): Core\Process\Handle` |

<a id="core-core-process-run"></a>
#### `Core\Process::run`

```nvs skip
Core\Process::run(string $path, array<string> $argv, { cwd?: string, env?: array<string>, timeout?: Core\Time\Duration }): Core\Process\Result
```

Runs the program at `$path` with the arguments in `$argv`, and waits until it ends. The program is started directly, never through a shell, so nothing needs escaping. Needs the `process.exec` capability for the program.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (sink) | The program to start, as an absolute path. A relative path must be a string written directly in the code. It is joined to the folder of the file that contains it. `PATH` is not searched, so `ls` means a file named `ls` in that folder. |
| `$argv` | `array<string>` | The arguments, one in each element: `["-n", "1", $host]`. An element with a space, a quote or a `;` in it is still one argument, on every platform. |
| `{ cwd: … }` | `string` (default `null`, sink) | The folder the program starts in, as an absolute path. A relative path must be written directly in the code, and is joined to the folder of this file. Without it, the program starts in the same folder as this program. |
| `{ env: … }` | `array<string>` (default `null`) | The environment variables of the program, as name => value. This replaces all of them, so a variable that is not in the array is not set. Without it, the program gets only these variables from this program: `PATH`, `HOME` or `USERPROFILE`, `TEMP`, `TMP`, `LANG`, and `SYSTEMROOT` on Windows. A `secret` value must be revealed first. |
| `{ timeout: … }` | `Core\Time\Duration` (default `null`) | The longest time the program may run, counted from the start. When it passes, the program is stopped and a `TimeoutError` is thrown. |

**Returns** `Core\Process\Result` — A `Core\Process\Result` with the exit code and everything the program wrote to its output and to its error output. The program cannot write to this program's own output, so the two never mix.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `process.exec` does not allow this program, or it is a `.bat`, `.cmd` or `.ps1` file. Those are not allowed on any platform, because Windows starts them through a shell. The error is also thrown when the program writes more than `[limits] max_output` in total. Then the program is stopped and nothing is returned. It is also thrown when `cwd` is a relative path, or when `timeout` is zero or shorter. An `env` name that is empty or has a `=` in it throws it too.; `TimeoutError` — The program was still running when `timeout` passed. The program is stopped and nothing is returned.; `IOError` — The program could not be started or waited for. For example, nothing is at the path, the file is not a program, or the `cwd` folder does not exist.

<a id="core-core-process-spawn"></a>
#### `Core\Process::spawn`

```nvs skip
Core\Process::spawn(string $path, array<string> $argv, { cwd?: string, env?: array<string>, timeout?: Core\Time\Duration }): Core\Process\Handle
```

Starts the program at `$path` with the arguments in `$argv`, and returns at once while the program runs. The handle it returns reads the program's output and writes to its input. The program is started directly, never through a shell. Needs the `process.exec` capability for the program.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (sink) | The program to start, as an absolute path or a path relative to the working directory. `PATH` is not searched. |
| `$argv` | `array<string>` | The arguments, one in each element. An element with a space, a quote or a `;` in it is still one argument, on every platform. |
| `{ cwd: … }` | `string` (default `null`, sink) | The folder the program starts in, as an absolute path. A relative path must be written directly in the code, and is joined to the folder of this file. Without it, the program starts in the same folder as this program. |
| `{ env: … }` | `array<string>` (default `null`) | The environment variables of the program, as name => value. This replaces all of them, so a variable that is not in the array is not set. Without it, the program gets only these variables from this program: `PATH`, `HOME` or `USERPROFILE`, `TEMP`, `TMP`, `LANG`, and `SYSTEMROOT` on Windows. A `secret` value must be revealed first. |
| `{ timeout: … }` | `Core\Time\Duration` (default `null`) | The longest time the program may run, counted from the start. When it passes, the program is stopped and a `TimeoutError` is thrown. |

**Returns** `Core\Process\Handle` — A `Core\Process\Handle` for the running program. Other requests keep running while this one waits on the handle. Call `wait` or `kill` on it before your script or request ends. A program that is still running then is stopped, and Novis reports an error.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `process.exec` does not allow this program, or it is a `.bat`, `.cmd` or `.ps1` file. Those are not allowed on any platform, because Windows starts them through a shell. It is also thrown when `cwd` is a relative path, or when `timeout` is zero or shorter. An `env` name that is empty or has a `=` in it throws it too.; `IOError` — The program could not be started. For example, nothing is at the path, the file is not a program, or the `cwd` folder does not exist.

<a id="core-core-process-result"></a>
### `Core\Process\Result`

Keywords: exitCode, stdout, stderr

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Process\Result->exitCode`](#core-core-process-result-exitcode) | `exitCode(): int` |
| [`Core\Process\Result->stdout`](#core-core-process-result-stdout) | `stdout(): bytes` |
| [`Core\Process\Result->stderr`](#core-core-process-result-stderr) | `stderr(): bytes` |

<a id="core-core-process-result-exitcode"></a>
#### `Core\Process\Result->exitCode`

```nvs skip
$result->exitCode(): int
```

Returns the exit code of the program. Most programs return `0` when they succeed, and another number when they fail.

**Returns** `int` — The exit code, as an `int`. On Linux and macOS, it is `-1` when a signal stopped the program before it could return an exit code.

<a id="core-core-process-result-stdout"></a>
#### `Core\Process\Result->stdout`

```nvs skip
$result->stdout(): bytes
```

Returns everything the program wrote to its standard output.

**Returns** `bytes` — The output, as `bytes`. A program can write data that is not valid text, so the result is not a `string`. Use `as string` to convert it to text. That throws an error if the output is not valid UTF-8.

<a id="core-core-process-result-stderr"></a>
#### `Core\Process\Result->stderr`

```nvs skip
$result->stderr(): bytes
```

Returns everything the program wrote to its standard error. Programs write their error messages and warnings there. This output is never mixed with `stdout`.

**Returns** `bytes` — The error output, as `bytes`. Use `as string` to convert it to text.

<a id="core-core-process-handle"></a>
### `Core\Process\Handle`

Keywords: readStdout, readStderr, writeStdin, wait, kill

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Process\Handle->readStdout`](#core-core-process-handle-readstdout) | `readStdout(): ?bytes` |
| [`Core\Process\Handle->readStderr`](#core-core-process-handle-readstderr) | `readStderr(): ?bytes` |
| [`Core\Process\Handle->writeStdin`](#core-core-process-handle-writestdin) | `writeStdin(bytes $data): void` |
| [`Core\Process\Handle->wait`](#core-core-process-handle-wait) | `wait(): Core\Process\Result` |
| [`Core\Process\Handle->kill`](#core-core-process-handle-kill) | `kill(): void` |

<a id="core-core-process-handle-readstdout"></a>
#### `Core\Process\Handle->readStdout`

```nvs skip
$handle->readStdout(): ?bytes
```

Waits until the program writes to its standard output, and returns what it wrote. Call it in a loop to read the output one part at a time while the program runs. Other requests keep running while this one waits.

**Returns** `?bytes` — The next part of the output, as `bytes`, up to 64 KiB. A part is whatever has arrived: it can be less than one line or several lines. At the end of the output the result is `null`, and every later call also returns `null`. Use `as string` to convert a part to text.

**Throws** `TimeoutError` — The `timeout` given to `spawn` has passed. The program is stopped, and every later call except `kill` throws this error too.; `IOError` — The operating system could not read the output. The output is then closed, so the next call returns `null`.

<a id="core-core-process-handle-readstderr"></a>
#### `Core\Process\Handle->readStderr`

```nvs skip
$handle->readStderr(): ?bytes
```

Waits until the program writes to its standard error, and returns what it wrote. Programs write their error messages and warnings there. It works like `readStdout`, and the two outputs are never mixed.

**Returns** `?bytes` — The next part of the error output, as `bytes`, up to 64 KiB. At the end of the error output the result is `null`, and every later call also returns `null`. Use `as string` to convert a part to text.

**Throws** `TimeoutError` — The `timeout` given to `spawn` has passed. The program is stopped, and every later call except `kill` throws this error too.; `IOError` — The operating system could not read the error output. The error output is then closed, so the next call returns `null`.

<a id="core-core-process-handle-writestdin"></a>
#### `Core\Process\Handle->writeStdin`

```nvs skip
$handle->writeStdin(bytes $data): void
```

Sends `$data` to the program's standard input. The call waits until the program has taken all of it. A `tainted` value is allowed here, because the program reads it as data and does not run it as a command.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$data` | `bytes` (neutral) | The data to send, as `bytes`. All of it is sent. Use `as bytes` to convert a `string`. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. The input stays open, so you can call `writeStdin` again. `wait` closes the input, and then the program sees the end of it.

**Throws** `TimeoutError` — The `timeout` given to `spawn` has passed. The program is stopped, and every later call except `kill` throws this error too.; `IOError` — The operating system could not send the data. This happens most often when the program has already ended, or after `wait`.

<a id="core-core-process-handle-wait"></a>
#### `Core\Process\Handle->wait`

```nvs skip
$handle->wait(): Core\Process\Result
```

Closes the program's standard input, waits until the program ends, and returns its result. While it waits, the server keeps handling other requests.

**Returns** `Core\Process\Result` — A `Core\Process\Result` with the exit code, and the output and error output that `readStdout` and `readStderr` did not read yet. If you already read all of the output, both are empty. A second call returns the same exit code and empty output.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The output that was not read yet is larger than `[limits] max_output`. The program is then stopped.; `TimeoutError` — The `timeout` given to `spawn` has passed. The program is stopped, and every later call except `kill` throws this error too.; `IOError` — The operating system could not read the output or get the exit code.

<a id="core-core-process-handle-kill"></a>
#### `Core\Process\Handle->kill`

```nvs skip
$handle->kill(): void
```

Stops the program at once, whatever it is doing. If the program has already ended, `kill` does nothing and throws no error. Call `kill` or `wait` before your script or request ends. A program that is still running then is stopped, and Novis reports an error.

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. Call `wait` afterwards to get the exit code. It is not `0` for a program that was stopped.

**Throws** `IOError` — The operating system could not stop the program.

<a id="core-core-time"></a>
### `Core\Time`

Keywords: time, current time, now, clock, timestamp, from timestamp, epoch, date, datetime, create a date, parse a date, date format, ISO 8601, sleep, immutable, now, monotonic, sleep, fromEpoch, fromIso, parse, at

`Core\Time` is where a time value starts: `now()` reads the clock as an `Instant`, `fromIso` and
`fromEpoch` build one from a timestamp, and `at` and `parse` build a `DateTime` from civil fields or
text. Every value it answers is immutable, and there is no ambient time zone — a `DateTime` is always
built in a `Zone` the call names, and an `Instant` becomes a calendar reading only through
`->in($zone)`. The two arithmetics are told apart by type: an `Instant` moves by an exact `Duration`
(`->plus(24h)`), a `DateTime` moves by a calendar step (`->plus(1, Core\Unit::Day)`), and across a
DST boundary the two land an hour apart. There is no free-form date text: each phrase such as
"next Monday" is a typed call, and a run-time offset such as `"30d"` is `Core\Time\Duration::parse`.

```nvs
<?nvs
var $utc = Core\Time\Zone::UTC;
var $meeting = Core\Time::at(2024, 3, 1, $utc, { hour: 9, minute: 30 });
echo $meeting->format('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm'), "\n";

var $parsed = Core\Time::parse('5 March 2024', 'd MMMM yyyy', $utc);
echo $parsed->format('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss'), "\n";

var $stamp = Core\Time::fromIso('2024-03-01T10:30:00+01:00');
echo $stamp->toIso(), "\n";
echo $stamp->compareTo($meeting->toInstant()) == 0 ? 'same instant' : 'different', "\n";

echo Core\Time::fromEpoch(0)->in($utc)->format('EEEE, d MMMM yyyy'), "\n";

var $berlin = Core\Time\Zone::of('Europe/Berlin');
echo $meeting->toInstant()->in($berlin)->format('HH:mm VV'), "\n";

var $eve = Core\Time::at(2024, 3, 30, $berlin, { hour: 12 });
echo $eve->plus(1, Core\Unit::Day)->format('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm'), "\n";
echo $eve->toInstant()->plus(24h)->in($berlin)->format('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm'), "\n";

try {
    Core\Time::at(2024, 2, 30, $utc);
} catch (RuntimeError $bad) {
    echo "30 February does not exist\n";
}
```
```output
2024-03-01 09:30
2024-03-05 00:00:00
2024-03-01T09:30:00Z
same instant
Thursday, 1 January 1970
10:30 Europe/Berlin
2024-03-31 12:00
2024-03-31 13:00
30 February does not exist
```

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Time::now`](#core-core-time-now) | `now(): Core\Time\Instant` |
| [`Core\Time::monotonic`](#core-core-time-monotonic) | `monotonic(): Core\Time\Duration` |
| [`Core\Time::sleep`](#core-core-time-sleep) | `sleep(Core\Time\Duration $d): void` |
| [`Core\Time::fromEpoch`](#core-core-time-fromepoch) | `fromEpoch(int $seconds, { nanos?: uint }): Core\Time\Instant` |
| [`Core\Time::fromIso`](#core-core-time-fromiso) | `fromIso(string $text): Core\Time\Instant` |
| [`Core\Time::parse`](#core-core-time-parse) | `parse(string $text, string $format, Core\Time\Zone $zone): Core\Time\DateTime` |
| [`Core\Time::at`](#core-core-time-at) | `at(int $year, uint $month, uint $day, Core\Time\Zone $zone, { hour?: uint, minute?: uint, second?: uint, nanos?: uint }): Core\Time\DateTime` |

<a id="core-core-time-now"></a>
#### `Core\Time::now`

```nvs skip
Core\Time::now(): Core\Time\Instant
```

Reads the current time from the system clock. Use `->in($zone)` to get the date and time of day in a zone.

**Returns** `Core\Time\Instant` — The current `Instant`, to the nanosecond.

<a id="core-core-time-monotonic"></a>
#### `Core\Time::monotonic`

```nvs skip
Core\Time::monotonic(): Core\Time\Duration
```

Reads a clock that only moves forward, for measuring how long something takes. Subtract two readings to get the time between them.

**Returns** `Core\Time\Duration` — A `Duration` since a fixed starting point. A later reading is never smaller than an earlier one.

<a id="core-core-time-sleep"></a>
#### `Core\Time::sleep`

```nvs skip
Core\Time::sleep(Core\Time\Duration $d): void
```

Waits for `$d`. Only this task waits, so other work on the same core keeps running. If the request is cancelled during the wait, it stops here.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$d` | `Core\Time\Duration` | How long to wait; zero or negative returns at once. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing.

<a id="core-core-time-fromepoch"></a>
#### `Core\Time::fromEpoch`

```nvs skip
Core\Time::fromEpoch(int $seconds, { nanos?: uint }): Core\Time\Instant
```

Builds the instant at a Unix timestamp. The `nanos` option is added after the second, so `-1` with `{ nanos: 1 }` is one nanosecond after `-1`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$seconds` | `int` | Whole seconds since `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z`; negative before it. |
| `{ nanos: … }` | `uint` (default `0`) | Nanoseconds to add on top of the second, below `1000000000`; the default is `0`. |

**Returns** `Core\Time\Instant` — The `Instant`.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `nanos` is not below `1000000000`, or `$seconds` is outside `-377705023201..=253402207200`. That is the time from `-9999-01-02T01:59:59Z` to `9999-12-30T22:00:00Z`.

<a id="core-core-time-fromiso"></a>
#### `Core\Time::fromIso`

```nvs skip
Core\Time::fromIso(string $text): Core\Time\Instant
```

Reads an ISO 8601 or RFC 3339 timestamp that includes its own offset, such as `2024-03-01T12:00:00Z` or `2024-03-01T13:00:00+01:00`. For a date and time with no offset, use `Time::parse` with a zone. For a relative time, use a method such as `plus` or `next`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$text` | `string` (neutral) | The timestamp text, with a date, a time and a `Z` or `±HH:MM` offset. |

**Returns** `Core\Time\Instant` — The `Instant` the text names.

**Throws** `ParseError` — `$text` is not such a timestamp. The error names the part of the text where reading stopped. It is also thrown for a time outside `-9999-01-02T01:59:59Z..=9999-12-30T22:00:00Z`.

<a id="core-core-time-parse"></a>
#### `Core\Time::parse`

```nvs skip
Core\Time::parse(string $text, string $format, Core\Time\Zone $zone): Core\Time\DateTime
```

Reads a date and time with a CLDR pattern and places it in `$zone`. A `$format` written directly in the code is checked when the program compiles. A malformed one is error `E0769`. A field the pattern does not contain is set to the start of its range.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$text` | `string` (neutral) | The text to read. The result does not keep a qualifier of the text, such as `tainted`. |
| `$format` | `string` (sink) | A CLDR pattern with date and time letters only, such as `yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm`. `$zone` gives the zone. A pattern is a small language, so a `tainted` pattern is not allowed. |
| `$zone` | `Core\Time\Zone` | The zone the date and time are read in. If the zone skips the time, the result moves forward past the gap. |

**Returns** `Core\Time\DateTime` — The `DateTime` in `$zone`.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$format` is not valid. It has a pattern letter that is not supported or a quote that is not closed. It is also thrown when `$format` has a zone or offset letter, because `$zone` already gives the zone. For a `$format` written directly in the code, only an invalid pattern is error `E0769`. A zone or offset letter is a valid pattern that only this method does not allow. So it throws this error however `$format` was written.; `ParseError` — `$text` does not match `$format`. Fixed text differs, a number has no digits, there is extra text at the end, or the parts together are not a real date and time. It is also thrown for a time outside `-9999-01-02T01:59:59Z..=9999-12-30T22:00:00Z`.

<a id="core-core-time-at"></a>
#### `Core\Time::at`

```nvs skip
Core\Time::at(int $year, uint $month, uint $day, Core\Time\Zone $zone, { hour?: uint, minute?: uint, second?: uint, nanos?: uint }): Core\Time\DateTime
```

Builds a date and time in `$zone` from its fields. The clock fields default to midnight. If the zone skips the time, such as 02:30 on the morning the clocks go forward, the result moves forward past the gap.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$year` | `int` | The year, within `-9999..=9999`. The time as a whole must also lie between `-9999-01-02T01:59:59Z` and `9999-12-30T22:00:00Z`. |
| `$month` | `uint` | The month, `1` to `12`. |
| `$day` | `uint` | The day of the month, which must exist in that month. |
| `$zone` | `Core\Time\Zone` | The zone the fields are read in. |
| `{ hour: … }` | `uint` (default `0`) | The hour, `0` to `23`; the default is `0`. |
| `{ minute: … }` | `uint` (default `0`) | The minute, `0` to `59`; the default is `0`. |
| `{ second: … }` | `uint` (default `0`) | The second, `0` to `59`; the default is `0`. |
| `{ nanos: … }` | `uint` (default `0`) | The subsecond nanoseconds, below `1000000000`; the default is `0`. |

**Returns** `Core\Time\DateTime` — The `DateTime` in `$zone`.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — A field is outside its range, or the fields together are not a date that exists, such as `30` February. Or the time is past either end of the range `$year` allows.

<a id="core-core-time-instant"></a>
### `Core\Time\Instant`

Keywords: instant, timestamp, epoch, Unix time, milliseconds, timeline, UTC, RFC 3339, ISO 8601, time difference, add hours, in, toEpochSeconds, toEpochMillis, toEpochMicros, plus, minus, since, compareTo, toIso

An `Instant` is a point on the timeline with no calendar attached: it has an epoch count and an
RFC 3339 rendering in UTC, and nothing else until `->in($zone)` places it on a calendar. It moves
only by an exact `Duration` — `plus(36h)` is thirty-six hours whatever a zone's clocks did in between —
and `since` measures the exact gap between two instants; a step in days or months is taken on the
`DateTime` that `->in($zone)` answers. Two instants are ordered with `compareTo`; the `<`, `>` and
`<=>` operators do not compile on an `Instant`.

```nvs
<?nvs
var $start = Core\Time::fromIso('2024-03-01T12:00:00Z');
echo $start->toIso(), "\n";
echo $start->toEpochSeconds(), "\n";
echo $start->toEpochMillis(), "\n";

var $end = $start->plus(36h);
echo $end->toIso(), "\n";
echo $end->since($start), "\n";
echo $start->minus(30m)->toIso(), "\n";
echo $start->compareTo($end), "\n";

echo $start->in(Core\Time\Zone::of('Asia/Tokyo'))->format('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm'), "\n";
echo Core\Time::fromEpoch(1709294400, { nanos: 500000000 })->toIso(), "\n";
```
```output
2024-03-01T12:00:00Z
1709294400
1709294400000
2024-03-03T00:00:00Z
1d12h
2024-03-01T11:30:00Z
-1
2024-03-01 21:00
2024-03-01T12:00:00.5Z
```

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Time\Instant->in`](#core-core-time-instant-in) | `in(Core\Time\Zone $zone): Core\Time\DateTime` |
| [`Core\Time\Instant->toEpochSeconds`](#core-core-time-instant-toepochseconds) | `toEpochSeconds(): int` |
| [`Core\Time\Instant->toEpochMillis`](#core-core-time-instant-toepochmillis) | `toEpochMillis(): int` |
| [`Core\Time\Instant->toEpochMicros`](#core-core-time-instant-toepochmicros) | `toEpochMicros(): int` |
| [`Core\Time\Instant->plus`](#core-core-time-instant-plus) | `plus(Core\Time\Duration $d): Core\Time\Instant` |
| [`Core\Time\Instant->minus`](#core-core-time-instant-minus) | `minus(Core\Time\Duration $d): Core\Time\Instant` |
| [`Core\Time\Instant->since`](#core-core-time-instant-since) | `since(Core\Time\Instant $earlier): Core\Time\Duration` |
| [`Core\Time\Instant->compareTo`](#core-core-time-instant-compareto) | `compareTo(Core\Time\Instant $other): int` |
| [`Core\Time\Instant->toIso`](#core-core-time-instant-toiso) | `toIso(): string` |

<a id="core-core-time-instant-in"></a>
#### `Core\Time\Instant->in`

```nvs skip
$instant->in(Core\Time\Zone $zone): Core\Time\DateTime
```

Shows this instant on the calendar and clock of `$zone`. This is the only way to get a date or an hour from an instant, so you always name the zone.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$zone` | `Core\Time\Zone` | The time zone to show the instant in. Its offset at this instant is used, including summer time. |

**Returns** `Core\Time\DateTime` — A `DateTime` at the same instant, in `$zone`. The instant does not change.

<a id="core-core-time-instant-toepochseconds"></a>
#### `Core\Time\Instant->toEpochSeconds`

```nvs skip
$instant->toEpochSeconds(): int
```

Returns the Unix timestamp of this instant: the whole seconds since 1 January 1970 in UTC.

**Returns** `int` — An `int`, negative before 1970. The part of a second is cut off, toward zero.

<a id="core-core-time-instant-toepochmillis"></a>
#### `Core\Time\Instant->toEpochMillis`

```nvs skip
$instant->toEpochMillis(): int
```

Returns the whole milliseconds since 1 January 1970 in UTC, as JavaScript counts time.

**Returns** `int` — An `int`, negative before 1970. The part of a millisecond is cut off, toward zero. Every instant fits.

<a id="core-core-time-instant-toepochmicros"></a>

```nvs skip
$instant->toEpochMicros(): int
```
