**Returns** `int` — An `int`, negative before 1970. The part of a microsecond is cut off, toward zero. Every instant fits.

<a id="core-core-time-instant-plus"></a>
#### `Core\Time\Instant->plus`

```nvs skip
$instant->plus(Core\Time\Duration $d): Core\Time\Instant
```

Moves the instant forward by an exact `Duration`. An instant has no time zone, so a change to or from summer time does not change the result. To add calendar days, use `$i->in($zone)->plus($n, Unit::Day)`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$d` | `Core\Time\Duration` | The duration to add. A negative duration moves the instant back. |

**Returns** `Core\Time\Instant` — A new `Instant`. The original instant does not change.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The result is before the year -9999 or after the year 9999.

<a id="core-core-time-instant-minus"></a>
#### `Core\Time\Instant->minus`

```nvs skip
$instant->minus(Core\Time\Duration $d): Core\Time\Instant
```

Moves the instant back by an exact `Duration`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$d` | `Core\Time\Duration` | The exact duration to subtract; a negative one moves the instant forward. |

**Returns** `Core\Time\Instant` — A new `Instant`; the receiver is unchanged.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The result lies outside the representable range, about ±9999 years.

<a id="core-core-time-instant-since"></a>
#### `Core\Time\Instant->since`

```nvs skip
$instant->since(Core\Time\Instant $earlier): Core\Time\Duration
```

Returns the exact time from `$earlier` to this instant, as a `Duration`. `$earlier->plus($later->since($earlier))` is `$later` again.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$earlier` | `Core\Time\Instant` | The instant to measure from. |

**Returns** `Core\Time\Duration` — A `Duration`. It is negative when `$earlier` is after this instant.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The two instants are more than about 292 years apart. That is the longest `Duration` there is.

<a id="core-core-time-instant-compareto"></a>
#### `Core\Time\Instant->compareTo`

```nvs skip
$instant->compareTo(Core\Time\Instant $other): int
```

Checks which of two instants comes first, as `Comparable` requires. The operators `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` and `<=>` use this method too. `==` on two instants checks whether they are the same object, so test for the same moment with `$a->compareTo($b) == 0`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$other` | `Core\Time\Instant` | The instant to compare against. |

**Returns** `int` — `-1` when the receiver is earlier than `$other`, `0` when they are the same instant, `1` when it is later.

<a id="core-core-time-instant-toiso"></a>
#### `Core\Time\Instant->toIso`

```nvs skip
$instant->toIso(): string
```

Returns the instant as RFC 3339 text in UTC. This is the date format that JSON and HTTP APIs use most.

**Returns** `string` — A `string` such as `2024-03-01T12:00:00Z`. It has a fraction of a second only when the fraction is not zero.

<a id="core-core-time-datetime"></a>
### `Core\Time\DateTime`

Keywords: date, time, datetime, format a date, add days, add months, date difference, weekday, day of year, leap year, immutable date, CLDR, format pattern, calendar arithmetic, DST, next monday, last day of month, format, plus, minus, next, previous, with, withTime, startOf, endOf, difference, toInstant, date, timeOfDay, zone, weekday, dayOfYear, isLeapYear

A `DateTime` is a civil reading — year, month, day, hour, minute, second, nanosecond — in one `Zone`,
built by `Core\Time::at` or `Core\Time::parse` or read off an `Instant` with `->in($zone)`. It is
immutable: every member answers a new value. Its arithmetic is calendar arithmetic: `plus(1,
Core\Unit::Month)` keeps the day-of-month clamped to the new month's length, `plus(1, Core\Unit::Day)`
across a DST boundary is a 23- or 25-hour day, and `difference` counts whole units in the receiver's
zone. `format` takes a **CLDR pattern**. `Core\Time::parse` reads the same patterns, and `Date::format`
and `TimeOfDay::format` use them for their own fields. A pattern written directly
in the code is checked when the program compiles, so a letter outside the table below is a compile error; a pattern
computed at run time throws a `LogicError` instead. Month and weekday names are always in English.

| Letter | Field | Counts |
|---|---|---|
| `y` | year | `yy` two digits; any other count zero-pads to it |
| `M` | month | `M`/`MM` numeric, `MMM` `Mar`, `MMMM` `March`, `MMMMM` `M` |
| `d` | day of month | numeric, zero-padded to the count |
| `D` | day of year | numeric |
| `E` | weekday | `E`–`EEE` `Tue`, `EEEE` `Tuesday`, `EEEEE` `T`, `EEEEEE` `Tu` |
| `a` | AM/PM | any count |
| `h` / `H` / `K` / `k` | hour 1–12 / 0–23 / 0–11 / 1–24 | numeric |
| `m` | minute | numeric |
| `s` | second | numeric |
| `S` | fractional second | one digit per count, truncated |
| `X` | offset, `Z` at zero | `X` `+01`, `XX` `+0100`, `XXX` `+01:00` |
| `x` | offset, never `Z` | the same three counts |
| `VV` | the zone's IANA identifier | `VV` only |

Text between `'…'` is printed as it is, and `''` is one apostrophe. `G`, `Q`, `w`, `W`, `L`, `c`, `F` and `u`
are refused.

```nvs
<?nvs
var $utc = Core\Time\Zone::UTC;
var $d = Core\Time::at(2024, 1, 31, $utc, { hour: 9, minute: 30 });
echo $d->format('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss'), "\n";
echo $d->format("EEEE, d MMMM yyyy 'at' h:mm a"), "\n";

echo $d->plus(1, Core\Unit::Month)->format('yyyy-MM-dd'), "\n";
echo $d->minus(1, Core\Unit::Week)->format('yyyy-MM-dd'), "\n";
echo $d->next(Core\Time\DateTime::Weekday::Monday)->format('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm'), "\n";
echo $d->with({ month: 3, day: 1 })->format('yyyy-MM-dd'), "\n";
echo $d->startOf(Core\Unit::Day)->format('HH:mm'), ' ',
    $d->endOf(Core\Unit::Month)->format('dd HH:mm:ss.SSS'), "\n";

echo $d->difference(Core\Time::at(2026, 8, 30, $utc), Core\Unit::Year), "\n";
echo $d->weekday() == Core\Time\DateTime::Weekday::Wednesday ? 'midweek' : 'other', "\n";
echo $d->dayOfYear(), ' ', $d->isLeapYear() ? 'leap' : 'common', "\n";
echo $d->toInstant()->toIso(), "\n";
```
```output
2024-01-31 09:30:00
Wednesday, 31 January 2024 at 9:30 AM
2024-02-29
2024-01-24
2024-02-05 09:30
2024-03-01
00:00 31 23:59:59.999
2
midweek
31 leap
2024-01-31T09:30:00Z
```

<a id="core-core-time-datetime-format"></a>
#### `Core\Time\DateTime->format`

```nvs skip
$dateTime->format(string $pattern): string
```

Turns the date and time into text with a CLDR pattern, such as `yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss` or `EEEE, d MMMM yyyy`. Day and month names always use CLDR's root locale.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$pattern` | `string` (sink) | A CLDR pattern, using the pattern letters that Novis supports. A pattern is a small language, so a `tainted` pattern is not allowed. |

**Returns** `string` — The rendered text.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$pattern` is not valid. It has a pattern letter that is not supported, or a quote that is not closed. A `$pattern` written directly in the code is checked when the program compiles, and an error there is `E0769`. So only a computed `$pattern` can throw this error. `Date::format` and `TimeOfDay::format` read the same patterns but are not checked when the program compiles. There, a bad pattern written in the code also throws.

<a id="core-core-time-datetime-plus"></a>
#### `Core\Time\DateTime->plus`

```nvs skip
$dateTime->plus(int $count, Core\Unit $unit): Core\Time\DateTime
```

Moves the value forward by `$count` calendar steps of `$unit`. `1, Unit::Month` gives the same day of the month, limited to the length of the new month. A day across a change to or from summer time is 23 or 25 hours long. For an exact step, use `$d->toInstant()->plus(24h)`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$count` | `int` | How many steps; negative moves back. |
| `$unit` | `Core\Unit` | The calendar unit of each step. |

**Returns** `Core\Time\DateTime` — A new `DateTime` in the same zone; the receiver is unchanged.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `$count` is too large for a calendar step, or the result lies outside the representable range, about ±9999 years.

<a id="core-core-time-datetime-minus"></a>
#### `Core\Time\DateTime->minus`

```nvs skip
$dateTime->minus(int $count, Core\Unit $unit): Core\Time\DateTime
```

Moves the value back by `$count` calendar steps of `$unit`. It is `plus` with the count negated. The two give the same results at the end of a month and at a change to or from summer time.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$count` | `int` | How many steps; negative moves forward. |
| `$unit` | `Core\Unit` | The calendar unit of each step. |

**Returns** `Core\Time\DateTime` — A new `DateTime` in the same zone; the receiver is unchanged.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `$count` is too large for a calendar step, or the result lies outside the representable range, about ±9999 years.

#### `Core\Time\DateTime->with`

```nvs skip
$dateTime->with({ year?: int, month?: uint, day?: uint, hour?: uint, minute?: uint, second?: uint, nanos?: uint }): Core\Time\DateTime
```

Replaces any of the seven date and time fields and keeps the others. If the zone skips the new time, the result moves forward past the gap.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `{ year: … }` | `int` (default `null`) | The new year, within `-9999..=9999`; omitted leaves the field alone. |
| `{ month: … }` | `uint` (default `null`) | The new month, `1` to `12`; omitted leaves the field alone. |
| `{ day: … }` | `uint` (default `null`) | The new day of the month; omitted leaves the field alone. |
| `{ hour: … }` | `uint` (default `null`) | The new hour, `0` to `23`; omitted leaves the field alone. |
| `{ minute: … }` | `uint` (default `null`) | The new minute, `0` to `59`; omitted leaves the field alone. |
| `{ second: … }` | `uint` (default `null`) | The new second, `0` to `59`; omitted leaves the field alone. |
| `{ nanos: … }` | `uint` (default `null`) | The new subsecond nanoseconds, below `1000000000`; omitted leaves the field alone. |

**Returns** `Core\Time\DateTime` — A new `DateTime` in the same zone; the receiver is unchanged.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — An option is outside its field's range, or the fields together are not a date that exists — `{ day: 31 }` on a June value.

Moves the value back to the first instant of the `$u` that contains it. `startOf(Unit::Day)` is local midnight, and `startOf(Unit::Month)` is the first day of the month. It is calculated on the date and time fields and then placed back in the zone.


Moves the value to the last instant of the `$u` that contains it, one nanosecond before the next one starts. `endOf(Unit::Month)` is the end of the month's last day. It is calculated separately from `startOf`. This matters on a day that is longer or shorter because of a change to or from summer time.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|

<a id="core-core-time-datetime-difference"></a>
#### `Core\Time\DateTime->difference`

```nvs skip

```

Counts the whole units of `$unit` from this value to `$other`, in this value's zone. Use it for an age in years or a term in months.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$other` | `Core\Time\DateTime` | The value to count to; it is read in the receiver's zone, so the two may differ in zone. |
| `$unit` | `Core\Unit` | The calendar unit to count in. |

**Returns** `int` — The whole count, truncated toward zero — negative when `$other` is earlier, `0` within one unit.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The count does not fit in an `int`. Only `Unit::Nanosecond` can reach this, for two values more than about 292 years apart.

<a id="core-core-time-date"></a>
### `Core\Time\Date`

Keywords: date, calendar date, day-month-year, zone-free, valid date, days in month, leap year, at, format, plus, minus, with, compareTo

A `Date` is the year, month and day alone — no time of day and no zone — built by `Date::at` or read
off a `DateTime` with `->date()`. There is no `Date::parse`: text is read with `Core\Time::parse`
(a pattern and a zone), and the `DateTime` it answers gives up its date. A date that does not exist throws where it is built.
It steps by `Core\Unit::Day` and larger, with the same month-end clamping as
`DateTime::plus`; a smaller unit is refused. `format` takes the date letters of the CLDR grammar
`DateTime::format` uses, and a time or zone letter in the pattern is refused because a `Date` has
none to render. Two dates are ordered with `compareTo`; the `<` operators do not compile on a `Date`.

```nvs
<?nvs
var $d = Core\Time\Date::at(2024, 1, 31);
echo $d->format('yyyy-MM-dd'), "\n";
echo $d->format('EEEE, d MMMM'), "\n";

echo $d->plus(1, Core\Unit::Month)->format('yyyy-MM-dd'), "\n";
echo $d->minus(1, Core\Unit::Day)->format('EEE d MMM'), "\n";
echo $d->with({ month: 3 })->format('yyyy-MM-dd'), "\n";
echo $d->compareTo(Core\Time\Date::at(2024, 2, 1)), "\n";

try {
    Core\Time\Date::at(2023, 2, 29);
} catch (RuntimeError $bad) {
    echo "2023-02-29 does not exist\n";
}

var $utc = Core\Time\Zone::UTC;
echo Core\Time::at(2024, 3, 1, $utc, { hour: 23 })->date()->format('d/M/yyyy'), "\n";
```
```output
2024-01-31
Wednesday, 31 January
2024-02-29
Tue 30 Jan
2024-03-31
-1
2023-02-29 does not exist
1/3/2024
```

|---|---|
| [`Core\Time\Date::at`](#core-core-time-date-at) | `at(int $y, uint $m, uint $d): Core\Time\Date` |
| [`Core\Time\Date->format`](#core-core-time-date-format) | `format(string $pattern): string` |
| [`Core\Time\Date->plus`](#core-core-time-date-plus) | `plus(int $count, Core\Unit $unit): Core\Time\Date` |
| [`Core\Time\Date->minus`](#core-core-time-date-minus) | `minus(int $count, Core\Unit $unit): Core\Time\Date` |
| [`Core\Time\Date->with`](#core-core-time-date-with) | `with({ year?: int, month?: uint, day?: uint }): Core\Time\Date` |

<a id="core-core-time-timeofday"></a>
### `Core\Time\TimeOfDay`

Keywords: wall clock, time of day, time without a date, clock reading, hour, minute, second, at, format, plus, minus, with, compareTo

A `TimeOfDay` is a clock reading — hour, minute, second, nanosecond — with no date and no zone, built by
`TimeOfDay::at` or read off a `DateTime` with `->timeOfDay()`. It steps by `Core\Unit::Hour` and
smaller and wraps within the day, so `23:30` plus an hour is `00:30`; `Core\Unit::Day` and larger are
refused, because a carry has no date to go to. `format` takes the time letters of the CLDR grammar
`DateTime::format` uses, and a date or zone letter is refused. `DateTime::withTime` puts a reading
back onto a date. Two readings are ordered with `compareTo`; the `<` operators do not compile.

```nvs
<?nvs
var $t = Core\Time\TimeOfDay::at(23, 30);
echo $t->format('HH:mm:ss'), "\n";
echo $t->format('h:mm a'), "\n";

echo $t->plus(1, Core\Unit::Hour)->format('HH:mm'), "\n";
echo $t->minus(45, Core\Unit::Minute)->format('HH:mm'), "\n";
echo $t->with({ second: 45 })->format('HH:mm:ss'), "\n";
echo $t->compareTo(Core\Time\TimeOfDay::at(9, 0)), "\n";

var $utc = Core\Time\Zone::UTC;
var $d = Core\Time::at(2024, 3, 1, $utc, { hour: 9 });
echo $d->withTime($t)->format('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm'), "\n";
echo $d->timeOfDay()->format('HH:mm'), "\n";
```
```output
23:30:00
11:30 PM
00:30
22:45
23:30:45
1
2024-03-01 23:30
09:00
```

|---|---|
| [`Core\Time\TimeOfDay::at`](#core-core-time-timeofday-at) | `at(uint $hour, uint $minute, { second?: uint, nanos?: uint }): Core\Time\TimeOfDay` |
| [`Core\Time\TimeOfDay->format`](#core-core-time-timeofday-format) | `format(string $pattern): string` |
| [`Core\Time\TimeOfDay->plus`](#core-core-time-timeofday-plus) | `plus(int $count, Core\Unit $unit): Core\Time\TimeOfDay` |
| [`Core\Time\TimeOfDay->minus`](#core-core-time-timeofday-minus) | `minus(int $count, Core\Unit $unit): Core\Time\TimeOfDay` |
| [`Core\Time\TimeOfDay->with`](#core-core-time-timeofday-with) | `with({ hour?: uint, minute?: uint, second?: uint, nanos?: uint }): Core\Time\TimeOfDay` |
| [`Core\Time\TimeOfDay->compareTo`](#core-core-time-timeofday-compareto) | `compareTo(Core\Time\TimeOfDay $other): int` |

<a id="core-core-time-timeofday-at"></a>
#### `Core\Time\TimeOfDay::at`

```nvs skip
Core\Time\TimeOfDay::at(uint $hour, uint $minute, { second?: uint, nanos?: uint }): Core\Time\TimeOfDay
```

Makes a time of day from an hour and a minute. The seconds and the nanoseconds are optional, and their default is `0`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$hour` | `uint` | The hour, `0` to `23`. |
| `$minute` | `uint` | The minute, `0` to `59`. |
| `{ second: … }` | `uint` (default `0`) | The second, `0` to `59`. The default is `0`. |
| `{ nanos: … }` | `uint` (default `0`) | The nanoseconds inside that second, `0` to `999999999`. The default is `0`. |

**Returns** `Core\Time\TimeOfDay` — The new `TimeOfDay`.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — A field is outside its range, for example an hour of `24`.

<a id="core-core-time-timeofday-format"></a>
#### `Core\Time\TimeOfDay->format`

```nvs skip
$timeOfDay->format(string $pattern): string
```

Returns the time as text in the pattern you give, such as `HH:mm:ss` or `h:mm a`. The pattern uses the letters of `DateTime::format`, but only the letters for a time.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$pattern` | `string` (sink) | The pattern, such as `HH:mm`. It may use letters for the hour, the minute, the second, parts of a second and AM or PM. A `tainted` pattern (text from outside the program) is not allowed. |

**Returns** `string` — The time as text.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$pattern` is not a valid pattern, or it uses a letter for a date or a time zone.

<a id="core-core-time-timeofday-plus"></a>
#### `Core\Time\TimeOfDay->plus`

```nvs skip
$timeOfDay->plus(int $count, Core\Unit $unit): Core\Time\TimeOfDay
```

Moves the time forward by `$count` steps of `$unit`. The result wraps around at midnight, so `23:30` plus one hour is `00:30`. To move a time across days, use `DateTime::plus`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$count` | `int` | How many steps. A negative count moves the time back. |
| `$unit` | `Core\Unit` | `Unit::Hour` or a smaller unit. |

**Returns** `Core\Time\TimeOfDay` — A new `TimeOfDay`. The original does not change.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$unit` is `Unit::Day` or larger. A time of day has no days to move.; `RuntimeError` — `$count` is too large for `$unit`.


#### `Core\Time\TimeOfDay->compareTo`

```nvs skip

```

Checks which of two times comes first in the day, as `Comparable` requires. The operators `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` and `<=>` use this method too. `==` on two times checks whether they are the same object, so test for the same time with `$a->compareTo($b) == 0`.

<a id="core-core-time-duration"></a>
### `Core\Time\Duration`

Keywords: duration, interval, time span, sleep, 1h30m, 250ms, nanoseconds, exact offset, parse a duration, timeout, nanoseconds, microseconds, milliseconds, seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, parse, toNanoseconds, toMicroseconds, toMilliseconds, toSeconds, plus, minus, multipliedBy, negated, compareTo, toString

A `Duration` is a signed count of nanoseconds. You write one directly in the code as a number and a
unit — `30s`, `250ms`, `1h30m`, `7d` — with the units `ns`, `us`, `ms`, `s`, `m`, `h`, `d` and `w`, and
`Duration::parse` reads the same grammar from text at run time. It is exact: `days(1)` and `1d` are
twenty-four hours, never a calendar day, which is what `Core\Time\DateTime::plus($n, Core\Unit::Day)`
is. `echo` renders a duration back in that same syntax, so its text round-trips through `parse`. An
argument to `parse` written directly in the code is read when the program compiles, so a bad one is a compile error; text
computed at run time throws a `ParseError`. Two durations are ordered with `compareTo`; the `<`
operators do not compile on a `Duration`.

```nvs
<?nvs
var $d = 1h30m;
echo $d, "\n";
echo $d->toSeconds(), "\n";

echo $d->plus(15m), "\n";
echo $d->minus(2h), "\n";
echo $d->multipliedBy(2), "\n";
echo $d->negated(), "\n";

echo Core\Time\Duration::parse('250ms')->toMilliseconds(), "\n";
echo Core\Time\Duration::minutes(90)->compareTo($d), "\n";
echo Core\Time\Duration::seconds(90061), "\n";
echo 1500ms->toString(), "\n";

string $flag = '--since=30 seconds';
try {
    Core\Time\Duration::parse(Core\Str::slice($flag, 8));
} catch (ParseError $bad) {
    echo "not a duration\n";
}
```
```output
1h30m
5400
1h45m
-30m
3h
-1h30m
250
0
1d1h1m1s
1s500ms
not a duration
```

| [`Core\Time\Duration::microseconds`](#core-core-time-duration-microseconds) | `microseconds(int $n): Core\Time\Duration` |
| [`Core\Time\Duration::milliseconds`](#core-core-time-duration-milliseconds) | `milliseconds(int $n): Core\Time\Duration` |

#### `Core\Time\Duration::parse`

```nvs skip

```

Reads a duration such as `30s`, `1h30m` or `7d` from text at run time. It uses the same syntax as a duration written in the code. Use it for an exact offset that comes from a config value or a flag. It accepts nothing else, so the result is not `tainted`, even when the text is.

<a id="core-core-time-zone"></a>
### `Core\Time\Zone`

Keywords: timezone, time zone, IANA, tz database, Europe/Berlin, UTC, offset, UTC offset, DST, daylight saving time, convert time zone, system time zone, of, fixed, system, offsetAt

A `Zone` is what turns an `Instant` into a calendar reading and back: `Zone::of` looks up an IANA
identifier such as `Europe/Berlin` in the bundled database and throws on one it does not have,
`Zone::fixed` is a constant offset with no DST rules, and `Zone::UTC` is the one constant. There is
no ambient zone: `Zone::system()` answers the host's zone as an ordinary value the program then
passes on, and no call sets a default zone for the program. A zone with DST has no single
offset, so `offsetAt` asks for the instant.

```nvs
<?nvs
var $berlin = Core\Time\Zone::of('Europe/Berlin');
var $jan = Core\Time::fromIso('2024-01-15T12:00:00Z');
var $jul = Core\Time::fromIso('2024-07-15T12:00:00Z');
echo $berlin->offsetAt($jan), "\n";
echo $berlin->offsetAt($jul), "\n";
echo $jul->in($berlin)->format('HH:mm xxx VV'), "\n";

var $india = Core\Time\Zone::fixed(5h30m);
echo $jul->in($india)->format('HH:mm xxx'), "\n";
echo Core\Time\Zone::UTC->offsetAt($jul)->toSeconds(), "\n";

echo Core\Time::at(2024, 7, 15, $berlin, { hour: 14 })->toInstant()->toIso(), "\n";

try {
    Core\Time\Zone::of('Mars/Olympus');
} catch (RuntimeError $unknown) {
    echo "not in the database\n";
}
```
```output
1h
2h
14:00 +02:00 Europe/Berlin
17:30 +05:30
0
2024-07-15T12:00:00Z
not in the database
```

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Time\Zone::of`](#core-core-time-zone-of) | `of(string $id): Core\Time\Zone` |
| [`Core\Time\Zone::fixed`](#core-core-time-zone-fixed) | `fixed(Core\Time\Duration $offset): Core\Time\Zone` |
| [`Core\Time\Zone::system`](#core-core-time-zone-system) | `system(): Core\Time\Zone` |
| [`Core\Time\Zone->offsetAt`](#core-core-time-zone-offsetat) | `offsetAt(Core\Time\Instant $i): Core\Time\Duration` |
| `Core\Time\Zone::UTC` | `Core\Time\Zone` = `Core\Time\Zone::of("UTC")` — The UTC zone — the only zone that is ever a default, and only where a call site writes it explicitly. |

<a id="core-core-time-zone-of"></a>
#### `Core\Time\Zone::of`

```nvs skip
Core\Time\Zone::of(string $id): Core\Time\Zone
```

Finds a time zone by its name, such as `Europe/Berlin` or `America/New_York`. The names come from the IANA time-zone database. A name that is not in the database throws an error.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$id` | `string` (neutral) | The name of the zone, such as `Asia/Tokyo`. An offset such as `+02:00` is not allowed here. Use `Zone::fixed` for an offset. |

**Returns** `Core\Time\Zone` — The `Zone` with that name.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `$id` is not a zone name in the database, or starts with `+` or `-`.

<a id="core-core-time-zone-fixed"></a>
#### `Core\Time\Zone::fixed`

```nvs skip
Core\Time\Zone::fixed(Core\Time\Duration $offset): Core\Time\Zone
```

Makes a zone that is always the same distance from UTC, such as `+05:30`. Its offset never changes for summer time. Use it for a timestamp that has an offset and no zone name, such as `2024-03-05T10:00:00+05:30`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$offset` | `Core\Time\Duration` | The distance from UTC as a whole number of seconds. It is negative for a zone west of UTC. |

**Returns** `Core\Time\Zone` — A `Zone` whose name is the offset, written `+HH:MM`, or `+HH:MM:SS` when it has seconds.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `$offset` has a part smaller than a second, or is more than 25:59:59 away from UTC.

<a id="core-core-time-zone-system"></a>
#### `Core\Time\Zone::system`

```nvs skip
Core\Time\Zone::system(): Core\Time\Zone
```

Returns the time zone of the computer the program runs on. There is no default zone, so you pass this `Zone` to each call that needs one.

**Returns** `Core\Time\Zone` — The computer's `Zone` with its IANA name, such as `Europe/Berlin`. When the computer has no zone name, the result is a fixed zone at its current offset, such as `+02:00`.

<a id="core-core-time-zone-offsetat"></a>
#### `Core\Time\Zone->offsetAt`

```nvs skip
$zone->offsetAt(Core\Time\Instant $i): Core\Time\Duration
```

Returns how far the zone is from UTC at one instant. A zone with summer time has two offsets in a year. `Europe/Berlin` is `+01:00` in January and `+02:00` in July.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$i` | `Core\Time\Instant` | The instant to read the offset at. |

**Returns** `Core\Time\Duration` — The offset as a `Duration` of whole seconds. It is positive east of UTC, negative west of UTC, and zero for UTC.

<a id="core-core-objectmap"></a>
### `Core\ObjectMap<K, V>`

Keywords: identity, object identity, object key, per-object data, side table, map, dictionary, lookup, set, get, has, remove, count, isEmpty, keys, values, clear

`Core\ObjectMap<K, V>` associates a value with an object, matched by **identity**: the one object is one
key however many variables hold it, and two objects that agree on every property are two keys. `array<T>`
cannot key on an object, so this is where a per-object side table lives. It is built with
`new Core\ObjectMap<K, V>()`, `get` answers `?V` rather than throwing — there is no `$m[$k]` subscript on it —
and `has` is the one member that tells an absent key from a stored `null`. The map is `Iterable`: a
`foreach` yields its **keys** in insertion order, walking a snapshot taken when the loop began, so the body
may `remove` what it is walking.

```nvs
<?nvs
class Tag
{
    public function constructor(public string $name)
    {}
}

var $red = new Tag('red');
var $blue = new Tag('blue');

var $weights = new Core\ObjectMap<Tag, int>();
$weights->set($red, 3);
$weights->set($blue, 7);
$weights->set($red, 4);

echo 'red=', $weights->get($red) ?? 0, "\n";
echo 'other red=', $weights->get(new Tag('red')) ?? -1, "\n";
echo 'count=', $weights->count(), "\n";

foreach ($weights as Tag $tag) {
    echo $tag->name, ' ';
}
echo "\n";

$weights->remove($blue);
echo $weights->has($blue) ? 'blue kept' : 'blue gone', "\n";
echo 'keys=', Core\Arr::count($weights->keys()), ' values=', Core\Arr::count($weights->values()), "\n";
```
```output
red=4
other red=-1
count=2
red blue
blue gone
keys=1 values=1
```

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|

<a id="core-core-objectset"></a>
### `Core\ObjectSet<T>`

Keywords: identity, object identity, set, membership, union, intersect, diff, deduplicate objects, add, has, remove, count, isEmpty, union, intersect, diff, clear

`Core\ObjectSet<T>` holds each object at most once, matched by **identity**: adding the same object twice
leaves one member, and a second object equal in every property is a second member. It is built with
`new Core\ObjectSet<T>()`; `add`, `has` and `remove` are the membership members, and the set is `Iterable`
— a `foreach` yields its members in insertion order, over a snapshot, so the body may `remove` what it is
walking. `union`, `intersect` and `diff` answer a new set and leave both operands untouched; the binary
types that new set as a bare `Core\ObjectSet`, so it can be counted, asked `has` and walked as `mixed`
(`foreach ($both as mixed $m)` and then `$m as Tag`), but a `foreach … as Tag $t` over it is refused.

```nvs
<?nvs
class Tag
{
    public function constructor(public string $name)
    {}
}

var $red = new Tag('red');
var $blue = new Tag('blue');
var $green = new Tag('green');

var $seen = new Core\ObjectSet<Tag>();
$seen->add($red);
$seen->add($blue);
$seen->add($red);
echo 'count=', $seen->count(), "\n";
echo $seen->has($red) ? 'has red' : 'no red', "\n";
echo $seen->has(new Tag('red')) ? 'has other red' : 'no other red', "\n";

var $wanted = new Core\ObjectSet<Tag>();
$wanted->add($blue);
$wanted->add($green);
echo 'union=', $seen->union($wanted)->count(), "\n";
echo 'both=', $seen->intersect($wanted)->count(), "\n";
echo 'only seen=', $seen->diff($wanted)->count(), "\n";

$seen->remove($red);
foreach ($seen as Tag $tag) {
    echo $tag->name, "\n";
}
echo $seen->isEmpty() ? 'empty' : 'not empty', "\n";
```
```output
count=2
has red
no other red
union=3
both=1
only seen=1
blue
not empty
```

| [`Core\ObjectSet->has`](#core-core-objectset-has) | `has(T $value): bool` |
| [`Core\ObjectSet->remove`](#core-core-objectset-remove) | `remove(T $value): void` |

<a id="core-core-heap"></a>
### `Core\Heap<T>`

Keywords: priority queue, heap, binary heap, min-heap, max-heap, smallest first, comparator, Comparable, compareTo, scheduling, push, peek, pop, count, isEmpty

`Core\Heap<T>` keeps its elements ordered so that `peek` and `pop` always answer the **smallest** one. The
order is decided once, at `new`: a comparator passed as the constructor's argument —
`new Core\Heap<T>(fn (T $a, T $b): int => …)`, answering negative, zero or positive as `Core\Arr::sort`'s does
— wins; without one, an object orders by its own `Comparable::compareTo`, and a scalar by its natural
order. A max-heap is therefore the min-heap with its comparator reversed, not another class. `peek` and
`pop` throw on an empty heap — ask `isEmpty` first — and a `foreach` over a heap yields its elements in
`pop` order without removing any of them.

```nvs
<?nvs
class Job implements Comparable
{
    public function constructor(public string $name, public int $cost)
    {}

    public function compareTo(Job $other): int
    {
        return $this->cost - $other->cost;
    }
}

var $jobs = new Core\Heap<Job>();
$jobs->push(new Job('deploy', 5));
$jobs->push(new Job('lint', 1));
$jobs->push(new Job('build', 3));

var $first = $jobs->peek();
echo 'next=', $first->name, ' of ', $jobs->count(), "\n";
while (!$jobs->isEmpty()) {
    var $job = $jobs->pop();
    echo $job->name, "\n";
}

var $largest = new Core\Heap<int>(fn(int $a, int $b): int => $b - $a);
$largest->push(3);
$largest->push(9);
$largest->push(5);
foreach ($largest as int $n) {
    echo $n, ' ';
}
echo 'still ', $largest->count(), "\n";
```
```output
next=lint of 3
lint
build
deploy
9 5 3 still 3
```

|---|---|
| `new Core\Heap` | `new Core\Heap(?callable(T, T): int $comparator = null): Core\Heap` |
| [`Core\Heap->push`](#core-core-heap-push) | `push(T $value): void` |
| [`Core\Heap->peek`](#core-core-heap-peek) | `peek(): T` |
| [`Core\Heap->pop`](#core-core-heap-pop) | `pop(): T` |
| [`Core\Heap->count`](#core-core-heap-count) | `count(): uint` |
| [`Core\Heap->isEmpty`](#core-core-heap-isempty) | `isEmpty(): bool` |

<a id="core-core-heap-constructor"></a>
#### `Core\Heap::constructor`

```nvs skip
new Core\Heap(?callable(T, T): int $comparator = null): Core\Heap
```

Builds an empty `Core\Heap<T>`, a priority queue. It is ordered by `$comparator` when one is given. Otherwise it uses `Comparable::compareTo`, or else the natural order of scalars.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$comparator` | `?callable(T, T): int` (default `null`) | An optional `fn ($a, $b)` that returns a negative number, zero or a positive number, like the comparator of `Core\Arr::sort`. With `null`, the heap uses `compareTo` or the natural order. |

<a id="core-core-heap-push"></a>
#### `Core\Heap->push`

```nvs skip
$heap->push(T $value): void
```

Adds `$value` to the heap in O(log n). The heap keeps duplicates, because it is a priority queue and not a set.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$value` | `T` | The element to add. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. If the comparator throws an error, `push` throws the same error.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The heap cannot compare `$value` with another element. There is no comparator or `compareTo`, and the two values have no natural order. Two numbers, two strings, two bools or two nulls have one. It also throws when the comparator returns `NaN`.

<a id="core-core-heap-peek"></a>
#### `Core\Heap->peek`

```nvs skip
$heap->peek(): T
```

Returns the element that `pop` would return, which is the smallest in the heap's order. The element stays in the heap.

**Returns** `T` — The first element. The heap does not change.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The heap is empty. Call `isEmpty` first to check.

<a id="core-core-heap-pop"></a>
#### `Core\Heap->pop`

```nvs skip
$heap->pop(): T
```

Removes the smallest element in the heap's order and returns it, in O(log n).

**Returns** `T` — The element that was first. The next element becomes first. If the comparator throws an error, `pop` throws the same error.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The heap is empty. It also throws when sorting the other elements meets two values with no natural order, or a comparator that returns `NaN`.

<a id="core-core-heap-count"></a>
#### `Core\Heap->count`

```nvs skip
$heap->count(): uint
```

Counts the elements in the heap, duplicates included.

**Returns** `uint` — The number of elements. An empty heap gives `0`.

<a id="core-core-heap-isempty"></a>
#### `Core\Heap->isEmpty`

```nvs skip
$heap->isEmpty(): bool
```

Checks whether the heap is empty. Call it before `peek` or `pop`, because they throw an error on an empty heap.

**Returns** `bool` — `true` for an empty heap, `false` otherwise.

<a id="core-core-random"></a>
### `Core\Random`

Keywords: random, random number, random integer, random float, random bytes, random element, shuffle, sample, token, CSPRNG, secure random, seed, seeded, reproducible, nonce, session token, int, float, bytes, token, pick, sample, shuffle

`Core\Random` is always a CSPRNG: there is no seeded or insecure generator under this name, and no
function sets a global seed. `int` draws from a closed range and throws on an empty one rather than swapping the bounds;
`pick`, `sample` and `shuffle` draw from an array and answer values — a fresh array for `shuffle`,
`null` from `pick` on an empty one. `token` is the hex text of `bytes`, two characters per byte, for a
session identifier or a reset link.

Reproducibility is a separate **type**, `Core\Random\Seeded`, built from an explicit seed with `new`
and carrying the same seven members: one seed is one sequence, every run, which is what a simulation
or a fixture wants and what a session token must never be. Because it is a type rather than a mode,
a parameter declaring which generator it takes cannot be handed the other one by mistake.

```nvs
<?nvs
echo Core\Random::int(7, 7), "\n";
int $face = Core\Random::int(1, 6);
echo $face >= 1 && $face <= 6 ? 'a die face' : 'out of range', "\n";

array<string> $only = ['ace'];
echo Core\Random::pick($only), "\n";
array<int> $deck = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
echo Core\Arr::count(Core\Random::shuffle($deck)), "\n";
echo Core\Arr::count(Core\Random::sample($deck, 2)), "\n";

echo Core\Str::length(Core\Random::token(8)), "\n";
echo Core\Bytes::length(Core\Random::bytes(16)), "\n";
float $f = Core\Random::float();
echo $f >= 0.0 && $f < 1.0 ? 'in [0, 1)' : 'outside', "\n";

array<int> $none = [];
echo Core\Random::pick($none) == null ? 'nothing to pick' : 'picked', "\n";
try {
    Core\Random::int(5, 1);
} catch (RuntimeError $empty) {
    echo "empty range\n";
}

var $left = new Core\Random\Seeded(42);
var $right = new Core\Random\Seeded(42);
echo $left->token(4) == $right->token(4) ? 'one seed, one sequence' : 'diverged', "\n";
echo $left->int(1, 6) == $right->int(1, 6) ? 'and it stays that way' : 'diverged', "\n";
```
```output
7
a die face
ace
5
2
16
16
in [0, 1)
nothing to pick
empty range
one seed, one sequence
and it stays that way
```

#### `Core\Random::bytes`

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|

**Returns** `bytes` — A `bytes` value with exactly `$count` raw bytes. For random bytes as a hex string, use `Core\Random::token`.

<a id="core-core-random-token"></a>
#### `Core\Random::token`

```nvs skip

```

Takes `$bytes` random bytes from the cryptographic random generator and returns them as lower-case hex. Use it for a session identifier or a reset link.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$bytes` | `uint` (default `32`) | How many random bytes to use, `32` by default. The string has twice as many characters. |

**Returns** `string` — A `string` of `2 * $bytes` hex digits, `0`–`9` and `a`–`f`.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `$bytes` is `0`, because an empty token is equal to every other empty token. It is also thrown when the result is larger than a buffer this process can allocate.

#### `Core\Random::sample`

<a id="core-core-random-shuffle"></a>

**Returns** `array<T>` — A new list of all the values, with the keys `0, 1, …`. The keys of `$a` are not kept, and `$a` is unchanged.

<a id="core-core-random-seeded-constructor"></a>
#### `Core\Random\Seeded::constructor`


**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `$min` is greater than `$max`. The method does not swap the two values.

**Returns** `float` — A `float` with 53 random bits. The result can be `0.0`, but never `1.0`.

<a id="core-core-uuid"></a>
### `Core\Uuid`

Keywords: uuid, GUID, unique id, random id, RFC 9562, RFC 4122, v4, v7, primary key, identifier, v4, v7, parse, tryParse, fromBytes, toString, toBytes

A `Uuid` is an opaque 128-bit value, not a string: `v4` draws a random one, `v7` a time-ordered one
whose leading bits are a millisecond timestamp — the right database key and the wrong public
identifier, since it tells the reader when the row was made. `parse` reads only the canonical
hyphenated `8-4-4-4-12` form, in either letter case, and refuses the unhyphenated, braced and
`urn:uuid:` spellings; asking whether text is a UUID is `tryParse($s) != null`. `toString` — and
`echo` — is the only way text comes back out, always lower-case. Two `Uuid` objects compare by
identity under `==`, so two values are compared through their text.

```nvs
<?nvs
var $id = Core\Uuid::v4();
echo Core\Str::length($id->toString()), "\n";
echo Core\Str::slice($id->toString(), 14, 1), "\n";
echo Core\Str::slice(Core\Uuid::v7()->toString(), 14, 1), "\n";

var $known = Core\Uuid::parse('123E4567-E89B-12D3-A456-426614174000');
echo $known, "\n";
echo Core\Uuid::tryParse('not-a-uuid') == null ? 'invalid' : 'valid', "\n";
echo Core\Uuid::tryParse('123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000') != null ? 'valid' : 'invalid', "\n";

var $again = Core\Uuid::parse('123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000');
echo $known == $again ? 'same object' : 'different objects', "\n";
echo $known->toString() == $again->toString() ? 'same value' : 'different values', "\n";

try {
    Core\Uuid::parse('{123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000}');
} catch (RuntimeError $bad) {
    echo "braces refused\n";
}
```
```output
36
4
7
123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000
invalid
valid
different objects
same value
braces refused
```

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Uuid::v4`](#core-core-uuid-v4) | `v4(): Core\Uuid` |
| [`Core\Uuid::v7`](#core-core-uuid-v7) | `v7(): Core\Uuid` |
| [`Core\Uuid::parse`](#core-core-uuid-parse) | `parse(string $s): Core\Uuid` |
| [`Core\Uuid::tryParse`](#core-core-uuid-tryparse) | `tryParse(string $s): ?Core\Uuid` |
| [`Core\Uuid::fromBytes`](#core-core-uuid-frombytes) | `fromBytes(bytes $b): Core\Uuid` |
| [`Core\Uuid->toString`](#core-core-uuid-tostring) | `toString(): string` |
| [`Core\Uuid->toBytes`](#core-core-uuid-tobytes) | `toBytes(): bytes` |

<a id="core-core-uuid-v4"></a>
#### `Core\Uuid::v4`

```nvs skip
Core\Uuid::v4(): Core\Uuid
```

Creates a new random UUID, such as `f9168c5e-ceb2-4faa-b6bf-329bf39fa1e4`. 122 of its 128 bits come from a secure random number generator. The other six bits say that it is a version 4 UUID.

**Returns** `Core\Uuid` — A new `Uuid`. Nobody can guess it, and it contains no date or time, so it is safe to show to other people.

<a id="core-core-uuid-v7"></a>
#### `Core\Uuid::v7`

```nvs skip
Core\Uuid::v7(): Core\Uuid
```

Creates a new UUID that starts with the current time, such as `0190d1e6-8e3c-7c2a-9a4b-1f2e3d4c5b6a`. The first 48 bits are the number of milliseconds since 1970. 74 of the other bits are random. Use it as a database key, because new keys sort after older ones.

**Returns** `Core\Uuid` — A new `Uuid`. It sorts after every UUID created in an earlier millisecond. Two UUIDs created in the same millisecond sort in a random order. Anybody who has the UUID can read the time it was created, so use `Core\Uuid::v4` for an ID that other people see. If the computer's clock is before 1970, the time part is zero.

<a id="core-core-uuid-parse"></a>
#### `Core\Uuid::parse`

```nvs skip
Core\Uuid::parse(string $s): Core\Uuid
```

Reads the text `$s` as a UUID. The text must be 32 hexadecimal digits in groups of 8, 4, 4, 4 and 12, joined by hyphens, such as `f9168c5e-ceb2-4faa-b6bf-329bf39fa1e4`. Upper case and lower case letters are both allowed.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$s` | `string` (neutral) | The text to read. It must be exactly 36 characters long. |

**Returns** `Core\Uuid` — The `Uuid` that the text gives. The version digit is not checked, so the nil UUID (all zeros) and the max UUID (all `f`) are both valid.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `$s` is not in that form. The 32 digits without hyphens, a UUID in `{}` braces and a UUID after `urn:uuid:` all throw this error too. The message quotes up to 48 characters of `$s`.

<a id="core-core-uuid-tryparse"></a>
#### `Core\Uuid::tryParse`

```nvs skip
Core\Uuid::tryParse(string $s): ?Core\Uuid
```

Reads the text `$s` as a UUID, like `Core\Uuid::parse`. When the text is not a UUID, it returns `null` and does not throw an error. Use it to check whether a text is a UUID.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$s` | `string` (neutral) | The text to read. It must be 32 hexadecimal digits in groups of 8, 4, 4, 4 and 12, joined by hyphens. Upper case and lower case letters are both allowed. |

**Returns** `?Core\Uuid` — The `Uuid` that the text gives, or `null` when the text is in any other form. The 32 digits without hyphens, a UUID in `{}` braces and a UUID after `urn:uuid:` all give `null`.

<a id="core-core-uuid-frombytes"></a>
#### `Core\Uuid::fromBytes`

```nvs skip
Core\Uuid::fromBytes(bytes $b): Core\Uuid
```

Reads sixteen bytes as a UUID. Many databases store a UUID in a binary column in this form, and binary protocols send it this way.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$b` | `bytes` (neutral) | The sixteen bytes, in the same order as the digits of the UUID's text. `$uuid->toBytes()` gives them in this order. |

**Returns** `Core\Uuid` — The `Uuid` that the bytes give. Any sixteen bytes are a valid UUID, so only the length is checked.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `$b` is not exactly sixteen bytes long. The message gives the length of `$b`.

<a id="core-core-uuid-tostring"></a>
#### `Core\Uuid->toString`

```nvs skip
$uuid->toString(): string
```

Returns the text of the UUID, such as `f9168c5e-ceb2-4faa-b6bf-329bf39fa1e4`. The digits are in groups of 8, 4, 4, 4 and 12, joined by hyphens. `echo $uuid` writes the same text.

**Returns** `string` — A string of 36 characters. The letters are always lower case, even when `parse` read them in upper case.

<a id="core-core-uuid-tobytes"></a>
#### `Core\Uuid->toBytes`

```nvs skip
$uuid->toBytes(): bytes
```

Returns the sixteen bytes of the UUID. Use it to store a UUID in a binary database column or to send it in a binary message. The text form of the same UUID is 36 bytes long.

**Returns** `bytes` — Sixteen bytes, in the same order as the digits of the UUID's text. `Core\Uuid::fromBytes` reads them back as the same UUID.

<a id="core-core-hash"></a>
### `Core\Hash`

Keywords: hash, md5, sha1, sha256, crc32, digest, HMAC, checksum, fingerprint, constant-time comparison, of, hmac, equals, stream

`Core\Hash::of` computes any `Core\Hash::Digest` case over a `string` or `bytes` and answers the raw
digest as `bytes` — never hex and never an `int` — so printing one goes through
`Core\Encoding::toHex`. `hmac` takes only the strong cases: `Core\Hash::Digest::Md5`, `Sha1`, `Crc32`,
`Crc32c` and `Blake3` are compile errors there, while `of` accepts every case for checksum interop.
Compare two digests with `equals`, which runs in constant time. Input that arrives in pieces goes
through `stream`, which opens a `Core\Hash\Stream`.

```nvs
<?nvs
bytes $digest = Core\Hash::of('abc', Core\Hash::Digest::Sha256);
echo Core\Encoding::toHex($digest), "\n";
echo Core\Encoding::toHex(Core\Hash::of('abc', Core\Hash::Digest::Md5)), "\n";
echo Core\Encoding::toHex(Core\Hash::of('abc', Core\Hash::Digest::Crc32)), "\n";

bytes $key = 'Jefe' as bytes;
bytes $mac = Core\Hash::hmac('what do ya want for nothing?', $key, Core\Hash::Digest::Sha256);
echo Core\Encoding::toHex($mac), "\n";

bytes $again = Core\Hash::of('abc', Core\Hash::Digest::Sha256);
echo Core\Hash::equals($digest, $again) ? 'same' : 'differ', "\n";
echo Core\Hash::equals($digest, Core\Hash::of('abd', Core\Hash::Digest::Sha256)) ? 'same' : 'differ', "\n";
```
```output
ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad
900150983cd24fb0d6963f7d28e17f72
352441c2
5bdcc146bf60754e6a042426089575c75a003f089d2739839dec58b964ec3843
same
differ
```

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Hash::of`](#core-core-hash-of) | `of(bytes\|string $data, Core\Hash::Digest $digest): bytes` |
| [`Core\Hash::hmac`](#core-core-hash-hmac) | `hmac(bytes\|string $data, secret bytes $key, Core\Hash::Digest::Sha224\|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha256\|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha384\|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha512\|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha512_224\|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha512_256\|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha3_224\|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha3_256\|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha3_384\|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha3_512 $digest): bytes` |
| [`Core\Hash::equals`](#core-core-hash-equals) | `equals(bytes $a, bytes $b): bool` |
| [`Core\Hash::stream`](#core-core-hash-stream) | `stream(Core\Hash::Digest $digest): Core\Hash\Stream` |

<a id="core-core-hash-of"></a>
#### `Core\Hash::of`

```nvs skip
Core\Hash::of(bytes|string $data, Core\Hash::Digest $digest): bytes
```

Computes the digest of `$data` with the algorithm `$digest`. The result is raw bytes. It is not hexadecimal text and not an `int`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$data` | `bytes\|string` (neutral) | The data to hash. A `string` is read as its UTF-8 bytes. |
| `$digest` | `Core\Hash::Digest` | The algorithm. Every `Core\Hash::Digest` case is allowed, also the broken ones. |

**Returns** `bytes` — The digest as `bytes`, with the length of the chosen algorithm. Every algorithm accepts any input, also an empty one.

<a id="core-core-hash-hmac"></a>
#### `Core\Hash::hmac`

```nvs skip
Core\Hash::hmac(bytes|string $data, secret bytes $key, Core\Hash::Digest::Sha224|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha256|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha384|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha512|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha512_224|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha512_256|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha3_224|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha3_256|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha3_384|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha3_512 $digest): bytes
```

Computes the HMAC of RFC 2104 for `$data`, with `$key` and the algorithm `$digest`. The result is raw bytes. Only a `StrongDigest` is allowed, so `Digest::Md5` or `Digest::Sha1` does not compile.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$data` | `bytes\|string` (neutral) | The data to sign. A `string` is read as its UTF-8 bytes. |
| `$key` | `secret bytes` (sink) | The secret key, of any length. A long key is hashed first, and a short key is padded with zero bytes, as RFC 2104 § 2 says. |
| `$digest` | `Core\Hash::Digest::Sha224\|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha256\|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha384\|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha512\|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha512_224\|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha512_256\|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha3_224\|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha3_256\|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha3_384\|Core\Hash::Digest::Sha3_512` | The algorithm, one of the ten SHA-2 and SHA-3 `Core\Hash::Digest` cases. |

**Returns** `bytes` — The MAC as `bytes`, with the length of the chosen algorithm.

<a id="core-core-hash-equals"></a>
#### `Core\Hash::equals`

```nvs skip
Core\Hash::equals(bytes $a, bytes $b): bool
```

Compares two digests in constant time. For two values of the same length, the time does not depend on where they first differ.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$a` | `bytes` (neutral) | One digest. |
| `$b` | `bytes` (neutral) | The other digest. |

**Returns** `bool` — `true` when the two have the same bytes, and `false` otherwise. Two values of different lengths return `false` at once. The length of a digest is not a secret.

<a id="core-core-hash-stream"></a>
#### `Core\Hash::stream`

```nvs skip
Core\Hash::stream(Core\Hash::Digest $digest): Core\Hash\Stream
```

Starts a digest with the algorithm `$digest` that you feed in parts. It returns a `Core\Hash\Stream`. Call `update` to add data and `finish` to get the digest.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$digest` | `Core\Hash::Digest` | The algorithm, any `Core\Hash::Digest` case. |

**Returns** `Core\Hash\Stream` — A new, open stream with no data in it yet.

<a id="core-core-hash-stream"></a>
### `Core\Hash\Stream`

Keywords: incremental hash, streaming digest, chunked input, hash a large file, checksum, update, finish

A `Core\Hash\Stream` is opened by `Core\Hash::stream` with a `Core\Hash::Digest` case and digests
everything `update` feeds it, in order, so `finish` answers exactly what `Core\Hash::of` answers
over the concatenation. `finish` consumes the stream: a second `finish`, or an `update` after one,
throws `RuntimeError`. Two digests of one input need two streams.

```nvs
<?nvs
var $stream = Core\Hash::stream(Core\Hash::Digest::Sha256);
$stream->update('a');
$stream->update('bc');
bytes $streamed = $stream->finish();
echo Core\Encoding::toHex($streamed), "\n";

bytes $whole = Core\Hash::of('abc', Core\Hash::Digest::Sha256);
echo Core\Hash::equals($streamed, $whole) ? 'same' : 'differ', "\n";

try {
    $stream->update('more');
} catch (RuntimeError $e) {
    echo "finished\n";
}
```
```output
ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad
same
finished
```

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Hash\Stream->update`](#core-core-hash-stream-update) | `update(bytes\|string $data): void` |
| [`Core\Hash\Stream->finish`](#core-core-hash-stream-finish) | `finish(): bytes` |

<a id="core-core-hash-stream-update"></a>
#### `Core\Hash\Stream->update`

```nvs skip
$stream->update(bytes|string $data): void
```

Adds `$data` to the stream. `finish` computes the digest of all parts in the order they were added.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$data` | `bytes\|string` (neutral) | The next part of the data. A `string` is read as its UTF-8 bytes. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. The stream keeps a reference to `$data` until `finish`.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The stream is already finished. A digest cannot change, so open a new stream.

<a id="core-core-hash-stream-finish"></a>
#### `Core\Hash\Stream->finish`

```nvs skip
$stream->finish(): bytes
```

Closes the stream and returns the digest of everything added with `update`. The result is the same as `Core\Hash::of` on all the parts joined together.

**Returns** `bytes` — The digest as `bytes`. After this call the stream is finished, and its data is freed.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The stream is already finished. A second call to `finish` throws this error.

<a id="core-core-uri"></a>
### `Core\Uri`

Keywords: parse a URL, validate a URL, URL encode, URL decode, form encoding, parse a query string, build a query string, URL, URI, query string, percent-encoding, parse, tryParse, encodeComponent, decodeComponent, encodeFormValue, decodeFormValue, parseQuery, buildQuery, scheme, userInfo, host, port, path, query, fragment, toString, with, queryParameter, withQueryParameter, resolve, compareTo, sign, verifySignature

`Core\Uri::parse` reads a URI *reference* and answers an instance whose readers report each
component exactly as written — still percent-encoded, in its own case. Every reader but `path` is
`?string` (`port` is `?int`) and answers `null` where the component was not written; `tryParse` is
the same read with `null` in place of `RuntimeError`, and is the spelling of "is this text a URI".
`with` and `resolve` answer a fresh `Uri`, and `compareTo` is the normalized content comparison —
`==` on two `Uri` objects is identity. `parseQuery` and `buildQuery` read and write the bracket
convention, and `queryParameter`/`withQueryParameter` are the same convention over **one** parameter
by name — a name `with` cannot take as a bag key, because a bag's keys are declared and a parameter's
name is chosen at run time. The name is top-level, so an array `$value` is what writes `a[b]`; a
`null` `$value` removes the pair, and removing the last one leaves no query at all rather than a bare
`?`. `encodeComponent` writes a space as `%20`, and `encodeFormValue` writes it as `+`.
The two **decoders answer `bytes`**, because percent-decoding is defined over octets and a client may
send any of them: `Core\Uri::decodeComponent("%FF")` has an answer, and text is one `as string` away —
which throws for octets no `string` can hold, exactly where a `string`-returning decoder would have.
`parseQuery` answers those same octets for a value; a name is the array key, so it is a `string`.

```nvs
<?nvs
var $u = Core\Uri::parse('https://example.com:8443/a/b%20c?x=1&y=2#top');
echo $u->scheme() ?? '-', ' ', $u->host() ?? '-', ' ', $u->port() ?? 0, "\n";
echo $u->path(), ' ', $u->query() ?? '-', ' ', $u->fragment() ?? '-', "\n";
echo $u->with({ path: '/c', fragment: 'end' })->toString(), "\n";
echo $u->resolve('../d?z=3')->toString(), "\n";

var $rel = Core\Uri::parse('/only/a/path');
echo $rel->scheme() == null ? 'relative' : 'absolute', "\n";
echo Core\Uri::tryParse('http://example.com/a b') == null ? 'not a uri' : 'a uri', "\n";

var $same = Core\Uri::parse('HTTPS://EXAMPLE.com:8443/a/b%20c?x=1&y=2#top');
echo $u->compareTo($same) == 0 ? 'same uri' : 'different', "\n";

var $q = Core\Uri::parseQuery('a=1&b[]=2&b[]=3');
echo Core\Str::join(Core\Arr::keys($q), ','), "\n";
array<mixed> $params = ['name' => 'a b', 'page' => 2];
echo Core\Uri::buildQuery($params), "\n";
echo $u->queryParameter('x') as bytes as string, "\n";
echo $u->withQueryParameter('y', null)->withQueryParameter('z', '3')->toString(), "\n";
echo Core\Uri::encodeComponent('a b&c'), ' ', Core\Uri::encodeFormValue('a b&c'), "\n";
```
```output
https example.com 8443
/a/b%20c x=1&y=2 top
https://example.com:8443/c?x=1&y=2#end
https://example.com:8443/d?z=3
relative
not a uri
same uri
a,b
name=a+b&page=2
1
https://example.com:8443/a/b%20c?x=1&z=3#top
a%20b%26c a+b%26c
```

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Uri::parse`](#core-core-uri-parse) | `parse(string $uri): Core\Uri` |
| [`Core\Uri::tryParse`](#core-core-uri-tryparse) | `tryParse(string $uri): ?Core\Uri` |
| [`Core\Uri::encodeComponent`](#core-core-uri-encodecomponent) | `encodeComponent(string $s): string` |
| [`Core\Uri::decodeComponent`](#core-core-uri-decodecomponent) | `decodeComponent(string $s): bytes` |
| [`Core\Uri::encodeFormValue`](#core-core-uri-encodeformvalue) | `encodeFormValue(string $s): string` |
| [`Core\Uri::decodeFormValue`](#core-core-uri-decodeformvalue) | `decodeFormValue(string $s): bytes` |
| [`Core\Uri::parseQuery`](#core-core-uri-parsequery) | `parseQuery(string $query): array<mixed>` |
| [`Core\Uri::buildQuery`](#core-core-uri-buildquery) | `buildQuery(array<mixed> $parameters): string` |
| [`Core\Uri->scheme`](#core-core-uri-scheme) | `scheme(): ?string` |
| [`Core\Uri->userInfo`](#core-core-uri-userinfo) | `userInfo(): ?string` |
| [`Core\Uri->host`](#core-core-uri-host) | `host(): ?string` |
| [`Core\Uri->port`](#core-core-uri-port) | `port(): ?int` |
| [`Core\Uri->path`](#core-core-uri-path) | `path(): string` |
| [`Core\Uri->query`](#core-core-uri-query) | `query(): ?string` |
| [`Core\Uri->fragment`](#core-core-uri-fragment) | `fragment(): ?string` |
| [`Core\Uri->toString`](#core-core-uri-tostring) | `toString(): string` |
| [`Core\Uri->with`](#core-core-uri-with) | `with({ scheme?: string, host?: string, port?: ?int, path?: string, query?: ?string, fragment?: ?string }): Core\Uri` |
| [`Core\Uri->queryParameter`](#core-core-uri-queryparameter) | `queryParameter(string $name): mixed` |
| [`Core\Uri->withQueryParameter`](#core-core-uri-withqueryparameter) | `withQueryParameter(string $name, mixed $value): Core\Uri` |
