<a id="core-core-config"></a>
### `Core\Config`

Keywords: nvs.toml, configuration, setting, read a setting, change a setting at run time, directive, [limits], memory, cpu_time, time limit, hard ceiling, get, set, restore, all, setting, secret

`Core\Config` reads and moves the configuration in force for the current request. Every value crosses as a
`string`, spelled as `nvs.toml` would spell it (`"512M"`, `"30s"`); a directive is named with dots
(`log.level`), and a bare limit name — `memory`, `cpu_time`, `wall_time`, `max_tasks`, `max_output` — is the
`[limits]` entry. `set` changes a directive for this request alone and answers `false`, leaving the value in
place, for anything it may not do: a directive only the file may set, an unknown name, a value of the wrong
shape, or a value above the `[limits.hard]` ceiling the operator kept. When `[limits.hard]` does not
set a limit, its ceiling is the value the request started with, so a program cannot raise it. A program you
start from the command line is the one exception: with no `[limits.hard] memory`, it may raise `memory` to any value. `restore` puts the file's value back,
or the built-in default when the file does not write the key. `get` and `all` give the built-in default of every key the file
does not write, such as `128M` for `memory`. A key with no default, such as `wall_time`, is `null`.

```toml file=nvs.toml
[limits]
memory = "256M"

[limits.hard]
memory = "512M"
```
```nvs
<?nvs
echo 'memory=', Core\Config::get('memory') ?? 'unset', "\n";

echo Core\Config::set('memory', '512M') ? 'raised to the ceiling' : 'refused', "\n";
echo Core\Config::set('memory', '1G') ? 'raised past it' : 'refused past the ceiling', "\n";
echo 'now=', Core\Config::get('limits.memory') ?? 'unset', "\n";

Core\Config::restore('memory');
echo 'restored=', Core\Config::get('memory') ?? 'unset', "\n";

echo Core\Config::set('no.such.directive', '1') ? 'set' : 'unknown name refused', "\n";
```
```output
memory=256M
raised to the ceiling
refused past the ceiling
now=512M
restored=256M
unknown name refused
```

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Config::get`](#core-core-config-get) | `get(string $name): ?string` |
| [`Core\Config::set`](#core-core-config-set) | `set(string $name, string $value): bool` |
| [`Core\Config::restore`](#core-core-config-restore) | `restore(string $name): void` |
| [`Core\Config::all`](#core-core-config-all) | `all(): array<string>` |
| [`Core\Config::setting`](#core-core-config-setting) | `setting(string $name): ?string\|int\|float\|bool\|array<mixed>` |
| [`Core\Config::secret`](#core-core-config-secret) | `secret(string $name): ?secret string` |

<a id="core-core-config-get"></a>
#### `Core\Config::get`

```nvs skip
Core\Config::get(string $name): ?string
```

Returns the value of one setting for this request. A setting this request changed with `set` gives the new value. Any other setting gives the value from the configuration file, or its built-in default.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$name` | `string` (neutral) | The dotted name of the setting, such as `log.level`. A limit name alone is the setting of that name in `[limits]`. The limit names are `memory`, `cpu_time`, `wall_time`, `max_tasks`, `max_output` and `max_regex_steps`. |

**Returns** `?string` — The value as text, written the way the configuration file writes it, such as `128M` or `30s`. The result is `null` for a setting with no default, such as `wall_time`. It is also `null` for a name that has a group of settings or a list. A secret setting, such as `db.main.password` or `http.csrf_key`, gives a `?secret string`. Your program cannot print it or write it to a log.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The name is a secret setting, and the call does not write it as a string literal. Write the name in the call, such as `Core\Config::get('db.main.password')`.

<a id="core-core-config-set"></a>
#### `Core\Config::set`

```nvs skip
Core\Config::set(string $name, string $value): bool
```

Changes a setting for this request only. Other requests do not see the change, and it ends when this request ends.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$name` | `string` (neutral) | The name of the setting, in the same form that `get` uses. |
| `$value` | `string` (neutral) | The value, written the way the configuration file writes it, such as `512M`, `30s` or `64`. |

**Returns** `bool` — `true` when the change was made. `false` when it is not allowed, and the previous value stays in place. It is not allowed for a setting that only `nvs.toml` may set, or for a name that is not a setting. It is not allowed for a value that is not a valid size, duration or count. It is not allowed for a value above the limit's ceiling. The ceiling is `[limits.hard]`, or the value the program started with when `[limits.hard]` does not set that limit. `set` never throws an error.

<a id="core-core-config-restore"></a>
#### `Core\Config::restore`

```nvs skip
Core\Config::restore(string $name): void
```

Deletes this request's change to one setting. The value from the configuration file is in force again, or the built-in default when the file does not write the setting.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$name` | `string` (neutral) | The name of the setting, in the same form that `get` uses. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. A name this request never changed is not an error. There is nothing to undo.

<a id="core-core-config-all"></a>
#### `Core\Config::all`

```nvs skip
Core\Config::all(): array<string>
```

Returns every setting in force for this request, with the dotted names as keys. A setting this request changed has the new value. A setting the configuration file does not write has its built-in default.

**Returns** `array<string>` — An `array<string, string>` sorted by name, with one entry per value. A name that has a group of settings gives one entry for each setting in it. A name that has a list gives no entry. A secret setting, such as `db.main.password` or `http.csrf_key`, has the value `<secret>`. `get` returns the real value.

<a id="core-core-config-setting"></a>
#### `Core\Config::setting`

```nvs skip
Core\Config::setting(string $name): ?string|int|float|bool|array<mixed>
```

Returns a value your program reads from the `[settings]` block of `nvs.toml`. A value in the `[app.settings]` block of the application replaces the value in `[settings]`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$name` | `string` (neutral) | The name of the value, such as `page_size`. A value in a table, such as `[settings.api]` with `base = "..."`, has the name `api.base`. |

**Returns** `?string|int|float|bool|array<mixed>` — The value with the type it has in the file. A TOML string is a `string`, an integer is an `int`, a float is a `float` and a boolean is a `bool`. A TOML array is an array, and a table is an array with the names as keys. The result is `null` when no block sets the name. Use `as` to convert it: `Core\Config::setting('page_size') as int` throws an error when the value is missing or is not a whole number.

<a id="core-core-config-secret"></a>
#### `Core\Config::secret`

```nvs skip
Core\Config::secret(string $name): ?secret string
```

Returns a secret your program reads from the `[secrets]` block of `nvs.toml`, such as an API key. A secret in the `[app.secrets]` block of the application replaces the one in `[secrets]`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$name` | `string` (sink) | The name of the secret, such as `api_key`. The block may write the value, or read it from a file with `api_key_file`. The name cannot come from the request. |

**Returns** `?secret string` — The secret as a `?secret string`. Your program cannot print it or write it to a log. You can send it in an outgoing header, a form field or a database parameter. The result is `null` when no block sets the name.

<a id="core-core-env"></a>
### `Core\Env`

Keywords: get, secret, all, mode, context

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Env::get`](#core-core-env-get) | `get(string $name): ?tainted string` |
| [`Core\Env::secret`](#core-core-env-secret) | `secret(string $name): ?secret string` |
| [`Core\Env::all`](#core-core-env-all) | `all(): array<tainted string>` |
| [`Core\Env::mode`](#core-core-env-mode) | `mode(): Core\Env::Mode` |
| [`Core\Env::context`](#core-core-env-context) | `context(): Core\Env::Context` |
| `Core\Env::EOL` | `string` = `"\n" ("\r\n" on Windows)` — The line ending this platform writes: `\r\n` on Windows and `\n` everywhere else. Use it to write text in the platform's own format. `Core\Str::lines` and `Core\IO::lines` do not use it, and split on all three line endings. |
| `Core\Env::OS` | `Core\Env::Platform` = `Core\Env::Platform::Linux (Windows or Darwin per platform)` — The operating system family, as a `Core\Env::Platform` case. Compare it with a case, such as `Core\Env::OS == Core\Env::Platform::Windows`. |
| `Core\Env::VERSION` | `string` = `"0.0.1"` — This runtime's version: three numbers separated by dots, the same string `nvs info` prints. To compare versions, split it with `Core\Str::split` and compare the numbers. |

<a id="core-core-env-get"></a>
#### `Core\Env::get`

```nvs skip
Core\Env::get(string $name): ?tainted string
```

Returns the value of the environment variable `$name`. The environment is read-only, so a program cannot change a variable.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$name` | `string` (sink) | The variable's name, with the same case as in the environment. It may not be `tainted`. A request that could choose the name could read every variable, one at a time. |

**Returns** `?tainted string` — The value as a `tainted string`, or `null` if the variable is not set. The value is `tainted` because it comes from outside the program. Clean it before you use it in SQL, HTML or a shell command.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The variable contains bytes that are not valid UTF-8, so its value is not a `string`. The method does not return `null` here, because `null` means the variable is not set. It does not repair the bytes either.

<a id="core-core-env-secret"></a>
#### `Core\Env::secret`

```nvs skip
Core\Env::secret(string $name): ?secret string
```

Returns the value of the environment variable `$name` as a `secret string`. Use it for a password or an API key. The value can go into an outbound HTTP header, a form field or a database password. `echo`, a log and a response body do not accept it.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$name` | `string` (sink) | The variable's name. It may not be `tainted`, so a request cannot choose which secret the program reads. |

**Returns** `?secret string` — The value as a `secret string`, or `null` if the variable is not set.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The variable contains bytes that are not valid UTF-8, so its value is not a `string`. The message names the variable and not its value.

<a id="core-core-env-all"></a>
#### `Core\Env::all`

```nvs skip
Core\Env::all(): array<tainted string>
```

Returns every environment variable, with the variable names as keys.

**Returns** `array<tainted string>` — An `array<string, tainted string>`, sorted by name. Every call returns the same order, on every platform. A variable whose name or value is not valid UTF-8 is left out. `get` with that name throws an error for it.

<a id="core-core-env-mode"></a>
#### `Core\Env::mode`

```nvs skip
Core\Env::mode(): Core\Env::Mode
```

Returns the mode the program runs in: production or development. You set the mode in `nvs.toml`, and `Core\Config` reads it like every other setting. No environment variable changes it, so a request cannot choose the mode.

**Returns** `Core\Env::Mode` — The mode as a `Core\Env::Mode` case. If the configuration does not set a mode, the result is `Production`, the stricter mode.

<a id="core-core-env-context"></a>
#### `Core\Env::context`

```nvs skip
Core\Env::context(): Core\Env::Context
```

Which kind of run the code is in: an HTTP request, a command-line program, a spawned script, a scheduled script, a queued job, a test or a connection. Use it to choose what a program does in each one.

**Returns** `Core\Env::Context` — The kind of run as a `Core\Env::Context` case. It is the same value for the whole run and for every task the run starts.

<a id="core-core-cap"></a>
### `Core\Cap`

Keywords: has

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Cap::has`](#core-core-cap-has) | `has(string $capability): bool` |

<a id="core-core-cap-has"></a>
#### `Core\Cap::has`

```nvs skip
Core\Cap::has(string $capability): bool
```

Checks whether the code running here has `$capability` at this point in the request. The check starts from the capabilities in `nvs.toml`. Any capability that the request or an enclosing isolate gave up is removed. This call grants nothing, and the guarded code is still checked when it runs.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$capability` | `string` (neutral) | A capability name as `nvs.toml` writes it, such as `fs.read` or `net.connect`. A literal name that is not a capability does not compile. A computed name that is not a capability returns `false`. |

**Returns** `bool` — `true` when the capability is granted for at least something, and `false` otherwise. A `true` does not mean every path or host is allowed. A grant limited to some paths still throws an error for a path outside them.

<a id="core-core-server"></a>
### `Core\Server`

Keywords: isDraining, traceId

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Server::isDraining`](#core-core-server-isdraining) | `isDraining(): bool` |
| [`Core\Server::traceId`](#core-core-server-traceid) | `traceId(): string` |

<a id="core-core-server-isdraining"></a>
#### `Core\Server::isDraining`

```nvs skip
Core\Server::isDraining(): bool
```

Returns `true` when the server has started to shut down. From then on, the server accepts no new connections and finishes the requests it already has.

**Returns** `bool` — `true` after the server stopped accepting new connections. `false` while it still accepts them. A program that no server runs, such as a command-line program, always gets `false`.

<a id="core-core-server-traceid"></a>
#### `Core\Server::traceId`

```nvs skip
Core\Server::traceId(): string
```

Returns the id of the current request. Every request has one. The server writes the same id into its log lines and into the `traceresponse` header of the response.

**Returns** `string` — 32 lower-case hexadecimal characters. If the request came with a `traceparent` header, the id is the one in that header.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The program is not handling a request. This is the case in a command-line program or a test.

<a id="core-core-signal"></a>
### `Core\Signal`

Keywords: onShutdown

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Signal::onShutdown`](#core-core-signal-onshutdown) | `onShutdown(callable(): mixed $handler): void` |

<a id="core-core-signal-onshutdown"></a>
#### `Core\Signal::onShutdown`

```nvs skip
Core\Signal::onShutdown(callable(): mixed $handler): void
```

Registers a function that runs when the process gets a signal to stop. The signal can come from Ctrl-C, from `SIGTERM`, or from the person who stops the server. The function runs once, between two statements. At that time `Core\Server::isDraining()` already returns `true`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$handler` | `callable(): mixed` | The function to run. It gets no arguments and returns nothing. Every stop signal has the same effect, so the function cannot tell which one arrived. If it throws an error or reaches the request's memory limit, the rest of it does not run. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. Each request has its own function, and a second call replaces the first. The function is deleted when the request ends, and other requests cannot see it. It cannot stop the shutdown or delay it.

<a id="core-core-budget"></a>
### `Core\Budget`

Keywords: memoryHeld, memoryPeak, memoryLimit

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Budget::memoryHeld`](#core-core-budget-memoryheld) | `memoryHeld(): uint` |
| [`Core\Budget::memoryPeak`](#core-core-budget-memorypeak) | `memoryPeak(): uint` |
| [`Core\Budget::memoryLimit`](#core-core-budget-memorylimit) | `memoryLimit(): uint` |

<a id="core-core-budget-memoryheld"></a>
#### `Core\Budget::memoryHeld`

```nvs skip
Core\Budget::memoryHeld(): uint
```

Returns the number of bytes **this request** uses right now. Novis frees a value as soon as nothing uses it. So the number goes down again when a request is done with a large value.

**Returns** `uint` — The number of bytes this request uses. It does not count the rest of the server process. `Core\Os::residentBytes` returns the memory of the whole process.

<a id="core-core-budget-memorypeak"></a>
#### `Core\Budget::memoryPeak`

```nvs skip
Core\Budget::memoryPeak(): uint
```

Returns the highest value `memoryHeld()` has had during this request. The number is recorded at every allocation, so it includes memory that was already freed again.

**Returns** `uint` — The highest number of bytes this request has used. It is never below what `memoryHeld()` returns. A program cannot reset it.

<a id="core-core-budget-memorylimit"></a>
#### `Core\Budget::memoryLimit`

```nvs skip
Core\Budget::memoryLimit(): uint
```

Returns the memory limit that `memoryHeld()` and `memoryPeak()` are measured against. It is the `[limits] memory` setting in bytes, minus the memory reserved for the limit handler. You do not need to parse `Core\Config::get('limits.memory')` yourself.

**Returns** `uint` — The limit in bytes. It is `0` when the request has no memory limit.

<a id="core-core-request"></a>
### `Core\Request`

Keywords: request, query string, query parameters, form fields, POST data, cookies, headers, request body, JSON body, multipart, upload, HEAD, request method, path, tainted input, method, isHead, path, query, queryArray, queryAs, header, headers, cookie, body, bytes, json, jsonAs, bodyStream, files, post, postArray, postAs, clientIp, scheme, host, route, mount

`Core\Request` is the whole of what arrived: `method`, `isHead`, `path`, `query`, `header`, `headers`,
`cookie` and the body readers, plus `route` and `mount` for where the router put it. The host never
fills a variable for the program. No lookup merges the query, the form fields and the cookies into
one. Every member throws `LogicError` in a program that is
not answering a request, so a CLI run, a scheduled script and a job worker say "no request arrived"
rather than answering empty.

**The body is read once, and every reader is one of two kinds.** `body()`, `post()`, `postAs<T>()`,
`json()` and `jsonAs<T>()` **buffer**: the first of them fills the request's hold, bounded by
`[limits] request_body`, and any of the five may follow any other in any order and answer the same
octets. `bodyStream()` and
`files()` **stream**: they hand the octets over as they arrive, keep none, and so consume the body — a
reader after one of those is refused, naming the member that consumed it. That refusal is a defect in
the program, never something a peer can provoke.

`json()` decodes the body as one JSON document and answers `mixed`; `jsonAs<T>()` hydrates it straight
into a class carrying `#[Core\Json\Derive]`, exactly as `Core\Json::decodeAs` does, so a handler names
the shape it expects instead of walking an array. Neither consults the `Content-Type` the peer
declared — a header is what a peer wrote, not what a body is — and both throw `ParseError` on a
document that is malformed, too deep, or absent altogether. `json()` keeps what it decoded and
`jsonAs<T>()` hydrates per call, so writing to what a second call answered leaves the first alone.

`queryAs<T>()` and `postAs<T>()` are that idea over the parameters rather than the body: each reads what
`query()` and `post()` parse as the type written at the call site — an inline shape, `{ page: uint }`, or a
class carrying `#[Core\Json\Derive]` — converting every named field with `as` and leaving the keys the
type does not name behind. Called with nothing, the whole parameter set is the subject, and that is the
only way a program reaches it: there is no `query(): array<mixed>`. Called with
`{ name: "filter" }`, the subject is the one bracket-named subtree under that name. A field that is absent,
or that holds a value `as` refuses for its declared type, is a `ParseError` listing every field that
failed at its own path — so a form reports the whole list rather than the first item of it.

Everything a peer chose is `tainted`, including the path, every header and the body, so it reaches a
sink only through a launderer named for that sink — `echo` escapes for HTML on its own. A class hydrated
from a body declares that on the fields receiving it: an unqualified `string` property is a compile
error at the `jsonAs<T>()` call rather than a silent laundering.

```nvs skip
<?nvs
#[Core\Json\Derive]
class Author
{
    public tainted string $name;
    public int $tags;

    public function constructor(tainted string $name, int $tags)
    {
        $this->name = $name;
        $this->tags = $tags;
    }
}

if (Core\Request::method() == Core\Http\Method::Post) {
    Author $author = Core\Request::jsonAs<Author>();
    echo 'hello ', $author->name, "\n";
}
```

That one needs a request in front of it; `examples/json-body.nvs` is the same program as a fixture, run
with `nvs run --request <file>`, which answers the request a file describes without standing a listener
up. Without one, this is what every member does:

```nvs
<?nvs
try {
    Core\Request::method();
    echo "not reached\n";
} catch (LogicError $none) {
    echo "no request here\n";
}
```
```output
no request here
```

<a id="core-core-request-method"></a>
#### `Core\Request::method`

```nvs skip
Core\Request::method(): Core\Http\Method
```

Returns the method of the request, such as `GET` or `POST`, as a case of `Core\Http\Method`. A `HEAD` request returns `Get`. Use `isHead` to tell the two apart.

**Returns** `Core\Http\Method` — The `Core\Http\Method` case of the request. It is never `Head`.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The program is not handling a request, such as a command-line program or a test. It is also thrown when the method is not one of the cases of `Core\Http\Method`. The server answers such a request with `501` before your program runs.

<a id="core-core-request-ishead"></a>
#### `Core\Request::isHead`

```nvs skip
Core\Request::isHead(): bool
```

Checks whether the request is a `HEAD` request. `method` returns `Get` for a `HEAD` request, so this is the only way to tell the two apart.

**Returns** `bool` — `true` when the request method is `HEAD`, and `false` for every other method. The server sends no body in the response to a `HEAD` request, so a program can skip the work of building one.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The program is not handling a request.

<a id="core-core-request-path"></a>
#### `Core\Request::path`

```nvs skip
Core\Request::path(): tainted string
```

Returns the request path without the prefix of the mount that matched. An application reads the same paths wherever it is mounted.

**Returns** `tainted string` — The rest of the path after the mount prefix, percent-encoded as it arrived. It is `tainted`. `mount()` returns the prefix that was removed.

**Throws** `LogicError` — This program is not handling a request.

<a id="core-core-request-query"></a>
#### `Core\Request::query`

```nvs skip
Core\Request::query(string $name): ?tainted string
```

Returns one query-string parameter by its name, as text. The query is read the same way `Core\Uri::parseQuery` reads it.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$name` | `string` (neutral) | The parameter's name, decoded. Upper and lower case are different. |

**Returns** `?tainted string` — The parameter's value as a `tainted string`, or `null` when the query has no parameter with this name. A name with square brackets, such as `tag[]=a`, also gives `null`. Read those values with `queryArray`. Use `as` to convert the text, for example `as ?int`.

**Throws** `LogicError` — This program is not handling a request.; `RuntimeError` — The query string has a percent escape that decodes to bytes that are not UTF-8.

<a id="core-core-request-queryarray"></a>
#### `Core\Request::queryArray`

```nvs skip
Core\Request::queryArray(string $name): array<tainted string>
```

Returns every value of one query-string parameter that has square brackets, such as `tag[]=a&tag[]=b`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$name` | `string` (neutral) | The parameter's name without the brackets. For `tag[]=a`, the name is `tag`. |

**Returns** `array<tainted string>` — An `array<tainted string>`. `tag[]=a&tag[]=b` gives `["a", "b"]`, and `filter[color]=red` gives `["color" => "red"]`. A name without brackets gives an array with its one value. A name that is not in the query gives an empty array.

**Throws** `LogicError` — This program is not handling a request.; `RuntimeError` — The query string has a percent escape that decodes to bytes that are not UTF-8.; `ParseError` — A value under this name has a second pair of brackets, such as `tag[a][b]=c`. Read nested values with `queryAs`.

<a id="core-core-request-queryas"></a>
#### `Core\Request::queryAs`

```nvs skip
Core\Request::queryAs<T>({ name?: string }): T
```

Reads the query string as the type `T` that you write at the call. It works like `Core\Arr::shapeAs` on what `query` reads, and converts each field with `as`. Without `name`, it reads all parameters. With `name`, it reads the nested value under that name.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `{ name: … }` | `string` (default `null`, neutral) | The parameter whose nested value is read, written without brackets. Brackets work the same way as in `query`. If you leave it out, the whole query string is read. |

**Returns** `T` — A new `T` with every field of its declared type, or one `T` for each entry for an `array<T>`. Nothing is kept. Every call reads the query string again, so two callers never get the same object.

**Throws** `LogicError` — This program is not handling a request. Or the query string has percent escapes that decode to bytes that are not UTF-8. Or `T` is a class without `#[Json\Derive]`.; `ParseError` — A field that `T` needs is missing, or `as` cannot convert its value to the declared type. It is also thrown when the value under `name` is not a set of fields. The error has one issue for each wrong field, at its own dotted path, so a form can show the whole list.

<a id="core-core-request-header"></a>
#### `Core\Request::header`

```nvs skip
Core\Request::header(string $name): ?tainted string
```

Returns the value of one request header by its name.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$name` | `string` (neutral) | The name of the header. Upper and lower case do not matter, so `Content-Type` and `content-type` are the same header. |

**Returns** `?tainted string` — The value as a `tainted` string, exactly as it arrived. The result is `null` when the request has no header of that name. When the header arrived on more than one line, the values are joined with `, ` in the order they arrived. `headers()` returns each line on its own.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The program is not handling a request.; `ParseError` — The value of this header is not valid UTF-8.

<a id="core-core-request-headers"></a>
#### `Core\Request::headers`

```nvs skip
Core\Request::headers(): array<array<tainted string>>
```

Returns every header of the request, grouped by name.

**Returns** `array<array<tainted string>>` — An `array<array<tainted string>>`. Each key is a header name in lower case. Its value is a list with one entry for each line of that header, in the order the lines arrived. The array is empty when the request has no headers.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The program is not handling a request.; `ParseError` — The value of a header is not valid UTF-8.

<a id="core-core-request-cookie"></a>
#### `Core\Request::cookie`

```nvs skip
Core\Request::cookie(string $name): ?tainted string
```

Returns the value of one cookie by its name.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$name` | `string` (neutral) | The name of the cookie, exactly as it was set. Upper and lower case are different, and `a.b` and `a_b` are two different cookies. |

**Returns** `?tainted string` — The value as a `tainted` string, exactly as it arrived. Nothing is decoded. The result is `null` when the request has no cookie of that name. When the name starts with `__Host-` and the cookie arrived twice, the result is `null` too.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The program is not handling a request.; `ParseError` — The value of this cookie is not valid UTF-8.

<a id="core-core-request-body"></a>
#### `Core\Request::body`

```nvs skip
Core\Request::body(): tainted string
```

Returns the whole request body as one string.

**Returns** `tainted string` — Every byte the client sent, in order and unchanged. The string is `tainted`. It is empty when the request has no body, and every call returns the same string.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The program is not handling a request. Or `bodyStream` or `files` already read the body, and those two do not keep it.; `RuntimeError` — The body is larger than `[limits] request_body`. The bytes past that limit are never stored.; `IOError` — The connection failed while the body arrived, or the client sent fewer bytes than its `Content-Length` said.; `ParseError` — The body is not valid UTF-8, so it cannot be a `string`. `bytes` returns the same body as `bytes`.

<a id="core-core-request-bytes"></a>
#### `Core\Request::bytes`

```nvs skip
Core\Request::bytes(): tainted bytes
```

Returns the whole request body as `bytes`. Use it for a body that is not text, such as an uploaded file.

**Returns** `tainted bytes` — Every byte the client sent, in order and unchanged. The value is `tainted`. It is empty when the request has no body. A body that is not valid UTF-8 is returned too, where `body` throws an error.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The program is not handling a request. Or `bodyStream` or `files` already read the body, and those two do not keep it.; `RuntimeError` — The body is larger than `[limits] request_body`. The bytes past that limit are never stored.; `IOError` — The connection failed while the body arrived, or the client sent fewer bytes than its `Content-Length` said.

<a id="core-core-request-json"></a>
#### `Core\Request::json`

```nvs skip
Core\Request::json({ maxDepth?: uint }): mixed
```

Reads the request body as one JSON document and returns the decoded value.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `{ maxDepth: … }` | `uint` (default `512`) | How deep the document may nest. The default is 512, and the value must be from 1 to 1024. A document with no array or object in it has depth 1. |

**Returns** `mixed` — The decoded value, the same as `Core\Json::decode` returns for the body. A JSON object becomes an array with string keys. Every string in it is `tainted`. Every call returns the same value.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The program is not handling a request. Or `bodyStream` or `files` already read the body, and those two do not keep it. Or `maxDepth` is not from 1 to 1024.; `ParseError` — The body is not one whole JSON document, or it nests deeper than `maxDepth`. An empty body throws this error too. The `Content-Type` header is not checked.; `RuntimeError` — The body is larger than `[limits] request_body`. The bytes past that limit are never stored.; `IOError` — The connection failed while the body arrived, or the client sent fewer bytes than its `Content-Length` said.

<a id="core-core-request-jsonas"></a>
#### `Core\Request::jsonAs`

```nvs skip
Core\Request::jsonAs<T>({ maxDepth?: uint }): T
```

Reads the request body as one JSON object and returns a new instance of the class `T`. The class needs `#[Core\Json\Derive]`. Write `array<T>` to read a JSON array with one object for each element.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `{ maxDepth: … }` | `uint` (default `512`) | How deep the document may nest. The default is 512, and the value must be from 1 to 1024. A document with no array or object in it has depth 1. |

**Returns** `T` — A new `T` with its properties read from the body, or one `T` for each element for an `array<T>`. Every call creates new objects, so two callers never get the same object.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The program is not handling a request. Or `bodyStream` or `files` already read the body, and those two do not keep it. Or `T` has no `#[Core\Json\Derive]` attribute. Or `maxDepth` is not from 1 to 1024.; `ParseError` — The body is not one whole JSON object, or it nests deeper than `maxDepth`. An empty body throws this error too. It is also thrown when a field is missing or has the wrong type. The `issues` list has one entry for each wrong field. The `Content-Type` header is not checked.; `RecursionError` — The call stack is full when a constructor runs. This happens when the call starts with the stack almost full, or when a constructor recurses deeply. A deep body within `maxDepth` does not throw this error.; `RuntimeError` — The body is larger than `[limits] request_body`. The bytes past that limit are never stored.; `IOError` — The connection failed while the body arrived, or the client sent fewer bytes than its `Content-Length` said.

<a id="core-core-request-bodystream"></a>
#### `Core\Request::bodyStream`

```nvs skip
Core\Request::bodyStream(): Core\Request\BodyStream
```

Returns the request body in pieces, in the order they arrive. Use it for a large body that you do not want in memory all at once.

**Returns** `Core\Request\BodyStream` — A value that a `foreach` loop reads once. Each piece is a `tainted bytes` value. How the body is split has no meaning. The loop runs zero times when the request has no body.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The program is not handling a request. Or `body`, `bytes`, `json`, `files` or `bodyStream` already read the body. After this call, those methods throw this error too.; `IOError` — The connection failed while the loop read the body. The pieces before the failure are still given to the loop.

<a id="core-core-request-files"></a>
#### `Core\Request::files`

```nvs skip
Core\Request::files(): Core\Request\Files
```

Returns the files that a form uploaded, one at a time in a `foreach` loop.

**Returns** `Core\Request\Files` — An `Iterable<Core\Request\Part>`. Each loop step gives the next file as it arrives. The text fields are not in the loop, and `post` reads them after it. The loop runs zero times when the request has no `multipart/form-data` body.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The program is not handling a request. Or `body`, `bodyStream` or `post` already read the body. After this call, `body`, `bytes`, `bodyStream` and `json` throw this error too. `post` still works after the loop.; `ParseError` — The request says it has a `multipart/form-data` body, but its `boundary` is missing, given twice or not valid. Or the body does not have the form that the request declared. Or the name, file name or `Content-Type` of a part is not valid UTF-8.; `IOError` — The connection failed while the loop read the body, or the body ended before its last boundary.

<a id="core-core-request-post"></a>
#### `Core\Request::post`

```nvs skip
Core\Request::post(string $name): ?tainted string
```

Returns one submitted form field by its name, as text. The fields are read the same way `query` reads them. The body can be `multipart/form-data`, where the parts that are not files are read, or urlencoded.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$name` | `string` (neutral) | The field's name, as the form declared it. Upper and lower case are different. |

**Returns** `?tainted string` — The field's value as a `tainted string`, or `null` when the form has no field with this name. A name with square brackets, such as `item[]=pen`, also gives `null`. Read those values with `postArray`. This method reads the body to its end. On a `multipart/form-data` request, call it **after** `files()`, because it skips the uploads on its way to the last field.

**Throws** `LogicError` — This program is not handling a request, or `body` or `bodyStream` already read the body of this request. Calling `post` after `files()` is allowed.; `ParseError` — The body is not the form it says it is, or a `multipart/form-data` body has no boundary.; `RuntimeError` — The name or value of a field is not valid UTF-8. In an urlencoded form, this includes a percent escape that decodes to bytes that are not UTF-8.; `IOError` — The connection failed while the body was read, or the body ended before the length it declared.

<a id="core-core-request-postarray"></a>
#### `Core\Request::postArray`

```nvs skip
Core\Request::postArray(string $name): array<tainted string>
```

Returns every value of one form field that has square brackets, such as `item[]=pen&item[]=book`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$name` | `string` (neutral) | The field's name without the brackets. For `item[]=pen`, the name is `item`. |

**Returns** `array<tainted string>` — An `array<tainted string>`. `item[]=pen&item[]=book` gives `["pen", "book"]`, and `size[shirt]=M` gives `["shirt" => "M"]`. A name without brackets gives an array with its one value. A name that is not in the form gives an empty array. Like `post`, this method reads the body to its end, so call it **after** `files()`.

**Throws** `LogicError` — This program is not handling a request, or `body` or `bodyStream` already read the body of this request.; `ParseError` — The body is not the form it says it is, or a value under this name has a second pair of brackets, such as `item[a][b]=c`. Read nested values with `postAs`.; `RuntimeError` — The name or value of a field is not valid UTF-8. In an urlencoded form, this includes a percent escape that decodes to bytes that are not UTF-8.; `IOError` — The connection failed while the body was read, or the body ended before the length it declared.

<a id="core-core-request-postas"></a>
#### `Core\Request::postAs`

```nvs skip
Core\Request::postAs<T>({ name?: string }): T
```

Reads the submitted form as the type `T` that you write at the call. It works like `Core\Arr::shapeAs` on what `post` reads, and converts each field with `as`. Without `name`, it reads the whole form. With `name`, it reads the nested value under that name.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `{ name: … }` | `string` (default `null`, neutral) | The field whose nested value is read, written without brackets. Brackets work the same way as in `post`. If you leave it out, the whole form is read. |

**Returns** `T` — A new `T` with every field of its declared type, or one `T` for each entry for an `array<T>`. Like `post`, this method reads the body to its end. On a `multipart/form-data` request, call it **after** the `files()` loop. Nothing is kept. Every call reads the form again, so two callers never get the same object.

**Throws** `LogicError` — This program is not handling a request. Or `body` or `bodyStream` already read the body of this request. Or `T` is a class without `#[Json\Derive]`.; `ParseError` — The body is not the form it says it is, for the same reasons as in `post`. Or a field that `T` needs is missing, or `as` cannot convert its value to the declared type. Or the value under `name` is not a set of fields. The error has one issue for each wrong field, at its own dotted path.; `IOError` — The connection failed while the body was read, or the body ended before the length it declared.

<a id="core-core-request-clientip"></a>
#### `Core\Request::clientIp`

```nvs skip
Core\Request::clientIp(): ?tainted string
```

Returns the network address of the client that sent this request. Behind a proxy that is listed in `[server] trusted_proxies`, the address comes from `X-Forwarded-For`.

**Returns** `?tainted string` — The address as a `tainted` string, such as `203.0.113.7` or `2001:db8::1`. An IPv6 address is always in its short form. The result is `null` when the request has no address, for example over a Unix socket.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The program is not handling a request. For example, it is a command-line program, a job or a test.

<a id="core-core-request-scheme"></a>
#### `Core\Request::scheme`

```nvs skip
Core\Request::scheme(): tainted string
```

Returns the scheme the request arrived over. A connection without TLS gives `https` only when a trusted proxy sends `X-Forwarded-Proto`.

**Returns** `tainted string` — `"http"` or `"https"`, as a `tainted` string. The result is never `null`, because every request arrived over one of them. A server that trusts no proxy always returns the scheme of the connection itself.

**Throws** `LogicError` — This program is not handling a request. For example, it is a command-line program, a scheduled script, a job worker or a test.

<a id="core-core-request-host"></a>
#### `Core\Request::host`

```nvs skip
Core\Request::host(): ?tainted string
```

Returns the host name the request was sent to, read from its `Host` header.

**Returns** `?tainted string` — The host name as a `tainted` string in lower case. A port and one dot at the end are removed, so `Shop.Example.com.:8443` returns `shop.example.com`. An IPv6 address keeps its brackets. The result is `null` when the request has no `Host` header. `header("host")` returns the header exactly as it arrived, with the port. Headers such as `X-Forwarded-Host` are never read.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The program is not handling a request.

<a id="core-core-request-route"></a>
#### `Core\Request::route`

```nvs skip
Core\Request::route(): ?Core\Router\Match
```

Returns the route this request matched. The server matches the route once, before your program runs. The CSRF check and the `route` metric label use the same match, so a handler never needs to match its own path again.

**Returns** `?Core\Router\Match` — A `Core\Router\Match` with the declared name and the captures of the path. The result is `null` when no route matches this method and path. Such a request is still served like any other, because a match does not decide which code runs. A program with no `#[Route]` has no route table, so the result is also `null`.

**Throws** `LogicError` — This program is not handling a request. For example, it is a command-line program, a scheduled script, a job worker or a test. The method throws this error and does not return `null`, because "no request arrived" and "no route matched" are different things.; `RuntimeError` — A capture percent-decodes to bytes that are not UTF-8, so it cannot be a `tainted string`. The error names the capture and the position of the first byte that is not valid in a `string`.

<a id="core-core-request-mount"></a>
#### `Core\Request::mount`

```nvs skip
Core\Request::mount(): Core\Request\Mount
```

Returns the mount that is serving this request. It gives the prefix the server removed from the path before `path()` returns it. It also gives the glob captures of that mount. A program served for many customers uses them to learn which customer this request is for.

**Returns** `Core\Request\Mount` — A `Core\Request\Mount`. The result is never `null`, because every request reaches the program through a mount. A mount with no prefix and no glob gives the prefix `""` and an empty array of captures.

**Throws** `LogicError` — This program is not handling a request. For example, it is a command-line program, a scheduled script, a job worker or a test. None of these is mounted.

<a id="core-core-request-mount"></a>
### `Core\Request\Mount`

Keywords: SCRIPT_NAME, PATH_INFO, base path, base URL, mount prefix, RewriteBase, subdirectory install, sub-folder deployment, virtual host, multi-tenant, subdomain routing, request URI, prefix, captures

`Core\Request\Mount` is what `Core\Request::mount()` answers with, and it holds two facts about the door
this request arrived at: `prefix()` is what the server took off the front of the path before
`Core\Request::path()` answered it, and `captures()` are the glob captures of the mount row that took the
request, in order — `{1}` is `captures[0]`. One member answers the pair because a request holding one
mount's prefix and another mount's captures is a bug the shape rules out.

**It is never `null`**, where `Core\Request::route()` is. Every request that reached a program reached it
*through* a mount, so a door that strips nothing and holds no glob answers `""` and an empty array rather
than an absence — there is no case to write for "served without a mount". With no request in front of it
at all, naming it refuses the way every reader of `Core\Request` does.

**A mount says where a request arrives and which file answers it, and nothing else.** Its key set is
closed — `prefix`, `host`, `scan`, `entry`, `origin` — and carries no mode, no limits and no capabilities;
what the code answering the request *may do* is the `[[app]]` block's, keyed on the entry file path. The
two usually cover the same tree, and reading one for the other is the mistake this split exists to
prevent: what you learn here is routing, never policy.

**The table expands at boot, not per request.** A `scan` glob is resolved against the disk once at
startup — and again at each configuration reload, in development also under hot reload's revalidation — into
ordinary mounts whose paths were each checked to lie inside `[server] root`. So a prefix reaching a
program is a row an operator wrote, and no path is ever derived from a URL at request time.

That is why the prefix is plain text and **the captures are `tainted`**: which row answers is the peer's
choice, and a capture is exactly what a multi-tenant program keys its data by. A capture reaching a query
or a path launders the way anything else off a request does. Nothing here is cached — both facts live on
the inbound request and this class is a reading of them — so a read costs one instance and one array of
the mount's own captures, a handful of values against a glob's one or two.

```nvs skip
<?nvs
// Served by a mount that scans `*/public/index.nvs` under `[server] root` and
// mounts each match at `/{1}`, so `/acme/orders` arrives here as `/orders`.
Core\Request\Mount $mount = Core\Request::mount();
tainted string $tenant = $mount->captures()[0];

echo 'serving ', $tenant, ' under ', $mount->prefix(), "\n";
```

A program therefore never derives its own base path from the request target, and `Core\Router::url`
prepends the prefix on the way back out, so the same compiled route table serves at `/ModuleA`, at
`/{1}` or at `/` with no recompile. Without a request, the class is unreachable in the ordinary way:

```nvs
<?nvs
try {
    Core\Request::mount();
    echo "not reached\n";
} catch (LogicError $none) {
    echo "nothing was mounted here\n";
}
```
```output
nothing was mounted here
```

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Request\Mount->prefix`](#core-core-request-mount-prefix) | `prefix(): string` |
| [`Core\Request\Mount->captures`](#core-core-request-mount-captures) | `captures(): array<tainted string>` |

<a id="core-core-request-mount-prefix"></a>
#### `Core\Request\Mount->prefix`

```nvs skip
$mount->prefix(): string
```

Returns the part the server removed from the start of the path before `Core\Request::path()` returns it. A program mounted at `/acme` sees `/orders` in `path()`, and `/acme` here.

**Returns** `string` — The prefix, with a slash at the start and none at the end. The result is `""` when the mount removes nothing. It is not `tainted`, because the server configuration sets every mount when the server starts. The prefix is the operator's text, and the client did not choose it.

<a id="core-core-request-mount-captures"></a>
#### `Core\Request\Mount->captures`

```nvs skip
$mount->captures(): array<tainted string>
```

Returns the glob captures of the mount serving this request, in order. `{1}` is `captures[0]`. One program that runs at many prefixes uses them to learn which customer the request is for.

**Returns** `array<tainted string>` — The captures as `tainted string` values. The array is empty for a mount whose prefix has no glob. They are `tainted` because the client chose which mount serves the request. Before you use one in a query or a path, check it as you check any other value from a request.

<a id="core-core-request-bodystream"></a>
### `Core\Request\BodyStream`

Keywords: raw request body, streaming request body, read the body in chunks, large upload, chunked body, chunk, Iterable bytes, memory limit,

`Core\Request\BodyStream` is what `Core\Request::bodyStream()` answers with: an `Iterable<tainted bytes>`
that a `foreach` walks once. It has no members — the walk is everything it does — and it holds nothing
but the chunk the loop body is looking at, so a body far larger than the machine's memory passes through
a program that never has more than one chunk of it resident. That is the whole difference from `body()`,
which fills the request's hold under `[limits] request_body` and can be read back any number of times.
This walk is under no such cap, because what a program keeps out of it is the program's own decision and
its own bill.

**A chunk boundary is the wire's, and carries no meaning.** It is where the octets happened to arrive, so
a program that needs lines, records or frames finds them itself, across chunks; nothing here aligns a
chunk to anything the sender wrote. Each chunk is copied out as the loop body receives it and stays valid
after the next pull, so keeping one keeps bytes the wire cannot revoke. The walk is empty where the
request carried no body at all.

**Naming the walk is the reading.** `bodyStream()` claims the body when the walk is built, long before a
single byte moves, so `body()`, `post()`, `json()`, `jsonAs<T>()` or `files()` after it is refused with
`LogicError` whether or not the loop ever ran — and refused the same way in the other direction. That
refusal is a defect in the program, never something a peer can provoke; the split between the readers
that share the body and the ones that consume it is
`rule:http-server/buffering-readers-share-the-body-and-streaming-readers-consume-it`, and `Core\Request`
is where all five readers are named together.

Every chunk is `tainted bytes`, like everything else a peer chose, so it reaches a sink only through a
launderer named for that sink. The common destination is disk, and `Core\IO::writeStream` takes this walk
directly — it is where every stream reaches a file, under a byte bound of its own, and it removes the
partial file if a write fails, so there is no half-written upload to clean up after.

```nvs skip
<?nvs
int $total = 0;
foreach (Core\Request::bodyStream() as tainted bytes $chunk) {
    $total = $total + Core\Bytes::length($chunk);
}
echo 'read ', $total, " bytes\n";
```

Or spent on a file instead, where the bytes never become a value the program holds. One request carries
one body, so this is the *other* program, not the next few lines of that one:

```nvs skip
<?nvs
Core\IO::writeStream('incoming.bin', Core\Request::bodyStream(), { max: 64 * 1024 * 1024 });
```

Both of those need a request in front of them. Without one, naming the walk is what every other member of
`Core\Request` does:

```nvs
<?nvs
try {
    Core\Request::bodyStream();
    echo "not reached\n";
} catch (LogicError $none) {
    echo "no request here\n";
}
```
```output
no request here
```

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|

<a id="core-core-request-files"></a>
### `Core\Request\Files`

Keywords: file upload, uploaded files, form upload, save an upload, multipart/form-data, large upload, streaming upload, temporary file,

`Core\Request\Files` is what `Core\Request::files()` answers with: an `Iterable<Core\Request\Part>` that a
`foreach` walks once, yielding each uploaded part as it comes off the wire. It has no members — the walk
is everything it does — and it is the only way a program receives an upload. There is no temporary file
and no directory the host chose: nothing lands on disk until the program names a path it holds the
`fs.write` capability for, so an upload nobody saves has cost the machine nothing but the bytes that
crossed the socket.

**The parse runs as the loop does.** The next part does not exist when the walk is named, so `files()`
holds one part at a time and nothing accumulates. A part is valid only while it is the walk's current one:
keeping one past the iteration that opened the next is holding a name for bytes the parse has already
drained, and it is refused rather than answered with the wrong part's content. Advancing past a part the
loop body never read simply drains it — skipping an upload the application does not recognise costs a walk
over bytes the door already charged for, and no memory at all.

**A part is a file part iff its `Content-Disposition` carries a `filename`**, which is RFC 7578's own
distinction and not a second one invented here. Every other part is an ordinary form field: the walk
buffers those as it passes them, and `Core\Request::post()` reads them back afterwards. That is why
`post()` on a `multipart/form-data` request is called **after** this walk and never before — the fields
are behind the uploads on the wire, and reading them first would mean draining the uploads to reach them.

The walk is empty where the request declared no `multipart/form-data` body, which is what a request
carrying no upload is. It throws `LogicError` where the program is not answering a request, or where
`body()`, `bodyStream()` or `post()` already read this body; `ParseError` where the request declared a
multipart body and then did not say how to read one — no `boundary`, two of them, or one outside the
grammar — since an ambiguous body is refused rather than guessed at; and `IOError` where the connection
failed under the body or the peer stopped short of the length it declared.

**What bounds it is the server, not this walk.** `[limits] request_body` bounds what is parsed into
memory and has nothing to say about a streamed body; the server carries at most 256M of one request body,
declared or chunked, refusing an oversize before the program runs and stopping a chunked one at the part
being read. That number is a constant today — the directive that makes it settable per deployment is not
on disk yet.

```nvs skip
<?nvs
foreach (Core\Request::files() as Core\Request\Part $part) {
    string $path = Core\IO::within('uploads', $part->filename());
    $part->saveTo($path);
    echo $part->name(), " saved\n";
}
```

`filename()` is `tainted`, so `Core\IO::within` above is not decoration: it is the one way a name the
client chose reaches a path. Without a request in front of it, naming the walk does what every member of
`Core\Request` does:

```nvs
<?nvs
try {
    Core\Request::files();
    echo "not reached\n";
} catch (LogicError $none) {
    echo "no request here\n";
}
```
```output
no request here
```

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|

<a id="core-core-request-part"></a>
### `Core\Request\Part`

Keywords: uploaded file, upload name, client filename, form field, Content-Disposition, Content-Type, multipart part, read an upload, save an upload, name, filename, contentType, content, readAll, saveTo

A `Core\Request\Part` is one file part of a `multipart/form-data` body, handed to the loop body by the
`Core\Request::files()` walk. Three members say what it declared about itself — `name()`, the form field
it arrived under; `filename()`, the name the client claimed; and `contentType()`, which answers
`text/plain` where the part declared none, RFC 7578's own default rather than a repair of a missing value.
All three are `tainted string`: they are what a peer wrote back, and a client is free to send a field name
the form never declared.

**`filename()` is a claim about a file on someone else's machine, and never a path on this one.** As a
`tainted string` it reaches a path only through `Core\IO::within`, which is the same refusal every other
untrusted string meets — and it is the refusal that matters most here, since the one place an upload could
choose where it lands is the one place the qualifier stands in the way.

**There is no `size`.** Nothing honest can be said about a part's length before it has been consumed, and
inventing a number is the kind of repair this language refuses everywhere. A program that needs the count
gets it from the bytes it read.

**Three ways to spend a part, and each of them spends it.** `readAll({max?})` pulls the whole part into
one `tainted bytes` — the reading for an upload small enough to hold — bounded by `[limits] request_body`
(8M) when `max` is omitted, by that number when it is named, and refusing outright a `max` larger than the
request's own `[limits] memory` rather than quietly clamping it. `content()` walks the part a chunk at a
time, holding none of it, for an upload that must never be resident whole. `saveTo($path, {max?,
overwrite?})` writes it straight to disk one chunk at a time — the path almost every upload takes — under
the `fs.write` capability for that path; it is `Core\IO::writeStream` underneath, so the path must not
already exist unless `overwrite` says so, and a write that fails leaves no partial file behind.

**All of them are valid only while this part is the walk's current one.** A part kept past the iteration
that opened the next names bytes the parse has already drained, so it is refused rather than answered with
the current part's content.

```nvs skip
<?nvs
foreach (Core\Request::files() as Core\Request\Part $part) {
    int $bytes = 0;
    foreach ($part->content() as tainted bytes $chunk) {
        $bytes = $bytes + Core\Bytes::length($chunk);
    }
    echo $part->name(), ' (', $part->filename(), ', ', $part->contentType(), '): ', $bytes, "\n";
}
```

The same part, held whole or sent to disk instead — one part is spent once, so these are two programs and
not two halves of one:

```nvs skip
<?nvs
foreach (Core\Request::files() as Core\Request\Part $part) {
    tainted bytes $whole = $part->readAll({ max: 1 * 1024 * 1024 });
    echo Core\Bytes::length($whole), "\n";
}
```

```nvs skip
<?nvs
foreach (Core\Request::files() as Core\Request\Part $part) {
    $part->saveTo(Core\IO::within('uploads', $part->filename()), { overwrite: true });
}
```

Every one of those needs a request in front of it; `Core\Request\Files` is where the walk that produces a
part is described, and what it does in a program answering no request.

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Request\Part->name`](#core-core-request-part-name) | `name(): tainted string` |
| [`Core\Request\Part->filename`](#core-core-request-part-filename) | `filename(): tainted string` |
| [`Core\Request\Part->contentType`](#core-core-request-part-contenttype) | `contentType(): tainted string` |
| [`Core\Request\Part->content`](#core-core-request-part-content) | `content(): Core\Request\PartContent` |
| [`Core\Request\Part->readAll`](#core-core-request-part-readall) | `readAll({ max?: uint }): tainted bytes` |
| [`Core\Request\Part->saveTo`](#core-core-request-part-saveto) | `saveTo(string $path, { max?: uint, overwrite?: bool }): void` |

<a id="core-core-request-part-name"></a>
#### `Core\Request\Part->name`

```nvs skip
$part->name(): tainted string
```

Returns the name of the form field this file was sent under. This is the `name` attribute of the `<input>`, as the client sent it.

**Returns** `tainted string` — The field name. It is `tainted` because the client chose it. A client can send a name the form never declared, so the name is untrusted input like every other byte of the part.

<a id="core-core-request-part-filename"></a>
#### `Core\Request\Part->filename`

```nvs skip
$part->filename(): tainted string
```

Returns the file name the client sent. It names a file on the client's computer. It is never a path on this server.

**Returns** `tainted string` — The name the client sent, `tainted`. It cannot be used as a file path until `Core\IO::within` checks it. This stops a client from choosing where its upload is saved.

<a id="core-core-request-part-contenttype"></a>
#### `Core\Request\Part->contentType`

```nvs skip
$part->contentType(): tainted string
```

Returns the media type this part declared. This is what the client said the bytes are. The bytes may be something else.

**Returns** `tainted string` — The declared type, `tainted`. The result is `text/plain` when the part declared no type, which is the default that RFC 7578 sets. To know what the bytes really are, read the bytes.

<a id="core-core-request-part-content"></a>
#### `Core\Request\Part->content`

```nvs skip
$part->content(): Core\Request\PartContent
```

Returns the bytes of this part, one piece at a time. Use it for an upload that must never be in memory all at once. `saveTo` and `readAll` both read the part this way.

**Returns** `Core\Request\PartContent` — An `Iterable<tainted bytes>` over the pieces of the part as they arrive. Each piece is a value of its own. The loop runs zero times for a part with no bytes. It works only while the `files()` loop is still on this part.

**Throws** `LogicError` — This program is not handling a request. Or the `files()` loop has moved to a later part, and the bytes of this part are gone.; `IOError` — The connection failed while the body was read, or the body ended before the closing boundary.; `ParseError` — The body is not the multipart body the request declared.

<a id="core-core-request-part-readall"></a>
#### `Core\Request\Part->readAll`

```nvs skip
$part->readAll({ max?: uint }): tainted bytes
```

Reads the whole content of this part into one value. Use it for an upload small enough to keep in memory.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `{ max: … }` | `uint` (default `0`) | The most bytes this call reads into memory. If you leave it out, the limit is `[limits] request_body`. If you give it, the limit is this number. A number larger than the request's own `[limits] memory` throws an error. It is not lowered to fit. |

**Returns** `tainted bytes` — Every byte of this part, in order and not decoded. The value is `tainted`. It is empty for a part with no bytes. That part was still sent by the client.

**Throws** `LogicError` — This program is not handling a request. Or the `files()` loop has moved to a later part. Or `max` is larger than this request may use at all.; `RuntimeError` — The part is larger than the limit. The bytes over the limit are never stored, because the error is thrown at the piece that would pass it. Use `content()` for a part that does not fit.; `IOError` — The connection failed while the body was read, or the body ended before the closing boundary.; `ParseError` — The body is not the multipart body the request declared.

<a id="core-core-request-part-saveto"></a>
#### `Core\Request\Part->saveTo`

```nvs skip
$part->saveTo(string $path, { max?: uint, overwrite?: bool }): void
```

Writes this part directly to `$path`, one chunk at a time. Use it to save an upload. It needs the `fs.write` capability for the path. The part's own `filename()` is `tainted`, so `Core\IO::within` must check it before it is used here.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$path` | `string` (sink) | The file to write the part to. It must not already exist, unless `overwrite` is `true`. |
| `{ max: … }` | `uint` (default `18446744073709551615`) | The most bytes to accept from this part. If you leave it out, there is no limit, because no other limit applies to a file on disk. `readAll` keeps what it reads in memory, so `[limits] request_body` limits it. |
| `{ overwrite: … }` | `bool` (default `false`) | Whether an existing file may be replaced. The default is `false`, because the path is usually built from a name the client sent. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. If the write fails partway, the partial file is deleted before the error is thrown. No later reader finds a cut-off upload that the program thinks is complete.

**Throws** `LogicError` — This program is not handling a request. Or the `files()` loop has moved to a later part, and the bytes of this part are gone.; `RuntimeError` — The configuration does not grant `fs.write` for this path, or the part is larger than `max` bytes.; `IOError` — A file is already at the path and `overwrite` is `false`. Or the operating system did not allow the file to be created or written. Or the connection failed while the body was read.; `ParseError` — The body is not the multipart body the request declared.

<a id="core-core-request-partcontent"></a>
### `Core\Request\PartContent`

Keywords: streaming upload, chunk, read in chunks, multipart/form-data, large file upload, memory limit, Iterable bytes,

`Core\Request\PartContent` is what `Core\Request\Part::content()` answers with: an `Iterable<tainted
bytes>` that a `foreach` walks once over one uploaded part. It has no members — the walk is everything it
does — and it holds nothing but the chunk the loop body is looking at, so a part far larger than the
machine's memory passes through a program that never has more than one chunk of it resident. It is the
reading for an upload that must never be whole in memory, and `readAll` and `saveTo` are both written
over it: those two are the bounded and the on-disk answers to the same question, and this is the one
where the program decides what to keep.

**A part is a position in a body, and this walk is only valid while it is the current one.** The `files()`
parse moves whether or not this walk is what moved it, so the part the walk was named on is remembered
and checked on every pull: once the loop over `files()` has advanced, a pull here refuses with
`LogicError` rather than handing back a later part's bytes. That is a defect in the program — a name kept
past the iteration that opened the next part — and never something a peer can provoke.

**A chunk boundary is the wire's, and carries no meaning.** It is where the octets happened to arrive, so
a program that needs lines, records or frames finds them across chunks; nothing here aligns a chunk to
anything the sender wrote. The walk is empty for a part that carried no bytes, which is an ordinary thing
for a form to send.

Every chunk is `tainted bytes`, like everything else a peer chose, so it reaches a sink only through a
launderer named for that sink — and the filename the part carries is tainted too, which is why a path is
built rather than concatenated. Where the destination is simply disk, `saveTo` is the shorter spelling of
this loop and bounds itself; reach for `content()` when the bytes are being counted, hashed, decoded or
forwarded rather than stored.

```nvs skip
<?nvs
foreach (Core\Request::files() as Core\Request\Part $part) {
    int $seen = 0;
    foreach ($part->content() as tainted bytes $chunk) {
        $seen = $seen + Core\Bytes::length($chunk);
    }
    echo $part->name(), ': ', $seen, " bytes\n";
}
```

Beyond the `LogicError` above, the walk carries the failures the body itself has: `IOError` where the
connection failed underneath it or the peer stopped short of the closing boundary, and `ParseError` where
what arrived is not the multipart body the request declared. Reaching the walk at all needs a request in
front of it, and without one the entry to it refuses the way every member of `Core\Request` does:

```nvs
<?nvs
try {
    Core\Request::files();
    echo "not reached\n";
} catch (LogicError $none) {
    echo "no request here\n";
}
```
```output
no request here
```

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|

#### `Core\Response::html`

```nvs skip
Core\Response::html(Core\Html\Markup $body): void
```

Sends the HTML page `$body` and adds the header `Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$body` | `Core\Html\Markup` | The page to send. It is a `Core\Html\Markup`, which is HTML that is already safe: an html template, ``html`…` ``, escaped the values in its `{...}`, or `Core\Html::escape` made it. It is sent as it is and nothing is escaped again. A `string` does not compile. |

<a id="core-core-response-json"></a>
#### `Core\Response::json`

```nvs skip
Core\Response::json(mixed $value): void
```

Converts `$value` to JSON, sends it, and adds the header `Content-Type: application/json`. It uses the same encoder as `Core\Json::encode`, and the JSON is on one line.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$value` | `mixed` | The value to send, of any type `Core\Json::encode` accepts. A `tainted` value is allowed anywhere inside it. Each string is written as a JSON string, so its quotes are escaped and it cannot change the JSON around it. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. Using this and `echo` in one response does not compile.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$value` contains something JSON cannot write: a `float` that is NaN or infinite, a value of a type JSON has no form for, an object of a class without `#[Core\Json\Derive]`, an object that points to itself, or nesting deeper than 1024 levels. Nothing is sent.

<a id="core-core-response-text"></a>

