<a id="core-core-crypto-generatekey"></a>
#### `Core\Crypto::generateKey`

```nvs skip
Core\Crypto::generateKey(): secret bytes
```

Creates a new random key for `seal` and `open`. It uses the same secure random number generator as `Core\Random`. There is no key size argument, because the cipher has one key size.

**Returns** `secret bytes` — 32 bytes as `secret bytes`. `secret` is part of the type, so you cannot assign the key to a plain `bytes`. You also cannot print it with `echo`, log it or put it in a `Throwable` message.

<a id="core-core-crypto-seal"></a>
#### `Core\Crypto::seal`

```nvs skip
Core\Crypto::seal(bytes $message, secret bytes $key, Core\Crypto::Cipher $cipher): bytes
```

Encrypts and authenticates `$message` with `$key`, using the cipher `$cipher`. Each call uses a new random nonce. There is no argument for a mode, a padding or an IV, and no cipher name as a string. You choose a `Core\Crypto::Cipher` case, and every case is authenticated.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$message` | `bytes` | The plaintext. A `secret` value is not allowed. To seal one, call `Core\Secret::revealBytes` first. Then a text search of your code finds every such place. |
| `$key` | `secret bytes` (sink) | A 32-byte key, such as `generateKey` returns. Both ciphers use a key of this size. |
| `$cipher` | `Core\Crypto::Cipher` | The cipher to use. There is no default. Use `XChaCha20Poly1305` when both ends are Novis, and `Aes256Gcm` when a browser must read the result. |

**Returns** `bytes` — The sealed message. It is 40 bytes longer than `$message` with `XChaCha20Poly1305`, and 28 bytes longer with `Aes256Gcm`. It is different on every call for the same inputs, because each call uses its own nonce.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$key` is not 32 bytes long, so it is not a key.; `RuntimeError` — This process does not have enough memory for a buffer the size of the sealed message.

<a id="core-core-crypto-open"></a>
#### `Core\Crypto::open`

```nvs skip
Core\Crypto::open(bytes $sealed, secret bytes $key, Core\Crypto::Cipher $cipher): bytes
```

Checks that `$sealed` is authentic for `$key` and `$cipher`, and returns the plaintext. If it is not authentic, it throws an error. A message with even one changed byte is not decrypted. This is why `Core\Crypto` has only authenticated ciphers.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$sealed` | `bytes` | A message `seal` produced. |
| `$key` | `secret bytes` (sink) | The 32-byte key that `$sealed` was sealed with. |
| `$cipher` | `Core\Crypto::Cipher` | The cipher that `$sealed` was sealed with. With the other cipher, the message throws the same error as a forged message. You never get wrong bytes. |

**Returns** `bytes` — The original plaintext, byte for byte.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$key` is not 32 bytes long, so it is not a key.; `RuntimeError` — `$sealed` is not an authentic message for `$key` and `$cipher`. It was changed, it is too short, or the key or the cipher is wrong. All these cases have the same message. A different message would tell an attacker which part of a forgery worked.

<a id="core-core-crypto-derivekey"></a>
#### `Core\Crypto::deriveKey`

```nvs skip
Core\Crypto::deriveKey(secret string $password, bytes $salt, uint $iterations): secret bytes
```

Derives a key from a password with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256. It computes `$iterations` rounds over `$password` and `$salt`. Use it for a value that a person typed. For material that is already uniformly random, use `expandKey`. The compiler does not stop you from passing a password to `expandKey`, so check which one you call.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$password` | `secret string` (neutral) | The password. A `secret` value is allowed, and it is not revealed. The result is `secret bytes` and contains no byte of the password. |
| `$salt` | `bytes` (neutral) | At least 16 bytes. Make a new salt for each password, and store it next to the derived key. `Core\Random::bytes(16)` makes one. The salt is not a secret. |
| `$iterations` | `uint` | How many rounds to compute, from 100,000 to 2,000,000. It is required and has no default. To derive the same key again later, you must use the same count as before. |

**Returns** `secret bytes` — 32 bytes as `secret bytes`, the key size that `seal` and `open` use. The result is not random: the same three arguments always give the same key.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$iterations` is less than 100,000 or more than 2,000,000, or `$salt` is shorter than 16 bytes. With fewer rounds, the key is easy to attack. With more rounds, one call uses so much CPU time that it blocks the process.

<a id="core-core-crypto-expandkey"></a>
#### `Core\Crypto::expandKey`

```nvs skip
Core\Crypto::expandKey(secret bytes $material, bytes $salt, string $info): secret bytes
```

Derives a key with HKDF-SHA256 from material that is already uniformly random. An example is a shared secret from a key agreement, or the root key of a service. `$info` names what the key is for. With a different `$info`, one secret gives a different key, so you never use the same secret in two places.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$material` | `secret bytes` (sink) | The secret to expand. It must already be uniformly random. For a password, use `deriveKey`. |
| `$salt` | `bytes` (neutral) | The salt of the extract step. It is not a secret, and it can be empty. An empty salt is the default of RFC 5869, a salt of zero bytes. |
| `$info` | `string` (neutral) | The context string. Two calls with the same `$material` and a different `$info` give unrelated keys. So one secret can give keys for two uses. |

**Returns** `secret bytes` — 32 bytes as `secret bytes`, the key size that `seal` and `open` use. The same three arguments always give the same key.

<a id="core-core-crypto-generatekeypair"></a>
#### `Core\Crypto::generateKeyPair`

```nvs skip
Core\Crypto::generateKeyPair(Core\Crypto\KeyKind $kind): Core\Crypto\KeyPair
```

Creates a new random private key of the kind `$kind`, and returns it as a key pair. It uses the same secure random number generator as `Core\Random`. There is no key size argument, because each kind has one size. Only the two RSA kinds would need a size, and this method does not create them.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$kind` | `Core\Crypto\KeyKind` | The kind of key to create. `P256` agrees and signs, `X25519` only agrees, and `Ed25519` only signs. The two RSA kinds are only read, never created. |

**Returns** `Core\Crypto\KeyPair` — The key pair, ready to sign or to agree. Its `write` method gives PKCS#8, which `Core\Crypto\KeyPair::read` reads back.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$kind` is `RsaPkcs1` or `RsaPss`. This method never creates an RSA key. You get an RSA key from whoever issued it, and `Core\Crypto\KeyPair::read` reads it.

<a id="core-core-crypto-agree"></a>
#### `Core\Crypto::agree`

```nvs skip
Core\Crypto::agree(Core\Crypto\KeyPair $mine, Core\Crypto\PublicKey $theirs): secret bytes
```

Computes a shared secret with ECDH, from your own key pair and the public key that the other side sent. The result is the raw shared value, and it is not a key. Pass it to `expandKey` with a context string to make the keys you need.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$mine` | `Core\Crypto\KeyPair` | Your own key pair, of kind `P256` or `X25519`. The other kinds can only sign. |
| `$theirs` | `Core\Crypto\PublicKey` | The public key of the other side. It must be of the same kind, because two keys on different curves cannot agree. |

**Returns** `secret bytes` — 32 bytes as `secret bytes`. This is the x-coordinate for P-256 and the u-coordinate for X25519. WebCrypto's `deriveBits` returns the same value for the same two keys.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The two keys cannot agree. One key is of a kind that cannot agree: `Ed25519` or an RSA kind. Or the two keys are on different curves.; `RuntimeError` — The X25519 point of the other side adds nothing, so the secret would be all zeros for any private key. The sender chose that point. So the error is about the sender, and it is not a bug in your program.

<a id="core-core-crypto-sign"></a>
#### `Core\Crypto::sign`

```nvs skip
Core\Crypto::sign(bytes $message, Core\Crypto\KeyPair $key): bytes
```

Signs `$message` with the private key of `$key`. There is no argument for the algorithm or the digest, because the kind of the key pair sets the scheme. `RsaPkcs1` and `RsaPss` use SHA-256, `P256` uses ECDSA with SHA-256, and `Ed25519` uses Ed25519. So a call cannot choose a scheme that does not match the key.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$message` | `bytes` (neutral) | The whole bytes to sign. You cannot pass a hash of the message in its place. A signature over a hash means something different. |
| `$key` | `Core\Crypto\KeyPair` | The key pair to sign with. It can be of any kind except `X25519`, which can only agree. |

**Returns** `bytes` — The signature. For `P256`, it is 64 bytes: the `r ‖ s` pair that JWS and WebCrypto use, never DER. For `Ed25519`, it is 64 bytes. For either RSA kind, it has as many bytes as the modulus. `RsaPkcs1` and `Ed25519` give the same signature for a message every time. `P256` and `RsaPss` use randomness, so two signatures of one message differ, and both verify.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$key` is an `X25519` key pair, which cannot sign. The kind is set when the pair is generated or read, so this is a bug in your program.

<a id="core-core-crypto-verify"></a>
#### `Core\Crypto::verify`

```nvs skip
Core\Crypto::verify(bytes $message, bytes $signature, Core\Crypto\PublicKey $key): void
```

Checks that `$signature` is a signature of `$message` by `$key`. If it is not, it throws an error. The algorithm comes from the key, as in `sign`. So nothing in the data you received chooses how it is checked.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$message` | `bytes` (neutral) | The bytes that the signature should cover. A `tainted` value is allowed, and it stays `tainted`. A valid signature tells you who sent the bytes. It does not tell you that their content is safe. |
| `$signature` | `bytes` (neutral) | The signature as `sign` returns it: `r ‖ s` for `P256`, never DER. |
| `$key` | `Core\Crypto\PublicKey` | The public key to check against, of any kind but `X25519`. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. For a valid signature, it returns. For a wrong one, it throws an error. So there is no `false` result that a `==` check could read wrongly.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The signature is not by this key for this message. It was changed, it has the wrong length for the algorithm of the key, or another key made it. All these cases have the same message, so the error does not say which part was wrong.; `LogicError` — `$key` is an `X25519` key, which cannot verify. It is your program's own key, not data you received, so this is a bug in your program.

<a id="core-core-crypto-publickey"></a>
### `Core\Crypto\PublicKey`

Keywords: read, write, kind

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Crypto\PublicKey::read`](#core-core-crypto-publickey-read) | `read(bytes $encoded, Core\Crypto\KeyKind $kind, Core\Crypto\PublicKey::Format $format): Core\Crypto\PublicKey` |
| [`Core\Crypto\PublicKey->write`](#core-core-crypto-publickey-write) | `write(Core\Crypto\PublicKey::Format $format): bytes` |
| [`Core\Crypto\PublicKey->kind`](#core-core-crypto-publickey-kind) | `kind(): Core\Crypto\KeyKind` |

<a id="core-core-crypto-publickey-read"></a>
#### `Core\Crypto\PublicKey::read`

```nvs skip
Core\Crypto\PublicKey::read(bytes $encoded, Core\Crypto\KeyKind $kind, Core\Crypto\PublicKey::Format $format): Core\Crypto\PublicKey
```

Reads a public key from `$encoded` and checks it. For `P256`, the point must be on the curve. For an RSA kind, the key size must be in the allowed range. For a JWK, its fields must match `$kind`. A key that fails the check throws an error here. So every method that takes a key gets a checked key.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$encoded` | `bytes` (neutral) | The bytes of the key, in `$format`. |
| `$kind` | `Core\Crypto\KeyKind` | The kind of the key. You must give it, because the bytes do not always say it. An RSA `SubjectPublicKeyInfo` says `rsaEncryption` for both `RS256` and `PS256` keys. Only your program knows which one the key is for. |
| `$format` | `Core\Crypto\PublicKey::Format` | The WebCrypto export format that `$encoded` is in. |

**Returns** `Core\Crypto\PublicKey` — The key, ready to verify a signature or to agree. Its `kind()` method returns the case it was read as.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The kind has no such format, for example `Raw` with an RSA kind. It is also thrown when the JWK has `d`, because that is a private key given as a public key.; `RuntimeError` — `$encoded` is not a public key of that kind in that format. For example, the point is not on the curve, or a coordinate has the wrong size. Or the modulus is outside the allowed range, the DER does not parse, or the JWK names another key type. All these cases have the same message. The key came from the sender, and a reason would tell the sender what was wrong.

<a id="core-core-crypto-publickey-write"></a>
#### `Core\Crypto\PublicKey->write`

```nvs skip
$publicKey->write(Core\Crypto\PublicKey::Format $format): bytes
```

Returns this key in `$format`. The formats are the ones that `read` accepts, so you can give a browser the key in the format it asks for. The output is made from the key, not from the bytes it was read from. So one key always gives the same bytes in each format.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$format` | `Core\Crypto\PublicKey::Format` | The format to write. `Jwk` gives the fields that RFC 7638 requires, sorted. A thumbprint is computed over this form. |

**Returns** `bytes` — The bytes of the key. For a JWK, this is its UTF-8 JSON.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$format` is `Raw` and the key has an RSA kind. An RSA key has no raw form, so there is nothing to return.

<a id="core-core-crypto-publickey-kind"></a>
#### `Core\Crypto\PublicKey->kind`

```nvs skip
$publicKey->kind(): Core\Crypto\KeyKind
```

Returns the `Core\Crypto\KeyKind` case of this key. This is the kind that `read` was given. It is not read again from the key.

**Returns** `Core\Crypto\KeyKind` — The case the key was read as. For an RSA key, it is `RsaPkcs1` or `RsaPss`. This is the scheme of the key, and it is set when the key is read.

<a id="core-core-crypto-keypair"></a>
### `Core\Crypto\KeyPair`

Keywords: read, write, publicKey

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Crypto\KeyPair::read`](#core-core-crypto-keypair-read) | `read(secret bytes $pkcs8, Core\Crypto\KeyKind $kind): Core\Crypto\KeyPair` |
| [`Core\Crypto\KeyPair->write`](#core-core-crypto-keypair-write) | `write(): secret bytes` |
| [`Core\Crypto\KeyPair->publicKey`](#core-core-crypto-keypair-publickey) | `publicKey(): Core\Crypto\PublicKey` |

<a id="core-core-crypto-keypair-read"></a>
#### `Core\Crypto\KeyPair::read`

```nvs skip
Core\Crypto\KeyPair::read(secret bytes $pkcs8, Core\Crypto\KeyKind $kind): Core\Crypto\KeyPair
```

Reads a stored private key, as DER PKCS#8 or as one PEM `PRIVATE KEY` block. A service-account file has this form. The key is parsed here, so later methods can use the pair without parsing it again.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$pkcs8` | `secret bytes` (sink) | The bytes of the key, as `write` returned them, or as the issuer of the key wrote them. |
| `$kind` | `Core\Crypto\KeyKind` | The kind of the key. You must give it, for the same reason as in `Core\Crypto\PublicKey::read`. A PKCS#8 key says that it is RSA, but not whether it is for `RS256` or `PS256`. |

**Returns** `Core\Crypto\KeyPair` — The key pair, ready to sign or to agree. Its `publicKey()` method returns the public key, which you can send to others.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$pkcs8` is not a PKCS#8 private key of that kind. For example, it is a key of another kind, or a PKCS#1 key. It can be an encrypted PKCS#8, which needs a password, and this method has no password argument. It can be an RSA key outside 2048 to 8192 bits, or any malformed data. A private key belongs to your program, never to the other side. So this error always means that your program was given a wrong key.

<a id="core-core-crypto-keypair-write"></a>
#### `Core\Crypto\KeyPair->write`

```nvs skip
$keyPair->write(): secret bytes
```

Returns this key pair as DER PKCS#8, as `secret bytes`. A server can store the key between requests and read it back with `read`. This is the only way to get the private key out of a pair.

**Returns** `secret bytes` — The PKCS#8 as DER. It is DER even when the pair was read from PEM.

<a id="core-core-crypto-keypair-publickey"></a>
#### `Core\Crypto\KeyPair->publicKey`

```nvs skip
$keyPair->publicKey(): Core\Crypto\PublicKey
```

Returns the public key of this pair, which you can send to others. It is computed from the private key and is not stored next to it. So it is always the public key of this pair, and never a different key that came with it.

**Returns** `Core\Crypto\PublicKey` — The public key, of the same kind as the pair. It is the same value that `Core\Crypto\PublicKey::read` returns for the key that the other side receives.

<a id="core-core-signedcookie"></a>
### `Core\SignedCookie`

Keywords: seal, open

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\SignedCookie::seal`](#core-core-signedcookie-seal) | `seal(string $name, string $value, array<secret bytes> $keys): string` |
| [`Core\SignedCookie::open`](#core-core-signedcookie-open) | `open(string $name, string $cookie, array<secret bytes> $keys): tainted string` |

<a id="core-core-signedcookie-seal"></a>
#### `Core\SignedCookie::seal`

```nvs skip
Core\SignedCookie::seal(string $name, string $value, array<secret bytes> $keys): string
```

Encrypts `$value` with the newest key in `$keys` and returns text for the cookie `$name`. Nobody without the key can read or change the value. `Core\SignedCookie::open` returns the value again for the same name.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$name` | `string` (neutral) | The name of the cookie, such as `cart`. `open` needs the same name. A cookie sent back under another name does not open. |
| `$value` | `string` | The value to store. `open` returns exactly this string. |
| `$keys` | `array<secret bytes>` | The keys, newest first. `$keys[0]` encrypts the value. The older keys are there so that `open` still accepts cookies made before you added a new key. A list of one key is `[$key]`. |

**Returns** `string` — The cookie text. It contains only `A-Z`, `a-z`, `0-9`, `-` and `_`, so a `Set-Cookie` header can carry it without escaping. It is about 4/3 × (length + 40) characters long. Each call returns different text for the same value, because each call adds new random bytes.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$keys` is empty, or its first key is not 32 bytes long. `Core\Crypto::generateKey()` returns a key of the right length.; `RuntimeError` — The request does not have enough memory left for the cookie.

<a id="core-core-signedcookie-open"></a>
#### `Core\SignedCookie::open`

```nvs skip
Core\SignedCookie::open(string $name, string $cookie, array<secret bytes> $keys): tainted string
```

Checks that `$cookie` was made by `Core\SignedCookie::seal` for the cookie `$name` with a key in `$keys`, and returns the value stored in it. A changed cookie throws an error. The value is `tainted` (it counts as input from outside the program), because your program may have stored text that a visitor sent.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$name` | `string` (neutral) | The name you gave `seal`. This is usually the name the cookie arrived with. |
| `$cookie` | `string` (neutral) | The cookie text as your program received it from the request. A `tainted` string is allowed here. |
| `$keys` | `array<secret bytes>` | The keys you gave `seal`, newest first. A cookie made with any key in this list is accepted. A cookie made with a key you removed from the list is not. |

**Returns** `tainted string` — The value that was given to `seal`, exactly as it was, as a `tainted string`.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$keys` is empty, or a key that `open` tries is not 32 bytes long. `open` tries the keys in order and stops at the first one that opens the cookie.; `RuntimeError` — `$cookie` was not made for `$name` with any key in `$keys`. This includes a changed cookie, an empty cookie, text that is not a cookie, a cookie made for another name, and a cookie made with a key you removed. All of these give the same message, so an attacker learns nothing from it.

<a id="core-core-csrf"></a>
### `Core\Csrf`

Keywords: token, issue, verify

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Csrf::token`](#core-core-csrf-token) | `token(): string` |
| [`Core\Csrf::issue`](#core-core-csrf-issue) | `issue(string $session, secret bytes $key): string` |
| [`Core\Csrf::verify`](#core-core-csrf-verify) | `verify(string $token, string $session, secret bytes $key): bool` |

<a id="core-core-csrf-token"></a>
#### `Core\Csrf::token`

```nvs skip
Core\Csrf::token(): string
```

Returns a CSRF token for the visitor's session. Put it in a form field named `_csrf`, in the `x-csrf-token` header or in a `_csrf` query parameter. The server checks it on the next request. Call `Core\Session::start()` first. If the visitor has no session yet, this call creates one and sends its cookie.

**Returns** `string` — A different string on every call. Each one is valid for the whole session. It uses only `A-Za-z0-9-_`, so a form field, a header and a URL carry it unchanged.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The request has not called `Core\Session::start()`, or `[http] csrf_key` is not set.; `LogicError` — The call runs inside a function passed to `Core\Task::afterResponse`, after the response was sent. The session cookie cannot be sent then.

<a id="core-core-csrf-issue"></a>
#### `Core\Csrf::issue`

```nvs skip
Core\Csrf::issue(string $session, secret bytes $key): string
```

Returns a CSRF token for `$session`, made with `$key`. Send it in a form field named `_csrf`, in the `x-csrf-token` header or in a `_csrf` query parameter. A form that uploads files must use the header or the query parameter. With `[http] csrf_key` set, the server checks the token before the handler runs. `verify` checks it with the same session and key.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$session` | `string` (neutral) | The value the token belongs to. This is a session id, or any other value that does not change while the token should be valid. A token made for one value never passes `verify` for another value. |
| `$key` | `secret bytes` (sink) | A 32-byte key, such as the one `Core\Crypto::generateKey()` returns. The key is not part of the token, so you can use the same key for every session. |

**Returns** `string` — A URL-safe base64 string without padding. It uses only `A-Za-z0-9-_`, so a hidden field, a header and a query string can contain it without escaping. Each call returns a different string for the same inputs. Two tokens for one session are never equal, so `==` cannot check a token.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$key` is not 32 bytes long. Such a value is not a key.; `RuntimeError` — The process does not have enough memory for the token.

<a id="core-core-csrf-verify"></a>
#### `Core\Csrf::verify`

```nvs skip
Core\Csrf::verify(string $token, string $session, secret bytes $key): bool
```

Checks that `$token` was made by `issue` for `$session` with `$key`. This is the only way to check a token. No method returns the expected token, so you cannot compare tokens with `==`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$token` | `string` (neutral) | The token from the request. A `tainted` value is allowed here, because a token always comes from a request. |
| `$session` | `string` (neutral) | The value you gave `issue`. A token made for a different session returns `false`. |
| `$key` | `secret bytes` (sink) | The key you gave `issue`. When you change the key, every token made with the old key returns `false`. |

**Returns** `bool` — `true` for a token made with this key for this session. `false` for any other text: a changed token, a token made with an old key, a token for another session, or text that is not base64. The comparison takes the same time in every case. All four cases return the same `false`, so an attacker cannot learn which check failed.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$key` is not 32 bytes long. A forged token returns `false` and never throws. Only a bug in the program throws here.

<a id="core-core-totp"></a>
### `Core\Totp`

Keywords: code, check

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Totp::code`](#core-core-totp-code) | `code(secret bytes $secret): string` |
| [`Core\Totp::check`](#core-core-totp-check) | `check(string $code, secret bytes $secret, int $after = 0): ?int` |

<a id="core-core-totp-code"></a>
#### `Core\Totp::code`

```nvs skip
Core\Totp::code(secret bytes $secret): string
```

Returns the current six-digit code for `$secret`. An authenticator app with the same secret shows the same code now. Use `check` to test a code that a user typed.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$secret` | `secret bytes` (sink) | The shared secret, at least 16 bytes long. `Core\Random::bytes(20)` makes one of the recommended length. |

**Returns** `string` — Six digits as a string, with leading zeros, such as `042311`. It is a string so that the leading zeros stay.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$secret` is shorter than 16 bytes, or the clock is outside the range of dates a code can have.

<a id="core-core-totp-check"></a>
#### `Core\Totp::check`

```nvs skip
Core\Totp::check(string $code, secret bytes $secret, int $after = 0): ?int
```

Tests a code that a user typed. It accepts the code of the current 30-second step and of the step before and after it. It returns the number of the step, or `null`. Store that number and pass it as `$after` next time. Then the same code cannot be used twice.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$code` | `string` (neutral) | The code the user typed. A string that is not six digits returns `null` and does not throw an error. |
| `$secret` | `secret bytes` (sink) | The same secret that `code` uses, at least 16 bytes long. |
| `$after` | `int` (default `0`) | The step number that the last accepted code returned. Codes of this step and earlier steps return `null`. The default is `0`, which accepts every code of the current steps. Use it only for the first code of an account. |

**Returns** `?int` — The step number of the code, or `null` when the code is wrong, too old, too new or already used.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$secret` is shorter than 16 bytes, or the clock is outside the range of dates a code can have.

### `Core\Passkey`

| Member | Signature |

| [`Core\Passkey::registerOptions`](#core-core-passkey-registeroptions) | `registerOptions(string $rpId, string $rpName, bytes $userId, string $userName, array<Core\Passkey\Credential> $existing = []): string` |
| [`Core\Passkey::verifyRegistration`](#core-core-passkey-verifyregistration) | `verifyRegistration(string $response, string $rpId, string $origin): Core\Passkey\Credential` |

| [`Core\Passkey::credentialId`](#core-core-passkey-credentialid) | `credentialId(string $response): bytes` |
| [`Core\Passkey::verifySignIn`](#core-core-passkey-verifysignin) | `verifySignIn(string $response, Core\Passkey\Credential $stored, string $rpId, string $origin): Core\Passkey\Credential` |

<a id="core-core-passkey-registeroptions"></a>
#### `Core\Passkey::registerOptions`

```nvs skip
Core\Passkey::registerOptions(string $rpId, string $rpName, bytes $userId, string $userName, array<Core\Passkey\Credential> $existing = []): string
```

Returns the options for `navigator.credentials.create()` as JSON. The options contain a new random challenge. The challenge is saved in the session, so call `Core\Session::start()` first.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$rpId` | `string` | The domain of your site, such as `example.com`. The passkey works only on this domain and its subdomains. |
| `$rpName` | `string` | The name of your site. The browser shows it to the user. |
| `$userId` | `bytes` | A unique id for the account, from 1 to 64 bytes. Do not use an email address or a name. `Core\Random::bytes(16)` makes a good id. |
| `$userName` | `string` | The name the user signs in with, such as an email address. The browser shows it in its list of passkeys. |
| `$existing` | `array<Core\Passkey\Credential>` (default `[]`) | The passkeys this account already has. A device that has one of them does not create a second one. |

**Returns** `string` — A JSON string. In the browser, pass it to `PublicKeyCredential.parseCreationOptionsFromJSON()`, and pass the result to `navigator.credentials.create()`.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The request has not started a session.; `LogicError` — `$rpId` is empty, or `$userId` is empty or longer than 64 bytes.

<a id="core-core-passkey-verifyregistration"></a>
#### `Core\Passkey::verifyRegistration`

```nvs skip
Core\Passkey::verifyRegistration(string $response, string $rpId, string $origin): Core\Passkey\Credential
```

Checks the browser's answer to `registerOptions` and returns the new passkey. Save the passkey with the account. A challenge can be checked only once, so a second call with the same answer throws an error.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$response` | `string` (neutral) | The credential that `navigator.credentials.create()` returned, as JSON. In the browser, `JSON.stringify(credential)` makes it. |
| `$rpId` | `string` (neutral) | The same domain that you passed to `registerOptions`. |
| `$origin` | `string` (neutral) | The address of your site in the browser, such as `https://example.com`. The answer must name exactly this origin. |

**Returns** `Core\Passkey\Credential` — The new passkey, with its id, its public key, its algorithm and its sign counter.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The request has not started a session, no registration is waiting, or the challenge is older than five minutes. It is also thrown when a check fails. The checks are the challenge, the origin, the domain, the user verification and the key algorithm. An answer longer than 64 KB also throws.

<a id="core-core-passkey-signinoptions"></a>
#### `Core\Passkey::signInOptions`

```nvs skip
Core\Passkey::signInOptions(string $rpId, array<Core\Passkey\Credential> $allowed = []): string
```

Returns the options for `navigator.credentials.get()` as JSON. The options contain a new random challenge. The challenge is saved in the session, so call `Core\Session::start()` first.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$rpId` | `string` | The domain of your site, such as `example.com`. Use the same domain as for `registerOptions`. |
| `$allowed` | `array<Core\Passkey\Credential>` (default `[]`) | The passkeys of the account that signs in. Leave it empty when you do not know the account yet. The browser then shows every passkey it has for your site. |

**Returns** `string` — A JSON string. In the browser, pass it to `PublicKeyCredential.parseRequestOptionsFromJSON()`, and pass the result to `navigator.credentials.get()`.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The request has not started a session.; `LogicError` — `$rpId` is empty.

<a id="core-core-passkey-credentialid"></a>
#### `Core\Passkey::credentialId`

```nvs skip
Core\Passkey::credentialId(string $response): bytes
```

Returns the passkey id in the browser's answer to `signInOptions`. Use it to find the saved passkey. The id is not checked yet, so the result is `tainted`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$response` | `string` | The credential that `navigator.credentials.get()` returned, as JSON. In the browser, `JSON.stringify(credential)` makes it. |

**Returns** `bytes` — The passkey id, from 1 to 1023 bytes.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The answer is not JSON or is longer than 64 KB. It is also thrown when the `id` is missing, is not base64url or is too long.

<a id="core-core-passkey-verifysignin"></a>
#### `Core\Passkey::verifySignIn`

```nvs skip
Core\Passkey::verifySignIn(string $response, Core\Passkey\Credential $stored, string $rpId, string $origin): Core\Passkey\Credential
```

Checks the browser's answer to `signInOptions` against the saved passkey. It returns the passkey with its new sign counter. Save it again. A challenge can be checked only once, so a second call with the same answer throws an error.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$response` | `string` (neutral) | The credential that `navigator.credentials.get()` returned, as JSON. |
| `$stored` | `Core\Passkey\Credential` | The saved passkey with the id that `credentialId` returned. |
| `$rpId` | `string` (neutral) | The same domain that you passed to `signInOptions`. |
| `$origin` | `string` (neutral) | The address of your site in the browser, such as `https://example.com`. The answer must name exactly this origin. |

**Returns** `Core\Passkey\Credential` — The passkey with its new sign counter.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The request has not started a session, no sign-in is waiting, or the challenge is older than five minutes. It is also thrown when a check fails. The checks are the passkey id, the challenge, the origin, the domain, the user verification, the signature and the sign counter. An answer longer than 64 KB also throws.

<a id="core-core-passkey-credential-publickey"></a>

<a id="core-core-passkey-credential-algorithm"></a>
#### `Core\Passkey\Credential->algorithm`


<a id="core-core-webpush-subscription"></a>
#### `Core\WebPush::subscription`

```nvs skip
Core\WebPush::subscription(string $json): Core\WebPush\Subscription
```

Reads a push subscription from the JSON that `PushSubscription.toJSON()` returns in the browser. It checks the endpoint URL and both keys. A subscription that fails a check throws an error here.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$json` | `string` (neutral) | The JSON text the browser sent, such as `{"endpoint": "https://…", "keys": {"p256dh": "…", "auth": "…"}}`. Other fields, such as `expirationTime`, are ignored. |

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — The text is not JSON or is longer than 8 KiB. Or the endpoint is not an `https:` URL, `p256dh` is not a P-256 public key, or `auth` is not 16 bytes. The message says which.

<a id="core-core-webpush-applicationserverkey"></a>
#### `Core\WebPush::applicationServerKey`

```nvs skip
Core\WebPush::applicationServerKey(Core\Crypto\KeyPair $vapid): string
```

Returns the public half of your VAPID key, as base64url text. Give it to `pushManager.subscribe()` in the browser as `applicationServerKey`. The private half is not in it.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$vapid` | `Core\Crypto\KeyPair` | Your application's VAPID key: a `Core\Crypto\KeyPair` of kind `P256`. Create it once with `Core\Crypto::generateKeyPair`, keep it secret, and use the same key for every message. |

**Returns** `string` — The public key: 87 characters of base64url, such as `BCVxsr7N_eNg…`.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$vapid` is not a key pair of kind `P256`.

<a id="core-core-webpush-send"></a>
#### `Core\WebPush::send`

```nvs skip
Core\WebPush::send(Core\WebPush\Subscription $to, bytes $payload, Core\Crypto\KeyPair $vapid, string $subject, int $ttl = 86400): Core\WebPush\Sent
```

Encrypts `$payload` for one browser and sends it to the browser's push service. The message is signed with your VAPID key. The program needs `net.connect` for the host of the endpoint.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$to` | `Core\WebPush\Subscription` | The subscription that `Core\WebPush::subscription` returned. |
| `$payload` | `bytes` (neutral) | The message, at most 3993 bytes. The browser's service worker receives it in its `push` event. |
| `$vapid` | `Core\Crypto\KeyPair` | Your application's VAPID key: a `Core\Crypto\KeyPair` of kind `P256`. Create it once with `Core\Crypto::generateKeyPair`, keep it secret, and use the same key for every message. |
| `$subject` | `string` (neutral) | A way for the push service to contact you: a `mailto:` or an `https:` URL, such as `mailto:admin@example.com`. |
| `$ttl` | `int` (default `86400`) | How many seconds the push service keeps the message while the browser is offline. `0` means the message is sent only if the browser is online now. |

**Returns** `Core\WebPush\Sent` — The push service's answer. Its `status()` is `201` when the service accepted the message.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$vapid` is not a key pair of kind `P256`.; `LogicError` — `$subject` does not start with `mailto:` or `https:`, or `$ttl` is negative.; `RuntimeError` — The payload is longer than 3993 bytes, the program may not connect to the host, or the push service cannot be reached.

<a id="core-core-jwt-sign"></a>
#### `Core\Jwt::sign`

```nvs skip
Core\Jwt::sign(array<string> $claims, Core\Time\Duration $lifetime, secret bytes|Core\Crypto\KeyPair $key, { kid?: string, typ?: string, embedKey?: bool }): string
```

Signs `$claims` into a JWT that expires `$lifetime` from now. `$key` signs the token, and the key decides the algorithm. This method always writes the expiry, so every token it returns has one.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$claims` | `array<string>` | The claims for the token, by name. This method writes `exp` and `iat`, so `$claims` may not contain them. Every other claim goes into the token unchanged. |
| `$lifetime` | `Core\Time\Duration` | How long the token is valid, such as `15m`, `1h` or `7d`. It must be greater than zero. A token that is already expired is a bug in the program. |
| `$key` | `secret bytes\|Core\Crypto\KeyPair` (sink) | A shared secret of at least 32 bytes, which signs with HS256. `Core\Crypto::generateKey()` returns one. A longer secret that you share with another service also works. The key can also be a `Core\Crypto\KeyPair`. It signs with ES256, EdDSA, RS256 or PS256, depending on its kind. There is no algorithm parameter, because the key decides the algorithm. |
| `{ kid: … }` | `string` (default `null`, neutral) | The key's name, written into the header. Use it when the receiver has several keys. By default there is no `kid`. The value is written exactly as given. It does not choose which key signs the token. |
| `{ typ: … }` | `string` (default `null`, neutral) | The header's `typ`. It is `JWT` if you leave it out. RFC 9068's access tokens use `at+jwt`. |
| `{ embedKey: … }` | `bool` (default `false`) | Writes the public key of the pair into the header, as a minimal JWK (RFC 7638). A DPoP proof needs this. It is off by default. With a shared secret it throws an error, because a secret has no public key. |

**Returns** `string` — The token as a string: a header, a payload and a signature in base64url, joined by two dots. You can put it in a header, a query string or a JSON body without escaping.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$key` is a secret shorter than 32 bytes, or an `X25519` pair, which cannot sign. `{ embedKey: true }` is used with a shared secret. `$lifetime` is zero or negative. `$claims` contains `exp` or `iat`, or an entry without a name.; `RuntimeError` — The process does not have enough memory for the token.

<a id="core-core-jwt-signobject"></a>
#### `Core\Jwt::signObject`

```nvs skip
Core\Jwt::signObject(object $claims, Core\Time\Duration $lifetime, Core\Crypto\KeyPair $key, { kid?: string, typ?: string, embedKey?: bool }): string
```

Signs a shape or an object `$claims` into a JWT that expires `$lifetime` from now. A key pair signs it, and the pair decides the algorithm. The claims are written the way `Core\Json::encode` writes them, with `iat` and `exp` added at the end.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$claims` | `object` | A shape, or an object of a class with `#[Core\Json\Derive]`. It is encoded as a JSON object. This method writes `exp` and `iat`, so `$claims` may not contain them. A value that cannot be encoded as JSON is a bug in the program. |
| `$lifetime` | `Core\Time\Duration` | How long the token is valid, such as `15m`, `1h` or `7d`. It must be greater than zero. A token that is already expired is a bug in the program. |
| `$key` | `Core\Crypto\KeyPair` | A `Core\Crypto\KeyPair`. It signs with ES256, EdDSA, RS256 or PS256, depending on its kind. A shared secret is not allowed here. A token with these claims is for another service, and `Core\Jwt::verify` reads only the string claims that `sign` writes. |
| `{ kid: … }` | `string` (default `null`, neutral) | The key's name, written into the header. Use it when the receiver has several keys. By default there is no `kid`. The value is written exactly as given. It does not choose which key signs the token. |
| `{ typ: … }` | `string` (default `null`, neutral) | The header's `typ`. It is `JWT` if you leave it out. RFC 9068's access tokens use `at+jwt`. |
| `{ embedKey: … }` | `bool` (default `false`) | Writes the public key of the pair into the header, as a minimal JWK (RFC 7638). A DPoP proof needs this. It is off by default. |

**Returns** `string` — The token as a string, in the same format that `sign` returns. The payload is the claims object, with `iat` and `exp` as its last two fields.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$claims` contains `exp` or `iat`. `$claims` cannot be encoded as JSON, for example a class without `#[Core\Json\Derive]`, a `secret` value, a `bytes` value or a cycle. `$key` is an `X25519` pair, which cannot sign. `$lifetime` is zero or negative.; `RuntimeError` — The process does not have enough memory for the token.

<a id="core-core-jwt-verify"></a>
#### `Core\Jwt::verify`

```nvs skip
Core\Jwt::verify(string $token, secret bytes $key): array<tainted string>
```

Checks that `$key` signed `$token` and that the token has not expired. Then it returns the token's claims. If a check fails, it throws an error. It never returns an empty value that a comparison could take for a valid token.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$token` | `string` (neutral) | The token as the request sent it, in its three-part form. |
| `$key` | `secret bytes` (sink) | The shared secret that was given to `sign`, or the issuer's secret. The method compares the token's `alg` with the key's algorithm. It never uses `alg` to choose the algorithm. |

**Returns** `array<tainted string>` — Every claim in the payload, by name, and each one is `tainted`. A signature shows who wrote a value, but not that the value is safe to use. The result includes `exp` and `iat` as strings of decimal digits.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$key` is shorter than 32 bytes, so it cannot be a signing key.; `RuntimeError` — The token was not signed with this key. The message is the same for every reason the signature check fails. It also throws when the token has expired, has no `exp`, or has a claim that is not a string.

<a id="core-core-jwt-verifyissued"></a>
#### `Core\Jwt::verifyIssued`

```nvs skip
Core\Jwt::verifyIssued<T>(string $token, Core\Jwt\KeySet|Core\Crypto\PublicKey $keys, string $issuer, string $audience, { leeway?: Core\Time\Duration, typ?: string, nonce?: string, maxAge?: Core\Time\Duration }): T
```

Checks a token from another service and returns its claims as the type you wrote. It checks the header, finds the one key that may have signed the token, and checks the signature. Then it checks the time and the registered claims, in that order. If a check fails, it throws an error. It never returns an empty value.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$token` | `string` (neutral) | The token as the request sent it, in its three-part form. A token longer than 8 KiB throws an error and is not read. |
| `$keys` | `Core\Jwt\KeySet\|Core\Crypto\PublicKey` | The issuer's key set, in which the header's `kid` names exactly one key. It can also be one public key. The method never tries every key. A token without a `kid` is checked only against a set with exactly one key. The method compares the token's `alg` with the key's algorithm. It never uses `alg` to choose the algorithm. |
| `$issuer` | `string` (neutral) | What the token's `iss` must equal, exactly. |
| `$audience` | `string` (neutral) | What the token's `aud` must be, or must contain. A token with more than one audience must also have an `azp` equal to this value. |
| `{ leeway: … }` | `Core\Time\Duration` (default `null`) | How much the clocks may differ, at the start and at the end of the valid time. It is 60 seconds if you leave it out. A negative value or more than 5 minutes throws an error. It makes the expiry check less strict, but never turns it off. |
| `{ typ: … }` | `string` (default `null`, neutral) | The `typ` the header must have. The comparison ignores case and an `application/` prefix. RFC 9068's access tokens use `at+jwt`. If you leave it out, any `typ` is allowed. |
| `{ nonce: … }` | `string` (default `null`, neutral) | The value the token's `nonce` claim must equal. It is compared in constant time. If you give it, a token without a `nonce` throws an error. |
| `{ maxAge: … }` | `Core\Time\Duration` (default `null`) | How old the token's `auth_time` may be. If you give it, a token without an `auth_time` throws an error. |

**Returns** `T` — An object of the type you wrote, decoded from the payload the way `Core\Json::decodeAs` decodes a document. Its string properties must be declared `tainted`, or the call does not compile. A signature shows who wrote a claim, but not that the claim is safe to use.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `leeway` is negative or more than 5 minutes. The type you wrote is a list, and a token's payload is never a list. The key is an `X25519` key, which cannot verify a signature.; `RuntimeError` — The token was not signed with this issuer's key. Its header has a parameter that is not allowed, or no key matches it. The message is the same for all of these. It also throws when a valid token is outside its valid time. A registered claim with the wrong value throws too, and the message names the claim.

<a id="core-core-jwt-keyset"></a>
### `Core\Jwt\KeySet`

Keywords: read

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Jwt\KeySet::read`](#core-core-jwt-keyset-read) | `read(string $jwks, { rsaScheme?: Core\Crypto\KeyKind }): Core\Jwt\KeySet` |

<a id="core-core-jwt-keyset-read"></a>
#### `Core\Jwt\KeySet::read`

```nvs skip
Core\Jwt\KeySet::read(string $jwks, { rsaScheme?: Core\Crypto\KeyKind }): Core\Jwt\KeySet
```

Reads the signing keys from a JWKS document. A token can then be checked with the one key its `kid` names. A key of a kind this class does not use is skipped. A document with an error throws an error, and no key from it is used.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$jwks` | `string` (neutral) | The document as the issuer published it. This method only reads it. Fetching, caching and replacing the keys is the job of a package. The method keeps no state between calls. |
| `{ rsaScheme: … }` | `Core\Crypto\KeyKind` (default `null`) | The scheme for an RSA key that has no `alg`: `RsaPkcs1` for RS256 or `RsaPss` for PS256. A key's own `alg` always wins. An RSA key with neither is not allowed, and the method does not guess. Other kinds of key have their own algorithm, so this option does not change them. |

**Returns** `Core\Jwt\KeySet` — A set of at most 16 public keys, each with the name the document gave it. A key is found in it by its `kid`. The set is never searched by trying every key.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `{ rsaScheme: … }` names a kind that is not one of the two RSA kinds. No other kind has two schemes to choose from.; `RuntimeError` — `$jwks` is not a valid key document. It is not JSON, or it has no `keys` array. A key has a private field, or a `kid` that is not a string. A key does not match its kind, such as an RSA modulus outside 2048 to 8192 bits. An `alg` does not fit its key's kind. Two keys have the same `kid`. The document has more than 16 keys that can be used. The document is longer than 1 MiB.

### `Core\Jwe`

Keywords: encrypt, decrypt

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Jwe::encrypt`](#core-core-jwe-encrypt) | `encrypt(string $payload, Core\Jwe\Key $key): string` |
| [`Core\Jwe::decrypt`](#core-core-jwe-decrypt) | `decrypt(string $token, array<Core\Jwe\Key> $keys): tainted string` |

<a id="core-core-jwe-encrypt"></a>
#### `Core\Jwe::encrypt`

```nvs skip
Core\Jwe::encrypt(string $payload, Core\Jwe\Key $key): string
```

Encrypts `$payload` with `$key` and returns a compact JWE token. The content is encrypted with `A256GCM`. The method that made `$key` sets the key algorithm.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$payload` | `string` | The text to encrypt. `decrypt` returns exactly this text, as a `tainted` value. |
| `$key` | `Core\Jwe\Key` | The key, made by one of the four static methods of `Jwe\Key`. That method also sets `alg`. A key made by `Jwe\Key::own` encrypts to its own public key. |

**Returns** `string` — Five base64url parts without padding, joined by dots. They are the protected header, the encrypted key, the 12-byte IV, the ciphertext and the 16-byte tag. The encrypted key is empty for `dir` and `ECDH-ES`. Each call uses a new IV, so the token is different every time.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The public key or key pair in `$key` has a point that gives no usable shared secret.; `RuntimeError` — This process does not have enough memory for a buffer the size of the token.

<a id="core-core-jwe-decrypt"></a>
#### `Core\Jwe::decrypt`

```nvs skip
Core\Jwe::decrypt(string $token, array<Core\Jwe\Key> $keys): tainted string
```

Decrypts `$token` with each key in `$keys`, in order, and returns the payload. If no key works, it throws an error. The result is **`tainted`**. Decrypting proves who wrote the payload, but not that its content is safe to use.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$token` | `string` (neutral) | The token text, as it arrived. A `tainted` value is allowed here, because tokens usually come from outside. |
| `$keys` | `array<Core\Jwe\Key>` | The keys to try, in order. A token encrypted with any of these keys can be decrypted. A key made by `Jwe\Key::password` must be the only key, because each try is slow. A key made by `Jwe\Key::recipient` is a public key and decrypts nothing. |

**Returns** `tainted string` — The payload, exactly as it was encrypted, as a `tainted string`.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$keys` is empty, or it contains a `Jwe\Key::recipient` key, or it contains a `Jwe\Key::password` key together with other keys.; `RuntimeError` — No key in `$keys` can decrypt `$token`. The token may not have five parts, or its header has fields this class does not read. Its `alg` may not match `$keys`, or the token was changed. All cases have the same message, so an attacker cannot learn which check failed.; `ParseError` — The token was decrypted, but its payload is not valid UTF-8 text.

#### `Core\Jwe\Key::shared`

```nvs skip
Core\Jwe\Key::shared(secret bytes $key): Core\Jwe\Key
```

Makes a key for `dir`. The shared key itself encrypts the content. No other key is derived or wrapped.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |

<a id="core-core-jwe-key-password"></a>
#### `Core\Jwe\Key::password`

```nvs skip
Core\Jwe\Key::password(secret string $password): Core\Jwe\Key
```

Makes a key for `PBES2-HS256+A128KW`. A key is derived from a person's password. A random content key is then encrypted with it.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$password` | `secret string` (neutral) | The password, of any length. It can come from `Core\Cli::secret` or a form field. It is not hashed for storage. Use `Core\Password` for that. |

**Returns** `Core\Jwe\Key` — A key that `encrypt` derives with the minimum iteration count. The count and the salt are written into the header, so the other side can derive the same key.

<a id="core-core-jwe-key-recipient"></a>
#### `Core\Jwe\Key::recipient`

```nvs skip
Core\Jwe\Key::recipient(Core\Crypto\PublicKey $key): Core\Jwe\Key
```

Makes a key for sending with `ECDH-ES`. It is the public key of the other party. Only that party's key pair can decrypt the token.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$key` | `Core\Crypto\PublicKey` | A `P256` or `X25519` public key, already validated by `Core\Crypto\PublicKey::read`. |

**Returns** `Core\Jwe\Key` — A key for `encrypt`. Each call makes a new temporary key pair and writes its public key into the header as `epk`. This key cannot decrypt, because it is a public key.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$key` is an `Ed25519` or RSA key. Neither can be used for key agreement.

<a id="core-core-jwe-key-own"></a>
#### `Core\Jwe\Key::own`

```nvs skip
Core\Jwe\Key::own(Core\Crypto\KeyPair $key): Core\Jwe\Key
```

Makes a key for receiving with `ECDH-ES`. It is your program's own key pair. It decrypts tokens that other parties encrypted to its public key.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$key` | `Core\Crypto\KeyPair` | A `P256` or `X25519` key pair, read with `Core\Crypto\KeyPair::read`. |

**Returns** `Core\Jwe\Key` — A key that `decrypt` uses with the `epk` of the token. With this key, `encrypt` encrypts to the pair's own public key.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$key` is an `Ed25519` or RSA pair. Neither can be used for key agreement.

<a id="core-core-signature"></a>
### `Core\Signature`

Keywords: sign, verify

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Signature::sign`](#core-core-signature-sign) | `sign(array<string> $payload, { keys: array<secret bytes>, until: ?Core\Time\Instant } $settings): string` |
| [`Core\Signature::verify`](#core-core-signature-verify) | `verify(string $token, array<secret bytes> $keys): array<tainted string>` |

<a id="core-core-signature-sign"></a>
#### `Core\Signature::sign`

```nvs skip
Core\Signature::sign(array<string> $payload, { keys: array<secret bytes>, until: ?Core\Time\Instant } $settings): string
```

Signs `$payload` with the newest key in `$settings.keys` and returns a token. The token contains the payload, and `Core\Signature::verify` returns it again. The same payload, keys and `until` always give the same token.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$payload` | `array<string>` | The values to sign, each under a name. The order of the names is not signed. `verify` returns the values sorted by name. |
| `$settings` | `{ keys: array<secret bytes>, until: ?Core\Time\Instant }` | The keys, and the time when the token stops being valid. You must write both. Keys: `keys` (array<secret bytes>) The keys, newest first. `$keys[0]` signs the token. The older keys are there so that `verify` still accepts tokens made before you added a new key. A list of one key is `[$key]`.; `until` (?Core\Time\Instant) The time after which `verify` throws an error for this token. The time is part of the signed data, so nobody can change it. Write `null` for a token that never expires. |

**Returns** `string` — The token. It contains only `A-Z`, `a-z`, `0-9`, `-` and `_`, so you can put it in a URL or a cookie without escaping it. It is about 4/3 × (payload + 40) characters long.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$settings.keys` is empty, or its first key is not 32 bytes long. `Core\Crypto::generateKey()` returns a key of the right length.

<a id="core-core-signature-verify"></a>
#### `Core\Signature::verify`

```nvs skip
Core\Signature::verify(string $token, array<secret bytes> $keys): array<tainted string>
```

Checks that `$token` was made by `Core\Signature::sign` with a key in `$keys`, and that it has not expired. It returns the signed payload, or throws an error. Every value in the payload is `tainted` (treated as input from outside). A signature shows who made the data. It does not show that the data is safe to use.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$token` | `string` (neutral) | The token as your program received it, for example from a URL. A `tainted` string is allowed here. |
| `$keys` | `array<secret bytes>` | The keys you gave `sign`, newest first. A token made with any key in this list is accepted. A token made with a key you removed from the list is not. |

**Returns** `array<tainted string>` — The signed payload, sorted by name. Every value is a `tainted string`.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$keys` is empty, or one of its keys is not 32 bytes long.; `RuntimeError` — `$token` was not made with any key in `$keys`. This includes a changed token, text that is not a token, and a token for a signed URL. All of these give the same message, so an attacker learns nothing from it. An expired token also throws `RuntimeError`, with a different message that gives the time it expired.

<a id="core-core-html"></a>
### `Core\Html`

Keywords: html, markup, template, html template, page, view, render, escape, escaping, xss, html entities, sanitize, parse, escape, join, later, toSource, parse, sanitize

`Core\Html\Markup` is the one type an HTTP request writes raw; every `string` written into a
page is escaped. A `Markup` is made in three ways: an ``html`…` `` template, whose text is trusted
because it was written in the source and whose `{$…}` holes are escaped; `Core\Html::escape`,
which escapes a string; and `Core\Html::sanitize`, which rebuilds an untrusted document with
only its safe parts. `+` joins two `Markup` values and `Core\Html::join` joins a list; `.` on a
`Markup` is a compile error. `Core\Html::toSource` is the only way back to a `string`, and it
takes a written reason. `Core\Html::parse` reads any document onto a `Core\Xml\Node` tree and
never fails.

```nvs
<?nvs
tainted string $name = '<script>alert(1)</script>';
string $bio = '<p>likes <b>tea</b></p><img src=x onerror=alert(1)>';
Core\Html\Markup $badge = html`<span class="badge">new</span>`;
Core\Html\Markup $line = html`<p>{$name} {$badge}</p>`;
Core\Html\Markup $safe = Core\Html::sanitize($bio);
echo $line + $safe, "\n";
echo Core\Html::join([$badge, $badge], html`, `), "\n";
echo Core\Html::toSource($badge, 'logging the fragment'), "\n";
```
```output
<p>&lt;script&gt;alert(1)&lt;/script&gt; <span class="badge">new</span></p><p>likes <b>tea</b></p><img src="x">
<span class="badge">new</span>, <span class="badge">new</span>
<span class="badge">new</span>
```

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Html::escape`](#core-core-html-escape) | `escape(string $text): Core\Html\Markup` |
| [`Core\Html::join`](#core-core-html-join) | `join(array<Core\Html\Markup> $parts, Core\Html\Markup $separator): Core\Html\Markup` |
| [`Core\Html::later`](#core-core-html-later) | `later(callable(): mixed $fn, { placeholder?: Core\Html\Markup, error?: Core\Html\Markup, deadline?: Core\Time\Duration }): Core\Html\Markup` |
| [`Core\Html::toSource`](#core-core-html-tosource) | `toSource(Core\Html\Markup $markup, string $reason): string` |
| [`Core\Html::parse`](#core-core-html-parse) | `parse(string $document): Core\Xml\Node` |
| [`Core\Html::sanitize`](#core-core-html-sanitize) | `sanitize(string $document): Core\Html\Markup` |

<a id="core-core-html-escape"></a>
#### `Core\Html::escape`

```nvs skip
Core\Html::escape(string $text): Core\Html\Markup
```

Escapes `&`, `<`, `>`, `"` and `'` in `$text` as character references. It also replaces every unterminated bidirectional control character with `�`. You can write the result into a page, where a `tainted` string is not allowed.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$text` | `string` (launder) | The text to write into an HTML document. It is shown as text, not read as HTML. |

**Returns** `Core\Html\Markup` — A `Core\Html\Markup` with the escaped text. It is safe in element content and in an attribute value with either kind of quotes. It is not a `string`, so the page does not escape it a second time. `toSource` returns its text as a `string`. Text without the five characters and without an unterminated control character does not change. The five characters are always escaped, and no option turns this off. Input that already looks like a reference is escaped again, because `&amp;` in the input is the text `&amp;`.

<a id="core-core-html-join"></a>
#### `Core\Html::join`

```nvs skip
Core\Html::join(array<Core\Html\Markup> $parts, Core\Html\Markup $separator): Core\Html\Markup
```

Joins a list of `Core\Html\Markup` fragments in order, with `$separator` between each two. It does the same as `Markup + Markup` for a whole list.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$parts` | `array<Core\Html\Markup>` | The fragments to join, in list order. |
| `$separator` | `Core\Html\Markup` | The markup written between each two parts. It is not written before the first part or after the last. With empty markup, nothing is written between parts. |

**Returns** `Core\Html\Markup` — A `Core\Html\Markup` with every part in order. An empty list gives empty markup. Nothing is escaped, because each part and the separator are already safe markup. Escaping them again would break that markup.

<a id="core-core-html-later"></a>
#### `Core\Html::later`

```nvs skip
Core\Html::later(callable(): mixed $fn, { placeholder?: Core\Html\Markup, error?: Core\Html\Markup, deadline?: Core\Time\Duration }): Core\Html\Markup
```

Runs `$fn` as a separate task and returns a placeholder. Write the placeholder where the output belongs. When the page is finished, the output of `$fn` replaces the placeholder. Several `later` calls run at the same time.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$fn` | `callable(): mixed` | The function to run. It takes no arguments. Its output is what it echoes, followed by the `Core\Html\Markup` it returns, if any. |
| `{ placeholder: … }` | `Core\Html\Markup` (default `null`) | The markup the page shows until the output is ready. The default is empty. |
| `{ error: … }` | `Core\Html\Markup` (default `null`) | The markup shown instead of the output when `$fn` throws an error or runs past its `deadline`. The default is empty. |
| `{ deadline: … }` | `Core\Time\Duration` (default `null`) | The longest time `$fn` may run. Without it, only the request's own limits apply. |

**Returns** `Core\Html\Markup` — A `Core\Html\Markup` placeholder. Outside an HTML response, `$fn` runs at once and the result is its output.

**Throws** `LogicError` — When the page writes the same placeholder twice. A placeholder that the page never writes is not an error: its `$fn` does not run, and a warning is logged.

<a id="core-core-html-tosource"></a>
#### `Core\Html::toSource`

```nvs skip
Core\Html::toSource(Core\Html\Markup $markup, string $reason): string
```

Returns the source text of a `Core\Html\Markup`. There is no `Markup as string` cast, so this is the only way to get the text. Each call needs a written reason, so it is easy to find in code.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$markup` | `Core\Html\Markup` | The markup whose text you need. |
| `$reason` | `string` (neutral) | Why this code needs the text and not the markup, written for the next person who reads it. Nothing else reads it. An empty reason is not allowed. |

**Returns** `string` — The source text of the markup, as a plain `string`. Typical uses are caching a rendered fragment, storing it in a database column, or writing it to a file. Another use is passing it to an output that is not HTML.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$reason` is empty. Each call must say why it needs the text.

<a id="core-core-html-parse"></a>
#### `Core\Html::parse`

```nvs skip
Core\Html::parse(string $document): Core\Xml\Node
```

Parses `$document` as HTML with the WHATWG algorithm, which browsers use. It returns the document node of the same kind of tree that `Core\Xml::parse` builds.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$document` | `string` (neutral) | The document text. Any text is a valid document, so this method never throws an error. |

**Returns** `Core\Xml\Node` — The `Core\Xml\Node` of kind `Document`. Its children are the top level of the parsed page. For any input that is not empty, this is one `html` element with `head` and `body` in it. That is true even when the text does not contain these tags. Missing tags, wrongly nested tags and stray content go exactly where a browser puts them. So the tree is the page a browser would show. A `<!DOCTYPE …>` gives no node, because the tree has no kind for it. Names are lower case in HTML. In SVG and MathML they get the correct case, as the algorithm says. Elements nested deeper than 1000 levels are placed at level 1000, so walking the tree can never run out of stack.

<a id="core-core-html-sanitize"></a>
#### `Core\Html::sanitize`

```nvs skip
Core\Html::sanitize(string $document): Core\Html\Markup
```

Parses `$document` as HTML and builds a new document from only the allowed elements and attributes. Use it for untrusted HTML. For untrusted text, use `escape`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$document` | `string` (launder) | The HTML to rebuild. Any text is a valid document, so this method never throws an error. |

**Returns** `Core\Html\Markup` — A `Core\Html\Markup` with the rebuilt document. You can write it into a page without escaping it again. The method builds a new document and does not edit the old one. An element that is not allowed loses its tag, but its content is kept. An attribute that is not allowed is not written. A `script`, `style` or other raw-text element is removed with its content. The list of allowed elements is fixed, and no argument can extend it. A list you write yourself could have security holes. The text and the order of the kept content stay as in the document.

<a id="core-core-xml"></a>
### `Core\Xml`

Keywords: parse, reader, writer

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Xml::parse`](#core-core-xml-parse) | `parse(string $document): Core\Xml\Node` |
| [`Core\Xml::reader`](#core-core-xml-reader) | `reader(string $document): Core\Xml\Reader` |
| [`Core\Xml::writer`](#core-core-xml-writer) | `writer({ indent?: string }): Core\Xml\Writer` |

<a id="core-core-xml-parse"></a>
#### `Core\Xml::parse`

```nvs skip
Core\Xml::parse(string $document): Core\Xml\Node
```

Reads a whole XML document and returns its document node. A document that is not well-formed throws a `ParseError`. Nothing is repaired or guessed. `Core\Html::parse` returns the same kind of tree, and repairs broken HTML instead of throwing.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$document` | `string` (neutral) | The document text. The five predefined entities, such as `&amp;`, and numeric character references, such as `&#65;`, are expanded. Any other entity reference throws a `ParseError`. Nothing is loaded from a file or from the network. |

**Returns** `Core\Xml\Node` — The document node. Its children are the root element and any comments or processing instructions next to it. Every string you read from the tree is `tainted`, which means it came from outside the program. This is true even when `$document` was not tainted.

**Throws** `ParseError` — The document is not well-formed. For example: a tag is never closed or is closed with a different name, there is more than one root element, an attribute is written twice, or an entity reference is not one of the predefined ones. A document type declaration also throws, and so do elements nested more than 1024 levels deep.

<a id="core-core-xml-reader"></a>
#### `Core\Xml::reader`

```nvs skip
Core\Xml::reader(string $document): Core\Xml\Reader
```

Returns a reader that goes through `$document` one node at a time. Call `read` until it returns `null`. The reader does not build a tree. It keeps the current node and the names of the elements that are open. This call reads nothing yet. The first `read` reads the first node.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$document` | `string` (neutral) | The document text. The reader does not copy it. Entity references are handled the same way as in `Core\Xml::parse`. |

**Returns** `Core\Xml\Reader` — A reader. Its first `read` returns the first node of the document.

<a id="core-core-xml-writer"></a>
#### `Core\Xml::writer`

```nvs skip
Core\Xml::writer({ indent?: string }): Core\Xml\Writer
```

Returns a writer that builds an XML document one node at a time. The writer remembers which elements are open, so `endElement` needs no name. Ending the document while an element is still open throws a `LogicError`. Every method that takes text escapes it, so you never escape text yourself.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `{ indent: … }` | `string` (default `""`, neutral) | The text for one level of indentation, such as two spaces. The default is `""`, which means no indentation. It may contain only whitespace. The writer never adds indentation next to text content, because that would change the text. |

**Returns** `Core\Xml\Writer` — A new writer with an empty document. Call `startDocument` first.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `indent` contains a character that is not whitespace.

<a id="core-core-xml-node"></a>
### `Core\Xml\Node`

Keywords: kind, name, namespaceUri, text, attributes, children, source

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|

<a id="core-core-xml-node-kind"></a>
#### `Core\Xml\Node->kind`

```nvs skip
$node->kind(): Core\Xml\Node::Kind
```

Returns what kind of node this is: an element, a text, a comment, a processing instruction or the document. Compare it with a `Core\Xml\Node::Kind` case, for example to skip everything that is not an element.

**Returns** `Core\Xml\Node::Kind` — A `Core\Xml\Node::Kind` case. There are exactly five cases, so a `match` over them covers every node.

<a id="core-core-xml-node-name"></a>
#### `Core\Xml\Node->name`

```nvs skip
$node->name(): tainted string
```

Returns the name of this node. For an element, this is the tag name. For a processing instruction, it is the target, such as `print` in `<?print fast?>`. A text node, a comment and the document have no name, so they return an empty string.

**Returns** `tainted string` — A `tainted` string. The name is written as in the document, with its prefix: for `<x:a/>` the result is `x:a`. To find the namespace of the prefix, use `namespaceUri`.

<a id="core-core-xml-node-namespaceuri"></a>
#### `Core\Xml\Node->namespaceUri`

```nvs skip
$node->namespaceUri(): ?tainted string
```

Returns the namespace URI of this element. For `<x:item>`, the URI comes from the nearest `xmlns:x` declaration on the element or above it. For a name without a prefix, it comes from the nearest `xmlns` declaration. An inner declaration replaces an outer one. The prefix `xml` always has the URI `http://www.w3.org/XML/1998/namespace`.

**Returns** `?tainted string` — A `tainted` string, or `null`. The result is `null` for a node that is not an element, for an element that no declaration covers, and for an element under `xmlns=""`. The name does not change: `name` still returns `x:item`.

<a id="core-core-xml-node-text"></a>
#### `Core\Xml\Node->text`

```nvs skip
$node->text(): tainted string
```

Returns the text of this node. For a text node, this is its characters. For a comment, it is the comment's content, and for a processing instruction it is the part after the name. An element and the document return an empty string. Their text is in their text children.

**Returns** `tainted string` — A `tainted` string. Entities such as `&amp;` and character references such as `&#98;` are expanded. A CDATA section gives the text written inside it.

<a id="core-core-xml-node-attributes"></a>
#### `Core\Xml\Node->attributes`

```nvs skip
$node->attributes(): array<tainted string>
```

Returns the attributes of this element, in the order the document wrote them. For a node that is not an element, the array is empty.

**Returns** `array<tainted string>` — An array keyed by attribute name. The name is written as in the document, with its prefix, such as `xml:lang`. Entities such as `&amp;` are expanded in the value. A tab or a line break written inside the value becomes a space, as XML requires. The values are `tainted`.

<a id="core-core-xml-node-children"></a>
#### `Core\Xml\Node->children`

```nvs skip
$node->children(): array<Core\Xml\Node>
```

Returns the children of this node, in the order of the document. For the document node, this is the root element and any comment or processing instruction beside it. For an element, it is everything between its start tag and its end tag. A text, a comment and a processing instruction have no children, so the array is empty.

**Returns** `array<Core\Xml\Node>` — An array with one `Core\Xml\Node` per child. The spaces and line breaks between two elements are text nodes, and they are in the array too.

<a id="core-core-xml-node-source"></a>
#### `Core\Xml\Node->source`

```nvs skip
$node->source(): tainted string
```

Returns this node and everything inside it as XML text. Use it to write a document, or one part of it, back out after you read it. Every element is written with an end tag, so `<e/>` is written as `<e></e>`. The XML rules apply, also to a tree from `Core\Html::parse`.

**Returns** `tainted string` — A `tainted` string, with no XML declaration at the start. In text, `&`, `<` and `>` are escaped. In an attribute value, `"`, a tab and a line break are escaped too. When you parse the result, you get the same tree again.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The tree contains something XML cannot write: a name that is not a valid XML name, a comment that contains `--` or ends with `-`, a processing instruction that contains `?>`, or a character XML does not allow. Only a tree from `Core\Html::parse` can contain these, because `Core\Xml::parse` does not accept them.

<a id="core-core-xml-reader"></a>
### `Core\Xml\Reader`

Keywords: read, depth

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Xml\Reader->read`](#core-core-xml-reader-read) | `read(): ?Core\Xml\Node` |
| [`Core\Xml\Reader->depth`](#core-core-xml-reader-depth) | `depth(): uint` |

<a id="core-core-xml-reader-read"></a>
#### `Core\Xml\Reader->read`

```nvs skip
$reader->read(): ?Core\Xml\Node
```

Reads the next node of the document and returns it. At the end of the document, it returns `null`. An element is returned when its opening tag is read. It has its name and its attributes, but no children. The nodes inside it are returned by the next calls to `read`. A closing tag is not a node, so use `depth` to see where an element ends.

**Returns** `?Core\Xml\Node` — The next node: an element, a text, a comment or a processing instruction. The result is `null` at the end of the document. Every string you read from the node is `tainted`, because it came from outside the program.

**Throws** `ParseError` — The document is not well-formed at the place the reader has reached. `Core\Xml::parse` throws the same errors. The nodes before that place were already returned. The reader does not move past the error, so the next `read` throws the same error again.

<a id="core-core-xml-reader-depth"></a>
#### `Core\Xml\Reader->depth`

```nvs skip
$reader->depth(): uint
```

Returns how deeply the node that `read` returned last is nested. The root element has depth `0`. A node inside the root element has depth `1`, and each level adds one. A closing tag is not a node, so the depth is how you see where an element ends. When the depth is the same as or smaller than an earlier element's depth, that element is closed.

**Returns** `uint` — A whole number. It is `0` before the first `read`, and `0` again after `read` returns `null`.

<a id="core-core-xml-writer"></a>
### `Core\Xml\Writer`

Keywords: startDocument, endDocument, startElement, endElement, content, attribute, comment, cdata, instruction, doctype
