<a id="core-core-db"></a>
### `Core\Db`

Keywords: connect, open, inList, quoteIdentifier

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Db::connect`](#core-core-db-connect) | `connect(string $name, { shared?: bool, timeout?: Core\Time\Duration }): Core\Db\Connection` |
| [`Core\Db::open`](#core-core-db-open) | `open({ driver: Core\Db\Driver::MySql\|Core\Db\Driver::MariaDb\|Core\Db\Driver::Postgres\|Core\Db\Driver::SqlServer, host: string, port?: uint, database: tainted string, user: tainted string, password: secret tainted string, tls?: Core\Db::Tls, timeZone?: Core\Time\Zone, timeout?: Core\Time\Duration, statementCache?: uint }\|{ driver: Core\Db\Driver::Sqlite, path: string, timeZone?: Core\Time\Zone, timeout?: Core\Time\Duration } $settings, { shared?: bool }): Core\Db\Connection` |
| [`Core\Db::inList`](#core-core-db-inlist) | `inList(array<mixed> $values): Core\Db\InList` |
| [`Core\Db::quoteIdentifier`](#core-core-db-quoteidentifier) | `quoteIdentifier(string $name): string` |

<a id="core-core-db-connect"></a>
#### `Core\Db::connect`

```nvs skip
Core\Db::connect(string $name, { shared?: bool, timeout?: Core\Time\Duration }): Core\Db\Connection
```

Opens the database connection that a `[db.<name>]` block of `nvs.toml` describes. Later calls in the same request return the same connection. The password is in the configuration file, not in the program. It needs the `db.connect` capability for that name.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$name` | `string` (sink) | The block to open. It must match exactly: `"main"` is `[db.main]`. Two blocks for the same server give two connections, because whoever wrote two blocks wanted two. |
| `{ shared: … }` | `bool` (default `true`) | Whether this call may return the connection that an earlier call opened. `false` opens a separate connection. You need one for a write that must stay after a rollback, for a session lock, or for a second statement during a `stream`. |
| `{ timeout: … }` | `Core\Time\Duration` (default `null`) | How long opening the connection may take, including the DNS lookup and TLS. Without it, only the server and the network limit the time. |

**Returns** `Core\Db\Connection` — A `Core\Db\Connection`. The same call twice in one request returns the same object, unless `shared` is `false`. The connection is closed when the request ends.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `db.connect` does not grant `$name`, or there is no `[db.<name>]` block of that name. It is also thrown when the block does not describe a valid connection. Examples are a missing `driver`, a setting of another driver, or a `time_zone` that is not an offset.; `IOError` — The host name does not resolve, or the connection, the TLS handshake or the login failed. It is also thrown when this CPU core already uses `[db.<name>.pool] max` connections with that name and none is free within `acquire`. When the server sends its own error message, the error includes it.

<a id="core-core-db-open"></a>
#### `Core\Db::open`

```nvs skip
Core\Db::open({ driver: Core\Db\Driver::MySql|Core\Db\Driver::MariaDb|Core\Db\Driver::Postgres|Core\Db\Driver::SqlServer, host: string, port?: uint, database: tainted string, user: tainted string, password: secret tainted string, tls?: Core\Db::Tls, timeZone?: Core\Time\Zone, timeout?: Core\Time\Duration, statementCache?: uint }|{ driver: Core\Db\Driver::Sqlite, path: string, timeZone?: Core\Time\Zone, timeout?: Core\Time\Duration } $settings, { shared?: bool }): Core\Db\Connection
```

Opens a connection to a server that the program names itself. Use it when a `[db.<name>]` block does not work. Examples are a customer whose database is stored as a row in another database, or an admin tool where a person types a host. It needs the `db.open` capability for that host. The address is fully checked against the blocked address ranges. This check is stricter than for `connect`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$settings` | `{ driver: Core\Db\Driver::MySql\|Core\Db\Driver::MariaDb\|Core\Db\Driver::Postgres\|Core\Db\Driver::SqlServer, host: string, port?: uint, database: tainted string, user: tainted string, password: secret tainted string, tls?: Core\Db::Tls, timeZone?: Core\Time\Zone, timeout?: Core\Time\Duration, statementCache?: uint }\|{ driver: Core\Db\Driver::Sqlite, path: string, timeZone?: Core\Time\Zone, timeout?: Core\Time\Duration }` | All settings of the connection. The object has one of two shapes, and `driver` selects the shape. Four of the five databases need a host, and SQLite needs a file path. Keys: `driver` (Driver) Which database this is. It selects which of the two shapes the rest of the object must have.; `host` (string) The server to connect to. Its certificate is checked against this name. It cannot be `tainted`, and no check can remove that, because no check on a string proves that a host is safe for a password.; `port` (uint) The port to connect to. Without it, the driver's default is used: 5432 for PostgreSQL, and 3306 for MySQL and MariaDB.; `database` (tainted string) The database or schema to use. It may be `tainted`, because it is sent as a separate value and never read as SQL.; `user` (tainted string) The role to log in as. It may be `tainted` for the same reason.; `password` (secret tainted string) The role's password. It is `secret`, so it cannot reach a log line, a message or a trace.; `tls` (Tls) How much of the certificate is checked. Only `VerifyFull` works, and it is the default. The three weaker modes throw an error.; `timeZone` (Core\Time\Zone) The time zone for reading a column that has no time zone. The server is also told to use it. The default is UTC.; `timeout` (Core\Time\Duration) How long opening the connection may take, including the DNS lookup and TLS.; `statementCache` (uint) How many prepared statements this connection may keep on the server. `0` turns the cache off.; `path` (string) The SQLite file, used in place of a host. It cannot be `tainted`, and it also needs the `fs.read` and `fs.write` capabilities. |
| `{ shared: … }` | `bool` (default `true`) | Whether this call may return the connection that an earlier call opened with the same settings. `false` opens a separate connection. |

**Returns** `Core\Db\Connection` — A `Core\Db\Connection`. It is closed when the request ends. Two calls with the same value in every setting return the same object, unless `shared` is `false`.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `db.open` does not grant the host, or the host's address is in a private range that `net.internal` does not allow. It is also thrown when this build cannot open a connection with these settings, or when `tls` names a mode weaker than `VerifyFull`.; `IOError` — The host name does not resolve, or the connection, the TLS handshake or the login failed. It is also thrown when this CPU core already uses its `max` connections with these settings and none became free in time.

<a id="core-core-db-inlist"></a>
#### `Core\Db::inList`

```nvs skip
Core\Db::inList(array<mixed> $values): Core\Db\InList
```

Binds `$values` as a list of values. The placeholder it is bound to becomes a list in parentheses with one placeholder per value, such as `IN (?, ?, ?)`. Nothing else in a statement changes the SQL text.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$values` | `array<mixed>` | The values to bind, one placeholder each, in the order of the array. Keys are ignored: the values fill positions inside one placeholder and have no names. |

**Returns** `Core\Db\InList` — A `Core\Db\InList` to bind to a single placeholder. It has no methods, and you can use it only as a bound parameter. Two lists of different lengths with the same SQL are two entries in the statement cache. The expanded statement has a different number of placeholders.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$values` is empty. An empty list means "match nothing" inside `IN` and "match everything" inside `NOT IN`. Check for an empty list in your code instead.

<a id="core-core-db-quoteidentifier"></a>
#### `Core\Db::quoteIdentifier`

```nvs skip
Core\Db::quoteIdentifier(string $name): string
```

Checks that `$name` is a plain SQL identifier: a letter or `_`, then letters, digits or `_`. It returns the name unchanged and no longer `tainted`, so you can write it into the text of a statement. Use it for a table or column name. It checks the syntax only. A visitor can still name any table or column, such as `users`. If a visitor chooses the name, check it against a list of allowed names first.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$name` | `string` (launder) | The identifier to check. It is returned exactly as given. Nothing is escaped, shortened or lower-cased, because a name that passes the check needs none of it. |

**Returns** `string` — The same text, without the `tainted` qualifier. It has no quotes around it. This method has no connection, so it has no SQL dialect. The five databases use different quote characters.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$name` is empty, starts with a digit, or contains a character that is not a letter, a digit or `_`. This includes a name that is valid only inside quotes. It is also thrown when the database reads `$name` as a value without quotes, such as `current_user`, `user` or `current_timestamp`, in upper or lower case.

<a id="core-core-db-connection-query"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Connection->query`

```nvs skip
$connection->query(string $sql, array<mixed> $params, { timeout?: Core\Time\Duration }): Core\Db\Rows<Core\Db\Row>
```

Runs one statement with its values bound, and reads every row it returns into memory. Every statement is prepared, so there is no separate prepare step. The connection is free again as soon as this returns. `stream` keeps the connection while you read.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$sql` | `string` (sink) | The statement, with a `?` or a `:name` for each value. Never write a value into the text. A `tainted` string does not compile here, and no escape function can make one allowed. |
| `$params` | `array<mixed>` | The values to bind. Use list keys for `?` and string keys for `:name`, and never both in one array. A `Core\Db::inList` element expands into several placeholders at its position. Nothing else expands. |
| `{ timeout: … }` | `Core\Time\Duration` (default `null`) | How long this statement may take. The limit covers the whole statement: the prepare, the execution and every row of the result. When the time passes, the statement stops with an `IOError`. The connection cannot be used again, because it stopped in the middle of a message. Without it, the statement waits as long as the server takes. |

**Returns** `Core\Db\Rows<Core\Db\Row>` — A `Core\Db\Rows<Core\Db\Row>` with every row the statement returned, in the server's order. A statement that returns no rows, such as an `update` or a `create table`, gives an empty result. It is not an error.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The call is wrong, not the database. The placeholders and the array use different styles or different counts, or a `:name` has no element. It is also thrown for an element that cannot be bound, such as an array or an object that is not an `inList`. A statement already streaming on this connection throws it too.; `Core\Db\DbError` — The server rejected the statement, for example for a syntax error, a constraint or a permission. The error has the server's `SQLSTATE` and message. It is also thrown for a column type this driver cannot read yet.; `IOError` — The connection failed while the statement was running, or `timeout` passed before it finished. The connection cannot be used for the rest of the request.

<a id="core-core-db-connection-queryas"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Connection->queryAs`

```nvs skip
$connection->queryAs<T>(string $sql, array<mixed> $params, { timeout?: Core\Time\Duration }): Core\Db\Rows<T>
```

Runs one statement as `query` does and returns each row as an object of the class written at the call site. `#[Db\Derive]` generates the mapping from the class's declared properties.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$sql` | `string` (sink) | The statement, bound the same way as in `query`. Use a `?` or a `:name` for each value, and never write a value into the text. A `tainted` string does not compile here. |
| `$params` | `array<mixed>` | The values to bind, with the same rule as `query`: one array, with list keys for `?` and string keys for `:name`. |
| `{ timeout: … }` | `Core\Time\Duration` (default `null`) | How long this statement may take. The limit covers the whole statement: the prepare, the execution and every row of the result. When the time passes, the statement stops with an `IOError`. The connection cannot be used again, because it stopped in the middle of a message. Without it, the statement waits as long as the server takes. |

**Returns** `Core\Db\Rows<T>` — A `Core\Db\Rows<T>` with one `T` per row, in the server's order. Each object is created when you read its row with `all`, `first` or a `foreach`. If you only count the rows, no object is created.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The type argument is an `array<...>`. A result is already a list of arrays, one per row. It is also thrown when `T` has no `#[Db\Derive]`, so there is no column mapping to create it from. Both errors come from the call itself, but they are found when the program runs.; `ParseError` — A row did not match `T`. A column is missing, or has a different type than the property. A SQL NULL is in a property that is not `?T`, or a property's type has no column mapping. Every bad column of the row is reported at once in `issues`, and each `path` is the column's name.

<a id="core-core-db-connection-execute"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Connection->execute`

```nvs skip
$connection->execute(string $sql, array<mixed> $params, { timeout?: Core\Time\Duration }): Core\Db\Write
```

Runs one statement that changes data, such as an `insert`, an `update`, a `delete` or a `create table`. It returns how many rows changed and the new key, if there is one. The values are bound the same way `query` binds them.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$sql` | `string` (sink) | The statement, with a `?` or a `:name` for each value. Never write a value into the text. A `tainted` string does not compile here, and no escape function can make one allowed. |
| `$params` | `array<mixed>` | The values to bind. Use list keys for `?` and string keys for `:name`, and never both in one array. This is the same rule as in `query`. |
| `{ timeout: … }` | `Core\Time\Duration` (default `null`) | How long this statement may take. The limit covers the whole statement: the prepare, the execution and every row of the result. When the time passes, the statement stops with an `IOError`. The connection cannot be used again, because it stopped in the middle of a message. Without it, the statement waits as long as the server takes. |

**Returns** `Core\Db\Write` — A `Core\Db\Write` with the number of affected rows as the server reported it, and the id that a `RETURNING` clause returned. Any rows the statement returned are read and discarded, so the connection is free again. Use `query` to keep rows.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The call is wrong, not the database. The placeholders and the array use different styles or different counts, or a `:name` has no element. It is also thrown for an element that cannot be bound, such as an array or an object that is not an `inList`. A statement already streaming on this connection throws it too.; `Core\Db\DbError` — The server rejected the statement, for example for a syntax error, a constraint or a permission. The error has the server's `SQLSTATE` and message.; `IOError` — The connection failed while the statement was running, or `timeout` passed before it finished. The connection cannot be used for the rest of the request.

<a id="core-core-db-connection-executemany"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Connection->executeMany`

```nvs skip
$connection->executeMany(string $sql, array<array<mixed>> $sets, { timeout?: Core\Time\Duration }): uint
```

Runs one statement once for each set of values and returns how many rows the whole batch wrote. The statement is prepared once, and all sets go to the server in one round trip.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$sql` | `string` (sink) | The statement, written once and bound once for each set. A `tainted` string does not compile here, as in `execute`. All sets use this one text. |
| `$sets` | `array<array<mixed>>` | One `$params` array for each run, each with keys as `execute` needs them. All sets must bind the same number of values. A set whose `inList` has a different length is a different statement. |
| `{ timeout: … }` | `Core\Time\Duration` (default `null`) | How long this statement may take. The limit covers the whole statement: the prepare, the execution and every row of the result. When the time passes, the statement stops with an `IOError`. The connection cannot be used again, because it stopped in the middle of a message. Without it, the statement waits as long as the server takes. |

**Returns** `uint` — The sum of the counts each run reported. A command that reports no count adds nothing. An empty `$sets` writes nothing and returns `0`. Rows from a `RETURNING` clause are discarded. There is no `lastId`, because no single run owns it.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The call is wrong, not the database. A set uses both list keys and string keys, two sets bind different numbers of values, or an element cannot be bound. A statement already streaming on this connection throws it too.; `Core\Db\DbError` — The server rejected one run, for example for a syntax error, a constraint or a permission. Each run is its own transaction, so the writes before the failed run stay. Use `transaction` to save all or nothing.; `IOError` — The connection failed while the batch was running, or `timeout` passed before it finished. The connection cannot be used for the rest of the request.

<a id="core-core-db-connection-stream"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Connection->stream`

```nvs skip
$connection->stream(string $sql, array<mixed> $params, { timeout?: Core\Time\Duration }): Core\Db\Stream<Core\Db\Row>
```

Runs one statement and gives its rows one at a time to a `foreach` loop. The connection stays open until the loop ends. The memory used stays the same however many rows there are. Use it instead of `query` for a large result.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$sql` | `string` (sink) | The statement, bound the same way as in `query`. Use a `?` or a `:name` for each value, and never write a value into the text. A `tainted` string does not compile here. |
| `$params` | `array<mixed>` | The values to bind, with the same rule as `query`. Use list keys for `?` and string keys for `:name`, and never both in one array. |
| `{ timeout: … }` | `Core\Time\Duration` (default `null`) | How long reading all the rows may take. The limit applies while the rows are being read, so it covers every row and not only the first call. When the time passes, the statement stops with an `IOError`, and the connection cannot be used again. Without it, the loop waits as long as the server takes. |

**Returns** `Core\Db\Stream<Core\Db\Row>` — The statement's rows for a `foreach` loop, each one a `Core\Db\Row`, in the server's order. No row has been read yet when this returns. The connection is busy until the loop reaches the last row, and no other statement can run on it. A loop that writes for each row needs a second connection (`{ shared: false }`), or `query` instead.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The call is wrong, not the database. The placeholders and the array use different styles or different counts, a `:name` has no element, or an element cannot be bound. It is also thrown when the connection is closed, or when a statement is already streaming on it.; `Core\Db\DbError` — The server rejected the statement, at the start or while the rows were read. The error has the server's `SQLSTATE` and message. It is also thrown for a column type this driver cannot read yet.; `IOError` — The connection failed while the statement or one of its rows was being sent, or `timeout` passed before the loop ended. The connection cannot be used for the rest of the request.

<a id="core-core-db-connection-streamas"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Connection->streamAs`

```nvs skip
$connection->streamAs<T>(string $sql, array<mixed> $params, { timeout?: Core\Time\Duration }): Core\Db\Stream<T>
```

Reads a result one row at a time as `stream` does, and builds each row into an object of the class written at the call site, as `queryAs` does. The memory used stays the same however many rows there are.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$sql` | `string` (sink) | The statement, bound the same way as in `query`. Use a `?` or a `:name` for each value, and never write a value into the text. A `tainted` string does not compile here. |
| `$params` | `array<mixed>` | The values to bind, with the same rule as `query`. Use list keys for `?` and string keys for `:name`, and never both in one array. |
| `{ timeout: … }` | `Core\Time\Duration` (default `null`) | How long reading all the rows may take, with the same rule as `stream`. The limit applies while the rows are being read, so it covers every row and not only the first call. Without it, the loop waits as long as the server takes. |

**Returns** `Core\Db\Stream<T>` — The statement's rows for a `foreach` loop, each one created as a `T`, in the server's order. No row has been read yet when this returns. The connection is busy, as with `stream`. Only one `T` exists at a time. That is the only difference from `queryAs`.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The call is wrong, not the database. The placeholders and the array use different styles or different counts, a `:name` has no element, or an element cannot be bound. It is also thrown when the connection is closed, or when a statement is already streaming on it. A `T` without `#[Db\Derive]` also throws it here, although the compiler already reports that.; `ParseError` — A row did not match `T`. A column is missing, or has a different type than the property. A SQL NULL is in a property that is not `?T`, or a property's type has no column mapping. Every bad column of that row is reported at once in `issues`, and each `path` is the column's name. The loop stops there, because the rest of the result is not read.; `Core\Db\DbError` — The server rejected the statement, at the start or while the rows were read. The error has the server's `SQLSTATE` and message. It is also thrown for a column type this driver cannot read yet.; `IOError` — The connection failed while the statement or one of its rows was being sent, or `timeout` passed before the loop ended. The connection cannot be used for the rest of the request.

<a id="core-core-db-connection-transaction"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Connection->transaction`

```nvs skip
$connection->transaction(callable(Core\Db\Transaction): T $fn, { isolation?: Core\Db\Isolation, readOnly?: bool, retries?: uint }): T
```

Runs `$fn` inside a transaction and returns what `$fn` returns. If `$fn` returns, the transaction is committed. If `$fn` throws, the transaction is rolled back and the error is thrown again. An early return cannot leave the transaction open.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$fn` | `callable(Core\Db\Transaction): T` | The work to run. It gets a `Core\Db\Transaction`, which has the same query methods as the connection. The function may declare that parameter or no parameter. |
| `{ isolation: … }` | `Core\Db\Isolation` (default `null`) | How much this transaction can see of other transactions running at the same time. Without it, the transaction uses the level set on the server. A nested call cannot set it. The level is for the whole transaction, not for a savepoint inside it. |
| `{ readOnly: … }` | `bool` (default `false`) | Writes are not allowed during the transaction, so the server can plan for reads only. The default is `false`. A nested call cannot set it, for the same reason as `isolation`. |
| `{ retries: … }` | `uint` (default `0`) | How many times `$fn` runs again when the commit reports a deadlock or a serialization failure. This applies to the outermost transaction only. The default is `0`, because a function with side effects should run again only when you ask for it. Nothing else is retried, and there is no wait between attempts. A conflict from a statement inside `$fn` is thrown and not retried. |

**Returns** `T` — What `$fn` returned, after the commit. A nested call on the same connection is a savepoint. So you can call a function that wraps its own writes in a transaction from inside another transaction.

**Throws** `Core\Db\RolledBack` — `$fn` called `rollBack`. This call throws it even if code inside `$fn` caught it, because the rollback is recorded on the transaction itself.; `LogicError` — A statement inside `$fn` was not allowed because of the way it was written. It is also thrown when the transaction is used after its `transaction()` call returned, or when a nested call sets its own `isolation` or `readOnly`.; `Core\Db\DbError` — The server rejected the `BEGIN`, or rejected the `COMMIT` after `$fn` returned, for example for a serialization failure or a deferred constraint. In both cases nothing is committed.; `IOError` — The connection failed while the transaction was open. The connection cannot be used for the rest of the request.

<a id="core-core-db-connection-close"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Connection->close`

```nvs skip
$connection->close(): void
```

Returns the connection to the pool before the request that opened it ends. After that, every other method of this connection throws an error. `isOpen` returns `false`, and a second `close` does nothing.

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. The only effect is that the connection goes back to the pool, and a program cannot use the pool directly.

<a id="core-core-db-connection-driver"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Connection->driver`

```nvs skip
$connection->driver(): Core\Db\Driver
```

Returns the database this connection uses. This is the `Core\Db\Driver` case that the `[db.<name>]` block or the `open` settings named.

**Returns** `Core\Db\Driver` — The connection's own `Core\Db\Driver` case.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The connection has been closed.

<a id="core-core-db-connection-serverversion"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Connection->serverVersion`

```nvs skip
$connection->serverVersion(): string
```

Returns the version the database server reported, exactly as it reported it. This is PostgreSQL's `server_version`, the greeting banner of MySQL and MariaDB, `major.minor.build` from the SQL Server login reply, or SQLite's library version. The server sent it when the connection opened, so reading it runs no statement. You can call it while a `stream` is using the connection.

**Returns** `string` — The version. It is never empty and never changed. A suffix that a distribution adds is part of it.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The connection has been closed.

<a id="core-core-db-connection-isopen"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Connection->isOpen`

```nvs skip
$connection->isOpen(): bool
```

Checks whether this connection can still be used. It returns `true` until `close` is called, and `false` after that. It is the only method that works on a closed connection.

**Returns** `bool` — `true` if statements can still run on the connection. `false` if `close` has returned it to the pool.

<a id="core-core-db-transaction-execute"></a>

Runs one statement that changes data, such as an `insert`, an `update`, a `delete` or a `create table`. It returns how many rows changed and the new key, if there is one. The values are bound the same way `query` binds them.

The error has the server's `SQLSTATE` and message.; `IOError` — The connection failed while the statement was running, or `timeout` passed before it finished. The connection cannot be used for the rest of the request.

<a id="core-core-db-transaction-executemany"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Transaction->executeMany`

```nvs skip
$transaction->executeMany(string $sql, array<array<mixed>> $sets, { timeout?: Core\Time\Duration }): uint
```

Runs one statement once for each set of values and returns how many rows the whole batch wrote. The statement is prepared once, and all sets go to the server in one round trip.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$sql` | `string` (sink) | The statement, written once and bound once for each set. A `tainted` string does not compile here, as in `execute`. All sets use this one text. |
| `$sets` | `array<array<mixed>>` | One `$params` array for each run, each with keys as `execute` needs them. All sets must bind the same number of values. A set whose `inList` has a different length is a different statement. |
| `{ timeout: … }` | `Core\Time\Duration` (default `null`) | How long this statement may take. The limit covers the whole statement: the prepare, the execution and every row of the result. When the time passes, the statement stops with an `IOError`. The connection cannot be used again, because it stopped in the middle of a message. Without it, the statement waits as long as the server takes. |

**Returns** `uint` — The sum of the counts each run reported. A command that reports no count adds nothing. An empty `$sets` writes nothing and returns `0`. Rows from a `RETURNING` clause are discarded. There is no `lastId`, because no single run owns it.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The call is wrong, not the database. A set uses both list keys and string keys, two sets bind different numbers of values, or an element cannot be bound. A statement already streaming on this connection throws it too.; `Core\Db\DbError` — The server rejected one run, for example for a syntax error, a constraint or a permission. Each run is its own transaction, so the writes before the failed run stay. Use `transaction` to save all or nothing.; `IOError` — The connection failed while the batch was running, or `timeout` passed before it finished. The connection cannot be used for the rest of the request.

<a id="core-core-db-transaction-stream"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Transaction->stream`

```nvs skip
$transaction->stream(string $sql, array<mixed> $params, { timeout?: Core\Time\Duration }): Core\Db\Stream<Core\Db\Row>
```

Runs one statement and gives its rows one at a time to a `foreach` loop. The connection stays open until the loop ends. The memory used stays the same however many rows there are. Use it instead of `query` for a large result.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$sql` | `string` (sink) | The statement, bound the same way as in `query`. Use a `?` or a `:name` for each value, and never write a value into the text. A `tainted` string does not compile here. |
| `$params` | `array<mixed>` | The values to bind, with the same rule as `query`. Use list keys for `?` and string keys for `:name`, and never both in one array. |
| `{ timeout: … }` | `Core\Time\Duration` (default `null`) | How long reading all the rows may take. The limit applies while the rows are being read, so it covers every row and not only the first call. When the time passes, the statement stops with an `IOError`, and the connection cannot be used again. Without it, the loop waits as long as the server takes. |

**Returns** `Core\Db\Stream<Core\Db\Row>` — The statement's rows for a `foreach` loop, each one a `Core\Db\Row`, in the server's order. No row has been read yet when this returns. The connection is busy until the loop reaches the last row, and no other statement can run on it. A loop that writes for each row needs a second connection (`{ shared: false }`), or `query` instead.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The call is wrong, not the database. The placeholders and the array use different styles or different counts, a `:name` has no element, or an element cannot be bound. It is also thrown when the connection is closed, or when a statement is already streaming on it.; `Core\Db\DbError` — The server rejected the statement, at the start or while the rows were read. The error has the server's `SQLSTATE` and message. It is also thrown for a column type this driver cannot read yet.; `IOError` — The connection failed while the statement or one of its rows was being sent, or `timeout` passed before the loop ended. The connection cannot be used for the rest of the request.

<a id="core-core-db-transaction-streamas"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Transaction->streamAs`

```nvs skip
$transaction->streamAs<T>(string $sql, array<mixed> $params, { timeout?: Core\Time\Duration }): Core\Db\Stream<T>
```

Reads a result one row at a time as `stream` does, and builds each row into an object of the class written at the call site, as `queryAs` does. The memory used stays the same however many rows there are.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$sql` | `string` (sink) | The statement, bound the same way as in `query`. Use a `?` or a `:name` for each value, and never write a value into the text. A `tainted` string does not compile here. |
| `$params` | `array<mixed>` | The values to bind, with the same rule as `query`. Use list keys for `?` and string keys for `:name`, and never both in one array. |
| `{ timeout: … }` | `Core\Time\Duration` (default `null`) | How long reading all the rows may take, with the same rule as `stream`. The limit applies while the rows are being read, so it covers every row and not only the first call. Without it, the loop waits as long as the server takes. |

**Returns** `Core\Db\Stream<T>` — The statement's rows for a `foreach` loop, each one created as a `T`, in the server's order. No row has been read yet when this returns. The connection is busy, as with `stream`. Only one `T` exists at a time. That is the only difference from `queryAs`.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The call is wrong, not the database. The placeholders and the array use different styles or different counts, a `:name` has no element, or an element cannot be bound. It is also thrown when the connection is closed, or when a statement is already streaming on it. A `T` without `#[Db\Derive]` also throws it here, although the compiler already reports that.; `ParseError` — A row did not match `T`. A column is missing, or has a different type than the property. A SQL NULL is in a property that is not `?T`, or a property's type has no column mapping. Every bad column of that row is reported at once in `issues`, and each `path` is the column's name. The loop stops there, because the rest of the result is not read.; `Core\Db\DbError` — The server rejected the statement, at the start or while the rows were read. The error has the server's `SQLSTATE` and message. It is also thrown for a column type this driver cannot read yet.; `IOError` — The connection failed while the statement or one of its rows was being sent, or `timeout` passed before the loop ended. The connection cannot be used for the rest of the request.

<a id="core-core-db-transaction-transaction"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Transaction->transaction`

```nvs skip
$transaction->transaction(callable(Core\Db\Transaction): T $fn, { isolation?: Core\Db\Isolation, readOnly?: bool, retries?: uint }): T
```

Runs `$fn` inside a transaction and returns what `$fn` returns. If `$fn` returns, the transaction is committed. If `$fn` throws, the transaction is rolled back and the error is thrown again. An early return cannot leave the transaction open.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$fn` | `callable(Core\Db\Transaction): T` | The work to run. It gets a `Core\Db\Transaction`, which has the same query methods as the connection. The function may declare that parameter or no parameter. |
| `{ isolation: … }` | `Core\Db\Isolation` (default `null`) | How much this transaction can see of other transactions running at the same time. Without it, the transaction uses the level set on the server. A nested call cannot set it. The level is for the whole transaction, not for a savepoint inside it. |
| `{ readOnly: … }` | `bool` (default `false`) | Writes are not allowed during the transaction, so the server can plan for reads only. The default is `false`. A nested call cannot set it, for the same reason as `isolation`. |
| `{ retries: … }` | `uint` (default `0`) | How many times `$fn` runs again when the commit reports a deadlock or a serialization failure. This applies to the outermost transaction only. The default is `0`, because a function with side effects should run again only when you ask for it. Nothing else is retried, and there is no wait between attempts. A conflict from a statement inside `$fn` is thrown and not retried. |

**Returns** `T` — What `$fn` returned, after the commit. A nested call on the same connection is a savepoint. So you can call a function that wraps its own writes in a transaction from inside another transaction.

**Throws** `Core\Db\RolledBack` — `$fn` called `rollBack`. This call throws it even if code inside `$fn` caught it, because the rollback is recorded on the transaction itself.; `LogicError` — A statement inside `$fn` was not allowed because of the way it was written. It is also thrown when the transaction is used after its `transaction()` call returned, or when a nested call sets its own `isolation` or `readOnly`.; `Core\Db\DbError` — The server rejected the `BEGIN`, or rejected the `COMMIT` after `$fn` returned, for example for a serialization failure or a deferred constraint. In both cases nothing is committed.; `IOError` — The connection failed while the transaction was open. The connection cannot be used for the rest of the request.

<a id="core-core-db-transaction-rollback"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Transaction->rollBack`

```nvs skip
$transaction->rollBack(string $reason): void
```

Rolls back this transaction. It records `$reason` and throws `Core\Db\RolledBack` with it. You cannot request a rollback and then continue in the same transaction. So no code has to remember to check a flag such as `setRollbackOnly`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$reason` | `string` (neutral) | Why the work is stopped. It becomes the `reason` property and the message of the thrown `RolledBack`, so write it for the person who reads the error. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. This method always throws.

**Throws** `Core\Db\RolledBack` — Always. The `transaction()` call throws it even if code between here and there catches it, because that call checks the recorded reason, not the thrown error.; `LogicError` — The transaction is used after its `transaction()` call returned, so there is nothing left to roll back.

<a id="core-core-db-rows-all"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Rows->all`

```nvs skip
$rows->all(): array<T>
```

Returns every row of the result, in the order the server sent them.

**Returns** `array<T>` — An `array<T>`. It is empty for a statement that returned no rows. `T` is a `Core\Db\Row` for `query`, and the class you named for `queryAs<T>`. The rows are already read, so this creates one object for each row and decodes nothing again.

<a id="core-core-db-rows-first"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Rows->first`

```nvs skip
$rows->first(): ?T
```

Returns the first row, or `null` if there is none. A second call returns the same row.

**Returns** `?T` — A `T`, as `all` describes it, or `null` for an empty result. Everywhere in `Core`, `?T` means that a value can be missing. A query that matched nothing is not an error.

<a id="core-core-db-rows-value"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Rows->value`

```nvs skip
$rows->value(): mixed
```

Returns the first column of the first row. Use it to read the result of a `select count(*)`.

**Returns** `mixed` — That column's value, or `null` if the result has no rows. A NULL column also gives `null`, because the declared type is `mixed`. To tell the two apart, call `count()` first.

<a id="core-core-db-rows-column"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Rows->column`

```nvs skip
$rows->column(int|string $key): array<mixed>
```

Returns the value of one column from every row, in the order the server sent them.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$key` | `int\|string` (neutral) | The column. An `int` is its position in the server's column list, counted from zero. A `string` is its label. |

**Returns** `array<mixed>` — An `array<mixed>` with one entry per row, empty for a result with no rows.

**Throws** `LogicError` — No column has that name, or the position is negative or past the last column. An empty result returns an empty array and does not throw.

<a id="core-core-db-rows-count"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Rows->count`

```nvs skip
$rows->count(): uint
```

Returns how many rows the statement returned. For the number of rows a write changed, use `Core\Db\Write::affected`.

**Returns** `uint` — The number of rows in the result. It is exact, because `query` reads all rows before it returns.

<a id="core-core-db-rows-columns"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Rows->columns`

```nvs skip
$rows->columns(): array<Core\Db\Column>
```

Returns a description of each column of the result, as one `Core\Db\Column` per column. The columns are in the order the server sent them.

**Returns** `array<Core\Db\Column>` — The columns. An empty result has them too. A `select` that matched nothing still describes the columns it would return, so you can read them before any row.

<a id="core-core-db-write"></a>
### `Core\Db\Write`

Keywords: affected, changed, lastId

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Db\Write->affected`](#core-core-db-write-affected) | `affected(): uint` |
| [`Core\Db\Write->changed`](#core-core-db-write-changed) | `changed(): ?uint` |
| [`Core\Db\Write->lastId`](#core-core-db-write-lastid) | `lastId(): ?uint` |

<a id="core-core-db-write-affected"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Write->affected`

```nvs skip
$write->affected(): uint
```

Returns how many rows the statement changed.

**Returns** `uint` — A `uint`. It is `0` for a statement that changed no rows. It is also `0` for a statement type that reports no count, such as `create table`. Use `changed` to tell the two apart.

<a id="core-core-db-write-changed"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Write->changed`

```nvs skip
$write->changed(): ?uint
```

Returns the same count, exactly as the server reported it. It is `null` when this type of statement has no row count. `affected` cannot show that case.

**Returns** `?uint` — A `?uint`. When it is not `null`, it is equal to `affected`. MySQL counts matched rows and changed rows separately. PostgreSQL does not send that difference, so there is no second count. A second count that always matched the first would mislead programs.

<a id="core-core-db-write-lastid"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Write->lastId`

```nvs skip
$write->lastId(): ?uint
```

Returns the key that this statement generated. The key belongs to this statement, so another statement on the same connection cannot change it.

**Returns** `?uint` — A `?uint`: the key this statement generated, or `null` if it generated none. A statement that inserted no row returns `null`. PostgreSQL has no last insert id, so the key comes from a `RETURNING` clause. It is the first column of the last row returned, if that column is declared as an integer. On MySQL it is the `AUTO_INCREMENT` value the server reports for this write. On SQLite it is the rowid of a row this statement inserted, which may be `0`. SQL Server always returns `null`, because the server does not send a generated key.

<a id="core-core-db-column"></a>
### `Core\Db\Column`

Keywords: name, type, nullable

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Db\Column->name`](#core-core-db-column-name) | `name(): string` |
| [`Core\Db\Column->type`](#core-core-db-column-type) | `type(): Core\Db\Column::Type` |
| [`Core\Db\Column->nullable`](#core-core-db-column-nullable) | `nullable(): bool` |

<a id="core-core-db-column-name"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Column->name`

```nvs skip
$column->name(): string
```

Returns the column's label as the server described it. If the `select` list gives the column an alias, the label is the alias.

**Returns** `string` — The label. It is not a unique key: `select a, a` gives two columns with one label. So read a column by its position in the array that `columns()` returns.

<a id="core-core-db-column-type"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Column->type`

```nvs skip
$column->type(): Core\Db\Column::Type
```

Returns the type the column was declared with, as a `Core\Db\Column::Type` case. Each database has its own type names, but the cases are the same for every database.

**Returns** `Core\Db\Column::Type` — The case. It describes the column, not the value you get when you read it. For example, a `JSON` column and a `TEXT` column both read as `tainted string`, and this case tells them apart. A type with no matching Novis type is `Other`. This includes every array and, on PostgreSQL, every `ENUM`.

<a id="core-core-db-column-nullable"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Column->nullable`

```nvs skip
$column->nullable(): bool
```

Checks whether the column can contain NULL. On PostgreSQL this is always `true`. The server does not send a NOT NULL flag with the result. Only an extra catalog query for each statement could find it, and this driver does not run one.

**Returns** `bool` — `true` for every column this driver describes, so treat every column as nullable. The typed methods of `Core\Db\Row` already do this, and each returns `?T`. A database that sends the flag gives its value here.

<a id="core-core-db-schema"></a>
### `Core\Db\Schema`

Keywords: fromArray, toArray, planAgainst, applySafe, applyIncludingRisky

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Db\Schema::fromArray`](#core-core-db-schema-fromarray) | `fromArray(array<mixed> $array): Core\Db\Schema` |
| [`Core\Db\Schema->toArray`](#core-core-db-schema-toarray) | `toArray(): array<mixed>` |
| [`Core\Db\Schema->planAgainst`](#core-core-db-schema-planagainst) | `planAgainst(Core\Db\Connection $connection): Core\Db\Plan` |
| [`Core\Db\Schema->applySafe`](#core-core-db-schema-applysafe) | `applySafe(Core\Db\Connection $connection): void` |
| [`Core\Db\Schema->applyIncludingRisky`](#core-core-db-schema-applyincludingrisky) | `applyIncludingRisky(Core\Db\Connection $connection): void` |

<a id="core-core-db-schema-fromarray"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Schema::fromArray`

```nvs skip
Core\Db\Schema::fromArray(array<mixed> $array): Core\Db\Schema
```

Creates a schema from its standard array form. This is the form that `toArray` returns, that a schema file contains and that `nvs schema dump` prints. Every rule is checked here, so any schema value works with all five databases.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$array` | `array<mixed>` | The schema, as `["tables" => [...]]`. A table has `name`, `columns`, and optionally `primary_key`, `unique` and `indexes`. A column has `name` and `type`, and optionally `null`, `identity` and a one-key `default`. A missing key means the empty list or `false`. |

**Returns** `Core\Db\Schema` — A `Core\Db\Schema` in **normalized** form: tables in name order, columns in declaration order, and every optional key filled in. So `toArray` returns the same array for every way to write one schema. This is what makes two schemas comparable.

**Throws** `LogicError` — A key is missing or has the wrong type of value, a type name is not supported, or an identifier is not a plain identifier. It is also thrown when the schema is not consistent. Examples are a table with no columns, a second identity column, an identity column outside the primary key, or an index on a missing column.

<a id="core-core-db-schema-toarray"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Schema->toArray`

```nvs skip
$schema->toArray(): array<mixed>
```

Returns the schema in its standard array form. You can save it to a file, pass it to `Core\Json::encode`, or compare it with another schema.

**Returns** `array<mixed>` — The array that `fromArray` reads back as the same schema. Tables are in name order. Columns are in the order they were declared, because `create table` keeps that order. Constraints and indexes are in name order, because the order they were added in has no effect.

<a id="core-core-db-schema-planagainst"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Schema->planAgainst`

```nvs skip
$schema->planAgainst(Core\Db\Connection $connection): Core\Db\Plan
```

Reads the database of this connection and returns every difference between it and this schema. The differences are in the order they must be fixed. Making a plan changes nothing. An empty plan means the database already matches the schema.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$connection` | `Core\Db\Connection` | The database to compare with. Planning only reads, so it needs only the `db.connect` capability this connection was opened with. |

**Returns** `Core\Db\Plan` — The plan. Each of its `steps()` has a grade, `Safe`, `Locking` or `Destructive`, and the complete SQL for the change. A table or column that the database has and this schema does not is a **report**. It is in the plan with the SQL that would remove it, but no `apply` ever runs it.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The database has a type, a default or an identifier that a schema cannot describe, so a plan could not cover every difference.

<a id="core-core-db-schema-applysafe"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Schema->applySafe`

```nvs skip
$schema->applySafe(Core\Db\Connection $connection): void
```

Makes a plan for this connection and runs it, but only if every step it would run is graded `Safe`. It needs the `db.schema` capability for the connection's block. Running DDL needs this extra permission, beyond access to the database.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$connection` | `Core\Db\Connection` | The database to change. `db.schema` is granted for the name of its `[db.<name>]` block. So you cannot use a connection from `Core\Db::open` here. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. Afterwards the database matches the schema. Only what the schema does not declare is different: it is reported and not changed.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The plan has a step that is not `Safe`, and the message names it. It is also thrown when the connection has no block to grant `db.schema` for, and for every error that `planAgainst` throws.; `RuntimeError` — The `db.schema` capability is not granted for this connection's block.

<a id="core-core-db-schema-applyincludingrisky"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Schema->applyIncludingRisky`

```nvs skip
$schema->applyIncludingRisky(Core\Db\Connection $connection): void
```

Works like `applySafe`, without the grade check. It runs every step of the plan. This includes steps that can hold a long lock, rewrite a table or fail on rows that already exist. The long name shows a reviewer the risk at the call.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$connection` | `Core\Db\Connection` | The database to change. It works as in `applySafe`, and needs the same `db.schema` capability. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. A reported drop still does not run, because a risky change is not the same as data loss. The step has the SQL for the drop if a program wants to run it.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The connection has no block to grant `db.schema` for. It is also thrown for every error that `planAgainst` throws.; `RuntimeError` — The `db.schema` capability is not granted for this connection's block.

<a id="core-core-db-plan"></a>
### `Core\Db\Plan`

Keywords: steps

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Db\Plan->steps`](#core-core-db-plan-steps) | `steps(): array<Core\Db\Plan\Step>` |

<a id="core-core-db-plan-steps"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Plan->steps`

```nvs skip
$plan->steps(): array<Core\Db\Plan\Step>
```

Returns every step of the plan in the order they must run, including reports.

**Returns** `array<Core\Db\Plan\Step>` — The steps. An empty array means the database already matches the schema. No `apply` runs a step whose `isRefused()` is `true`.

<a id="core-core-db-plan-step"></a>
### `Core\Db\Plan\Step`

Keywords: grade, reason, sql, isRefused

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|
| [`Core\Db\Plan\Step->grade`](#core-core-db-plan-step-grade) | `grade(): Core\Db\Plan\Step::Grade` |
| [`Core\Db\Plan\Step->reason`](#core-core-db-plan-step-reason) | `reason(): string` |
| [`Core\Db\Plan\Step->sql`](#core-core-db-plan-step-sql) | `sql(): string` |
| [`Core\Db\Plan\Step->isRefused`](#core-core-db-plan-step-isrefused) | `isRefused(): bool` |

<a id="core-core-db-plan-step-grade"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Plan\Step->grade`

```nvs skip
$step->grade(): Core\Db\Plan\Step::Grade
```

Returns the worst risk of this step.

**Returns** `Core\Db\Plan\Step::Grade` — `Safe`, `Locking` or `Destructive`. The grade is the worst case, not the likely case. When there is no rule for a change, it gets the higher grade. Too high a grade costs one confirmation, and too low a grade can cost an outage.

<a id="core-core-db-plan-step-reason"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Plan\Step->reason`

```nvs skip
$step->reason(): string
```

Returns one sentence for a person that says why the step has its grade.

**Returns** `string` — The sentence. It is written for the same database as the SQL. So it gives the reason for that database, such as a table rewrite that this server does and another does not.

<a id="core-core-db-plan-step-sql"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Plan\Step->sql`

```nvs skip
$step->sql(): string
```

Returns the complete SQL of this step, with terminators, in the right dialect for the database. It is never shortened, also for a step that no `apply` runs. Some applications cannot run DDL and give the plan to a database administrator. A summary does not help there.

**Returns** `string` — The statements, one per line. Most steps are one statement, and you can pass it directly to `Core\Db::execute`. SQLite's table rebuild is four statements. A person pastes those, and a program does not run them.

<a id="core-core-db-plan-step-isrefused"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Plan\Step->isRefused`

```nvs skip
$step->isRefused(): bool
```

Checks whether this step is a report. A report is a table, column or key that the database has and the schema does not name.

**Returns** `bool` — `true` for a step that no `apply` ever runs. Something missing from the schema is never deleted. A database is often shared with a queue, a reporting view or tables an administrator added. A program that wants the drop runs this step's `sql()`.

### `Core\Ldap`

Keywords: connect, open

| Member | Signature |
|---|---|

| [`Core\Ldap::open`](#core-core-ldap-open) | `open({ url: string, user?: tainted string, password?: secret tainted string, tls?: Core\Ldap::Tls, timeout?: Core\Time\Duration, base?: Core\Ldap\Dn\|string } $settings): Core\Ldap\Connection` |

<a id="core-core-ldap-connect"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap::connect`

```nvs skip
Core\Ldap::connect(string $name): Core\Ldap\Connection
```

Opens the directory named by an `[ldap.<name>]` block in `nvs.toml`. A second call with the same name in one request returns the same connection. Needs the `ldap.connect` capability for that name.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$name` | `string` (sink) | The block to open: `"corp"` is `[ldap.corp]`. |

**Returns** `Core\Ldap\Connection` — A `Core\Ldap\Connection`, logged in as the block's `user`. It is closed when the request ends.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `ldap.connect` does not grant `$name`, or no `[ldap.<name>]` block has that name.; `IOError` — This core already has the block's `pool.max` connections open, and none was free within the block's `timeout`.; `Core\Ldap\LdapError` — No URL in the block responded, or the server did not accept the block's user and password. `$kind` says why.

<a id="core-core-ldap-open"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap::open`

```nvs skip
Core\Ldap::open({ url: string, user?: tainted string, password?: secret tainted string, tls?: Core\Ldap::Tls, timeout?: Core\Time\Duration, base?: Core\Ldap\Dn|string } $settings): Core\Ldap\Connection
```

Opens a directory at a URL the program gives. Needs the `ldap.open` capability for the URL's host. The host's address is also checked against the addresses no program may reach, such as private networks.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$settings` | `{ url: string, user?: tainted string, password?: secret tainted string, tls?: Core\Ldap::Tls, timeout?: Core\Time\Duration, base?: Core\Ldap\Dn\|string }` | The directory to open and the account to log in with. Keys: `url` (string) One `ldaps://` or `ldap://` URL. It cannot be `tainted`, because the password is sent to this host.; `user` (tainted string) The account to log in as, as a DN, `user@example.test` or `EXAMPLE\user`. Left out, the connection does not log in.; `password` (secret tainted string) The account's password. An empty password throws before anything is sent. A password with a zero byte (`\x00`) throws before it is sent.; `tls` (Tls) `Tls::Required`, the default, encrypts the connection. `Tls::None` sends everything as plain text, and needs the host in `[capabilities.ldap] cleartext`.; `timeout` (Duration) How long one operation may take. Left out, it is 30 seconds.; `base` (Dn\|string) The DN a search starts from when it does not give its own `base`. Text cannot be `tainted`. |

**Returns** `Core\Ldap\Connection` — A `Core\Ldap\Connection`. It is closed when the request ends.

**Throws** `RuntimeError` — `url` is not an `ldap://` or `ldaps://` URL, `ldap.open` does not grant its host, or the host's address is one no program may reach.; `Core\Ldap\LdapError` — The server did not respond, the connection is not encrypted and the host may not use plain text, or the server did not accept the user and password. `$kind` says why.

<a id="core-core-ldap-connection-whoami"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap\Connection->whoami`

```nvs skip
$connection->whoami(): string
```

Returns the account the connection is logged in as, as the server reports it.

**Returns** `string` — `dn:` and then the account's DN, or `u:` and then its login name. The result is an empty string when the connection did not log in.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The connection is closed.; `Core\Ldap\LdapError` — The server did not respond, or it returned an error. `$kind` says why.

<a id="core-core-ldap-connection-authenticate"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap\Connection->authenticate`

```nvs skip
$connection->authenticate(string $login, secret tainted string $password): void
```

Checks a user's login and password. It opens a new connection to the same server, logs in as the user and closes that connection. The connection you call it on stays logged in as before.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$login` | `string` (neutral) | The user's DN, `user@example.test` or `DOMAIN\user`. It can be `tainted`, such as a name from a login form. |
| `$password` | `secret tainted string` | The user's password. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing. The login and password are correct when no error is thrown.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The connection is closed.; `Core\Ldap\LdapError` — `$kind` is `InvalidCredentials` for a wrong password and for a user that does not exist, so the error does not show which users exist. An empty login or password is also `InvalidCredentials`, and nothing is sent. So is a password with a zero byte (`\x00`), and it is not sent. Active Directory gives other reasons as their own kinds, such as `AccountDisabled`, `AccountLocked` or `PasswordExpired`.

<a id="core-core-ldap-connection-search"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap\Connection->search`

```nvs skip
$connection->search(Core\Ldap\Filter $filter, { base?: Core\Ldap\Dn|string, scope?: Core\Ldap\Connection::Scope, select?: array<string>, pageSize?: int, sizeLimit?: int, sort?: string, descending?: bool, offset?: int, window?: int, showDeleted?: bool }): Core\Ldap\Entries
```

Finds the entries that match a filter. The server sends the entries in pages, and the next page is read when a `foreach` loop reaches it.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$filter` | `Core\Ldap\Filter` | Which entries to return, such as `Filter::equals('sAMAccountName', $login)`. |
| `{ base: … }` | `Core\Ldap\Dn\|string` (default `null`, sink) | The DN the search starts from, as a `Dn` or as text. Left out, it is the `base` of the `[ldap]` block. Text cannot be `tainted`. |
| `{ scope: … }` | `Core\Ldap\Connection::Scope` (default `Core\Ldap\Connection::Scope::Subtree`) | How far below `base` the search looks. The default is `Scope::Subtree`. |
| `{ select: … }` | `array<string>` (default `null`) | The attributes each entry has, such as `['cn', 'mail']`. Left out, an entry has every attribute the connection's account can read. |
| `{ pageSize: … }` | `int` (default `1000`) | How many entries the server sends at once. The default is 1000. |
| `{ sizeLimit: … }` | `int` (default `0`) | The most entries the search may find. The default, 0, is the server's own limit. |
| `{ sort: … }` | `string` (default `null`, sink) | The attribute the server sorts the entries by, such as `cn`. Left out, the entries come in the server's own order. |
| `{ descending: … }` | `bool` (default `false`) | `true` sorts from the largest value to the smallest. It needs `sort`. The default is `false`. |
| `{ offset: … }` | `int` (default `0`) | How many sorted entries the window skips. It needs `window`. The default is 0. |
| `{ window: … }` | `int` (default `0`) | How many sorted entries to return, starting after `offset`. It needs `sort`. With `{ sort: 'cn', offset: 20, window: 10 }`, the search returns entries 21 to 30. `total()` then returns how many entries there are in all. The default, 0, returns every entry. |
| `{ showDeleted: … }` | `bool` (default `false`) | `true` also finds deleted entries. Active Directory keeps a deleted entry for some time, with most of its attributes removed. `isDeleted()` checks whether an entry is one of them. The account needs the right to read deleted entries. The default is `false`. |

**Returns** `Core\Ldap\Entries` — A `Core\Ldap\Entries`. Use it in a `foreach` loop to get each `Core\Ldap\Entry`.

**Throws** `LogicError` — A name in `select` or `sort` is not an attribute name, a number is out of range, `window`, `offset` or `descending` is given without the option it needs, the search has no `base`, or the connection is closed.; `Core\Ldap\LdapError` — The server returned an error, such as `NoSuchObject` for a `base` that does not exist. A search that finds more entries than `sizeLimit` throws `SizeLimitExceeded` in the loop.

<a id="core-core-ldap-connection-changes"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap\Connection->changes`

```nvs skip
$connection->changes(Core\Ldap\Filter $filter, { base?: Core\Ldap\Dn|string, select?: array<string>, cookie?: tainted bytes }): Core\Ldap\Changes
```

Finds the entries that changed since the last call, with Active Directory's DirSync. Store the `cookie()` of the result, and give it to the next call. That call returns only the entries that changed after it.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$filter` | `Core\Ldap\Filter` | Which entries to return, such as `Filter::equals('objectClass', 'user')`. |
| `{ base: … }` | `Core\Ldap\Dn\|string` (default `null`, sink) | The root of the domain, as a `Dn` or as text. Left out, it is the `base` of the `[ldap]` block. Active Directory throws an error for any other DN. Text cannot be `tainted`. |
| `{ select: … }` | `array<string>` (default `null`) | The attributes to watch, such as `['cn', 'mail']`. A changed entry has only the attributes that changed. The attributes `filter` uses and `isDeleted` are always watched too. Left out, every attribute is watched. |
| `{ cookie: … }` | `tainted bytes` (default `null`) | The `cookie()` of an earlier result. Left out, the result has every entry that matches `filter`. |

**Returns** `Core\Ldap\Changes` — A `Core\Ldap\Changes`. Use it in a `foreach` loop to get each changed `Core\Ldap\Entry`. A deleted entry has `isDeleted()` set to `true`.

**Throws** `LogicError` — A name in `select` is not an attribute name, there is no `base`, or the connection is closed.; `Core\Ldap\LdapError` — The server returned an error. A server without DirSync throws `Unsupported`.

<a id="core-core-ldap-connection-read"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap\Connection->read`

```nvs skip
$connection->read(Core\Ldap\Dn|string $dn, { select?: array<string> }): ?Core\Ldap\Entry
```

Reads the one entry at a DN.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$dn` | `Core\Ldap\Dn\|string` (sink) | The entry's DN, as a `Dn` or as text such as `CN=Staff,OU=Groups,DC=example,DC=test`. Text cannot be `tainted`. Build a DN from user input with `Dn::of` or `child`. |
| `{ select: … }` | `array<string>` (default `null`) | The attributes the entry has. Left out, it has every attribute the connection's account can read. |

**Returns** `?Core\Ldap\Entry` — A `Core\Ldap\Entry`, or `null` when no entry has this DN.

**Throws** `LogicError` — A name in `select` is not an attribute name, or the connection is closed.; `Core\Ldap\LdapError` — The server returned an error other than "no such entry".

<a id="core-core-ldap-connection-add"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap\Connection->add`

```nvs skip
$connection->add(Core\Ldap\Dn|string $dn, array<mixed> $attributes): void
```

Adds a new entry to the directory.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$dn` | `Core\Ldap\Dn\|string` (sink) | The entry's DN, as a `Dn` or as text. Text cannot be `tainted`. Build a DN from user input with `Dn::of` or `child`. |
| `$attributes` | `array<mixed>` | The entry's attributes, keyed by name, such as `['objectClass' => ['top', 'group'], 'cn' => 'Staff']`. A value is written in the form the methods of `Entry` return it, and a list writes one value per element. A value may be `tainted`. A name that can come from outside the program does not compile. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing.

**Throws** `LogicError` — An attribute name is not a valid name, a value has no LDAP form, such as a `float`, or the connection is closed.; `Core\Ldap\LdapError` — The server returned an error. `$kind` says why, such as `NoSuchObject`, `AlreadyExists`, `InsufficientAccess` or `ConstraintViolation`.

<a id="core-core-ldap-connection-modify"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap\Connection->modify`

```nvs skip
$connection->modify(Core\Ldap\Dn|string $dn, array<Core\Ldap\Change> $changes): void
```

Changes the attributes of one entry. The server makes every change in the list, in order, or none of them.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$dn` | `Core\Ldap\Dn\|string` (sink) | The entry's DN, as a `Dn` or as text. Text cannot be `tainted`. Build a DN from user input with `Dn::of` or `child`. |
| `$changes` | `array<Core\Ldap\Change>` | The changes, each made with `Change::add`, `remove`, `removeAll` or `replace`. The list cannot be empty. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing.

**Throws** `LogicError` — An attribute name is not a valid name, a value has no LDAP form, such as a `float`, or the connection is closed.; `Core\Ldap\LdapError` — The server returned an error. `$kind` says why, such as `NoSuchObject`, `AlreadyExists`, `InsufficientAccess` or `ConstraintViolation`.

<a id="core-core-ldap-connection-delete"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap\Connection->delete`

```nvs skip
$connection->delete(Core\Ldap\Dn|string $dn): void
```

Deletes one entry. An entry with entries below it cannot be deleted.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$dn` | `Core\Ldap\Dn\|string` (sink) | The entry's DN, as a `Dn` or as text. Text cannot be `tainted`. Build a DN from user input with `Dn::of` or `child`. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing.

**Throws** `LogicError` — An attribute name is not a valid name, a value has no LDAP form, such as a `float`, or the connection is closed.; `Core\Ldap\LdapError` — The server returned an error. `$kind` says why, such as `NoSuchObject`, `AlreadyExists`, `InsufficientAccess` or `ConstraintViolation`.

<a id="core-core-ldap-connection-rename"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap\Connection->rename`

```nvs skip
$connection->rename(Core\Ldap\Dn|string $from, Core\Ldap\Dn|string $to): void
```

Gives an entry a new DN. The entry moves when the new DN has another parent.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$from` | `Core\Ldap\Dn\|string` (sink) | The entry's DN now, as a `Dn` or as text. Text cannot be `tainted`. |
| `$to` | `Core\Ldap\Dn\|string` (sink) | The entry's new DN, such as `CN=Shop,OU=Groups,DC=example,DC=test`. Text cannot be `tainted`. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `from` or `to` is text that is not a DN, or the connection is closed.; `Core\Ldap\LdapError` — The server returned an error, such as `NoSuchObject` or `AlreadyExists`.

<a id="core-core-ldap-connection-setpassword"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap\Connection->setPassword`

```nvs skip
$connection->setPassword(Core\Ldap\Dn|string $dn, secret tainted string $password): void
```

Sets a new password for a user account, as an administrator does. It works only over TLS.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$dn` | `Core\Ldap\Dn\|string` (sink) | The user account's DN, as a `Dn` or as text. Text cannot be `tainted`. |
| `$password` | `secret tainted string` | The new password. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `dn` is text that is not a DN, or the connection is closed.; `Core\Ldap\LdapError` — `$kind` is `EncryptionRequired` when the connection does not use TLS. Nothing is sent then. It is `PasswordPolicy` when the domain does not accept the new password, and another kind for any other error the server returns.

<a id="core-core-ldap-connection-changepassword"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap\Connection->changePassword`

```nvs skip
$connection->changePassword(Core\Ldap\Dn|string $dn, secret tainted string $old, secret tainted string $new): void
```

Changes the password of a user account from `$old` to `$new`, as the user does. The server checks `$old` and the password history. It works only over TLS.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$dn` | `Core\Ldap\Dn\|string` (sink) | The user account's DN, as a `Dn` or as text. Text cannot be `tainted`. |
| `$old` | `secret tainted string` | The password the account has now. |
| `$new` | `secret tainted string` | The new password. |

**Returns** `void` — Nothing.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `dn` is text that is not a DN, or the connection is closed.; `Core\Ldap\LdapError` — `$kind` is `EncryptionRequired` when the connection does not use TLS. Nothing is sent then. It is `PasswordPolicy` when the domain does not accept the new password, and another kind for any other error the server returns.

<a id="core-core-ldap-connection-compare"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap\Connection->compare`

```nvs skip
$connection->compare(Core\Ldap\Dn|string $dn, string $attribute, mixed $value): bool
```

Checks whether an entry has a value. The server compares the value by the rules of the attribute, so `staff` matches `Staff` in a name.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$dn` | `Core\Ldap\Dn\|string` (sink) | The entry's DN, as a `Dn` or as text. Text cannot be `tainted`. Build a DN from user input with `Dn::of` or `child`. |
| `$attribute` | `string` (sink) | The attribute's name, such as `department`. It cannot be `tainted`. |
| `$value` | `mixed` | One value, in any form a write accepts, such as a `string`, an `int` or a `Dn`. |

**Returns** `bool` — `true` when the entry has the value, and `false` when it does not.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `attribute` is not an attribute name, `value` is `null`, a list or has no LDAP form, or the connection is closed.; `Core\Ldap\LdapError` — The server returned an error. `$kind` is `NoSuchObject` when there is no entry with this DN.

```nvs skip

```

**Returns** `array<tainted string>` — The URLs in the order the server sent them. The list is complete after the loop ends, and it is empty when the server named no other server.

```nvs skip

```

**Returns** `?int` — The number of entries, or `null` when the search did not use `window`.

<a id="core-core-ldap-changes-cookie"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap\Changes->cookie`

```nvs skip
$changes->cookie(): tainted bytes
```

Returns the cookie for the next call to `changes`. Store it, for example in a database, after the loop ends. If you stop the loop early, the cookie covers only the entries you read, so the next call returns the others again.

**Returns** `tainted bytes` — The cookie. It is `tainted`, because the server sent it.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The connection is closed.

<a id="core-core-ldap-entry-uuid"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap\Entry->uuid`

```nvs skip
$entry->uuid(string $name): ?Core\Uuid
```

Returns a GUID attribute, such as `objectGUID`, as a `Core\Uuid`. Active Directory stores the first three groups of a GUID in reverse byte order. This function puts them in the usual order, so the text is the same as Windows shows.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$name` | `string` (neutral) | The attribute's name, such as `mail`. Upper and lower case are the same. |

**Returns** `?Core\Uuid` — The UUID, or `null` when the entry has no value for the attribute.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The attribute has more than one value, or its value is not in the form this function reads. The message names the attribute.

<a id="core-core-ldap-entry-instant"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap\Entry->instant`

```nvs skip
$entry->instant(string $name): ?Core\Time\Instant
```

Returns a time attribute as a `Core\Time\Instant`. It reads both forms a directory uses. One is a number of 100-nanosecond steps since the year 1601, as in `pwdLastSet`. The other is text such as `20240101120000.0Z`, as in `whenCreated`.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$name` | `string` (neutral) | The attribute's name, such as `mail`. Upper and lower case are the same. |

**Returns** `?Core\Time\Instant` — The instant, or `null` when the entry has no value for the attribute. It is also `null` when the number is `0` or `9223372036854775807`. Active Directory uses those two numbers for "never".

**Throws** `LogicError` — The attribute has more than one value, or its value is not in the form this function reads. The message names the attribute.

<a id="core-core-ldap-entry-duration"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap\Entry->duration`

```nvs skip
$entry->duration(string $name): ?Core\Time\Duration
```

Returns a length of time, such as `maxPwdAge` or `lockoutDuration`, as a `Core\Time\Duration`. Active Directory stores it as a negative number of 100-nanosecond steps.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$name` | `string` (neutral) | The attribute's name, such as `mail`. Upper and lower case are the same. |

**Returns** `?Core\Time\Duration` — The duration, or `null` when the entry has no value for the attribute. It is also `null` when the number is `-9223372036854775808`. Active Directory uses that number for "never".

**Throws** `LogicError` — The attribute has more than one value, or its value is not zero or a negative number, or it is longer than a `Duration` can be. The message names the attribute.

Matches the entries that have any value for an attribute.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$attribute` | `string` (sink) | The attribute's name, such as `sAMAccountName`. It cannot be `tainted`. |

**Returns** `Core\Ldap\Filter` — A `Core\Ldap\Filter`.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$attribute` is not an attribute name.

<a id="core-core-ldap-filter-atleast"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap\Filter::atLeast`

```nvs skip
Core\Ldap\Filter::atLeast(string $attribute, string $value): Core\Ldap\Filter
```

Matches the entries where a value of an attribute is equal to or greater than this value. LDAP has no "greater than" filter. Use `not` and `atMost` for it.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$attribute` | `string` (sink) | The attribute's name, such as `sAMAccountName`. It cannot be `tainted`. |
| `$value` | `string` (neutral) | The value to compare with. It may be `tainted`. The server compares by the attribute's own order, so `'10'` comes after `'9'` for a number. |

**Returns** `Core\Ldap\Filter` — A `Core\Ldap\Filter`.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$attribute` is not an attribute name.

<a id="core-core-ldap-filter-atmost"></a>

```nvs skip
Core\Ldap\Filter::atMost(string $attribute, string $value): Core\Ldap\Filter
```

| `$value` | `string` (neutral) | The value to compare with. It may be `tainted`. The server compares by the attribute's own order, so `'10'` comes after `'9'` for a number. |

**Returns** `Core\Ldap\Filter` — A `Core\Ldap\Filter`.

**Throws** `LogicError` — `$attribute` is not an attribute name.

```nvs skip
Core\Ldap\Filter::approx(string $attribute, string $value): Core\Ldap\Filter
```

<a id="core-core-ldap-filter-parse"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap\Filter::parse`

```nvs skip
Core\Ldap\Filter::parse(string $text): Core\Ldap\Filter
```

Reads LDAP filter text, such as `(&(objectClass=user)(cn=Ann))`, and returns the filter it describes. Use it for a filter that you wrote, for example in a configuration file.

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$text` | `string` (sink) | The filter text, as RFC 4515 writes it. It cannot be `tainted`. Build a filter from user input with `equals` and the other functions of this class. |

**Returns** `Core\Ldap\Filter` — A `Core\Ldap\Filter`. Its `toString` returns text that `parse` reads back as the same filter.

**Throws** `LogicError` — The text is not a filter, it has a name that is not an attribute name, or it has more than 100 levels of filters inside each other. The message gives the position of the first wrong character.

<a id="core-core-ldap-filter-tostring"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap\Filter->toString`

```nvs skip
$filter->toString(): tainted string
```

Returns the filter as LDAP filter text, such as `(&(objectClass=user)(cn=Ann))`. Use it to write the filter to a log. A search does not use this text.

**Returns** `tainted string` — The text. A `*`, `(`, `)` or `\` in a value is written as `\` and two hex digits. The text is `tainted`, because a value in the filter may be.

```nvs skip
Core\Ldap\Dn::parse(string $text): Core\Ldap\Dn
```
