<a id="core-enums"></a>
### `Core` enums

Every enum `Core` declares. A case is written `Core\Arr::Order::Asc` and is an `int` underneath (see the enums chapter); a member's signature names the enum it takes.

<a id="enum-core-arr-order"></a>
#### `Core\Arr::Order`

The direction `Core\Arr::sort` and `sortByKey` put elements in. It is the `{ order: … }` option, and it is `Asc` when you leave it out.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Arr::Order::Asc` | Smallest first. This is the default when `{ order: … }` is left out. |
| `Core\Arr::Order::Desc` | Largest first. |

<a id="enum-core-arr-seton"></a>
#### `Core\Arr::SetOn`

Which part of an entry `Core\Arr::diff` and `intersect` compare. It is the `{ on: … }` option, and it is `Values` when you leave it out. `by` and `comparator` apply to the part it selects.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Arr::SetOn::Values` | Compares the value alone. |
| `Core\Arr::SetOn::Keys` | Compares the key alone. With `by`, the callback changes the key before the comparison. |
| `Core\Arr::SetOn::Both` | Compares the key and the value together. |

<a id="enum-core-str-normalform"></a>
#### `Core\Str::NormalForm`

The four Unicode normal forms (UAX #15) that `Core\Str::normalize` can change text into. A form is either composed or decomposed, and either canonical or compatibility.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Str::NormalForm::Nfc` | Canonical composition. `é` is one code point. Only canonically equivalent text becomes the same string. Use this form to store and compare text. |
| `Core\Str::NormalForm::Nfd` | Canonical decomposition. `é` is `e` followed by a combining acute accent. Only canonically equivalent text becomes the same string. |
| `Core\Str::NormalForm::Nfkc` | Compatibility composition. This is `Nfc`, and it also changes a character that only looks like another one into that character, such as `ﬁ` or `①`. This change cannot be undone. |
| `Core\Str::NormalForm::Nfkd` | Compatibility decomposition. This is `Nfd`, and it also changes the same look-alike characters that `Nfkc` changes. |

<a id="enum-core-roundmode"></a>
#### `Core\RoundMode`

Chooses how `Core\Math::round` rounds a value that lies between two results. Four cases decide what happens to a value exactly halfway, and two always round in one direction.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\RoundMode::HalfUp` | A value exactly halfway rounds away from zero. This is the default of `round`. |
| `Core\RoundMode::HalfDown` | A value exactly halfway rounds toward zero. |
| `Core\RoundMode::HalfEven` | A value exactly halfway rounds to the even neighbour. This is banker's rounding. Over many values, the rounding errors do not add up in one direction. |
| `Core\RoundMode::HalfOdd` | A value exactly halfway rounds to the odd neighbour. |
| `Core\RoundMode::Up` | Every value rounds away from zero, whether or not it is exactly halfway. This is `ceil` for a positive number and `floor` for a negative one, at any precision. |
| `Core\RoundMode::Down` | Every value rounds toward zero, whether or not it is exactly halfway. This is truncation, at any precision. |

<a id="enum-core-charset"></a>
#### `Core\Charset`

The encoding that a `Core\Encoding` text conversion reads or writes. There is one case for each encoding in the WHATWG Encoding Standard, in the same order. `Ascii` and `Latin1` are separate cases from `Windows1252`. There is no `Replacement` case, because a conversion is exact or it throws an error.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|

<a id="enum-core-unit"></a>
#### `Core\Unit`

The calendar step a `DateTime`, `Date` or `TimeOfDay` moves by, and the unit `startOf`, `endOf` and `difference` count in. A change to or from summer time, or a short month, can make one step longer or shorter. The cases are listed smallest first.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Unit::Nanosecond` | One nanosecond. This is the smallest step any of these values can have. |
| `Core\Unit::Microsecond` | One microsecond — 1000 nanoseconds. |
| `Core\Unit::Millisecond` | One millisecond — 1 000 000 nanoseconds. |
| `Core\Unit::Second` | One second of the civil clock. |
| `Core\Unit::Minute` | One minute of the civil clock. |
| `Core\Unit::Hour` | One hour of the civil clock. |
| `Core\Unit::Day` | One calendar day. It is 23 or 25 hours on a day the zone changes to or from summer time. |
| `Core\Unit::Week` | Seven calendar days; `startOf(Unit::Week)` is the Monday, ISO 8601's first day. |
| `Core\Unit::Month` | One calendar month, with the day-of-month clamped to the target month's length. |
| `Core\Unit::Quarter` | Three calendar months, so `plus(1, Unit::Quarter)` is `plus(3, Unit::Month)` and `startOf` returns the start of January, April, July or October. |
| `Core\Unit::Year` | One calendar year, with 29 February clamped to the 28th where the target has none. |

<a id="enum-core-time-datetime-weekday"></a>
#### `Core\Time\DateTime::Weekday`

A day of the week, in ISO 8601 order with Monday first. `$d->weekday()` returns one, and `next` and `previous` take one. The cases are numbered from zero: `Monday as int` is `0` and `Sunday` is `6`.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Time\DateTime::Weekday::Monday` | The first day of the ISO week. |
| `Core\Time\DateTime::Weekday::Tuesday` | The second day of the ISO week. |
| `Core\Time\DateTime::Weekday::Wednesday` | The third day of the ISO week. |
| `Core\Time\DateTime::Weekday::Thursday` | The fourth day of the ISO week. |
| `Core\Time\DateTime::Weekday::Friday` | The fifth day of the ISO week. |
| `Core\Time\DateTime::Weekday::Saturday` | The sixth day of the ISO week. |
| `Core\Time\DateTime::Weekday::Sunday` | The seventh and last day of the ISO week. |

<a id="enum-core-hash-digest"></a>
#### `Core\Hash::Digest`

The algorithm a `Core\Hash` method computes. It includes checksums and the two broken digests that other systems still use, and BLAKE3. `StrongDigest` is the ten SHA-2 and SHA-3 cases, which `Core\Hash::hmac` accepts.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Hash::Digest::Crc32` | CRC-32/ISO-HDLC, a 4-byte checksum. It detects accidental corruption only. |
| `Core\Hash::Digest::Md5` | MD5, 16 bytes. It has been broken since 2004. Use it only to work with other systems. |
| `Core\Hash::Digest::Sha1` | SHA-1, 20 bytes. It has been broken since 2017. Use it only to work with other systems. |
| `Core\Hash::Digest::Sha256` | SHA-256, 32 bytes. This is the usual choice. It is a `StrongDigest`. |
| `Core\Hash::Digest::Sha384` | SHA-384, 48 bytes. It is a `StrongDigest`. |
| `Core\Hash::Digest::Sha512` | SHA-512, 64 bytes. It is faster than SHA-256 on 64-bit hardware. It is a `StrongDigest`. |
| `Core\Hash::Digest::Sha224` | SHA-224, 28 bytes. It is a `StrongDigest`. |
| `Core\Hash::Digest::Sha512_224` | SHA-512/224, 28 bytes. It is SHA-512 cut to 28 bytes, with its own starting values (FIPS 180-4 § 5.3.6). It is a `StrongDigest`. |
| `Core\Hash::Digest::Sha512_256` | SHA-512/256, 32 bytes. It has the speed of SHA-512 and the length of SHA-256. It is safe against length-extension attacks. It is a `StrongDigest`. |
| `Core\Hash::Digest::Sha3_224` | SHA3-224, 28 bytes. SHA-3 (FIPS 202) uses the Keccak design, which is different from SHA-2. It is a `StrongDigest`. |
| `Core\Hash::Digest::Sha3_256` | SHA3-256, 32 bytes. It is a `StrongDigest`. |
| `Core\Hash::Digest::Sha3_384` | SHA3-384, 48 bytes. It is a `StrongDigest`. |
| `Core\Hash::Digest::Sha3_512` | SHA3-512, 64 bytes. It is a `StrongDigest`. |
| `Core\Hash::Digest::Crc32c` | CRC-32C/Castagnoli, 4 bytes. S3 and GCS use this checksum for stored objects. |
| `Core\Hash::Digest::Blake3` | BLAKE3, 32 bytes, and the fastest here. It is not a `StrongDigest`, because it has its own keyed mode and does not use HMAC. |

<a id="enum-core-compress-codec"></a>
#### `Core\Compress::Codec`

The format a `Core\Compress` method reads or writes. The first three are one deflate stream under three different headers. The last two are the other two `Content-Encoding` formats in use.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Compress::Codec::Gzip` | RFC 1952: a deflate stream under a gzip header. This is `Content-Encoding: gzip`. |
| `Core\Compress::Codec::Zlib` | RFC 1950: the same stream under a zlib header. In HTTP, this is what `Content-Encoding: deflate` means. |
| `Core\Compress::Codec::Deflate` | RFC 1951: the stream with no header at all. |
| `Core\Compress::Codec::Brotli` | RFC 7932, `Content-Encoding: br`. |
| `Core\Compress::Codec::Zstd` | RFC 8878, `Content-Encoding: zstd`. |

<a id="enum-core-crypto-cipher"></a>
#### `Core\Crypto::Cipher`

The authenticated encryption that `seal` and `open` use. There is no default, so each call names its cipher. Both cases are authenticated, so a message that was changed never opens.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Crypto::Cipher::XChaCha20Poly1305` | ChaCha20-Poly1305 with a 192-bit nonce (a random value used once). Prefer it when both ends are Novis. A nonce this long is never chosen twice, and the cipher is fast on a computer without AES instructions. The sealed message is `nonce(24) ‖ ciphertext ‖ tag(16)`. |
| `Core\Crypto::Cipher::Aes256Gcm` | AES-256-GCM, the cipher to use with other systems. A browser's WebCrypto encrypts with it, so the other end can open a sealed message. The sealed message is `nonce(12) ‖ ciphertext ‖ tag(16)`. This is the output of WebCrypto with its IV in front. Its nonce has 96 bits, so a repeated nonce becomes a risk at about 2^32 messages with one key. For more messages, use `XChaCha20Poly1305`. |

<a id="enum-core-crypto-keykind"></a>
#### `Core\Crypto\KeyKind`

The kind of an asymmetric key: its curve or its RSA scheme. There is no default, and one kind cannot replace another. `P256` and `X25519` agree on a shared secret (Diffie-Hellman). `P256`, `Ed25519` and the two RSA cases sign.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Crypto\KeyKind::P256` | NIST P-256. It agrees on a shared secret (ECDH) and signs (ECDSA with SHA-256). A signature is the 64-byte `r ‖ s` that a browser and JWS both use. Every WebCrypto implementation has this curve, so use it for a key pair that you share with other systems. |
| `Core\Crypto\KeyKind::X25519` | Curve25519 key agreement only. A key pair of this kind cannot sign. Prefer it to `P256` when you choose the curve for both ends, because a call needs no extra check to be safe. |
| `Core\Crypto\KeyKind::Ed25519` | Ed25519 signatures only. A key pair of this kind cannot agree on a shared secret. Prefer it for signing when both ends are Novis. The keys and the signatures are short, and there is no scheme to choose. |
| `Core\Crypto\KeyKind::RsaPkcs1` | An RSA key that signs with RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 and SHA-256. This is `RS256` in JWS, and most identity providers still issue it. An RSA key is read, never generated. This case sets the scheme of the key when it is read. |
| `Core\Crypto\KeyKind::RsaPss` | The same RSA key with RSASSA-PSS, SHA-256 and a 32-byte salt. This is `PS256` in JWS. It is a separate case and not a separate key type, because the key does not say which of the two schemes it is for. |

<a id="enum-core-crypto-publickey-format"></a>
#### `Core\Crypto\PublicKey::Format`

The encoding that a public key is read from or written to. The three cases are the export formats of WebCrypto, with the same names. So you can give a browser a key in the format it asks for.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Crypto\PublicKey::Format::Raw` | The key alone: the 65-byte uncompressed point for `P256`, and 32 bytes for `X25519` and `Ed25519`. An RSA key has no raw form, so `Raw` with either RSA kind throws a `LogicError`. |
| `Core\Crypto\PublicKey::Format::Spki` | DER `SubjectPublicKeyInfo`: the key together with the identifier of its algorithm. Every kind has this form. A certificate and a `.pem` public key use it. An RSA key can be read and written in this format and in `Jwk`, and in no other. |
| `Core\Crypto\PublicKey::Format::Jwk` | A JSON Web Key, as UTF-8 JSON bytes. A read accepts what a browser exports, including `ext` and `key_ops`. A key with `d` throws an error, because `d` makes it a private key, and a private key given as a public key is a bug. A write gives the fields that RFC 7638 requires, sorted. A thumbprint is computed over this form. |

<a id="enum-core-passkey-credential-algorithm"></a>
#### `Core\Passkey\Credential::Algorithm`

The signature algorithm of a passkey. A passkey with another algorithm cannot be registered.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Passkey\Credential::Algorithm::ES256` | ECDSA with the P-256 curve and SHA-256. Almost every device supports it. |
| `Core\Passkey\Credential::Algorithm::Ed25519` | Ed25519 signatures. Some devices support it. |

<a id="enum-core-mime-type"></a>
#### `Core\Mime::Type`

The kind of file that `Core\Mime::detect` found in some bytes. The list of cases is fixed, so your program compares the result with a case. Every text format gives `Unknown`.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Mime::Type::Unknown` | The bytes match no known file format. This is the usual result for text, such as JSON, CSV, SVG and HTML. |
| `Core\Mime::Type::Png` | `image/png`. |
| `Core\Mime::Type::Jpeg` | `image/jpeg`. |
| `Core\Mime::Type::Gif` | `image/gif`, both the 87a and 89a versions. |
| `Core\Mime::Type::Webp` | `image/webp`. This is a RIFF container of the form `WEBP`. |
| `Core\Mime::Type::Tiff` | `image/tiff`, in either byte order. |
| `Core\Mime::Type::Avif` | `image/avif`. |
| `Core\Mime::Type::Heic` | `image/heic`. Many phone cameras save photos in this format. |
| `Core\Mime::Type::Pdf` | `application/pdf`. |
| `Core\Mime::Type::Mp4` | `video/mp4`, by its ISO base media brand. |
| `Core\Mime::Type::Ogg` | `application/ogg`. This container can contain audio or video, and only its content says which one. |
| `Core\Mime::Type::Wav` | `audio/wav`. This is a RIFF container of the form `WAVE`. |
| `Core\Mime::Type::Zip` | `application/zip`. This includes every format that is a zip archive, such as `.docx`, `.xlsx`, `.odt` and `.jar`. |
| `Core\Mime::Type::Gzip` | `application/gzip`, the format `Core\Compress::Codec::Gzip` writes. |
| `Core\Mime::Type::Zstd` | `application/zstd`, the format `Core\Compress::Codec::Zstd` writes. |
| `Core\Mime::Type::Xz` | `application/x-xz`. |
| `Core\Mime::Type::Wasm` | `application/wasm`, a binary WebAssembly module. |
| `Core\Mime::Type::Ebml` | `video/matroska`. This is the EBML container of every `.mkv` and every `.webm` file. Only the `DocType` element inside the file says which of the two it is. Detection does not read that far, so this case is never `video/webm`. |

<a id="enum-core-xml-node-kind"></a>
#### `Core\Xml\Node::Kind`

The kind of a node in a parsed document. There are exactly five kinds. `Core\Xml::parse`, `Core\Html::parse` and `Core\Xml\Reader` all return nodes of these kinds, so code that checks the kind works the same with each of them.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Xml\Node::Kind::Element` | A tag and its content. It is the only kind that has attributes. |
| `Core\Xml\Node::Kind::Text` | Character data. A CDATA section also gives a text node, because it contains the same characters written in another way. |
| `Core\Xml\Node::Kind::Comment` | A comment, such as `<!-- … -->`. Comments are kept in the tree, because they are part of the document. |
| `Core\Xml\Node::Kind::ProcessingInstruction` | A processing instruction, such as `<?target data?>`. Its target is the node's name, and its data is the node's text. The XML declaration is not a processing instruction. |
| `Core\Xml\Node::Kind::Document` | The root of the tree that a parse returns. It is never a child of another node. A parse returns it directly, and you reach every other node through it. |

<a id="enum-core-log-level"></a>
#### `Core\Log::Level`

How serious a log record is. Each of the five cases has the number of its syslog severity, so a `syslog` target can use it directly. A smaller number is more serious.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Log::Level::Debug` | Details for the person who is debugging this run. `Core\Debug::dump` writes at this level inside a web request. In production, a `Debug` record is kept only when `[log] level` is `"Debug"`. |
| `Core\Log::Level::Info` | Something the program did that the person who runs the server wants to see in the log. |
| `Core\Log::Level::Warn` | Something went wrong, and the program continued. Examples are a retry, a fallback, or a deprecated path that is still in use. |
| `Core\Log::Level::Error` | An operation failed. An uncaught `Throwable` is written at this level. |
| `Core\Log::Level::Critical` | The most serious level. It is used when a resource limit stops a request. It is also used when a program has stopped and Novis writes the record for it. |

<a id="enum-core-env-mode"></a>
#### `Core\Env::Mode`

The mode a program runs in. There are two modes. A mode sets the defaults of five settings, and you can still change each of those settings on its own.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Env::Mode::Production` | The stricter of the two modes. A server with no configuration runs in this mode. The mode fixes which defaults it sets, so a program does not need to compute them. |
| `Core\Env::Mode::Development` | The less strict of the two modes. Only `nvs.toml` selects it. An environment variable, a hostname or a build does not. A request can switch to it with `Core\Config::set` only if `[mode] ceiling` allows `Development`. |

<a id="enum-core-env-context"></a>
#### `Core\Env::Context`

The kind of run the code is in. `Core\Env::context()` returns one of these seven cases.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Env::Context::Request` | The code handles an HTTP request, under `nvs serve` or inside `Core\Test::request`. `echo` writes to the response body. |
| `Core\Env::Context::Command` | The code runs from the command line: a script started with `nvs run`, or a `#[Command]` method. `echo` writes to stdout. |
| `Core\Env::Context::Isolate` | The code runs in a script started with `spawn script`. A spawned script has no request, even when a request started it. |
| `Core\Env::Context::Schedule` | The code runs as a `[[schedule]]` entry that the server started at its time. |
| `Core\Env::Context::Job` | The code runs as a queued job, in a worker. |
| `Core\Env::Context::Test` | The code runs in a `#[Test]` method under `nvs test`. |
| `Core\Env::Context::Connection` | The code serves a connection that a request upgraded, a socket or an event stream. The request that upgraded it has already ended. |

<a id="enum-core-env-platform"></a>
#### `Core\Env::Platform`

The operating system family the program runs on. `Core\Env::OS` is one of these six cases.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Env::Platform::Windows` | Microsoft Windows. |
| `Core\Env::Platform::Darwin` | macOS and iOS. |
| `Core\Env::Platform::Linux` | Linux, and Android. |
| `Core\Env::Platform::BSD` | FreeBSD, OpenBSD, NetBSD and DragonFly BSD. |
| `Core\Env::Platform::Solaris` | Solaris and illumos. |
| `Core\Env::Platform::Unknown` | Any other operating system. |

<a id="enum-core-router-refusal"></a>
#### `Core\Router\Refusal`

The reason `Core\Router::dispatch` did not call the method of a route. Your `Core\Router\Gate` gets it in `refused()`. The response already has the status that each case names.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Router\Refusal::NotFound` | No route has this path. The status is `404`. A `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE` from another origin is `Csrf`, even when no route has its path. |
| `Core\Router\Refusal::MethodNotAllowed` | A route has this path, but not for this HTTP method. The status is `405`. The `Allow` header lists the methods that the path accepts. |
| `Core\Router\Refusal::UnknownMethod` | The HTTP method is not a case of `Core\Http\Method`. The status is `501`. |
| `Core\Router\Refusal::Denied` | `allows()` returned `false` or threw an error. The status is `403`. |
| `Core\Router\Refusal::Csrf` | The server did not accept the CSRF token or the origin of the request. The status is `403`. The server checks the origin before it looks for a route. |
| `Core\Router\Refusal::BodyTooLarge` | The request body is larger than the limit of the server. The status is `413`. |
| `Core\Router\Refusal::BadCapture` | A value in the path or in the query string cannot be converted to the type of its parameter. For example, the `parse` method of its class threw an error. A required query key that is missing, or a query key that is written twice, gives this case too. The status is `400`. |

<a id="enum-core-http-method"></a>
#### `Core\Http\Method`

The HTTP methods that a `#[Route]` can use and a request can have. There are eight, and `CONNECT` is not one of them. The safe methods come first. The four methods from `Post` on are the ones the CSRF check covers.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Http\Method::Get` | Reads a resource. It is safe, so there is no CSRF check. |
| `Core\Http\Method::Head` | The same as `Get`, without a response body. It is safe. |
| `Core\Http\Method::Options` | Checks what a resource supports. It is safe. |
| `Core\Http\Method::Trace` | Sends the request back to the client. It is safe. |
| `Core\Http\Method::Post` | Sends data and can change state. It is the first of the four methods the CSRF check covers. |
| `Core\Http\Method::Put` | Replaces a resource. The CSRF check covers it. |
| `Core\Http\Method::Patch` | Changes part of a resource. The CSRF check covers it. |
| `Core\Http\Method::Delete` | Deletes a resource. The CSRF check covers it. |

<a id="enum-core-audience"></a>
#### `Core\Audience`

The one access value that `Core` gives for `#[Access(allow: …)]`. `Public` is for a route that is open to everyone. The compiler checks this name, so it is not a magic string. The enum will not get a second case, because `Core` does not define access levels.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Audience::Public` | The route is open to everyone. For any other access rule, use an enum case or a class constant of your own program. |

<a id="enum-core-api-schemetype"></a>
#### `Core\Api\SchemeType`

The kind of security scheme that an `#[Api\Scheme]` declares. The generated OpenAPI file writes it as the scheme's `type`. Each kind needs its own fields.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Api\SchemeType::ApiKey` | A key in a header, a query parameter or a cookie. It needs `in` and `parameter`. |
| `Core\Api\SchemeType::Http` | An HTTP `Authorization` scheme, such as `bearer` or `basic`. It needs `scheme`, and `format` is optional. |
| `Core\Api\SchemeType::MutualTls` | A client certificate. It needs no other field. |
| `Core\Api\SchemeType::OAuth2` | OAuth 2.0. It needs `flows`. |
| `Core\Api\SchemeType::OpenIdConnect` | OpenID Connect. It needs `url`, the address of the provider's configuration. |

<a id="enum-core-api-keyin"></a>
#### `Core\Api\KeyIn`

Where the key of an `ApiKey` security scheme is sent. You write it as `in:` in an `#[Api\Scheme]`.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Api\KeyIn::Query` | In a query parameter of the URL. |
| `Core\Api\KeyIn::Header` | In a request header. |
| `Core\Api\KeyIn::Cookie` | In a cookie. |

<a id="enum-core-response-redirect"></a>
#### `Core\Response::Redirect`

The kind of redirect a response sends. Every browser handles these three statuses in the same way, so the browser does exactly what your program says.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Response::Redirect::SeeOther` | `303`. The browser loads the new address with `GET`, whatever the method of the request was. Use it after a form post. This is the default. |
| `Core\Response::Redirect::Temporary` | `307`. The browser sends the same request again to the new address, with the same method and body. This is for this one time only. Nothing is cached, and the old address stays valid. |
| `Core\Response::Redirect::Permanent` | `308`. The browser sends the same request again to the new address, with the same method and body. The new address replaces the old one from now on. Caches and search engines may remember it. |

<a id="enum-core-response-samesite"></a>
#### `Core\Response::SameSite`

Which requests from other sites send a cookie. The three cases are the values of the cookie's `SameSite` attribute. The default is `Lax`. A cookie that is sent with requests from other sites makes a CSRF attack possible.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Response::SameSite::Lax` | The browser sends the cookie when a person opens a page of this site, also from another site. It does not send it with an image, a form post or a `fetch` from another site. This is the default, with or without configuration. |
| `Core\Response::SameSite::Strict` | The browser never sends the cookie with a request from another site. This is also true when a person opens a page. So a visitor who follows a link from another site is logged out. For this reason, it is not the default. |
| `Core\Response::SameSite::None` | The browser sends the cookie with requests from other sites. It needs `Secure`, because browsers ignore the cookie without it. Without `Secure`, it throws an error, and in the configuration it stops the server from starting. |

<a id="enum-core-cli-stream"></a>
#### `Core\Cli::Stream`

One of the three standard streams a process starts with. Whether output goes to a terminal is always checked for one stream, not for the whole process.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Cli::Stream::In` | Standard input. Prompts read from it, and piped data arrives on it. |
| `Core\Cli::Stream::Out` | Standard output. `echo` writes to it, and the colour depth is checked for it. |
| `Core\Cli::Stream::Err` | Standard error. It is for diagnostic messages, which stay visible when output is redirected. |

<a id="enum-core-cli-colordepth"></a>
#### `Core\Cli::ColorDepth`

How much colour standard output can show. The cases are in increasing order, so you can compare two depths.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Cli::ColorDepth::None` | No colour at all. This is the case for a pipe, a file, `NO_COLOR` or `TERM=dumb`. All styling is removed. |
| `Core\Cli::ColorDepth::Ansi16` | The eight ANSI colours and their bright halves, which every terminal has. |
| `Core\Cli::ColorDepth::Ansi256` | The 256-entry indexed palette, reported by a `TERM` naming `256color`. |
| `Core\Cli::ColorDepth::TrueColor` | 24-bit colour, reported by `COLORTERM=truecolor` and by a Windows console that accepted virtual terminal processing. |

<a id="enum-core-command-shell"></a>
#### `Core\Command::Shell`

Which shell `Core\Command::completions` writes a completion script for. There are four cases and no case for other shells. Each script uses the syntax of its own shell, so each case needs its own generator.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Command::Shell::Bash` | GNU Bash, whose script registers a function with `complete -F`. |
| `Core\Command::Shell::Zsh` | Z shell, whose script is a `#compdef` function driving `_arguments`. |
| `Core\Command::Shell::Fish` | fish, whose script is one `complete -c` line per command and per option. |
| `Core\Command::Shell::Pwsh` | PowerShell 7 and Windows PowerShell. The script calls `Register-ArgumentCompleter`. |

<a id="enum-core-reflect-typekind"></a>
#### `Core\Reflect::TypeKind`

The kind of a value while the program runs. There are ten cases, and every value matches exactly one of them.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Reflect::TypeKind::Null` | The `null` value. |
| `Core\Reflect::TypeKind::Bool` | A `bool`, `true` or `false` alike. |
| `Core\Reflect::TypeKind::Int` | A signed `int`. |
| `Core\Reflect::TypeKind::Uint` | An unsigned `uint`. It is a type of its own, so it has a case of its own. |
| `Core\Reflect::TypeKind::Float` | A `float`. |
| `Core\Reflect::TypeKind::Decimal` | A `decimal`, which is an exact number. A `float` with a round value is a `Float`. |
| `Core\Reflect::TypeKind::Text` | A `string`. A string is always valid UTF-8. |
| `Core\Reflect::TypeKind::Bytes` | A `bytes` value. It is like `Text`, but its content does not have to be valid UTF-8. |
| `Core\Reflect::TypeKind::Array` | An `array<T>`. |
| `Core\Reflect::TypeKind::Object` | A class instance. A callable is also an object here, so there is no `Callable` case. |

<a id="enum-core-io-filemode"></a>
#### `Core\IO::FileMode`

What an open handle may do. There is no binary or text mode: every handle reads and writes the bytes unchanged.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\IO::FileMode::Read` | Reading only, from the start of a file that must already exist. |
| `Core\IO::FileMode::Write` | Writing only. The file is emptied first, and it is created if it does not exist. |
| `Core\IO::FileMode::Append` | Writing only, always at the end of the file, even if something else wrote to it since. The file is created if it does not exist. |
| `Core\IO::FileMode::ReadWrite` | Reading and writing. The file is created if it does not exist, and its content is kept. |

<a id="enum-core-cldr-pluralcategory"></a>
#### `Core\Cldr::PluralCategory`

The six CLDR plural forms. The names are labels for the forms of a language, not numbers. Only `Other` means the same thing in every language. Most languages use only some of the six.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Cldr::PluralCategory::Zero` | The form for none of something. Arabic and Welsh have it, and most languages do not. |
| `Core\Cldr::PluralCategory::One` | The singular of the language. It is 1 in English, 1, 21 and 31 in Russian, and 0 and 1 in French. |
| `Core\Cldr::PluralCategory::Two` | The form for two things. Arabic, Welsh, Slovenian and Irish have it. |
| `Core\Cldr::PluralCategory::Few` | The form for some small counts. It is 2 to 4 in Russian, 3 to 10 in Arabic, and only 3 in Welsh. |
| `Core\Cldr::PluralCategory::Many` | The form above `Few` in a language that has both. It is 5 to 20 in Russian. Some Romance languages use it for whole millions. |
| `Core\Cldr::PluralCategory::Other` | The form that every language has. In a language with no plural forms, every count gives `Other`. |

<a id="enum-core-script-exitreport-reason"></a>
#### `Core\Script\ExitReport::Reason`

How a script ended, as `Core\Script\ExitReport::reason()` returns it. A `FATAL` error and a cancelled script have no case, because they run no exit function.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Script\ExitReport::Reason::Normal` | The last top-level statement ran. |
| `Core\Script\ExitReport::Reason::ExitCall` | `exit`, `exit($n)` or `exit("msg")` ended the script. No `finally` block runs after `exit`. |
| `Core\Script\ExitReport::Reason::UncaughtThrow` | An exception reached the top of the script and nothing caught it. `Core\Script\ExitReport::error()` returns that exception. |
| `Core\Script\ExitReport::Reason::Finish` | `Core\Script::finish()` ended the script. Every `finally` block runs, and no `catch` block catches it. The status is `0` and there is no error. |

<a id="enum-core-db-driver"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Driver`

Which database a connection uses. It is the first field of the settings object that `Core\Db::open` takes. The driver sets which of the two shapes the rest of that object has: a server needs a `host`, and SQLite needs a `path`.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Db\Driver::MySql` | MySQL, over its own client protocol. |
| `Core\Db\Driver::MariaDb` | MariaDB. This is a separate driver, not a MySQL option. MariaDB has its own authentication methods and its own error codes. |
| `Core\Db\Driver::Postgres` | PostgreSQL, over the extended-query protocol. |
| `Core\Db\Driver::Sqlite` | SQLite. It uses a file named by `path`, and no host. |
| `Core\Db\Driver::SqlServer` | Microsoft SQL Server, over TDS. |

<a id="enum-core-db-tls"></a>
#### `Core\Db::Tls`

How much a TCP connection checks the server's identity before it sends credentials. Every connection uses `VerifyFull`, and it is the default when the settings name no mode. The three weaker modes throw an error. A connection that checks less than it promises is a security hole.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Db::Tls::Disabled` | No TLS at all. Not allowed: it throws an error. |
| `Core\Db::Tls::Required` | TLS, but the certificate is not checked. Not allowed: it throws an error. |
| `Core\Db::Tls::VerifyCa` | The certificate must chain to a trusted root certificate, but its name is not checked. Not allowed: it throws an error. |
| `Core\Db::Tls::VerifyFull` | The certificate must chain to a trusted root certificate and must be issued for the host in the settings. This is the default, and the only mode a connection uses. |

<a id="enum-core-db-isolation"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Isolation`

How much a transaction can see of other transactions running at the same time. This is the `isolation` option of `transaction`. Without it, the connection's own level is used. A driver that cannot offer the requested level throws an error. It does not run `$fn` at a weaker level.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Db\Isolation::ReadUncommitted` | A statement may read rows another transaction has written and not committed. This applies only on a database that supports this level. |
| `Core\Db\Isolation::ReadCommitted` | A statement sees the rows committed before that statement began. |
| `Core\Db\Isolation::RepeatableRead` | Every statement in the transaction sees one snapshot of committed rows. |
| `Core\Db\Isolation::Snapshot` | The transaction reads from one snapshot taken when it began. Conflicting writes fail and do not wait. This is SQL Server's own level. Databases that keep row versions call it `REPEATABLE READ`. |
| `Core\Db\Isolation::Serializable` | Transactions that run at the same time give the same result as if they ran one after another in some order. A transaction that cannot do this is rolled back, so the caller can retry it. |

<a id="enum-core-db-column-type"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Column::Type`

The type a result column was declared with. It describes the column, not the value you get when you read it. For example, a `JSON` column and a `TEXT` column both read as `tainted string`. This type tells them apart, if the database has a separate type for each.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Db\Column::Type::Int` | A signed integer column: `SMALLINT`, `INTEGER` or `BIGINT`. A `TINYINT(1)` on MySQL and MariaDB is also `Int`, not `Bool`. |
| `Core\Db\Column::Type::Uint` | An unsigned integer column: an `UNSIGNED` integer on MySQL and MariaDB, an `oid` on PostgreSQL. |
| `Core\Db\Column::Type::Float` | `FLOAT`, `REAL` or `DOUBLE`. |
| `Core\Db\Column::Type::Decimal` | An exact numeric column: `DECIMAL`, `NUMERIC` or `MONEY`. |
| `Core\Db\Column::Type::Text` | A text column: `CHAR`, `VARCHAR`, `TEXT` or `ENUM`. A JSON column is also `Text` on a database where JSON is only another name for a text type. |
| `Core\Db\Column::Type::Bytes` | A binary column: `BINARY`, `BLOB` or `BYTEA`. This includes the `BINARY(16)` column that MySQL schemas use to store a UUID. |
| `Core\Db\Column::Type::Bool` | `BOOLEAN`, and `BIT(1)`. |
| `Core\Db\Column::Type::Date` | A `DATE`. Reading it gives a `Core\Time\Date`. |
| `Core\Db\Column::Type::Time` | A `TIME`. Reading it gives a `Core\Time\TimeOfDay`. |
| `Core\Db\Column::Type::DateTime` | A `DATETIME` or `TIMESTAMP` without a time zone. Reading it gives a `Core\Time\DateTime` in the time zone set for the connection. |
| `Core\Db\Column::Type::Instant` | A column that stores its own offset: `TIMESTAMPTZ`, or SQL Server's `datetimeoffset`. Reading it gives a `Core\Time\Instant`. |
| `Core\Db\Column::Type::Uuid` | A `UUID` or a `uniqueidentifier`. Reading it gives a `Core\Uuid`. |
| `Core\Db\Column::Type::Json` | A column that the database declares as JSON. Reading it still gives a `tainted string`, because JSON is never decoded for you. A database with no JSON type of its own reports the column as `Text`. |
| `Core\Db\Column::Type::Other` | Every other column: one with no matching Novis type, and every array. This case is not an error. It means a column list can describe every column a server can send. |

<a id="enum-core-db-dberror-kind"></a>
#### `Core\Db\DbError::Kind`

Why the server rejected a statement. The cases are the same for every driver, so a program can check the condition without knowing each database's own error code. `Core\Db\DbError::$kind` returns one of these. For anything more specific, read the raw `SQLSTATE` beside it.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Db\DbError::Kind::UniqueViolation` | A row with this key already exists. |
| `Core\Db\DbError::Kind::ForeignKeyViolation` | A referenced row does not exist, or a referencing one still does. |
| `Core\Db\DbError::Kind::NotNullViolation` | A column that may not be null was written null. |
| `Core\Db\DbError::Kind::CheckViolation` | A `CHECK` constraint rejected the row. |
| `Core\Db\DbError::Kind::Deadlock` | Two transactions each wait for a lock the other has, so the server stopped this one. SQLite's `SQLITE_BUSY` and `SQLITE_LOCKED` also give this kind, so a retry works on SQLite too. |
| `Core\Db\DbError::Kind::SerializationFailure` | The transaction conflicted with another transaction running at the same time, and the server stopped it. This is normal under `REPEATABLE READ` or a stronger level. |
| `Core\Db\DbError::Kind::ConnectionLost` | The connection is gone, or the server is going away. |
| `Core\Db\DbError::Kind::Timeout` | A statement or an idle transaction ran past a time limit and was cancelled. |
| `Core\Db\DbError::Kind::Syntax` | The server cannot run the statement: a syntax error, an undefined table, or a type it cannot resolve. |
| `Core\Db\DbError::Kind::Permission` | The database role is not allowed to do this. |
| `Core\Db\DbError::Kind::Other` | Any condition the driver does not map to a kind above, including one that only one database has. A `Core\Db\DbError` that a program creates itself also has this kind, because no server classified it. |

<a id="enum-core-db-plan-step-grade"></a>
#### `Core\Db\Plan\Step::Grade`

The worst risk of one step of a schema plan. A deployment can use it to run only the steps it is willing to run without a person watching.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Db\Plan\Step::Grade::Safe` | Cannot lose data, cannot fail on rows that already exist, and cannot hold a long lock. |
| `Core\Db\Plan\Step::Grade::Locking` | Cannot lose data, but can fail on existing rows or block writes for a long time. Examples are a unique key on data with duplicates, `NOT NULL` on a column with data, or a type change that rewrites the table. |
| `Core\Db\Plan\Step::Grade::Destructive` | Can lose data. Every drop has this grade. So does SQLite's table rebuild (create, copy, drop, rename), because it always copies the data. |

<a id="enum-core-ldap-ldaperror-kind"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap\LdapError::Kind`

Why an LDAP operation failed. `Core\Ldap\LdapError::$kind` is one of these, and `$code` beside it is the LDAP result code the server sent.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Ldap\LdapError::Kind::InvalidCredentials` | The login or the password is wrong. An account that does not exist gives this kind too, so the error does not show which accounts exist. |
| `Core\Ldap\LdapError::Kind::AccountDisabled` | The account is disabled. Active Directory sends this as `data 533`. |
| `Core\Ldap\LdapError::Kind::AccountLocked` | The account is locked after too many wrong passwords. Active Directory sends this as `data 775`. |
| `Core\Ldap\LdapError::Kind::PasswordExpired` | The password has expired. Active Directory sends this as `data 532`. |
| `Core\Ldap\LdapError::Kind::MustChangePassword` | The user must set a new password before they can log in. Active Directory sends this as `data 773`. |
| `Core\Ldap\LdapError::Kind::AccountExpired` | The account has expired. Active Directory sends this as `data 701`. |
| `Core\Ldap\LdapError::Kind::NotAllowedNow` | The account may not log in at this time or from this computer. Active Directory sends this as `data 530` or `data 531`. |
| `Core\Ldap\LdapError::Kind::EncryptionRequired` | The server needs an encrypted connection for this operation. |
| `Core\Ldap\LdapError::Kind::PasswordPolicy` | The new password does not meet the directory's password rules. |
| `Core\Ldap\LdapError::Kind::NoSuchObject` | The entry, or the base of the search, does not exist. |
| `Core\Ldap\LdapError::Kind::AlreadyExists` | The entry, or the attribute value, already exists. |
| `Core\Ldap\LdapError::Kind::InsufficientAccess` | The connection's account is not allowed to do this. |
| `Core\Ldap\LdapError::Kind::ConstraintViolation` | The directory's schema does not allow this value or this change. |
| `Core\Ldap\LdapError::Kind::SizeLimitExceeded` | The search found more entries than the server or the search allows. |
| `Core\Ldap\LdapError::Kind::TimeLimitExceeded` | The search ran longer than the server allows. |
| `Core\Ldap\LdapError::Kind::Referral` | The server sent a referral to another server. Novis never follows a referral. |
| `Core\Ldap\LdapError::Kind::ReadOnly` | The server only allows reads, and the operation was a write. |
| `Core\Ldap\LdapError::Kind::Unsupported` | The server does not support this operation or this option. |
| `Core\Ldap\LdapError::Kind::Unavailable` | The server cannot be reached, or it closed the connection. |
| `Core\Ldap\LdapError::Kind::Timeout` | The operation took longer than the connection's `timeout`. |
| `Core\Ldap\LdapError::Kind::Protocol` | The server sent a message the LDAP protocol does not allow, or a result code no other kind covers. A `LdapError` you create yourself has this kind. |

<a id="enum-core-ldap-tls"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap::Tls`

Whether a connection to a directory is encrypted.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Ldap::Tls::Required` | The connection is encrypted. An `ldaps://` URL starts with TLS, and an `ldap://` URL switches to TLS before it logs in. |
| `Core\Ldap::Tls::None` | The connection is not encrypted. The password and every result are sent over the network as plain text. The host must be in `[capabilities.ldap] cleartext`. |

<a id="enum-core-ldap-connection-scope"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap\Connection::Scope`

How far below its `base` a search looks.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Ldap\Connection::Scope::Base` | Only the `base` entry itself. |
| `Core\Ldap\Connection::Scope::OneLevel` | The entries directly below `base`, and not `base` itself. |
| `Core\Ldap\Connection::Scope::Subtree` | `base` and every entry below it, at any depth. This is the default. |

<a id="enum-core-ldap-entry-accounttype"></a>
#### `Core\Ldap\Entry::AccountType`

What kind of object an entry is, read from `sAMAccountType`.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Ldap\Entry::AccountType::Domain` | The domain itself. |
| `Core\Ldap\Entry::AccountType::Group` | A global or universal security group. |
| `Core\Ldap\Entry::AccountType::NonSecurityGroup` | A global or universal distribution group. |
| `Core\Ldap\Entry::AccountType::Alias` | A domain local security group. |
| `Core\Ldap\Entry::AccountType::NonSecurityAlias` | A domain local distribution group. |
| `Core\Ldap\Entry::AccountType::User` | A user account. |
| `Core\Ldap\Entry::AccountType::Machine` | A computer account. |
| `Core\Ldap\Entry::AccountType::Trust` | A trust with another domain. |
| `Core\Ldap\Entry::AccountType::AppBasicGroup` | An application group. |
| `Core\Ldap\Entry::AccountType::AppQueryGroup` | An application group whose members come from a query. |

<a id="enum-core-queue-state"></a>
#### `Core\Queue::State`

The state of a background job, as `Core\Queue::status` returns it. There are five states and no `Failed` state. A failed attempt is retried, so the job goes back to `Pending`.

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Core\Queue::State::Pending` | The job waits for a worker. This includes jobs whose `runAt` time is still in the future, and jobs that wait between two attempts. |
| `Core\Queue::State::Claimed` | A worker is running the job. If that worker stops, the job goes back to `Pending` after the `[queue] visibility` time. |
| `Core\Queue::State::Succeeded` | The job ran to the end. A job can run more than once, so this means the work happened at least once. It does not mean the work happened exactly once. |
| `Core\Queue::State::Dead` | The job used all its attempts and is now in the dead-letter table. The table keeps its data and the error of every attempt. Only `purge` and `delete` delete it from there. |
| `Core\Queue::State::Cancelled` | `cancel` removed the job while it was still waiting, so no worker runs it. A job that a worker already started never gets this state. `cancel` does not stop work in progress. |

# Part C — The toolchain

<a id="tools-cli"></a>
## C.1 The nvs command

Keywords: nvs, nvs run, nvs check, nvs test, nvs build, --compile, --openapi, nvs api diff, nvs config check, nvs config dump, nvs info, nvs meta --json, nvs ast, nvs fmt, formatter, --check, --diff, --stdin, --config, --dump-ir, --dump-asm, --filter, --format, exit status, exit code, .nvs, shebang, cache, single-file executable, bundle, syntax check, version, licenses, nvs debug, --tail, --once, debug index, recorded requests, debug viewer, --listen, replay, compare requests, open in editor

### One binary

Everything is one executable, `nvs`. It takes a subcommand, then that subcommand's options, then
usually one file:

    nvs run hello.nvs
    nvs check src/app.nvs
    nvs test tests/
    nvs --version          # prints `nvs 0.0.1 (commit 16a26500b, 2026-09-24)`

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `nvs run <file>` | check, compile and run a program |
| `nvs check <path>` | parse, resolve and type-check a file or a directory, reporting every diagnostic; runs nothing |
| `nvs test <paths>...` | run a program's `#[Test]` methods, or a tree of `.nvst` cases |
| `nvs build --compile <file>` | write a single-file executable holding the program's source |
| `nvs build --openapi <file>` | write the program's OpenAPI 3.1 document to standard output |
| `nvs api diff <old> <new>` | classify every change between two OpenAPI documents |
| `nvs init` | write a `nvs.toml` with every key commented out, into the working directory or to the one path `--config` names — see [Installing on a host](#tools-install) |
| `nvs config check [files]` | resolve the configuration tree and report what it holds |
| `nvs config dump [files]` | print every configuration key in force |
| `nvs info` | build, host and third-party licensing information |
| `nvs meta --json` | the whole `Core` registry as JSON |
| `nvs agent <verb>` | the same registry for a coding agent: a primer, an index, a search, one card — and the pointers `init` installs |
| `nvs ast [--json] <file>` | parse one file and print its syntax tree |
| `nvs fmt [paths]...` | rewrite files in the one standard layout, or with `--check` list the files that would change |
| `nvs debug` | read recorded requests into the debug index, and keep reading |

Every subcommand also takes `--config <PATH>` (see `nvs run`), `--data <PATH>` and `-h`/`--help`.
`--data` names the data folder, where Novis keeps its own files (see
[Installing on a host](#tools-install)). Every operation is a subcommand: there is no `-i`, `-a`,
`-r`, `-f` or lowercase `-v`.

**In other chapters:** `nvs serve` and `nvs service` are in
[the server chapter](#tools-server); `nvs lsp` and `nvs lsp-test` are in
[the editor chapter](#tools-editor).

**Not in this chapter yet:** `nvs queue`, `nvs schema`, `nvs tmp`, `nvs doc` and
`nvs stubs` are in the binary and answer `--help`, but their sections here are unwritten.
`nvs --help` lists every subcommand this build carries.

### Files, extensions and tags

- A program is a `.nvs` file. The extension is a convention, not a rule: the front end never reads
  it, `nvs run` accepts any path, and what matters is the content. `nvs test` is the one command
  that decides anything from an extension, because it has two suites to choose between.
- `<?` alone is not a tag. The file stays in HTML mode, and `<?` is copied to the output as text.
- A `#!` first line opens code mode. When the first two bytes of a file are `#!`, Novis skips that
  line and reads the rest as code, as if `<?nvs` stood there, so `#!/usr/bin/env nvs` makes a
  script you run as `./tool` on Linux and macOS. An `<?nvs` in such a file before any `?>` is
  `E0009`. `#!` anywhere else is ordinary text.

```nvs
#!/usr/bin/env nvs
echo 'This line runs as code.', "\n";
```
```output
This line runs as code.
```

### nvs run

    nvs run <file> [--config <path>]... [--dump-ir | --dump-asm]

`nvs run` checks the file the way `nvs check` does, stops with the same diagnostics if any, and
otherwise compiles and runs it with the current directory as its working directory. Before running
it reads the configuration:

- `./nvs.toml` in the working directory, if there is one.
- If there is none, `nvs.toml` in the data folder. The data folder is `.nvsdata` next to the `nvs`
  program, or the folder that `--data` names.
- If neither file exists, `nvs run` writes `nvs.toml` into the data folder and reads it. Every key
  in that file is commented out, so the program runs with an empty configuration. `--no-init`, or
  the environment variable `NOVIS_NO_INIT`, stops `nvs run` from writing the file. `nvs run` never
  writes a file into the working directory.
- `--config <path>` names a file to read *instead*. Then `nvs run` reads neither `nvs.toml`. Repeat
  the flag to read several files in order. A named file that does not exist stops the run with
  `E0605`. Relative paths inside a configuration file start at that file's own directory. The
  configuration chapter has the file format.

Two debugging flags replace running with printing: `--dump-ir` prints the lowered intermediate
representation of every function in the program, and `--dump-asm` prints the generated machine
code. Both are for reading the compiler's output, not the program's.

#### Exit status

| Status | When |
|---|---|
| `0` | the program ran to the end, or called `exit`/`exit(0)`/`exit("message")` |
| `n` | the program called `exit(n)` |
| `1` | a diagnostic stopped the check, an uncaught throwable ended the program, or a resource limit was breached (`FATAL: …` on standard error) |
| `2` | the command line itself was wrong (an unknown subcommand or flag) |

`exit("message")` prints the message and exits `0`. An uncaught throwable writes one log record to
standard error: its message, its class and one entry per frame. `[log] format` picks how the record
is written — one JSON line by default, and readable text with one `#n Class::method() at file:line`
line per frame under `format = "text"`. Nothing about it reaches standard output.

```nvs exit=3
<?nvs
echo 'bye', "\n";
exit(3);
```
```output
bye
```

```nvs exit=1
<?nvs
echo 'before', "\n";
throw new LogicError('boom');
```
```output
before
```

### nvs check

    nvs check <path> [--autoload-map] [--root <folder>]

Prints `no errors` and exits `0` when the file and everything it reaches through `require` and
`autoload` type-checks; otherwise prints every diagnostic found and exits `1`. Nothing runs, so it
is the command for an editor, a pre-commit hook or CI.

The path can also be a directory. Then `nvs check` checks all the `.nvs` files under it as one
program. This is the same program `nvs test` runs for that directory. A class that one file declares
can be used in another file.

Each diagnostic has one shape:

```text
error[E0401]: expected `int`, found `string`
   --> bad.nvs:11:9
   |
11 | $o->add("seven");
   |         ^^^^^^^ this is `string`

error[E0405]: `Order` has no property named `totl`
   --> bad.nvs:12:6
   |
12 | echo $o->totl, "\n";
   |      ^^ referenced here

error: aborting due to 2 errors
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```

A code is `E` followed by four digits for an error and `W` for a warning; the location is
`file:line:column`; the caret marks the span; optional `= help:` and `= note:` lines follow. The
code is stable and is what the tables in this reference cite. The last line is printed once, after
all the diagnostics. `nvs agent show E0401` prints what the error `E0401` means and how to fix it.
`nvs check --json` does not print this line.

`nvs check --count` also prints one line on standard error with how much work the compiler did. For
a file that contains only `<?nvs` and `echo "Hello, World!\n";`, the line is:

```text
compile: tokens=7 nodes=2 names=0 exprs=0
```

`tokens` is the words and symbols in the source. `nodes` is the parts of the syntax tree. `names`
is the classes, interfaces, enums, type aliases and `use` imports. `exprs` is the expressions that
were given a type. The numbers are the same on every machine for the same program, so you can
compare a small program with a large one to see how compile time grows. `nvs run --count` prints
the same line before the program starts, with `ir`, the number of compiled instructions, added.

You can check one class file of a program, such as `nvs check app/User.nvs`. A class file that a
program loads with `autoload` cannot declare `autoload` itself. So when the file uses a class that no
file declares, `nvs check` looks for the program that loads this file with `autoload` or `require`. It searches the `.nvs` files in
the project folder in path order and uses the first program it finds. Then it checks the file with that
program's `autoload` lines, and the result is the same as for the whole program. The project folder is
the folder that `--root <folder>` names. Without `--root`, it is the folder of the `--config` file,
or else the folder you run the command in. The search skips `vendor`, `target` and folders whose
names start with a dot. If no program loads the file, the errors are reported as usual. The first
error about an unknown class then has a note. The note names the folder that was searched.

A test file in a `tests` folder is checked the same way. It uses the `autoload` lines that
`tests/bootstrap.nvs` loads. A `require` in a comment or a string does not count. A test file
with its own `require` is a program of its own.

`--autoload-map` prints the resolved `autoload` map instead of `no errors` — every prefix, what a
`discover` glob skipped, what was shadowed, and every root that does not exist — so an autoload
declaration can be audited without running anything. A `{..}` prefix segment is shown as the
directory name it resolved to.

```nvs error
<?nvs
class Counter
{
    public int $n = 0;
}
Counter $c = new Counter();
$c->n = 'one';
```
```output
E0401
```

### nvs test

    nvs test <paths>... [--filter <text>] [--format human|json|junit] [--update]
                        [--coverage-lcov <file>] [--coverage-clover <file>]
                        [--coverage-cobertura <file>] [--mutate]

One subcommand runs two kinds of test, and which one is meant is read off the path:

- **A `.nvs` path is a program**, and its `#[Test]` methods are run. Every `public`
  `void` instance method carrying `#[Test]` is one test; classes are reported in name order and
  methods in declaration order; a test that asserts nothing fails; `#[Test(skip: "why")]` skips
  with its reason. The `Core\Test` section has the assertions and the attribute's options.
- **A directory holding `.nvs` files is one program** that requires every one of them, subdirectories
  included, in name order, and its `#[Test]` methods are run. One file in the directory requires the
  application's bootstrap file, which gives the whole directory its `autoload` declarations. A
  directory holding both `.nvs` and `.nvst` files is refused.
- **Anything else is a `.nvst` case file, or a directory walked for `*.nvst`.** A case is one
  program with its expected output, and the report is a conformance summary
  (`3 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped`). This is the one place an extension decides anything, so a
  program in a file not named `.nvs` is read as a case tree here and fails to parse as one.

The two are not mixed in one invocation. The exit status is non-zero if any test or case failed;
a skipped one is not a failure. *Which kind of test to write*, in [testing](#lang-testing), says
when to use each.

```nvs test
<?nvs
use Core\Test;

final class MathTest
{
    #[Test]
    public function addsTwoNumbers(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(2 + 2, 4);
    }

    #[Test(skip: 'not written yet')]
    public function dividesByZero(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(1, 1);
    }
}
```
```output
MathTest
✓ addsTwoNumbers
- dividesByZero
skipped: not written yet
0 failed, 1 passed, 1 skipped, 0 flaky
```

- `--filter <text>` runs only the tests whose name contains the text: a `.nvst` case's path, or a
  program's `Class::method` — so `--filter Class::` selects one class's `#[Test]` methods.
- `--format` chooses how a *program's* run is reported: `human` (the default — one line per test as
  it runs, then `N failed, N passed, N skipped, N flaky in N ms`), `json` (one versioned document
  on standard output at the end: `schemaVersion` is `2`, then `summary`, and one `tests[]` entry per
  test with `class`, `method`, `file`, `line`, `column`, `verdict`, `durationMs`, and
  `reason`/`failures`/`attempts` where they apply; with a coverage flag `schemaVersion` is `3` and
  each test also has `coverage`, each file name mapped to the sorted lines that test reached),
  or `junit` (JUnit XML). In the machine formats, what the tests themselves `echo` goes to standard
  error so that standard output is the document alone. Naming a machine format beside a `.nvst`
  tree is refused.
- `--list` writes what the program declares without running any of it: under `human`, one
  `Class::method  file:line` per test; under `json`, a `schemaVersion: 2` document whose `listed`
  array holds one `{class, method, file, line, column}` per test and no summary, because nothing
  ran. `--filter` selects the same tests it would select in a run, and `--format junit`, `--update`
  and a `.nvst` tree are each refused beside it.
- `--coverage-lcov <file>` writes the run's coverage to the file in the lcov format.
  `--coverage-clover <file>` writes the same coverage as Clover XML, a format many CI
  services read. `--coverage-cobertura <file>` writes the same coverage as Cobertura
  XML, the format GitLab and Azure DevOps read. You can give all three in one run. Each line where
  a statement starts is listed with the number of times it ran. A line that no test reached has the
  count `0`. Each branch is listed too. A branch is a condition, such as the one in an `if`, a
  `while` or an `&&`. The file says how many times its true side ran and how many times its false
  side ran. The lcov and Clover files also list each function with the number of times it was
  called. A file is named relative to the directory you run `nvs test` in, so run it from your
  repository's root for your CI service to find the files. Under the `human` format, the run
  prints one more line, `N of N lines run (N%)`. The top-level statements of a file do not run
  under `nvs test`, so they have the count `0`. Naming any of these flags beside a `.nvst` tree
  or `--list` is an error.
- `--mutate` checks whether your tests notice a wrong line. See
  *nvs test --mutate* below.
- `--update` rewrites each failed `Core\Test::assertMatchesInline` snapshot in the source that
  wrote it, and is **the only spelling under which `nvs test` writes to a source file**. It
  replaces the `$expected` string and nothing else: a passing snapshot is untouched, and so is
  every other line of the file. The verdicts do not change — the tests that produced a new
  snapshot are still reported as failed, and the re-run is what says the new text is the one you
  meant. Write the snapshot as `''` and let the first run fill it in. Where one method holds two
  snapshots with the same text, neither is written and the run says so: there is no way to tell
  which rendering belongs in which string. Naming it beside a `.nvst` tree is refused — a case's
  expectation is its `--EXPECT--` section, which nothing rewrites.

A `.nvst` case is a sequence of `--SECTION--` headers: `--TEST--` (one line saying what the case
pins), `--FILE--` (the program, run as `nvs run`), `--EXPECT--` (its exact standard output) or
`--EXPECTF--` (with `%s`/`%d`/`%f` placeholders), `--EXPECTF-ERROR--` (standard error), an
optional `--FILE name--` for each extra file written beside it (`nvs.toml` included), and an
optional `--RUN--` naming another subcommand to run in that directory instead — `test`,
`config dump --origin`.

```text
--TEST--
a read outside the granted roots is refused
--FILE nvs.toml--
[capabilities.fs]
read = ["data"]
--FILE data/note.txt--
note
--FILE--
<?nvs
echo Core\IO::read("data/note.txt");
--EXPECT--
note
```

### nvs test --mutate

    nvs test <paths>... --mutate [--filter <text>] [--format human|json] [--jobs <n>]

`--mutate` checks whether your tests notice a wrong line. A line can run in a test while no
assertion checks its result. Coverage counts that line as tested. A mutation run finds it.

The run has two steps:

1. The tests run once, with coverage. If a test fails here, no mutant runs and the run fails.
2. For each place in the program that can change, Novis builds a copy with that one change. This
   copy is a **mutant**. The tests that ran the changed line run again against it.

These are the changes Novis makes:

| Change | Example |
|---|---|
| a comparison moves its boundary | `<` to `<=`, `>=` to `>` |
| an equality test is reversed | `==` to `!=` |
| an arithmetic operator is swapped | `+` to `-`, `*` to `/` |
| a logical operator is swapped | `&&` to `\|\|` |
| a boolean value is flipped | `true` to `false` |
| an `if` or loop condition is reversed | `if ($ok)` runs as `if (!$ok)` |

Each change keeps the types of the code, so every mutant compiles. A test method, and every line
inside it, never changes. A change that would give a value the wrong type is not made: `*` and `/`
swap only on `float` and `decimal` values.

Some conditions tell Novis the type of a value inside the `if`. These conditions are not changed:

- an `is` test, such as `$x is int`
- an `==` or `!=` that compares a value with `null`, a literal or a constant, when the value can
  have more than one type, such as `?int`, `int|string` or `mixed`

`if ($n == 10)` is changed when `$n` is an `int`. `if ($n == null)` is not changed when `$n` is a
`?int`.

Each mutant has one of four results:

| Result | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `killed` | a test failed, so the tests noticed the change |
| `survived` | every test passed, so no test checks this line's result |
| `timed out` | a test ran past its time limit, which also counts as noticed |
| `not reached` | no test ran the line, so no test ran again |

The **mutation score** is the `killed` and `timed out` mutants as a percentage of the reached
ones. A changed loop condition can make a loop run forever. A test can have no time limit from
`#[Test(timeout: ...)]` or `[limits] wall_time`. Under `--mutate`, such a test gets a limit of ten
times the slowest test's time, plus one second.

Under `human`, the run prints the normal test report, then the four counts, the score and each
survived mutant with its file, line and change:

```text
  mutants: 3 killed, 1 survived, 1 timed out, 1 not reached
  mutation score: 80.0% (4 of 5 reached mutants made a test fail or time out)
  survived  counter.nvs:10  `>=` to `>`
```

Under `json`, `schemaVersion` is `4`. The document has a `mutants` array with one `{file, line,
change, outcome, tests}` record for each mutant. `tests` is the number of tests that ran the
mutant's line. A survived mutant does not make the run fail, so the exit
status is the one of the first step.

Each mutant compiles the program again, so a run costs one compile and a few tests per mutant. The
mutants run one at a time, and each mutant's tests run across `--jobs` cores. `--mutate` runs a
program's `#[Test]` methods only. `--format junit`, `--list`, `--update`, `--watch` and a `.nvst`
tree are each an error beside it.

### nvs debug

    nvs debug [--once] [--tail <file>]... [--listen <address>]

With `[debug] store = true` in `nvs.toml`, every request is recorded. The records are written to
files in `debug/spool` in the data folder. `nvs debug` reads those files into one SQLite database,
`debug/index.sqlite`, and deletes each file once it is read. Then it waits for new files.

You usually do not start it yourself. A `nvs serve` in development starts `nvs debug` when
`store` is on, and stops it when the server stops. A production server never starts it. On a
production host, you run `nvs debug` yourself, when and where you choose.

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--once` | read the files that are ready, delete old records, then exit |
| `--tail <file>` | also read this log file, and each line added to it later; you can give it more than once |

A `--tail` file must use the `json` log format (`[log] format = "json"`). `nvs debug` never changes
that file. It remembers how far it read, so a restart goes on from there. When the file is rotated,
it first reads the rest of `<file>.1`.

Only one `nvs debug` runs for a data folder. A second one prints an error and exits with status
`1`. A server that finds one running uses it.

The index deletes a request's records once they are older than `[debug] index_age` (`7d`). When it
grows past `[debug] index_max` (`1G`), the oldest requests are deleted first. A line that cannot be
read is kept as an error record, and the lines after it are read as usual. A file that cannot be
read is tried again later, and the other files are read in the meantime.

**What a record contains.** In development, a record has the request's method, path, query,
headers and body, and the response's status, headers and body. The values of `Authorization`,
`Cookie`, `Set-Cookie` and `Proxy-Authorization` are replaced with `[redacted]`. A body is stored
as the program read it, up to `[limits] request_body`. A longer body is cut at that size. A body the
program did not read is not stored. A program can read a body into a class with
`Core\Request::jsonAs<X>()` or `postAs<X>()`. The decoder fills each `secret` property of `X`, and
the stored body has `[redacted]` in place of that value. If Novis cannot find those values in the
body, the body is not stored. That is the case for a multipart form, for example. A body the program
read another way is stored as it was read, so a password in it is in the index. The files are in a
folder that only your account can open. In production, a record has no headers and no body.

### The debug viewer

    nvs debug [--listen <address>]

`nvs debug` also serves the debug viewer, a page that shows the recorded requests in a browser. It
prints the page's address when it starts. The address is `http://127.0.0.1:8137/` unless
`[debug] listen` or `--listen` sets another one. If that port is in use, `nvs debug` stops with an
error. It does not pick another port, so a link to the viewer still works after a restart.

| Page | What it shows |
|---|---|
| `/` | the requests, newest first: method, route, status, duration, queries, dumps and exceptions |
| `/requests/<trace id>/<span id>` | one request: its timeline, its queries, dumps and log lines, and its input |
| `/stream` | every record of every request, as one list you can filter |
| `/log` | the log lines |
| `/search` | a full-text search over requests, dumps, logs, queries and exceptions |
| `/exceptions` | one row for each exception class and the line that threw it, with a count |
| `/compare/...` | two requests side by side |

New rows appear at the top while you watch. Press `p` or scroll down to pause the list. The list
then counts the new rows and does not move. Each page and each filter has its own link, which still
works after a reload. You can paste a trace id, or the value of a `traceresponse` header, into the
search box. The viewer then opens that request.

Every key is listed when you press `?`. `j` and `k` move the selection, `Enter` opens it, `/` goes to
the search box and `s` saves a filter. `m` marks a request, and the next request you open is
compared with it. `c` compares a request with the previous request to the same route.

`r` replays a request: it sends the recorded request to your development server again. The handler
runs again, with all its side effects, so the viewer asks first. Replay works only when `nvs serve`
started `nvs debug`. `t` makes a test from a request, the same test `nvs debug to-test` prints.

Every `file:line` in the viewer is a link that opens the file in your editor. Pick the editor in
the **Editor** dialog. The choices are `vscode` (the default), `vscode-insiders`, `vscodium`,
`cursor`, `zed`, `idea`, `phpstorm` and `custom`. With `custom`, you write the link yourself, with
`{file}`, `{line}` and `{column}` in it. A path mapping replaces the start of a recorded path. Use
one when the program ran in a container and its paths differ from yours. The viewer saves these
settings and your saved filters next to the index.

A profile that `Core\Debug::startProfile` wrote has a download link. In VS Code, it also has a link
that opens it in the Novis extension. When the server ran with `[debug] mode = ["coverage"]`, a
request's page shows which lines of each source file ran, and how often.

The viewer is for you alone. On a loopback address, it answers only its own page. A page on another
site cannot read it. When `listen` is not a loopback address, for example in a container,
`nvs debug` serves the viewer over HTTPS. It creates a certificate and a token, and prints a link
that contains the token. Your browser warns about the certificate once. `[debug] tls_cert_file`,
`tls_key_file` and `token_file` name your own files instead.

### nvs debug to-test

    nvs debug to-test <trace id> [--span <span id>] [--write <file>]

`nvs debug to-test` prints a test made from one recorded request. The test sends the same request
to your program with `Core\Test::request`, and checks that the response is the same. Save it in your
project and run it with `nvs test .`.

The test checks the status, the `Content-Type` header, the `Location` header of a redirect, and the
body. A JSON body is read with `json()` and compared with the recorded JSON as data, so spaces do
not matter. The keys must be in the same order. Any other body is compared byte for byte. Headers
such as `Date` change with every request, so the test does not check them.

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--span <span id>` | choose one request when several requests have the same trace id |
| `--write <file>` | write the test to a new file; if the file exists, nothing is written |

A header the record has as `[redacted]`, such as `Authorization`, gets the value `'redacted'`, with a
comment above it. Put a test credential there. If the recorded request body is not complete, no
test is printed, because part of a body is a different request. If the recorded response body is
not complete, the test checks the status and the headers only.

The request needs its input in the index, so it must come from a development server with
`[debug] store = true`. The viewer's `t` key shows the same test, with a button that copies it.

### Profiling

    nvs run <file> --profile callgrind|speedscope [--profile-out <file>]
    nvs test <paths>... --profile callgrind|speedscope [--profile-out <file>]

`--profile` measures how long each function call takes. When the program or the tests end, it
writes the result to a file. You do not change the program for this.

| Format | The file | Open it with |
|---|---|---|
| `callgrind` | `callgrind.out.<pid>` | KCachegrind or Webgrind |
| `speedscope` | `profile.<pid>.speedscope.json` | speedscope, or the *View Profile* command in VS Code |

`<pid>` is the process ID of the run. The file is written in the current folder.
`--profile-out <file>` writes it to another file instead. At the end, the run prints
`profile: <path>` on standard error.

A Callgrind file has totals for each function. One total is the time in the function itself. The
other includes the time of the functions it called. The file also lists who called each function.
A speedscope file has every call on a timeline, in the order the calls ran.

Under `nvs test`, each test has its own timeline in a speedscope file. A program that `spawn`
starts also has its own timeline. A Callgrind file adds the totals of all of them together. The
time a program waits for a spawned program is also in that sum, so the total can be larger than
the time the run took.

The timing adds a cost to every call. In a speedscope profile, it is about 170 nanoseconds per call
on a current desktop processor. Every call pays the same cost, so code with many small calls looks
slower in a profile than it is. A `.nvst` tree has no
profile. On `nvs run`, `--profile` is an error beside `--dump-ir`, `--dump-asm` or `--count`.

A program can also profile one part of itself. `Core\Debug::startProfile` and
`Core\Debug::stopProfile` write a speedscope file around the code between them. The configuration
must allow this. `[debug] mode` must include `"profile"`, and `[capabilities.debug] profile` must
allow the file's folder. `--profile` needs neither of them, because only the person who runs the
command can add the flag.

### nvs build --compile

    nvs build --compile <file> [-o <path>]

Writes a **portable single-file executable**: a copy of the `nvs` binary itself with the program's
source appended — the entry file plus every file its `require` graph reaches, as a flat list of
paths and bytes, followed by a small footer. No compilation result is stored; the bundle compiles
its source when it starts, exactly as `nvs run` would.

```text
$ nvs build --compile report.nvs -o disk-report
wrote disk-report (1 source file(s))
$ ./disk-report
uploads: 420 MB
total: 420 MB
```

- `-o <path>` says where to write it; the default is the entry file's stem in the current directory
  (`routes.exe` on Windows, `routes` elsewhere). The command reports `wrote <path> (N source
  file(s))`.
- Running the bundle runs the program. **Its whole command line belongs to the program**: a bundle
  never interprets `run`, `check`, `--help` or any other `nvs` argument, so an application whose
  first argument happens to be `run` keeps it.
- A bundle reads `./nvs.toml` from the directory it is *run in*. If there is none, it reads
  `nvs.toml` in the `.nvsdata` folder next to the bundle. A file with an error stops the run. A
  bundle never writes a `nvs.toml`. Ship the configuration beside it, or run it from a directory
  that has none.
- Files reached only through `autoload` at run time, or opened with `Core\IO`, are not in the
  bundle: it carries the static `require` graph and nothing else.
- Each `.nvsx` file that the build's configuration lists under `[[extension]]` goes into the
  bundle, with its `sha256` and its `grants`. The bundle checks each `sha256` when it starts and
  loads these extensions before the ones in the configuration file it reads. A file that does not
  match its `sha256` stops the build.
- On Windows, the executable shows the program's own name, version and icon in Explorer and in
  Task Manager. They come from the nearest `package.toml`, found from the current directory: the
  package's `name` and `version`, and the `.ico` file `[bundle] icon` names. Without a
  `package.toml`, the executable shows the icon and version of `nvs`.

### nvs build --openapi

    nvs build --openapi <file>

Writes an OpenAPI 3.1 document for the program's `#[Route]` methods to standard output: `openapi:
"3.1.0"`, an `info` block whose `title` is the entry file's stem and whose `version` is the nearest
`package.toml`'s `version` (`0.0.0` without one), and one `paths` entry per route
with its method, an `operationId` of `Class.method`, its path parameters with their schemas, and
its responses. Nothing runs. `nvs build` with neither `--compile` nor `--openapi` is refused rather
than doing nothing. The output below, for a program with one route, is trimmed at the `...`.

```text
$ nvs build --openapi orders.nvs > openapi.json
$ cat openapi.json
{
  "info": {
    "title": "orders",
    "version": "0.0.0"
  },
  "openapi": "3.1.0",
  "paths": {
    "/orders": {
      "get": {
        "operationId": "Orders.index",
        ...
        "summary": "Lists every open order."
      }
    }
  }
}
```

### nvs api diff

    nvs api diff <old.json> <new.json>

Reads two OpenAPI documents — typically the last release's and the one `nvs build --openapi` just
produced — and prints one line per change, classified `breaking`, `additive` or `cosmetic`, then a
summary; `no change` when they agree. It exits `1` when any change is breaking, so it is a CI gate:

```text
breaking: paths./users/{id} — path removed, with every operation on it
additive: paths./users.get.query.q — optional parameter added
2 change(s): 1 breaking, 1 additive, 0 cosmetic
```

### nvs config check and nvs config dump

    nvs config check [files]... [--as <account>]
    nvs config dump [files]... [--origin] [--toml]

Both read the configuration tree offline and run nothing, so a tree can be validated in CI before
it is deployed. With no files named they read `./nvs.toml`. If there is none, they read `nvs.toml` in
the data folder. If there is neither, they report an empty configuration, which is not an error.
Naming files positionally is the same as `--config`. Neither command creates the data folder.

- `config check` resolves the whole tree — includes, `[[app]]` blocks, secrets — and prints one
  line: `ok: 2 files, 4 directives set, 1 override, 0 warnings`. It exits `1` on anything the tree
  refuses: a TOML syntax error, an unknown key (`E0601`), a missing or cyclic include (`E0605`,
  `E0606`), an `[[app]]` block naming both `root` and `entry` or neither (`E0609`), a secret with
  both `password` and `password_file` (`E0608`). It does **not** check whether a value is a valid
  quantity, or whether a default lies under its own `[limits.hard]` ceiling: `memory = "12
  bananas"` passes `config check` in this build.
- `config check --as <account>` also checks who owns each file and who can write it. It checks the
  files for `<account>`, the account that will run `nvs serve`. A file that `nvs serve` would not
  read as that account is `E0607`, with the same help `nvs serve` prints. On Unix, `<account>` is a
  user name or a uid. On Windows, it is an account name, `LocalSystem` or `NT SERVICE\<service>`.
  An account that does not exist on this machine is `E0662`. The check reads the files on this
  machine as they are now. Without `--as`, `config check` does not check ownership. `config dump`
  does not take `--as`.
- `config dump` prints every key in force, one per line in dotted-key order, with array-of-tables
  blocks numbered (`app.0.root`, `include.1.path`). A value or a table name that holds a new line, a
  control character or a right-to-left mark is written as a TOML escape, such as `\n` for a new
  line. Each key stays on one line, and you can see text that a terminal would hide. `--origin` adds the file each key was written
  in, and the file it overrode; `--toml` prints the resolved tree as one canonical TOML document,
  for diffing two environments.

```text
app.0.capabilities.script.spawn = true
app.0.origin                    = "https://example.test"
app.0.root                      = "."
limits.hard.memory              = "512M"
limits.memory                   = "256M"
```

### nvs ext new and nvs ext build

    nvs ext new --lang rust|c <dir>
    nvs ext build [project]

An extension is a `.nvsx` file. It is a WebAssembly component that adds one class to Novis. You
write the code in Rust, C or another language that compiles to WebAssembly. `nvs ext` is the tool
