not a CDN: there is no `max-age` and no precompressed lookup.

### What a program reads about its door

The matched prefix is stripped before the program runs, so `Core\Request::path()` is the
remainder and one compiled program serves at `/`, at `/shop` or at `{1}` with no change.
`Core\Request::mount()` returns the rest: `prefix()` is what was stripped, `captures()` the glob
captures of the mount that matched, in order, `tainted` because which mount answers is the
client's choice. It is never `null` — a program served without a mount table reads `""` and an
empty array — and outside a request it throws.

```nvs skip
<?nvs
// Mounted by `scan = "*/public/index.nvs"` at `prefix = "/{1:lower}"`, so
// `/acme/orders` arrives here with `path()` equal to `/orders`.
Core\Request\Mount $mount = Core\Request::mount();
tainted string $tenant = $mount->captures()[0];
echo 'serving ', $tenant, ' under ', $mount->prefix(), "\n";
```

`Core\Router::url` puts the same prefix in front of every link it builds, so a link is never
assembled from a route's declared path by hand, and `Core\Router::urlAbsolute` prepends the
mount's `origin`, falling back to the `[[app]]` block's. A program run from the command line is
mounted nowhere: the prefix is empty and nothing else changes.

### Behind a proxy: `trusted_proxies`

```toml
[server]
listen          = ["127.0.0.1:8000"]
trusted_proxies = ["10.0.0.5", "10.1.0.0/16"]   # one address, and one block of addresses
```

`trusted_proxies` lists the proxies whose forwarding headers the server reads. An entry is one
address or one block of addresses, IPv4 or IPv6. The server prints a note at start for an entry
that is neither, and does not use that entry. A change to the list applies to the next request,
without a restart.

**The list is empty.** This is the default, and the server reads no forwarding header.
`Core\Request::clientIp()` returns the address that connected, and `Core\Request::scheme()` returns
`http`. A program can still read `X-Forwarded-For` with `Core\Request::header`, as a `tainted`
string.

**The list has the address that connected.** `clientIp()` returns the last address in
`X-Forwarded-For` that is not in the list. A client can send its own `X-Forwarded-For`, and the
proxy adds the real address after it, so the server does not use the addresses the client wrote.
`scheme()` returns `https` when the last value in `X-Forwarded-Proto` is `https`, and only the
response to such a request has the HSTS header. `X-Forwarded-For` is the only address header the
server reads.

```nvs skip
<?nvs
// The proxy at 10.0.0.5 sent `X-Forwarded-For: 192.0.2.99, 203.0.113.7`
// and `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`.
?tainted string $client = Core\Request::clientIp(); // "203.0.113.7"
tainted string $scheme = Core\Request::scheme(); // "https"
```

`clientIp()` returns `null` when the proxy wrote `unknown` in place of the address. A port after
the address is not part of the result. When the address the server would use is not an IP address,
the server answers `400` and runs no program.

**The address that connected is not in the list.** The server reads no forwarding header of that
request, the same as with an empty list.

**A Unix socket.** When the list is not empty, the server also reads the forwarding headers of a
request that arrives over a Unix socket. The operating system decides who may connect to the
socket, so it needs no entry of its own. With an empty list, `clientIp()` returns `null` for such a
request.

A production server whose configuration has a `[server]` block prints one warning at start when
`trusted_proxies` is empty and every address it listens on is a loopback address or a Unix socket.
A server like this is usually behind a proxy, and without the list every request has the address of
the proxy, or none.

### What reaches a running server

A running server takes a change without a restart, except a change to three keys.

**A code change.** The server checks every file a program has loaded once per `[opcache]
revalidate_freq`, off the request path. When a file changed, the server waits until no file of the
program has changed for `[opcache] settle`: `1s` in production, `100ms` in development. Then it
compiles the whole program again, and the next request runs the new code. A request that is already
running finishes on the code it started with. A file added where the program looks for one, or a
file removed, is a change too. This works in every mode, and a deploy has no step to run after it.

A change that does not compile fails the requests that reach it, with its diagnostic. The server
does not serve the last version that compiled in its place. When the file is fixed, the next check
finds the fix.

**A configuration change.** The server checks its own configuration files every two seconds. When
you save a file, the server reads all of its configuration files again and checks them. Then the next
request uses the new configuration. Every reload writes one `configuration reloaded` line to the log.
Its `applied` field lists the keys that changed. Its `ignored` field lists the changed keys that need
a restart. `invalidated` is the number of compiled program files that the server compiles again.

A file with an error changes nothing. The server writes `configuration reload refused` to the log
once, with the error and its line, and keeps the configuration it has. A saved file is the only
thing that starts a reload. No signal and no command from a service manager starts one.

**Four keys need a restart**: `[server] listen`, `[server] socket_mode`, `[server] workers` and
`[server] watchdog_margin`. A port below 1024 needs a privilege the server gave up after it opened
the socket. `socket_mode` is applied only when a socket is opened, and `workers` sets how many cores
accept requests. `watchdog_margin` is how long a worker may stay past the deadline of its oldest
request before the server reports that the worker has stopped. A changed one takes effect at the
next start. Until then, the server writes `configuration restart pending` to the log once, with the
key, the running value and the new one. The shipped `nvs.toml` ends each of these four lines with
`restart required`:

```toml
[server]
#listen = ["127.0.0.1:8000"]          # default; restart required
#socket_mode = "0660"                 # default; restart required
#workers = 4                          # default: one per core; restart required
#watchdog_margin = "5s"               # default; restart required

[opcache]
#revalidate_freq = "2s"               # how often the server checks the files a program loaded
#settle = "1s"                        # how long they must stay unchanged before a compile
```

#### Deploying

Copying files into place is safe, even when the copy takes a few seconds. The server compiles only
after the program's files have stopped changing for `settle`. If a file changes while it compiles,
it throws that compile away and starts again.

An upload that can pause for longer than `settle`, over a slow link or with a large archive, goes
into a new directory. When the upload is complete, switch a link such as `current` to it. The server
resolves the link at the start of each compile and again at the end, so it never builds one program
from two releases. Under `nvs serve <file>` the next compile after the switch reads the new release,
and static files still come from the release the server started with. A `[[server.mount]]` table
resolves its links when the server starts, so a switch reaches it at the next start.

#### What no compiler can check

The compiler checks that the new code agrees with itself. It cannot check data that the old code
wrote and the new code reads: cache entries, sessions, queued jobs and database rows. Requests that
started before a change finish on the old code, so for a short time both versions write. Write the
new code so that it reads what the old code wrote. For example, a job that gains a field needs a
default for the jobs queued without it.

### Stopping and reloading: the drain

A stop makes the server drain. A stop is `Ctrl-C`, `nvs service stop` or a stop from the service
manager. The server accepts no new connection, finishes the work it has, and then exits:

- A request that is running is answered in full, and then its connection closes.
- A connection with no work closes at once. This is a kept-alive connection between two requests,
  a WebSocket whose program waits for a message, and an event stream with nothing to write.
- A WebSocket or an event stream whose program keeps writing is closed a short time later.

A WebSocket is closed with the code `1001` (`going away`), so its client can connect again.

`drain_timeout` is the longest time that a connection with no request stays open after it sees
the drain. `false` and `0` are not allowed:

```toml
[server]
drain_timeout = "30s"                 # default
```

While the server drains, `[server] health_path` answers `503`. A program reads the same state with
`Core\Server::isDraining()`, which returns `false` in a program that no server runs. A long request
can test it between two steps and end early:

```nvs skip
<?nvs
array<string> $orders = ['A-1001', 'A-1002', 'A-1003'];
foreach ($orders as string $order) {
    // `true` after the server was told to stop. The loop ends, and the answer is still sent.
    if (Core\Server::isDraining()) {
        break;
    }
    echo 'invoice sent for ', $order, "\n";
}
```

**A reload drains the connections that are open.** When the server applies a saved configuration
file, it closes each connection that was opened before the reload, the same way a stop does. A
request that is running finishes with the configuration it started with, and then its connection
closes. The server still accepts new connections, and they use the new configuration. The health
path still answers `200`, and `Core\Server::isDraining()` still returns `false`.

### When the client goes away

A client can close its connection before the answer is sent. For example, the user closes the
browser tab. The request still runs to its end, and the server throws its answer away:

- A write to the answer returns at once and does not throw an error. This is true for `echo`,
  for `Core\Response` and for `Core\Response\Stream::write`. The bytes are thrown away.
- Work that the request gave to `Core\Task::afterResponse` still runs.
- The request keeps its place in `[server] max_in_flight` until it ends.
- When the server drains, it waits for this request as for any other, up to `drain_timeout`.

A request with a `wall_time` stops at its `wall_time`, as it does with a client. A request with no
`wall_time` stops when `disconnect_grace` has passed since the client went away. `false` and `0`
are not allowed:

```toml
[limits]
disconnect_grace = "30s"              # default
```

`cancel_on_disconnect` lists request methods. A request with a listed method stops as soon as its
client goes away. The names are compared exactly, so `GET` and `get` are two different methods:

```toml
[limits]
cancel_on_disconnect = ["GET", "HEAD"]   # default: []
```

A request that stops runs no more code of your program. No `catch` block runs. Both keys can also
be written in `[app.limits]` for one application. A request cannot change them while it runs, and
a program cannot test whether its client has gone. These keys do not apply to an event stream
(`Core\Sse`) or a WebSocket.

### nvs service

    nvs service install <name> [options] -- <nvs arguments>
    nvs service unit <name> [options] -- <nvs arguments>
    nvs service start | stop | status | run | uninstall <name>

`nvs service` installs a server as a service of the operating system. The service manager starts a
service at every boot, and starts it again after a failure. The service manager is systemd on Linux
and the Service Control Manager on Windows.

**`install`** stores one `nvs` command under a name that you choose. Everything before `--` is an
option of the installer. Everything after `--` is the command that the service runs. Run `install`
as root on Linux, and in a terminal started as administrator on Windows:

```text
$ nvs service install shop -- serve /srv/shop/public/index.nvs --config /srv/shop/nvs.toml
installed service `shop`; `nvs service start shop` starts it
```

The installer checks the command first. When a check fails, it prints an error and changes nothing:

| The check | Error |
|---|---|
| The command is `serve` or `run`. No other command keeps running. | `E0630` |
| `serve` with no file needs a configuration with a `[[server.mount]]` entry that is on disk. | `E0630` |
| Every path is a full path. This includes `--config`, `--data`, and `[log] target`, `[opcache] file_cache_dir` and `[io] temp_root` in the configuration. | `E0631` |
| The installer can create and use the data folder, when the service reads the `nvs.toml` in it. | `E0653` |
| On Linux, the account that `--account` names exists. | `E0654` |
| The command line has no `--password`. Other users of the machine can read a command line. | `E0633` |
| A bundled executable does not install itself. Install the `nvs` binary. | `E0634` |

Without `--config`, the service reads the `nvs.toml` in its data folder. The data folder is
`.nvsdata` next to the `nvs` program, or the folder that `--data` names after `--`. The installer
adds `--config` and the full path of that file to the command that it stores. It creates the folder
and the file when they do not exist. A file that already exists is not changed.

The error names what failed the check:

```text
$ nvs service install shop -- serve index.nvs --config /srv/shop/nvs.toml
error[E0631]: `the entry file` is relative: `index.nvs`
  = note: a service does not start in the directory of this terminal, so a relative path names another file there and the service fails at its first start
  = help: write the path absolutely

error: aborting due to 1 error
To read what a code means and how to fix it, run `nvs agent show <code>`.
```

The options of the installer:

| Option | What it sets |
|---|---|
| `--account <account>` | The account that the service runs as. The default is the local system account. |
| `--start automatic`, `delayed` or `manual` | When the service starts after a boot. The default is `automatic`. |
| `--restart on-failure` or `never` | What happens after a failure. The default is `on-failure`. |
| `--depends-on <service>` | A service that must start first, such as a database. You can repeat it. |
| `--description <text>` | The text that an administrator sees beside the name. |
| `--dry-run` | Prints every step and changes nothing. |

With `--account`, the service account can read the data folder and every configuration file. It can
write only to the `cache`, `tmp`, `lsp` and `logs` folders in the data folder, and to a log, cache or
temporary folder that the configuration names. The service cannot change its own configuration.

On Linux, the installer sets owners and modes. The data folder belongs to `root` with mode `0750`,
and its `nvs.toml` with mode `0640`. Both are in the group of the account, so the account can read
them. Each folder that the service writes to belongs to the account, with mode `0700`. The
installer creates such a folder when it does not exist. A `--config` file in another folder is not
changed, and the installer prints a warning when the account cannot read it. `uninstall` gives
every one of these paths back to `root`, readable only by `root`.

A service has no terminal. When the configuration does not set `[log] target`, a service writes its
log to `logs/nvs.log` in the data folder. When that file reaches `[log] max_size`, Novis renames it
to `nvs.log.1` and starts a new file, and it keeps `[log] keep` old files. If the data folder cannot
be used, the log goes to the standard error stream. `nvs service install --help` prints one whole
command line for each platform.

**`unit`** prints what `install` would store, and changes nothing. It makes the same checks, and it
needs no administrator. On Linux it prints a systemd unit. On Windows it prints a `New-Service`
command:

```text
$ nvs service unit shop -- serve /srv/shop/public/index.nvs --config /srv/shop/nvs.toml
[Unit]
Description=Novis service shop
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=notify
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/nvs serve /srv/shop/public/index.nvs --config /srv/shop/nvs.toml
WatchdogSec=30
NoNewPrivileges=true
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=true
ReadWritePaths=-/usr/local/bin/.nvsdata/cache -/usr/local/bin/.nvsdata/tmp -/usr/local/bin/.nvsdata/lsp -/usr/local/bin/.nvsdata/logs
PrivateTmp=true
CapabilityBoundingSet=
RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_UNIX
SystemCallFilter=@system-service

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

On Linux, `install` writes this unit to `/etc/systemd/system/shop.service` and enables it. The unit
has no reload command. The server applies a saved configuration file by itself.

`ProtectSystem=strict` makes every file read-only for the service. `ReadWritePaths` lists the folders
that the service can write: the `cache`, `tmp`, `lsp` and `logs` folders in the data folder, and a
log, cache or temporary folder that the configuration names. The `-` before
each path tells systemd to skip a folder that does not exist. If the `nvs` binary, the program or one
of these folders is in `/home`, `/root` or `/run/user`, the unit has `ProtectHome=read-only`. With
`ProtectHome=true` the service could not read or write there.

**`start`** and **`stop`** send the request to the service manager. After a stop the server drains
(§ *Stopping and reloading: the drain*). **`status`** prints the state that the service manager
reports:

```text
$ nvs service status shop
active
```

On Windows the state is a word such as `running` or `stopped`. While the service runs, `status`
also lists each mount that did not compile when the server started:

```text
$ nvs service status shop
active
Mounts that did not compile at start:
  the mount at `/blog` serves `/srv/www/Blog/public/index.nvs`, which did not compile at start, ...
```

The list comes from the last lines that the server wrote to its log. A server that has written many
lines since it started may list none. **`run`** runs the stored command in your
terminal, so you can read what the server prints when it does not start as a service.
**`uninstall`** removes the service and everything that `install` added.

The installation chapter has where the binary, the configuration and the logs go and which folder
permissions are checked.

<a id="tools-php-differences"></a>
## C.5 Coming from PHP: how Novis is different, and how to port a program

Keywords: PHP, coming from PHP, switch from PHP, differences, port, porting, rewrite, migration, converter, AI agent, coding agent, nvs agent, PHPUnit, PHPStan, Psalm, PHP CS Fixer, PHP_CodeSniffer, Composer

This page is for somebody who already knows PHP. Novis looks like PHP, but it is a different
language. This page explains how Novis is different, what Novis can do that PHP cannot, and how to
port a program.

PHP code does not run in Novis. There is no converter. There is also no list that gives the Novis
method for each PHP function. A PHP program and a Novis program are built from different parts:
Novis has no traits, no magic methods and no global functions. A tool cannot choose the new design
for your program, so you write it yourself, or with the help of an AI coding agent.

### The short list

Ten ideas explain most of the differences:

- **Every variable, parameter and property has a type**, and you write it once. A value never
  changes its type. `mixed` is the type for a value that can have more than one type.
- **Every function is a method of a class, and every constant is a constant of a class.** This is
  true for the built-in ones too. Novis has no global variables, so `$_GET`, `$GLOBALS` and
  `global` do not exist.
- **The `Core` classes are the standard library.** All their methods use the same order of
  arguments and accept named arguments. A method that fails throws an error. It does not return
  `false`.
- **There is one equality operator.** `==` never converts its operands, and `===` does not exist.
  Comparing two values of unrelated types does not compile.
- **A `string` is UTF-8 text** and counts graphemes (what a person counts as one character). Binary
  data has its own type, `bytes`.
- **An array keeps its insertion order, and its keys are always strings.** It declares the type of
  its elements. Assigning an array to a second variable gives a copy.
- **Novis has no `eval`, no references and no magic methods.** The constructor is named
  `constructor`. A parameter marked `inout` is the only way a method can change a variable of its
  caller.
- **Concurrency is built in.** `Core\Task` and channels run work at the same time. `spawn script`
  starts a separate script that shares no memory with yours.
- **Security is part of the program.** A program needs a permission in `nvs.toml` to read a file or
  to open a network connection, for example `fs.read` or `net.connect`. `tainted` and `secret` are
  part of a type, and the compiler checks where those values go.
- **Tests are part of the language.** You write `#[Test]` methods and run them with `nvs test`. See
  *The tools you do not install* below.

This short program uses several of them. The function is a static method, the constant belongs
to the class, and `==` compares two strings without converting them to numbers:

```nvs
<?nvs
class Stock
{
    public const string UNIT = 'pcs';

    public static function total(array<int> $counts): int
    {
        int $sum = 0;
        foreach ($counts as int $count) {
            $sum += $count;
        }
        return $sum;
    }
}

echo Stock::total(['apples' => 12, 'pears' => 5]), ' ', Stock::UNIT, "\n";
echo '12' == '012' ? 'equal' : 'different', ' ', Core\Str::length('Café'), "\n";
```
```output
17 pcs
different 4
```

#### What Novis can do that PHP cannot

Three things in Novis are part of the language, and a library cannot add them to PHP:

- **SQL injection and leaked secrets are compile errors.** Text from a request is `tainted`. A
  password or a key is `secret`. The program does not compile if such a value is used in an unsafe
  place, for example tainted text in an SQL query.
- **Every request runs in its own isolate.** An isolate is a separate part of one server process,
  with its own memory. Each request, job and script has its own limit for memory, CPU and time, and
  one request cannot read another request's data.
- **Any function can wait.** A method that reads a file or calls a server waits without blocking the
  other requests. There is no `async` keyword, so you never write a second version of a function.

### Porting a program

To port a PHP program, read it to learn what it does. Then write that again with the parts Novis
has. Do not translate it line by line. A trait, a magic method or a global helper function has no
direct form in Novis, and you choose the new design.

1. Write down what the program does: its pages, its jobs, and the data it reads and writes.
2. Write the types first: the classes, their typed properties and the enums.
3. Write each part again with the `Core` classes. `nvs agent find` with the name of a task finds
   the method for it.
4. Run `nvs check` after each part. It shows every line that still needs a change.
5. Write tests as `#[Test]` methods, and run them with `nvs test`.

For a large program, you can give this work to an AI coding agent. `nvs agent init` writes a file
that tells the agent about `nvs agent`. The agent then reads `nvs agent primer`, and it looks up
each method with `nvs agent find` and `nvs agent show`. See [agents](#tools-agents).

This is a small cart program written in Novis. The function `total` is a method of the class
`Cart`, and its parameter has the type `array<int>`. `as int` converts the text `"7"` to the number
`7`, and `&&` is the way to write "and":

```nvs
<?nvs
class Cart
{
    public const int FREE_SHIPPING = 50;

    public static function total(array<int> $prices): int
    {
        int $sum = 0;
        foreach ($prices as int $p) {
            $sum += $p;
        }
        return $sum;
    }
}

array<int> $prices = [20, 35];
int $total = Cart::total($prices);
string $input = '7';
int $qty = $input as int;

echo $total, ' ', ($total >= Cart::FREE_SHIPPING && $qty > 0) ? 'ships free' : 'pays', "\n";
echo Core\Str::slice('Novis', 0, 1), ' ', 7 <=> 3, ' ', 1 == 1.0 ? 'eq' : 'ne', "\n";

[int $first, int $second] = $prices;
var $double = fn(int $n): int => $n * 2;
echo $first, ' ', $second, ' ', $double($qty) as int, "\n";

try {
    throw new RuntimeError('stock');
} catch (RuntimeError $e) {
    echo $e->message, "\n";
}
```
```output
55 ships free
N 1 eq
20 35 14
stock
```

### The tools you do not install

A PHP project usually installs a set of development tools with Composer. Novis has their work built
into the toolchain or into the language itself:

- **PHPUnit** → `#[Test]` methods, `Core\Test` assertions and `nvs test` are the framework — data
  rows, fixtures, skip-with-reason, retries, JUnit and JSON output. See [testing](#lang-testing).
- **PHPStan / Psalm** → `nvs check` is the compiler, and it already checks what their strictest
  levels check: every variable typed, every method resolved at compile time, every path returning,
  every property initialized — plus `tainted`/`secret` flow, which is Psalm's taint mode as a type
  rule. There are no levels and no baseline file, because there is no untyped code to bridge.
- **PHP CS Fixer / PHP_CodeSniffer** → the style rules that catch bugs are compile errors here —
  identifier casing, a written visibility on every member, one way to write each construct — with
  no suppression and nothing to configure.

A test is a method with `#[Test]` in any class. `nvs test` runs this file and reports three tests:
one for each `#[TestWith]` row, and one that is skipped with its reason.

```nvs test
<?nvs
use Core\Test;
use Core\Test\TestWith;

final class Price
{
    public static function withTax(int $cents, int $percent): int
    {
        return $cents + Core\Math::intDiv($cents * $percent, 100);
    }
}

final class PriceTest
{
    #[TestWith(cents: 1000, percent: 20, want: 1200)]
    #[TestWith(cents: 999, percent: 10, want: 1098)]
    #[Test]
    public function taxIsAdded(int $cents, int $percent, int $want): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Price::withTax($cents, $percent), $want);
    }

    #[Test(skip: 'refunds are not written yet')]
    public function aRefundGivesTheTaxBack(): void
    {
        Test::assertSame(Price::withTax(-1000, 20), -1200);
    }
}
```
```output
  PriceTest
    ✓ taxIsAdded#0
    ✓ taxIsAdded#1
    - aRefundGivesTheTaxBack
      skipped: refunds are not written yet
  0 failed, 2 passed, 1 skipped, 0 flaky in
```

`nvs check` reports a method that does not return a value on every path. No analyser is set up
for it:

```nvs error
<?nvs
class Stock
{
    public static function label(int $count): string
    {
        if ($count > 0) {
            return 'in stock';
        }
    }
}

echo Stock::label(3), "\n";
```
```output
E0739
```

<a id="tools-packages"></a>
## C.6 Packages: grants, package.toml, adding, fetching, updating, packing and publishing packages, and API versions

Keywords: nvs pkg audit, nvs pkg advise, version range, advisory, advisories, log/advisories, second copy, checkpoint copy, package.toml, grants, nvs pkg add, nvs pkg fetch, nvs pkg vendor, nvs pkg update, nvs pkg outdated, nvs pkg pack, nvs pkg download, nvs pkg provide, [[download]], SHA-256, download cache, archive, package.lock, --locked, vendor, vendor/packages.nvs, registry, registries, dependencies, git dependency, digest, BLAKE3, released, retracted, withheld, unlisted, install, E0317, transparency log, checkpoint, signed note, Ed25519, fork, nvs registry key, nvs registry log append, nvs registry log verify, nvs registry index sign, nvs pkg api, nvs pkg diff, public API, breaking change, version, semantic versioning, major, minor, patch, [grants], namespace, package, vendor, dependency, capability, capabilities, required, optional, Core\Cap::has, E0655, E0656, E0657, E0658, E0659, E0660, E0661, permission, supply chain, third-party code, nvs pkg login, nvs pkg whoami, nvs pkg publish, nvs pkg retract, nvs pkg unlist, publish token, nvsreg_, pending, passkey, publish

### Grants: what each namespace may do

The `[grants]` table says which capabilities the code in each namespace may use. A capability is a
right such as `fs.read` or `net.connect`. The table is in the `package.toml` file of your
application:

```toml
[grants]
'Acme\Http\*' = ["net.connect"]
'Acme\Cache'  = []
```

Novis finds this file in the directory of the entry file, or in the nearest directory above it. The
entry file is the file you pass to `nvs run` or `nvs serve`. The current directory does not matter.

Each key is a namespace. Each value is a list of capability names. `'Acme\Cache'` matches only the
namespace `Acme\Cache`. `'Acme\Http\*'` matches `Acme\Http` and every namespace below it, such as
`Acme\Http\Client`. An empty list gives the namespace no capability.

The check happens when the program compiles. A call to a `Core` method that needs a capability
compiles only if the namespace of the code that makes the call has that capability. The namespace is
the one in the file's `namespace` line. An anonymous function has the namespace it is written in. A
`use` line does not change anything. A missing capability is error `E0658`. The message shows the
line to change.

```toml file=package.toml
[grants]
'Acme\Cache' = []
```
```nvs file=lib/Store.nvs
<?nvs
namespace Acme\Cache;

final class Store
{
    public static function load(): string
    {
        return Core\IO::readText('note.txt');
    }
}
```
```nvs error
<?nvs
autoload 'Acme\Cache' from './lib';

echo Acme\Cache\Store::load(), "\n";
```
```output
the namespace `Acme\Cache` does not have the capability `fs.read`
```

When several keys match a namespace, the longest key wins. Length is counted in namespace parts. A
key without `\*` wins over a key with `\*` of the same length. Only the winning line applies. A
longer key never adds to a shorter one.

A namespace that no key matches has every capability of the application. So a program without a
`[grants]` table compiles exactly as before. A namespace with a line has only what the line lists.

The table can only take capabilities away. `nvs.toml` still decides what the program may do at
all, and each path or host a call uses is still checked when the call runs. A call can do only what
both files allow.

These lines are errors:

| Line | Error |
|---|---|
| a key that is not a namespace, a value that is not a list, an unknown capability | `E0655` |
| `'\Acme\Http'` next to `'Acme\Http'`: a `\` at the start changes nothing, so both keys are the same | `E0656` |
| a key that names `Core` or a namespace below it | `E0657` |

#### A package's own `package.toml`

A package is a directory with its own `package.toml`. Its name is a vendor and a name, such as
`Acme\Disk`. The file lists the capabilities the package needs:

```toml
[package]
name = 'Acme\Disk'

[capabilities]
required = ["fs.read"]
optional = ["fs.write"]
```

This list grants nothing. It only tells you what to write in `[grants]`. A file of your program
belongs to the package when the package's `package.toml` is in the file's directory or in a directory
between the file and the entry file. A `package.toml` in the entry file's directory, or above it, is
your application's own file. A bad package file is error `E0659`.

A capability in `required` that the package's grant line does not list is error `E0658`, as above.
A capability in `optional` that the line does not list compiles. A call that needs it throws a
`RuntimeError` when it runs. Before the call, the package can check the capability with
`Core\Cap::has`:

```nvs skip
if (Core\Cap::has('fs.write')) {
    Core\IO::write('cache.txt', $text);
}
```

`Core\Cap::has` returns `true` only when the grant line of the calling namespace and `nvs.toml`
both allow the capability.

#### The rules for a package's files

Every file of a package declares the package's namespace or a namespace below it. A file of
`Acme\Disk` may declare `namespace Acme\Disk;` or `namespace Acme\Disk\Index;`. Any other
namespace is error `E0660`. So a package cannot use the grant line of your application or of another
package.

A `require` or `autoload` path in a package must stay inside the package's directory. A path that
leaves it with `..`, with an absolute path or through a symbolic link is error `E0661`.

### package.toml

`package.toml` describes your application or a package. The `nvs pkg` commands read all of it.
When your program compiles, Novis reads only `[grants]` of your application's file, and only
`[package] name` and `[capabilities]` of a package's file. Your program never reads the file when it
runs.

A file with a `[package] name` is a package's file. A file without one is an application's file.
This is an application's file:

```toml
[dependencies]
'Acme\Slug' = "1.2.0"
'Acme\Fork' = { git = "https://git.example.com/acme/fork.git", rev = "4f2a9c0e1b7d3a5f6e8c9b0a1d2e3f4a5b6c7d8e" }

[registries]
Acme = { url = "https://packages.example.com", key = "packages.example.com+6c1a1f0e+AW0nQ8Kq3s9xUjvL4kz5Ff2hN1pYc7RbT0eGdMiSo8Ax" }

[grants]
'Acme\Slug\*' = []  # required: fs.read
'Acme\Fork\*' = []
```

| Table or key | What it says |
|---|---|
| `[package] name` | the package's name, which is also its namespace, such as `'Acme\Slug'` |
| `[package] version` | the package's version, `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, such as `"1.2.0"` |
| `[package] files` | the files the package carries beside its `src` folder, such as `["data/words.txt"]` |
| `[package] supersedes` | the package this package replaces, such as `'Acme\Http'` for `'Acme\HttpNext'`. The registry shows it on the package page |
| `[dependencies]` | each package your code needs, with the lowest version it works with |
| `[registries]` | the registry each vendor's packages come from |
| `[capabilities]` | the capabilities a package needs, as `required` and `optional` |
| `[grants]` | the capabilities each namespace may use, in an application's file only |
| `[[download]]` | a large file a package downloads from another host, with its size and SHA-256 hash |
| `[bundle] icon` | the `.ico` file a Windows executable from `nvs build --compile` shows, as a path from this file's folder |

On Windows, `nvs build --compile` writes the package's name and `version` into the executable. Explorer
and Task Manager show them. Without a name, the executable shows its file name, and without a version, `0.0.0`.

`version`, `files`, `supersedes`, `[capabilities]` and `[[download]]` are allowed only in a package's file. Any
other key is error `E0659`, and the `nvs pkg` commands stop.

A package's name has two parts, a vendor and a name: `Acme\Slug`. On the command line and in a URL,
you write it in lower case with `/`: `acme/slug`. No package may be named `Core` or take the name of a
built-in component, such as `Novis\Image`.

A dependency is written with its namespace, the same way as in `[grants]`. Its value is the lowest
version your code works with. `nvs pkg fetch` may choose a higher version, as
[nvs pkg fetch and nvs pkg vendor](#nvs-pkg-fetch-and-nvs-pkg-vendor) says.

A dependency can also come from a git repository. Write its URL and the full commit hash as `rev`. A
branch or a tag is not allowed, because it can point to other code later. Only your application's
file may have a git dependency. When a package's file has one, `nvs pkg fetch` stops with an error.

Each vendor's packages come from one registry. `[registries]` names the registry for a vendor. Every
other vendor's packages come from `https://registry.novis-lang.org`. A registry URL starts with
`https:`, or with `file:` for a folder on your disk. `nvs pkg fetch` never looks for a vendor's
package in a second registry. So nobody can publish a package with your vendor's name in another
registry and have it used.

The `key` is the public key of the registry's log. You get it from the people who run the registry.
`nvs pkg` uses a package only if the log contains it. The log is a list of every change to the
registry, and nobody can rewrite it. If the log does not continue the one `nvs pkg` saw last time,
`nvs pkg` stops with an error and fetches nothing.

### nvs pkg add

    nvs pkg add <package>
    nvs pkg add <package>@<version>

`nvs pkg add acme/slug` adds the newest released version of `acme/slug` to `[dependencies]`. Then it
does what `nvs pkg fetch` does. With a version, such as `acme/slug@1.2.0`, it adds exactly that
version.

Before the command changes any file, it prints each package it adds, with the capabilities that
package requests. The packages that `acme/slug` needs are included:

```text
`Acme\Slug` 1.2.0 needs 1 other package(s). Each one requests:
  `Acme\Slug` 1.2.0: required fs.read
  `Acme\Text` 1.0.0: no capabilities
There is no package.lock yet, so every package is new:
  `Acme\Slug` 1.2.0 is new. It requests required fs.read.
  `Acme\Text` 1.0.0 is new. It requests no capabilities.
added to [grants]: 'Acme\Slug\*' = []  # required: fs.read
added to [grants]: 'Acme\Text\*' = []
2 package(s), 2 written to vendor/
```

Each new grant line is empty, so the package may use no capability yet. The comment says what the
package requests. You add a capability to the line when you agree with it.

A new version of a package is released seven days after it is published, or earlier when an owner of
the package confirms it. `nvs pkg add` without a version chooses only a released version. A version
that waits for its release, or that its owners unlisted, is added only when you write its number.

A retracted version has a known problem. The command stops with an error that gives the reason and
the version with the fix. A version that the registry withheld, such as malware, also stops the
command. In both cases, no file changes.

A dependency that is already in `[dependencies]` keeps its version when that version is higher. With
`@<version>`, the command writes that version. The comment on the line stays.

When a package also downloads files from other hosts, the command lists each host and the total
size. Those hosts see the address of the computer that runs `nvs pkg fetch`.

### nvs pkg fetch and nvs pkg vendor

    nvs pkg fetch [--locked]
    nvs pkg vendor [--locked]

`nvs pkg fetch` downloads every package in `[dependencies]`, and every package those packages need.
Run it in the folder of your application, next to `package.toml`. It writes these files:

| File | What it contains |
|---|---|
| `vendor/<vendor>/<name>/` | each package's files: `package.toml`, the `src` folder and the files it lists |
| `vendor/packages.nvs` | one `autoload` line for each package |
| `vendor/package-files.toml` | the files of each package, which its own code may read with no grant |
| `package.lock` | the version, the source and the digest of every package |
| `package.toml` | one new grant line in `[grants]` for each new package |

Your program loads every package with one line:

```nvs skip
require './vendor/packages.nvs';
```

`vendor/packages.nvs` looks like this:

```nvs skip
<?nvs
// Generated by `nvs pkg` from package.lock. Do not edit.
autoload 'Acme\Slug' from './acme/slug/src';
autoload 'Acme\Text' from './acme/text/src';
```

When two packages need different versions of a third package, the higher version is used. A version
is only chosen when a package asks for it, so a new release does not change your program until you
run `nvs pkg add` or `nvs pkg update`.

The digest of a package is the BLAKE3 hash of its archive. `package.lock` has the digest of every
package. Commit `package.lock` with your code. The next `nvs pkg fetch` checks each archive against its
digest and stops with an error when one does not match. `--locked` also stops when `package.lock` is
missing a package or has to change, so CI uses exactly the versions you tested.

No code of a package runs during `nvs pkg fetch`. A package's code runs only when your program calls
it. A file that `autoload` loads may only declare a class, an interface, an enum or a type. Any other
statement at the top of the file is error `E0317`.

A new grant line gives the package no capability. A line that is already in `[grants]` is never
changed, so a capability you added stays. A package's own code may read the files that
`vendor/package-files.toml` lists for it with no grant, when the path is a string in the code. It may
not write them.

`nvs pkg fetch` keeps a package folder whose files still match `package.lock`. `nvs pkg vendor` does the
same work, but it downloads every package again and replaces its folder. Use it when a file in
`vendor/` was changed. Both commands remove only the folders of packages they wrote before, so code
you copied into `vendor/` yourself stays.

A package that contains a file named `nvs.toml`, in any folder, stops the fetch with an error that
names the file. Only the person who runs the server writes that file. The package is not written to
`vendor/`, and `package.lock` does not change.

When a package contains an extension, the fetch prints the entry that loads it. The path is relative
to the folder of your application:

```text
`Shop\Ledger` contains an extension. To load it, add this entry to your `nvs.toml`:

[[extension]]
path   = "vendor/shop/ledger/ledger.nvsx"
sha256 = "3112cf3359166c7a83a052ca0f21537ef8e1f87a6873d0b4c7d96b8b7fd4e1b6"
```

The fetch never writes `nvs.toml`. It prints the entry again only when the package is new or has a
new digest. The entry has no `grants`. Read what the extension needs with `nvs ext inspect`, and add
the grants yourself.

### nvs pkg update and nvs pkg outdated

    nvs pkg update [<package> ...]
    nvs pkg outdated

`nvs pkg outdated` lists each package that has a newer released version. It changes no file:

```text
`Acme\Slug` 1.2.0 -> 1.3.0
`Acme\Text` 1.1.0 -> 2.0.0 (a new major version)
```

`nvs pkg update acme/slug` raises the minimum of `acme/slug` in `[dependencies]` to its newest released
version. Without a package, the command raises every dependency. A minimum is only raised, never
lowered. The comment on the line stays. Then the command does what `nvs pkg fetch` does.

Before the command changes any file, it prints what changed since `package.lock`:

```text
`Acme\Slug`: the minimum is raised from 1.2.0 to 1.3.0.
Changes since package.lock:
  `Acme\Slug` 1.2.0 -> 1.3.0
    now requests net.connect (optional)
    owners were acme and are now acme, newcomer
```

The report lists each new version, each capability a package now requests or no longer requests, a
change of owners and a change of repository. A new package and a package that is no longer needed are
listed too. The report changes no grant line, so a capability that a package now requests stays
refused until you add it.

When two packages need different major versions of a third package, the higher version is used. The
report then names the packages that asked for the older version. Your program is checked when it
compiles, so a change that breaks your code is a compile error.

A retracted version that `package.lock` already has stays in use, so you can update the other packages.
The command never chooses a retracted version that is not in `package.lock`. A git dependency is not
updated by these commands. Change its `rev` in `package.toml` instead.

### package.lock and --locked

    nvs pkg fetch --locked
    nvs pkg vendor --locked

`package.lock` lists every package your application uses. `nvs pkg fetch`, `nvs pkg vendor`,
`nvs pkg add` and `nvs pkg update` write it. Commit it with your code, and do not edit it. One entry
looks like this:

```toml
[[package]]
name = 'Acme\Slug'
version = "1.2.0"
source = "https://packages.example.com"
digest = "ad5fbbc3700675923bf1fcd46f4c46775db50fe76f05385b9d40782b75447d75"
repository = "https://git.example.com/acme/slug"
commit = "4f2a9c0e1b7d3a5f6e8c9b0a1d2e3f4a5b6c7d8e"
owners = ["acme"]

[package.capabilities]
required = []
optional = []
```

| Key | What it says |
|---|---|
| `name`, `version` | the package and the version that is used |
| `source` | the registry URL, or `git+` and the repository URL for a git dependency |
| `digest` | the BLAKE3 hash of the package's archive |
| `repository`, `commit` | where the package's source code is |
| `owners` | the accounts that may publish the package |
| `[package.capabilities]` | the capabilities the package requests |
| `hosts` | the hosts its downloaded files come from, when it has any |

Every command checks each archive against the digest in `package.lock`. When a digest does not match,
the command stops with an error and writes no file. So a changed archive or a changed digest in the
file is never used.

With `--locked`, the command also stops when `package.lock` has to change. That happens when a package
is missing from it, has another version, or is no longer needed. Use `--locked` in CI, so the build
uses exactly the versions you tested.

### nvs pkg pack

    nvs pkg pack [<dir>] [--out <file>]

`nvs pkg pack` builds the archive of the package in `<dir>`. The default is the current folder. The
archive contains only these files:

- every `.nvs` file under `src`;
- `package.toml`;
- the license, readme and notice files next to `package.toml`, such as `LICENSE`, `README.md` and
  `NOTICE`;
- each file that `[package] files` lists.

The command prints each file with its size, the total and the digest of the package:

```text
       241  LICENSE
       112  package.toml
       530  src/Slug.nvs
       883  total, 3 files
acme/slug 1.2.0  blake3:ad5fbbc3700675923bf1fcd46f4c46775db50fe76f05385b9d40782b75447d75
wrote acme-slug-1.2.0.tar
```

The same files always give the same archive and the same digest, on every system. The archive does
not contain the time, the owner or the permissions of a file.

A package must have a license file, such as `LICENSE` or `COPYING`. It has at most 5,000 files, and at most 16 MiB together. Every path must work on Windows, macOS
and Linux. A symbolic link is not allowed. For a larger file, use `nvs pkg download`. A file named
`nvs.toml` is not allowed in any folder.

A package may contain one extension, a `.nvsx` file that `[package] files` lists. This is an
extension package. Its Novis code under `src` can call the extension:

```toml
[package]
name    = 'Shop\Ledger'
version = "1.0.0"
files   = ["ledger.nvsx"]
```

`nvs pkg pack` loads the extension and checks it the way `nvs ext verify` does. The class of the
extension must be the package's namespace or a class under it. The Novis code inside the extension
must also be under that namespace. A package with two `.nvsx` files does not pack.

### nvs pkg download and nvs pkg provide

    nvs pkg download <url> --to <path>
    nvs pkg provide <file>

A package can use a file that is too large for its archive, such as a font or a data set. Run
`nvs pkg download` in the folder of your package:

    nvs pkg download https://files.example.com/fonts/Big.otf --to fonts/Big.otf

The command downloads the file, saves it at `fonts/Big.otf` and adds this entry to `package.toml`:

```toml
[[download]]
path = "fonts/Big.otf"
urls = ["https://files.example.com/fonts/Big.otf"]
sha256 = "9f2c4e6a8b0d1f3e5a7c9b2d4f6e8a0c1b3d5f7e9a2c4b6d8f0e1a3c5b7d9f2e"
size = 734212
```

You can add more URLs to `urls`, and a `license` such as `"OFL-1.1"`. Every URL must start with
`https://`. The path may not be under `src` and may not end in `.nvs`.

When somebody fetches your package, `nvs pkg fetch` downloads each file and checks its size and its
SHA-256 hash. A file that does not match is not used, and the next URL is tried. A redirect to an
internal address, such as `127.0.0.1`, is not allowed. Nothing in the file runs. The package's own code
may read the file with no grant.

Each file is kept once in a download cache in the Novis data folder. Every project that needs the same
file uses that copy.

When no URL of a file works, get the file in another way. Then run `nvs pkg provide` with it:

    nvs pkg provide Big.otf
    nvs pkg fetch

`nvs pkg provide` adds the file to the cache only when its size and its hash match a file that a
package in `package.lock` lists.

### The transparency log

    nvs registry key <file> --name <name>
    nvs registry log append <dir> --key <file> --origin <name>
    nvs registry log verify <dir>
    nvs registry index sign <dir> --key <file> [--log <dir>] [--at <seconds>]

A registry keeps a log of every change it makes. Each publish, retraction, withhold, unlist and
change of owner is one entry. An entry is never changed or removed, so the log only grows. The log
uses the C2SP formats `tlog-tiles` and `signed-note`, which other transparency logs also use.

A checkpoint is the signed summary of the log. It has the log's name, its number of entries and a
SHA-256 hash of all the entries:

```text
packages.example.com
2
ivAZfe0T7wcstVA1V/8iXOr5+LHx+fw6Zb25ASoaPxU=

— packages.example.com fI4DleVohE11yxi/MdYzFqIELlvHFJqbjAVI3m1yHkn8Bk16LjuP/DWSeKcUgFTsIsrHIUvEb7l8TV2h7+phl5tdMAc=
```

The last line is an Ed25519 signature. The `key` of the registry's line under `[registries]` is the
public key that checks it. `nvs pkg` never takes the key from the registry itself.

Every `nvs pkg` command that reads a registry does these checks:

- **The log continues the one it saw last time.** `nvs pkg` keeps the newest checkpoint of each
  registry in the Novis data folder. A new checkpoint must contain every entry of the kept one.
  When it does not, the registry changed its history. `nvs pkg` stops with an error that says the
  log was forked, and it fetches nothing.
- **Each archive is in the log.** Each version in an index file names its publish entry. The entry
  must have the same package, version, digest, repository and commit. An archive that is not in
  the log is not used.
- **Each index file is signed.** `registry.json` and each package's index file are signed with
  the same key. Each one has the time it was signed and the checkpoint it was signed with. A file
  with a wrong signature, or a time more than an hour in the future, is not used. `nvs pkg` then
  tries the next file host.

`nvs pkg add`, `nvs pkg update` and `nvs pkg outdated` also need an index file signed in the last
seven days. They choose versions, and an old file could hide a newer release or a retraction. A
build from `package.lock` and `nvs pkg fetch --locked` choose nothing, so they still work when the
registry is down.

The `nvs registry` commands are for the people who run a registry. `nvs registry key` makes the
signing key and prints the public key for `[registries]`. `nvs registry log append` reads one JSON
entry per line and signs a new checkpoint. If one entry is wrong, it adds nothing.
`nvs registry log verify` checks every file of a log from the start. `nvs registry index sign` signs
`registry.json` and every index file again. Run it at least once a day.

### nvs pkg api and nvs pkg diff

    nvs pkg api <dir>
    nvs pkg diff <old> <new> [--from <version>] [--to <version>] [--json]

The public API of a package is every public class, interface, enum and type in it, with their
methods, properties and constants. A version number of a package is `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, such as
`1.4.0`. From `0.1.0` on, only a major release may break the public API.

`nvs pkg api` prints the public API of the package in `<dir>` as JSON. It reads every `.nvs` file
under `<dir>/src` and checks the program. It does not run any of the code. Each type is written with
its full name, so an alias, a `use` line or a change in formatting is not a change.

`nvs pkg diff` compares two versions. `<old>` and `<new>` are each a package directory or a JSON file
that `nvs pkg api` printed. Each change prints on one line, as `breaking` or `additive`:

```text
breaking: Api\Client::send() — method removed
1 change(s): 1 breaking, 0 additive
1.2.0 to 1.3.0 is a minor release, so no breaking change is allowed.
```

A breaking change is a change that can stop code that uses the package from compiling:

- a public class, method, property, constant or enum case is removed or renamed;
- a method is added to an interface, or an abstract method is added;
- a case is added to an enum, because a `match` over every case no longer covers it;
- a parameter accepts fewer types, or a return type has more types;
- a required parameter is added, or a parameter is renamed.

A change that the comparison cannot decide is a breaking change. There is no way to allow one
breaking change and not the others.

The versions decide which changes are allowed. Each version is the `version` key in the
`package.toml` of the directory. `--from` and `--to` replace the two versions.

| From and to | Breaking changes |
|---|---|
| a `0.0.x` version on either side, such as `0.0.4` to `0.1.0` | allowed: `0.0.x` is experimental |
| a higher major, such as `1.2.0` to `2.0.0` | allowed |
| a higher minor or patch, such as `1.2.0` to `1.3.0` | not allowed |
| a new version that is not higher than the old one | not allowed |
| a side without a version | not allowed |

`nvs pkg diff` exits with `1` when a breaking change is not allowed, so you can run it in CI before
you publish. `--json` prints the changes as JSON. The JSON also has `from`, `to`, `step` and
`allowed`.

The check is about the shape of the API only. The behaviour of a method may change in any release.

### nvs pkg login and nvs pkg whoami

    nvs pkg login [--registry <url>]
    nvs pkg whoami [--registry <url>]

To publish, you need a publish token. You make the token on the registry's website. A token can
publish one vendor, such as `Acme`, or one package, such as `Acme\Http`. This is its scope. A
token expires after one year at most. Every token starts with `nvsreg_`.

`nvs pkg login` reads the token from standard input. Paste it when the command asks, or pipe it
in:

    nvs pkg login < token.txt

The command never takes the token as an argument, because other programs and your shell history
can see an argument. It sends the token to the registry first. If the registry does not accept it,
nothing is stored. Otherwise the command stores the token in the Novis data folder, where only your
account can read it:

```text
Logged in to `https://registry.novis-lang.org`.
Account: 3f2a9c0b7d4e4a1c9b8e2f6d0a5c7e13
Scope: Acme
Expires: 2027-10-28 (UTC)
The token is stored in `/home/ana/.nvsdata/tokens/5e0c8d4b2a7f19e3c6b1d0a4f8e2c7b9`.
```

`nvs pkg whoami` sends the stored token to the registry and prints the same account, scope and
date. It also prints each release of your vendors that is not available yet, and that you did not
confirm:

```text
Registry: https://registry.novis-lang.org
Account: 3f2a9c0b7d4e4a1c9b8e2f6d0a5c7e13
Scope: Acme
Expires: 2027-10-28 (UTC)
Releases that are not available yet:
  Acme\Http 1.4.0 will be available at 2026-11-04T09:12:00Z.
```

If you did not publish a release in this list, somebody else has a token for your vendor. Revoke
the token on the website, and retract the version. Each token works only with the registry it was
made for. `--registry` names another registry. The default is `https://registry.novis-lang.org`.

A token that a file or a log shows is easy to find, because of `nvsreg_`. Secret scanners look for
it. If a token leaks, revoke it on the website at once.

### nvs pkg publish

    nvs pkg publish [--repository <url>] [--dry-run] [--registry <url>]

`nvs pkg publish` publishes the package at the last commit of its git repository. Run it in the
folder of the package. It sends no file. It sends the repository's URL, the commit, the version
from `package.toml` and the package's folder in the repository. The registry downloads that commit
and builds the archive itself, so push the commit first. Changes that are not committed are not
published.

The repository must be public, and its URL must start with `https://`. The default is the URL of
the remote `origin`. `--repository` names another one.

Before it sends anything, the command builds the archive from the same commit on your computer. It
uses the same code as the registry, so both get the same digest. `--dry-run` stops there and
prints every file:

```text
acme/http 1.4.0
Repository: https://git.example.com/acme/http.git
Commit: 5b1e0c4f9a7d2e8b3c6a1f0d4e9b8a7c6d5e4f3a
       241  LICENSE
       132  package.toml
      2106  src/Client.nvs
      2479  total, 3 files
Digest: blake3:9d2c41e07a5b3f68c1d0e4a2b7f9c3d58e6a1b0c4d7e2f9a3b5c8d1e0f4a7b6c
This was a dry run. Nothing was sent to `https://registry.novis-lang.org`.
```

Without `--dry-run`, the registry checks the package and prints what happens next:

```text
Digest: blake3:9d2c41e07a5b3f68c1d0e4a2b7f9c3d58e6a1b0c4d7e2f9a3b5c8d1e0f4a7b6c
`Acme\Http` 1.4.0 is published. It is pending until 2026-11-04T09:12:00Z. An owner can release it now with a passkey on the website.
```

A release that is sent with a token is pending for seven days. You can download a pending version
by its exact version, but `nvs pkg add` and `nvs pkg update` do not choose it. An owner who signs
in with a passkey on the website can release it at once. In the seven days, every owner of the
vendor gets a message, so a release from a stolen token can be stopped. The first version at
`0.1.0` or higher waits until an owner confirms its API with a passkey.

The registry does not publish the package when:

- the token's scope does not include the package;
- the version was published before;
- a file declares a namespace outside the package's name;
- the package has an `nvs.toml` file or a git dependency;
- a minor or a patch version breaks the API of the version before;
- the archive breaks a rule of `nvs pkg pack`;
- your account has no verified notification channel on the website;
- your account had no activity in the last 60 days.

Activity is a sign-in with a passkey, or the answer to a reminder that the registry sends to your
devices. Using a token is not activity. After 60 days with no activity, sign in with a passkey on
the website to publish again. The first publish of a package like `Acme\Http` makes your account the
owner of the vendor `Acme`. Then only its owners can publish packages under `Acme`.

If no owner of the vendor has a working notification channel, the command prints a warning. If a
publish fails while the registry writes its files, publish the same commit again.

### nvs pkg retract and nvs pkg unlist

    nvs pkg retract <version> --reason <text> [--fixed-in <version>] [--registry <url>]
    nvs pkg unlist [<version>] [--undo] [--registry <url>]

Run these commands in the folder of your package. A version is never deleted. A retracted or
unlisted version can still be downloaded, so a `package.lock` that names it still works.

`nvs pkg retract` marks a version as broken or unsafe. `nvs pkg add` and `nvs pkg update` do not
choose a retracted version. The package index shows the reason, which has at most 500 characters.
`--fixed-in` names the version that fixes the problem:

    nvs pkg retract 1.4.0 --reason "Client::send drops the last header." --fixed-in 1.4.1

With a token, the retraction starts seven days later. Every owner gets a message, and an owner can
make it start at once with a passkey on the website:

```text
Version 1.4.0 is retracted from 2026-11-04T09:12:00Z. An owner can retract it now with a passkey on the website.
```

`nvs pkg unlist` hides a package, or one version of it, from search and listings. Without a
version, every version is hidden. `--undo` shows it again. Only an owner who signs in with a passkey
can unlist. With a token, the command prints the page where an owner confirms it:

```text
To unlist it, sign in with a passkey and confirm on https://registry.novis-lang.org/packages/acme/http.
```

When the registry saved the change but could not update the package index yet, the command also
prints this line. The registry updates the index on its next run.

```text
The registry saved the change. It updates the package index on its next run.
```

The people who run the registry cannot delete or change a version. They can only withhold a version
that contains malware, or that a court orders them to remove. A withheld version cannot be
downloaded, and the package index shows the reason.

### nvs pkg advise

    nvs pkg advise <package> <versions> <summary> [--registry <url>]

`nvs pkg advise` sends a security advisory for a range of versions of your package. `nvs pkg
audit` then reports every locked version in the range. The versions stay in the package index,
and `nvs pkg add` can still choose them. To stop that, use `nvs pkg retract`.

The range has two forms. `1.2.0..1.2.4` is the versions from 1.2.0 up to 1.2.4, without 1.2.4.
The second version is the version that fixes the problem. `1.2.0..` is every version from 1.2.0,
when no version fixes it yet. For a second range, send a second advisory. The summary has at most
500 characters.

    nvs pkg advise acme/http 1.2.0..1.2.4 "Client::send logs the session cookie."

You can write the package as `acme/http` or as `Acme\Http`.

With a token, the advisory is in the registry's list of advisories seven days later. Every owner
gets a message. An owner can send the same advisory again with a passkey on the website, and then
it is in the list at once. The registry gives each advisory an id, such as `acme/http-1`:

```text
The advisory acme/http-1 is in the feed from 2026-11-04T09:12:00Z. An owner can send it again now with a passkey on the website.
```

### nvs pkg audit

    nvs pkg audit [--json]

Run this command in the folder of your application. It reads `package.lock` and lists each locked
version that has an advisory. An advisory is a retraction or a withhold of a version, or an
advisory that an owner sent for a range of versions with `nvs pkg advise`. For each one, the
command prints the reason and the smallest version that fixes it:

```text
`Acme\Http` 1.4.0 is retracted: Client::send drops the last header.
  Update to 1.4.1 or newer.
1 locked version has an advisory.
```

For an advisory from `nvs pkg advise`, the first line has its id, and the reason is its summary:

```text
`Acme\Http` 1.2.1 has the advisory `acme/http-1`: Client::send logs the session cookie.
  Update to 1.2.4 or newer.
```

When the fix is in a new major version, the second line also says `This is a new major version.`
When no released version fixes it yet, the second line is `No released version fixes it yet.`
The command exits with an error while a locked version has an advisory, so you can run it in CI.
An unlisted version has no advisory. A package from a git repository is not checked.

The registry publishes its advisories in the file `log/advisories`, signed with the key of its
transparency log. Every advisory is also an entry in the log. The command reads the whole log and
compares the two. When the file leaves out an advisory that the log has, the command stops with an
error. A registry cannot hide an advisory from you without the change showing.

A registry can name a second copy of its log's checkpoint, on another host. The command checks that
both copies show the same log, and prints a line when they do:

```text
The log of `https://registry.novis-lang.org` matches its second copy at `https://copy.example.com/checkpoint`.
```

When the two copies show different logs, or the copy cannot be read, the command stops with an
error. A registry that names no copy gets one note, and the command goes on.

The command also checks your `[grants]` table. Code in a namespace that no grant line matches has
every permission of your application. `nvs pkg fetch` writes a line for each package, so this
warning names code that somebody copied in by hand. It also names the source folder of your
application. After you add a grant line for a namespace, the command no longer names it:

```text
warning: no line in `[grants]` matches `Acme\Legacy`, loaded from `lib/Legacy`. Its code has every permission your application has.
  If it is not your application's own code, add a line for `Acme\Legacy\*` to `[grants]` in `package.toml`, with the permissions it needs.
```

A warning does not change the exit code. `--json` prints the same report as one JSON object, with
the lists `advisories`, `registries` and `unmatched`.

### The registry website

The registry's website finds packages and shows what the registry knows about each one. It is a
Novis program, and its code is in the folder `apps/registry/` of the Novis repository.

A search matches the words you type in the name of a package, in the first paragraph of its readme
and in its doc comments. Then you choose the order:

| Order | The first package is |
|---|---|
| `default` | the one with the highest score (see below) |
| `date` | the one with the newest release |
| `activity` | the one with the most months with a release |
| `downloads` | the one with the most downloads in the last 90 days |
| `name` | the first one in alphabetical order |

The same search is `GET /api/search?q=<words>&sort=<order>`, which returns JSON:

    curl 'https://registry.novis-lang.org/api/search?q=http+client&sort=downloads'

The score is a number from 0 to 1. Half of it comes from facts that the registry saw itself. These
are the months with a release, the age of the newest release, the time since the first publish, the
size of the public API, the share of it with a doc comment, and the retractions that name a fixed
version. The other half comes from the downloads of the last 90 days. The whole formula is the file
`apps/registry/src/Ranking.nvs`, and every package page links to it.

The dates and the commits in a git repository do not change the score, because anybody can write
them.

The page of a package, `/packages/<vendor>/<name>`, shows:

- each version with its state: released, pending, unlisted, retracted or withheld;
- the commit that each version was built from, and the package it replaces;
- the owners of the vendor, and when each one was added or removed;
- each retraction and withhold, with its reason;
- every fact the score uses, and the score itself;
- the readme of the newest version, as plain text.

The page of a version, `/packages/<vendor>/<name>/<version>`, also shows the capabilities that the
version needs and what changed from the version before. It shows the changes to the API, every file
in the archive with its size, and every file the package downloads from another host.

#### Your account and your packages

An account is one or more passkeys. It has no email address and no password. You create one on
`/signup`. Your browser first does a short calculation, and then it makes a passkey on your device.
The page then shows ten recovery codes. Each code signs you in one time when you have no passkey.
Write them down, because the registry shows them only once.

You sign in on `/signin`, with a passkey or with a recovery code. Some changes need a passkey
sign-in from the last 15 minutes. When your sign-in is older, the page asks for your passkey first.
A recovery code is not enough for these changes.

Your account page, `/account`, shows your passkeys, your tokens and your vendors. It also shows your
devices and webhooks, your messages and the days left before you must sign in to publish again. On
it you can:

- add a passkey, for example on a second device;
- make a publish token for a vendor or a package, and revoke it;
- add and remove the other owners of your vendors;
- get messages in this browser, or at a webhook address, and check that each one works.

When you own the vendor of a package, its page also has the forms that change it:

- **Unlist** and **List again**, for one version or for every version;
- **Retract**, with a reason and the version that fixes the problem;
- **Send the advisory**, for a range of versions such as `1.0.0..1.2.0`;
- **Move the package**, to another repository or another folder in it.

The page of a pending version has a **Release now** button. The first version at `0.1.0` or higher
waits until an owner confirms its API. Its page shows that API, and **Confirm the API and release**
releases it. After that, only a new major version may break this API.

The page `/policy` says what the people who run the registry can do with a package.

<a id="tools-editor"></a>
## C.7 The editor: nvs lsp, nvs lsp-test, nvs dap and the VS Code extension

Keywords: nvs lsp, language server, LSP, Language Server Protocol, editor, IDE, VS Code, stdio, initialize, hover, go to definition, completion, autocomplete, semantic tokens, syntax highlighting, document symbol, outline, selection range, folding, document link, code action, quick fix, refactor, convert to html template, publishDiagnostics, nvs/redactions, secret, position encoding, utf-8, utf-16, nvs lsp-test, .lspt, --coverage, extension, vsix, TextMate grammar, nvs.path, nvs.lsp.enable, nvs.secrets.redact, nvs.taint.mark, reveal secret, restart language server, activation, nvs dap, debugger, debug adapter, DAP, Debug Adapter Protocol, launch.json, breakpoint, conditional breakpoint, hit count, logpoint, step over, step into, step out, exception breakpoints, skipFiles, pathMappings, stopOnEntry, nvsCommand

### nvs lsp

    nvs lsp

The language server. It is started by an editor and not by a person: it reads Language Server
Protocol 3.17 frames on standard input and writes them on standard output, so a terminal that runs
it sees nothing and appears to hang. Nothing else in the process writes to standard output — a
stray line there would be read as a protocol frame and end the session.

It takes no arguments. Everything configurable arrives in `initialize`, because the editor owns
those settings and a flag here would be a second, staler copy of them.

One server answers every editor. There is no per-editor logic in it: a client is a shell that
starts the process, forwards requests and renders answers, so what this section describes is what
every editor gets.

#### What it answers

The list is closed. Every capability below is declared at `initialize`, and a client never asks for
anything else, because nothing else is offered.

| Request | What comes back |
|---|---|
| `textDocument/publishDiagnostics` | every diagnostic for the open document, with the phase gate below applied. A notification, sent on open, on every edit, and once more with nothing in it when the document is closed |
| `textDocument/hover` | the `///` run attached to the declaration the name resolves to, handed over as Markdown; a `Core` member's registry row; or, where neither exists, the declared type of what the cursor is on — in that order. Inside the prefix of an `autoload` line, the hover shows the namespace it maps and the folders a class in it is looked for in, in order, and says which folder does not exist. A `{..}` part of the prefix shows the folder name it stands for. Inside the string of `'App\User' as class<Model>`, the hover is the one the class name `App\User` has, and the same is true for a class name you pass to `Core\Reflect::forClass` or `Core\Test::assertThrows`. Inside a path you pass to a function that reads or writes a file, such as `Core\IO::read('data/x.json')`, the hover shows the full path and says whether a file or a folder is there |
| `textDocument/definition` | the declaring span, anywhere in the `require` graph the analysis loaded. The name is resolved by the type checker and read back here, so an imported name lands where the compiler says it does. Inside the string of `'App\User' as class<Model>`, it is the declaration of the class the string names. The string must be the whole class name: `use` lines and the current namespace do not apply, the same as when the program runs |
| `textDocument/completion` | the members reachable off a receiver whose class was resolved, the static members and constants reached through a class name, an enum's cases after `Type::`, and — at a bare position — the keywords that may be written there with the variables in scope. A row reads like the declaration: `name(params)` with the return type at the right, `NAME = value` for a constant, a class with its namespace in brackets. Accepting a method writes its parentheses and opens signature help. Inside the path of a `require`, an `autoload` root or an `autoload discover` glob, the list is the folders and `.nvs` files in the folder the path reaches so far, relative to the file you are editing. An `autoload` path offers folders only. Typing the opening quote or a `/` opens this list, and accepting a folder opens it again for the next part of the path. Inside the prefix of an `autoload` line, the list is the namespaces your code declares. Inside the string of `'App\User' as class<Model>`, the list is the classes your program declares that are a `Model`. Inside a class name you pass to `Core\Reflect::forClass`, the list is every class your program declares, and for `Core\Test::assertThrows` it is the error classes. These lists give whole names, such as `App\Blog`. Inside a path you pass to a function that reads or writes a file, the list is every file and folder in the folder the path reaches, relative to the file you are editing. This is true for a `Core` function such as `Core\IO::read` and for your own function whose parameter has `#[Core\Path]`. A path that starts at a root, such as `/srv/data/`, lists that folder |
| `completionItem/resolve` | the description of the one row the editor is showing — a `Core` member's reference card, a class's or enum's own line, a `///` comment above your own declaration — read only when the editor asks, so the list itself stays small. In VS Code, press Ctrl+Space a second time while the list is open to show that panel, and it stays open from then on |
| `textDocument/semanticTokens/full` | what every name in the document *is*, for the colour a regular expression cannot choose |
| `textDocument/documentSymbol` | the outline of the entry file: every declaration it writes, as a tree |
| `textDocument/selectionRange` | the chain of nodes the cursor is inside, innermost first, so expand-selection walks the tree |
| `textDocument/foldingRange` | every construct written over three lines or more, plus the comment blocks |
| `textDocument/documentLink` | each `require`'s path, with the file it reached, and each `autoload` root and `discover` glob, with the folder it names. A glob links to the folder before its `*`. A root that does not exist has no link. The prefix of an `autoload` line links to the first of its folders that exists. A path you pass to a function that reads or writes a file links to that file or folder, if it exists. In VS Code, Ctrl+click on a folder link shows that folder in the Explorer |
| `textDocument/codeAction` | the quick fixes, the refactor and the source action below |
| `nvs/redactions` | the byte ranges the editor must conceal. Novis's own request; the protocol has no shape for it |

Every quick fix is a fix that the diagnostic which reported the problem already contains. Examples
are the rename that corrects an identifier's casing, and the rewrite of a legacy cast to `expr as T`.
A fix the compiler would have to compute for itself is not offered. The fixes are `quickfix` actions.
They are also grouped under `source.fixAll.nvs`, so an editor can run them on save.

One action is not a fix: **Convert to html template**, of kind `refactor.rewrite.htmlTemplate`. Put
the cursor on a string, or select it, and the action rewrites the string as an
``html`…` `` template that prints the same text:

```nvs
var $name = 'Ada';
echo "<p class=\"note\">Hello, $name</p>";
echo html`<p class="note">Hello, $name</p>`;
```

On an operand of a `.` chain, the action converts the whole chain. A variable, or a property or
array read on one, becomes a `{$…}` hole. Any other value becomes a `<?= … ?>` hole:

```nvs
var $name = "Ada";
echo "<b>" . $name . "</b> is " . Core\Str::upper("here") . '!';
echo html`<b>{$name}</b> is <?= Core\Str::upper('here') ?>!`;
```

The action changes what the line prints. Text from a plain string is escaped when it is printed,
and the text of an html template is printed as markup. So the action is never applied on save. Read
the preview before you apply it. It is offered for a double-quoted or single-quoted string. It is
not offered for a heredoc or nowdoc, for an array key, a `case` or `match` condition, a constant, or
the path of a `require` or `use`.

**Order class members** is a source action, of kind `source.orderMembers.nvs`. It puts the members of
every class and interface in the file in one order. Types come first, then constants, then
properties, then methods. In each group, `static` members come before the others. Then `public` comes
before `protected`, and `protected` before `private`. The constructor is the first method after the
`static` methods. Members that are equal in this order keep the order you wrote them in.

A member moves with its comments and its attributes. Enum cases and constructor parameters do not
move. The file is formatted as `nvs fmt` formats it. The action is offered when you ask for it, and
never on save. If the action changes the JSON key order of a class with `#[Core\Json\Derive]`, you see
the change in the edit. A class with `#[Core\Json\KeepKeyOrder]` keeps its properties in the order you
wrote them.

#### Diagnostics, and the phase gate

What is published is what `nvs check` reports, filtered: **a file whose parse failed publishes the
parse error alone**. A broken tree makes name resolution and the type check say things about a
program nobody wrote, and mid-edit every document is a broken tree, so the diagnostics from the
phases that read the tree are held back for that file until it parses.

The filter is by code. `E00xx` (the lexer) and `E01xx` (the parser) are the two phases that build
the tree; an error in either suppresses `E03xx` (name resolution) and `E04xx`, `E07xx` and `E08xx`
(the type check) for the same file. Nothing is rewritten and nothing is re-analysed: the walk runs
in full and the editor is shown a subset of it.

Diagnostics are published for open documents. A document that requires another is re-analysed when
that other file changes, so fixing a class in one buffer clears the error in the buffer that used
it.

#### Positions, encodings and document sync

A Novis span is a byte offset, and LSP positions are line and character. The two encodings the
protocol allows are negotiated at `initialize`: **`utf-8` is taken whenever the client offers it**,
and `utf-16` — the protocol's own default — is what a client that offers nothing gets. Every
column is converted for that client and for no other, so a multi-byte line reports the same place
to both.

The document is synchronized in full, not by range. Each analysis reparses the whole document
anyway, so applying a range edit here would buy nothing and add a second place a document's text
could be wrong.

#### Semantic tokens

Colour is two layers, and this is the second one. A TextMate grammar in the editor colours what a
regular expression can see — a keyword, a string, a type position — and the server colours what
only a parse can answer, staying silent wherever saying would mean guessing.

The legend it declares, in the order that **is** the wire encoding:

```text
namespace  class  interface  enum  enumMember  type
method  property  parameter  variable  typeParameter
```

with three modifiers: `defaultLibrary`, which marks a `Core` class so the standard library is
